Hebrews 11 11 Through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed, and was delivered of a child when she was past age, because she judged him faithful who had promised. 12 Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable. 13 These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. 14 For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country. 15 And truly, if they had been mindful of that country from whence they came out, they might have had opportunity to have returned. 16 But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city. Mother Sarah, as much as Mary, is blessed by God, given the honor of the seed, which is Jesus Christ. Announced by God, Himself. Brought to conceive by a miracle. Genesis 21 And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said, and the Lord did unto Sarah as he had spoken. For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him. Luke 1 28 And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women. 29 And when she saw him, she was troubled at his saying, and cast in her mind what manner of salutation this should be. 30 And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God. 31 And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name Jesus. 32 He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David: 33 And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end. 34 Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man? 35 And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God. 36 And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren. 37 For with God nothing shall be impossible. ... 68 Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people, 69 And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David; 70 As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: 71 That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us; 72 To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant; 73 The oath which he sware to our father Abraham, 74 That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear, 75 In holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. 76 And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways; 77 To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins, 78 Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, 79 To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace. Like Sarah was visited by the Lord God and bore Isaac, so too was Israel visited by God in Christ Jesus, through Mary. Bookends of faith, a covenant fulfilled. Now, as the Bible in Galatians 4 says, regarding the story of Sarah and Isaac, that these things be an allegory, the children of the promise in Sarah, the children after the bondage of the law, in Hagar. That the true seed of Abraham isn't after the flesh, as Ishmael was by the bondwoman Hagar, but by the miracle of God, Issac, conceived in faith through Sarah. The life story of Sarah represents Old Testament Israel, faithful believing Israel, who were saved through faith in the promise made to Abraham. An allegory, as the Bible says. When we first meet Sarah, as a young wife to Abraham, we are told she was barren. Without hope of conception. She journeys to Canaan, the promised land. Later, due to famine, she sojourns into Egypt, is captured by Pharaoh, and God for Sarah's sake visits plagues upon the Pharaoh's house until he relents and sends Sarah, Abraham, Lot and their cattle and belongings out from Egypt. Just as the Israelites spoiled Egypt, and went out with them, a mixed multitude. Sarah, despite her faith and love of God lapses in faith, and brings adultery to the bed of Abraham, with Hagar. Sarah's impatience with God's promise has her seek to find an heir after the flesh. Just as the Israelites lapsed in faith and brought the adultery of strange gods at times, and eventually sought an earthly king to rule them, frustrated at the timing of God. And like Israel, which would at times repent and turn back to God, admitting their error, Sarah says to Abraham; My wrong be upon thee: I have given my maid into thy bosom; and when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised in her eyes: the Lord judge between me and thee. And Hagar, having fled from Sarah with Ishmael the heir after the law, representing Israel after the flesh, not of faith, was given another chance by God, so too were the Jews of Jesus earthly ministry, to receive the adoption by faith that they though was theirs by law. And Sarah, believing Israel, gave them a home until the coming of Isaac. We are told of another captivity, Sarah taken by a king, and freed not by plagues but by the fear of the Lord upon Abimelech, convicted of his error, just as Babylonian captivity was. And when Isaac was born, Ishmael mocked the heir of the promise, and Sarah cast out the bondwoman and her son, though it grieved Abraham, the father. But God agrees with Sarah that son after the flesh, the heir according to the law be cast out, so that the son of faith may come in to his inheritance in full. Just as the non-believing Jews were cut off. (God, in His mercy offers salvation to Hagar if she just believe. And a well of water giving her salvation, just as any seed of Abraham after the flesh can still repent towards Christ today) Finally, Sarah having seen her son born of a miracle and come to be offered as a sacrifice, (I believe at 33 upon a hill in Jerusalem, spared by God, a picture of Jesus) she passes away a year later, at 127 years old and is honored, being given a place with the patriarchs, our being told of her end, chronicled by scripture. And in her faith, she was saved, and through her, all nations and kindreds were blessed. And so with this better understanding of the allegory, of recognizing that the entire Old Testament is about Christ Jesus and salvation by faith alone in him, to redeem us, offered by God the father in love and grace, we can understand the righteous anger of Paul writing unto the Galatians. The Church of the Galatians being swayed by judaizers into accepting another gospel, one of bondage to the law. Whereby they were being told that they must circumcise, keep the days and the months and the dietary laws in the carnal ordinances to be saved. Being dragged back to Hagar, the Bond woman and rejecting Sarah and the son of the promise. Of faith. And Paul writes, "O foolish Galatians! who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?" The Apostle is angry, he says he fears them. He says that he doubts their salvation, which he had labored with them and questions if it was in vain. Paul saying that only an unsaved person who didn't believe the gospel of Faith he presented them would be susceptible to the judaizers dragging them back under the law and away from the liberty of Christ. My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you,I desire to be present with you now, and to change my voice; for I stand in doubt of you. Tell me, ye that desire to be under the law, do ye not hear the law? For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman. But he who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman was by promise. Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants. He says that he's willing to go through this again with them that they may come to Jesus. That they seeking to be brought back under the law, he says don't you even hear the law? And this is what prompts his use of Sarah and Hagar as an allegory. As a teaching moment taken from scripture that they may understand the difference between salvation by faith alone and the bondage of the law. This is the same message we can give to those claiming Christ who have added works of the law to the salvation given in the simple Gospel of reconciliation and faith. These judaizers and those bewitched by them will claim that, "Yes it's by faith alone but you have to do the works of the law to be saved. You have to adhere to our vain traditions. To our carnal ordinances. To our dietary restrictions. You don't expect to just be handed salvation? Do you?" And so they bring people to be the seed after Hagar, not Sarah. And like Ishmael, they do not receive the inheritance which is given by faith in God's promise, not by heirs according to the law. Just as Sarah was barren from birth, and brought to old age, it took a miracle of God, visited upon her, to bring her the promise. Not by anything she did, for she was not capable, but in God all things are possible. This is the lesson. Do you not hear the law? If you're trusting in your own works, if you're sewing your own fig leaves, if you're offering the fruit of your garden, instead of the firstling of the flock, if you're committing adultery with Hagar to produce your salvation, repent. Hear the law. Salvation is given us by God, in His grace, through His Son, Jesus Christ, killed for our sins, a burnt offering, raised from the dead, that we may be redeemed in faith and sealed by the Holy Spirit unto the day of redemption. A free gift that once accepted cannot be lost. Eternal life. Heir to the Kingdom. Sons of God.

The faith of Abraham and the servant brought Isaac a wife in Rebekah. In uncertain times and strange lands, leading the servant to where he needed to be. An angel of the Lord lighting the path and preparing the way. So many young men seek their Rebekah, and go where they should not, doing what they should not and not trusting in the Lord to guide them. But Abraham knew in faith such a thing was possible. I am firmly convinced of the same, with the longview of being an old head and seeing God's angels bringing me where I needed to be, and watching faith move in other's lives the same way. Don't be discouraged. And young ladies seeking a spouse, live Godly with hospitality, grace and kindness, and the man for you will show himself. Amen.

Up too late to do Genesis 25 justice. I will post the first half, regarding Abraham today. We will delve into the second half, and it's spiritual application over the weekend. I think I will skip the more obscure theories regarding this. My studies are meant for first timers and seldom readers and disputations regarding genealogies are often a stumbling block to the spiritual. Abraham was 175 when he died. He was 137 when Sarah died, and here it says he remarried and had at least 6 sons with Keturah, and they begat many sons, but the physical inheritance and the spiritual blessing, given Abraham by God concerning Jesus, Abraham passes down to Isaac. The child of faith. And Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac. Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full of years; and was gathered to his people. And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is before Mamre; The field which Abraham purchased of the sons of Heth: there was Abraham buried, and Sarah his wife. Abraham died and was gathered to his people, in heaven. It couldn't be into his own "bosom" after all. But the patriarch is given an end of days and an account of his death, which the Bible uses to signify the humanity of the fathers and the prophets. Christ Jesus comments on the faith of Abraham and his joy at the fulfillment of the promise made to him in John 8; Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad...Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am. And so it was that Abraham's seed was a blessing to the whole world, especially of those who believe. Galatians 3 For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus. And if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise. Let this comfort you who believe, and drive to envy those of you still on the fence, trusting your own righteousness to provide your own salvation, bringing you to repent. Knowing Abraham trusted God and obtained the righteousness of Christ, and so to do we. For God is not slack concerning His promises. And we who are of Abraham's seed in Christ Jesus are joint heirs with Him. Rejoice! Malachi 1:2-3 I have loved you, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us? [Was] not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob, And I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the dragons of the wilderness Romans 9 4 Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; 5 Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen. 6 Not as though the word of God hath taken none effect. For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel: 7 Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children: but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called. 8 That is, They which are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God: but the children of the promise are counted for the seed. 9 For this is the word of promise, At this time will I come, and Sarah shall have a son. 10 And not only this; but when Rebecca also had conceived by one, even by our father Isaac; 11 (For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;) 12 It was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger. 13 As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. 14 What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid. 15 For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. Hebrews 12 14 Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord: 15 Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled; 16 Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. 17 For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears. Issac, at 60 years old, finally becomes a father. In an echo of his own birth, Rebekah is as barren as Sarah was. Yet God intervenes, and the couple conceive twin boys. As God says to Rebekah, there are two nations striving within her. One shall be strong, and the elder will serve the younger. Esau, the first born, hair red as the pottage he'd sell his birthright for. Red is the meaning of Edom. Jacob, second born, holding on to Esau's foot, as they are taken from their mother. And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents. And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob. God wastes no time on irrelevant details. Isaac's life story is briefly skimmed over. Only the details of the inheritance and blessing matter to the story God is telling. Of the elder serving the younger. Of the law and of faith. And so, we come to adult Esau and Jacob, men established as a hunter, and a man of the field, while the younger tends flocks, living in tents. No great hero and hunter, proficient with weapons like his elder brother, but a plain man. Jacob makes a red pottage, a lentil soup. Esau, hungry and tired, saying "Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint." Most interpret this to just mean normal hunger. Not truly fainting or starving in a serious sense. Just ravenous from being out in the field hunting, and wanting to please his flesh by eating the pottage. Jacob says he will feed his brother in exchange for his birthright. And despising his birthright, that is not caring about it, willing to trade it for a momentary satisfaction of the flesh, Esau agrees. Paul uses this illustration in Hebrews 12 regarding fornicators among the believers, who have the inheritance but lose the blessings that come with the birthright we share in Christ Jesus for the same momentary satisfaction of the flesh. That later, though he repented of giving away his inheritance by law to his younger brother, having a change of heart too late, and losing the eventual blessings meant for him. Christians who live carnally, after the flesh, despising their birthright received through Christ, losing blessings of God for their own morsel of meat, a simple bowl of pottage, are like Esau. And while we still retain sonship, and gain a share in the kingdom, the blessings we lose here in this life and in the time to come are lost or diminished, regardless of how tearfully we may regret it when our flesh dies. It's a grave warning. We know, having hindsight what a fool Esau, now Edom was. Yet how many times do we do the same, for much less than even a bowl of lentils? Now, the Bible says that God hated Esau, and Jacob He loved. This is referring to the nations that come from each, Jacob giving birth to the 12 patriarchs of Israel, Esau the nations of Edomites. Much is made of this distinction, but the fate of Edom is not necessarily reflected in the life of its patriarch, Esau. In the next chapter we will look more closely at that. For now, the parallels to Cain and Abel, Sarah and Hagar, Isaac and Ismael, Jews and Gentiles, even Jesus and Barabbas, the free will choices given to show that God favors faith over the law, spirit over the flesh, blesses them that trust His promises and do His will, giving them the inheritance for their faith, and the casting out of those who are after the flesh, even if by law they have a birthright claim. The entire Old Testament serves as a pattern for the salvation to come offered in Christ. Both the choice to believe, placing faith above flesh, explaining the theology of the New Testament with examples from the Old. And continually we see the eldest by law passed over, to serve the younger, who by faith receives both the birthright and blessing. When applied to the Jews and Gentiles, this is called "replacement theology," which is a misnomer. Like Esau, Jews sought an earthly kingdom from an earthly messiah, to satisfy their fleshly desires. They sold their birthright, despising their inheritance, by choosing to kill Christ. By rejecting the blessing that had carried them from Canaan to Egypt, back to the promised land. Through wars, invasions and captivity, they lost everything, for the younger, the Gentiles, to gain. It's not replacement, it's rejection. Spiritual Edom. And like Edom after the flesh, they were made desolate by the Lord. Jeremiah 49 10 But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he is not. 11 Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me. 12 For thus saith the Lord; Behold, they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup have assuredly drunken; and art thou he that shall altogether go unpunished? thou shalt not go unpunished, but thou shalt surely drink of it. 13 For I have sworn by myself, saith the Lord, that Bozrah shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste, and a curse; and all the cities thereof shall be perpetual wastes. 14 I have heard a rumour from the Lord, and an ambassador is sent unto the heathen, saying, Gather ye together, and come against her, and rise up to the battle. 15 For, lo, I will make thee small among the heathen, and despised among men. 16 Thy terribleness hath deceived thee, and the pride of thine heart, O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, that holdest the height of the hill: though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the Lord. 17 Also Edom shall be a desolation: every one that goeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss at all the plagues thereof. 18 As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighbour cities thereof, saith the Lord, no man shall abide there, neither shall a son of man dwell in it. God didn't "replace" Esau with Jacob. Edom with Israel. The choice is made in man's heart. And the Jews who killed Jesus and the prophets and persecuted the Gentiles who received the inheritance in faith, are spiritually Edom. The wrath of God abides upon them to the uttermost. They are a byword and a parable. A warning. Modern, dispensationalist Christians who have elevated Jews to coequal status, even giving them honor as "older brothers," claiming that inheritance of the flesh, in the law means they retain the birthright and blessing they rejected when they reject Christ, are carnal and risk going the way of Edom themselves. They so despise their birthright in Christ they are willing to give it up to Jews for a morsel. For less than a bowl of pottage. They say the "church age" ends in failure. Taken up in a pre-trib rapture to make way for the Jews to receive the Kingdom that is ours in Jesus' name. They question the judgment of God and ignore these warnings found throughout the Bible, in exchange for...what? The false teachers get paid. Hagee and the televangelists and evangelical pastors who promote dispensationalism get filthy lucre, for sure. Vipers being rewarded in the flesh. But the flock, many who are believers, they get nothing of value but the brief and fleeting feeling of approval by a group of people who resent and hate them. "If I bless them I will be blessed!" If you are saved in Christ you've already been blessed! If you live in the spirit, doing the will of the Father, the blessings are ours, in abundance. But for the meaningless approval of man, they sell it all to the wicked, spiritual Edomites. And like Esau, they will see eventually that their choice robbed them of the blessings, and with tears they will repent, but it will be too late.

Quite a cliffhanger. Having already gone over the spiritual application of Jacob vs Esau, the inheritance and blessing going to the younger, to be served by the elder, and what it means for Christians and the Jews in the last chapter, we see the drama play out here. Jacob, covered by the skins of the goats slain. A picture. Gains the blessing passed down from Abraham to Issac, now Issac to Jacob. Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine: Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother's sons bow down to thee: cursed be every one that curseth thee, and blessed be he that blesseth thee. This blessing being fulfilled in Christ. It seems wrong, to be dishonest this way to receive the blessing, but even Esau understood he'd already lost the birthright to Jacob by his own choice. The blessing goes with it. And though he repented with tears, Esau understood the finality of it all. And he begs Issac for a blessing as well. Behold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above; And by thy sword shalt thou live, and shalt serve thy brother; and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck. Hebrews 11 By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. We will see this pay off with the Israelites and Edomites, both in Genesis, and in Exodus, Numbers etc, when Moses, who in the Spirit wrote Genesis, reminds them they are Israel. We will get there soon enough. Anyway, Genesis 28 will continue this story, and we will get into some of the implications of Edom and Israel. I want to flesh out who is Edom, which is a minor theme going forth in the OT. One many have some ideas regarding, ideas that may have some merit regarding earthly things, and application we can take for spiritual. Have a blessed Sunday.

Genesis 26 34 And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: 35 Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah. Genesis 27 46 And Rebekah said to Isaac, I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth: if Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me? To catch us up, Esau, the oldest and heir by law to the inheritance of Issac, and by the blessing passed from Abraham to Isaac, heir to the promise of God, had sold his birthright to his younger twin, Jacob for a bowl of lentils. Jacob then, many years later, under direction of Rebekah, fooled Issac into also giving him the blessing. Esau had also taken two wives of the Hittites, a heathen people of Canaan. This had greatly displeased their mother, Rebekah and Isaac. And so Esau's anger at Jacob, a murderous rage, presented an opportunity; send Jacob away to Rebekah's people, Abraham's cousins, to find a suitable wife and return once Esau had calmed down. And so, Jacob flees back to Padanaram, to the house of Bethuel thy mother's father; and take thee a wife from thence of the daughers of Laban thy mother's brother. Before leaving, Issac gives Jacob his blessing again, this time without guile or subterfuge. God Almighty bless thee, and make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, that thou mayest be a multitude of people; And give thee the blessing of Abraham, to thee, and to thy seed with thee; that thou mayest inherit the land wherein thou art a stranger, which God gave unto Abraham. Seeing Issac blessing his brother, that he was sent to the daughters of Laban for a wife and knowing his own wives disappointed his parents, Esau tries to work to regain their favor by marrying a daughter of his uncle, Ishmael. Thinking this will help, but like most of our efforts to please people after making mistakes, it only compounds his trespass now having multiple wives. Poor Esau, now Edom. We find in life, as well as before God, what others want isn't for us to "make it right" so much as to stop digging, and be sincere in asking for forgiveness. Penance isn't how we earn forgiveness. Forgiveness is given by grace and mercy, charitable love extended to a sincere change of heart and contrition, acknowledging what we've done and how it impacted others. Isaiah 1:18 Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool. Isaiah 55:7 Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. 1 John 1:9 If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. We see this idea of Biblical contrition and forgiveness in the parable of the Prodigal Son, who realizing his sin, turns back to his father, repenting of his decision to waste his inheritance with harlots and wine; Luke 15 18 I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, 19 And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants. 20 And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. 21 And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son. 22 But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet: 23 And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry: 24 For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry. Esau, not yet forgiving Jacob, holding hate in his heart for how he's been wronged, doesn't understand this concept, and seeks instead to "make things right" by his own judgment. How often do we do the same? With others we love, and with God himself? Now went out from Beersheba, and went toward Haran. And there he camped for the night. Using stones as pillows, he slept and dreamed. He dreamt of a ladder, extending to Heaven, with angels of the Lord ascending and descending. And in this vision, Jacob sees the Lord God above, and God blesses Jacob; I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed; And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south: and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed. And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land; for I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of. Jacob wakes up in dread and fear, thinking that this place is itself the gate to Heaven, and that the Lord must dwell here, that it was the house of God. And so, to consecrate the place, he stacks the rocks he'd slept on during the dream, into a pillar. And the pillar he anoints with oil, renaming the place Bethel, from Luz. This is the first time we see the concept of a house of God. 1 Timothy 3:15 But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. It's a concept that we obviously will see more of as we progress. And it reminds of this, from Revelation 3:12: Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name. Jacob also vows to the LORD, calling upon His name; If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on, So that I come again to my father's house in peace; then shall the Lord be my God: And this stone, which I have set for a pillar, shall be God's house: and of all that thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee. A faithful vow to honor a faithful God. And note, he is set a pillar for the the house of God, like we who believe and overcome the world in Christ, (and don't miss this, he swears to tithe therein, 10 percent) People who, like Esau, seek to find forgiveness in their own works, or like the Prodigal Son, by thinking they are no longer welcome as a son, but have to work as a servant to repay what they did wrong, will often say "salvation by faith alone isn't in the Bible," or "Once saved, always saved" isn't. And yet, in dozens of clear verses, and in parable and story, we see how God rates forgiveness, how His sons are always His sons. That we are heirs to the kingdom through Christ, adopted to the promise. Not servants to work off debt. Not fumbling Esau, trying to emulate Jacob and regain favor. The idea of forgiveness and adoption, being sealed by the Spirit, a son of God, by our faith, and maintained, preserved by God who is just and merciful, who forgets our sins when we confess them, who chastises us when we fail to recognize our error, who blesses us with abundance, in grace, unearned favor, is the entire theme of the Bible. The love of God for we who believe. It's everything.

And so Jacob finds Laban, and his beautiful daughter Rachel. Offering to work 7 years for her hand, Laban tricks Jacob into taking Leah, the oldest daughter instead. Angry, but still wanting Rachel, Jacob agrees to work another 7 years for the chance to wed her. 14 years of labor for one woman. Incel powers, activate! When Jacob comes upon the well where Rachel will be watering her flock, it echos Rebekah, Laban's sister, and her meeting Abraham's servant. But rather than Rebekah watering the strangers camels, here Jacob waters Rachel's sheep. The passages surrounding the well seem to also carry some prophetic symbolism of Christ, the gathering of the lost sheep, and the well of living water that is the Spirit. We cannot, until all the flocks be gathered together, and till they roll the stone from the well's mouth; then we water the sheep. Rolling the stone away. Gathering all the sheep unto them, all who thirst. It's hard not to see the parallel. Laban himself is a foreshadowing of Egypt and the time of Joseph, Jacob's son by Rachel, and the captivity itself. We see that the wife who Jacob despised was blessed with fertility from God, while the woman he desired, Rachel had, like Sarah and Rebekah, remained barren. Judah, of whom the seed of Abraham would continue till Christ, was born of Leah and was the fourth born, not even first. We see again it is God's will, not man's what will be. And the inheritance of the law isn't what interests God, but the inheritance of the spirit and the promise. The law says, in Deuteronomy 21 15 If a man have two wives, one beloved, and another hated, and they have born him children, both the beloved and the hated; and if the firstborn son be hers that was hated: 16 Then it shall be, when he maketh his sons to inherit that which he hath, that he may not make the son of the beloved firstborn before the son of the hated, which is indeed the firstborn: 17 But he shall acknowledge the son of the hated for the firstborn, by giving him a double portion of all that he hath: for he is the beginning of his strength; the right of the firstborn is his. Pay attention to the double portion owed the eldest, it will come up shortly at Jacob, then Israel's, passing, and how he blessed the 12 sons he will have. It's easy to see that the switch Laban tricks Jacob with, tricking him into marrying the elder sister, as payback for his own deception with Esau, and tricking Issac for the blessing. The hurt he feels likely was a shadow of the pain he caused his brother. Revenge of the first born. Again, the first born being rejected for the second appears, which is a picture of the Jews and Gentiles after Christ's resurrection. And again Leah he hated, but Rachel he loved being an allegory that makes up much of Genesis. But Leah, we see, is faithful unto the Lord, praising God with the naming of her sons, and her desire to have Jacob love her as he does Rachel. Reuben, because the Lord looked upon her affliction. Simeon, because the Lord knew she was hated. Levi, the hope that three sons would win Jacob's favor. Judah, because she praised the Lord regardless. This is the faith in God Leah had, despite Jacob. And it was rewarded in her children of not by her spouse. The Bible says she left bearing after Judah, but we see that God answered her faith, even if what she desired and what she received weren't perfectly aligned, still she praised Him. Another parallel in Genesis 29, we can see that back in chapter 24, that Abraham and his servant sought a wife for Issac by faith, asking God to bring a suitable wife to them, where as Jacob offers to work for his wife and even after all his labors, ends up not getting who he sought. Our faith allows God to give to us what we need, while our works often end up just tying us further to bondage without getting what we wanted. My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of his correction: For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth. As a parent who loves his children unconditionally is a picture of how God sees His children. A parent who sees love as a transaction, selfishly, doesn't seem to correct their child but control them. It's important to understand the difference and seek to magnify the love of God, shining it on to your children so that they will understand the truth of God.

In the 14 years Jacob has been laboring for his uncle Laban, Laban has prospered. And with his wives and their maidservants, Jacob has produced many sons and a daughter. God's blessings upon Jacob has remained, despite his servitude and despite his sin of marrying multiple times. God has heard the prayers of Leah and Rachel, and given them the sons they desire, even by their maids, Bilhah and Zilpah. Joseph, Rachel's first born son, among them. This practice of multiple wives and laying with servants is not God's plan for man. We are to marry once, and forever. For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder. But, even our sin God may use to His purpose. And the multitudes of the 12 tribes to come spring from Jacob who is Israel. Children are a blessing from God. He frees and shuts up the womb, determining when we conceive and when we don't. There are examples throughout the Bible of this opening and closing of the womb, and children being a blessing from Him. Psalms 127:3 Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward This is why birth control and abortion are such grave sins. God is our goalie. We are to become one flesh, husband and wife, trusting in Him to provide and prevent. But man is often impatient, as Jacob's wives here. As Sarah was. Today we see it the opposite way, rather than not trusting the Lord to provide a child, we don't trust in Him to prevent one. In our hearts we should understand His ways and that he won't give His faithful children they cannot handle. And so many Christians today act as the fornicators of the world, and use chemicals to sterilize the wombs, to artificially make their wives barren. It's a shame. We should be producing multitudes of Godly children. It is the main way we increase the Lord's blessing in the world, other than soul winning. (I've done my part, believe me) Now Laban is loathe to see Jacob leave with his wives and children back to Canaan and the land promised him of God. He knows that God's blessing of Jacob has benefited him. He asks, what wage would you take to stay a while? His nephew/son in law says he would take the off-color cattle; sheep and goats who had spot, brown or blemishes. That he would leave the white to Laban (his name means White). Laban agreed, but again seeks to trick Jacob by hiding his existing flocks with these markings 3 days away from their main herd, limiting the number Jacob could potentially take as his own. But Jacob, in faith, devised a plan to increase his herd. He uses the wood of 3 trees, stripped bare, to the trough they feed at, and they that conceive bare him brown and spotted kids. He withheld this practice from the weak and the scrawny. And God, who blesses all creatures with children after their kind, provided Jacob with many kids with the markings that make them his. And so, miraculously Jacob's deal pays off and Laban's attempt fails. This seems like a picture of Jesus, coming for the sheep who had blemish, who were stained in sin. Who would hear their shepherd's voice and know they belonged to Him. Laban sought by his works, and trickery, to gain the lambs without blemish unto himself. A picture of works trying, and failing, to gain righteousness. Again and again we see that God is patient and longsuffering, and in His mercy he uses the less than perfect, who in faith trust Him to deliver them, calling upon His name because they come up short. For all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. We see faith is rewarded, and works and schemes backfire. We see imperfect men, made righteous by faith, used by God for something greater, often not seen in their own lifetime, and not even in the lives of their children. Sometimes without their even understanding how God will profit from them, but having faith that He will. It's a beautiful reminder of our own imperfections and encouraging reminder that it's not all about us, but the long-term glory of God. Humbling and yet cozy. Christianity is the only explicitly anti-jew ideology. This is what God says about the antichrists calling themselves Jews: Jews, Who both killed the Lord Jesus, and their own prophets, and have persecuted us; and they please not God, and are contrary to all men: Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they might be saved, to fill up their sins alway: for the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost. What's interesting is the people claiming to be on our side maintain the same position as the Jews they claim to oppose. They are all antichrists There is no other ideology or philosophy of men that explains the jew, and why they hate Gentiles in general, Christian White's specifically, and behave the way they do. Being contrary to all men, being liars, being of their father the devil... Literally nothing else except Christianity opposes them explicitly. The fact that non-saved Christian sects that have been thoroughly judaized and subverted, defend Jews and our pro-zionist etc, isn't a failure of Christianity. It's the weakness of men.

And so Jacob, after 20 years sojourning in service, flees Laban with his wives, servants and children, and the flocks he obtained by God's blessing. The parallel of Laban as Egypt/Pharaoh and the passing over of the river to flee back to the land of Isaac and Abraham seems to be the picture here. Laban however listens to the warning of God, rather than hardening his heart. The theft of his household idols by his daughter, Rachel is an odd thing, and one only God would know. Her either clinging to these dead images and hedging her bets, or spiting her father, or taking them as inheritance due, is up for debate, but her theft risked her life when Jacob offered to allow Laban to slay whomever stole them. Just as fleeing Egypt (sin) to the promised land (salvation), through the Red Sea (baptism/Christ's death, burial and resurrection) all has symbolic meaning, Rachel's theft of the idols of her father could be seen as that nagging sin we sometimes see a saved Christian take with them into their new, born again life. The risks and harm of it can still affect us, even when we have crossed from death to life in Jesus. The covenant they forge by the God of Abraham and the pillar anointed, show Laban feared the true God even as he had idols to dead ones.

Jacob, having left behind Laban and having his wives and children, cattle and riches with him, now faces the thing that drove him from his father's land to begin with; Esau's murderous vow against him for deceiving Isaac and taking the blessing from his older brother. (Jacob means deceiver/grabber). He can't go back, having just escaped and made covenant with his father-in-law. But in pressing forward, he may lose everything. His life has been blessed by God, despite his schemes and his dishonesty. Despite taking advantage of Esau's hunger to take the inheritance. Despite his fooling his father. Despite his haggling with and ultimately tricking Laban. Now, his vow to God at Bethel is come due. He was taken care of and blessed by God, now it's time he fully commit and serve the Lord, even if it means dying there at the hands of his brother. Quite a spiritual crisis. As they make their way, Jacob looks and sees the hosts of heaven, angels all about him. 2 Kings 6:17 And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha. Psalm 91:11-12 For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone. Hebrews 1:14 Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation? Anyone who has been a saved Christian for any meaningful length of time will testify to the fact that the Lord places angels over us, protecting us, often from ourselves. Providing a path out of sin and temptation. Guarding us from the worst of the consequences of our foolish actions or placing us directly in the path of them, if it brings us closer to God. We are given understanding to just how protected we are that God may have the glory. It's often at a time where our own sin is wrestling with us to try and fix things ourselves, as a reminder that God is prepared to if we had but the faith to let him. Jacob now facing this moment of crisis. Messengers to his brother return saying Esau is following with 400 men. It looks fire. This is the crisis he feared, one he built for himself. And though God allowed him to see the hosts of angels about him, yet he begins to plot and scheme, as is his way. He splits the troop in two. He concocts a bribe and a script for all to say, hoping it would stave off his brother. He tells them to say to Esau that he is here as his servant. That these gifts are a sign of respect. He's hoping on his own devices to save all he has, but his real battle is with the God who has blessed him, and his vow to serve Him. Genesis 28 And Jacob vowed a vow, saying, If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on, So that I come again to my father's house in peace; then shall the Lord be my God: And this stone, which I have set for a pillar, shall be God's house: and of all that thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee. The moment of truth. Will God deliver or will Jacob be killed? And if he puts his full trust in God, recognizing His power, having faith he will be delivered safely to his father's house in peace, he will have to honor his vows. Sometimes we as Christians, especially when we haven't been walking with Christ, maybe backslidden or just stubbornly trying to fix and control things in our lives, we will make vows to God if He would provide. God holds us to the vows we make in His name. Numbers 30:2 If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth Ecclesiastes 5:4 When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Psalms 76:11 Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared. At the same time, God delights in our reminding Him of His promises, in prayer and supplication. Because God is not slack concerning His promises. He keeps His side of every covenant. And our acknowledging of this and trusting Him to do so brings Him joy and glory. It is not tempting God to remind Him, by our recognition, realizing all He does is in grace and mercy to us, as sinners, that He is true to His word and won't let us down. And in Christ we have the authority to boldly go before the Father, and all we ask shall be delivered. Ephesians 3 8 Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ; 9 And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ: 10 To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God, 11 According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord: 12 In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him. 13 Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory. 14 For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, 15 Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named, 16 That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man; 17 That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, 18 May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; 19 And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God. 20 Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, 21 Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen. And so, Jacob having prepared his own ways to protect what he has is now alone in the wilderness. And there, he finds himself wrestling with a man, and there wrestled with him until the breaking of the day. Jacob, an old man by our standards. Likely 60-70 years old at this point. Having been a rancher for decades, but still not a young man, endures this wrestling all night unto morning. And as the dawn came and the man saw he was in a stalemate with Jacob, touches his thigh and shrinks the sinew of his hip and lames Jacob, and doing this says "Let me go." Essentially telling the exhausted and now hobbled Jacob to give up and surrender. And Jacob defiantly says no, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The man asks, "What is thy name?" "Jacob." And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed. And Jacob asked him, and said, Tell me, I pray thee, thy name. And he said, Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name? And he blessed him there. And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved. The man he'd wrestled with all night was Christ Jesus, God in the flesh. And having overcome, was born again, given a new name. (As Jesus we know is want to do) Face to face with God, halted and lame for his experience, he is blessed as a prince, inheritor of the blessing, recognizing God come in the flesh. And he passes through the river Penuel, a sort of baptism, the sun rises to warm him, Israel goes to meet his fate. >pulls the pin< >throws verse< Isaiah 60:13 The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious. >Runs away shouting "let every man be persuaded in his own mind! Christ is born! Hallelujah!"

The reunion Jacob, now Israel, dreaded with Esau, now Edom. And Edom embraced Israel and kissed his brother and gave to him safety and security in his land and giving his men, brought Israel and his children into Canaan, to the promised land. And there Israel set an altar, calling it "EleloheIsrael," or "the Lord God is the God of Israel." Perhaps this past week, with the holidays and families getting together, in Christ's name, put dread in your heart for a wrong committed, or a trespass against you by another. Maybe time and distance had been put between you, perhaps it is a fresh cut, still sore. But God who has forgiven us asks that we too be forgiving. And He promises that of we have a contrite heart and come meekly to the matter, others will come to forgiveness with us as well. Now, make no peace with evil. But, as much as possible, live peaceably with all men. Recompense to no man evil for evil. Ernest forgiveness is the fruit of our salvation, the reflection of the charity and mercy God has shown us, while we are yet sinners. That understanding should influence our relationships. Not in a foolish "love everyone, don't judge" way, but with humble discernment, that we may bring the Gospel of reconciliation to them with whom we are reconciled.

Dinah and Shechem's doomed romance. The slaying of the Hivites as they recover from the circumcision they'd agreed to in a covenant with Jacob and his sons, who were plotting evil against them for spoiling their sister like a harlot. There's symbolism and a picture of the purity of God's people, and not suffering a harlot among the daughters of Israel. Especially where the Hivites wanted to become one people with Jacob's clan. Marrying daughters of men to sons of God type situation. But I have come to notice that when God is absent a narrative given in the Old Testament, that often it's the imaginations of men which guide their actions, and God is teaching us more about ourselves with these retellings of events. Moses was writing this to the Israelites who were to come into the promised land, and a warning and application of not being diluted as a people by intermarriage with the heathen was necessary. Unequal yoke marriage is still relevant today. And the spoiling of a daughter should still provoke wrath in men, rather than quiet acceptance of fornication. But, Shechem and his father did the thing God's law calls for in these instances; making it right with a wedding and a dowry, only to be tricked by Simeon and Levi. Jacob tells them that their actions have endangered them all in the land they'd not yet been given. That they shared with other people. I really appreciate how God doesn't just show us perfect people, cardboard villains and heroes. These are real people with complex character and who do wicked things out of the abundance of their hearts, and yet find grace in God and His blessings when they turn to him.

He is Esau who is Edom. He is Esau the father of the Edomites. We are given the genealogies of Esau, who is Edom, which God repeats for us several times, to drive home the point. The primary target for this scripture were the Israelites in Moses' day, sharing their people's story and the story of the people of Mt Seir, who they are coming up against as we will see later in scripture. Cousins really. One with the blessing and the promise for the seed that is Christ to come. Esau himself is often painted in a negative light, primarily due to a Calvinist reading of Romans 9:13: As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. Which is itself taken from the prophet Malachi 1:3-4 And I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the dragons of the wilderness. Whereas Edom saith, We are impoverished, but we will return and build the desolate places; thus saith the Lord of hosts, They shall build, but I will throw down; and they shall call them, The border of wickedness, and, The people against whom the Lord hath indignation for ever. And your eyes shall see, and ye shall say, The Lord will be magnified from the border of Israel. Note, these are the Edomites generations later, being cursed by God. Not Esau, who is Edom. And why were they cursed by God for destruction? In Deuteronomy 2:1-5, God orders the Israelites to tread carefully through the land of Seir so as not to worry the Edomites. That their land was promised Esau: Then we turned, and took our journey into the wilderness by the way of the Red sea, as the Lord spake unto me: and we compassed mount Seir many days. And the Lord spake unto me, saying, Ye have compassed this mountain long enough: turn you northward. And command thou the people, saying, Ye are to pass through the coast of your brethren the children of Esau, which dwell in Seir; and they shall be afraid of you: take ye good heed unto yourselves therefore: Meddle not with them; for I will not give you of their land, no, not so much as a foot breadth; because I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession. We see at this point God is still allowing the nations of Edom, who is Esau to continue with His blessing of a promised land to their patriarch. God loved Esau, despite his failings. He made a promise to him and kept it, even in those days, 400yrs later. Esau was saved by the same faith as Jacob, and their fathers. But his descendents became wicked. Numbers 20:14-21 And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh unto the king of Edom, Thus saith thy brother Israel, Thou knowest all the travail that hath befallen us: How our fathers went down into Egypt, and we have dwelt in Egypt a long time; and the Egyptians vexed us, and our fathers: And when we cried unto the Lord, he heard our voice, and sent an angel, and hath brought us forth out of Egypt: and, behold, we are in Kadesh, a city in the uttermost of thy border: Let us pass, I pray thee, through thy country: we will not pass through the fields, or through the vineyards, neither will we drink of the water of the wells: we will go by the king's high way, we will not turn to the right hand nor to the left, until we have passed thy borders. And Edom said unto him, Thou shalt not pass by me, lest I come out against thee with the sword. And the children of Israel said unto him, We will go by the high way: and if I and my cattle drink of thy water, then I will pay for it: I will only, without doing anything else, go through on my feet. And he said, Thou shalt not go through. And Edom came out against him with much people, and with a strong hand. Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his border: wherefore Israel turned away from him. Later we see Edomites war with Israel, and eventually David conquers and takes them as servants, slaves. 2 Samuel 8:13-14 And David gat him a name when he returned from smiting of the Syrians in the valley of salt, being eighteen thousand men. And he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom put he garrisons, and all they of Edom became David's servants. And the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went. Later, under King Joram, they revolted and gained their eventual freedom. 2 Kings 8:20–22 So Joram went over to Zair, and all the chariots with him: and he rose by night, and smote the Edomites which compassed him about, and the captains of the chariots: and the people fled into their tents. Yet Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah unto this day. But the real betrayal was during the Babylonian captivity, where the Edomites would raid Judah and took pleasure in their being made servants to Babylon. And so God curses Edom. Ezekiel 25:12-14 Thus saith the Lord God; Because that Edom hath dealt against the house of Judah by taking vengeance, and hath greatly offended, and revenged himself upon them; Therefore thus saith the Lord God; I will also stretch out mine hand upon Edom, and will cut off man and beast from it; and I will make it desolate from Teman; and they of Dedan shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel: and they shall do in Edom according to mine anger and according to my fury; and they shall know my vengeance, saith the Lord God Contemporary prophet to Ezekiel, Jeremiah, 49:7–22 Concerning Edom, thus saith the Lord of hosts; Is wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished? Flee ye, turn back, dwell deep, O inhabitants of Dedan; for I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time that I will visit him. If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough. But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he is not. Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me. For thus saith the Lord; Behold, they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup have assuredly drunken; and art thou he that shall altogether go unpunished? thou shalt not go unpunished, but thou shalt surely drink of it. For I have sworn by myself, saith the Lord, that Bozrah shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste, and a curse; and all the cities thereof shall be perpetual wastes. I have heard a rumour from the Lord, and an ambassador is sent unto the heathen, saying, Gather ye together, and come against her, and rise up to the battle. For, lo, I will make thee small among the heathen, and despised among men. Thy terribleness hath deceived thee, and the pride of thine heart, O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, that holdest the height of the hill: though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the Lord. Also Edom shall be a desolation: every one that goeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss at all the plagues thereof. As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighbour cities thereof, saith the Lord, no man shall abide there, neither shall a son of man dwell in it. Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan against the habitation of the strong: but I will suddenly make him run away from her: and who is a chosen man, that I may appoint over her? for who is like me? and who will appoint me the time? and who is that shepherd that will stand before me? Therefore hear the counsel of the Lord, that he hath taken against Edom; and his purposes, that he hath purposed against the inhabitants of Teman: Surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them. The earth is moved at the noise of their fall, at the cry the noise thereof was heard in the Red sea. Behold, he shall come up and fly as the eagle, and spread his wings over Bozrah: and at that day shall the heart of the mighty men of Edom be as the heart of a woman in her pangs. As we see in Obadiah, God's judgment is carried out against Edom.

Genesis 37 begins the tale of Joseph and Judah, the other brothers and how the sons of Jacob came to be in Egypt. The generations of Israel, told by God through Moses. In this narrative, there lays prophecy of Christ Jesus, both as a figure in Joseph and in the blessing upon Judah, which we will see later near the end. But keeping in mind the picture of Jesus in Joseph and the traits of man in the brothers, especially Judah/Jews of Christ's time, there's a lot to digest. First, we are given the timing and situation; Joseph, the first son born unto Rachel, Jacob's first love, and so the father's favorite. Joseph, out with his half brothers tending the flocks returns to his father, bringing an "evil report." Bringing word to the father that the children are in sin. And the brothers hate him for it. Much the same way today the world hates a faithful Christian for the reminder of their sin we bring. The light shined on their inequity. As Jesus says in John 3:20: For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved. Christians standing fast against sin bring an evil report of the wicked hearts of men. The world resents it. John 15:18 If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you. Joseph's brothers hated him for the same reason. Sinners hate preaching against sin. Standards and morality. God's word, which convicts them. Christians who bring an evil report to their deeds. And like Joseph's brothers, the world plots and schemes ways to shut us up. To sully Christ's name by our own failings. To discredit God's word. To subvert His people. To call good evil and evil good. Isaiah 5:20 Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter! And so, we understand the setting. They hate the favoritism Jacob gives his son, Joseph and that he's tattled on their sin. They hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him, and to compound matters, Joseph tells them of his dream. For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf. And his brethren said to him, Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us? And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words. In parallel to Christ, we see the resentment. Like Jews resentment of Christians, the older hating the younger because of the prophecy of who will reign. Not exact but echos. And Joseph dreams again. And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me. And he told it to his father, and to his brethren: and his father rebuked him, and said unto him, What is this dream that thou hast dreamed? Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth? Here Jacob interpreting the dream for us, that he is the sun and his mother, the moon. The brothers the stars. All bowing before Joseph. The brothers hated him even the more, but Jacob observed the saying. The prophetic dreams about Joseph are from God, given by the Holy Ghost. We will see later how tied to dreams and prophecy Joseph is. But note the building resentment of the brothers mirrors Israel's resentment of Christ, where Jesus speaks to the Jews about how the prophets spoke of Him; John 5:46 For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me; for he wrote of me. Luke 24:44 These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me They had the word of the prophets and hated Jesus because of it. In spite of it. Despite the truth of the prophecy being the hope of salvation, they hated the idea of bowing to Christ the Lord. Joseph's brothers didn't understand that his dream of preeminence was to prophesy their physical salvation. And so, stage set, Jacob sends Joseph to find the brothers and their flocks. But they are "lost"... He sent him out of the vale of Hebron, and he came to Shechem. And a certain man found him, and, behold, he was wandering in the field: and the man asked him, saying, What seekest thou? And he said, I seek my brethren: tell me, I pray thee, where they feed their flocks. And the man said, They are departed hence; for I heard them say, Let us go to Dothan. And Joseph went after his brethren, and found them in Dothan. My feeling is the certain man was an angel of the Lord (if not Jesus Himself), pointing Joseph, a figure of Christ, to the "lost sheep of Israel." Not where they are supposed to be in Shechem. Again, another picture. And there, while still in the distance approaching, the brothers plot his demise. Behold, this dreamer cometh. Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit, and we will say, Some evil beast hath devoured him: and we shall see what will become of his dreams. And Reuben heard it, and he delivered him out of their hands; and said, Let us not kill him. And Reuben said unto them, Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit that is in the wilderness, and lay no hand upon him. Like Pilate, Reuben, the eldest brother seeks to keep his hands free of the innocent blood shed. He appeals to them to simply put him in the pit so that he could later return Joseph to their father. The brothers agree. But in Reuben's absence, they devise another scheme. Seeing merchants coming their way, men of Ishmael, Midianites, Judah says; What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood? Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother and our flesh. And his brethren were content. Like the Jews use of Romans to do their dirty work, the brothers are convinced that this compromise will keep their hands clean. And like Judas, Judah takes the silver to betray Joseph. Echos. Twenty Pieces of Silver for Joseph. Thirty Pieces of Silver for Christ. Joseph is taken by the merchants to Egypt as a slave. When Reuben returns, and sees the pit empty; a picture of Christ's tomb, he tends his clothes believing his brothers killed him. The child is not; and I, whither shall I go? The brothers then took the coat of many colors which Joseph wore, and dipped it in the blood of a goat, sacrificed to cover up their sin. The coat of many colors may represent the nations of the world saved by the blood of Christ, who covers our sin, spotless white robes washed clean in His blood. I think it does. Nothing in the Bible is coincidental, accidental or incidental. They bring the blood-soaked coat to Jacob, who mourns the death of his favored son in anguish. And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh's, and captain of the guard. Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain: Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.

Today on Judah Springer.... Judah, the son of Israel who had led his brothers to sell Joseph to bondage, is not a good guy. One of the reasons the brothers hated the young brother Joseph was that he brought an evil report back to their father, and we see from this synopsis of Judah's life, there was plenty of evil to report. Judah falls in with a rough crowd of heathens, being best friends with an Adullamite. He marries a Canaanite woman and bears sons wicked enough to be slain by the Lord. The eldest, Er, isn't detailed what all he did, but it was wicked enough to get God's attention. And when his wife was left childless by his death, Judah does try to do what is right by her and give her a child by his son Onan. This custom mirrors the law given by God to Moses. Deuteronomy 25:5 If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her. This is the law and what's right in the eyes of God. Of course, we see in the Gospels that the Sadducees use this to tempt Jesus; Matthew 22 23 The same day came to him the Sadducees, which say that there is no resurrection, and asked him, 24 Saying, Master, Moses said, If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother. 25 Now there were with us seven brethren: and the first, when he had married a wife, deceased, and, having no issue, left his wife unto his brother: 26 Likewise the second also, and the third, unto the seventh. 27 And last of all the woman died also. 28 Therefore in the resurrection whose wife shall she be of the seven? for they all had her. 29 Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God. 30 For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven. 31 But as touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God, saying, 32 I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. 33 And when the multitude heard this, they were astonished at his doctrine. It is in this context we see Judah offering Onan unto his daughter-in-law Tamar. But Onan refuses to give a son to his dead brother, knowing Tamar but spilling his seed on the ground. For this wicked act, God slays Onan as well. Many think Onan's sin was pulling out, in general. That's not the case, it was the specific act of denying seed to his dead brothers wife, breaking the law and dishonoring everyone involved. And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother. And the thing which he did displeased the Lord: wherefore he slew him also. This misunderstanding of the scriptures has led to the term Onanism to describe a sin of not completing in a woman, and is often associated with masturbation. The more you know. Tamar is then promised to the next youngest son of Judah, Shelah, who isn't old enough at that point to fulfill his duty. As time passes and he comes of age, Tamar is left a widow in her father's house, and disrespected and dishonored by Judah's failure to provide her a child and a husband. And so, hearing that the widowed Judah is coming her way to sheer his sheep, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite. So, she awaits him by the roadside veiled as a harlot. Judah, being a not so great guy, sees her and decides to go in unto her, as a whoremonger. Offering her a kid from his flock to lay with her, she asks for a surety to back his promise, receiving his signet, bracelets and staff. Afterwards, he seeks to pay her the kid and get his things back, he sends the Adullamite, but he cannot find her and no one there knows anything about any harlot. But Tamar is pregnant, and when Judah hears, he assumes she was whoring and seeks to have her killed. Hypocritical. But when confronted, Tamar reveals he was the man who impregnated her, to his shame. He failed to provide for her, to give her to his son when he was old enough as it was written. He was as wicked as his sons in that regard. And Judah acknowledged them, and said, She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son. And he knew her again no more. Now Tamar gives birth to twins by Judah, sons. And it came to pass, when she travailed, that the one put out his hand: and the midwife took and bound upon his hand a scarlet thread, saying, This came out first. And it came to pass, as he drew back his hand, that, behold, his brother came out: and she said, How hast thou broken forth? this breach be upon thee: therefore his name was called Pharez. And afterward came out his brother, that had the scarlet thread upon his hand: and his name was called Zarah. The scarlet thread represents the lineage of Christ. The blood of Jesus which saves. In the genealogy given in Matthew 1, we see the lineage passes through Judah to Zarah.

Now catching up with Joseph, we see the contrast between him and his brother Judah. Who being free and rich, fell in to the wrong crowd, was taken by lust and had sons slain by the Lord for their wickedness, while Joseph was a slave who strived to do right in the eyes of the Lord and was blessed exceedingly. As a worker, we who are saved should strive to be as Joseph. Working hard, loyally and having faith God will bless our hand if we do. Joseph in the worst of conditions, even prison, rises to the top because of his faith. The wife who trapped him with a lie did a wicked evil to him. He could have given in, he could have cursed God for his fate, he could have been bitter or angry. Instead he just does what's right even in jail. And God continues to bless him. Philippians 4:12 I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. Proverbs 28:20 A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent. Psalm 41 Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the Lord will deliver him in time of trouble. 2 The Lord will preserve him, and keep him alive; and he shall be blessed upon the earth: and thou wilt not deliver him unto the will of his enemies. 3 The Lord will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness. 4 I said, Lord, be merciful unto me: heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee. 5 Mine enemies speak evil of me, When shall he die, and his name perish? 6 And if he come to see me, he speaketh vanity: his heart gathereth iniquity to itself; when he goeth abroad, he telleth it. 7 All that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt. 8 An evil disease, say they, cleaveth fast unto him: and now that he lieth he shall rise up no more. 9 Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me. 10 But thou, O Lord, be merciful unto me, and raise me up, that I may requite them. 11 By this I know that thou favourest me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me. 12 And as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, and settest me before thy face for ever. 13 Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen.

Continuing the narrative of Joseph and his time in Egypt, we see the spirit for prophetic dreams and interpretation is given unto Joseph, and in his bonds he has an opportunity to use the gift in an attempt to find favor and get Pharaoh to release him. Joseph predicts that in 3 days the cupbearer will be saved, and the butler will be hanged. Symbols of the grape, and the juice of the vine, coming to salvation. Interesting. Psalm 105:17-22 He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant: Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron: Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him. The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free. He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance: To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom

This is fairly cut and dry narrative. I would note that Joseph makes certain to give God the glory for the interpretation of the Pharaoh's dreams. He shows it as well in naming his sons, giving God credit in gratitude for all that is done to bless him, even in his bondage. Despite his condition. Abased or abounding. And like the 7 years of plenty, we store up the blessings given us by the Lord that when we may face 7 years of famine, we have what we need and more, enough to be a blessing for others.
