Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness. Not by the law. Not by circumcision, for Abraham was saved decades before God gave circumcision as an ordinance. But by believing God. Abraham didn't repent of his sins, follow the law, or grovel for mercy. God in His amazing grace, offered salvation unto him, and out of free will, Abraham accepted. His faith was such that Abraham willingly offered his only begotten son upon the altar, knowing God would keep His word, and by this act, his faith was made perfect. That one may look upon that and see Abraham justified by men. But not before God. It was faith alone that saved him. If it were his willingness to obey God, then Abraham would have the glory. But all the glory is God's. He did it all. We just have to trust Him as Abraham did. That while we are yet sinners, Christ died for us. I know I am bringing two lines of thought together; the study of Leviticus and its ordinances and statutes for sanctification, and the current heresy that I have been hammering against with scripture. And forgive me if I failed to fit the two pieces together elegantly enough. But I think it is a complimentary study to see how God looks at things, rather than man, and how consistent He is in how He extends His mercy to us while we are yet sinners, His grace to those that believe, and the precious salvation that comes from His Son. That all glory is his. Not of ourselves, least any man should boast. That by understanding this, we may be conformed to His purpose, without being holier than thou scolds and hypocrites, lacking mercy and judgment. But in the Spirit, a light to the lost and a comfort to the broken hearted. That God may have the increase. Repentance, or metanoia, having a change of heart, coming to a new understanding that is (by grace, led of the Spirit); discernment. We gain discernment regarding the will of God and the state of ourselves and man in relation to Him, when we repent. When we believe the scriptures that say God would offer a sacrifice of His own making to free us from death and Hell. That that sacrifice is the Son of God, Jesus Christ. That discernment, if the new man created at salvation is fed, leads to a change in attitude towards sin. It becomes less desirable. The lusts of the flesh can lose their appeal. Even disgusting us. If that new man isn't fed, and they continue walking in the flesh, they are still saved by the knowledge of the truth, but that discernment is dulled and God may have to chasten the person to work godly sorrow in their heart. If they remain backslidden, God may call them home. But they are still saved. Saying "real repentance WILL mean you turn from sin, and WILL walk in the Spirit," is false. We must pick up our cross daily. It is a choice to engage in sanctification. But salvation is of Christ, not ourselves. It is by grace, not of ourselves.

Chapter 21 contains more of the Levitical priesthood laws regarding the holiness of the priests, the sons of Aaron. That they may not defile themselves by touching or being around a corpse other than close kin. That they should be the husband of one wife, just as pastors must be, and their wives must be virgins. Not a widow or divorced, or profane. 1 Timothy 3:2-12 A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous; One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?) Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless. Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well. While the holiness of a Levitical priest is unique, the cleanliness rituals both practical and ceremonial, and can be mirrored in the qualifications for pastor, it is important to recognize that we who are believers are part of a holy priesthood too. And for us, we should seek to be as separated spiritually as they were in the flesh. There are further provisions against a priest acting as a pagan priest, with rending of clothes, cutting the corners of their beard or hair in the fashion of the Egyptian and Canaanite priests. Acting in a profane way, desecrating the temple of God. This holiness extended to not allowing the halt, lame, deaf and blind, broken, crippled or birth defects enter into the holy places or to offer the sacrifice. God does say they may eat of the portion given to the Levitical priests and their families. This isn't a eugenic command, simply relating to the office itself. And may point to the current time, that in Christ we are healed and allowed to boldly go before the Father, but those who haven't been made righteous in the blood of Christ may not, not being spiritually made without blemish.

A free will offering. Without blemish. The Lord is who sanctifies, it is the Lord which hallows you, because you are His people. He took us out of bondage to be our God. And so be ye holy for He is holy. Amen

Now we are here in Leviticus chapter 23, and in it God provides the basic terms of the sabbaths and holy days to be kept by the children of Israel. Understanding that sabbaths means rest, and that the prohibition of doing work on the sabbath is a picture of Christ Jesus, and the rest we enter into in Him. That we are saved by the rest given to us by the Lord and not our own works. That if a child of Israel works on these days, he is cut off, just as anyone trusting in their works for salvation is likewise cut off from the Kingdom of God. It is an undeniable truth that is repeated over and over again throughout the Bible, from the creation through Revelation. We are saved by Christ's perfect work, not our own. Not by being a "good person" or contrite or "trying to avoid sin" or how well we make "Jesus the Lord of our life." Jesus paid it all in full, and the Spring feasts of Passover, unleavened bread and Pentecost all serve as ordinances to the Israelites as a picture of Christ. I covered much of this in the Gospel studies, recently in a study of Luke. It is fascinating and amazing how God set this before the people and thousands of years later, we see it pay off with Jesus, the Passover lamb, slain on a sabbath, in Hell for 3 days and nights, all sabbaths, and risen again, only to ascend into Heaven on Pentecost, the feast of the first fruits held 50 days after Passover. The day in which the disciples went out to the multitude of gathered Jews preaching the Gospel in every tongue. The 5,000 saved that day being the first fruits of the spring harvest. Then we see the Fall feasts (which I touch on in this study of Revelation). Which with the trumpets and gathering of the harvest, is a picture of the day of the Lord. The second coming of Jesus Christ, to gather the elect, the dead first reborn to glorified bodies, then those who are alive and remain, changed in a twinkling of an eye, all to meet the Lord in the sky, caught up together in the clouds. The day of our redemption. Amen. The details and how each of the ordinances given by the Lord unto the people corresponding to and a picture of the things to come, is fun to study out, but the knowledge of His giving us these things that we may know Him and build in faith, that He is true to His word and His word is consistent, over thousands of years and many authors, given by the Spirit and preserved by God for all time. We can trust His word because He has shown us in it a singular voice, and the theme that is Christ. Everything points to Him. Jesus is found in every book of the Bible. The faith of the Old Testament saints was the same as New; believing on the Lord to save us, a gift given in grace from our Father because He so loved us. That while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Amen

The Levitical feasts are also important to understand for our study of Revelation going forward. They are a picture of Christ. Last Easter I gave a rundown of the ways Jesus fulfilled the spring feasts, Passover, the feast of unleavened bread and Pentecost. These were a picture of His first coming. Likewise, the fall feasts God commands in Leviticus 23 represent Christ at His second coming. The timing, the harvest, the gathering. The blowing of trumpets. The dwelling in houses made by God, while singing His praises. All point to end times Bible prophecy. ("Booths" were tabernacles, tents, made from branches and boughs, rough cut and gathered from nature). The timing of things mirrors events in Revelation, as we will see. One incredibly important point of the feasts, these Sabbaths; NO WORK was to be done by the people. This is the reinforcement by God of His grace in giving us a free gift of salvation in Jesus, who is the Sabbath. Three days of no works, 3 Sabbaths in a row, from His crucifixion to His resurrection, Jesus doing all the work. And like the Spring feasts, the convocations or gathering of the congregation/church, there is no work allowed, for Jesus did it all. For whatsoever soul it be that shall not be afflicted in that same day, he shall be cut off from among his people. And whatsoever soul it be that doeth any work in that same day, the same soul will I destroy from among his people. These are those unsaved who are appointed to wrath. Notice it is both the unbelieving, those not afflicted by the atonement made by the sacrifice, and those who do any work who are cast out and destroyed. So too will it be in the second coming. We should all be familiar with Matthew 7:21-23: Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity. Romans 4:6-8 Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Psalm 32 Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man unto whom the Lord imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile. With this background established, we will get into Revelation 2 tomorrow. But really consider how God's word is one story, and all of creation testifies to the truth that He is our salvation. His law, a picture of Christ and everything points to the final days and the harvest. His servants bringing in the sheaves. The chafe and tares being burned. How to increase your faith? The Bible tells us: Romans 10:17 So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. Read the word and listen to preaching from His word. James 1:22-24 But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. By living the word we begin to rely more of God and less on ourselves. The word becomes part of us, shoring up faith. Psalm 51:12-14 Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; And uphold me with thy free spirit. Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; And sinners shall be converted unto thee. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: And my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness. Pray for faith. Malachi 3:10 Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it. God says to prove, or test Him. Obey His word (go to church, pay tithes in this example) and see how His blessings reward your faith in being a doer of the word. God keeping His promises is a huge way to learn to trust Him with more.

1 Samuel 21 Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why art thou alone, and no man with thee? 2 And David said unto Ahimelech the priest, The king hath commanded me a business, and hath said unto me, Let no man know any thing of the business whereabout I send thee, and what I have commanded thee: and I have appointed my servants to such and such a place. 3 Now therefore what is under thine hand? give me five loaves of bread in mine hand, or what there is present. 4 And the priest answered David, and said, There is no common bread under mine hand, but there is hallowed bread; if the young men have kept themselves at least from women. 5 And David answered the priest, and said unto him, Of a truth women have been kept from us about these three days, since I came out, and the vessels of the young men are holy, and the bread is in a manner common, yea, though it were sanctified this day in the vessel. 6 So the priest gave him hallowed bread: for there was no bread there but the shewbread, that was taken from before the Lord, to put hot bread in the day when it was taken away. Matthew 12 At that time Jesus went on the sabbath day through the corn; and his disciples were an hungred, and began to pluck the ears of corn and to eat. 2 But when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto him, Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day. 3 But he said unto them, Have ye not read what David did, when he was an hungred, and they that were with him; 4 How he entered into the house of God, and did eat the shewbread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for them which were with him, but only for the priests? 5 Or have ye not read in the law, how that on the sabbath days the priests in the temple profane the sabbath, and are blameless? 6 But I say unto you, That in this place is one greater than the temple. 7 But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless. 8 For the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath day. Leviticus 24 begins with the command to have the lamps of the Tabernacle burn continually, dusk to dawn. A statute for ever. That there is light in the place of God. And God commands that there be bread baked as a memorial, continually, as an offering before the Lord, and eaten by the Levitical priests. This is called the shewbread, concentrated by the Lord. The light symbolizes the truth of God throughout the Bible, and so it is never dark before Him. The bread is both the life given the people by God's grace and His word. This shewbread becomes a means of feeding David and his men as they flee Saul, who was in a murderous rage against the future king. Even as it was offered to God and holy, but to the Lord's purpose, it fed His favored in a time of need. Likewise, as Jesus rebukes the Pharisees when He and His disciples gleaned corn on the Sabbath to eat, Jesus points to how these things are the Lord's, and not just blind tradition and meaningless ritual. That He is the Lord of the sabbath. Often religion becomes rote practices, that forget the meaning behind them as the Pharisees had. Using these things to condemn. Jesus says had they understood who He was, that He was present for mercy in His death and resurrection to come, that the sacrifices of the temple were a picture of Him who had come not to condemn but to save, that they'd understand why it was acceptable for them to eat of their work, as the Levites were allowed on the sabbath. Because they did the work of God. The second half of the chapter begins with a narrative of a child of Egyptian heritage born into the Tribe of Dan, blaspheming God, and God's instructions to take him without the camp and those who heard the blasphemy to stone him to death. God reiterates that even strangers among them are under His law, both to their good, and to their punishment for violating it. He says His law is justice, that a murderer be put to death. That blemish, or physical harm, be answered in a like manner; breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. This concept of God's law has been understood for millennia, preserved for all time, but in 1901 a Babylonian relic was found that contained what is called Hammurabi's Code, a list of laws credited to the ancient king by archeologists, which included the eye for an eye form of justice. During the 20th century, what was part of God's perfect law (repeated from Exodus 21:24-25 Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, Burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe) began to be credited to a man, and after it had permeated culture that the concept of an eye for an eye actually originated from Hammurabi's Code, people began to mistakenly think it wasn't God's perfect law. And once they'd managed to mislead people with that, they then began to discredit the concept as barbaric, a remnant of ancient Babylon and not the commandments of God. And so by the close of the 20th Century, most people had no idea that this was found in scripture, and were taught to think of it as a savage injustice. If the concept was raised by Christians at all, it was in the context of Matthew 5:38-39; Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. And this was taught as somehow Jesus contradicting the concept, as if He wasn't the author of it. When Jesus says love thy neighbor, The same people pretend it was a new commandment when it comes from Leviticus as well. But Jesus calling those who are saved by faith in Him to love even our enemies, to pray for them, to not answer violence with violence, but to show mercy and love to them, isn't saying that the law itself is unjust, for it will be the law in the Millennial Kingdom. He's talking about our hearts storing up wrath, vengeance, and hatred. Before a magistrate, the eye taken for an eye would still be justice. 1 Timothy 1:9-11 Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers, For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine; According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust. But we who are righteous should forgive those who wronged us and show mercy to those in need. These two concepts aren't contradictory but complimentary. Our mercy doesn't upend the law. Our being at liberty from the law spiritually means we should be more circumspect in how we view our enemies. Our trust in God for vengeance taking priority over our executing our own wrath. But if the law demands restitution, so be it. The sword is not wielded in vain. What those who seek to undermine confidence in scripture do is trust that Christians won't be able to rightly divide the word of God, and this higher level concept would escape us, and lead us to showing perverse judgment. If you notice, by abandoning the law for the unrighteous, instead of mercy and love and limited restitution to a like-for-like code, we have a "justice system" that either punishes the wrong doer far exceeding what is right in the eyes of God, or not doing anything to rightly punish the wicked and protect the innocent. Those that deserve death still live, often freed to offend again. Those who deserved perhaps the loss of a tooth, or to pay restitution for damages end up incarcerated for years to no one's profit. It is skewed and unjust and it encourages vengeance, hatred and variance, instead of mercy and love. The nuance required to understand these differences, The worldly application of biblical principles with people who aren't believers versus how believers should respond personally. This causes confusion for many in other applications such as application of Romans 13 and 14. Christians are called to be meek, to be peacemakers, to be humble in realizing that our condition is by the grace of God and not of ourselves. To be understanding of our enemies that by love, we may overcome it and bring them to the same peace that we have found in the grace of God. But that doesn't mean that in this world, God's law shouldn't be upheld. And if we were to stone to death, someone for a capital violation, We should not do so gleefully and with vengeance but with understanding. And after applying just mercy. By not walking this line, we have a society wherein there is no justice and there is no mercy. We have courts that are grossly unfair. We have a criminal justice system that can't decide between rehabilitation and punishment and so attains neither. We don't put to death those who have their own blood upon them. And we lock up people who could have simply worked off the harm they caused. The application of the law becomes arbitrary and capricious rather than circumspect and done with discernment. I don't know if I'm explaining this concept well, and I myself struggle with the seeming dichotomy. But we have to understand that it isn't God's law that is imperfect, it is us. We want vengeance and God wants justice. We want mercy when it applies to us but deny it to others, Just as God's mercy is extended to us by His grace, but the wages of sin is a debt we all owe. And a person's blood is upon themselves when they violate God's law. This I think is why it's so important to stay in God's word, to feed the new man. These concepts become clearer and we begin to see the nuances and glory in how perfect God's judgment is.

Leviticus chapter 25 brings us the law of Jubilee, a perpetual sabbatical observation of the 7th year, in the land of Canaan which the Lord brought the children of Israel, culminating in the 49th year, 7 times 7, a jubilee, a proclamation of liberty, wherein all God's children shall be redeemed. Of course this parallels with Christ, and the redemption from the bonds of sin He makes for us, as the near kin, the Son of man, setting us free. The particulars of this law, which wouldn't take effect for the Israelites until they had settled the land, driving out the former inhabitants and dividing by lot the tribes and the habitations thereof, showed not only the foresight of God's providence, but His terms as the actual owner, the land Lord so to speak, of the land He gives them. And so, 6 years the fields are sown and the vineyards dressed, but in the 7th, there was no work to be done in the land. God promises them that the 6th year will be bountiful enough to tide them over to the 9th year, that they could live off their stores, because God provides all. Not of their own works. The timing of the jubilee, which was marked in the 49th year, 7 sabbaths, was marked at the end of the fall feasts by the trumpets at the end of the day of atonement. Just as Pentecost is celebrating the 7th sabbath after Passover, the spring feasts, represent Christs work here at His first coming, then the Jubilee is marked by the fall feast, which is emblematic of His second, and the day of redemption for believers. The trumpet sounds to announce the victory of the Lord, the atonement bought with blood, the redemption from bondage and the liberty given all, rich or poor. And so, the land given to the people by lot would return to them, and if it had been sold during the proceeding years to be worked by another, it would be redeemed back to the inheritors. Thus the price must be fair, and match the nearness of the jubilee; less time, less expensive. By this God provided that no family ever be perpetually destitute. And while being sold into servitude, it was always to be released in the jubilee. Not as bondsmen, or chattel slaves. No usury given to a brother, either. And no defrauding them in buying or selling. The Lord gives these things as a soft reset that allows for everyone to partake in His bounty and that none becomes rich by the accumulation of land and houses. (Except in the cities, where this didn't apply, being hubs of commerce and safety, not home.) Isaiah 5:8 Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth! God hates unfair dealings, taking advantage of others for profit, especially in their poverty. Unjust weights and measures. Mistreatment of servants. Usury among His people and the accumulation of property and capital, to the exclusion of others. Basically, Capitalism. But that is not to say He endorsed Communism, either. But fair and righteous trade and checks on over accumulation of wealth, or subjugation of His people. Productive enterprise and free markets (little f, little m), were the way He provided. This system was fair and just and kept in remembrance of God being who we rely on, who provides for all. Rich or poor, servant or free. The right of return to their own place, the inheritance they claim, enabled the genealogies to be recorded, and kept the tribes separated as He had ordained through the lots when it was eventually divided. It kept the integrity of nations, as a people, as kin. The genealogies also then served a purpose, bringing us to Christ's human family being perfect in its generations as it is given in the Gospel. And the real jubilee being the ultimate sabbath, which is Jesus. The elegance and perfection of this law shouldn't be lost in the allegory or spiritual application, however. It really is the way that we should live, even today. Ultimately, the ordinances of jubilee serve as a sobering reminder that we are servants of God, and we cannot be given or taken in bondage to any other master. We may work and toil for another, to pay our way and support our family, but not as slaves, because we are bought for a price already, by the blood of Christ. And so, even as we work here on this earth, we answer to Him. And so, the admonitions in the epistles to be good employees, hard working and honest, because we work for God, is the lived implication of this truth, that we are His. It reminds us that He provides. That even the ground we must toil to work, the curse of Adam, is His. That bounty or dearth, it is of God. That we can rest in His promise. That when He says we need not work, but that He will give us what we need, we can believe it. It's a constant reminder to the Israelites the thing we as Christians take comfort in, in the Spirit. Imagine if the economists and "experts" studied and followed these rules laid out by God? That practices like Jubilee, Liberty and redemption, resting the land, returning it to the tribe it belongs to, trusting God, allowing gleaning of the fields to support the poor, temporary servitude when necessary, but freedom and forgiveness once the acceptable year of the Lord has come. This is the closest to a perfect system we could expect in this life. And like all of God's perfect law, the fault isn't with it, but us.

Leviticus 26 is one of the many times God reiterates the warning to Israel, that if they don't keep the conditions of the covenant God has made with them, he will curse them 7-fold, remove them from the land and set their enemies up over them. This held specific meaning to the Hebrews in the wilderness, entering into Canaan, but it is true of all people who call themselves by His name. 2 Chronicles 7:14 If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land. The curse against His people comes with a remedy. Because the Lord is a forgiving and merciful God. If they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers, with their trespass which they trespassed against me, and that also they have walked contrary unto me; And that I also have walked contrary unto them, and have brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised hearts be humbled, and they then accept of the punishment of their iniquity: Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land. (Note the physical circumcision availa them nothing. It is the circumcision of the heart, made without hands, in Christ Jesus; In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ. ... But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.) This covenant is and always has been kept in Christ. It was to Abraham's seed, who is Jesus, and those blessings fall on those adopted into the promise by faith in Him. Those calling themselves Jews today could repent to be partakers of the promise, but note that they'd have to admit not only that they forsook God and didn't walk in His statutes, rejecting Christ, and deserved their punishments, but they'd have to also testify that God has walked contrary to them, and that His judgment was right. In the various captivities and tribulations of the OT Israelites, this repentance led to their being restored. But modern Jews, so-called, maintain in their being scattered, in their being cursed, in their being kept from peace in the land, they keep the fiction that they remain God's chosen people. That they aren't being cursed for their unbelief, but that it is we who believe, those circumcised of the heart, who afflict them unjustly. And upon them that are left alive of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth. This is seen in the ADL and the cries of "antisemitism," seeing swastikas and threats of genocide in construction markings and preaching from the Bible. The wicked flee where none pursue. They are faint of heart, as the Lord promises. Talmudic rabbinical Judaism shows that they despise God's statutes and abhor His judgements, so that they do not keep His commandments but instead find loopholes and rationalizations in the vain traditions of men, doctrines they invented taught as commandments of God. His tabernacle is not set in their midst, who is Jesus. They are contrary to all men. God's wrath abides upon them to the uttermost. God's people, Israel, has always been a nation of believers who, by faith, carry the circumcision of the heart. Today it is believing Christians, and our nations are blessed by the few within it who keep the word of God, and cursed when we who call ourselves by His name reject His judgement. Dispensationalists miss all of this, and they feed into apostasy and leading those who call themselves by His name astray. Chasing after vanity, false gods, making idols of Jews. They teach that the promises, blessings and inheritance that believers receive aren't for us. They seek to turn Christians, who are Jacob, into Edom, spiritually, and despising our birthright. It is wicked as Hell. It should go without saying that our God, Whose name is Jealous, and Who demands by His righteousness all the glory, hates Idolatry. He hates the veneration and worship of idols, especially by those claiming to be of His people. The Second Commandment is again hammered home here in the opening verse; Ye shall make you no idols nor graven image, neither rear you up a standing image, neither shall ye set up any image of stone in your land, to bow down unto it: for I am the Lord your God. Those who call themselves by His name who bow before statues of stone, standing images and molten and graven idols, are what spark His wrath. Catholicism and Orthodox Christianity, so called, the apostates who reject salvation by grace, and set up images to be served and bowed before in supplication, are the leading reason why Europe and America are suffering today. Why these curses and others spelled out by God throughout the Old Testament, are afflicting our land today. When Asa became king and he took away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made, the Bible says he did what was right in the eyes of the Lord. If we were to have a return to doing what was right in the eyes of the Lord, we who are His people would need to destroy every image and idol, from the blasphemy of St. Patrick's Cathedral, to every profane "crucifix," to every bathtub Mary in every Catholic yard, throughout the land.

The last chapter of Leviticus, the law of the vow, offering and tithe. These are the general conditions for the sake of clarifying what goes into the surety of a vow or, rather the amount held until completion of the vow, that could be redeemed upon completion, or the case of land and other things offered to the priesthood outside of what is proscribed earlier, for the sake of a special promise to God. It is an idea later corrupted, where we see Jesus in the Gospels call out the Pharisees for allowing an adult son to place his things in such a vow, to avoid his responsibility to honor his father and mother, caring for them in their old age, or "Corban." But ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free. The idea of temporarily giving or using collateral to ensure keeping of a vow before God, and redemption, is reflected in salvation, where Jesus is offered, the vow made, the Spirit serving as surety until the day of redemption. Hebrews 7 18 For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof. 19 For the law made nothing perfect, but the bringing in of a better hope did; by the which we draw nigh unto God. 20 And inasmuch as not without an oath he was made priest: 21 (For those priests were made without an oath; but this with an oath by him that said unto him, The Lord sware and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec:) 22 By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament. And 2 Corinthians 1 19 For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. 20 For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us. 21 Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God; 22 Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts. 23 Moreover I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth. We see these examples of promises of God are made with an application of earnest, the surety of a vow. The blood of a testimony. Redemption at the day appointed. To be paid in full as God vows. He gave His word. This concept of contractual law is the basis of everything God does. And why He detests bearing false witness, perjury, false weights and measures, cheating and stealing...It is ultimately why salvation is by faith accepted by believing a witness testimony, the Gospel shared by a believer. Why we must be blameless, that in judgment a man may trust our confession of faith. And it is why we see the emphasis in the law of trusting multiple witnesses who testify of the same thing. It's why we have 4 Gospels. For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And Jesus saying; If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. There is another that beareth witness of me; and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true. The Bible is, regardless of anything else, the testimony of God to His promises, and faith is believing He is true. God's word. Not the words of God. If that makes sense. And we can believe His vow, that we will be redeemed, after He gave his Son as surety and the Spirit as earnest. Amen This law also calls to mind the story in Acts 5: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession, 2 And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet. 3 But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land? 4 Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God. 5 And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost: and great fear came on all them that heard these things. 6 And the young men arose, wound him up, and carried him out, and buried him. 7 And it was about the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what was done, came in. 8 And Peter answered unto her, Tell me whether ye sold the land for so much? And she said, Yea, for so much. 9 Then Peter said unto her, How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? behold, the feet of them which have buried thy husband are at the door, and shall carry thee out. 10 Then fell she down straightway at his feet, and yielded up the ghost: and the young men came in, and found her dead, and, carrying her forth, buried her by her husband. 11 And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things. As for vows and swearing to God before men, Jesus says in Matthew 5: 33 Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: 34 But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: 35 Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. 36 Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. 37 But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. We have no obligation to make vows, to give earnest, and to do these things before God. The law being a schoolmaster brings us to the truth that Jesus is conveying; that a just man doesn't need to prove by vow what his word is, because by being honest in all things, and keeping it to yes or no, and meaning it, we uphold the spirit of the law and its intention. Men will believe us or not. And our vows to these things, be it God, or your life or heaven or things of the earth, all are His and we have no real right to put them up for earnest. And so we've reached the end of Leviticus. I know I got a better understanding of the book from this read through. And I hope other people may have benefited from it. Before diving right into numbers, which has a similar bad reputation for people who struggle to get through these books of the law when trying to read the entire Bible, I think I'm going to take a slight diversion. I feel as though Jeremiah and lamentations would be a nice study to contrast what we've just learned and before getting into Numbers. And I may need to revisit a New Testament book for my own interest. I think everyone who took the time to read the scripture even if you skipped over my commentary. Encourage everyone to read at least 15 to 20 minutes of Bible a day with a purpose. Not just as some devotional. But seeking the deeper things of God.

Here we go. God is a God of separation. The Bible has example after example of division, separating one thing from another. Day from night. The creatures after their own kind. Woman from man. Man from the Garden. Cain and Abel. The descendents of Seth, the sons of God that called upon the name of the Lord and the children of men who did not. Noah and his perfect generations from fallen man. The animals of the ark. The nations of Noah's sons. The people of Babel and their languages. The habitations of the nations. Abraham out of Ur. Ishmael and Isaac. Jacob and Esau. Joseph and his brothers. Hebrews out of their land and into Egypt. Out of Egypt and back in the land. The covenant with Moses that they would be a holy people. Separated from other nations. Even here, in Numbers, each tribe separated and counted. And the Levites separated even further. Luke 12:51 Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: The division. The separation. Making holy a people of God. Separating Israel from Judah. And Jesus from the root of Jesse. Believing Israel from the non-believing Jews. The tares from the wheat. Sheep from goats. Israel after the flesh and Israel after the Spirit. Unfruitful branches cut off and cast into the fire. The election in Christ chosen to be graft in. Deuteronomy 7:6 For thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God: the LORD thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth. Isaiah 62:12 And they shall call them, The holy people, The redeemed of the LORD: and thou shalt be called, Sought out, A city not forsaken. 1 Peter 2:9 But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light; Winnowing the chaff from the wheat. The earth is His threshing floor. The harvest is ongoing. We are in the last days, and have been since the first fruit of Christ, and the harvest of 5,000 made by the disciples on Pentecost. In Numbers 2, the Lord commands Moses to organize the camp of Israel around the Tabernacle. First the Levites divided into four smaller camps, to the South, West, North and East of the Tabernacle. With the tent of worship at its heart, the entrance facing East, that the morning sun would shine into it. God then told them to make four camps; to the East, the standard of Judah. To the South, the standard of Reuben. To the West, the standard of Ephraim. To the North, the standard of Dan. Each banner with the ensign, the emblem of that tribe. And within each camp, the other tribes would muster. In the East, first camped Judah, then next to them the tribe of Issachar, then the tribe of Zebulun. 186,400 of the armies total of the three tribes. And when the camp would go out and move, they would fall in ranks in that order. Leading the march. Next, to the South, first came Ruben. And those that pitched by them, Simeon. Then next to Simeon, Gad. 151,450 men. And when they marched, the camp of Ruben would fall in behind the camp of Judah. And the disassembled Tabernacle and the Levites, behind them, in the midst of the march. On the West, in the camp of Ephraim camped according to their armies, with Manasseh camped next to them, with Benjamin then next. 108,100 men. On the North, under the standard of Dan fell their tribe, then by him was the tribe of Asher, followed next by Naphtali. 157,600. The camps of Ephraim and Dan following in line when the camp of the children of Israel were on the move. Now, to the point. What Numbers 2 lays out is a picture of the camp, surrounding the Tabernacle, the heart of the camp where the Spirit of God appears as a cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. The Levites to each direction, serving the 4 camps. The rectangular tent of the Tabernacle facing East would see the camp of Judah. Larger than the others. West, a bit smaller. North and South, almost equal. There are two schools of thought on this, presented above. One school teaches that each camp surrounded the Tabernacle in a square, the tribes each side by side. The other sees the camp laid out in a nearly perfect cross. With the camps laid out by one tribe, next to them another, and then another. A cross with the heart being the holy place of God. Where the blood was shed for sacrifice, a picture of Christ. Facing East, looking towards Judah. Jesus being the morning star. Revelation 22:16 I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star. While we cannot know with 100% certainty that the layout was a cross, it certainly is what is described in my opinion. I cannot see it any other way, and Numbers has many references to Jesus, as we will see. The idea it would just be an uneven box-shaped camp seems absurd. Not to get to any spoilers, consider this passage from Numbers 24; And Balaam lifted up his eyes, and he saw Israel abiding in his tents according to their tribes; and the spirit of God came upon him. And he took up his parable, and said, Balaam the son of Beor hath said, and the man whose eyes are open hath said: He hath said, which heard the words of God, which saw the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance, but having his eyes open: How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel! Balaam, a character we shall encounter soon enough, is looking down at the camp of Israel and the Spirit of God came upon him and he marveled at the layout of the camp. I don't believe that he was viewing a rough square. I believe he was looking towards the cross. The debate over this is definitely tertiary doctrine. No one has to believe one way or another about it. But the picture of Christ should inform everything we read in the Old Testament. God's promise of His Son is found in every book. Moses wrote of Him. To Jesus did all the prophets give witness. We've already covered the pictures of Christ and His sacrifice found throughout Exodus and Leviticus. Numbers, as we will see God willing, has much more, and touches heavily on the theme that we are all sinners and all have fallen short. That we all need God to deliver us. Themes Numbers teaches throughout. The next few chapters can be rough. But all scripture is given for our profit. It was written for our edification and to build faith in us. Things like the layout of the camp builds faith that God's plan was always, from everlasting. Jesus the same yesterday today and forever. Numbers 4 sees God lay out the calling to each family of the Levites for ministering to the Tabernacle concerning the movement of the camp, the storage and transport of those holy things. And each man of each clan given a role, specific to them. With the whole given to the purpose of God. Just as today, we who are saved are given different ways to be ministers of the faith and to edify the church, carrying that which is holy forth, into the world. Never boast of your calling or think it beneath you. Never covet another's as better than yours. If you are apt to teach, teach well with longsuffering. Chapter 5 of Numbers is divided into three sections, highlighted by God restating or clarifying previous commands given in Exodus and Leviticus, and adding another, the law of jealousy. First, God reiterates the law of the unclean, those with leprosy, issues which means blood issues, sores or boils, or other kinds of sickness that causes the body to release fluids, and those unclean having come in contact with the dead. That these people be put without the camp that their uncleanliness doesn't affect others. We have already read these things and the timing of the exile. Leprosy being contagious and generally incurable, the person would be permanently removed, although a ritual with the Levites and a method for determining they be clean if healed was laid out in Leviticus 14:1-9 (covered here and here) Issues potentially carrying some kind of contagious disease, withdrawn until it has cleared or they are healed. We see a woman with blood issues her whole life healed by simply touching the hem of Jesus' cloak in Luke 8:43-48. The law about being unclean by the touching of a carcase was given against the Levites with general instructions and is mentioned here, with more specific rules given in Numbers 19:11; The one who touches the corpse of any person shall be unclean for seven days....With purification rituals attached. Physically they are instructions to keep diseases from spreading. To stop outbreaks of illness that could spread from person to person. Spiritually, all are a picture of sin, and the exile similar to church discipline, the removal of leaven that can spoil a whole lump. It also pictures the removal of our own sin in our lives, that can grow and metastasize until we are castaway in our backslidden state. Useless to the Lord. You can also see how it pictures separation from the world, keeping the unclean from that which is holy, the temple of God within us, where the holy Spirit dwells; that shall ye put out, without the camp shall ye put them; that they defile not their camps, in the midst whereof I dwell. We should be mindful of these applications, understanding that the physical revelation of the Old Testament carries with them the spiritual applications for our lives as Christians today. I'm am always struck by the very nature of creation and the things we experience and witness, all serve as a parable to bring us understanding of the spiritual things of God. Even death and disease serve as a method for God to teach His people about the nature of sin, or the need for cleansing in Christ. The world is the way it is for our benefit. God is revealed from Heaven that we may better understand Him. That it is all to His purpose. Amen Next is the law of recompense for trespasses against another. That when a man or woman commit any sin (which is transgression of the law), they trespass against the Lord, and if guilty, they must confess the trespass and pay the person it was against whatever it cost them in damages, plus 20% for their trouble. And if it could not be paid to the person, then paid to their kin. And without kin, brought to the priest and offered to the service of God that atonement may be made for them. Note the recompense is due God, and for every sin. God demands payment plus the fifth, which when you consider the sins of man in a given day, if all were to be covered, even a righteous and godly man could be bankrupt by the end of a few days. But the redemption is covered in Christ. God's recompense for our sin paid for by the blood of Jesus, a propitiation for our sin, atonement given that we may be justified in that reckoning. The concept of the ledger and the debt incurred by sin is given that we may know we can never do enough to offset it. Our only hope is in Christ. Numbers 5:9-10 touches on that which a man reserves for the priests, a holy gift given independently of a sin or trespass offering. For the holy service of God. Also called 'corban.' Given the context here, I think it was an understanding that the offered thing, money or wealth, or animal, which would be given the Levites at an appointed time or in death or when an animal reached age to be sacrificed, was set aside and belonged to the priest and not to be used as recompense. I could be wrong. But the concept of this being abused, appears in the Gospels. And ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother; Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye. People used the Corban to get out of honoring, that is financially supporting, their parents in their later years. The obligation nullified by the promise of wealth to the temple, and thus being exempt from paying for their needs. The letter of the law being used to justify corruption, while ignoring the weightier things of the Spirit of the law. The intentions of God subverted by the Pharisees loopholes and reasoning, which Jesus calls out. Exodus 34:13-14 But ye shall destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves: For thou shalt worship no other god: for the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God... The law of jealousy, outlined here in chapter 5 of Numbers, refers to the Biblical meaning of holding that which is yours as precious and sacred. Loving that which is yours. A name of God is Jealous, and in and of itself it is good and holy. And the infidelity of the Israelites with false gods and idols demonstrated that they did not regard God's jealousy, and instead held it in contempt. It is not the same as envy, which our modern vernacular has added to the word, and the negative connotations that come with it, which is covetousness. It also is not the obsessive overprotection of something that isn't rightly yours, like some use it. But it is a godly emotion, which all of us can have. And like wrath and love itself, it is a good thing when appropriate, but that can be made toxic and lead us to sin because we are flesh. And so, in seeking to give man the perfect law, God instituted a way for a husband who may be jealous for his wife, to determine if that were warranted, and for women dealing with an obsessive husband to have protection. God says that if a woman has a secret affair and is defiled by adultery, and the husband doesn't have any actual proof, but suspicion, he is to take her to the priest with an offering of plain barley. The priest will then prepare water set aside for the altar and dust of the ground of the Tabernacle, and mix it. Then he shall shave the woman's head, give her the barley to hold, with the water in his hand, have her swear an oath that she has been faithful. But if she lies and is guilty the water will be bitter, causing her thighs to rot and her belly to swell. And the woman was to say amen, amen to this and drink. The curse written down and blotted out with the water. It was left for God to judge. The priest offered the offering upon the altar. And the water was left to either curse or clear. Verse 28 indicates to me that the lying unfaithful woman may have been left barren by the experience, as the cleared wife "shall conceive seed." So we can see that by having an outlet for this gave both spouses a form of protection and an incentive to be both chaste in their dealings, never leading their husbands to jealousy, even falsely as a manipulation, and to keep husbands from inordinately accusing their wives. The wife's head was shorn and uncovered regardless of the outcome. The shame of it would be for both to bear. The woman would become a curse and a warning to others. The man, a cuckold, or potentially one, bringing him shame as well. Thus the perfect law of God always sought to discourage wrong doing, even as it punished those that did transgress the law. 1 Corinthians 11:1-16 Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ. Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you. But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God. Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonoureth his head. But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven. For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered. For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man. For the man is not of the woman: but the woman of the man. Neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man. For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels. Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God. Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered? Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him? But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering. But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God. Just to be clear, the woman being uncovered means shorn, her hair cut short to the scalp with a razor. Some take it to mean a hat or veil, but the context here is a man with long hair in the church being a dishonorable thing, just as a woman shorn or shaven. People get hung up in the slight diversion Paul takes to establish the order of "heads," the hierarchy that the woman is of the man and the man of Christ's, that we are all under God. The "head" in this regard is not the physical body part but the ruler. The higher power each submits to. And the "because of the angels" line seems like a non sequitur, or an instruction that if a woman doesn't put a hat on when praying the angels have a problem with it. It is a line that is open to some interpretation, but the larger point is hair length, and that can be discerned by the surrounding text. My thoughts are that in giving the hierarchy, a woman is subject unto the man because of Eve and the temptation of Satan, an angel, and the curse put upon Eve in the garden. Genesis 3:16 Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee. But that's just my opinion. Before leaving 1 Corinthians though, take note of the warning against bringing God to jealousy 1 Corinthians 10:21-22 Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils. Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he? Rather than hold jealousy in our hearts in a relationship, turning trust toxic, we should instead seek to not being God to jealousy by the things of this world. Especially by not separating ourselves from idolatry and the wicked beliefs of the unsaved who worship the created more than the Creator who is blessed forever amen.

Numbers 6 gives the vow of the Nazarite, the law of the vow and the consecration into service unto the Lord. Not to be confused with Nazarene, someone from Nazareth as Christ Jesus was, the Nazarite was someone, male or female, who took a vow for a time to dedicate themselves to special service for the Lord. The rules laid out are simple, no wine or fermented wine, "strong drink," nor vinegar or wine vinegar, or grape or seed or skin. Nothing from the vine. (This is the clearest indication in scripture that "wine" means unfermented juice, as the distinction with wine vs strong drink or liquors indicates) They were not to take a razor to their hair, but let it grow out during the period of service. They had to avoid being unclean, especially the uncleanliness of being near or touching the dead. We get very little in scripture by way of the why someone would take the vow, the specific time it would last, if any, or the details of that service. What we do know from the special cases of Samson, Samuel and John the Baptist, who were dedicated at infancy to this vow that the separation was made to be in great service to the people and to God. Were the lifelong Nazarites long-haired or just simply not shorn with a razor? Did Sampson have to offer numerous sacrifices for the dead he had slain? Why was his gift great strength when Samuel and John were not? While they showed great fear of God and meekness, Samson was bold and given to women and wrath. I don't know. Vows were made for various purposes and reasons, just as the Nazarites. People vowed special offerings, gifts to the priests of money and items, fasting was often accomplished by vow. And vows to God should always be taken seriously and not haphazardly. Ecclesiastes 5:4-6 When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay. Numbers 30:2 If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth. Even in the New Testament, there were some who swore vows, and the expectations of the grave nature of it was the same. We see in Acts 5 the vow made by Ananias and his wife to offer the price of a sold property to the church at Jerusalem, only to withhold a portion for themselves. But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession, And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet. But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land? Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God. And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost: and great fear came on all them that heard these things. And the young men arose, wound him up, and carried him out, and buried him. The Bible says 3 hours later, Sapphira was confronted with the same dereliction of their vow, and suffered the same fate as her husband. The Bible shows Paul taking various vows, as in Acts 18:18 which appears to be Nazarite; And Paul after this tarried there yet a good while, and then took his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila; having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow. And Paul takes a vow in Acts 21 at the behest of James, the brother of Jesus, that results in his arrest at Jerusalem. As we see throughout Acts and the early epistles, Paul sought to bridge the gap between the believing Jews and Gentiles, with the Gospel of grace, because of his love for his brothers after the flesh, and his disentanglement from the practices of the Jews came over time, mainly through his opposition to Judaizers. But should we as New Testament Christians take vows? Matthew 5:33-37 Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. James 5:12 But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation. We are already called to live consecrated lives in service of the Lord. Separated unto the Gospel. And as such, are supposed to be dedicated to the purposes of God without vow, but as His. And in doing so, we see that the more important thing is that our testimony be without question or ill repute. Blameless. Honest in our dealings that when we say to someone the reason for our hope, we are a good witness for the Gospel that they might be saved. And while times of fasting or dedication to a specific task for God may be something we do for specific favor, or time offered in service for thanksgiving, we should live separated lives daily, with joy and thanksgiving. Psalms 61:8 So will I sing praise unto thy name for ever, that I may daily perform my vows. Numbers 6 22 And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, 23 Speak unto Aaron and unto his sons, saying, On this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel, saying unto them, 24 The Lord bless thee, and keep thee: 25 The Lord make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: 26 The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace. 27 And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them. I don't want this law of blessings to be lost in all the vow talk, because it is important. The Lord instructs the priests to bless the children of Israel in His name, giving various examples. The purpose is to out His name upon them. That they understand where and Who the blessings are from. That it is His name upon them that brings these glad tidings. That they may understand and appreciate Him in their daily lives. We should do the same, as a priesthood of believers, especially with our family, but everywhere in our lives. People need to be reminded that the blessings that come to them are of God.

This is tough. It is the same offering given 12 times, and described in detail each time, with names that are difficult to pronounce. His offering was one silver charger, the weight whereof was an hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary; both of them full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering: One golden spoon of ten shekels, full of incense: One young bullock, one ram, one lamb of the first year, for a burnt offering: One kid of the goats for a sin offering: And for a sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five he goats, five lambs of the first year: this was the offering... Again and again. Numbers 7 has derailed more "read the Bible in a year" plans of young and old for centuries. I confess I really struggle with this type of verse. But there's a cliff hanger payoff at the end. To touch on this, we see the distribution of oxen for the purpose of carrying forth the Tabernacle, given to the camps of the priests. Then the consecration of the Tabernacle by the gifts and sacrifices, given of each tribe. A burnt offering, a sin offering, a peace offering. Precious vessels of silver and gold. Fine flour and incense, mingled with oil. The pictures of the sacrifice and life of Christ Jesus.

And so the detailed separation of the Levites unto the service of God continues, and the offerings of sanctification and atonement given. A shadow of what is to come. Hebrews 9 Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary. 2 For there was a tabernacle made; the first, wherein was the candlestick, and the table, and the shewbread; which is called the sanctuary. 3 And after the second veil, the tabernacle which is called the Holiest of all; 4 Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant; 5 And over it the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat; of which we cannot now speak particularly. 6 Now when these things were thus ordained, the priests went always into the first tabernacle, accomplishing the service of God. 7 But into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood, which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people: 8 The Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest, while as the first tabernacle was yet standing: 9 Which was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience; 10 Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation. 11 But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building; 12 Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us. 13 For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh: 14 How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? 15 And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance. 16 For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator. 17 For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth. 18 Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood. 19 For when Moses had spoken every precept to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of calves and of goats, with water, and scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book, and all the people, 20 Saying, This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you. 21 Moreover he sprinkled with blood both the tabernacle, and all the vessels of the ministry. 22 And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission. 23 It was therefore necessary that the patterns of things in the heavens should be purified with these; but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. 24 For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us: 25 Nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest entereth into the holy place every year with blood of others; 26 For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. 27 And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment: 28 So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation.

We are in Numbers 9, and we see this the 3rd Passover, held in the wilderness and the Lord tells Moses not to forget the ordinance that He has established, using the Passover in Egypt and the physical salvation of Israel as a picture of Christ and the individual salvation of man. I've done larger studies on the parallels and processes before. But it is always good to note that it was a reminder of Christ to come, just as the Lord's supper is a reminder of Christ for us now. Here, God provides Moses with a few guidelines given circumstance. That the ceremonially unclean and those sojourning participate in Passover just the same, that strangers among them that wish to are invited, and those that don't participate are cut off and bear their own sin. The parallels are pretty clear as to how this corresponds to individual salvation in Jesus. Anyone. Even the unclean. Even those afar off from God, get to participate in the sacrifice and the blood. Even the stranger among them. The sinner, the worldly, the Gentile...all are invited to take part in the salvation by the blood, in the faith of Jesus Christ. And those who don't are cut off and made to pay for their sin. It is that simple. People try to overcomplicate salvation because they want to make it about themselves or to make it a sensual experience that they can "feel," or see. Because they lack faith, which is the evidence of things unseen. And then we are called to follow Him. Just as the movement of the Tabernacle and the camps was dictated by the movement of God upon them, the pillars of smoke and fire. At the commandment of the Lord they moved. At His command they rested. And so it is to be in our lives, that after salvation we follow the Lord. It is right and good to follow the Lord, moving to His commandments. And accepting His will for our lives. But again, people conflate or confuse the order of things. The salvation out of sin of Egypt had already taken place, with the shedding of blood of the Passover lamb. The baptism of the waters of the sea followed. The understanding of the law given. The sanctification of the people. The continuous atonement with burnt offerings and blood of the sacrifices. The command to follow where God takes us after that. Being led into the promised land. The order of things is given that there can be no misunderstanding. God is not the author of confusion. People want to add and mix things based on their own ideas, not the word of God.

Isaiah 58:1 Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins. 1 Corinthians 15:52 In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” Revelation 11:15 And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever. A trumpet to gather the Israel of God. A trumpet to move them. A trumpet to sound the alarm. A trumpet to go to war. There will be a trumpet. He will return with a shout and gather the elect, the dead in Christ and they that are alive and remain. Changed into incorruptible bodies, redeemed as promised of God. And the nations of the earth and the kingdoms of this world will be given unto Him. Amen

...would God that all the Lord'S people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit upon them! Amen. With Numbers 11, we enter into the more narrative-driven portion of the book. Less difficult to get through, no less full of doctrine. Here we see the children of Israel as they are typically shown throughout the exodus and wandering in the wilderness, complaining and in disfavor of the Lord. They and the mixed multitudes among them, begin to lust. To put their carnal desires above their love of God. To look back to Egypt as better than their miraculous salvation. To miss the life they had and the things of the world they fared on, and resenting the heavenly bread which God provided. The like picture of our salvation today, the longing for the old ways of our sinful lives. Nostalgia for the wickedness of the world and the various temptations available in it. The separation and sanctified life of the Christian can often feel like this. Working, reading scripture, praying, church...a routine that sees little variance, and if we aren't careful, can become stale and boring. When I first read through Exodus and Numbers, as a younger babe in Christ, I would be angry at the Israelites and look down on them, saying "no wonder God is so angry with them. He's providing them food from heaven and they still complain!" Now, as a more mature Christian, I feel more sympathetic, and see how my own walk with God has likely angered Him, as I have gone after lusts of the world. It has strengthened my walk to see myself in them, and made me more understanding for those struggling. Give us this day our daily bread...live by every word of God. Be hungry for the manna. Don't be distracted from the word with the temptations of the worldly. Appreciate that God has inspired and preserved His word for all generations. The privilege we have to study it day and night. And that we are called to prophesy, preaching His word to every creature. That the Spirit is upon our hearts. It isn't just manna to feed us, but to feed others. In that spirit, we can appreciate God's chastisement of the Hebrews, giving them the meat they crave, in abundance. Ye shall not eat one day, nor two days, nor five days, neither ten days, nor twenty days; But even a whole month, until it come out at your nostrils, and it be loathsome unto you: because that ye have despised the Lord which is among you, and have wept before him, saying, Why came we forth out of Egypt? If you have experienced this, where you backslide and fall away from walking in the spirit, longing for the old life you left behind when you were born again, and starve the new man to feed the old, you've witnessed this same thing. Phone calls or texts from an old drinking buddy. A woman at work suddenly seems interested in you. The gang from high school wants to get together. The dealer you used to score from you run into unexpectedly. It is more than a test. It's often a lesson of excess in the thing you were lusting after, and you find if you should stumble back into sin, that it doesn't hold the same appeal. That you can't enjoy it. Even if you run greedily after whatever it is you missed about spiritual Egypt, your time in bondage, in short order you'll see it as repulsive and gross. You will have it coming out of your nostrils. Some prefer that misery. Even eating the metaphorical quail long after it has spoiled and sickened them. But for many Christians it is a wake-up call and a reminder of how good we have it walking with the Lord. For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. Thank God for His love and correction. If dispensationalists tried reading the New Testament I would ask them why they think the Jews were so angry at Paul and the other apostles and evangelists. If they still have the kingdom because "All Israel shall be saved" then why would they care if Gentiles were grafted in, to the point where they persecuted and murdered people in multiple countries across half a continent? Why are the Jews the villain?

So, we are here in Numbers chapter 12, and we have a story of the brother and sister of Moses, Aaron and Miriam, and their sedition against Moses because of his marriage to an outlandish woman, an Ethiopian. Claiming they were on par with Moses, having had the Spirit of the Lord upon them and having then preached His word through them, they presumed to speak with authority over the appointed man of God. Moses in his meekness didn't speak against them, but the Lord in His anger did, saying that His inspiration to prophecy given men in visions and dreams wasn't the same thing as His relationship with Moses which was direct and personal, speaking mouth to mouth. Not in "dark speeches," or dark sayings as parables and metaphors used to teach doctrine are called in the New Testament. But directly. Frankly. In person. God asks why they are not afraid to speak out against Moses given that obvious position of favor and authority that had been granted him. And His wrath was kindled, and Miriam became leprous, skin as white as snow. Aaron seeing this begged for forgiveness to Moses, who then intercedes on Miriam's behalf. But the Lord, to show Miriam and others who might rise in sedition a lesson, has her put without the camp for 7 days of shame. This chapter has been used to justify or argue something about mixed marriages with other nations, races, kindred, religion...to justify miscegenation, and to condemn those who oppose taking a stranger as a spouse. The "Ethiopian wife" and the "white as snow" punishment of Miriam, has added to this debate. But it's not what the chapter is about.
