Those saved and in the promised land, delivered by the Lord to their inheritance. It is a parallel that shows that there are many nations blessed by God in Christ, the seed of Abraham, but there is one Kingdom we shall inherit.

The final chapter in the book of Joshua, and another recap of all that God had done for the people, and reminder that by agreeing to be His people, and He their God, they are accepting the blessings and the curse should they fall away as a nation. The Lord reminds them through Joshua that their fathers, Terah and the Chaldeans served false gods beyond the flood, the Euphrates river, but for Abram, who God led out of Ur and into Canaan. And he begat Issac who begat Jacob, who begat Joseph, bringing them from the land of promise to Egypt. And by God's mighty hand were they led out of bondage, through the Red Sea, through the wilderness and into the promised land. And so, now the children of Israel had a choice; to return to the strange gods of their fathers, or to serve the Lord. And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. And as Joshua dies, an exemplar for the faith and living in obedience to God, we learn that the people for at least the generations alive during this time, did indeed choose to serve the Lord. Honoring their pledge, the rock at Shechem serving as witness to the covenant the people made with Joshua there.

Just to recap the theme going into the Book of Judges; God having delivered the people into the promised land commanded them to utterly destroy the inhabitants and to smash down their altars to the false gods they worshipped. The Lord had been with them in every battle (save one, thanks to the abomination of Achan). He had driven out the people that Joshua and his armies went against. He delivered 33 Kings into their hands. The Lord God rained hail the size of boulders, drove men out with hornets, felled the walls of cities with the shout and trumpets of the Israelites. But yet they did not fully eradicate the Canaanites and others in the land. They resorted to allowing them to stay in tribute. Valuing their gold more than the commandments of God. They had the knowledge of the will of the sovereign God, and chose, of their own will, to ignore His word, to do as they saw was right in their own eyes. Despite all their valiant deeds and the miracles they witnessed while obeying Him, they slacked off in their duty to do that which was comfortable. Easy. To leave the work unfinished. By their choice. By free will. And God responded by removing the hedge of protection around them. By allowing them to feel the consequences of their actions. By using these nations as a thorn in the side of Israel, to prove her that they may learn the ways of war, rather than peace. To be a snare with their false gods, so that the glory of God could be known. That in their tribulation they would call out to the Lord for salvation, and He would place His Spirit on a judge He would raise up to deliver them. The Bible is the record of God's will for man, in Christ Jesus. And it demonstrates that He gave His word as a testimony, that man should believe Him. The Godhead being three persons, that the witness be true, just as the law requires. Jesus appeared resurrected to witnesses that others believed their report. The Spirit indwells believers, that it testify to them they have eternal life, that they may know. The Bible exists, inspired and preserved, that we may hear the word and have faith that it is true, and obey His commandments beginning with the gospel of Christ. It is always a choice. And God uses our choices to His purpose, even when we are disobedient. Even when some don't believe the report. Even when people fall away from the truth. Calvinism demands that a sovereign God removes that choice, the need for His word as testimony, the Spirit to believe, and makes all of man's shortcomings God's responsibility. It denies the power of God to see His will done despite our failings. To use our sins as a means of shaping the clay as a Potter. The covenants become worthless, because why make promises and give blessings for man's obedience when the obedience is given to them? The Israelites failed to harken to the commandments of God, and lost those blessings and protections. Just as the covenant with Moses in the wilderness established as terms; I will be your God, and ye shall be My people. But if they took up the gods and abominations of those in the land, it would be a curse, and they would be troubled until they turned back to the Lord. The covenant was glorious, but the fault was with them. None of this makes sense in a Calvinistic world view. There is no lesson to learn from it. If they were predestinated to disobey, then the punishment they received wouldn't be to prove them and provoke them to repentance. God's decision to let them suffer the consequences to teach them their need for salvation in Him wouldn't make any sense. There's no need for the law to be a schoolmaster if faith and obedience is handed down by the good will of a sovereign Lord, on whomever He will. And it limits God, showing He needs total control of man's actions in order to have the outcome He desires, rather than the glory and power of His will being done despite man's disobedience. And it makes Christ's obedience to the Father's will unto death meaningless, for if man's obedience is forced upon them, why would the Son saying "not my will, but the Father's" mean anything at all to us? How would that perfect obedience save us? How is it an inspiration to strive for that perfection? The gospel of the Calvinist is a hopeless thing, and their false god is weak and capricious. 2 Timothy 2:16-19 But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus; Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some. Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity. Acts 1:6-11 When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel? And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power. But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. And while they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel; Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven. 2 Peter 3:1-4;8 This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you; in both which I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance: That ye may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour: Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation...But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.

Judges 1 & 2 sets the stage for the next era of Israel, following the death of Joshua. The various tribes failed to utterly destroy the Canaanites in the land God had given them to possess, and instead made tributaries of them. Valuing their gold more than God. Keeping these people among them, that they become thorns in their sides. The corruption of the following generations, who turned from the deliverance of God and His covenant, was sown in the remnants of the heathen among them. They turned to worship Baal and Asteroth, 'the queen of heaven." They were beset and spoiled constantly by the remnants of the nations. The children of Israel were even taken as slaves. And periodically, when the complaints of the Israelites were heard by God, he sent a judge. A deliverer to save them from their plight. And when the judge was dead, they returned to corruption and adultery with idols, following other gods. The picture of Christ, the judge who delivers us from death and bondage, but who never dies, living forever the first fruits of the resurrection. Who will judge the quick and the dead at the judgment seat of Christ for saints, the great white throne for the unregenerate. It is Christ Jesus, the angel of the Lord who appears before them to let them know that He would no longer drive the heathen from them, because they had not thrown down their altars and slain the people. The covenant He would never break was broken, finding fault with them. Christians in the world, delivered by the most High Judge, Christ Jesus will see, their children and grandchildren fall away to the world, just as the tribes of Judah did. But the promise of His deliverance remains forever, that they may turn to Him and call upon His name and be saved. We will see this patterned for us in Judges, again and again.

The pattern of falling away, turning to God for deliverance, and God sending a judge to free the children of Israel begins. We see that God determines that the heathen in the land that they had failed to utterly remove will serve as a means to test the people, to keep them ready for war, to humble them, to tempt them to marry their outlandish woman and worship their false gods. And when they suffered the fruit of their adultery, and came to see their need for God's salvation, repented towards Him, and called upon His name, He would send a deliverer. In the same way, tribulation and sin in the world serve to test man, and as a schoolmaster, bring people to be humbled before God and seek His help. To call upon the name of Christ, the judge of all, to deliver us. The Jews, who say they are but are not and do lie, exist in this world for the same reason these Canaanites do. The same with every evil organization of men. They are here to keep us spiritually equipped for war. To tempt us into sin and worship of false gods. To test us and try us. To bring us to Him. You can almost hear an ancient Israelite saying "of God real, why bad things happen? Why Chushanrishathaim attack us?" Here in Judges we see exactly why. And it is to glory God. Now in the narrative we see the early history of the Israelites in the promised land. The 5 lords of the Philistines, Sidonians, Hivites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Moabites, Jebusites, and Canaanites in general, are both bordering and among the land inherited by each tribe. The king of Mesopotamia, Chushanrishathaim comes against them and leads them as captives 8 years, and Caleb's nephew Othniel has the Spirit of the Lord come up on him, and he as judge delivers the Mesopotamian into his hands. And for 40 years they knew peace. And Othniel dies. The 40 year pattern is a generational cycle used by God throughout history. The wandering in the wilderness. The cycle of judges and kings. The time between Pentecost and the ascension of Jesus to the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem in 70AD...God provides a span of these generations to allow man to get right, as He judges nations. Next we see Moab come up against Israel as the agent of God's wrath for Israel for falling away again. The children of Ammon and Amalek, who take possession of Jericho, the city of palm trees. And for 18 years the children of Israel serve under Eglon. And when Israel cried unto the Lord for deliverance, Ehud, a Benjamite was raised up by the Lord as judge. And Ehud, the left-handed judge slays Eglon in God's name, in one of the most gruesome deaths of the Bible. Judges has some of the best narratives ever, better than those Netflix and HBO could ever imagine. And after the destruction of the Moabites under Ehud, the land knows rest for 80 years. Then we learn of Shamgar son of Anath, who slew 600 Philistines with an ox goad, an unimaginable feat, yet relegated to a single verse. (We will see another mention of Shamgar in a few chapters, in the song of Deborah) But we see the pattern. The harder the times, the more likely the people turn to the Lord. The better the times, the quicker they fall away. In our Christian life, we may see similar patterns. There's a tendency towards leaning on God, turning to prayer more often, reading the Bible more, increasing church attendance, maybe even fasting...but when the deliverance comes, many begin to shirk those things. And rather than walk in the Spirit, backslide towards walking in the flesh. God uses tribulation to prove us. That we may learn to trust Him more, to increase our faith. To learn mercy and judgement. To increase patience. We see it throughout the Epistles. Romans 5:1-5 Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. It's the same pattern, spiritual rather than physical, but similar. A picture of our Christian life.

Judges 4 begins with the generation following the death of Ehud the judge, and the Israelites falling once again into sin. The Lord sells them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, and his captain Sisera. For 20 years he oppressed the children of Israel. Meanwhile, a prophetesses by the name of Deborah was a judge of Israel at that time. Things were bad, a woman held the knowledge of the word of God and had set up a place of judgment at a palm tree in Ephraim, where the people came to her for judgment. Isaiah 3:12 As for my people, children are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, they which lead thee cause thee to err, and destroy the way of thy paths. Deborah was righteous in the sight of the Lord and wise by her understanding of His word. There is no indication that her judgment was wrong, and matters brought before her must have been answered satisfactorily to the parties, or all Israel wouldn't seek her out, there beneath the palms. But it was not God's intention that a woman shall rule. It is a sign of weak and faithless men where they feel the need to. Happy international women's month. Now this prophetess goes to a man named Barak, asking him why he had not harkened to a command by God to rise an army of 10,000 men from Naphtali and Zebulun, to go against Sisera, which presumably Barak was aware of, that God had promised to deliver the Canaanite army into Barak's hand. And Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go. Very similar to Moses when he asked the same of God; Exodus 33:14-17 And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest. And he said unto him, If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence. For wherein shall it be known here that I and thy people have found grace in thy sight? is it not in that thou goest with us? so shall we be separated, I and thy people, from all the people that are upon the face of the earth. And the Lord said unto Moses, I will do this thing also that thou hast spoken: for thou hast found grace in my sight, and I know thee by name. Barak saw the Lord was with Deborah, and in his own way, needed reassurance from the Lord that He was with him and his men, setting out to do this seemingly impossible thing. Fear is a lack of faith. Barak did not know the Lord was with him, but knew He was with Deborah. For his lack of faith, Deborah prophesied the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. The honor of victory would go to a woman, since the man lacked faith. And Deborah went with him. Next, we are introduced to Heber the Kenite, descended from Moses father in law, who separated himself from his people, who had allied themselves with Sisera, and who told the captain of Barak's plan to attack. Sisera prepares his armies and their chariots of iron, and lay in wait for Barak and his men. The odds of defeating him even worse now that he was prepared. 900 iron chariots. Horsemen and infantry, against the 10,000 Israelites. Hopeless but for the Lord. To God's glory, the opposing armies were discomfited, set in disarray and scattered, and they fell by the sword before Barak. Sisera fled the battle on foot, as the Israelite army slew all of his men. And finding the tent of Heber, the Kenite, and presuming their allegiance, Sisera sought refuge from Jael, Heber's wife. And Jael took him in, and gave him comfort. Milk and a mantle to keep warm by. Promising to hide him from any seeking him. And lulling Sisera to sleep. Then the goodly woman took a tent stake and hammer, and drove it through his temple to the ground. Barak, in pursuit of Sisera, finds Jael who shows him what had become of the oppressor of Israel. And the glory was God's, who subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel, ultimately leading to his defeat at the hands of the children of Israel. Amen. Women in the word of God are not as some haters of God would claim. Weak, and incidental. But godly women are used mightily by Him, for the Lord's purpose. Yes they are called to be submissive to their fathers and husbands, but submission isn't total helplessness. It is just the order of delegation of authority, God, lords, husband, wife, children, each with a role to play. Each requiring both sacrifice and responsibility. It isn't a lack of agency, but an acknowledgement of the proper order of things, that it be well with the people. Deborah setting up a place of judgment, as someone who knew the law and understood His word, in the absence of men stepping up wasn't rebellion, it was of necessity. But even so she didn't seek to usurp authority over the man. She didn't raise an army to lead it. She didn't travel the land to be its queen. She sat beneath a palm tree, and her God given wisdom brought people to her. Barak was a leader of men, but weak in faith. He needed Deborah to goad him into action and trust in the Lord. Still, Deborah went to him, to lead. But God reveals to Deborah that a woman will be given the honor of victory, to the shame of Barak. God wants strong men, full of faith, to take their role seriously, gravely. To be the leader of their home, loving their wives as an extension of themselves. To turn away from temptation and chasing adultery, fornication and false gods. But women play a role, in supporting and encouraging men. Being keepers at home, instructing their children in the right paths. And like Jael, honoring their husband's decisions, leaving their people for the plains of Zaanaim, even when it means brutally killing a man who her husband had given up family to reject allegiance with. That's the strength that comes from submission. How God uses the weak to destroy the strong. How He reveals His mighty hand, in impossible situations. It is why we are called to submit to whatever higher authority is in our lives, knowing that in doing so we are serving God. Not in rebellion. That the Lord will reward us for our faith, and use us in our weakness to confound the mighty. Amen. Proverbs 31:10-31 Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies. The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil. She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life. She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands. She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar. She riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth meat to her household, and a portion to her maidens. She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard. She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms. She perceiveth that her merchandise is good: her candle goeth not out by night. She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff. She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy. She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet. She maketh herself coverings of tapestry; her clothing is silk and purple. Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land. She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant. Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come. She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness. She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness. Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her. Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised. Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates. This is the virtuous woman according to the Bible. She isn't weak. She isn't helpless. She submits to her husband and is a proper mother to her children, a keeper at home, and industrious for her family. Wise, from the word of God. Diligently seeking opportunities to improve her family's lives while caring for the poor, and raising Godly children. Being a helpmeet for her husband. Strong in the Lord.

The Song of Deborah and Barak recounting their victory by the hand of the Lord and the action of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, is a poetic look at the state of things in their time, when Deborah judged and Jabin the Canaanite king ruled over them. That they led captivity captive overthrowing their oppressors. Praising Jael, a Gentile, as most blessed above women (a similar phrase given to Mary) and mocking Sisera's mother and loved ones in their presumed growing concern at not returning from battle and their impending grief. There's a lot there. Mocking other tribes of Israel who did not fight. Giving praise to the Lord for giving Barak dominion over the mighty and His righteous acts towards Israel when they willingly offered themselves to Him. The willing turn towards God to save them, contradicting the idea that man cannot willingly turn to God, another nail in Calvinism's coffin. We memorialize things in song to remember them by. This isn't a Bollywood movie where they break out into song at the end of the story. This has purpose and meaning in worship of the Lord. We should sing hymns and psalms to His glory. And again, after this deliverance by the Lord, they had 40 years of peace. Some use the term "captivity captive" to promote the idea that Jesus freed souls from Hell, or "Abraham's bosom." I linked a study I did last year about it and debunking that false doctrine, linked above.

Judges 6, in which we meet one of the most doubting men chosen of God in the Bible. Gideon is not as well known as Thomas, but his need for reassurance and signs of God being with him, because his faith was weak, is matched only by the great things God uses him for. A simple farmer in his father's house, under oppression of the Midianites and surrounded by Baal worship, even in his own family. The story of Gideon shows even the weakest of faith is stronger than dead idols and great armies. The angel of the Lord appears to Gideon, and the Lord speaks to him saying Surely I will be with thee, and thou shall smite the Midianites as one man....Thou shalt save Israel from the hands of the Midianites: have I not sent thee? What I believe is an OT appearance of Jesus, the angel of the Lord speaks to Gideon, the word of God either way, and yet the poor farm boy needs more. He says, "show me a sign." How often in our lives, when we know the right thing to do, but are afraid, do we delay doing it and place the burden on the Lord to show us a sign? To put the ball in God's court as a means of procrastinating, allowing fear to overwhelm our faith? I believe every Christian has had a moment like this. A clear path, the word of God unmistakable, understanding what must be done of His will, and rather than answering the call of "Have I not sent thee?" with "Show me a sign that you are with me oh Lord?" We may not have an angel or Jesus appear to us, tell us directly, and then even consume a sacrifice on an altar with fire to convince us the next right thing the Lord has for us to do. It may be a Bible reading, a sermon we hear, subtle and not so subtle answers to prayers, divine appointment...God speaks to us every day if we are listening. And He has works for each of us who hear the call. But fear, doubts, comfort in our own situations, may keep us from doing what we should. By asking for a sign, we put it off, when the sign of God actually speaking to us and presenting the task or challenge should be sign enough. But man is stubborn and often needs the carrot and the stick. Fear the stick and give praise for the carrot is what I have learned, begrudgingly over time. As God does here for Gideon, He will do for us to shape us into the vessels He needs. And the sooner we go with the flow, usually the better it works out. Be not afraid and trust in the Lord. Gideon, the son of Joash, from the Abiezrite clan, was of the tribe of Manasseh, living in Ophrah, which is on the promised land side of the Jordan, where the western half tribe of Manasseh resided. The Midianites, on the eastern side of the Jordan south of Edom and Moab. This is how extensive the reach of the Midianites were, as they rated Israel to take as spoil everything they planted. God sent them against Israel for their falling away and worship of Baal. And to drive home the point of how extensive that abomination was, We see that all of the people living in Ophrah including his own father, worshiped at an altar and a grove dedicated to the Canaanite god. Gideon was clearly a believer in the Lord, though he questioned why they suffered so. But he knew why, He was surrounded by it. It was punishment for their adultery. Today many Christians, especially those of us who may have gotten saved from a Bible way to heaven video, or through talking to people online, or by a door-knocker on a missions trip or soul-winning marathon. They believe in the Lord and call upon Jesus name and are saved, yet they are surrounded by people who believe in a false god. It can be very difficult in those situations to stand up for the Lord against the popular opinion of those around us. Including our families. It can be hard to do the right thing. But we see Gideon instructed to tear down the altar and burn the wood of the grove, and he does so. And when the men come inquiring who did it, Gideon's active faith in service to the Lord. Reveals the dead idol that they had been worshiping, his wayward father leading his defense. Often that is all it takes to bring other people to the understanding of the Lord. To just stand up and do the next right thing as He is presented it to you. Our faithful obedience can convince people far more than our words. And often the only hindrance to doing something great for the Lord that brings others around to the truth is our own fear. And Joash said unto all that stood against him, Will ye plead for Baal? will ye save him? he that will plead for him, let him be put to death whilst it is yet morning: if he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar. Therefore on that day he called him Jerubbaal, saying, Let Baal plead against him, because he hath thrown down his altar. This rebuke by Joash against the Baal-worshipping lynch-mob that had come against his son is such a perfect illustration of how empty paganism and idolatry are compared to serving the living God. "Let Baal plead against him." Jerubbaal becomes one of Gideon's names. Our God destroys those who come against Him, without need of an unruly mob insulted by the exposure of their vanity. Then all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the children of the east were gathered together, and went over, and pitched in the valley of Jezreel. But the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon, and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered after him. And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh; who also was gathered after him: and he sent messengers unto Asher, and unto Zebulun, and unto Naphtali; and they came up to meet them. A battle looms in the fertile plains of Megiddo, in the heart of Israel. The armies of the East camped there, and the Spirit of the Lord comes upon Gideon, who gathers his kin, and sends word to the surrounding tribes for men. Amassing his own army to go and fight. And yet Gideon doubts that the Lord is with him. And again, seeks a sign, dew on a piece of wool, and God grants him the sign, not only dew upon the flax, but soaking it. But doubtful Gideon, afraid, asks for another. Dew on everything else but the wool, and God grants him his sign. God is longsuffering and willing to work with us, but ultimately we have to accept on faith the word of God and do the right thing. Even when it is scary and uncertain by man's wisdom, it is to the glory of God that he uses the weak to defeat the strong. Amen

The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion. Continuing the story of Gideon, AKA Jerubbaal, who the Lord has chosen to deliver Israel from the hands of the Midianites. We read in Judges 6 that Gideon had assembled men for war against the camp of the Midians in the valley of Meggado. There Gideon asked the Lord for not one, but two signs that He was with them and would deliver the host into his hands, and the Lord granted him these signs. Gideon's doubt was great but with a sign (or two), he turned his fear into faith. It is the same for us as believers. We may have all the faith we think we need, but when tried, fear comes. We are saved, we know His word is true, we know through Him all things are possible. And yet... I often think about the father in Mark 9, who came to Jesus to have his son healed of the dumb spirit that possessed him. The father thought Jesus could save him, but still he feared there was no hope for his son. He was conflicted between fear and faith. Mark 9:23-24 Jesus said unto him, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth. And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. In the same way, we often search for faith in our tribulation, not because we doubt God, but we have doubts about ourselves. Our own weakness. The impossible odds we seem to face. But with faith, all things are possible. And while the signs Gideon had asked for were given him, the dew on the wool and the ground, and Gideon's believed that God would deliver the enemy, God wasn't through increasing his faith. Helping his unbelief. The host of Midianites were as a sea of grasshoppers in the valley, Israel had only mustered 32,000 men, and were outnumbered. The Lord says to Gideon that he has too many men. They would credit themselves for the victory, and so He instructs Gideon to send home those too scared to fight, and immediately 22,000 depart. But the 10,000 are still too many, says the Lord, and He instructs Gideon to take them to water, and the men who vow down to the water to drink, send home. Keeping only those that lapped the water from their cupped hand. 300 remained. When you ask God for assurance in faith, be prepared to have that faith come by testing it mightily. For whom much is given, much is expected. Gideon wanted a sign that the Lord, Who was speaking to him, whose Spirit had come over him, who had brought Gideon to this place and God answered his need for signs, was now telling Gideon that the hosts of Midianites that were as sand, too numerous to count, we're going to be delivered into his hands with a force of 300. You wanted faith, here it is. God not only uses the weak to confound the strong, He makes us weaker that we may become strong. Having purged the army of Israel down to the 300, the Lord tells Gideon to get down to the enemy's camp that he may know God has already won the victory for him. And, knowing Gideon is sometimes afraid, tells him to take his servant Phurah with him if he's afraid. (Phurah goes, so that answers that) There the pair hear the men of the camp discussing a dream that when interpreted reveals they are afraid of Gideon, knowing the Lord was with him. Gideon understanding their state of, probably relating to it, returns to his camp and the 300, with a plan. Dividing the men into groups, surrounding the camp on three sides, Gideon tells the men to do as he does. Each with a trumpet, and a clay pot with a lamp inside, Gideon tells them when he blows his trumpet, shout The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon. The judge who needed signs to turn his fear into faith was preying upon the fears of his enemy. And so just after midnight, they follow Gideon's lead and blow the trumpets and smash the pitchers and hold up the lamps and shout, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon! And they stood their ground. And the sound and the sight and the battle cry all worked on the fear of the Lord in them, and they not only scattered and retreated but in panic slaughtered one another with their own swords. And as the remnant of the Midianites and Amalek host fled East, towards the Jordan, men from throughout Israel joined Gideon in pursuit, killing two princes, and bringing their heads to Gideon. Sometimes Christians get the mistaken idea that tribulations and temptations and attacks by adversaries are sent by God to test our faith, to prove ourselves worthy of His love. And so they will try to go it alone to show God how strong they are. This is a mistake. Romans 5:6-8 For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die. But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. God loves us so much, despite our weakness, that He sent His only begotten Son. That Jesus so loves us, He died for us while we were yet sinners. Yes, God wishes us to grow in faith, and shapes us by our experiences to be better vessels for His purpose. But increased faith doesn't mean relying more and more upon yourself, but rather leaning more and more upon Him to deliver us. Like Gideon, we may have fears and doubts, and require signs. But the Lord knows and understands, and will surely provide us with a way out. He will provide us with a Phurah, to go with us into the breach. Like Barak needed Deborah with him. He will ask for our trust, and to stand firm and do as He commands, but the battles are already won by Him. The Lord delivered us already. We have overcome. This is how He increases our faith. How He helps our unbelief. God uses the weak. He uses foolish things to confound the wise. No one would think that 300 men blowing trumpets and smashing pots and shouting could rout tens of thousands. What a foolish plan! But they had already been delivered into Gideon's hands by the Lord. Just as the Israelites were delivered from Egypt. Just as Jericho fell. Just as Jael the housewife had victory over Sisera. Just as the giants were destroyed and the land was delivered, and 33 Kings were toppled in a single campaign. Just as death and Hell have been conquered. By the mighty hand of God. When we are tempted, tested and tried, remember this, God has already given us victory. We just have to obey His word, be watchful and ready to act on the opportunities He will provide. 1 Corinthians 10:13 There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. 2 Corinthians 4 Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not; 2 But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. 3 But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: 4 In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them. 5 For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. 6 For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. 7 But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 8 We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; 9 Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed; 10 Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body. 11 For we which live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh. 12 So then death worketh in us, but life in you. 13 We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak; 14 Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you. 15 For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God. 16 For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. 17 For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory; 18 While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal. The pitchers with lamps within of Gideon's story are a picture of us as believers, and the light of God within us. Earthen vessels given to the ministry of God, His servants, with His light that shines even brighter from us when we are broken, but unafraid. Troubled on every side, but yet not distressed. We have the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. For which cause we faint not. For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God.

Chapter 8 of Judges begins abruptly, carrying the narrative of chapter 7, where as Gideon and the 300 pursued the host of the Midianites back east, across the Jordan, he sent messengers to the tribes of Israel in the area to join in the pursuit, and we saw the men of Ephraim capture two princes of the Midianites. Here, the chapter opens with the the men of Ephraim angry that Gideon had not called them to the initial battle. Of course of all the men Gideon gathered, God dismissed most before He used the acts of the 300 to drive the army from the land. Gideon answers them tactfully and with humility; What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? Abiezer being the family of Manasseh Gideon belonged to, the men of Ephraim in "gleaning" or opportunistically had subdued two princes of the host, God delivering them to their hands. This simple acknowledgement of their role stayed their resentment, allowing the forces to continue their chase of the armies of the East. Proverbs 15:1 A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger. As Gideon and his men continue to go after them, they pass through Succoth, a place in the wilderness that Israel had passed through, and Gideon as captain asks them for bread to feed his men, and they refuse. I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. And the princes of Succoth said, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? The men of the next community, Penuel respond the same way. Gideon vows that when he returns, he will take thorns as scourges against the men of Succoth and tear down the tower of Penuel. A vow he fulfilled after he and his men capture the fleeing princes, Zebah and Zalmunna, whipping and killing the men and razing the tower. Gideon tells his captives, Zebah and Zalmunna, that had they spared lives of those at Tabor, an apparent raid they'd conducted in Israel, he would have spared their lives. Gideon asks his young son to take the heads of the princes, but by his youth he can't do it. Gideon takes them instead, after Zebah and Zalmunna mock him. So the armies were defeated and the children of Israel took the spoil and returned back across the Jordan, hailing Gideon for delivering them out of the hands of the Midianites. They call for Gideon to be made king and his son and future sons to rule over them. But Gideon meekly declined, giving glory to God. However, he does ask for tribute. The gold earrings of the men slain, which when taken together was a substantial weight of gold. And while judging Israel the rest of his days, back in Ophrah of Manasseh, he takes the gold of his spoil and makes himself an ephod. A golden vestment of the office of the high priest. This is the snare of Gideon. This causes the children of Israel to go a whoring. Some interpretations of this make the ephod an idol that is worshipped, but it seems unlikely that Jerubbaal, aka Gideon, a smasher of idols, "the accused of Baal," would set up an idol and there's no indication that they worshipped the ephod itself. It is more likely in my opinion to mean that Gideon, despite his declining to be a king, allowed his popularity and fame to make him seek to usurp the place God chose, Shiloh, and the office of the high priest to whom the Ephod crafted by Moses belonged. And rather than go to Shiloh for spiritual matters, many in Israel came down to Ophrah and Gideon. The number of wives and sons he produced showed that he did take advantage of his glory, despite deferring the glory of the victory to God. The spoils he took as tribute became a snare, and caused the Israelites to go whoring, away from the commandment of the Lord. So we see, even Gideon, full of fear. Requiring signs. Witnessing the miracle of their defeat of a troop of over a hundred and fifty thousand with 300 men, let his success go to his head. Leading him to sin. This is a trap some very successful Christians fall in to. Who have been used mightily for God, and done great works for Him. For all their humility and understanding that it was not of them, pride eats away at their character. God's success begins to seem to them to be a partnership. And their idea of what God wants take the place of what God actually wills for them. We can apply this to great modern preachers of the word, who have won thousands of souls to Christ, and then, building an empire from the success, sow the seeds their own downfall. And the people who they helped forget these men, after they've died. And their children turn to wickedness. Worshiping Baal as the Israelites do. The children of these great soldiers for God not turning out to be godly men, but wicked, like Gideon's son, Abimelech.

Judges 8:33-34 And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baalberith their god. And the children of Israel remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side Here in Judges 9 we are given the story of Abimelech, one of the 70 sons of Gideon, also known as Jerubbaal, and his brief, violent and wicked time as king over Shechem. Shechem is a city north of Jerusalem and south of Samaria, in the center of Canaan, on the west Bank of the Jordan. It is where Abraham built an altar to God upon the covenant he received, and where Jacob pitched his tents. It is where his sons, Levi and Simeon killed all the men, after their sister Dinah was raped. Shechem is where Joshua assembled the children of Israel and asked them to choose this day whom they would serve, the gods of Babylon, beyond the Euphrates; Baal and Asteroth who were the gods of the Canaanites or the living God Who had led them from Egypt and given them the promised land. It became a Levitical city in Ephraim, a city of refuge. Gideon had taken a concubine from among the people of Shechem, from among the ruling families, and her son was Abimelech. And so, after the death of Gideon, with the people of Israel forgetting the Lord God and worshiping Baal-Berith, they had built a temple to the false "god of the covenant" there, and it is in Shechem Abimelech goes to seek power. Not content to share the diminishing power of being a son of Gideon with his 70 brothers, Abimelech curries favor with his mother's kin in Shechem, and in exchange for a piece of silver from the temple of Berith, one per brother, gathers a gang of base fellows, vain and light, to set about slaying them. They succeeded in murdering them all up on a rock, save one, Jotham. Jotham curses Abimelech and the men of the city for their treachery, saying by allegory that Israel had great men before it that refused to be king, represented by the olive, the fig and the vine, and yet they chose the worst, a briar. The bramble. And that by doing so Abimelech would destroy them by fire. Jotham then flees, hiding in Beer. And so for 3 years, the cruel king rules in Shechem, and the men of the city grow disillusioned by their choice because God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem. Their trust was diminished, and they sought to deal with their king treacherously. They hired a band of men to lay in wait for him in the mountains, men who robbed all who passed by, and Abimelech was made aware of their plans. The bandits failing them, the men turned to one of their own, Gaal son of Ebed. Gaal, his men and the men of the city get drunk, and Gaal curses Abimelech, Zebul his chief officer and ruler of the city, and promises to rule in place of the king after overthrowing the son of Jerubbaal. Zebul hears of it and informs Abimelech, and they plot to surround the city and take it to put down the rebellion. When Gaal sees the companies of men surrounding the city, Zebul at first taunts him, questioning his senses, saying he is afraid of shadows. But then tells Gaal that here is his chance, go out and fight Abimelech the same who he had cursed. Abimelech defeats the men, and they flee into the city but Zebul throws the rebels out. Abimelech's men slay them and turn towards the city and take it. Slaughtering the men and burning down the tower and the temple and salting the earth, Jotham's curse fulfilled. Not satisfied with the destruction of Shechem, Abimelech moves on the city of Thebez, which too has a strong tower, a keep in the center of the city. The last refuge for siege in the walled cities. And like the tower of Shechem, Gideon's son begins to light fire to the door, to burn the tower down with the people inside. And a woman throws down a piece of millstone, that grinds the wheat to flour, and it hit Abimelech in the head, breaking his skull. And the wicked wannabe king calls his armourbearer and begs him to run him through with a sword, so no one could say he was killed by a woman. Reminiscent of the death of Sisera by the hand of Jael. And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they departed every man unto his place. The brief civil war was over. Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren: And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal. The book of Judges is better than any Hollywood blockbuster or Netflix series. The Sopranos has nothing on Jerubbaal, Abimelech and the rest of these men. I love God's word. Abimelech serves as a picture of a type found throughout scripture, and the pattern we see even today. Mighty man of the Lord does great works and has a son that's prodigal or worse, wicked. Some misguided, some reprobate. The children of Jacob, to varying degrees. The sons of Aaron. Gideon and Abimelech. David and Absalom. Ultimately, it is a picture of God and fallen man. The Good King and his wayward or wicked son. The pastor and the pastor's son. It seems that great men of God, who do good and mighty works for the Lord, often produce a child or two who openly rebel against them. Who become prodigal. And at times the father is unable to handle the truth and enables their offspring's wickedness. And others who do the right thing, choosing God over their own, and casting them out to be destroyed by their own wickedness. We as parents have an obligation, a Godly duty, to be a picture of God's unconditional love and grace, forgiving our children's sins without enabling them. Chastening them when needed, but like the father of the Prodigal, rushing to meet them when they come home. To not be hypocrites. To live the example that we hold them to. To be strong enough to cast out the reprobate. To bring an unruly son to the gates to be stoned. Our behavior as parents is how children learn about God. It is an awesome responsibility, and one even the most separated fathers can fail at. Even as we, knowing God, fall away to sin, children will ultimately choose their way. And so you have examples of men like Jack Hyles, who built an ephod of the spoils given him by God. A Bible college. A high school. Bus ministries and other things he took pride in, put his name on, along with the fame and respect that came with it. And he had a son, David, who was wicked as Hell. An Abimelech. But these things do not detract from the great works of the Lord, who uses men to do His will. They just show the weakness of the vessel. Jack Hyles was a mighty preacher, won hundreds of not thousands to the Lord. But the snare of pride led to the downfall of what he built. It's tragic and sad. But it does not undo the mighty works done by God, just as Abimelech didn't change the deliverance of Israel under his father. If you know any pastors who may be struggling with an unruly son or daughter, pray for them. Use discernment. Keep the works of God separate from the failures of men. God will repay.

What man is he? Who will judge the children of Israel? Who will God use to deliver them? Having fallen away, again and again, and having shorter periods of peace and longer periods of tribulation, the people again turn back the Lord of their fathers. And the Lord has grown weary of them. He reminds them of all the times He has delivered them. Yet ye have forsaken me, and served other gods: wherefore I will deliver you no more.Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your tribulation. They put away their strange gods, they served the Lord...and the Lord's soul grieved for their misery. There will be a deliverer, Jephthah, who we will meet in Judges 11. Sometimes God will allow the wages of our sin to overcome us. To give us the recompense for our error. Even if we vow to change. Even if we clean up our act. Sometimes it is too late to undo the consequences of our action. But He still grieves for us. As a good Father who chastens a son, it hurts Him more than it hurts you. And for our sakes tribulation will be cut short. Sometimes, that's by being called home. If we have unresolved sin in our lives, now is the time of reconciliation. We are forgiven already. Turn to God with your whole heart and soul, for deliverance. Before it is too late.

We are here in Judges 11, and the story of Jephthah the Gileadite, son of a whore and the eponymous patriarch of Gilead. We are told he was a mighty man of valor, who by the jealousy and resentment of his half-brothers, was cast out of the community. He went to the wasteland, the land of Tob, and there he formed a gang of vain men, outlaws. But when the children of Ammon came and made war against them, the elders of Gilead called for him to return and to be captain of their troops. Jephthah agrees so long as they pledge to make him their ruler, and they vow to God they will if he delivers them from the Ammonites. Now, we know Jephthah is a man of faith, who uttered all his words before the Lord, taking on the responsibility of leadership in His name. He also is given honorable mention in the 'Hall of Faith' in Hebrews 11:32-34; And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets: Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions. Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens. And so, after his own pledge and profession of his faith, he rode out with men of Gilead and confronted the king of Ammon. Jephthah asks why they are attacking Israel, and the king responds that it is retribution for the taking of their land 300 years prior, as the children of Israel approached the promised land. Jephthah, showing knowledge of their history, reminds them that the Ammonites brought it up on themselves, attacking the Israelites as they sought to pass between their coasts. That in the centuries since, the Ammonite kings accepted their loss of land. He says that since the Lord God had given the children of Israel the land by driving out the previous inhabitants, it was theirs. And he taunts their false god Chemosh, saying wouldn't they accept any land as their possession of it drove out the people? And after this history lesson, Jephthah calls on the Lord the Judge to judge between them. And the Spirit of the Lord comes down, He delivers the Ammonites into the hands of Israel. The Spirit of the Lord was upon him. He was definitely a man of faith. But yet, as Barak needed Deborah with him, and Gideon needed the dew upon the flax, Jephthah vowed a vow unto the Lord to assure his victory over the children of Ammon. That he would sacrifice whatsoever crossed his doorway when he returned from battle victorious, if the Lord delivered the enemy into his hands. Returning victorious, he came to Mizpeh and his house, and there was his only child, his young daughter come to meet him. He rent his clothes and cried; Alas, my daughter! His daughter tells him he must honor his vow to the Lord. Especially now that He had delivered victory and given him his enemies in vengeance. She only asks to have 2 months to travel the mountains lamenting her death in virginity, which he grants. Sacrificing her as he vowed to do. Her story creating a custom in Israel among her daughters, that 4 days a year they lamented her plight. As Jesus says, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. God does not need our vows, our promises to do good or to perform works in order to deliver us. He simply asks we trust in Him and let our yea mean yea. Jephthah would have won victory over the children of Ammon by the power of the Lord. He did not need to add his own works as part of God's plan. But God holds us to vows; Ecclesiastes 5:4 When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. So it should not be done in an idle fashion. But if possible, a vow to God in exchange for His favor should not be done at all. Godly living and honest character do not require such a thing. It is by God mighty hand that we are delivered. Not of works of ourselves. Jephthah paid a price he needn't have, because he placed a portion of his faith in his own hands.

After Jephthah's tragic victory in Judges 11, he finds himself in a similar situation as Gideon had a century earlier, back in Judges 8; And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply. Here in Judges 12, rather than deescalate the conflict with the men of Ephraim with kind words as Gideon had, Jephthah chooses conflict and he and his men smite the men of Ephraim, driving them back across the Jordan. It is here we get the term 'Shibboleth,' a word that the Ephraimites struggled to pronounce as the Gileadites did. By asking the fleeing men to say it, knowing it would betray them as of Ephraim, Gilead put them to the sword. This shows that even just a few hundred years since Moses and the settling of the land by Israel, that distinct dialects and regional accents had occurred. The tribes of Israel were themselves nations. And subgroups like Gilead, which was the name of part of the land settled by Gad, on the east bank of the Jordan, had grown to be its own thing. God sets boundaries and habitations, dividing nations by blood and language, shifting over time as He judges them. We often see the term 'Shibboleth' used today as a derogatory way of describing a longstanding belief that a group of people may share that separates them from others. A way of gatekeeping looked down upon by those with modernist views, seeking to infiltrate and influence the older group. There have been those who have accused fundamentalists of maintaining Shibboleths, from matters of separation to the sole use of the KJB, and even to the nature of the gospel...All have been attacked as 'archaic' means of resisting change in the modern era, and to that we should say "Amen!" Scripture tells us repeatedly of how we can recognize false teachers and warns of those creeping in privily, unawares, to spy out our liberty and to lead believers astray. The main shibboleth being the gospel of grace and reconciliation through faith in Christ. If someone brings a false gospel, we know they are not of God but accursed. Galatians 1:8-9 But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed. A healthy church maintains the landmark shibboleths of the faith. And so we see that Jephthah judges Israel a short 6 years, and died. Ibzan of Bethlehem and his 30 sons followed, for seven. Then Elon of Zebulun for 10, and Abdon son of Hillel, and his 40 sons, another eight. These judges often overlapped with others. Deborah and Gideon were contemporaries, Sampson was during the time of Jephthah, Elon and the others, near the end of the Judges period. And they often ruled through the strength of their sons, the significance of the colts of an ass that they rode meant there was distance and area they could cover. I always picture it as the patriarchs of the 'Wild West,' or the families that acted as semi-autonomous gangs that would run cities. Chinese Tongs and Mafia families. We know that they judged, but we also know that during some of these judges' time Israel fell away to worshiping the gods of the Canaanites, and doing evil in the sight of the Lord. As the Bible says several times of the era of Judges; In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes. But as Proverbs 21:2 says; Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts.

Judges 13 tells of the circumstances of the miraculous birth of Sampson; the appearance of the angel of the Lord to his parents, and that he would be under a vow his entire life from conception. I believe, like many of the similar appearances of the Lord as a man, or messenger, that this was a pre-incarnate visitation of Jesus, His name secret at this time. But it may just be just an angel, a messenger, of God. His instructions to the mother and father of Sampson are simple; as a Nazarite, she was not to eat of the vine, drunk its unfermented wine, or the fermented strong drink of wine. His head was to not see a razor. He was to be dedicated to God from the womb. And the sacrifice of the kid by the visiting angel, acting as a high priest in giving the burnt offering upon a rock, before ascension into Heaven is what makes this appear to be a theophany, an appearance of Christ Jesus. The parents agree, and God had chosen Sampson to be a judge to deliver his people from the Philistines. Dan was on the Mediterranean coast, west of Judah, and the Gaza strip south of Dan was possessed by the Philistines who came up out of the Sinai. The children of Israel had done evil in the sight of the Lord and so He delivered the people into the hands of the Philistines, just as He had used the Amorites and the others to oppress the disobedient tribes of Israel during this time. To show His glory and mercy, the Lord sent a savior, miraculously conceived, to deliver them by his own sacrifice. A picture of the Son. We have noted in the past that certain heresies come in waves. That there is a tendency for some unbiblical doctrines to pop up, stir up contention, and then fade as another breaks upon the rock of scripture. There is currently a host of false doctrines regarding the understanding of the spiritual state of infants making the rounds. From what is being referred to as "Baalgate" in the so-called Reform movement of Calvinism that most babies are damned from birth, to the reaffirmation of 'original sin' and this a need for pedobaptism by mainline Protestants (displaying their Roman Catholic roots), to weird doctrines held by some Baptists that newborn babies sin, claiming they are under a special form of grace unheard of in the Bible. I want to take a look at these heresies and give what the Bible says about the innocence of a child, the notion of an age of accountability, and how the debate surrounding these false ideas today likely reflects how early church first schismed over claims of spiritual regeneration by baptism and the logical end-result of needing to baptize babies. This is something I will develop over the weekend, God willing. But I want to park this here until then. Romans 7:8-13 But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin was dead. For I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. And the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death. For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me. Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good. Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful.

Now in Judges 14 we meet Samson in earnest. The miraculous birth to a barren mother and a lifetime vow of cleanliness as a Nazarite as instructed by the angel of the Lord in chapter 13 meets the reality of Samson as a grown young man. A man who the Spirit of the Lord moves upon to deliver his people from the Philistines, but whose own methods and ways lead to rather interesting conflicts with that vow. Numbers 6:1-12 And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When either man or woman shall separate themselves to vow a vow of a Nazarite, to separate themselves unto the Lord: He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried. All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk. All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the Lord, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow. All the days that he separateth himself unto the Lord he shall come at no dead body. He shall not make himself unclean for his father, or for his mother, for his brother, or for his sister, when they die: because the consecration of his God is upon his head. All the days of his separation he is holy unto the Lord. And if any man die very suddenly by him, and he hath defiled the head of his consecration; then he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing, on the seventh day shall he shave it. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtles, or two young pigeons, to the priest, to the door of the tabernacle of the congregation: And the priest shall offer the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering, and make an atonement for him, for that he sinned by the dead, and shall hallow his head that same day. And he shall consecrate unto the Lord the days of his separation, and shall bring a lamb of the first year for a trespass offering: but the days that were before shall be lost, because his separation was defiled. Samson begins the story by going into the cities of the Philistines, down from Dan to Timnath, and a Philistine girl there catches his eye. He returns to his parents and tells them to get her for him to wife. Naturally, his parents are upset at this, that he would want an outlandish woman, unclean, to wed. They ask why not a woman from their tribe or from Israel, a fellow believer, a daughter of the circumcision. He insists and they relent, not knowing that this was of the Lord. That it was an opportunity for Samson to get in with the Philistines who were oppressing Israel. As he makes his way back to Timnath, he encounters a young lion and tears it apart with his bare hands, by the power of the Spirit of the Lord. It is a supernatural act of strength, as an unarmed man rends a lion apart as a normal man could a baby goat. Samson, having touched an unclean thing, tells not his father or mother. Samson talks with the woman, and she pleases him. Time passes, and on his way back to take her as a wife, he notices the carcass of the lion and that a bee hive has set up in it, producing honey. He reaches into this dead, unclean carcass and takes of the honey with his bare hands, and eats it and gives it to his parents to eat, without telling them where it came from. The wedding is arranged and Samson makes a feast lasting 7 days, and having no groomsmen among the people, 30 Philistine men are made his companions. Samson offers them a bet in the form of a riddle, the stakes, 30 sheets and 30 sets of clothes. The men agree, and Samson says Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness, referring to the lion and the honey. An impossible riddle that even his parents would be unable to solve. And after 3 days of fruitless guessing, the 30 men threaten the would-be bride and her family to pry the answer from Samson. She begs and pleads for the next several days and on the final day of the feast, Samson tells her the answer. His physical strength is mighty, but his weakness, as we will see throughout his story, is women. The 30 companions tell Samson the answer, and he knows they cheated. If ye had not plowed with my heifer, ye had not found out my riddle. And the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, and he travels to a neighboring city and slays 30 Philistines in Ashkelon, taking from their unclean dead bodies the spoils of 30 sheets and sets of raiment, to pay of his bet. Samson then returns to his father unmarried, and the girl is given to one of the 30 Philistine men who served as his companions. It is always interesting to me when I read the story of Samson, how often he violated the vow of separation he was meant to live by. His being with unclean women and unclean carcasses, even eating from one, and yet the Spirit of the Lord remained on him. He was used for mighty works. But his temper and his love of women would be his undoing.

Continuing the story of Samson, Judges 15 picks up some time later, where he decides to visit his betrothed Philistine woman with a baby goat, and discovered that her father had married her off to another. Samson then, feeling vindictive as the one who was "wronged," captures and sets loose 300 foxes with torches between their tied-together tails, destroying the corn fields of the Philistines. When they learn of this and why, the Philistines burn to death the girl and her father, Timnite. Not satisfied, Samson slaughters many of them, then leaves for Lehi in Judah, upon the rock of Etam. The armies of Philistine camp against Judah, and the men of the tribe come to Samson and are wroth with him. They have submitted to being ruled over by the heathens, and Samson is causing problems. He asks if they are there to slay him, and they say no. But to be bound and delivered. So tied up in cords, they bring him to the camp of men, and there the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, the bands snap like burnt cotton. Freed, the Nazarite picks up a freshly dead jawbone of an ass and slaughters 1000 men. Heaps upon heaps. And casting the jawbone aside, he names the place Ramathlehi, the hill of the jaw-bone. After the slaughter, Samson thirsts and cries out to the Lord; Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised? And out of the hollow of the jawbone sprung up a fountain, named Enhakkore, the fountain of the crier, and from this dead thing in the midst of a thousand corpses, Samson drank and was revived. Again, we see Samson, under a lifetime vow of cleanliness and separation, using unclean things to cause havoc, and consuming that which sprung up from death. Like the honey from the lion, now the water from the jawbone of an ass. And yet the Spirit of the Lord still came up on him. His strength hadn't failed. He judged Israel for 20 years in the days of the Philistines. The secret of his strength not yet revealed.

Samson's story ends with a bang. His weakness revealed; Women. He is nearly caught because of his visit to a harlot in Gaza. And just as his riddle was given away to the daughter of Timnath for her pleading, Delilah the Philistine manages to get Samson to tell her his heart, and his belief that the Lord was with him due to his hair, kept unshaved due to his lifelong vow. Women, and their persistence with him, was Samson's undoing. The lifelong vow of the Nazarite that he violated so often, being unclean with dead bodies, eating from carcasses, drinking from bloody bones, and laying with harlots, included not taking a razor to his hair. And that's where he drew the line. Many times as Christians, we do the same thing. We know what we ought to do and that which we should not. And we set an arbitrary line around one particular thing, that we fool ourselves into thinking we are right with God so long as that one thing isn't violated, even as we sin all around it. And God is patient and longsuffering. But when our heart, our trust, is in that one thing, especially under a vow, and not Christ, He will punish us when we break it. Delilah was the means. The hair she shaved, the 7 locks he had, was just the thing, the vow, he used as a fig leaf. Once gone, the Spirit given strength he had was gone. Samson was made blind. Tied to posts and mocked. And even with stubble growing back, was still weak. Led around by a boy. But Samson called upon the Lord for deliverance. O Lord God, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes. And the Lord answered his prayers, and sacrificing himself, Samson killed 3,000 Philistines including their lords, gathered to offer sacrifices to their false god. In the end it was faith that delivered Samson. In the end God was the source of his strength. Amen

Judges 17 begins the story of Micah, not to be confused with the later prophet, but here, a young Ephraimite in the time of the judges; In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes. Micah had stolen 11,000 shekels of silver from his mother. Apparently conflicted by this, he confesses to her and returns the money, saying he had sought to bring it to a founder in order to make a graven image. A molten image. His mother, rather than be offended at his theft or his Idolatry, blesses the endeavor by giving 200 of the shekels to the founder herself, and commissions the graven image and the molten image to satisfy her son. Micah and his mother both were of Israel and recognize the Lord as their God, but had fallen so far from His way for them that they sought after idols of silver. The Bible says Micah had an house of gods, a church full of graven and molten images. He made an ephod, the priestly garment, and teraphim, which we would call icons, or relics. Items of worship. Micah even consecrated his young son to serve as a priest. Micah was an Ortho-bro, setting up a shrine. But an unnamed Levite, out of Judah strikes out on his way to find a place to serve. Coming to mount Ephraim, he finds Micah, and stays with him. Micah offers the Levite the role of spiritual father, to be his priest for hire. Paying him ten shekels a year, and clothing and food. The Levite agrees and takes on the role of house priest. Micah says Now know I that the Lord will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest. Micah, doing what seems good in his eyes, thinking in some way he is following the Lord, has sought to establish his own religion, his own church, even as the Tabernacle is in Shiloh. His family appears to be wealthy, his mother's riches and her spoiling of her son, catering to his whims even after his theft is revealed, shows that in many ways, Micah is blessed. Born into a peaceful area, with silver enough to make idols, and even to hire a priest to legitimize his endeavor. Naturally, not knowing better, having a zeal for the Lord but not after knowledge, Micah believes his efforts are blessed of the Lord. He thinks by his accumulating idols and images, an ephod and teraphims, and even a genuine Levite to be his priest, to call "father," that the Lord will do him good. Micah creates a building full of gods, a priest called "father." A place of worship to the Lord that violates the commands set forth by the word of God, because it seemed right in his own eyes. If you have children or grandchildren and are looking for a present to give them on Easter, pick up this KJVO-coloring book telling the story of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden. Made by a saved Christian woman and put together by her husband, to help support their young family. You may want to refamiliarize yourself with Judges 17 and Micha, the first Ortho-bro. His story continues in chapter 18...

Joshua 19:47 And the coast of the children of Dan went out too little for them: therefore the children of Dan went up to fight against Leshem, and took it, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and possessed it, and dwelt therein, and called Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their father. Judges 17-18 tells the story of Micha, his creation of his own church full of idols and icons, an ephod and teraphim, and his recruiting of a young Levite to be his personal house priest, calling him "father." In those days there was no king in Israel. And men did as seemed right in their own eyes. The story presented occurs during the period immediately after Joshua's death, where Dan had not fully gone out to take their inheritance from those that dwelled there. Joshua 23:4-5 Behold, I have divided unto you by lot these nations that remain, to be an inheritance for your tribes, from Jordan, with all the nations that I have cut off, even unto the great sea westward. And the LORD your God, he shall expel them from before you, and drive them from out of your sight; and ye shall possess their land, as the LORD your God hath promised unto you. Joshua had waxed old and died before the tribes had finished the work to go out and possess the land given them. Dan especially was shown to be dragging behind the other tribes. And here they are seeking to go out and find land to take. In Judges 18, we find that the troop of spies stop at Mt Ephraim, and lodge at the house of Micha. There they recognized the young Levite, and inquire why he's there. He tells them of the arrangements made with Micha, his hire and role as a private priest over a house of gods. They ask him for God's blessings in finding a suitable city to take, and he says reassuring words that God had blessed their endeavors. And so, 600 Danites set forth to go into the land, armed for war. They come up on the house of Micha and the spies tell their army about the gods and the silver graven image and the ephod and priest, and they go in and take all the idols and ephod for themselves. The priest protests and they tell him to come with them and be their priest, and he agrees. Micha seeing this runs out with some men from his town and Micha confronts them. The much larger force of men gathered for war tell him to stop, or he may forfeit his and his family's lives. And so Dan finds the city of Laish, or Leshem, and the people there living simple and peaceful lives, and take it for themselves, renaming the city Dan. And the young priest of the Levites turns out to be the son of Gershom, he and his sons, with their stolen idols and icons and fake Ephod, become the priests for the tribe of Dan until the captivity of the land. The seeds of their own downfall sown by rejecting the way of the Lord and turning to idols. A people can seem mighty, and put many simple peasants to the sword while carrying the banner of conquest, and relying on idols and images. Unqualified priests. But in the end, God will judge them and their abominations. Danites went marching on a crusade with their apostate priest and easily took the land, but lost their understanding. The parallel with Roman Catholics should be obvious. The end of those people being captivity and destruction, if they don't turn from Idolatry, repenting towards the Lord. Joshua 19:47 And the coast of the children of Dan went out too little for them: therefore the children of Dan went up to fight against Leshem, and took it, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and possessed it, and dwelt therein, and called Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their father. Judges 17-18 tells the story of Micah, his creation of his own church full of idols and icons, an ephod and teraphim, and his recruiting of a young Levite to be his personal house priest, calling him "father."
