First Saul asks for the ark of God, but the noise increased and so Saul says to the priest, "stay thy hand." Where Jonathan went out by faith, Saul leaned on the ark, and it failed him. And so assembling his men, and the men disorderly came together, including the Hebrews among the Philistines and those in hiding, rallying to the battle Jonathan had begun. Jonathan by faith showed leadership and courage that became infectious. And Saul, who had remained behind struggled to find the faith and leadership his son had displayed. Courage that brought out of hiding the fearful Israelites to attack the enemy camp. Despite the success, Saul commanded the men not eat until evening, a fast he decided to decree after the victory had already begun. The Lord had already saved Israel that day. By faith, not of their own works. But Saul had commanded a fast. And the men of Israel, exhausted obeyed. But Jonathan who hadn't heard his father's order, dipped his spear in honey that had by chance fallen on the ground, and ate it, the rush of it lighting up his eyes. Enlightened. While the men all looked on with fear knowing the vow Saul had foolishly made, Jonathan points out how even the taste he had of it had enlightened him, say; How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? for had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines? A picture of the Spirit that quickens those who eat freely of Christ, how much greater the victory had they gone by faith and Saul had not taught for commandments the doctrines of men. And so they smote the Philistines and yet were faint with hunger, and so when they fell upon the spoils of sheep, ox and cow, they ate them straight away, with the blood. And so Saul's foolish vow, adding works of righteousness to what was won by faith alone, led the men of Israel to sin. And so King Saul commands the spoil be brought to him and he again sets up an altar and offers the meat that it be drained of blood and the men may eat thereof. But again, this wasn't his place to do it, and so again Saul does wrong trying to do right. Afterwards Saul sought council of the Lord as to whether to continue through the night to spoil the Philistines, yet God does not answer. Saul assembled the men and asks the current high priest, Ichabod who was the grandson of Eli, to cast the lots to separate the men and find the sin that he felt was preventing the Lord's blessing. The Thummim and Urim of the High Priest's ephod. And so, by lot the men are separated until it is revealed that it was Jonathan who had broken Saul's foolish vow. Saul had made a big show of it during the casting of the lots, that even if it were his very own son, they would be out to death. And when it is, Saul is convinced that he must slay Jonathan. But the people stand with Jonathan and say as God lives they would defend his life. And so Saul forgets about it and leaves off following the Philistines, allowing them to go back to their place. Yet again, Saul compounds his error without admitting to it, and rather than repent or ask forgiveness, he just lets it go. Just as when Samuel tells him in chapter 13 that his impatient sacrifice had cost him the kingdom, the blessing and inheritance, Saul just went and numbered his men and did what he was going to do anyway. Christians can often be stubborn in this way. Knowing they've sinned and having been called out on it and consequences compounding, and yet they seek not forgiveness nor admit they were wrong. Saul keeps allowing the will of the people to decide for him as well. To please them he offered that sacrifice. To please them he reneges his vow. Saul is a weak leader and his faith is not always enough to keep him from folly, because he does what he thinks is right rather than follow the word of God. Saul may have had the victory over the Philistines that day, but his error and his making everything worse meant he had to deal with Philistines until his death. They were a garrison in his heart. The sin that undoes so many of the faithful. He won many great victories, he delivered Israel from enemies. He smote the Amalekites. He had sons and daughters and a wife. But the Philistines remained a threat. And, as Samuel had warned the people, when Saul found a strong or valiant young man, he drafted them. Bringing them into his army. Leading them off to war. It really can be difficult to recognize that Saul was saved. He believed on the Lord. It becomes harder and harder to keep that perspective going forward, as we read through Samuel. But Saul was certainly saved by grace through faith in the Lord. His victories, the times the Lord used him for good for His people, where he was blessed personally, all show that even a less than perfect Christian can still have a great impact. But there are pitfalls and snares that we all face. And our end can be as tragic as Saul's if we allow ourselves to forget the word of God and to stay on the path He leads us. If we lean on our own understanding. If we don't recognize our error when chastised, and ask for forgiveness. The longsuffering of God has limits and He will take from us blessings and eventually even call us home if we no longer can be useful to His works that He has crafted us to do.

Chapter 15 of 1 Samuel, and the tragic story of King Saul continues. The first king over Israel is given yet another chance to do the will of God, and again leaning on his own understanding, Saul does not obey God's word. Told to wipe out all Amalek, from the king to the infants, and all the livestock, Saul allows the men with him to spoil the best sheep and other livestock, and keeps king Agag of the Amalek alive as a captive. Samuel had told Saul clearly the word of God, and all he had to do was obey. And God repents of His choice of Saul as king, because he did not follow His commandments. Samuel grieves all night at the word of the Lord, and sets out to meet Saul in the morning. Saul greets the prophet saying I have perform the commandment of the Lord, yet Samuel points to the noise of the sheep and oxen, asking what is it, knowing full well. And Saul said they were the best of the Amalekites, taken in spoil and how he plans on offering them as sacrifice to the Lord. Seemingly oblivious to the fact that it contradicted the word of God. Samuel recounts what the Lord had commanded, and this was not part of it. Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? And the king begins to argue why his disobedience was actually righteous, and in doing so admits the problem; the people took of the spoil, and to please them Saul compromised between them and the word of God. Saul acknowledges his sin, that because he feared the people, he obeyed their voice not the Lord's. And full of regret, Saul begs for forgiveness and that Samuel remain with him, but Samuel breaks fellowship, telling Saul the Kingdom had been rent from him the way Saul had rent his clothes in anguish at the truth of his cowardice and compromise, when he was told he'd been rejected as king. And also the Strength of Israel will not lie or repent: for He is not a man that He should repent. Samuel allows Saul to worship God. Saul slays the king of Amalek. And Samuel departs the company of Saul not to see him again until the day of his death. And Samuel mourns Saul: and the Lord repented that He had made Saul king over Israel. This chapter contains some key scripture and doctrines, but the primary message for Christians here is the understanding God will give us multiple chances to be used by Him for His purpose, if we harken to His word. Follow His commandments. And every time we turn rather to what seems right in our own eyes, or add too or diminish His word, or compromise to please men, He is grieved. Saul, His anointed remains king until his death. But the Lord is no longer with him. The word of the Lord taken away with Samuel. Saul was castaway. He never stopped believing, never lost his salvation, but he no longer would receive the blessings and benefits, and he would backslide into vanity and wickedness. Pride and paranoia, until he lost everything including his own life. People who doubt the gospel will often slanderously report that we teach a license to sin. But in truth, we who are saved are held to a higher standard. To whom much is given, much is expected. The chastisement of God is fierce against our sin. Obedience to the Lord is not for our spiritual salvation, but rather that it be well with us and we may be His workmen doing great things for the Lord. When we compromise with the world, seek approval from men, we are dealt with more harshly. When God sent Saul to slay the Amalek, he and the people had no problem with the genocide to be carried out when it was against things that were vile and refuse. But when they saw nice things, the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, they stayed their hand and thought better of themselves than what God commands. Christians do this too. It is easy to eliminate many sins in our lives. To stop doing vile things, while in the Spirit. But the sin that is appealing, that seems good and profitable in our eyes. That we struggle with eliminating. And sometimes, like Saul, we even convince ourselves God can use it to His glory. That by not eliminating it from our lives we are actually doing right. Rationalizing evil by calling it good. But God will not be impressed with our rebellion. Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Isaiah 1:11 To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats. Hebrews 10:1-14 For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect. For then would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins. But in those sacrifices there is a remembrance again made of sins every year. For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me: In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure. Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God. Above when he said, Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and offering for sin thou wouldest not, neither hadst pleasure therein; which are offered by the law; Then said he, Lo, I come to do thy will, O God. He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second. By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God; From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool. For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. God never took pleasure in the sacrifices. He doesn't care about our religious trappings and ceremony. He doesn't care about rites and sacraments. He cares about obedience to His word. Trust and faith and fearful respect. Obeying His word. Even unto death as Jesus Christ His Son. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king. Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. This is so hard for people trapped in false religion to grasp. They believe their own righteousness must be offered in sacrifice, even if it means going against the command of God to believe on His Son's righteousness instead. They will dress it up as Saul did. That they are offering the best. Buildings made of marble and images laid with gold, and sacrifices made to idols representing, in their minds, Christ. Doing all these works that they reasoned for themselves as good. That their logic of men and vain traditions came up with, often through compromise and fear of the people. God despises it. It is witchcraft. Rebellion.

1 Samuel 16 introduces us to David, son of Jesse and God's anointed. Having taken His Spirit off of Saul, the Lord sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint His new king-elect. And there Samuel brings the heifer for a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and all his to the service. Samuel supposed Jesse's son, Eliab, who looked the part to the prophet. But the Lord says to him; Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart. This is an important doctrine, that reinforces the seeming dichotomy of Romans 4 and James 2 that so many struggle with. That we are justified before God by our faith and justified before men by our works. Our appearance. That men are respecters of persons. James 2:1-14 My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him? But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats? Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by the which ye are called? If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well: But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors. For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all. For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law. So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty. For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment. As Jesus teaches in John 7:24; Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. And so when David is fetched from the flocks he shepherded, Samuel anoints him. A man after God's own heart. God knows our hearts and the spirit by which we do things. As we see Saul, who is discomforted and growing more and more bitter, no longer having the favor of God upon him, an evil spirit is taken him. His servants decide he needs a harpist to soothe the king when his temper is raised, and knowing David is a skilled harpist, they send for him. Saul loves him as a son and makes the man of Judah his armourbearer. And David plays to calm the king down, the Spirit of the Lord upon the soon-to-be king. Note that David was sent to bring peace, riding on an ass, provisioned with wine, bread and a kid, pictures of the Christ to come. The anointed of the Lord, who is the bread of life. Whose body was broken for our sins. Whose blood is the blood of testimony, sprinkled on the mercy seat. The kid, a sacrifice without blemish. It's a neat detail that shows that David is also a picture of Christ.

The familiar story of David and Goliath. How a shepherd boy slew the giant with one smooth stone. It is one of the most well known stories in the world, a feat everyone has heard of and a byword for overcoming impossible odds. But the world doesn't see the lesson; that it wasn't David who overcame Goliath, but the Lord. David's faith wasn't in himself, or his weapon of choice, but the power of God to deliver him. The Lord that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine... ...Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied. This day will the Lord deliver thee into mine hand; and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee; and I will give the carcases of the host of the Philistines this day unto the fowls of the air, and to the wild beasts of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. And all this assembly shall know that the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord's, and he will give you into our hands. It is not by works we have done. It is not by our own cunningly made devices and armor. Our sword or our strength, but His. And all the earth knows there is a God in Israel, that our God is true and delivered David. That God doesn't save by sword and spear but He wins the battle and delivers salvation into our hands. The parallel with the spiritual things of God, the Christian life of trusting in the Lord. Our victories are His, that the assembly may know that it is the Lord that delivers us. The battle is His. David believed God and it was counted for righteousness. He was anointed to be king. He had been to Saul to play the harp, be an armourbearer for the troubled king. Yet he remained a humble shepherd. Obedient to his father, he leaves to provide provision for his brothers who had been drafted into the kings service (as Samuel had warned), and to bring honor to their captain, that he may bring back word to Jesse. Goliath taunting the men of Israel is as the scoffers of this world. Mocking them and putting them to open shame. When David hears this he is angered that all the army, including his brothers, have been cowardly, allowing Goliath to humiliate them and by extension the power of God. His brothers, rather than be stirred by his faith, instead question David's motives. Make light of it. Just as we as Christians have family members who do just the same. Who are ashamed by our faith and their doubts, and rather than be strengthened, turn to resent us. To impugn our intentions. David remains steadfast, and word reaches the king. Saul, once again, is far from battle. He hears our David and naysays against him; You are too young and small, with no experience fighting. David replies that God had already delivered unto him a bear and a lion, and that He will deliver David out of the hand of the Philistine. Saul hearing his testimony tells David to go, and may the Lord be with him. Saul, as appointed leader, as a king who stood literally head and shoulders above all other men in Israel, who had years of battle experience, sends off a youth to do what should have been his responsibility. Goliath may have been 9ft tall and mighty, but Saul probably was a physical match, with the best coat of mail and helmet of brass, and a sword. Fully equipped. But he sent other men's sons out to battle. In typical Saul fashion, he attempts to fit David with his kit, giving him the armour and sword, but David refuses the king, saying he cannot trust those things, having not proved them. Saul's trust was in those things, David's in God. God who had proved to the shepherd that He was with him. And so the future king, David, confronts the Philistine champion, and with his faith, slays the giant with one blow. And using Goliath's own sword, slays him and decapitates him. The Philistines flee, the emboldened Israelites pursue and slaughter them and spoil their camp. David returns to the king, with the trophy of his victory with him. Earlier in the story, when David learned of Goliath, the men of the camp had rumoured that whosoever slay the giant would be rewarded by the king; Have ye seen this man that is come up? surely to defy Israel is he come up: and it shall be, that the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel. This is a picture of the victory Christ gives us, the reward we are elected into for allowing God to deliver us in Him, by faith. We are rewarded with eternal life, and are made His sons. And we become free, that is are set at liberty. In David's case, the family of Jesse would live tax free in the kingdom. In ours, we live free of the tax on our sin, the wages of death. And so with the victory won, David brought the head of the giant to Jerusalem, but kept the armor as spoil. Saul, as he sent off David, asks his captain of the host, Abner, whose son is this youth? Abner doesn't know but seeks to find out. Saul, who had known David, been soothed by the boy's harp and psalms, who had offered to bear his armor, hadn't bothered to know anything of him. After the fact, Abner brings David and his trophy before the king, who asks "whose son are you?" David answered Jesse of Bethlehem, but this is a picture of Jesus Christ. There's an echo of Jesus being brought before Herod, accused of the Jews for saying truthfully that He was the son of God.

And so with the Spirit of the Lord upon David, and an evil spirit of envy and paranoia upon Saul, the king begins to despise the shepherd. The heir, Jonathan vowed friendship to David, loving him. And Jonathan gave to David his royal garment, his sword and bow. A sign of fealty. The women of Israel hailed David returning from battle, giving him more glory for slaughter of the Philistines than Saul. And while Saul demanded David stay with him, and play the harp as before, it no longer soothed the king but enraged him. And trying to kill David himself by spear as he played, and failing, fear came over Saul. And because David had the love of the people, which Saul had always sought and desired, even to the disobedience to God's word, Saul was afraid to act directly on David. And so Saul sought that David would be killed in battle by the Philistines (mirroring what would come to be David's greatest sin with Uriah). But David returned with victory every time, and grew to be more beloved. Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with David. Saul became David's enemy continually. David walked wisely. He knew Saul's heart and yet kept himself loyal to the king, and obedient to the throne. He was wise, keeping himself blameless. Executing his orders. Saul's daughter Michal loved David, just as all the people did, and so when Saul sought to snare him with his daughter Michal (after offering his eldest daughter and slighting David by marrying her to someone else, I think hoping to get him to react angrily and failing), David demurs, humbling himself saying he was not worthy. But when Saul hears this he foolishly offers a dowry of the foreskins of 100 Philistines, and David gladly accepted the challenge, bringing the king 200 and taking Michal to wife, becoming the son-in-law to the king. Saul's efforts only make David stronger.

And so, here in 1 Samuel 19 we are given more details of the murderous spirit King Saul has against David, adding to the narrative established in the previous chapter. In the opening of chapter 18 we saw Jonathan's love for David, and here in chapter 19 it opens with Jonathan's father telling him to kill David. Jonathan tells David to hide while he speaks to his father, and while they are out and about, he convinces Saul that David is a loyal servant and it would be wrong to kill him. And Saul, as we have seen before, makes a foolish vow; As the Lord liveth, he shall not be slain. But like all Saul's people-pleasing oaths, his sincerity is in question and his inability to follow through shows itself again after David has another victory over the Philistines. The evil spirit of the Lord again comes up on the king, and he attempts to slay David with a javelin as he plays the harp. David as we know, slips away and is aware of the king's intentions. And as we saw in the last chapter, Michal, David's wife, Saul's daughter, loves David very much. She tells David of a plot to kill him in their home, and she helps him escape out a window as she sets up an image in the bed, with a wig to fool the men dispatched by the king. Saul has lost the confidence of his people, his family, the prophet Samuel, and ultimately, God. David seeks out Samuel, and he and the prophet go out to Naioth, Ramah to dwell. Saul, finding out, sends his messengers to see Samuel and find him in the company of prophets, all in the Spirit, preaching the word of God. And the messengers themselves are overtaken by the Spirit and begin to prophesy also. Saul, hearing this, sends yet more servants, and they too are used by the Lord to preach His word. And yet a third time Saul sends men who are added to the prophets with Samuel and overcome by the Spirit. Finally, Saul himself goes forth to see them, and has to be directed where to go, which I find to be a sign of the blindness that had come over the king. He had sent three groups of messengers to the prophet Samuel, and yet he himself has to ask others for directions. As he drew near to Naioth, the king also had the Spirit of God come upon him, and he prophesied all the way to their camp. There he strips out of his clothes, naked, laying down before Samuel and prophesying the word of God. Just as when Saul first went out before Samuel, anointed, where the Spirit came over him and he prophesied with the prophets he met in the way, Saul again is compelled by God. And again the people say, Is Saul also among the prophets?

Here in chapter 20 we find Jonathan, the son of the king and presumed heir torn between his loyalty to his father and to his friend, David, whom he loved like a brother. Saul had previously vowed before Jonathan that "as the Lord liveth he would not harm David." Unbeknownst to Jonathan, Saul broke that vow and tried to kill David in his sleep, and then at Naioth, where he'd fled with Samuel. Jonathan believes his father wouldn't do such a thing without telling him, but as David says, Saul knows their bond. Jonathan had already pledged his sword and bow to David. David makes a similar vow, swearing truly as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, there is but a step between me and death. A very similar oath as made by Saul. But unlike Saul, David and Jonathan aren't so easily swayed from keeping their word. While Saul is a saved believer, an evil spirit had come on him from the Lord as recompense for his constant wavering between keeping the word of God and pleasing others. Between being in faith and not fear. Now all the king knew was fear. And from that fear came envy and worry. David and Jonathan are also brothers in the faith, believing on the living God. They hatch a plan. The king would host a feast for the new moon, and when David failed to be there, Jonathan would tell his father that David was gone to Bethlehem for a family sacrifice, and had asked permission of Jonathan who'd granted him leave. If Saul was unperturbed by the news, all was well. But if he were to react in anger, Jonathan would know his heart and David's life was threatened. To communicate this, David would hide in a field, 3 days, and Jonathan would come with his bow and shoot arrows toward the hiding place. Jonathan devised a code; when he'd tell his young squire to fetch the arrows, of all were well, then he'd say "Behold the arrows are in this side of thee" and if Saul was wroth, he would say "Behold, the series are beyond thee." At the first night of the feast, Saul looked for David but made assumptions that his son-in-law must have been unclean. That he wouldn't knowingly miss the feast of the king. But the second night, he sought David and Jonathan told him their planned alibi. Saul instantly knows Jonathan has betrayed him for David, and shouts obscenities as his own son, calling him a son of a whore, saying that as long as David lives, Jonathan will not be established. That he will not inherit the kingdom of Israel. He then throws his javelin at his own heir, to smite him. Jonathan has his answer, and knows that David was correct. Saul seeks His friend's life. On the 3rd day, Jonathan goes to the field and fires his arrows and gives the signal that David must flee as his lad fetches the arrows. Giving his bow and quiver to the lad and sending him back to the city, Jonathan finds David and they make a tearful and tragic goodbye. And, as they had pledged to one another a covenant before in the name of the Lord, Jonathan reminds that David had swore not to kill Jonathan or his children when he comes to power. Jonathan reiterates this oath; Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord, saying, The Lord be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever. It is impossible to read this chapter, and miss the number of times both Jonathan and David appeal to the Lord in their communication with each other. God forbid; thou shalt not die... David sware moreover...truly as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, there is but a step between me and death. And Jonathan said unto David, O Lord God of Israel, when I have sounded my father about to morrow any time, or the third day, and, behold, if there be good toward David, and I then send not unto thee, and shew it thee; The Lord do so and much more to Jonathan: but if it please my father to do thee evil, then I will shew it thee, and send thee away, that thou mayest go in peace: and the Lord be with thee, as he hath been with my father. And thou shalt not only while yet I live shew me the kindness of the Lord, that I die not...But also thou shalt not cut off thy kindness from my house for ever: no, not when the Lord hath cut off the enemies of David every one from the face of the earth. So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, Let the Lord even require it at the hand of David's enemies... If I expressly say unto the lad, Behold, the arrows are on this side of thee, take them; then come thou: for there is peace to thee, and no hurt; as the Lord liveth. But if I say thus unto the young man, Behold, the arrows are beyond thee; go thy way: for the Lord hath sent thee away. And as touching the matter which thou and I have spoken of, behold, the Lord be between thee and me for ever... And Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord, saying, The Lord be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever. The parallel with salvation, calling upon the living God, the Lord God of Israel, literally of the seed of David, and these paths sworn between Jonathan and David are obvious. Saul, like the remnant of unbelieving Jews, having the kingdom taken from him, and given to another, and so he seeks the son of Jesse's life. Just as they sought Christ's. But Jonathan loves David more than his own father, more than his own earthly reward, more than even inheriting a kingdom of man. No greater love. We should love our brothers in Christ this much. We should love Jesus like this and more. And when thou hast stayed three days, then thou shalt go down quickly, and come to the place where thou didst hide thyself when the business was in hand, and shalt remain by the stone Ezel. From what I gather, Ezel may mean separation/departure, and the stone may have marked the way away from the city, a place where travelers would say goodbye to those departing on the way. But In the margin notes made by the KJV translators, they note Ezel is the stone "that showeth the way." Just as Jesus is the rock and the way. It is where Jonathan and David call upon the name of the Lord. Where Jonathan vows to love David's seed forever. Where they both speak of the living God, and make a covenant. I don't know, I wondered about it and this is what I found and how it seems to me.

Luke 6 And it came to pass on the second sabbath after the first, that he went through the corn fields; and his disciples plucked the ears of corn, and did eat, rubbing them in their hands. 2 And certain of the Pharisees said unto them, Why do ye that which is not lawful to do on the sabbath days? 3 And Jesus answering them said, Have ye not read so much as this, what David did, when himself was an hungred, and they which were with him; 4 How he went into the house of God, and did take and eat the shewbread, and gave also to them that were with him; which it is not lawful to eat but for the priests alone? 5 And he said unto them, That the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath. 6 And it came to pass also on another sabbath, that he entered into the synagogue and taught: and there was a man whose right hand was withered. 7 And the scribes and Pharisees watched him, whether he would heal on the sabbath day; that they might find an accusation against him. 8 But he knew their thoughts, and said to the man which had the withered hand, Rise up, and stand forth in the midst. And he arose and stood forth. 9 Then said Jesus unto them, I will ask you one thing; Is it lawful on the sabbath days to do good, or to do evil? to save life, or to destroy it? 10 And looking round about upon them all, he said unto the man, Stretch forth thy hand. And he did so: and his hand was restored whole as the other. 11 And they were filled with madness; and communed one with another what they might do to Jesus. Here in 1 Samuel 21 we find the story referenced by Jesus in Luke 6, where David fleeing Saul seeks food from the priest at Nod. All that is present is the shewbread, sanctified and hallowed. He asks that David than those with him are clean, and acquiesces to give it to them. And David, lying to say he was on urgent business of the king, asks if there be a weapon there, and providentially enough, there is the sword of Goliath whom he had slain. Doeg the Edomite, chief over Saul's herdsmen sees David. This comes into play in the next chapter. But it's interesting that David, son of Jacob who is Israel, the good shepherd who will be king, is betrayed by a son of Esau who is Edom, the evil shepherd, whom Saul trusted over his flocks. Fleeing from Nob, David crosses to the land of the Philistines, his sworn enemies, and seeks sanctuary from Saul at Gath, and their king Achish. The men at the gate recognize David, and even acknowledge what Saul feared, that David was truly the king of Israel, having the love of the people. But David's fame is a problem, and he fears the king will have him taken. And so he changes his behavior to that of a mad man, pounding on the gate. The king chastised the guards saying not to bring a madman into his house. Another interesting parallel with Luke 6 is that the Jews become stricken with madness, determined to seek the life of Jesus, who heals the man with the withered hand in their house on a Sabbath. The rulers of the Jews, like Saul, understood that the Son of Jesse was a threat to their power, like David to Saul. And like Saul, they had an evil spirit fall on them and knowing they were rejected of God, they sought Jesus' life.

Psalm 52 Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? the goodness of God endureth continually. 2 The tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully. 3 Thou lovest evil more than good; and lying rather than to speak righteousness. Selah. 4 Thou lovest all devouring words, O thou deceitful tongue. 5 God shall likewise destroy thee for ever, he shall take thee away, and pluck thee out of thy dwelling place, and root thee out of the land of the living. Selah. 6 The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him: 7 Lo, this is the man that made not God his strength; but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness. 8 But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever. 9 I will praise thee for ever, because thou hast done it: and I will wait on thy name; for it is good before thy saints. Psalm 57 Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast. 2 I will cry unto God most high; unto God that performeth all things for me. 3 He shall send from heaven, and save me from the reproach of him that would swallow me up. Selah. God shall send forth his mercy and his truth. 4 My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword. 5 Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; let thy glory be above all the earth. 6 They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down: they have digged a pit before me, into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves. Selah. 7 My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise. 8 Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early. 9 I will praise thee, O Lord, among the people: I will sing unto thee among the nations. 10 For thy mercy is great unto the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds. 11 Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: let thy glory be above all the earth. David, on the run from King Saul, who is seeking his life, continued to write psalms, songs of worship and praise, thanksgiving and faith in the Lord to deliver him, even while hiding in a cave in the wilderness. His trust in the Lord giving him hope, even as all of Saul's resources are turned against him. We see David return to Judah and seek refuge for his father and mother in Moab. Once safe there, his brothers other men gathered to join him in hiding, about 400 men. And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him. This is a picture of Christ, gathering the distressed and discontent, those carrying the debt of sin unto Him. Despite persecution. Knowing that He shall deliver us. Saul hears of David's movements and those that went to him, the king abode in Gibeah under a tree in Ramah, having his spear in his hand, surrounded by his kinsmen the Benjamites, his servants. He implied that David would not treat them as well as he has, that they have land and power through Saul, appealing to their own greed. And chastising them out of paranoia for not telling him that Jonathan had betrayed him with David, aiding his escape. It is in this setting that Doeg the Edomite enters the court to approach the king, having witnessed David at Nob, seeking aid from the priest there, Ahimelech the son of Ahitub. Saul calls for the all the priests of Nob to come before him. Saul said unto him, Why have ye conspired against me, thou and the son of Jesse, in that thou hast given him bread, and a sword, and hast enquired of God for him, that he should rise against me, to lie in wait, as at this day? David received holy bread and a mighty sword from the priest while calling upon the Lord. An image of the bread of life that is come down from Heaven, Christ Jesus, and His word, sharper than any two-edged sword, which is given us who seek after God. The priests tell the king that they had no reason to suspect David was anything but an honored servant to Saul, his very son-in-law. Despite their plea of ignorance, the king said, Thou shalt surely die, Ahimelech, thou, and all thy father's house. Saul orders his footmen, his personal guard made up of Israelites, and tells them to execute the priests, but they all refuse the kings orders. They feared God more than Saul. And so Saul turned to Doeg to do it for him, which the Edomite gladly did, killing 85 men that day, and then leading a sack of Nob, killing man, woman, child and beast. Saul like many today, turned to spiritual Edom. Away from Israel and the things of God. And one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped, and fled after David. And Abiathar shewed David that Saul had slain the Lord's priests. David realizes that he was betrayed by Doeg, knowing the Edomite would tell Saul. Taking blame for the deaths of his father's house, David promises safety to Abiathar. It may be Doeg David writes about in Psalm 52, who loves evil more than good. And lying more than righteousness. And in his tribulation, David again sang unto the Lord; Psalm 142 I cried unto the Lord with my voice; with my voice unto the Lord did I make my supplication. 2 I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble. 3 When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path. In the way wherein I walked have they privily laid a snare for me. 4 I looked on my right hand, and beheld, but there was no man that would know me: refuge failed me; no man cared for my soul. 5 I cried unto thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my refuge and my portion in the land of the living. 6 Attend unto my cry; for I am brought very low: deliver me from my persecutors; for they are stronger than I. 7 Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name: the righteous shall compass me about; for thou shalt deal bountifully with me.

And so we see as David is hiding out the Philistines make a raid on a city in Judah and David inquires of the Lord if he should go down and deliver the people. And God tells him yes. Go, and smite the Philistines, and save Keilah. David and his men repel the Philistines successfully, and Saul hearing of it gathers his men to go up against the city thinking he could trap David there. Having a priest there with the ephod, which has the Urim and Thummim, David inquires of the Lord what he should do. Saul however acts of his own accord. David asks of God if the people he just saved will betray him to the king, and the answer is yes. David even shows further concern for the city that would betray him, Saul would destroy it simply to get at him. So David and his men flee. And so we see a cat and mouse game develop between Saul and David. And the people who David hides among, offer him up to be killed despite his heroism. Again, another picture of Christ Jesus in David. Jonathan again seeks out. David and the friends again strengthen their commitment, Jonathan pledging that when David is king he will serve by his side. The heir apparent is willing to sacrifice his own kingdom for the kingdom God ordained. Again, a wonderful picture of giving up the worldly for the Kingdom of Heaven. Trusting the person whom God sent. The pursuit of David continues, Saw getting close with his befores to David and his men. They circle around a mountain seeking escape and David is delivered when Saul is called away with his forces to another battle with the Philistines. They call that place Selahammahlekoth, which means the rock of escape, or the rock of separation. David's time in the wilderness being sought after by the enemies of the world is similar to the life of a Christian as they go from Ezel, The rock of the way, to Selahammahlekoth, the mount of separation. These subtle details are included to not only provide a narrative that we can follow and understand but contain the deeper things of God. His word really is beautiful.

1 Peter 2:20-23 For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously Proverbs 25:21-22 If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord shall reward thee. Romans 12:19-20 Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Matthew 5:38-42 Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: but I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also. And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away. Psalm 7:8-9 The LORD shall judge the people: Judge me, O LORD, According to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me. Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end; but establish the just: For the righteous God Trieth the hearts and reins. Psalm 43 Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man. For thou art the God of my strength: why dost thou cast me off? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy? O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles. Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God. Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God. The living God is the God of judgment and vengeance, delivering His sons and bringing his wrath on our enemies. As followers of Christ, we are called to love our enemies and give them a chance to repent of the evil they seek to do to us. Even to support them in their need, and to forgive them if they turn away from their anger. Matthew 5:44-48 But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so? Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect. This is one of the hardest doctrines to accept for many Christians. It can be the thing that snares them and keeps them from being perfect, complete, in their faith. Of course, to be saved, we must have trust in God's promise of salvation and eternal life in Christ Jesus. We have to believe that He can deliver us from wrath. We may believe that He can heal us of our sins, removing thorns from our heart and conforming us to His purpose. We will pray for our physical well-being and the safety and health of our loved ones, trusting His tender mercies and that He will help us in our affliction. We might even develop faith deep enough to not fear when hard times come, when money is tight, when we need food or clothing or shelter. That He will provide. But when we are wronged by another, when we are unfairly persecuted, or others hold us in contempt and seek our harm, it is often difficult to trust in the Lord to deliver us. To bring to nothing their schemes. We want to fight back, answer railing for railing, to protest and proclaim our righteousness loudly, to all who will listen, so they know that our enemies cause is not just. But what sayeth scripture? When David has the opportunity to end this one-sided feud with King Saul, he chooses to let God judge. To allow the Lord to deliver him. By his kindness to Saul, humiliating the paranoid king by showing that mercy and his good intentions to all the men present, Saul was left no choice but to withdraw. David's faith in God and the righteousness of obedience to His word, not only saves his life and the life of his men, but heaps coals upon his enemy's head. And as we know, God's vengeance against Saul is coming, his destruction is assured. Saul knows it too, and asks favor from David, to spare his seed after David is king, a covenant David had already made with Jonathan. By trusting in the Lord, without a single blow, David has been delivered and his enemy made weak. Saul, with 4,000 men surrounding the cave, could have easily turned and destroyed the upstart and his small band. Instead he slunk away in defeat. This is the kind of faith that makes us perfect, Jesus says. The lack of fear, trusting in the righteousness established in us by Christ, testified of by the Spirit, knowing the power of the Father to deliver us. With that sure knowledge, loving your enemies becomes our strength. It is a mercy given them by victors, even if that victory hasn't been seen yet. A victory we have already received in Jesus, having overcome the world. And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. We may have friends and family that don't have the faith to understand this strength. They may see the opportunity to exact vengeance as a sign from God, as David's men did. They may be afraid, and look for the easiest way out, and push you into taking it with the best of intentions. It can be hard to do the right thing in the presence of that kind of peer pressure. It is notable that while Saul consistently bowed to that sort of pressure, choosing to please man rather than do as God said, David does the right thing and silences his men by keeping to the principles of righteousness as God has given us. Had he done as they thought best, doing what seemed good to him, rather than what is good to the Lord, who knows what may have happened, but it's a good bet that they'd be in worse straits, surrounded and outnumbered and without the protection of God, having not trusted in Him. So take heart. Faint not. Trust in the Lord. Do what's right in His eyes. The rest takes care of itself.

Here in chapter 25 of 1 Samuel, with several more chapters left, and a whole 2nd Samuel to come, the titular prophet himself dies. Even with all he had done for the Lord and the 40 years he'd judged Israel and stood as its moral compass, his death is a paragraph. His life is not wasted, his eternity secure, and the impact of his work for the Lord reverberating even now, to us today, but his death is hardly a mention. It is a fitting way to view things for the saved Christian. We will all die physically, but that's just a moment in time. We are dead to the flesh as it is, and sealed by the Spirit unto redemption and eternity awaits in Christ. So we should live as Samuel, while we draw breath and not worry about the moment God takes us home to be with Him. And with the prophet's death, David goes down to Paran, still hiding in the wilderness, 600 men with him in his band. And while staying there, they were near a wealthy man's fields near Carmel, where this man, Nabal had his flocks. And Nabal was married to a beautiful, believing woman named Abigail. But Nabal was mean and greedy, a son of Belial according to his servants. Churlish and evil in his doings. David, hearing Nabal had come down to sheer his flock, sent 10 young men to see the rich man, and to ask of him some food and supplies, seeing as how David's men had helped guard the area and protect his herds and herdsmen from harm. He sends them in peace, reiterating this three times. And Nabal, hearing their plea mocks David, railing against him that he was in rebellion to the king, an obvious lie. He tells the young men to leave with nothing, saying he doesn't know them or owe them anything. David, hearing this, is outraged. He tells 400 of his men to gird up and grab their swords, for to go an slay Nabal and all his servants, the menfolk, those who pisseth against the wall. Now one of the servants of Nabal makes an appeal to Abigail, telling her the circumstances and fearing for his life. She puts together a fitting tribute of provisions, sending it before her, and sets out an ass to see David and plead her case. David, still angry at being used and railed against by her husband, meets up with her, and she bows before him, begging his forgiveness in the name of the living God. Nabal, the very name meaning foolish, has acted rashly, she says. Abigail says that her meeting him is a divine appointment, an act of the Lord, staying David's hand from shedding blood and taking vengeance for himself. She prophesies that surely David is the Lord's anointed, that the spirit is upon him, and soon enough he would be king and his enemies would be destroyed. And when that surely comes to pass, the insults of Nabal will mean nothing to him. And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand. David takes her gifts and sends her away in peace. Abigail finds Nabal drunken, holding a feast fit for a king, his heart merry within him, so she holds off on telling him what she had done. His reveling showing his greed, that if he had that much food and drink to waste at a party, it would have been nothing to him to spare what David had asked for. But in the morning, when his wife tells him, the Bible says, his heart died within him. If he wasn't a reprobate, a true son of Belial, before, he was now. And ten days later, the Lord smote Nabal and he died. Vengeance is His. David, upon hearing the news that the Lord had avenged him, immediately sends for Abigail to wife. But least we think this was a good and proper thing, or see some romance in it, the Bible also mentions immediately after that David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel to wife. But Saul had gave Michal his daughter, wife of David, away to another man, Phalti, which will come into play later on. It is interesting that just a chapter after David had trusted in the Lord, by passing on the opportunity to slay Saul and end his exile, showing great faith and patience, David reacts so strongly to the railing of Nabal. Not only had David humiliated the king, heaping coals on his head, and gained more favor in the eyes of the Lord by not rebelling against the appointed leader over him, despite Saul's murderous heart, David had shown the Christian spirit to his men who wanted him to kill the king. Being a great example to them, and by extension to all of us who have read this. But sometimes, especially after a victory in the Christian's life, we face temptations. The world turns harder against us. We become less guarded against our own sins, and fall victim to our flesh, just as we should be growing more in the Spirit. Sometimes it feels like we are determined to sabotage what God has wrought in us, and the Devil is all too happy to give us the opportunity to stumble and fall, that he can accuse us before the Lord. Sometimes we catch ourselves. Other times our passions run so hot, we need another saved person to act as our better angel, advising us against the evil we are set to do, as Abigail does here for David. And often, even if we turn from the worst that we might do, we settle on a lesser sin to scratch that itch within our flesh. The thorn in our hearts. Abigail, a godly woman and beautiful, was loyal to her wicked husband. She didn't betray Nabal or allow David to take him off her hands, rather she saved his life. She did right by the Lord and by her husband and it worked out for her that the Lord destroyed Nabal. But David is married, and yet seeks her for his wife. While Abigail does nothing wrong. Being a window, David falls into sin. And not only with Abigail, which may have been a great love story, but with yet another woman, making Abigail a sister wife to Ahinoam. David's sin affects her, and will lead him to greater sin with Bathsheba, and eventually will serve as a bad influence on his son Solomon, who will have a thousand wives and concubines. This is why we can't rest on our victories, we can't become complacent just because we have done the right thing, and God has blessed us for it. We should always keep in mind 1 Peter 5:8; Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour I hope you aren't skipping Bible reading

Psalm 35:1-3 Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me: Fight against them that fight against me. Take hold of shield and buckler, And stand up for mine help. Draw out also the spear, and stop the way against them that persecute me: Say unto my soul, I am thy salvation. Once again, Saul sets out to seek David's life. The men of Ziph again betraying his whereabouts. And, again David has opportunity to slay the king who pursues him, and declines choosing to obey the Lord rather than go against His anointed. He and his man sneak into the camp, standing over a sleeping Saul, his trusty javelin stuck in the earth by the kings head. When David's man, Ahimelech suggests taking the spear and ending it, David stays his hand. David said furthermore, As the Lord liveth, the Lord shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish. Prophesying the death of Saul. They take his spear and head off, up I to the wilderness, the Lord sending a deep sleep on the men of Saul's camp. Reaching a hill afar off, David cries out to the king's right hand man. Abner. David mocks Abner, if he is such a valiant man, how is it he failed to protect the king? He was worthy of death for allowing such a thing to happen. And as proof of David's accusation, he produces the king's spear and cruse of water. Saul, recognizing David's voice calls out to his "son." David replies, as he had outside the cave earlier, asking why the king sought his faithful servant. David challenges Saul's integrity before the Lord, saying if Saul's actions are of God, then let it be revealed. But if not, let them be cursed for driving him out from the inheritance of the Lord. David once again calls on the Lord to determine the just cause here, and trusted in Him to deliver him from Saul. And Saul, again humbled and left exposed and embarrassed by his deeds again repents and sorrowfully apologies to David and after David returns his spear, David praises the Lord who delivers him from tribulation, and Saul blesses David, and they depart from one another again. David continues to show the faith in the Lord to deliver us from tribulation if we remain obedient to Him. 1 Corinthians 10:11-13 Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come. Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. People who criticize biblical fundamentalism and the inerrancy of scripture, or worse, cast doubt on the accuracy or origin of the accounts, will point to the repetitive narrative of Samuel, and other books of the Old Testament, to sow doubtful disputations. But we know better. That's Satan's oldest trick. The Spirit tells us that these things happened, and for a reason; as examples and admonition for us, that we understand the will of God for us. So we may know His deliverance is real. So we may trust in Him as David trusted in Him. We can know that these aren't merely stories and folklore, but actual events, and they played out for a purpose, even if it was unbeknownst to those involved at the time. And they were recorded in scripture for us to take heart, to rest easy, knowing that the Lord delivers. Amen

And so David took up residency with the hated Philistines, he and his band of men and their families. Living there for 16 months. During that time, raiding the other Canaanite nations, while returning with spoil to king Achish, while telling him that they were invading Israel. Again we see the pattern of David trusting in the Lord for deliverance, and then falling back to his own understanding, doing what seems right in his own eyes. He flees out of fear of Saul, despite knowing the Lord's hand was upon him. He sets himself up in tribute to the enemy of Israel, and covered for his sin by doing "good," while lying about it. What a picture of how Christians can fall back into sin, from fear and trying to create their own path, when the path God has laid out seems hard. David will be reminded to turn to the Lord in tribulation a few chapters from now.

Now David, encamped with the Philistines, is in a bind. His false loyalty to the king is about to be sorely tested as the Philistines mount an invasion of Israel. Samuel the prophet is dead. And King Saul, having gathered his armies to meet the invaders is afraid. And he has no guidance from the Lord; And when Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets. The Lord has left him to his fear. Now Saul was not the best leader, and wasn't the most dedicated believer, but he had the decency to cast out and kill the abominable; the mediums and necromancers and wizards from the land. But now, seeking any guidance whatsoever, he disguises himself to go visit a woman with a familiar spirit, someone who claims she talks to the dead. His servants found the witch at Endor. He asks the witch to show him Samuel that he could enquire of the prophet from beyond the veil. The woman recognizes the king and says she fears he's tricking her to kill her, but the desperate king assures her, again foolishly swearing to the Lord. Saul's habit of making foolish vows to the Lord while disobeying Him is a trait that has cost him the kingdom. And soon his life. He asks to speak to Samuel. And the woman is shocked to see Samuel. Saul says be not afraid, describe what you've seen, and the witch says I saw gods ascending out of the earth. Spirits of leaders and lords going up into Heaven. And an old man, covered in a mantle, coming towards them. Saul knows this is Samuel. And we, the reader can know it too, as the Spirit inspired narrator confirms it is actually him; And Samuel said to Saul, Why hast thou disquieted me, to bring me up? And Saul answered, I am sore distressed; for the Philistines make war against me, and God is departed from me, and answereth me no more, neither by prophets, nor by dreams: therefore I have called thee, that thou mayest make known unto me what I shall do. I believe this is the first time the familiar actually has seen the spirits of the dead. I believe that, as most sorcery and divinations, are scams that prey on people's weaknesses, fear and depression. And are satanic in their practice because of it. But every so often, they are used by evil spirits, or even allowed a glimpse of the spirit world by God, to His purpose, as was the case here. Samuel upbraids Saul, and reminds him of the prophecy Samuel had already told the king; the kingdom was lost to him and would be David's. Because thou obeyedst not the voice of the Lord, nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek, therefore hath the Lord done this thing unto thee this day. The spirit of Samuel goes on to say the Philistines will be victors, and that in a day, Saul and his sons will lose their lives to the heathen. Saul is devastated, and already fasting, refused food. But the witch convinces the doomed king to eat, finally, a fattened calf and unleavened bread, and sends the king to meet his fate. Sometimes, I feel as though Christians may say that they feel like David. But for the most part I think most act more like Saul.

David is placed in a precarious position due to his faltering faith in chapter 27, sending himself to live among the Philistines, pretending to serve their king for fear of Saul. And now all Philistine has risen against the hosts of Israel under King Saul, and so David and his men ride towards the battlefield with the enemies of their people. But the leaders of the Philistines question their king, saying they fear David would turn on them in battle to reconcile with Saul. And so, king Achish sends David away, back to the town they've been staying in, to their families. David may have felt relief in this moment. When we have sinned against God and the consequences for our sin rise up to chasten us, the Lord may take us out of the calamity we have made for ourselves, only to deposit us in the place where he wants us, so that He may show us our error in His own way, as David will soon see.

Now, David had gone to Ziklag originally out of fear of Saul. Unlike the doomed king, David had the word of God, the ephod with the Urim and Thummim, the blessing of the prophet Samuel, and the Spirit of the Lord upon him. The Lord had delivered David multiple times, and rewarded him for his faithful service to Him and to his king, despite Saul's persecution. David had all those, but in the midst of tribulation, he fled to his enemies the Philistines, and took up residency in Ziklag. There, he and his men and their wives and children, along with the priest Abiathar lived for over a year, spoiling the Amalekites and other heathens, giving a portion to King Achish of the Philistines, claiming he was taking it from Judah. Living a lie, in deception out of fear. That lie nearly cost he and his men everything, as they went up with Achish and his legions to invade Israel, setting them against their own brethren. But God had another plan for him, and the princes of the Philistines told the king they didn't trust him, and so the king sent David and his band home. There's a time when we are tried that we may do what seems right in our eyes. Where our faith isn't perfect, and our trust in the Lord to deliver us is overwhelmed by fear, and we make bad choices. We sin. We fall back into the world. We hide our faith to fit in with the world, and tell ourselves that we are still doing the work of the Lord, even though we are hiding it from the unsaved around us. Lying to them and ourselves. The Lord may still save us from the worst consequences of our actions, but He may also let us twist in the wind a little bit, to help us develop the faith we should have had in the first place. This is true of David, as the Amalekites had raided their town, and taken captive their wives, sons and daughters, spoiling the village and burning it to the ground. The men with David are distraught, some seek to stone him, blaming his poor leadership for bringing this desolation to their door. They weep and wait until they cannot anymore, David with them, his wives gone into captivity as well. In their despair, David encouraged himself in the Lord his God. Doing what he should have done 16 months before. Determined, he seeks the Lord's council and calls for the ephod, enquiring what he should do. The Lord tells him to go and overtake the spoilers, and they will recover all without fail. So David and his 600 men head out, but partway there, by the brook of Besor, 200 men, exhausted fall out and remain behind. But David and the 400 pursued the raiders, and finding an Egyptian boy, a servant to the captors, they play him with food and water and he agrees to take them to their camp. There David and his men smite the Amalekites from dusk through dawn and into the next evening, sparing none but 400 camel riding men who fled. All of their families were safe and sound. Their possessions accounted for plus spoils beside. As they return to Ziklag, they reunite with the 200 who had stayed behind, and some of the men with David, reprobates, sons of Belial, tried to deny those who hadn't made it to the camp any portion. But David insisted that they be compensated as much as the rest. The blessings of God had been given them by His grace, and would be shared throughout. Blessings so abundant, David had enough to send forth to Judah and his friends, saying; Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the Lord. Having learned a hard lesson, nearly losing everything, David turned again to the Lord and the Lord delivered him, and with more than he had feared he had lost. Keep this in mind when you fear the worst. When you want to flee to Ziklag. When you want to seek your own way, better the way of the Lord. And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. So keep the faith. Psalm 23 The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever. Encourage yourself in the Lord your God.

1 Chronicles 10 Now the Philistines fought against Israel; and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. 2 And the Philistines followed hard after Saul, and after his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul. 3 And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him, and he was wounded of the archers. 4 Then said Saul to his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. So Saul took a sword, and fell upon it. 5 And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise on the sword, and died. 6 So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together. 7 And when all the men of Israel that were in the valley saw that they fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, then they forsook their cities, and fled: and the Philistines came and dwelt in them. 8 And it came to pass on the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Saul and his sons fallen in mount Gilboa. 9 And when they had stripped him, they took his head, and his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to carry tidings unto their idols, and to the people. 10 And they put his armour in the house of their gods, and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon. 11 And when all Jabeshgilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, 12 They arose, all the valiant men, and took away the body of Saul, and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh, and buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh, and fasted seven days. 13 So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the Lord, even against the word of the Lord, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; 14 And enquired not of the Lord: therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse. Acts 13:20-22 And after that he gave unto them judges about the space of four hundred and fifty years, until Samuel the prophet. And afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave their testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.... Acts 13:9 Then Saul, (who also is called Paul,) filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him. Romans 11:1 I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. And so we come to the end of Saul, a Benjamite, son of Cis, or Kish as it is in the Old Testament. A man head and shoulders above the other men of Israel. Anointed by God to be their first king. And while Saul was most assuredly saved, his life as king was not the example of a Christian walk that we aspire too. We see him developing from a loyal son, seeking the lost donkey of his father, to an unsteady and uncertain leader, plucked from the least tribe of Israel, just a generation removed from their decimation for harboring sodomites. Every bit the part of king, but with none of the heart to lead. Saul spends his time as King worrying about what others think of him, what they may do or say. Caring about the world over the word of God. Indecisive. Prone to bad choices. And ultimately paranoid and wrathful, knowing the Lord had repented of his kingship and had chosen another to take his place. David, the apple of God's eye. A man after the Lord's own heart. Now to Saul and his sons would have been the promises given to David. But his transgressions against the Lord were too great. And even with warning after warning, Saul back slid further and further. Had this Saul repented, and confessed his sin and asked for forgiveness, he may have been restored. But he was blinded by the evil spirit given him by God for his disobedience. Seeking the witch of Endor was the final straw, and God gave him an ignoble death, and a fitting end, along with his sons. It is fitting that of all the people God could choose to use to spread the gospel to the Gentiles, He found a man of Benjamin named Saul, also known as Paul (his Roman name), the name and the tribe redeemed by Paul's dedication to the word of God. We see that, following his conversion on the road to Damascus, where he was blinded by God but restored by His word, when he sought out Ananias and was healed, Saul/Paul did his best to keep the word of God, and to not be castaway. Mortifying his flesh against sin. Preaching hard against backsliding and for separation from the world. A man who risked being rejected by his own people, being tortured, stoned, persecuted, arrested, held in bonds for years, and likely died for the cause of Christ. The two Saul's of Benjamin couldn't have been more different. But both were the anointed of God.

Here, in 2 Samuel 1 we learn of how David and his men in Ziklag learned of Saul and his sons' death at the hands of the Philistines. A son of a stranger, an Amalekite sojourning in Israel comes to the camp, and proclaims the king was defeated by the enemy, and all Israel smitten and fled. Pressed for details, he falsely claims that he came across a wounded Saul, begging for him to put him out of his misery. He tells David that he did just that, and with Saul's crown and a bracelet as evidence, he came to tell David thinking he'd win the praise of the exiled son of Judah, knowing that his enemy was dead. David has the man killed for his own testimony, that he had killed God's anointed. We, the reader know the truth, that Saul took his own life. But as David says, the Amalekite's own blood is upon him. The men of the camp rend their clothes and David mourns the loss of the king, and especially his son Jonathan, who was closer than a brother to him. Also he bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow, behold, it is written in the book of Jasher. This verse is mildly controversial, referencing a lost, deuterocanonical book, the Book of the Righteous, transliterated from Jasher. In the King James, this verse has use of the added before the bow to make it easier to understand. The bow being the preferred weapon of Jonathan, David instructed that the sons of Judah be instructed in it, to be proficient archers like his slain friend. Without having this apocryphal book, the preserved and inspired word of God gives us the only information we need about what it contains. Many forgeries claiming to be The Book of Jasher have been passed off over the years, but the important content is preserved by God for all ages. I personally believe there is a double meaning here, and that the Bow is also the name of the song David wrote to honor the mighty who have fallen, King Saul and Jonathan, lamenting their deaths, celebrating his friendship and calling all Israel to mourn. How are the mighty fallen is yet another wildly used phrase in popular culture, that comes from the beauty of the King James Bible translation. As an idiom, it has come to mean that someone once in power has been toppled. The song of David's mourning is far more valuable and insightful than just this poetic turn of phrase. We see David demonstrate true sadness at the loss of Saul. Forgiveness that he extended to someone who had been his bitter enemy for years. Someone who had tried to kill him multiple times. We expect the future king to mourn the loss of his beloved friend Jonathan, but his kind remembrance of the fallen first King of Israel, recalling his valiance and goodness to the daughters of Israel, shows the forgiveness that Christians should have towards one another. Especially in death, knowing that we ourselves will be transformed as fully new men, and our past sins forgotten and forgiven by the Lord. David strived to make peace with Saul while the king was alive. And in death, honored the Lord's anointed. No resentment or bitterness. But more; In the death of those who've hurt us, or were against us, we should also offer this spirit of forgiveness and let go of any enmity to those who may not have been saved. To our unsaved parents who've wronged us, to family we've felt betrayed us. To friends and neighbors and coworkers who may have done us wrong, without cause. We should let go of the animosity and hurt feelings we may have had, because we know that they have their punishment. That God is just and He will repay. We should only lament that they weren't won to Christ in life, and let go of the pain of the past. This attitude of forgiveness is one of the key aspects of Christian life. It is part of what allows us to live peacefully with all men. To have a productive life filled with love, joy and longsuffering. Building our faith. If you have animosity towards a brother or sister in Christ, let it go. And if they've passed on, joyfully look for them in the resurrection. And if it be that they never believed, rest easy knowing that the Lord is just. I hope those who skim my channel, the 100 or so daily visitors, stop for a moment and read that last post, and take it to heart. When you see the forgiveness of David, a man after God's own heart, you can learn from it and find peace.

Following the death of Saul, when Judah made David King over them, and a Benjamite captain, Abner made one of Saul's sons, Ishbosheth, king over the rest of Israel. David at first appealed to the men of Gilead, and others, but they followed after Abner. And eventually to rectify the matter, the two camps met at the pool of Gibeon, and agreed to allow a small battle of their respective camps to determine the matter.
