Twelve each, in what became known as the 'land of sharp blades,' Helkathhazzurim. David's men were victorious, and Abner beaten, fled. We hear of the hero Asahel, fleet of foot, who pursued the Benjamite captain. And Abner repeatedly sought to deter Asahel, wishing to spare him. But in the end Abner slew his pursuer, and made it to Benjamin to seek refuge. Seeing that the only resolution in this was an all out battle between Judah and Benjamin, Abner asked for peace and Joab, that captain of David's men held back from attacking. They returned to David and buried their Asahel as a hero. David lost 19 men total, Abner's men lost 360. First, we see David, a man after God's own heart, inquire of the Lord if he should go unto Judah, into Hebron. And the Lord answered saying yes. David further sought peace with the men of Israel, specifically Jabeshgilead who had honored Saul by retrieving his body from the enemy, and informing them all that Judah had anointed him king. A peaceful offer to do the same. Letting them all know he was willing to honor them. We see even though Abner's plans were different, that he took sought an outcome that was as peaceful as possible. They agree to a battle of champions, 12 vs 12. When that doesn't go his way, and he flees, Abner seeks peace with the one pursuing him. When the men of Judah arrive and see the gathered forces of Benjamin, again he cries out for peace. There is an honor in being a peacemaker. Regardless of the righteousness of the cause or the bitterness of the disagreement, or whatever else has been done to wrong the different parties. Especially between brothers. The most peaceful solution should always be sought, even when that solution is rejected and more forceful action is required. Even if peace creates an uneasy result, it is preferable than brothers going to war with one another. Matthew 5:9 Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God. If a brother is your enemy, and you have defeated him and he offers you a chance to let it go, you should consider it. Asahel did not. Joab did. And while both are heroes, one lived to fight another day. The other paid the price.

There is war between David and Judah and the son of Saul, Ishbosheth, under the hand of Saul's captain Abner. And David, King in Judah had many sons by many wives. The two he had taken in his exile bore him sons, and wives he took for himself in Hebron. Ahinoam bore Amnon David's firstborn, Abigail, Chileab. Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur who bore Absalom. Adonijah son by Haggith.his sixth sin Ithream, born of Eglah. All born heirs in Hebron. And yet David still desired his first wife, Michal. And while the conflict between Judah and Benjamin wore on, David grew stronger and Saul's house grew weaker. And when the former King's son accused his general Abner of going in to Saul's concubine, Abner had enough. And so the loyal servant grew determined to make peace and place David as King throughout all of Israel. He sent word to David and promised to deliver him the support of the elders of Israel. David agreed to meet and discuss peace, asking only that they bring him his espoused, Michal, whom Saul had given to another man. Agreeing, Abner took her from Phaltiel her illegitimate husband, bringing her to King David. (Phaltiel didn't take it well, following behind them, weeping until Abner sent him away). Abner gain support for David among the elders of Israel, and all recognized God's hand upon the king. In Hebron, David made a feast and agreed to peace, forgiving Abner, and sending him on his way to secure the support of David. But David's man, Joab and his band return to David and learning that Abner had been there, became furious. Their brother was Asahel, who had pursued Abner from the battle at the pool of Gibeon. Whom Abner begged to stop, before killing Asahel. Joab wanted revenge. And so the captain of David's men sent them to capture Abner and return him to Hebron. And in anger, Joab slew the Benjamite in revenge. When David hears this he becomes distraught, mourning greatly the loss of Abner, and making certain all Israel understood he played no part in his death. David curses Joab and his entire family. David ordered a day of mourning and he himself fasted until sundown. These things pleased the people of Israel, seeing him as innocent of the blood of Abner. Even as the anointed king, David commends Joab to the vengeance of God, saying let the Lord reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness. The theme of the last few chapters of 1st Samuel, and these opening chapters of 2nd, continues to be the right place for wrath and the importance of forgiveness. While David is not perfect, his taking of multiple wives, seemingly unsatisfied with those he had, even taking Michal back from her second husband, was sinful. But his love for God and trust in the Lord to carry him through, seeking peace with his enemies and leaving vengeance to the Lord made him a man after God's own heart. That kind of leadership pleased the people far more than the fear of Saul, who acted impulsively trying to please everyone but God.

Once again we see that the judgment of the world, taking vengeance for themselves, seeking favor by slaying David's enemies, is a sin in the eyes of the Lord. But forgiving and trying to make peace, trusting the Lord to judge, is the path we are told to take. As the Lord liveth, who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity...This is the faith we should have when we are beset by our enemies. They will either come to be friends or their own actions will be judged by God, but it is not our place to seek their hurt. We are supposed to love them, and pray for their well-being. Seeking peace. This is considered weakness by the world, but we see in the story of David how well it served him. The Lord delivered him out of all adversity, in His time, in His way. It is one of the hardest lessons of faith and longsuffering we can learn. Luke 6:27-38 But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you. And unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other; and him that taketh away thy cloke forbid not to take thy coat also. Give to every man that asketh of thee; and of him that taketh away thy goods ask them not again. And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise. For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them. And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same. And if ye lend to them of whom ye hope to receive, what thank have ye? for sinners also lend to sinners, to receive as much again. But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful. Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven: give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again. Proverbs 24:17-18 Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, And let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: Lest the LORD see it, and it displease him, And he turn away his wrath from him. It is important to note that both Saul and his son Ishbosheth were saved. David calls the son of the king "righteous." Enmity among brothers is a serious matter, and forgiveness between saved believers is commanded of us. Matthew 18:21-22 Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.... Jesus gives a parable of forgiveness and the destruction God the Father gives an unforgiving man, So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses. So let us pray for our enemies and trust in the living Lord to rightly judge, delivering us from our torment because we continuously seek out peace.

If you remember from Joshua 15, the Jebusites had been a remnant of Canaan that the Israelites had failed to remove from the land. As for the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out; but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day. Even unto the days of the prophet Ezra, centuries after David took Jerusalem from them, they were in the land, teaching their abominations to the children of Israel, along with other nations God had commanded to be destroyed. Ezra 9:1 Now when these things were done, the princes came to me, saying, The people of Israel, and the priests, and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the people of the lands, doing according to their abominations, even of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. But we see that under David, they were taken from the heart of Zion. This is a picture of the nature of sin in the Christian life. David is representative of Israel getting right. Walking in the Spirit. Accepting and doing God's will. Driving sin from your heart. As we see, this isn't permanent. As long as the flesh lives, we sin. And if we turn away from walking in the Spirit, doing what's right in God's eyes, it can fester and destroy us. We must crucify ourselves daily. Seeking the will of God. Now the Philistines, hearing of David's anointment, begin to come up against him and Israel. When we walk closer to Jesus, when we seek the things of God, the enemies of God will come against us. Tribulation will come. There's no getting around it. It may be family that turns against us. Mocking us. It could be coworkers and bosses. Friends who cut us off, hating us for His name's sake. The closer our walk, the more we live a Christian life, the more the world hates us. But as David does, seeking first the will of God, we can defeat them. We can smash their idols and burn their images. Purging the things of this world from our life and having victory in Christ. So never be discouraged. Trust in the Lord. And though you enter the valley of death, know He shall deliver you to the green grass beyond.

1 Chronicles 13 And David consulted with the captains of thousands and hundreds, and with every leader. 2 And David said unto all the congregation of Israel, If it seem good unto you, and that it be of the Lord our God, let us send abroad unto our brethren every where, that are left in all the land of Israel, and with them also to the priests and Levites which are in their cities and suburbs, that they may gather themselves unto us: 3 And let us bring again the ark of our God to us: for we enquired not at it in the days of Saul. 4 And all the congregation said that they would do so: for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people. 5 So David gathered all Israel together, from Shihor of Egypt even unto the entering of Hemath, to bring the ark of God from Kirjathjearim. 6 And David went up, and all Israel, to Baalah, that is, to Kirjathjearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up thence the ark of God the Lord, that dwelleth between the cherubims, whose name is called on it. 7 And they carried the ark of God in a new cart out of the house of Abinadab: and Uzza and Ahio drave the cart. 8 And David and all Israel played before God with all their might, and with singing, and with harps, and with psalteries, and with timbrels, and with cymbals, and with trumpets. 9 And when they came unto the threshingfloor of Chidon, Uzza put forth his hand to hold the ark; for the oxen stumbled. 10 And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzza, and he smote him, because he put his hand to the ark: and there he died before God. 11 And David was displeased, because the Lord had made a breach upon Uzza: wherefore that place is called Perezuzza to this day. 12 And David was afraid of God that day, saying, How shall I bring the ark of God home to me? 13 So David brought not the ark home to himself to the city of David, but carried it aside into the house of Obededom the Gittite. 14 And the ark of God remained with the family of Obededom in his house three months. And the Lord blessed the house of Obededom, and all that he had. Psalm 96 O sing unto the Lord a new song: sing unto the Lord, all the earth. 2 Sing unto the Lord, bless his name; shew forth his salvation from day to day. 3 Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people. 4 For the Lord is great, and greatly to be praised: he is to be feared above all gods. 5 For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the Lord made the heavens. 6 Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary. 7 Give unto the Lord, O ye kindreds of the people, give unto the Lord glory and strength. 8 Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name: bring an offering, and come into his courts. 9 O worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth. 10 Say among the heathen that the Lord reigneth: the world also shall be established that it shall not be moved: he shall judge the people righteously. 11 Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof. 12 Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice 13 Before the Lord: for he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth: he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth. King David's first thought at being anointed over all Israel was the restoration of the ark of God, and so he sought to return it from where it has been since being recaptured from the Philistines. During Saul's reign, he apparently never thought to do so. And they take it down to Jerusalem, singing praise and playing instruments and dancing before the Lord. But the oxen stumble, and Uzzah falters and touches the ark, disrupting the peace, and is struck down by God then and there. Was Uzzah's sin not trusting in the Lord to deliver His ark to the house of David? I think so. But his death set David back, and the king questioned his own wisdom in bringing the ark down. Fearing God he sought a sign and left the ark with the house of Obededom, the Gittite. It always makes me laugh thinking about how Obededom must have felt about that. But the grace of God was upon him, and his house blessed, and David knew it was God's will to finish the journey and bring the ark to His city. Where God had placed His name. Where Abraham had offered tithes to Melchizedek, to the Lord. Where Abraham offered Isaac. Where Christ would one day suffer and rise again in glory. David's first wife, Saul's daughter Michal, who had loved David, now despises him. And in her hatred she mocks the king for his celebration of God before the ark. Trying to shame him for his behavior. In the end her bitterness costs her a chance to bear an heir. She dies childless. Consumed by resentment towards her one time love, and the failures of her father. It's tragic, but all too common in this world today. Many women find themselves like Michal. Facing adversity and tribulation, they turn to misery and not to God. It is a sad, lonely life. Often ending in reprobation. It is important for fathers and mothers to show their daughters the love of Christ early and often, that they may believe and in faith accept what ever comes. Blessings and temptations. Having a solid foundation in Jesus.

Here in 2 Samuel 7, God gives us the foundation of the Davidic Covenant, the promise made to David that in his seed would come the Christ, and that son of David would rule His people forever. That in Jerusalem He would set Him. Nathan the prophet is introduced here, and this tiding to David, who has received what would have been Saul's. Another example of God giving to the second choice. The younger. And David humbly goes before the Lord, and praises Him, and in faith believes the promise. Let the house of thy servant be blessed forever. Amen. We as saved Christians are co-heirs with Christ, heirs to this promise, to be princes in the Kingdom of God. The Heavenly Kingdom ruled by Jesus, the Son of David. The Son of God. The living Lord. The judgements and discernment and the call to study to be approved by God, to understand His ways and to obey His commandments and to respect His hierarchy...it is all in training to be wise and just rulers, that we may rule and reign with Christ. To be faithful servants to the King of kings. To be as David was here, humble and faithful, with the fear of God guiding Him. Psalm 110 The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool. 2 The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies. 3 Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth. 4 The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. 5 The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath. 6 He shall judge among the heathen, he shall fill the places with the dead bodies; he shall wound the heads over many countries. 7 He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head. Matthew 22:41-46 While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them, Saying, What think ye of Christ? whose son is he? They say unto him, The son of David. He saith unto them, How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying, The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool? If David then call him Lord, how is he his son? And no man was able to answer him a word, neither durst any man from that day forth ask him any more questions. Acts 2:33-35 Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear. For David is not ascended into the heavens: but he saith himself, The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, Until I make thy foes thy footstool.

1 Chronicles 18 Now after this it came to pass, that David smote the Philistines, and subdued them, and took Gath and her towns out of the hand of the Philistines. 2 And he smote Moab; and the Moabites became David's servants, and brought gifts. 3 And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. 4 And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them an hundred chariots. 5 And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadarezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. 6 Then David put garrisons in Syriadamascus; and the Syrians became David's servants, and brought gifts. Thus the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went. 7 And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadarezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. 8 Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass. 9 Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah; 10 He sent Hadoram his son to king David, to enquire of his welfare, and to congratulate him, because he had fought against Hadarezer, and smitten him; (for Hadarezer had war with Tou;) and with him all manner of vessels of gold and silver and brass. 11 Them also king David dedicated unto the Lord, with the silver and the gold that he brought from all these nations; from Edom, and from Moab, and from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek. 12 Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the valley of salt eighteen thousand. 13 And he put garrisons in Edom; and all the Edomites became David's servants. Thus the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went. 14 So David reigned over all Israel, and executed judgment and justice among all his people. 15 And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, recorder. 16 And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Abimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Shavsha was scribe; 17 And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief about the king. Having been made king over all Israel, David establishes an empire, conquering the surrounding areas, from the city of Gath of the Philistines, where David had sought refuge, up to the Syrians and the border of the Euphrates River, and down to the Moabites and the Edomites over the Jordan, making all the surrounding nations into vassals paying tribute to Israel. David reserved the gold and brass and silver for the Lord, and God was with David in all he did. Critics of the Authorized Version of the King James Bible, and nonbelievers alike, will point to an apparent discrepancy in the telling of these events taken from 2 Samuel 8 and its parallel in 1 Chronicles 18, a matter of horsemen and chariots. David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates. And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: and David houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them for an hundred chariots. vs And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them an hundred chariots. The difference between the two numbers is "corrected" in many modern versions, while others leave it but attempt to change the wording in a way to square the seeming contradiction. But is there a contradiction? The number of chariots and horses, 100, remains consistent, as David cut the hamstrings of the other horses taken, and only kept 100 chariots. To me it reads that David did the same with the horsemen themselves, decimating them and reserving 700 out of 7000, for the hundred chariots and horses he reserved. Matthew Henry agrees with the King James reading and offers this explanation: "The horsemen are here said to be 700, but 1 Chronicles 18:4 they are said to be 7000. If they divided their horse by ten in a company, as it is probable they did, the captains and companies were 700, but the horsemen were 7000." The fact that God inspired the retelling of much of these histories in two places written years apart, for our own knowledge and admonition, is a blessing. That they have been preserved for us is a providential miracle. Seeming discrepancies that can be explained by simple understanding, comparing the two accounts, should be understood to be a different view of the same event, not in error but giving an additional detail not given in the other. Or a clarification of a point God wished us to have. That modern versions use these to cast doubt or to inject their own words is a mistake that comes from a lack of faith in the preservation of the word. And how do we know we can trust the KJV? If there's a discrepancy like this, could it be wrong? Thankfully, we can compare scripture with scripture; 2 Samuel 10:18 And the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew the men of seven hundred chariots of the Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen, and smote Shobach the captain of their host, who died there. 1 Chronicles 19:18 But the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand men which fought in chariots, and forty thousand footmen, and killed Shophach the captain of the host. And so we see that for 1000 chariots we have 7000 men, and so with the decimation of the company of chariots and horsemen, a 7-1 ratio, both accounts in Samuel and Chronicles are correct. Psalm 60 O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us, thou hast been displeased; O turn thyself to us again. 2 Thou hast made the earth to tremble; thou hast broken it: heal the breaches thereof; for it shaketh. 3 Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment. 4 Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah. 5 That thy beloved may be delivered; save with thy right hand, and hear me. 6 God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth. 7 Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the strength of mine head; Judah is my lawgiver; 8 Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe: Philistia, triumph thou because of me. 9 Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom? 10 Wilt not thou, O God, which hadst cast us off? and thou, O God, which didst not go out with our armies? 11 Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man. 12 Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.

1 Samuel 20:15-17 But also thou shalt not cut off thy kindness from my house for ever: no, not when the Lord hath cut off the enemies of David every one from the face of the earth. So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, Let the Lord even require it at the hand of David's enemies. And Jonathan caused David to swear again, because he loved him: for he loved him as he loved his own soul. Here in 2 Samuel 9, we see David, now King of Israel, honoring the covenant made with Jonathan, the son of Saul. He extends not only mercy and forgiveness to Mephibosheth, but provides him with his inheritance, servants to care for him, and that he shall eat at the king's table, forever. Mephibosheth is a picture of a sinner, seeking grace in the eyes of the King, who is a picture of Christ. He was crippled in youth, as we are in sin, and custom would have the heirs of the previous king killed, yet David not only pardons him that fate, but sets him up as an adopted son, welcome at his table. This is the mercy and grace we are to show to people. David, unlike the paranoid Saul, does this kindness and keeps his oath and is rewarded by the loyalty of Mephibosheth later during an uprising, when the young lord is betrayed by the servant, Ziba, who David had placed under him. (Ziba is a picture of the Jews who were unfaithful servants, as we will see in chapter 19) The world today would see David's actions as weak and foolish, but as we see again and again his faith in the Lord and willingness to forgive and make peace has led to David being strong, bringing the whole region under his control. Blessed by God, his enemies destroyed before him. This lesson, to be as David, to show the mercy and grace God showed us on others, is a lesson in faith.

1 Chronicles 19 Now it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his stead. 2 And David said, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me. And David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father. So the servants of David came into the land of the children of Ammon to Hanun, to comfort him. 3 But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun, Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee? are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land? 4 Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away. 5 Then there went certain, and told David how the men were served. And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return. 6 And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syriamaachah, and out of Zobah. 7 So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people; who came and pitched before Medeba. And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle. 8 And when David heard of it, he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men. 9 And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array before the gate of the city: and the kings that were come were by themselves in the field. 10 Now when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, he chose out of all the choice of Israel, and put them in array against the Syrians. 11 And the rest of the people he delivered unto the hand of Abishai his brother, and they set themselves in array against the children of Ammon. 12 And he said, If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee. 13 Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the Lord do that which is good in his sight. 14 So Joab and the people that were with him drew nigh before the Syrians unto the battle; and they fled before him. 15 And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem. 16 And when the Syrians saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they sent messengers, and drew forth the Syrians that were beyond the river: and Shophach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them. 17 And it was told David; and he gathered all Israel, and passed over Jordan, and came upon them, and set the battle in array against them. So when David had put the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. 18 But the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand men which fought in chariots, and forty thousand footmen, and killed Shophach the captain of the host. 19 And when the servants of Hadarezer saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they made peace with David, and became his servants: neither would the Syrians help the children of Ammon any more. Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the Lord do that which seemeth him good. Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the Lord do that which is good in his sight. This encouraging message of faith given by Joab before what could have been a haplessly outnumbered battle, with his forces split and surrounded, should be a mantra for Christians, especially Christian men. Too often today, professing Christian men come off as afraid, behave with no honor or duty to their people, and do not trust in the Lord to do what He sees as right. We see it daily, especially among the "conservatives," and even the more right-wing. Men, who seeing the odds and thinking that it's "so over," that the "West has fallen," either cower in fear, retreat from the world to hide, or take up blindly reactionary causes to "do something!" and force outcomes without any faith in the Lord to provide victory. But the Bible tells us again and again to have no fear. In the life of David we see that he behaved like a man, valiantly. Having the morality of God to guide him and following His word. Trusting in the Lord to deliver him and his people. And in his leadership, King David's faith and attitude trickled down to his captains, and from them to their men. And eventually to all Israel, rising up to put an end to the threats facing them, when God delivered victory against their enemies. That's the secret to winning. To win souls and obey God, live righteously and trust in Him when the battle comes.

The famous story of David and Bathsheba, and the King's gravest sins. Coveting, adultery, lying and murder. David not being with his men in battle during the time for war left him opportunity for sin. Idle hands are the devil's tools. His gaze falling on another man's wife and her nakedness, compounded by the covetous nature of the lust it stirred in him. His use of his station to bring her in unto him to lay with her. All stemming from that initial dereliction to his duty. A Christian who sins often finds themselves in that situation by a similar set of circumstances. We are to crucify our flesh daily and walk in the Spirit. The Bible tells us that we should wake in the morning in prayer. Beginning the day getting right with the Lord. But David tarried in bed, rather than in battle. And rather than refresh himself in the Spirit, thinking of the things of the Lord, he wandered. When we do that, blow off our commitments, "take a day off" from prayer or study, we often wander, too. Temptations that we would not normally experience present themselves, and with our minds not on the spiritual things of God, we can give in to them. Of course David's actions have consequences. Our Father often lets those consequences of our willful sin have repercussions that are for our admonition and instruction. A chance to make it right. And yet often our sinful nature leaves us making it worse. David seeks to cover up Bathsheba's pregnancy by sending for her husband, Uriah. Hoping the Hittite would take the opportunity of coming from the front lines to Jerusalem to visit his wife and lay with her, covering up the pregnancy. But Uriah has more honor than that, and refuses the comfort of home while his fellows are encamped for war. His commitment to his duty contrasting with David's initial dereliction. David tries again, all but ordering Uriah to his home, sending a feast from his own royal kitchen, and still Uriah stays with the guards and servants. David's attempts to get Uriah to do the wrong thing fail, so the King takes more desperate measures to cover for his sin. He orders his general, Joab, to send Uriah into the hottest of battles, that he may be smitten dead. David goes from a momentary lapse in duty and honor to premeditated murder. This is how Christians backslide. This is how sin compounds. Of course, David takes Bathsheba as his wife, one of many. He lives with his sin and the poor decisions he has made. But the Lord is displeased and David's actions won't remain hidden for long. Hebrews 12:6-7 For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? Hebrews 10:26-27 For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins, But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries. That fearful looking for judgment, the guilt we feel when we disobey God's word, the pangs of our conscience, is a powerful motivation to get right with the Lord. To call out to Christ our redeemer for forgiveness, to repent of our actions and seek to do the right thing. Especially knowing that, as adopted children, our Father will not spare the rod, and the sins we do in secret will be revealed in the light. Psalms 90:8 Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance. Proverbs 28:13 He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. Luke 8:17 For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.

Psalm 51:1-6 Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: According unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions. Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, And cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: And my sin is ever before me. Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: That thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest. Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; And in sin did my mother conceive me. Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: And in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom. Psalm 32 Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man unto whom the Lord imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile. When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah. I acknowledge my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah. For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: surely in the floods of great waters they shall not come nigh unto him. Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah. I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye. Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee. Many sorrows shall be to the wicked: but he that trusteth in the Lord, mercy shall compass him about. Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye righteous: and shout for joy, all ye that are upright in heart. Here in 2 Samuel 12 the prophet Nathan is sent by the Lord to expose David's sin in taking another man's wife and doing it dishonestly through murder. Nathan speaking the words of God tells David a parable of a rich man with abundant flocks who takes the poor man's only ewe. David is outraged at the story and demands the rich man be put to death for his lack of mercy, only to be told by the prophet that the rich man is the King. The Lord knows our secret sin, and the things we are ashamed of will be revealed in due time. But God is also merciful, in that while we may sin and while we may face temporal punishment for it, He will not impute our sin against us, because we are justified in Christ. And David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the Lord. And Nathan said unto David, The Lord also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. We who are saved in Christ shall not die. Our sin has been put away by the washing of the regeneration given to us by the Spirit, by trusting in the blood of the Lamb. But in this life we will be punished, that we may learn and the glory of God be known, not just by His mercy but His wrath. As an example for others. And so the prophet tells the king that David's wives will be taken from him, and what he did in darkness will be done to him in broad daylight. That the Lord would raise up evil against him from his own house. And finally, that the son Bathsheba gave him will surely die. David acknowledges his sin and understands his plight is of his own making, and ultimately accepts God's judgment against him. This is a model for us to follow. This is how we get right with God. And so David's son is stricken with illness, and for seven days the king refuses to eat or any comfort, hoping that God may repent and spare his son. But on the 7th day, his infant child dies. The servants are hesitant to tell the king, but David sees their whispering and asks is the child dead, and they say yes. David arises from his mourning and asks for food, and the servants are amazed that he took the news so well. But David says, while the boy lived he hoped that the Lord might turn from his judgement, but now that he's dead he knows he will someday see him again. This is the comfort we have in the death of a young child. That they are with Christ in Heaven. It is curious that many professing Christians teach the lie of original sin condemning infants, innocents who have not sinned themselves, and will often use Psalm 51 to do it, while the Psalm was written by David during his despair, saying he himself was wicked beyond measure, using hyperbole to describe his own condition in this very matter, not to condemn his own child. And so in time the Lord blessed David and Bathsheba with a son they name Solomon, telling Nathan to tell them to call him Jedidiah, because the Lord loved him. Solomon is the Lord showing them that they are forgiven, a sign of His grace towards them. Reconciled by a son, born to a king, whom the Lord loves. A sort of picture of Jesus. Meanwhile, the war against Ammon continued, and Joab has their capital in hand. He sends word to the absent King David to come with his armies to finish the job, lest Joab takes it and the crown himself. This is a jab at David for his dereliction that led to the sin with Bathsheba. And David does as Joab says, taking the city. Unlike previous conquests which were led by David and given victory by the Lord, where David took the spoil of gold and silver and dedicated to God, here he takes the golden crown for himself and places it upon his own head after a victory he played no real part in. And then subjecting the Ammonites to be servants of Israel, enslaving them, so soon after being forgiven by God. After all the mercy and grace God showed him, and for all his regret for what he had done, David seems to still not be fully right with the Lord. It is important to note that God primarily punished David for given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord. We who are professing believers are supposed to live like it. To be blameless before others. Not sinless, which is an impossible standard while we live in the flesh, but blameless. Trying to do the right thing, being a good example. Living like we have eternal life. Princes of the Kingdom. Keeping that perspective can be difficult at times. But forgiveness, mercy and grace, charitable love, meekly displaying the joy we have in the hope of Christ, goes a long way towards bringing others to the truth of Jesus. His light shining through us. And so when we wilfully sin, and bring shame on the gospel, giving great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, do not be shocked when you are chastened by the Lord.

There is a lot going on in this verse, but I wanted to focus on something, where Nathan the prophet says to David, after ripping face on him and his sin, he says "The Lord also hath put away thy sin." It's a faint assurance, that God won't kill him dead for his murder of Uriah and adultery with Bathsheba. But it's also a statement of David's being a saved son of God, who's sins are not imputed. Who shall not die, but have eternal life. We are punished here on earth for our sins. For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. Sometimes very harshly. Sometimes with death. And so God punished David, yet He put away David's sin, because he had the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ. His faith in God's word.

Leviticus 20:17 And if a man shall take his sister, his father's daughter, or his mother's daughter, and see her nakedness, and she see his nakedness; it is a wicked thing; and they shall be cut off in the sight of their people: he hath uncovered his sister's nakedness; he shall bear his iniquity. Deuteronomy 22:28-29 If a man find a damsel that is a virgin, which is not betrothed, and lay hold on her, and lie with her, and they be found; Then the man that lay with her shall give unto the damsel's father fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife; because he hath humbled her, he may not put her away all his days. Exodus 20:13 Thou shalt not kill. The continued consequences for David's sin and his poor example as father have begun to compound, just as Nathan prophesied. His multiple wives have led to near siblings lusting after another. David's growing comfort as King has led to his being soft with his sons, and esteeming their feelings and his feelings for them over the love of God and His commands. And so David's son Amnon is sick with desire for his half sister Tamar. Tamar is sister of Absalom, both children of David and his 4th wife Maacah, the daughter of Tamil, the king of Geshur. Under the subtle provocation of his cousin, Jonadab, who tells Amnon to fake like he's sick and ask for Tamar to come prepare food for him, he enacts the plot and takes the opportunity to rape his half-sister, who the Bible tells us was a virgin. As he begins to force her, she says to stay his hand and simply ask the King to give her as wife, a request she says David would grant. This, to me, says a lot about how spoiled David had made his sons. But it may have just been a desperate attempt by the princess. And as soon as Amnon has raped her, his feelings of lust are replaced by hate, hating her more than the love he'd previously felt. Often in sin, we crave what we ought not and then despise the thing we'd craved. It is the nature of sin. Pleasure for a moment and pain for a lifetime. The prince casts her out of his house, further compounding her shame. In anguish and no longer a virgin, Tamar rends her colorful dress that marked her chastity and returns to her brother's house. This thing done in secret is known throughout the kingdom. Absalom is furious and promises revenge. David hears and is angry, but does nothing. Had he followed the law of God, there were remedies. He could have had his son executed. He could have forced their marriage. But he did nothing for fear of his children more than the Lord. This sets in motion a series of terrible events. After two years of inaction, Absalom devises a plot for revenge. He calls all the brothers and even the King to the shearing of his flocks. David declines but the princes agree and go to the feast prepared as a trap for Amnon. And there, when Amnon was drunken, Absalom ordered his servants to murder the prince. The other brothers flee, Absalom as well, going north to his grandfather's Kingdom of Geshur. David at first hears that all his sons are dead, and suffers this anguish before the wicked cousin Jonadab tells him the news that it was only Amnon. The rest returned and mourned with David. And despite it all, David longed to reunite with Absalom, which would be soon enough. Parents do their children no favors by withholding punishment from them. God the Father scourges every son He receives. It should always be done in love, and appropriately, not to frustrate the child but to edify and bring them to understanding. Proverbs 13:24 He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes. The weakness of David for women, and his longing for his sons' earthly happiness kept him from loving them as he should. And he is reaping what he had sown.

And so, with Absalom self-banished to his grandfather's kingdom, and David yearning for his son, his captain, Joab seeks to get David to bring the prince home. To do so he has a woman go before the king with a story of her sons, one slaying the other and revengers seeking to take her remaining heirs life. David pledges that no one would harm her son, despite the blood on his head. And she speaks on, saying if the king ruled justly for her, then why is his own still banished? David discerned that it was Joab who put her up to this and why, and ordered Joab to fetch Absalom from Geshur. Is this right judgment? Absalom has not shown any sign of regret in his actions, taking a life of a brother in revenge and adding blood to the charge of Israel. In the woman's story, her son slayed his brother impulsively, in a fight. Absalom plotted and murdered Amnon deliberately and with guile. Amnon who himself should have been slain by the king for his wicked actions. Sin compounds. Absalom comes home but is not allowed to see his father. The Bible tells us of his outer beauty, his hair which he glories in, allowing it to grow out long, only cutting it once a year for the weight. But it says nothing about his heart except his own vanity. After 2 years, and not having audience with his father, he decides to force the issue with Joab by burning his barley fields. Joab takes the act of arson, and does what Absalom wishes and reunited the king with his son. But this behavior being rewarded again and again will have consequences.

And so, Absalom, having been forgiven and embraced by his father David for murdering his brother, begins to plot a coup. With vanity and flattery, he captures the hearts of Israel. He builds himself a small army, with horsemen and chariots. He subverts the judgment of the King by intercepting those come to seek judgment, and disingenuously pronouncing everyone who comes seeking resolution to a conflict as being right and just, while insinuating his father David is failing them. All under David's nose. With this support established, Absalom tells his father that he had vowed a vow to God for his 40th birthday, to return to his place of birth in Hebron to offer himself to the Lord. And so, blessed by David, the prince begins his seditious plan. Sending spies throughout Israel, he tells them when the trumpets sound, to announce that Absalom has been anointed king in Hebron. David's chief councilor, Ahithophel goes with Absalom as part of the conspiracy, and to grow the upstarts support. Eventually, David is informed of the plot and it's progress, and to protect the lives of the people of Jerusalem, he evacuates the city to the wilderness, to the mount of Olives, where Jesus so often went to preach and pray. David's humility and faith, and his concern for the bloodshed that would come up on Israel is contrasted with his son's disregard for the people, only seeking power. Lying about an oath to the living God, and misleading 200 men to accomplish it. David does leave behind some people. 10 of his concubines to keep the house. He sends the priest Zadok and his sons and the ark back to Jerusalem, saying it is where it belongs regardless of God's judgment upon him. Loyal servants follow David, and a testimony of one who had just arrived under David's house refused to leave him, even as the King gave him permission to flee and not face their fate. Ittai the Gittite, in my opinion, is a picture of a new believer in Christ, who comes to believe during tribulation. The messianic imagery of the loyal servants following the king into the wilderness to praise God during peril, a picture of the great tribulation. Especially that Gentiles like the Gittite are among them, while disloyal men of Judah plot the murder of the King. Hushai the Archite came to meet David, another council of his house. David says to return to the city and spy on Absalom and pass information on to the Zadok and Abiathar, to relay it to the king. And Absalom came into Jerusalem without a fight.

2 Samuel 12:7-12 And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul; And I gave thee thy master's house, and thy master's wives into thy bosom, and gave thee the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that had been too little, I would moreover have given unto thee such and such things. Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment of the Lord, to do evil in his sight? thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and hast taken his wife to be thy wife, and hast slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon. Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house; because thou hast despised me, and hast taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be thy wife. Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun. For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun. David continues his exile in the wilderness, passing through Benjamin. There he encounters Ziba, servant of Saul to whom David commanded keep watch over the lame son of Jonathan, Mephibosheth. Ziba has brought asses to ride and food and provisions for the king and his party. David enquires why, and Ziba claims Mephibosheth has gone to claim the throne in Jerusalem, but Ziba declares loyalty to David. This is a ploy by the servant to become master over the inheritance of Saul, and for now, it works. David grants Ziba control over the holdings, purchased by lies and a few hundred loaves of bread. Again Ziba represents the unbelieving Jews, who are bad servants seeking to steal the inheritance for themselves. Mephibosheth the sinners saved by the King. A picture of things to come. Then Shimei, of the house of Saul comes out and begins cursing David as he and his party pass. Throwing rocks and dust and shouting "Come out, come out thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial!" Blaming David for the downfall of Saul. David's men seek permission to behead him for his insolence, but David humbly accepts this as God's doing, and says if he suffers it perhaps God would bless him for it. It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day. Again, the meekness of allowing God to judge and repay, holding to His esteem rather than the esteem of men is what we as Christians are called to do. Then we see Absalom in Jerusalem has fallen under the sway of Ahithophel, who had advised his father before him, and now saw opportunity to have power through the rebellion of the son. Seeking his council, Ahithophel tells Absalom to go in until his father's 10 concubines that had remained in the palace, and take them for himself that the people of Israel would know he was utterly despised of David. Absalom not only does so, but sets up a tent on the roof that all Israel may see his sin. This fulfilling the prophecy given by Nathan that while David took a man's wife in secret, his would be taken before all Israel, in the sight of the sun. And more, on the same roof where David first coveted Bathsheba. Of course this is an abomination to the Lord and a grave sin under the law, but this was the sway Ahithophel held over the would-be king.

So Absalom has set himself up as king over Israel, defiled his father's wives in front of the people and under the sun, and now seeks David's life. Ahithophel, the wicked counsel who had betrayed David, advises Absalom to allow him choice men to ride and take David in the wilderness and slay him, and return his people to Jerusalem. Absalom is pleased with this plan, but Hushai, whom David had sent to be his man in Jerusalem and to counter Ahithophel, says instead to assemble an army out of all Israel and ride himself into battle against David. Ahithophel's council is rejected, and the author of the sedition goes and hangs himself. A picture of Judas who betrayed the anointed. Hushai gets word to the priests, Zadok and Abiathar, they get word to Jonathan and Ahimaaz via a wench, (a young girl or possibly prostitute), and the spies take off with word to David. But they are seen by a young boy who tells Absalom. The spies are hidden in a well by the woman of a house loyal to David, and finally make their harrowing way to the exiled King. Absalom assembles a host of men, and places Amasa as its captain over Joab, and pursued David into Gilead. David crosses the Jordan unto Mahanaim and there the sons of Ammon, Lodebar and Gilead all come to give him provisions, in return for the blessing David had been to them in the past. The only reason this has not been adapted for mass entertainment is the glory to God and the picture of Christ found throughout the story of Saul, David, Solomon and Samuel. It is a compelling tale of intrigue and war and relationships that Hollywood constantly seeks to emulate. But they can only pump out pale imitations full of corruption and profanity.

Psalm 9 I will praise thee, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will shew forth all thy marvellous works. 2 I will be glad and rejoice in thee: I will sing praise to thy name, O thou most High. 3 When mine enemies are turned back, they shall fall and perish at thy presence. 4 For thou hast maintained my right and my cause; thou satest in the throne judging right. 5 Thou hast rebuked the heathen, thou hast destroyed the wicked, thou hast put out their name for ever and ever. 6 O thou enemy, destructions are come to a perpetual end: and thou hast destroyed cities; their memorial is perished with them. 7 But the Lord shall endure for ever: he hath prepared his throne for judgment. 8 And he shall judge the world in righteousness, he shall minister judgment to the people in uprightness. 9 The Lord also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble. 10 And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, Lord, hast not forsaken them that seek thee. 11 Sing praises to the Lord, which dwelleth in Zion: declare among the people his doings. 12 When he maketh inquisition for blood, he remembereth them: he forgetteth not the cry of the humble. 13 Have mercy upon me, O Lord; consider my trouble which I suffer of them that hate me, thou that liftest me up from the gates of death: 14 That I may shew forth all thy praise in the gates of the daughter of Zion: I will rejoice in thy salvation. 15 The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: in the net which they hid is their own foot taken. 16 The Lord is known by the judgment which he executeth: the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands. Higgaion. Selah. 17 The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God. 18 For the needy shall not always be forgotten: the expectation of the poor shall not perish for ever. 19 Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail: let the heathen be judged in thy sight. 20 Put them in fear, O Lord: that the nations may know themselves to be but men. Selah. Here we see the final end for Absalom. He betrayed the King and ended up hanging from a tree, only to be brought down, belly burst from the darts of Joab, and buried in a field with no sons or legacy but his betrayal. And David wept, mourning for his lost son. Absalom is a picture of Judas, that man of perdition who betrayed Christ for earthly gain. Hung and split open and buried in an unmarked grave. In a like manner, the Bible says God's will is that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. And it grieves the Father when men perish in their sins, without Jesus. Now Psalm 9 is often called 'The death of the son," and it is believed by some to be written by David following Absalom's end, praising God and calling upon the Lord to show mercy on believers and to show judgment against the unbelieving, to put fear upon them that they may know they are but men, and that the Lord will always prevail. Joab has again gone against the King and taken the blood of David's enemies against his will. David's cries for Absalom will cause some conflict with the general in the next chapter.

Absalom is dead and the King weeps for his lost son, despite the betrayal. And practical Joab, his general tells David that his sorrow for his son who had risen up all Israel against David and his people is making those loyal to him feel shame. That David hadn't appreciated what a threat Absalom was, and what they risked in defending David. And so David is rebuked and takes back up the mantle of King. He sends to Judah the priests, and shames the men of Judah who had supported Absalom in the rebellion, into coming to call back David to Jerusalem, and David and his people begin their journey back over the Jordan to the promised land. Absalom is a picture of the antichrist, and the rise of the false king put in power by men of Judah. David and his loyalists, the persecuted believers. The restoration of the king, the millennial reign. And the forgiveness of David a picture of Christ. One by one we see those that had blessed David be rewarded, those that had cursed David forgiven when mercy is asked for with Shimei. Ziba the unfaithful servant comes, and Mephibosheth whom Ziba had accused of betrayal arrives and David sees that the son of Jonathan had been faithful this whole time. David to bring peace between them orders that they share the inheritance, but Mephibosheth says let Ziba have it all, that he just wished to be with David in the kingdom. A picture of the Jews and their obsession with the land, and the Christian rather seeking the kingdom. The men of Israel come down to David as he makes his way back to Jerusalem, angry at Judah for not including them in bringing back the king. The initial seed of the rift that will manifest after Solomon's death and the dividing of the kingdom. In my opinion there is a picture here of the believing Jews after Pentecost, and the other nations who should be partakers in the kingdom being shut out by the failure of the church at Jerusalem to preach to the Gentiles at first, as exemplified in Acts 10, by Peter being sent by the Spirit to Cornelius to win him and his house to Christ; While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word. And they of the circumcision which believed were astonished, as many as came with Peter, because that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the Holy Ghost.

Chapter 20 of 2 Samuel picks right up from the end of 19; where the other tribes of Israel come down to Judah to complain they were not called to bring King David back from his exile; And, behold, all the men of Israel came to the king, and said unto the king, Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away, and have brought the king, and his household, and all David's men with him, over Jordan? And all the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, Because the king is near of kin to us: wherefore then be ye angry for this matter? have we eaten at all of the king's cost? or hath he given us any gift? And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, and said, We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more right in David than ye: why then did ye despise us, that our advice should not be first had in bringing back our king? And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel. But all Israel had backed Absalom in his coup attempt and their heart was not with him, despite their claim to having more part in David than Judah. Here in chapter 20, when the reprobate Sheba, of Benjamin comes and says "We have no part in David," the men of Israel depart to follow Sheba. It is interesting to note that Sheba, a son of Belial, a reprobate says also "Neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse," which is, ultimately Jesus Christ. He is the inheritance, the root of Jesse, promised to David by the Lord. David returns to his house, and put the concubines defiled by Absalom away, as widows. Cared for but no longer David's to go in unto. David calls to Amasa, the general Absalom had elevated over Joab during the insurrection. When David returned across the Jordan, Amasa had begged for mercy and David diplomatically kept him as a captain, and here tells him to pursue after Sheba, to nip this new civil war in the bud. The king orders Amasa to make haste to prevent the rebel from reaching a fortified city, giving him three days to muster and depart. But Amasa took his time, and delayed and likely was giving Sheba time to get away. And so David orders Abishai to gather Joab and his men to take off after Sheba. Amasa joins them, going to the front to lead them, and Joab comes to him subtly and pretends to be greet his rival, and when Amasa leans in, Joab stabs him and leaves him to die. Yet another murder by Joab. Yet another time where Joab's doing right in his own eyes led to his second guessing the King. Joab is a faithful servant to the King, but he leans on his own understanding and executed his own judgement repeatedly. Like many believers, he would choose what was expedient over what his master willed. Taking matters into our own hands, we may think what sins we do are justified by the outcome we are seeking, that the ends justify the means. But the Bible teaches us faith and patience, especially in trouble, temptation and tribulation. After the murder of Amasa, the men choose to follow after Joab, to finish their mission. And finding Sheba in the city of Abel, they set to besiege them. But a wise woman of the city calls to Joab and asks if he is willing to slaughter them to do it, and Joab says he would rather not. Aho she strikes a bargain with him, and after consulting with the people of Abel, they kill Sheba and throw his head over the wall to Joab, in peace. And Joab retires his men and returns to Jerusalem, captain of the guard again. And David's government is reestablished.

As we move into the final chapters of 2 Samuel, the narrative is no longer a chronological telling, but a sort of summary of events that occurred outside the main narrative, given by God for example and instruction. The first half of chapter 21 deals with a crime of Saul that has had lingering repercussions for Israel. Saul had gone and killed men of Gibeon. The Gibeonites were the city of Canaan that had tricked Joshua into a vow of non-aggression back in Joshua 9. Joshua swore before God without consulting the Lord, that no harm would come to them after they presented themselves as impoverished strangers from a far land, rather than their near neighbors, afraid of the Israelites. Joshua, upon finding out their trickery kept the vow, but made them be laborers for Israel. Now, years later, Saul in his zeal had gone to smite them and drive them from the land. David, now king, faced a famine that had lasted years. He inquired of the Lord, and He said it was due to the blood shed by Saul against the Gibeonites. To make peace with God and repay the blood debt, David offers up 7 sons of Saul, including the five sons of his first wife, Michal, daughter of Saul who had been given to another man during David's exile. She had despised David in the end and this likely did nothing to improve that relationship. He also took two sons of Rizpah. David spared Mephibosheth because of his vow to Jonathan. The Gibeonites hanged the men, and as the harvest began, Rizpah mourned in sackcloth upon the rocks of the field, from the beginning of the harvest to the later rain. David, moved by her mourning went and gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabeshgilead, and the seven sons, and delivered them to the sepulchre of Kish, that they may sleep with their fathers. And this pleased the Lord and the famine ended. The second half of the chapter deals with wars against the Philistines, and David's eventually being too old to go out to battle, falling faint. The sons and brother of Goliath sought to slay David and the Israelites, and all were killed by the hand of David and his servants. There is a controversy created by modern Bible versions that incorrectly claim that it was Goliath himself killed by Elhanan, which of course creates a contradiction in scripture, as David famously slew the giant. Check out these posts from a brother Just to put a pin on this, we know that the KJV is correct and the LXX and other sources wrong, because of 1 Chronicles 20:5 And there was war again with the Philistines; and Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear staff was like a weaver's beam. God preserves His word for all time. Without error. Amen

Note, this song of David is found in Psalm 18:1-50, with slight changes to the lyrics. 2 Samuel 22 being spoken unto the Lord, Psalm 18 as given to the chief musician for accompaniment. The praise of the LORD God as the rock, and the God of the rock of salvation, and clear imagery of God's might, the protection He extends to those that are His, God's recompense for our keeping to His statutes and walking in His paths, the wrath against our enemies, and deliverance from our affliction coupled with the understanding of spiritual salvation and undertones of Christ, the shield of salvation, and the mercy towards us in the Lord are key themes. As we saw during key points of David's life, as much as it lay within him, he tried to live peaceably with all men. He trusted in the Lord. He rarely did what seemed expedient to others, preferring to wait on the Lord. The few times David did what was right in his own eyes, he was sorely punished, and accepted the chastening of God with regret and repentance. And in all things gave thanks and praise to God.

The end of David's life is come, and the final words of the King are recorded, and they begin with a beautiful recitation of faith and doctrine. David, the anointed of God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel, acknowledges that he was inspired by God, Who spoke through him in the Psalms. In case there was any doubt about the inspiration of the Psalms of David, which were quoted throughout the New Testament by Jesus and the Apostles. The Spirit of the Lord spake by me, and His word was in my tongue. David goes further to say the God of Israel, the Rock of Israel, spake to him and advised that he as King must be just, ruling in the fear of God. This is the truth, and a standard that David, being human didn't always achieve. But it is undeniable as we read his life story that he strove to rule as a God fearing judge, with mercy and faith. An example in patience and longsuffering for Christian believers. He tried to be as the light of the morning, which is how Jesus is described in scripture, that the people of Israel would be as the tender grass covered in dew springs forth at the light. Putting the profit of others before himself, something we are commanded to in scripture; Philippians 2:3-5 Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus David is a picture of the king as servant. A picture of Christ, and an example for us who follow after Jesus. David then says; Although my house be not so with God; yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure: for this is all my salvation, and all my desire, although he make it not to grow. What a wonderful description of salvation! Although his house was not always right with God, his sin and the sin of his sons, still God had made a covenant with David in Jesus, the everlasting Kingdom to come of his seed. His salvation, and all David wanted. The Lord delivered regardless of David's worthiness and his own humble acknowledgement that it was undeserving, but for the grace of God. David says that despite God delivering him and all he desired, all the good things that came from God, the Lord kept him from coveting more. Leaving him satisfied. We know that wasn't always true, but it wasn't of God when David coveted Bathsheba, but his sin was punished in this life, and David is looking at his eternal life to come, where his sin is remembered no more. 2 Samuel 23:5 is such a wonderful testimony of the grace of God and the undeserved favor of His promises and salvation, that of course modern perversions twist it to mean the opposite; a picture of salvation by grace and not of works changed to make grace no more grace. To make the blessings, promises and covenant David received, including his salvation, into something he worked to deserve. Only the KJB renders this verse properly, in the context of David's life and without any contradiction of the gospel of grace. David then begins to give praise and honor for his mighty men, the Thirty, (although there are 37 named, and one hinted at but left out), providing a form of immortality that even today thousands of years later, we know their name, their people and their exploits. Again, David humbly giving credit where it is due, rather than to himself. The list is extensive, and some we know from other places in the Bible, and others only appear here and in 1 Chronicles 11, where a similar list is given. One noticeably absent name, although he is mentioned several times, but never given honor himself; Joab. I suspect Joab was one of the second three, who is skipped over in the telling. Likely due to his eventual betrayal of David, but his absence is something that stands out. The rest of these men of valor, who slew multitudes of the enemies of Israel, giants and hosts of men, all in service to the King, were clearly dear to David. And the most tragic of all, is the final mention of Uriah the Hittite, whom David had murdered after committing adultery with his wife.

The final chapter of 2 Samuel tells a tale from some point in King David's reign, where God is angry with the people of Israel, and in His anger he allows Satan to tempt David into sin that they may be punished. And so David comes to desire a census of the people, ordering Joab and his captains to number the people. David as king wants to know the number of men for his own purpose, and neglects to do it in accordance with the word of God. The Lord requires a tithe of a half shekel at the numbering, to support the tabernacle and His priests. Something the sweet psalmist of Israel should know, as David writes in the Psalms, O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day. And yet... So with the numbering done the wrong way and the punishment in Exodus being a plague against Israel, the means and reason for punishment are established because David did not resist Satan in this thing. God sends a prophet named Gad to tell David of His displeasure, and the Lord offers David a choice of punishment, (though we know from Exodus how this will end up going) and David throws himself and all Israel on the mercy of the Lord. The angel of death comes upon them, and 70,000 men are slain. But as the destroyer came to Jerusalem, the Lord repents and stays the angel's hand, by the threshing floor of Araunah. This is similar in a way to the Great Tribulation; Matthew 24:21-22 For then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be. And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened. Jesus tells us that for the sake of the believers on earth midway through the Tribulation, before the Rapture and the wrath to follow, God cuts short the works of the beast, least no flesh remain. And David as a picture of Christ, takes on the sin of Israel and asks the Lord to punish him alone for the sake of his "sheep." God through the prophet Gad, speaks to David and tells him to set up an altar at the threshinghouse, and David buys the place and the animals for sacrifice which Araunah had offered to give, knowing that David must pay for the sins of the people that the plague may be stayed. Just as Jesus paid it all that we be spared Hell. This is a pretty deep story, and it can be confusing because it relies on knowledge of scripture to discern what exactly is going on. Especially when the sin of David is not spelled out and the account in 1 Chronicles 21 adds Satan into the mix. But like anything else in the Bible, the answer to our confusion is found by comparing scripture with scripture. Too often, Christians can be led away with foolish doctrine because they don't know the word of God. Satan will tempt us when God allows it, and often our reaction is used by God to get our attention, to show us our error. To give us a chance to get right, as in this case. God always provides a means of escape; 1 Corinthians 10:13 There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. And the means of Satan's testing begins with making us either question the word of God (Ye, hath God said?) or taking advantage of our ignorance that we may be led into sin; Hosea 4:6 My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children. The law of God is perfect. It serves a wonderful purpose. It allows us to have knowledge and understanding of the mind of the Lord, and His will for us. People get bogged down in theology and vain philosophy of men, and lose sight of the purpose of the word. Christians should study to be approved before God, reading His word daily, our daily bread. The words of eternal life given to us by the inspiration of God. Wrapping up 2 Samuel is bittersweet. The story of David is told again in 1 Chronicles, but it is for a different purpose and while equally important, there's something about the humanity of David in Samuel that resonates with me. I hope everyone takes the time to read through the scripture I have presented, even if you scroll past my commentary. I may take a few days to explore some other parts of the Bible before resuming with 1 Kings. Exodus 30:11-16 And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the Lord, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them. This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the Lord. Every one that passeth among them that are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering unto the Lord.The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when they give an offering unto the Lord, to make an atonement for your souls. And thou shalt take the atonement money of the children of Israel, and shalt appoint it for the service of the tabernacle of the congregation; that it may be a memorial unto the children of Israel before the Lord, to make an atonement for your souls. Malachi 3:8-10 Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings. Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation. Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it. 1 Chronicles 21:1-7 And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel. And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people, Go, number Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it. And Joab answered, The Lord make his people an hundred times so many more as they be: but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord's servants? why then doth my lord require this thing? why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel? Nevertheless the king's word prevailed against Joab. Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem. And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David.
