Offering sacrifice to them. They have the appearance of righteousness but are still evil in His sight. This is why the push by Catholicism to establish a "Christian Nationalist" fervor in America as an answer to the wickedness of the godless sodomites and Jews is so appealing to so many. But we see over and over again in God's word that it isn't enough to say you are worshiping God when you are doing it your way. Man's way. It is His way or nothing. And so the King of Moab, who had paid tribute to Ahab rebels against the son, and refuses to pay what was promised to Israel. Jehoram seeks war. The King of Israel goes to Jehosaphat, King of Judah and asks if he will aid him, and of course, faithful Jehosaphat agrees. They go by way of Edom and the King of Edom joins them with his armies. But as they pass on the way to Moab, they cannot find water for their men or their cattle, and are afraid their campaign is over before it begins. But Jehoshaphat, faithful to the Lord, asks if there is a prophet they can ask for guidance. Jehoram says yes, and they call for Elisha. Elisha makes it clear that he has no respect for Jehoram, and is only responding due to the faith of the King of Judah. He tells them to dig trenches, and the Lord would provide the water. But that they had to utterly destroy Moab. Ruining wells and fields. They dig and the water comes by way of Edom. They drink. But Moab looks towards their camp and sees the water reflected red as blood and assumes the three kings turned on one another. Racing for spoil, they meet the armies of the 3 kings and are defeated, retreating to Moab where the armies kill the men and destroy the wells and fields. But they leave one city, attacking it but not putting the stones in the field. Falling short of their promise. The King of Moab desperately offers his only male heir to the fire, sacrificed to his false gods to no avail.

Reading this chapter, it should stand out how similar in form and content it is to how the Gospels are written. The anointed one of God going forth and having average people come to him seeking something, and miraculously receiving it by faith. Parallels with Christ are there; Elijah as John the Baptist, a voice in the wilderness, Elisha as he who came after him, with twice the spirit of the Lord upon him. The sons of the prophets as disciples. Bringing the word of God to the people. In the first story, we find a certain woman, wife of a man of God, a believer in the Lord. Her husband's death, leaving them in debt. Her and her sons, about to be sold into bondage to pay it. Elisha asks what does she have, and she replies only a little oil. He tells her to go out to her neighbors and ask for empty containers, and not a few. As many as she can get, and fill them from the pot. And she does as he says, acting on her faith. She fills every vessel they have, and yet there was still more in the pot. She tells Elisha, who says go and sell them and pay her debt, and her and her sons live off what's left over. In scripture, oil is almost always a picture of the holy Spirit. Debt and bondage, sin and the wages of sin, which is death. Her husband feared the Lord. He left her with nothing but oil. The Spirit. And she takes that oil and fills the vessels of her neighbors and more. Just as we who are saved are filled with the Spirit, and we can fill others, as vessels, infinitely. It never runs out. The Spirit is enough to not only pay for our debt but to live on, forever. As men, we should do well to leave our wives and children that inheritance. Greater than any other, the surety of the Spirit in our house, by faith in Christ Jesus. The second story, of the Shunammite woman, a great woman the Bible says, has similar parallels. She, understanding that Elisha is a holy man of God, not only feeds him daily bread, but makes room for him in her house. Setting up a bed, chair and table, with a candlestick, in a chamber for him to come into. This is a clear picture of how we are to seek to place Christ, the holiest Man of God, in our hearts. She sought first the daily bread, the word of God. And by faith that comes from the word, perceive the truth of Christ, in her case that Elisha was of God. And then make room in our hearts for Christ to come into and stay. The candlestick, often a symbol of the Spirit. The light of God that shines forth from believers. And the woman did all this not wanting for anything in return, but the prophet through his servant asks, what does she truly desire. Just as the Spirit brings our prayers to God through Christ. Romans 8:26-27 Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God. Gehazi the servant may also be as a picture of a believer, praying on behalf of another. The Shunammite woman longs for a son. Her husband great in years, she has been left childless. Elisha through Gehazi, his messenger, tells her that her desire will be granted and she will bear a son, miraculously. Again, an echo of the angel Gabriel, a messenger of God, telling Mary of a miraculous birth. Also of Sarah, etc. God opens and closes wombs. And sure enough, she bears a son. And when he has grown enough to go with his father to the reaping of the harvest (another common picture of soul winning), that he said unto his father, My head, my head. They took the boy to his mother, and he died in her arms. She places the dead boy in the chamber she had prepared for Elisha. Again, a symbol of her own heart and the space she made for God. She asks for an ass and a rider to bring her to Elisha. From afar off, he sees her and recognizes her, but says he doesn't know why she came. God had not revealed it to him. (I find that interesting, that the humanity and lack of omniscience reminds us that he is just a man, only a picture of Christ, not actually Christ) He sends his servant, Gehazi, to ask her if all is well, and she tells the servant yes. But when she reaches the prophet, she throws herself at her feet, lamenting her child. The pain of being given what she asked for, but losing it is likely far worse than if she'd never been given him at all. At least in that moment. You can really feel for her as a parent. Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me? Heartbreaking. Elisha sends his servant, saying to slow down or stop for nothing, and lay my staff upon the face of the child.The mother, with Elisha, follow behind. Gehazi comes back to meet them saying the staff did not work. Elisha himself comes into the house, finding the son dead. Elisha shuts the door and lays upon the child, praying to the Lord. He leaves the child and paces the house, and returns and lays upon him again and the child sneezed, 7 times (symbolic of something, seven being a number of perfection of the Lord). And so, the son was alive. And he called Gehazi, and said, Call this Shunammite. So he called her. And when she was come in unto him, he said, Take up thy son. Then she went in, and fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground, and took up her son, and went out. Next, we find Elisha in Gilgal, where there is a famine in the land. He tells his servant to set a pot for pottage, to make a stew to feed the sons of the prophets, (again a term meaning believers or disciples, in my opinion). And one went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full, and came and shred them into the pot of pottage: for they knew them not. They go to eat and realize that the gourds of the wild vine have apparently poisoned the stew. The allegory here shows how a group of saved believers, of the true vine that is Christ, welcoming in the fruit of a wild vine, can lead to death. O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof. Just as Peter warns the churches of Christ in the NT; 2 Peter 2:1-2 But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction. And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of. But Elisha adds to the stew some meal, the ground barley that makes bread, and casts it into the pot, and makes it safe to eat again. Just as the word of God preached, the daily bread, can cleanse a church of the false doctrines of false teachers. Finally, this story; And there came a man from Baalshalisha, and brought the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley, and full ears of corn in the husk thereof. And he said, Give unto the people, that they may eat. And his servitor said, What, should I set this before an hundred men? He said again, Give the people, that they may eat: for thus saith the Lord, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof. So he set it before them, and they did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the Lord. A familiar miracle, one Christ did many times; feeding the masses with but a few loaves of bread. If the bread is a representation of the word of God, you can see how, as His servants, we can "feed" an unlimited number of people, giving them the bread of life. The words of eternal life that Christ Jesus brought down from Heaven. The bread that, if eaten, means ye shall never hunger again. So he set it before them, and they did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the Lord. John 6:63-69 It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life. But there are some of you that believe not. For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him. And he said, Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father. From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God.

Here in 2 Kings 5, we find the Syrian captain, Naaman, stricken with the incurable disease, leprosy. And a servant girl, captive out of Israel, tells Naaman's wife of the prophet of the Lord in Samaria, that is Israel. With permission of his king and loaded with treasure, Naaman and servants go into the King of Israel, asking he be recovered of his leprosy. The king becomes upset, thinking this is a trap. How can he heal a man of something that is untreatable? The King of Syria would hold it against him, he rends his clothes in distress. Elisha heard of this and sends for Naaman, and when the Syrian comes to him, the prophet's servant comes to him with a message; Wash yourself in the Jordan seven times and be healed. At first, Naaman is offended. He expected the man of God to come and lay hands and make a show and heal him there in the spot. He questions why he just go to the Jordan, when Syrian rivers are superior in his mind, and more convenient. But his servants convince him to try, and he does as the prophet said, and is healed. Cleaned of the leprosy. He returns to Elisha, and confesses that now he believes there is no other God in all the earth, but in Israel. And he offers the treasure he has brought to the prophet. Elisha refuses, in the name of the Lord. Naaman asks then for two burdens of earth, soil from Israel, that he would make sacrifices of burnt offerings only to the Lord. As he had previously believed the waters of the rivers were different in Syria, now he assumes the mounds of Israeli dirt would matter in the sacrifice to God. He also asks for pardon, for Elisha's blessing, that when he returned to Syria, that when he went in to the house of Rimmon, a temple to idols, and bow himself down, that the Lord forgive him. He is indicating that while he believes that the Lord is the only true God, he would still go before idols and bow down before them, because of custom and what others might think. Asking for permission, and the Lord's blessing to be unfaithful to the Lord he proclaimed, Elisha offers nothing, but says "Go in peace." Whether Naaman actually believed on the Lord is doubtful. He seemed caught up in the moment and the miracle that had occurred, and yet still carnal. Seeing the water as important, rather than following the word of God. Seeing the soil as different. Pledging with one hand to worship only the Lord, and at the other admit he would continue in the false religion of his people. In many ways, this is the experience many have when given the Gospel. They are resistant to the truth, show doubt and disdain when told there is only one way to salvation, faith in Christ Jesus. They may taste of the Heavenly gifts as the Spirit works in them to help bring them to the truth. They may even confess that this IS the truth, and they promise they will do whatever it takes to convince God, the person who gave them the gospel, other Christians. But in the end, they are already thinking about the ways they will back out of their promise. They are already back to their old beliefs before the words of the promise had come out of their mouths. They never accepted the truth in their hearts. They are like the seed sown on the pathway in the parables of the Sower; Behold, a sower went forth to sow; And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up. When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side. An all too common occurrence. Some get confused by Elisha's telling him to go in peace, that by this he was blessing Naaman's request to pardon his sin of returning to the worship of his false gods. But really, he doesn't acknowledge it, and politely sends him on his way. It may also be why he refused any of the rewards. Not just for keeping himself from filthy lucre, but that it wasn't a sincere conversion and Naaman may well have taken the wrong idea, that he could buy God's favor. But we see covetousness and greed strike Elisha's servant Gehazi, who rides after and makes up a story to get some of that silver and clothing for himself. He then lies to Elisha when he returns, but the Lord reveals to the prophet the truth. And so, fittingly, Gehazi is stricken with leprosy, and cursed to his entire lineage. There's also a lesson here for saved Christians. Those who are the rocky soil, who receive the truth of the word with gladness and hope, but because they have no root in themselves, with her and die without producing fruit. It is possible to receive the gospel and believe unto salvation and yet return to the same old life. Healed, washed, clean and reborn the way the Syrian Captain was, and yet living in the old flesh doing the same old things. Seeking pardon for not living the way you should, knowing that you've been forgiven. Of course, if good works and sanctification came automatically with salvation, the New Testament wouldn't be filled with encouragement from the apostles to do good works. To pursue sanctification by walking in the spirit rather than in the flesh. To feed the new man rather than the old. It's also why we are to disciple those that we help lead to Christ. Or to be edifying and supportive in the lives of those who we come across. Encouraging them to walk in the Spirit. There are quite a few professing Christians and even entire denominations that teach that works come automatically, and without evidence of a changed life, we should doubt the salvation of someone. While faith without works is dead, not being profitable to others, and we are justified before men by our good works, we should be careful to be understanding rather than judgmental. To encourage rather than condemn. We have all been as Naaman, excited about the Lord and turning back towards the things that we were trusting in before. We should have some Grace and understanding for people who aren't where we are in our spiritual walk. Not to condone sin. But to not be confrontationally judgmental. Elijah could have lectured Naaman. But he told him to go in peace. I think there's a lot that can be taken from that.

2 Kings 6 8 Then the king of Syria warred against Israel, and took counsel with his servants, saying, In such and such a place shall be my camp. 9 And the man of God sent unto the king of Israel, saying, Beware that thou pass not such a place; for thither the Syrians are come down. 10 And the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of, and saved himself there, not once nor twice. 11 Therefore the heart of the king of Syria was sore troubled for this thing; and he called his servants, and said unto them, Will ye not shew me which of us is for the king of Israel? 12 And one of his servants said, None, my lord, O king: but Elisha, the prophet that is in Israel, telleth the king of Israel the words that thou speakest in thy bedchamber. 13 And he said, Go and spy where he is, that I may send and fetch him. And it was told him, saying, Behold, he is in Dothan. 14 Therefore sent he thither horses, and chariots, and a great host: and they came by night, and compassed the city about. 15 And when the servant of the man of God was risen early, and gone forth, behold, an host compassed the city both with horses and chariots. And his servant said unto him, Alas, my master! how shall we do? 16 And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them. 17 And Elisha prayed, and said, Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the Lord opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha. 18 And when they came down to him, Elisha prayed unto the Lord, and said, Smite this people, I pray thee, with blindness. And he smote them with blindness according to the word of Elisha. 19 And Elisha said unto them, This is not the way, neither is this the city: follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom ye seek. But he led them to Samaria. 20 And it came to pass, when they were come into Samaria, that Elisha said, Lord, open the eyes of these men, that they may see. And the Lord opened their eyes, and they saw; and, behold, they were in the midst of Samaria. 21 And the king of Israel said unto Elisha, when he saw them, My father, shall I smite them? shall I smite them? 22 And he answered, Thou shalt not smite them: wouldest thou smite those whom thou hast taken captive with thy sword and with thy bow? set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master. 23 And he prepared great provision for them: and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. So the bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel. Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them. Have that kind of faith, even when you cannot see the chariots of fire about you. (Splitting the chapter up, as the second half carries over into chapter 7) Here in 2 Kings 6, we find another series of acts of Elisha, the prophet of God. Similar to the structure of the Gospels and Acts of the Apostles, they are stories that provide a window into the faith of the man who had double the measure of the Spirit as the great Elijah. While 2 Kings paints a picture of a man of great faith, it is careful to also let us know he is just a man, and that it is God that guides and protects him. Here, he and his disciples, at their behest, set off to the banks of the Jordan to build a dwelling for them, as their current place in Carmel isn't big enough. I take this to mean that the prophet had gathered a good number of the sons of the prophets. They ask if they may, and he agrees. They ask him to come and he does. While felling trees for beams, the iron ax head of one of the men falls off into the waters. Seemingly lost. Because the tool has been borrowed, the man is upset, being responsible for another's property. But Elisha simply asks where, and breaking off a stick, casts it into the stream, and the iron floats to the surface. The iron did swim. With God, all things are possible. With faith enough, even iron did swim. The casual way Elisha trusted in the Lord, is a testament to his great faith. As Jesus spoke to the Apostles; Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you. The amount of faith needed to receive Christ and be saved is infinitesimal. The Apostles were unable to cast out a certain demon in a man, yet Jesus said it was a lack of faith. That the faith the size of a tiny mustard seed could move mountain. Elisha demonstrates this kind of faith, and is an example to us. When the King of Syria sets a trap for the King of Israel, Elisha having had it revealed to him, warns the king, saving him multiple times. The Syrian King, frustrated by the failure of his ambush, suspects a traitor in his court had been tipping off the King of Israel. But his men explain that it is Elisha, who knows even the things whispered in his bed chamber. (I wonder how they know, unless there be spies in the other kings house, telling them!) And so the Syrian King sends his army to get Elisha. And surrounds the city he is in with a multitude of troops. Panicked, Elisha's servant goes to the prophet in fear, asking what shall they do against such an array. Elisha calmly tells him to not be afraid, for those with them are many more. Elisha prays, asking the Lord to open the servant's eyes to see, and the young man looks and all around him are horses and chariots of fire, surrounding the prophet. We should remember this in times of distress. If we are walking in the Spirit and doing the work of the Lord, we should fear no man. And as Elisha prayed to open the young servant's eyes, he prays for blindness to fall on the Syrian host. And, they being blind to it, are led by Elisha into the very heart of Samaria, delivered unto the king. The King of Israel asks for permission to gleefully slay them, but the prophet says not so. They are captives. Feed them and give them drink and send them to their master. And so they do, and peace comes between the kingdoms for a time.

So another tale of Elisha, the siege of Samaria by the Syrians. A host of Syrians lay encamped about the city, to starve the king out. And the people were so desperate for food they boiled the heads of asses, and ate the dung of the birds. Even boiling their own children to eat, as one grieving mother tells the King. She was tricked into offering her own child with the promise of another woman to then cook her own. We cannot imagine such tribulation and hunger. We are blessed beyond measure. And still we complain. We have food in abundance, clothing, shelter. Relative peace and security. We are free to worship God, to attend church, to read the Bible, free to give the gospel to the lost...All things denied Christians for hundreds of years. Things that could be a death sentence in the past. Yet how many people claiming Christ do them? How many exercise the liberty we have? One of the reasons Israel was so often afflicted was, that when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish hearts were darkened. They turned to the worship of idols and worse. They held the truth of God in unrighteousness. But first, they took for granted the blessings of the liberty they had from the Lord. As longsuffering and merciful as God is, the Lord's patience runs out. With individuals, and with a nation. How many Christians spend their time complaining about how bad they have it, how fearful they are about the state of things, and yet do not pray everyday in thanksgiving, glorifying God for what they have? How many neglect their Bible? How many forsake the assembly? How many make excuses as to why they don't have to go to church, they don't have to live separated lives, they don't have to win souls and be a light? And the excuses always are ridiculous. "There are no good churches! No good pastors! The Bible is hard to read! It's easier to listen to a podcast or to watch YouTube debates!" Itching ears, taking every rationalization they are fed, while rejecting the word preached, and complaining all the while. America may end up as Samaria. Under siege and eventually overrun. But today we have unprecedented freedoms to turn to the Lord and to make an impact with His light so shining. We don't have to wait until it's too late because of fear. And so, as bad as it is, the King sends one of his lords to fetch Elisha, blaming the prophet of the Lord for their troubles. Seeking his head for their misery. For the testimony of the word of the Lord. This is, in my opinion, the real fear that drives some Christians to reject our role in this world. They are afraid of the backlash that comes from rebuking the wicked by God's word. The tribulation that may come from standing firm against sin and wickedness. Being a light against those that love darkness. They don't want people to think they are a peculiar person. They don't want people to think they are "judgemental." They don't want people to point out their own sin, and call them out as hypocrites, because they are comfortable in their sin. They become codependent with the world. But Elisha knows that regardless of what the reaction may be, God's will be done. So, he tells the messenger that by that same time the following day, the famine will be ended. That barley and flour will be so plentiful, that they will sell for a shekel at the gate. The lord sent by the king mocks this, asking if the Lord will open windows in heaven to make it so. Elisha says that while he will see this come to pass, he won't himself eat thereof. And so, God in the night scares off the hosts of Syria, thinking they hear hoofs of an army approach. They run where none pursued, leaving behind their fully provisioned camp. Some beggars, with leprosy, waiting by the gate, decide to go to the Syrian camp to seek food, and find the camp abandoned. They spoil some things for themselves, but think better of not telling anyone inside the city. So they go and tell the King. The King, fearful of a trap, sends out scouts and they return with the news, and the people of the city trample the lord Elisha had prophesied against, in their haste to gather the spoils. And so it came to pass, just as the prophet had said. One of the biggest hurdles to overcome in doing the right thing, is that if you begin, you know you will have to continue. If you begin reading the Bible every day, you're admitting that you should. And if you know that you should, you know it's wrong if you don't. And now you are without excuse. If you haven't been to church in a while, and you go once, you are admitting you should be going regularly, and now you don't have an excuse. If you haven't been living a separated life, as blameless as you can, and you try to clean it up, and get rid of worldly things in your life, you will have to continue in it. If you begin to testify for the gospel, people who know you will judge all those sins they've witnessed you do. And now you're forced to show genuine faith and a change. This can be terrifying. It makes us make rationalizations. Or empty promises and vows to "do better tomorrow." While living for today. But we are to be doers of the word, not hearers only. We are supposed to let our light shine. A prophet is not without honor, except in his home country. We will have family and friends who aren't Christian who will roll their eyes. Who will feel threatened by your newfound dedication to the Lord. Who will look for chinks in the whole armour of God you try to put on. You will fail sometimes. It's ok. God's mercies are new every morning. Yes, you will be making yourself obligated to doing the right thing by acknowledging it is the right thing. That is the Spirit working in you. Accept it. Accept people will be put off by the change. Accept some will make fun of you, mockers. It's ok. Because this tribulation is nothing compared to eternity. God will bless you in this life and the next.

Here in the first part of 2 Kings 8, we see the Shunammite woman from chapter 4, whose son was miraculously born and who was raised from the dead, warned by the prophet Elisha of a 7 year famine in the land. He sends her off to sojourn where she could escape it. She takes his advice and goes unto the Philistines. Upon return, she appeals to the king to have her land of her inheritance restored. He, hearing the story of Elisha and her son, agrees and makes her whole, including the fruit of the field while she was away. This reminds me of this passage in Revelation 12:6; And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days. The woman who gave miraculous birth to the child who was raised from the dead, hid for 3.5 years of Tribulation. Restored to all her possessions and more by the king I know it isn't exact parallel, but it's something. The judgment seat of Christ giving to us our reward, the fruit of our fields at the end of the 7 years of Tribulation and then wrath. I won't claim that this is the interpretation of things, but it's what came to me this time through. Next we are told Elijah is in Damascus, and Benhadad the king of Syria is sick. He sends his servant, Hazael to greet the prophet with great gifts, to ask the Lord if he shall recover. Elisha says yes, but says the Lord has shown him the King will surely die. He begins to weep, and Hazael asks why. Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child. The Lord has shown Elijah that Hazael would be king. And sure enough, Benhadad recovered from his illness, only to be smothered in his sleep by his servant, who takes the throne for himself, and makes war with Israel and Judah. Next we are given news of the kinds of Judah, and their slide into the same abominations as Israel, the ways of Ahab. And their falling away led to Edom and other nations revolting from being tributaries. Blessings given to David and Solomon now wasted. Yet the Lord would not destroy Judah for David his servant's sake, as he promised him to give him alway a light, and to his children. That promise is to David, and the light is Christ Jesus. Dispensationalism makes the promise to the wicked Jews, and the light their own being. We can see plainly that the only thing keeping Judah from being utterly destroyed as Israel soon will be, is the promise to David for a King to rule forever in Jerusalem, the place where the Lord puts His name. God had delivered on the covenant made in the wilderness to bring the children of Israel to the promised land. He kept His covenant that as long as they kept their end of the deal, and didn't turn to false gods and the abominable things the Canaanites did, He would be their God. But that covenant was already failing by this time. Hebrews 8:7-9 For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second. For finding fault with them, he saith, Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord. Just another example of the unbiblical nature of Dispensationalism and the idea that Jews remain God's chosen people, or that they have any promises other than Christ remaining.

Here in 2 Kings 9, we are given at last the fulfillment of the task given Elijah against Ahab, where God sent him to anoint Hazael over Syria, Jehu over Israel and Elisha as his successor in 1 Kings 19:15-18. Because Ahab had humbled himself before the Lord at the prophesying of Elijah, God had forestalled His judgment, but now it was come due upon Ahab's son and against that wicked Jezebel. Elisha sends his disciple to the front in the war against Syria by the northern and southern kingdoms, and anoints Jehu, telling him the Lord has chosen him as king over Israel. And that he is the instrument of God's judgment against Jordan and Ahaziah, king over Judah. Jehu rides furiously with his host to the King's residence in Jezreel, and spying his approach, Joram sends messengers to ask if it be peace, and Jehu turns both sent to his side, as they fall in behind him. Finally, they can tell by his manner that it is Jehu, captain of the men approaching, and so the two kings ride out against him, ironically (or providentially) meeting at the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite, whom Jezebel had murdered to procure his vineyard for Ahab. And it came to pass, when Joram saw Jehu, that he said, Is it peace, Jehu? And he answered, What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many? And Jordan fled, but an arrow from Jehu fell him, straight through his heart. They cast his body in the field of Naboth, to be eaten by the field if the air as the Lord had spoke. Ahaziah, King of Judah flees, but Jehu smites him as well. He continues, wounded to Megiddo, dying there and was taken to Jerusalem to be buried with David and his fathers. Jehu then sets off to the city, and there Jezebel paints her face and readies her hair and looked out a window to see. She cries out an accusation against Jehu, comparing him to the ill-fated Zimri, who ruled for 7 days after his coup against Elah. Jehu calls out to the others inside the keep with her, and asks who is on his side. And a couple of eunuchs took and threw her down from her window, and horses trod on her blood underfoot. Jehu sends to have her buried, but only a portion remained of her corpse, the rest eaten of dogs as God had cursed. The carcase of Jezebel shall be as dung upon the face of the field in the portion of Jezreel...what a fitting and terrible fate. God's judgments are true, and will come. Turning from wicked ways may bring God to repent of the evil He would do, but the chastisements will come, eventually. For rulers, for nations, for His sons and daughters who have backslidden and ignored His chastening. Eventually, for the whole unbelieving world.

One of the most epic chapters of 2 Kings, the story of Jehu and his consolidation of power and carrying out the command of the Lord by the prophet Elisha, utterly destroying the house of Ahab and killing all the servants of Baal. For his faithfulness in this task, the Lord promises Israel will be reigned over by his sons to the 4th generation. But due to his leaving the golden calves of Jeroboam, where Israel was made to sin before God, worshiping them in His name, God afflicted the nation with the armies of Syria, under Hazael (who was anointed as well to do just that). Jehu had great zeal for the Lord, and was ruthless in his execution of it. When the throne was his, he had to deal with securing it from an heir to Ahab, who had 70 sons. Rather than waiting or riding himself, he wrote to the men entrusted with their care challenging them to rise up against him. When they pledge loyalty out of fear, he immediately calls them on it, demanding the heads of all 70 sons. And they deliver. He has the heads piled at the gates, and says to the people who may have judged him as an usurper for slaying the king of Israel (and Judah); Ye be righteous: behold, I conspired against my master, and slew him: but who slew all these? The power of doing mighty works for God lay in the number of others who will do likewise at your example. The number of folks that will follow your lead and do their part and great things are accomplished for the furtherance of Christ. Being able, when persecuted and accused for your faith and your witness, to point at results greater than anything you've personally achieved, and say "Who slew all these?" is a powerful rebuke to those who hate Christ, and seek to oppose the Lord. Then the brethren of Ahaziah, the King of Judah whom Jehu had also slain, came riding to "pay their respects" to the family of Ahab and Jezebel, as it were. They likely came for vengeance, and the very act was disrespectful to Jehu as king. He has the 42 men taken alive, cast into a pit and slaughters them there, together. Then he meets with Jehonadab the Kenite, son of Rechab. The Rechabites, mentioned in Jeremiah, are non-Israelites who lived among them as nomads, never owning land, planting vineyards or drinking wine. Fierce followers of the Lord. Jehu, seeking his approval and support meets with Jehonadab and shaking hands in peace, invites him into his chariot, saying; Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord. They then set out and slew all the men loyal to Ahab, and those of his seed, according to the saying of the Lord, which he spake to Elijah. We, as Christians, like to think of ourselves as Jehu in this moment, and with other believers, show our zeal. I know I have been fired up for the Lord and eager to do His bidding and to show that zeal to others. It is a line of scripture that always has my heart stirring and gets me pumped up. I think we can learn a lesson from this to not allow our zeal to burn bright and fade away, as it did for Jehu to some extent. In his zeal, he did the things the Lord set before him with gusto. But long term, the Bible says; But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the Lord God of Israel with all his heart: for he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam, which made Israel to sin. Sometimes, especially for new Christians, that initial zeal can be lost and faded over time. We are better to stoke our zeal for the Lord as a fire, and keep it going as warm embers for our entire life, than burn out quickly and fade like Jehu. But the flame of Jehu's zeal is awesome, none the less. To rid the land of Baal, Jehu calls an assembly, telling the priest and followers of Baal to gather in their temple for a feast. He makes out as if he is with them, and they all gladly come to curry favor with the new king. There he has the assembly of Baal look for any followers of the Lord snuck in among them. Then gives them special clothing, vestments for Baal (all the easier for the soldiers outside to recognize them). Then, as they sacrifice their false god, he orders his men to slaughter them. They do, and break down the houses of Baal, destroying the images and idols. Turning their temple Into an outhouse. Thus Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel. This story always gladdens my heart and makes me long for the day we break down the idols and drive the false priests of the Roman church and its harlot daughters out of our land. Finally, I have to share with you one of my favorite sermons of all time, Who slew all these? by Pastor Roger Jimenez at the 2022 Red Hot Preaching Conference. If you want to get fired up for the Lord today, please give it your time

Here in 2 Kings 11, the focus shifts to the Southern Kingdom of Judah. As we read, Jehu had slain their king, Ahaziah, and his mother, the queen regent, sensed an opportunity to take the throne for herself. She orders all the heirs of her son killed, even her own grandchildren. But his sister by their father Joram, takes her one year old nephew, Joash, and hides him in the temple. There Joash is raised for 6 years under the tutelage of the high priest, Jehoiada while Athaliah ruled as queen. When the prince turned seven, Jehoiada sent for the rulers of Judah, the captains of the guard who were sworn to protect the kings. There, he made a deal with them by oath, to anoint the boy as king, and that they would protect the proceedings from the wicked queen. And so the captains of the guard do as planned, and armed with the spears and shields dedicated to the temple, they went out on the sabbath, protecting the temple of the Lord as Jehoiada brought out Joash, and crowned him, giving him the testimony of the Law, and anointing him king. The assembled cheered "God save the king!" And when Athaliah heard the commotion from the palace, she rushed to the temple to find the boy by the pillar, in the place of the king. And looking round she saw the people cheering and trumpets sounding and all the people rejoicing. She rent her clothes and cried out "Treason, Treason." Jehoiada ordered her captured and taken without the temple to be slain, and all who were with her. The guards killed her in the horses gate. Ignominious end to her corrupt reign. And all the people went out and tore down the house of Baal that the queen had allowed to be set up, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, and destroyed the images. And so, the rule of seven year old Jehoash began.

2 Kings 12 provides more detail of Jehoash, King of Judah, who the Bible says reigned rightly in the sight of the Lord while being guided by Jehoiada, the high priest that had raised him. He reigned for 40 years, brake down the house of Baal and destroyed the idols, as we read in chapter 11. But we see that many of the people of Judah still worshipped in the high places and burnt incense there. And Jehoash orders the priests to use the money they received from dedications, from extra donations given by men, (Corban as the NT calls it) and money they acquired themselves outside of tithes and offerings, and use that money to help them repair the Temple. They do not see to the repairs themselves and their own money they don't use for it, and so Jehoash orders them to not receive the money any longer. The impression is that they were to fundraise and rather than dedicate that money to the repairs, they spent it in other ways. It doesn't indicate if it was misappropriation (although they did not do as the King commanded so, it would be regardless). But the system didn't work as intended. But Jehoiada creates a donation box, and set it at the entrance, and by and by it is filled with money. This money was gathered and used for the hire of workmen who repaired the Temple. None of the extra money was used to increase the treasure of the house of the Lord, only to upkeep. And the men who did the work and the priests that paid them did so honorably and honestly. I think this is a story of the best intentions of the King, but a lack of wisdom in how to carry it out. Where his chief advisor, the high priest Jehoiada's plan works to achieve the same end, illustrating the King's need for that guidance. Because, Jehoash did that which was right in the sight of the Lord all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him. And when the King of Syria, Hazael, set his face to go up to Jerusalem to make war, King Jehoash took all of the wealth of his house that was dedicated to the Lord, hallowed things of his fathers and his own, and even of the Temple, and sent it as ransom to Hazael, who accepted it and left Jerusalem alone. Again, the wisdom of such a thing is questionable. Giving that which was the Lord's to save him, rather than trusting in the Lord to deliver them from their enemies. A shortsighted lack of faith. The next event is his assassination at the hands of his servants, and it seems to be a consequence of his poor decisions after no longer having the priest to guide him. And so, as 2 Kings turns to the Southern Kingdom, we see Amaziah, his son, take the throne.

Here in 2 Kings 13, we are back in the Northern Kingdom of Israel, and Jehoahaz the son of Jehu. The Lord had promised Jehu his sons would reign to the 4th generation, and this promise is kept here in this chapter, as we are also told of Jehoahaz' son, Joash and his son, Jeroboam, all taking the throne. It is a speed run through the lineage, and more is told of their reigns in Chronicles. During this time, God was using Syria to punish Israel for their continued sin, worshiping idols in His name, and Baal in the groves and high places. Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz. At some point, despite the evil he had done, Jehoahaz besought the Lord, and the Lord hearkened unto him. And the Lord provided a savior to Israel, allowing them some relief. Jehoahaz visits the dying Elisha, who gives to him a bow and arrow, and tells him to smite the ground with it. Jehoahaz smites the ground three times, and Elisha says that it would have been better had he done it more, but now God will deliver victory against the Syrians three times, and as we see, He does. Syria still will ultimately destroy Israel, but not as yet. God for the sake of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob forestalls their final judgement. But Israel are still in great tribulation, forced to live in tents as their fathers did. No longer tied to the land by inheritance. Hazael of Syria died, and his son Benhadad rules in his stead and continued the affliction of Israel. Elisha's death occurs in this chapter, and a miracle concerning the prophet; Moabites invade and while burying a man, they spied a band coming, a s so they cast the dead man into the sepulchre of Elisha, and when he was lowered into the tomb, he touched the prophet's bones and revived. This one short verse is used, primarily by the Orthodox Church, but by many Roman Catholics as well, to justify their veneration and worship of corpses, skulls and bones. Relics, they say, of "holy men," the "saints." They claim the bones have power, that there is Spirit still invested in them, and that this power can be transferred to those that touch them, pray to them, and worship them in rites and rituals. This pagan cult of relics, worshiping death, serving the dead things of the flesh, is wicked as Hell. As Proverbs says; all they that hate me love death. They store the skeletal remains, usually of unknown origin but with grandiose claims or being Apostles, certain saints, in special places. Temples of death. In glass cases to be paraded about, being served. Miracles are attributed to these abominations. Forgeries abound. But Scripture gives no such accounting. A miracle occurred. The how and the why aren't given. Elisha isn't exhumed and carted around to temples. No Israelites lined up to seek to be healed by the relics of a finger bone or skull. No instruction is given by the inspiration of God to do anything of the sort. In fact, we are told repeatedly by the word of God that to do so is unclean. It's gross. Numbers 19:13 Whosoever toucheth the dead body of any man that is dead, and purifieth not himself, defileth the tabernacle of the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from Israel; because the water of separation was not sprinkled upon him, he shall be unclean; his uncleanness is yet upon him. Most of the profane and false doctrines of Rome that have trickled down to the various offshoots of that false church, come from similarly dubious reasoning, where they take a single verse or incident, remove whatever context exists in scripture, and make assumptions and assertions that rely on the foolish reasoning of man, rather than the clear word of God. This is why we as saved Christians should only take doctrine from clear, undeniable scripture. Proving all things. Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. Searching the scriptures to see if something is so.

Here in 2 Kings 14, we are given more history of the Kings of Israel and Judah, and see the first open war between the kingdoms, when Amaziah of Judah and Jehoash of Israel met in battle, Judah losing to their brothers, and Jerusalem sacked. The Bible says that Amaziah did right in the eyes of the Lord, but did not have the heart of David. He kept Baal worship out of Judah as his father did, but allowed the high places and sacrifices there to continue. He did right by not slaying the sons of the servants who had murdered his father, killing only the assassins themselves. The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children be put to death for the fathers; but every man shall be put to death for his own sin. A reminder that the concept of "original sin," the false idea that we are born condemned by the son of Adam, rather than having his same sinful nature, is unbiblical and goes against the teachings of God. Amaziah went against Edom and had success. This prompted his challenge to Jehoash in Israel, who taunted his challenge saying that he was a thistle compared to his mighty cedar. Jehoash did evil in the sight of the Lord, and so too his son Jeroboam who was crowned after his death. But the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai spoke to him the word of God, that he expand and shore up the territory of Israel due to the affliction He saw in the land. He used the wicked king to be a deliverer for the people, while the lukewarm king of Judah, who did that which was right but wasn't sold out for the Lord, was not as successful in ruling. He was overthrown by a seditious plot, as was his father. And like him, his son was placed on the throne. A key element to the stories of the kings of Judah is their unwillingness to drive all the sin from the land. They may break down the house of Baal and destroy the images and slay the priests, but they never turn to the high places. They leave sin in the land. While Israel continues its slide towards destruction and promoting a false religion, they have varying success and failures, afflictions and victories, as the will of God found necessary. But Judah, who are as a saved Christian, trusting the Lord and getting right on major sin, never fully commit. And God chastens them for it. We can take that lesson and apply it to our own lives as saved believers. We should seek to have a heart like David's, and not be lukewarm in our walk, but strive to remove the high places in our hearts.

2 Kings 15 shows decades of rule in Israel and Judah. Israel, in constant turmoil, betrayal and seditions. Each king doing evil. And we begin to see Assyrian Kingdom grow in power and demand tribute and take land from the Northern Kingdom. In the Southern Kingdom of Judah, we find a steady succession of David's lineage, who so right in the sight of the Lord, but they leave the lingering sin of the high places in the land, and God punishes these kings for it. Chastening them. Giving Azariah leprosy, and sending the Syrians and even Israelites against Judah. In many ways, Kings and Chronicles, its parallel book, serve as an indictment against the children of Israel. God demonstrating His long suffering, His chastisements, His providing generations for these people to get right, and then letting them slide into desolation and destruction, as they condemn themselves. It is a testimony, where we are called to rightly judge and see it from God's point of view, where we may read and know the beginning from the end, and see His judgments are good.

Wicked King Ahaz, of Judah, who took the gods of the high places and passed his son through the fire, and brought the gods and altar of the Assyrians to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem. Had his fathers rid Judah of the high places, and kept to the faith of their fathers, would Ahaz had the opportunity or desire to be tempted away to heathenism? As with the Philippian jailer and Cornelius, often the lead of the father, the patriarch, brings whole households to the Lord. Other times, even the most righteous men have wicked sons. It is no guarantee. But if you walk in the paths God provided us, and raise up your child in the way they should go, and remove the high places in your heart, keeping your house, your kingdom, unspotted from the world, you increase the odds that your children will do the same. A sincere man who is a believer, who walks in the ways of righteousness, and loves his wife and children with the same love as God shows us; longsuffering, kind, merciful but uncompromising on what is right, firm but fair, as a doer of the law, who visits the widow in their affliction and is a good judge to the fatherless, will more likely have children who do. Some Christian men make the mistake of being iron fisted and provoking their children to wrath, and think that is the way to rule their household. They fear the world and its influence so much that they believe the only way to protect their children from it is as a tyrant, trying to control everything they do. Their fear shows their children a lack of faith, and it can often drive them away from the Lord. We can raise our kids rightly, not sparing the rod of correction, chastening them betimes, training them up in the way they should go, while also showing them the unconditional love and mercy of the Father. Being an example of the same tender mercies God showed us in our salvation. Some men think that is weakness. God is not weak when He does this for us. Don't think it weak to follow His example.

2 Kings 17 contains the judgment of God against the tribes of Israel in the Northern Kingdom, and their utter destruction. It is the fulfillment of the covenant that God made with Israel in the wilderness; Deuteronomy 30:11-20 For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go up for us to heaven, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? Neither is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it. See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil; In that I command thee this day to love the Lord thy God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments and his statutes and his judgments, that thou mayest live and multiply: and the Lord thy God shall bless thee in the land whither thou goest to possess it. But if thine heart turn away, so that thou wilt not hear, but shalt be drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce unto you this day, that ye shall surely perish, and that ye shall not prolong your days upon the land, whither thou passest over Jordan to go to possess it. I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:That thou mayest love the Lord thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days: that thou mayest dwell in the land which the Lord sware unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them. The children of Israel chose death. And they perished from the land. Dispensationalists and modern Jews will always ignore the if/then nature of the covenant with the children of Israel, the promise to be their God and they to be His people, so long as they walked in His statutes and kept the fear of the Lord. They ignore the destruction of Israel found here in this chapter. They ignore the warnings given of the prophets that spike against the sin of Israel. They ignored the famines and the plagues and invasions and spoiling by their enemies. They forgot about the bounty and blessings and impossible victories given to their fathers. Howbeit they did not hearken... And the Lord, longsuffering and merciful, finally has enough, and destroys them. The country of Samaria is filled with outlandish people, who know not the Lord. And while they are taught to fear Him, they never turn to Him, but do as they like, worshipping their gods. Burning incense in the high places, serving idols and passing their children through the fire as sacrifices. When God sends lions in the land to provoke them, the king of Assyria sent a priest of Israel among them, to teach them of the God of the land, but they still made gods of their own. If there will be a stubborn and wicked people, bowing and serving false gods in the land, better they not be carrying the name of Israel, better to not be claiming to be His people. A lesson modern Israel should heed. As for the Southern Kingdom of Judah, God had made a promise to David for an eternal King from his lineage, and a promise to put His name upon Jerusalem. But the Jews themselves? Also Judah kept not the commandments of the Lord their God, but walked in the statutes of Israel which they made. And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, and afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of spoilers, until he had cast them out of his sight. The Lord rejected ALL the seed of Israel. So, while Judah had protection for a while longer, and was then carried away to captivity in Babylon for 70 years, and though they were returned when some had turned back to the Lord, were allowed to rebuild the temple and dwell in the land, they were never again given the blessings that came as a nation to the children of Israel. We will see as we go through scripture, that they were under Babylon, Persia and the Medes, the Greeks, and by the time of Christ, under the Roman empire. The Jews, the remnant of Judah and Benjamin and Levi that returned to Judea after being freed from 70 years captivity, were only kept from utter destruction until the promise of Christ came. And once Jesus ascension was done, and the gospel went out to all the world, the temple was destroyed and the remnant of unbelieving Jews were put to the sword, scattered and destroyed. God regarded them no more.

Here in chapter 18, we begin to learn of King Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, king of Judah. And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father did. He not only did that which was right, but broke down the high places and the images, and cut down the groves where the heathen worshiped. He even destroyed the brazen serpent, called Nehushtan, which Moses had made when the fiery serpents were killing the children of Israel in their camp in the wilderness. Numbers 21:8-9 And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live. And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived. This was, of course, a picture of Christ. John 3:14-15 And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. While Nehushtan's original purpose was to serve as a picture of Christ, showing that the children of Israel looked to it and lived, just as we look to Christ lifted up on the cross and have eternal life, the brazen serpent was never itself meant to be an object of worship. Men weren't to bow and serve it. It had a specific purpose, and that purpose was past. Catholics and their schismatics in other denominations, use the brazen serpent to justify their idolatry. They say that if God told Moses to make this particular image, then the making of any image is allowed. And they proceed to bow and serve them, lighting candles and incense to them, and pray at their feet. They seldom have ever heard of Nehushtan. They don't know the story of Hezekiah. They don't know he destroyed it because the children of Israel were treating it the way Catholics treat images of the crucifix, of Mary and various other humans. That the word of God says Hezekiah did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord and destroyed it. They err not knowing scripture, determined to keep their groves and high places and their images they make. To worship outside of the ways God had given in His word. Keeping to vain traditions and dead works. Hezekiah kept to the word of the Lord, and the ways God commanded of Moses, and the Lord was with him, and he prospered. He rebelled against the Assyrian King and defeated the Philistines. This summary is given, and the remaining chapter, as well as the next, details Hezekiah's rebellion against the Assyrians. I will take the remaining chapter and 2 Kings 19 together, tomorrow, God willing.

As we saw in 2 Kings 18, Hezekiah the son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign. And he did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord. He had a heart like David, trusting in the Lord for all things. He rid the land of the high places, the groves and the idols. And he rebelled against the king of Assyria. When Senna cherub, king of Assyria came against Jerusalem, Hezekiah paid a ransom and a tribute for peace, even cutting off gold plate from the doors of the Temple to appease him. Yet he wasn't satisfied. And so, the king of Assyria, the king sent his host from the city of Lachish, and the captains, Tartan and Rabsaris and Rabshakeh, to siege the city. They taunt Hezekiah, his servants and the men of the city. They say that if he is counting on the king of Egypt to save them, that is like leaning on a broken reed that will stab you in the hand. Then, they mock Hezekiah's faith in the Lord, scoffing. Eliakim, Hezekiah's chief of staff, asks they speak Syrian to them that the men on the wall not understand, but Rabshakeh scoffs and speaks Hebrew, that they all understand his words. He says that they have taken city after city and destroyed god after god, and that the same will happen here. Let not Hezekiah deceive you: for he shall not be able to deliver you out of his hand: Neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord, saying, The Lord will surely deliver us, and this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. He promises the men that they will be taken to a land just as good, and allowed to have their own prosperity there, demoralizing the king and slandering the Lord with blasphemy. And so Hezekiah and his servants rent their clothes and went to the Lord in sackcloth and supplication, and asked after Isaiah the prophet for the word of God. The king acknowledges the trouble they are in, the rebuke they are due, and in that tribulation he asks that the living God hear the blasphemy of the Assyrians, and deliver Jerusalem out of their hands. Isaiah tells the king not to fear, the Lord has decided to cause the king to hear a rumor, to return to his own land and to fall by the sword there. And so, the king of the Assyrians, out warring, hears a rumor that the king of Ethiopia is come out against him for Judah, and sends word to Hezekiah with the same threats and blasphemy as before. And lists the gods and the nations that served them that he has made desolate. But Hezekiah brings the letter before the Lord and prays to Him, worshipping the living God who is over all things and the Creator of Heaven and Earth. That while Assyria has cast their gods into the fire: for they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them, that they see the might of the Lord. And Isaiah brings the king the word of the Lord, promising that the remnant of Judah in Jerusalem will be safe, and Assyrians will be chastened. The Lord says that their success against these other cities and destruction of their gods was allowed by Him. But; Because thy rage against me and thy tumult is come up into mine ears, therefore I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest. And in this, a prophecy of Jesus; And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall yet again take root downward, and bear fruit upward. For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion: the zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this...For I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake. Note again, as we have seen multiple times, God is doing this for His own sake, and for His promise to David. God's plan is for a root to spring up in Zion, the place where He placed His name; Jerusalem. And the Christ, King of Kings He promised by covenant to David. This is not a promise to the Jews, the people had done wickedly. It was not to all Israel, who by this time were being destroyed utterly by the same Assyrians. It was being done for God's will and David's sake. And so, in the night an angel of death came over the camper of the Assyrians, slaying 185,000 men. And they fled back to their land. And Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, and while worshiping his god, Nisroch, was slain by his own sons. Just as the word of God spoke. Amen.

Here in 2 Kings 20, the final tales of good King Hezekiah of Judah. First, we find the King near death. The prophet Isaiah comes and tells him to get his things in order, for the word of the Lord says he will surely die. Now we know from his introduction in chapter 18 that Hezekiah did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, and walked in His ways. So hearing of his pending untimely death, he turned in prayer to the Lord. He reminded God of his faithfulness and his living according to God's precepts, and asks to be spared this fate, in tears. And before Isaiah had gone out of the courtyard, God repents and grants Hezekiah 15 more years. That after 3 days, when he is clean, he shall go up to the house of the Lord. (This seems like a picture of Christ, and the healing power of the Spirit to me). And Hezekiah asks for a sign, to know that what Isaiah speaks is true, and he offers that the Lord can make the shadow of the sundial move forward 10 degrees, or backwards 10. Hezekiah asks for the sub to move backwards in the sky, being a more sure sign of God's might, and it does. And the Lord promises; I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria; and I will defend this city for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake. Note again, it isn't for the Jews and it isn't for Hezekiah that the Lord preserved Jerusalem. But for His own sake and the covenant He made with David, that is Christ. Hezekiah asked for a sign that the word of God spoken of Isaiah was true. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 1:22-24; For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: but we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; but unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. In the Old Testament, the Hebrews often asked for a sign, and were given them. Sometimes, God offered a sign that they may know His word was true. But we have the Spirit testifying within us, and the more sure words of prophecy of the Bible. In our life, when we are praying to God to deliver us from bad things, illness, family members in trouble, whatever, we are reassured by the Spirit confirming the word of God and His promises to us. That according to His will, He is faithful to deliver us. This is sign enough. But often we need more. As the tearful father said to Jesus, asking Him to bring back his daughter unto him, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. Or as the apostles said to Christ, Lord, Increase our faith. We can ask God for reassurance. We can ask for things we've hoped for, and see the work of the Spirit bringing it about. Increasing our faith. Helping our unbelief. It doesn't mean we doubt our salvation, or that God can't deliver. It just means we are human, and the flesh fears. This is why it is important to be in good standing with the Father, as Hezekiah was. Able to go before God to ask of Him what we need. By walking 3the Spirit and being right with the things of God, our faith is made stronger, and our trust in him when we are weak will come more naturally. But when we are in sin, and ashamed, and walk in the flesh, our doubts and fears increase. Our faith that God will save us falters, knowing we don't deserve His mercy. Thankfully, He is faithful to us, that if we turn to Him, and confess our sins, He will forgive us. 1 John 1:5-9 This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. 1 John 5:13-15 These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him. So, like Hezekiah, let us walk in the light that we may have confidence in the Lord to deliver us from our troubles. But a story of an Old Testament saint wouldn't be complete without an example of their sin. For all have sinned and come short of the glory of God. And Hezekiah was no different. The king of Babylon sends his regards, having heard of hezekiah's illness. And the recovered Hezekiah entertains the servants of the king. The Bible doesn't tell us that Hezekiah praised the Lord for his recovery, but rather showed them all of the riches of his kingdom, the city, his household and in the Temple. His sin is pride. Boasting of his riches while just a short while before he was on his deathbed. This is possibly the most common thing that I have experienced myself and witnessed in others; a great triumph of the Lord acting miraculously in our lives, followed by a low point where we forget the trouble we were in, and grow comfortable, taking it for granted. It is so easy for sin to creep in when this happens. One of the ways to avoid it is to not only go to God in our troubles and with supplications, but to praise the Lord for when He acts mightily in our lives. Bragging on him rather than ourselves. Staying humble. Because of Hezekiah's sin, Isaiah comes to him and tells him that God has judged and that all of the treasures he had shown off to Babylon would be carried away there. And that his son s will be eunuchs to their King. Hezekiah accepts the rebuke and the judgment. And is thankful that it won't be in his day. But that small comfort isn't worth the moment of sin. Judah will soon learn a lesson in humility. And while God won't destroy them yet, because of his own interests and his promise to David, they will be made desolate for 70 years.

2 Chronicles 33:10-20 10 And the Lord spake to Manasseh, and to his people: but they would not hearken. 11 Wherefore the Lord brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon. 12 And when he was in affliction, he besought the Lord his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers, 13 And prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the Lord he was God. 14 Now after this he built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entering in at the fish gate, and compassed about Ophel, and raised it up a very great height, and put captains of war in all the fenced cities of Judah. 15 And he took away the strange gods, and the idol out of the house of the Lord, and all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the Lord, and in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city. 16 And he repaired the altar of the Lord, and sacrificed thereon peace offerings and thank offerings, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel. 17 Nevertheless the people did sacrifice still in the high places, yet unto the Lord their God only. 18 Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer unto his God, and the words of the seers that spake to him in the name of the Lord God of Israel, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel. 19 His prayer also, and how God was intreated of him, and all his sins, and his trespass, and the places wherein he built high places, and set up groves and graven images, before he was humbled: behold, they are written among the sayings of the seers. 20 So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his own house: and Amon his son reigned in his stead. Manasseh may have been the most wicked King of Judah and Israel, doing abominable things, but he also is a testimony to God's grace and mercy, and the healing that comes by repentance towards faith. Reading the entry in 2 Kings 21, it would be difficult to ever imagine that such a person could call upon the name of the Lord and be forgiven. And yet, 2 Chronicles 33 shows us that even the worst of sinners can hear the word of God be preached and believe unto righteousness. The consequences of Manasseh's sins were great, however. And the punishment against Jerusalem was assured, the innocent blood and the evil and provocation of the people against God needing vengeance. And he set a graven image of the grove that he had made in the house, of which the Lord said to David, and to Solomon his son, In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all tribes of Israel, will I put my name for ever: Neither will I make the feet of Israel move any more out of the land which I gave their fathers; only if they will observe to do according to all that I have commanded them, and according to all the law that my servant Moses commanded them. Because they have done that which was evil in my sight, and have provoked me to anger, since the day their fathers came forth out of Egypt, even unto this day. It is important to keep beating this drum, but the Old Testament is filled with clear teaching and doctrines that God repeats, over and over again, that destroy dispensationalism. As we have seen, the Lord destroyed Israel. The remnant of Judah existed only for the promise to David and that Jerusalem is where He chose to place His name forever. That the Jews were as abominable as the nations that dwelt there before them. Isaiah 1:9 Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah. There is no special dispensation to the Jews. There is redemption in Christ or death and hell. Verily I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.

1 Kings 14 21 And Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty and one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city which the Lord did choose out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. And his mother's name was Naamah an Ammonitess. 22 And Judah did evil in the sight of the Lord, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins which they had committed, above all that their fathers had done. 23 For they also built them high places, and images, and groves, on every high hill, and under every green tree. 24 And there were also sodomites in the land: and they did according to all the abominations of the nations which the Lord cast out before the children of Israel. 1 Kings 15 And in the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel reigned Asa over Judah. 10 And forty and one years reigned he in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom. 11 And Asa did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, as did David his father. 12 And he took away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made. 13 And also Maachah his mother, even her he removed from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove; and Asa destroyed her idol, and burnt it by the brook Kidron. 14 But the high places were not removed: nevertheless Asa's heart was perfect with the Lord all his days. 1 Kings 22 41 And Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel. 42 Jehoshaphat was thirty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. 43 And he walked in all the ways of Asa his father; he turned not aside from it, doing that which was right in the eyes of the Lord: nevertheless the high places were not taken away; for the people offered and burnt incense yet in the high places. 44 And Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel. 45 Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he shewed, and how he warred, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? 46 And the remnant of the sodomites, which remained in the days of his father Asa, he took out of the land. Josiah becomes King of Judah, and does that which is right in the eyes of the Lord. He seeks the truth and is given it, when the scribe and priest find a copy of the Law, the word of God, and deliver it to him. The young king reads it and rends his clothes knowing the sin of their fathers, and the people not harkening to all that which was written. He seeks to know God's will, and enquires of a prophetess who tells them that God will judge Judah harshly, with desolation, but that because of the tender heart of the King, and Josiah's humble and faithful reaction to hearing the word of God and believing it, judgment is spared for the length of his reign. The story of King Josiah is a picture of the coming of Christ. Where some were seeking truth, hearts meet for repentance, and the Word of God came among them, and they believed, and because of that faith, are spared the wrath of God. This applies to the 1st century Jews who accepted Christ, and the desolation of Jerusalem in 70AD. It also applies to believers in general, who hear the word of God with tender hearts and humble spirits, and are delivered from the wrath that will pour out in the world at Christ's return.

We are here in 2 Kings 23, and the reign of Josiah, King of Judah. A godly man, who sought the Lord and, when finding the law of God and reading the covenant that had been ignored for generations, uses his power as king to set things right; to honor the covenant of the Lord. He orders that all, great and small, come to the temple and he reads the entire book of the law to the people, and standing by the King's pillar, makes a covenant with God to walk in His commandments, keeping His statutes with all their heart and soul. He leads a revival. Now the pillar he stood by, the same as that which other kings had, I believe is a picture of Christ. The promise of Him, shown to us as that unmoving pillar of the king whereby Josiah stands firmly in the word of God. And Josiah's zeal for the Lord is excellent. He destroys all of the groves, altars, high places, images, idols, and other abominations to false gods, not only throughout Judah, but even into the territory of Israel, whereby Jeroboam had led Israel to sin.
