But the purpose of this retelling, like the previous chapters, is to give inspiration to the returning captives and to provide saved Christians insights and examples, in our own way leaving the captivity of Babylon by our salvation in Christ. Solomon's wisdom and judgment were a good report throughout the world. By his faith and putting God first, others sought him out to learn how and why he was so blessed, and glory was given to the Lord by his example. We know Solomon wasn't perfect. He had flaws. But by honoring God, honoring his father, by seeking to do right for others, he became a beacon drawing others to God. Happy are thy men, and happy are these thy servants, which stand continually before thee, and hear thy wisdom. Blessed be the Lord thy God, which delighted in thee to set thee on his throne, to be king for the Lord thy God: because thy God loved Israel, to establish them for ever, therefore made he thee king over them, to do judgment and justice. This statement by the Queen of Sheba can also be seen as a prayer to the Lord God the Father about His holy Son. Happy are His servants, blessed is the Lord our God. The Israel of God established forever. Amen.

Matthew 11:28-30 Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. Revelation 9:3-12 And there came out of the smoke locusts upon the earth: and unto them was given power, as the scorpions of the earth have power. And it was commanded them that they should not hurt the grass of the earth, neither any green thing, neither any tree; but only those men which have not the seal of God in their foreheads. And to them it was given that they should not kill them, but that they should be tormented five months: and their torment was as the torment of a scorpion, when he striketh a man. And in those days shall men seek death, and shall not find it; and shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them. And the shapes of the locusts were like unto horses prepared unto battle; and on their heads were as it were crowns like gold, and their faces were as the faces of men. And they had hair as the hair of women, and their teeth were as the teeth of lions. And they had breastplates, as it were breastplates of iron; and the sound of their wings was as the sound of chariots of many horses running to battle. And they had tails like unto scorpions, and there were stings in their tails: and their power was to hurt men five months. And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon. One woe is past; and, behold, there come two woes more hereafter. Revelation 20:1-10 And I saw an angel come down from heaven, having the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain in his hand. And he laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years, And cast him into the bottomless pit, and shut him up, and set a seal upon him, that he should deceive the nations no more, till the thousand years should be fulfilled: and after that he must be loosed a little season. And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them: and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years. But the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years. And when the thousand years are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog, and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea. And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them. And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever. Continuing the theme of 2 Chronicles showing David as the first coming of Christ Jesus, Solomon's reign a picture of the millennial Kingdom, now we have Rehoboam, Solomon's son taking the throne, and Jeroboam the son of Nebat who was in Egypt for fear of King Solomon, loosed for a season and come, deceiving the people into rebellion against the King, to make himself King over Israel. Of course the picture isn't precise, but we can see the outline and shape through the glass darkly. The yoke of Solomon wasn't grievous. The people had wealth and servants and peace, but as a picture of the law, the yoke was indeed heavy. None being able to be saved by works of the Law. Just as Jeroboam comes in his father's name, so too has Christ, and offered a lighter yoke; salvation by grace. Just as the wise advisors told the young King; be kind to this people, and please them, and speak good words to them. But the young who advise him say make the yoke worse, and chasten not with whips, but worse, with scorpions. The Father does chasten us, scourging every son. Jesus does being the wrath of God upon the unbelieving world, including scorpion-locusts from Hell. Again it isn't a perfect one to one picture of things, but you can see the shape and draw the lesson. This same event is told in 1 Kings 12 which we also covered here and discussed some of the other take-aways from the tale. Focusing more on the details than the bigger picture. Check it out if you're interested or need a refresher.

And so Rehoboam, son of Solomon and Naamah the Ammonite, becomes King, and like his father, he desired many wives, marrying cousins and others, having 28 sons and threescore daughters. He served as the first King of Judah after the division, wherein Jeroboam took Israel as King. We see that Judah, having Benjamin among them already, also absorbs the Levites fleeing the north, as Jeroboam causes Israel to sin with a false priesthood worshiping idols in God's name. The term "Jew" will begin to be used as a designation for those residing in Judah, including Benjamin, Levi and those who fled to Jerusalem, wishing to serve the Lord God only. It also would include any of the people who reside there from the Canaanites and Edomites, etc. Which is why the term Jew is so imprecise and difficult to pin down, even to this day. We see that, as King faxing rebellion, Rehoboam's first instinct is to raise a mighty army to go up against the other tribes, but God through His prophet says not to, and Rehoboam obeys. We know that a few hundred years later, a wicked Israel is utterly destroyed by the Assyrians. God's justice comes in His own time and manner.

Continuing the chronicles of Rehoboam as King over Judah, we see that despite his beginning fearing the Lord and obeying His words against their going to war with Jeroboam, and enjoying the blessings of his inheritance from his father King Solomon, and the blessings God had bestowed on him directly, Rehoboam turned his heart from following the Lord. And as the king went, so too the people. And so God brought a challenge out of Egypt, to conquer Judah and put them in servitude. The walled cities and stores came into the hands of Shishak King of Egypt. But before their utter destruction, as Jerusalem was surrounded and the king and his princess huddled there in fear, the prophet of the Lord came. Shemaiah preached to them that the Lord had forsaken them as they had Him. Hearing this the king and his princes humbled themselves and got right with God, and while they suffered loss for their behavior, God showed mercy upon them. Very familiar to a lot of Christians, who after conversion and with the support of those before them to edify them, do great things for the Lord and are blessed, but soon their passion dies and they turn from the path of righteousness. And God chastens them. But He is merciful to send His word as warning before destruction to get right with Him. Many listen. We see many young Christians saved as children, blessed to be in a Christian home with parents raising them in the admonition of the Lord, who backslide entering into adulthood. They often lose the blessings they inherited, and suffer loss and the consequences of their sin, and chastened, hearing the word, get right with God and live out their days humbled, serving Him. Some don't, and are destroyed. If you have experienced this, and we're prodigal, you know the longsuffering and mercy of God, His forgiveness, and the regret of wasted time. If you're in rebellion now, repent. You are always welcome in the Father's house, as sons and daughters. He will deliver you from what you deserve, that you may have a chance to serve Him. The Lord is righteous. Amen

Here in 2 Chronicles 13, we are given the story of the short-lived reign of King Abijah, son of Jeroboam. He reigned 3 years, and in that time Rehoboam King of Israel rose up an army to spoil Judah. In the depiction given by the chronicler, he stood mighty upon mount Zenaraim in Ephraim, with 400,000 valiant men, while Rehoboam met him with twice as many, and surrounded his forces by ambush. But King Abijah, standing defiantly calls upon the name of the Lord, and reminds us of the thing by which Jeroboam caused all Israel to sin; turning from the Lord, building golden calves to worship, casting out the priests of Aaron, and the Levites whom God gave a covenant of salt to; Numbers 18:19 All the heave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer unto the LORD, have I given thee, and thy sons and thy daughters with thee, by a statute for ever: it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD unto thee and to thy seed with thee. And reminds us that God's covenant with David is also a covenant of salt; Ought ye not to know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt? These are the only two appearances of the term, and it is given that these two covenants are preserved like as by salt, in perpetuity. Contrasting with Jeroboam, a false king, and his priesthood, made up of baser men of the lewd sort, where anyone who could bring a young bullock and 7 rams could buy their way in. The true King and true Priest vs the false, the counterfeit. Very much a picture of Christ Jesus, Who is both King and High Priest, forever vs the beast and his antichrist, and their false prophet. Abijah gives a good accounting of faithful Judah and the Levitical ceremony and sacrifices kept as God had given them, fundamentalist, the Old Paths, vs these modernist perversions and Idolatry. The Lord is with the armies of Abijah, and they slay 500K Israelites, routing them and taking Bethel and other lands from the North. As well as this victory, we are told Abijah had 22 sons by 14 wives, and referred to the book of the prophet Iddo, material we do not have preserved as such. But there is a possibility that the books of the Kings may have been written by prophets, like Iddo. We have an account of Abijah there, anyway; 1 Kings 15:1-8 Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam the son of Nebat reigned Abijam over Judah. Three years reigned he in Jerusalem. and his mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom. And he walked in all the sins of his father, which he had done before him: and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as the heart of David his father. Nevertheless for David's sake did the Lord his God give him a lamp in Jerusalem, to set up his son after him, and to establish Jerusalem: Because David did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, and turned not aside from any thing that he commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life. Now the rest of the acts of Abijam, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. And Abijam slept with his fathers; and they buried him in the city of David: and Asa his son reigned in his stead. Of course, this account is less flattering. Chronicles leaves much of the flaws of David, Solomon and their sons out of the retelling, focusing more on the Temple and the priesthood, which was inspiration to the returning Jews out of Babylon, and their construction of the 2nd Temple. Abijah's walk with the Lord wasn't perfect. He sinned after the same manner of his father. But he was clearly a believer, and saved. And as we see by his victory against Jeroboam, even flawed and sinful believers can do great things for the Lord. And the blessings and promises of God to those who, like David, strive to walk in His ways, can still be a blessing to their children and grandchildren, as we will see in the story of Asa.

1 Kings 15:9-12 And in the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel reigned Asa over Judah. And forty and one years reigned he in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom. And Asa did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, as did David his father. And he took away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made. King Asa was one of few righteous kings in Judah, who walked with the Lord as David had. Who did that which is right, building up the altar of God at Jerusalem, and tearing down the idols and many, if not all, the high places. He took the sodomites out of the land. And we see members of the other tribes of Israel came to Judah because they saw that the Lord was with Asa. And God gave them peace, stood up for them in war, built up their cities, blessed them in all their doings. Again, we see the story of a king reflected in our Christian life. As an example. When we turn from idols and walk the paths God instructed us in His word, we know peace. We have a champion in war. We are blessed. And we bring others to the light. Because we have sought the Lord our God, we have sought him, and he hath given us rest on every side. This is a promise of God. Something worthy to place our faith in. Hebrews 11:6 But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. Matthew 7:7-8 Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. 1 John 5:14-15 And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him. It will be in His time. It may not look like what you imagined. It may be what you need not what you want. But He will answer our prayers, and deliver us with His mighty hand from whatever troubles us. We simply have to trust Him. Amen

Continuing the theme from yesterday's reading, we see that those who seek the Lord diligently are blessed. Even when the nation has gone the way of Baal, if they humble themselves and repent towards the Lord, He is faithful to forgive them. Here all Judah takes an oath, and promises to serve the Lord with all their hearts. And the word of the Lord comes upon the prophet to encourage them to continue in it, because of they break the oath, the Lord will certainly forsake them. The Lord granted them peace all around. But the oath made in their zeal also carries a burden, God holds them to their oath. But the high places were not taken away out of Israel: nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect all his days. Jesus said it is better to swear not at all. To just be doers of the word. Don't promise to seek God in all things, just do it. As we will see in the next chapter, it isn't the well intentioned promise that God respects, but faith. The promise to kill any who did not seek after the Lord the way the people swore to, was not from the Lord, but their own imagination. While reprobates and sodomites in the land were driven out, and the law was kept for abominations, and idols destroyed, the open ended oath left a lot of room for hypocrisy. Asa destroyed the images of his own mother, which was good, removing her as queen mother (a position that isn't respected in Biblical accounts, sorry Caths), he failed to remove all the high places. None of us are perfect and paths to be perfect will fail and prove us liars. Better to rely on God's mercy, than make promises in our excitement, that we in the flesh cannot keep.

As mentioned in yesterday's study, Asa over time turns his trust from the Lord to himself. To his treasure (that the Lord provided), to men, physicians, and ceased from going to God first. Especially after swearing oaths and vows to serve God with his whole heart. Now, when we are beset by enemies, we may find allies and win friends to help defeat them, but first go to God and He will bring these things into being. If we are sick, there's nothing wrong with using doctors, medicines, etc...but first go to God in prayer. Place your trust in Him, not men or things. Those men and those things may be the tools with which God heals you or delivers you, but it is God's mighty hand that we need. For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars. God's greatest means of punishment, the most brutal cord of scourging, is His withdrawal of protection against our suffering the consequences of our own sin. Thus we should seek His tender mercies everyday. Thanking Him for not judging us in His hot displeasure. Humbling ourselves before the Lord. We see righteous Asa put the prophet of God into prison for preaching the word of the Lord, that in his own pain and misery, he treated his subjects cruelly. He had war for the rest of his days and he suffered disease of the foot, and died, miserable it seems. Many Christians get this way, backslidden and resentful over time. It is a sad state of affairs. Walk with the Lord in meekness and in fear. Endure chastisements as one who is wise, and turn towards Him in all things. It is never too late to get right with God.

Jehosaphat becomes King over Judah, and strengthens his hand against Israel, built up the cities his father had won from the northern kingdom, built stores and had a mighty army of valiant men...but the Lord was with Jehosaphat because he walked in the first ways of his father, David. He sought not unto Baalim. But sought to the Lord God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not after the doings of Israel. Jehosaphat had peace, and wealth. The other kingdoms gave to him tribute. He had riches and honor in abundance. What he did, he did for the Lord. And was rewarded. He took away the high places and groves that his fathers failed to remove. And he established a ministry of preaching, sending his princes with the Levites, to preach the law of God. This not only had the effect of God blessing his reign, and Judah, but bringing the fear of the Lord to their neighbors. The preaching of the word more powerful than even his chariots and mighty men in bringing peace and subduing enemies, turning them into friends. This again is a picture of the millennial Kingdom, the peace, prosperity and the blessings of having the King of Kings rule and reign. It is also a standard we should pray for in our leadership, and hold as an example for our own lives and that which God has given us rule over. Spread the word, win souls, be a light to our neighbors and seek first the Lord in all things.

2 Corinthians 6:14 Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? 2 Thessalonians 2:10-12 And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness. Here in 2 Chronicles 18, we find King Jehosaphat, whose reign in Judah has been blessed by God, and who has walked as David walked, pleasing to the Lord, Yoking himself to wicked King Ahab of the northern Kingdom of Israel. This retelling of the story found in 1 Kings 22 retains the facts of the matter, Jehosaphat visiting Samaria, the feast given by Ahab, the proposal to retake Ramothgilead from the Syrians. The false prophets given the lying spirit of the Lord. Righteous Jehosaphat asking that they inquire of a true prophet of God. Micaiah the prophet is called for, whom Ahab despised. He speaks the word of God and tells Ahab he will die in the battle, the men scattered and going home to their tents for lack of a leader. And of course, all this comes to pass. But here, in 2 Chronicles, and the perspective of how blessed and faithful Jehosaphat is, his alliance with the wicked Ahab is surprising. Especially his willingness to commit to going to war with the prophecy of Micaiah, knowing it is a doomed endeavor. How often in our Christian life do we find ourselves in a similar situation? Where maybe we seek peace, or not to offend, or a fruitful partnership with someone who is unsaved, and wicked. And in our desire to please men, join them in things that the word of God has told us are wrong. Jehosaphat, wearing his kingly robes at Ahab's suggestion, becomes the target of the Syrians. If not for calling out to the Lord, he would have been slain then and there. The wicked taking advantage of mistaken loyalty to save their own skin is one of the biggest risks of finding yourself in the position of being allied with them. Meanwhile, Ahab disguised himself, as if to fool God. So, a random arrow fired by a certain man finds him, and slays him. But Jehosaphat, who walked righteously, spread the word of God, removed the sodomites and high places and groves, and who had prospered in all things, does suffer a decline. We are given this information in I Kings 22:48, after the death of Ahab; Jehoshaphat made ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Eziongeber. This was a significant thing Solomon had done to increase his wealth and power, but Jehosaphat fails, his ships wrecked. Is it the fruit of his alliance? Maybe. It could just be the way things go. But we shouldn't risk being unequally yoked with the wicked. Psalm 26:5 I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked.

In the matter of Ahab, and Jehosaphat's allegiance with the northern kingdom of Israel, the word of the Lord came upon the prophet Jehu. Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the Lord? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the Lord. Being yoked to the wicked, even your own brothers after the flesh, which is what Jehosaphat used to justify it, does not please God. How much more then the Zionism of many Christians today? If God's wrath is upon unbelieving Jews to the uttermost, how much more those that place them as our "greatest allies?" People who should know better, whom God's word is the final authority, and yet they join light for darkness. Blessing antichrists who curse the holy name of Jesus. But despite that lapse of judgement (one he would commit again) Jehosaphat's faith was great and he did lead a revival in Judah. He preached the Lord throughout the land, placed faithful judges over the people and encouraged and empowered the priests of the Levites to fulfill their role before God for the people. Jehosaphat calls to the men he placed in judgment over Judah to do right judgment with fear of the Lord. Not as respecters of persons. Serving the Lord faithfully and with a perfect heart. And proclaiming the righteousness of the Lord, warning against trespass, that His wrath not be kindled against them or the land. Deal courageously, and the Lord shall be with the good. This is our calling as Christians, to be just servants over those in our responsibility. To seek others profit more than our own. To deal fairly. To work as to the Lord. To obey authority. It is an Old Testament lesson of leadership that we see throughout the New Testament applied to all Christians. We are to judge righteously. Serve as to God. Hebrews 13:17 Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you. Romans 13:1 Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.

Revelation 20:6-10 Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years. And when the thousand years are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog, and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea. And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them. And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever. The final entry in the Chronicles of Jehosaphat's reign. We see here that the godly king's faith, and his efforts in leading revival among the people brings them to be able to call upon the Lord in adversity, and know He would not forsake them, but deliver them as He has promised. While not perfect in all his ways, Jehosaphat consistently sought the Lord. Even when he yoked with Ahab in their failed battle with Syria, he insisted the wicked king inquire of the prophet Micaiah. And so, when the armies of Ammon and Moab and Mt Seir assemble against Jerusalem and her king, Jehosaphat calls the people together. A called out assembly in fast, and prayer, and singing songs in praise of God. Calling on Him to remember His promise, showing they have faith in His word. Because of all the legwork, soul-winning, hard preaching, keeping the word of the Lord, Judah is right with God and able to do this in good conscience. They weren't perfect. There were high places still in the land. Not all their hearts were continuously with the Lord. But, generally the people were faithful and believed. And so in time of tribulation, with the armies gathered as the sand of the sea, the Lord confounded them, turning them on one another until they were all dead. Just as He will defeat the armies of Satan after the millennium. While we stand firm and sing praises to His name. A Christian who walks in the Spirit, who first seeks the things of God, praying and reading the Bible, going to church. Putting the profit of others above their own, can boldly go before God to ask for deliverance, knowing He is faithful and true. We are also given more context of the one real setback of Jehosaphat; the ships of Eziongaber, set to go to Tarshish for gold, as Solomon had done. In 1 Kings, we are told these ships were destroyed and never made it. Here we learn it wasn't his alliance with Ahab that sunk them, but Ahab's even more wicked heir, Ahaziah. Again, Jehosaphat allowed family ties to cloud his judgement. And God did not allow their unequal yoke to flourish.

The chronicles of Jehoram, King of Judah tell us that unlike his father Jehosaphat and grandfather Asa, or David, Jehoram was wicked. He married Ahab's daughter, likely a cause of Jehosaphat's uneasy allegiance with Israel in his reign. And the wickedness of Israel, he slayed his own brothers, worshiping false gods, restored high places, and fornication was brought in as he led Judah to sin. Elijah prophesies against him, great plagues against the people, that he himself will die of bowel disease, his very intestines coming out of him in the end. A fitting end. All his wives and most of his sons were dead. He had only one son living, his youngest, Jehoahaz. The least influenced by his wicked father, keeping the promise to David of the Messiah to come.

Here we are given the chronicles of King Ahaziah, a wicked king in Judah. He was the product of his father being married to the evil daughter of Ahab, Athaliah. This unequal yoke led to Ahaziah joining his cousin Joram, king of Israel in an ill-fated battle against Syria, and the anointing of Jehu by the word of God to be king. Jehu riding out with zeal to slay Joram, and being used by God to also slay Ahaziah. Ahaziah walked in the ways of his grandfather, Ahab, and brought Judah to sin as Ahab had Israel. Like a fish rotting from the head, the Bible teaches us that leadership can bless or curse a people. Wicked Athaliah would seize power as Queen of Judah, and slay all the heirs of her son, save one, Joash, who was spirited away and hid in the temple for 6 years while she reigned over the land. Isaiah 3:12 As for my people, children are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, they which lead thee cause thee to err, and destroy the way of thy paths. While each of us are given some dominion over something in our lives, male or female, the order of things as given by God is for men to rule in positions of power in the family and the nation. To be ruled by women is a shame and a curse. This extends to the household as much as it does to government. To the extent that women may usurp the authority of men, it is always the fault of men for abdicating their authority first. Adam, knowing the word of God forbidding the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden, took it and ate it to please Eve. When men rule poorly, weakly or without love for their subjects, cruel and ungodly, the results can end poorly for all concerned. Judah is about to experience 6 years of pain for the sin brought about by their kings' poor choices. Just as America is threatened with the same for ours.

Athaliah meets her end, as the plot of Jehoiada the priest is carried out, anointing the King's son, Joash to reign over Judah. There is a picture of the millennium in this, where Athaliah is a picture of the whore of Babylon, and her plaintive cry of "Treason!" fails to save her from the wrath, as the anointed of God is lifted up to his throne. Jehoiada the priest placing a 7 year old boy on the throne, a son of David, picturing an innocent King. The smashing of the altars of Baal, and the execution of the false prophet, Mattan, fits in there as well. But like all OT end time prophesies, it is a picture through a glass darkly. Echos back in time from the true end of days. The emphasis in Chronicles of the role of the persists and the importance of the Temple, as well as reinforcement of the rejoicing and sacrifices of burnt offerings, as it is written in the law of Moses, (a picture of Christ), is for the instruction of those returning from captivity in Babylon, centuries later.

The child-king, Joash began to reign at the age of 7, but was under the council of the high priest, Jehoiada. And all the days of Jehoiada, the Bible tells us, Joash did that which was right in the sight of the Lord. But, as we will see, once the influence of Jehoiada was gone, after his death, Joash allowed idols and groves and wickedness to flourish in Judah. 2 Chronicles 24 gives a slightly different view than what is given in 2 Kings 12, regarding the collection for the restoration of the Temple, and added context to the story. I notice we are told that Jehoiada took a second wife, and immediately afterwards, Joash orders the collection to restore the house of "your God." The King chastises the priests and his vizier, Jehoiada for their not making haste in doing as he commanded. This story, and the context of some recent events, set me of mind about the relationship between father figures and sons, of the flesh or spiritually, and the dynamic that ofttimes plays out. Nothing in the Bible is accidental, coincidental or incidental. Joash is riding the faith and judgment of his spiritual father, Jehoiada. He is walking in the ways because his mentor is. When Jehoiada takes another wife for himself, Joash makes a demand for a great work to be undertaken, and then complains that it isn't being done fast enough to his liking. How often do we see the sons or daughters of a Christian man, who have been kept holy by their father's holiness, kept in subjection, and seeing a crack in their father's character (for all have fallen short), grow to resent them. Grow to hate them. In that resentment and hate, their own sinful desires find an outlet, a justification. And they often will set an impossible standard, or a subjective measurement to meet for the authority figure, in an arbitrary way, just so they can claim a moral high-ground from which to rebel. Here, Joash demands a great work to ("your") God. Was it objectively a good thing? Probably. Did it come from prayer and seeking God first? There is no indication. Joash has created a way to outwardly show how righteous he is, while using it to claim Jehoiada and the priests are falling short of it. This is as a rebellious son, wanting to justify their own sin and unrighteousness by tearing down the reputation of the man who they have decided is a hypocrite, because that man reminds them daily of their own shortcomings. They feel judged continuously, because they feel guilty. And rather than look to themselves and get right with God, they tear down the moral authority in their life. And once that authority is removed from them, they sink further and further into sin. Many such cases. A lesson for fathers here, too. You cannot exert your own righteousness and salvation onto your children. Individuals have free will. We aren't given to micromanage our children, but to; Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it. We should not spare the rod. We should raise our children to fear the Lord, and be an example to them. When we fall short, demonstrate the mercy of God on us, and keep the same longsuffering mercy God shows us, and apply it to them. And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. But we shouldn't try to carry their salvation on ourselves, that they never learn and build their own relationship with God. Joash did that which was right in the sight of God while under Jehoiada's influence. But it sounds like he was never saved. If he was, the King allowed his own resentment for Jehoiada to fester, and then to justify being backslidden. Either way, it is a lesson in leadership. ...Now after the death of Jehoiada came the princes of Judah, and made obeisance to the king. Then the king hearkened unto them. And they left the house of the Lord God of their fathers, and served groves and idols: and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this their trespass. Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again unto the Lord; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear. And the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, which stood above the people, and said unto them, Thus saith God, Why transgress ye the commandments of the Lord, that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the Lord, he hath also forsaken you. And they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the Lord... Matthew 23:33-35 Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell? Wherefore, behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes: and some of them ye shall kill and crucify; and some of them shall ye scourge in your synagogues, and persecute them from city to city: That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar. Such is the fate of prophets, who preach the word of God against the wickedness of man. A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house. We can see how the history of the Kings, their Chronicles, judges these figures, Jehoiada being buried among the Kings, with David and the fathers. Joash, having been king over the spiritual decline of Judah, murder of a prophet of the Lord, judged by God by the Syrians, forced to give tribute from the very treasure he ordered collected for the restoration of the temple, he is murdered in his chambers, bed-ridden from disease, and is not buried in the sepulchres of the kings.

The reign of Amaziah, son of Joash, King of Judah, lasted 29 years. With a heart towards God in the first, and obeying the word of God given by the prophet, in the end he turned towards other gods and would not harken to the word of the Lord. When he set to go to war against Edom, he hired men from Ephraim, of the northern kingdom to bolster his ranks. When the prophet of the Lord came and told him he would not prosper with them, that God would ensure his loss, Amaziah sent the men away. But only after being assured the money he had paid for their hire would be restored to him by God. They left, angrily, and spoiling Judah on their way. Amaziah wins the battle at Mt Seir, defeating the Edomites, but slaughters his captives and takes their idols and set them up to be worshipped in Jerusalem. Wicked. And from there, the puffed up king sought to ally with wicked Israel, and was instead humiliated by their King Joash, both in word and battle. He refused council with the prophet of God, threatening to have him slain. Instead, he eventually is chased into hiding and slain, because he had turned from the Lord. The bitter end of an apostate, someone who has an understanding intellectually of the things of God, even tasting of the gifts, but in the end rejecting Him. Their destruction is greater than those who simply never sought the truth. Hebrews 6:4-8 For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, And have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, If they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame. For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God: But that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned. Now it came to pass, when the kingdom was established to him, that he slew his servants that had killed the king his father. But he slew not their children, but did as it is written in the law in the book of Moses, where the Lord commanded, saying, The fathers shall not die for the children, neither shall the children die for the fathers, but every man shall die for his own sin. The law of God is clear, the sons are not guilty of the blood owed by their fathers. Every man shall die for their own sin. This principle is just and right, from the perfect law of God. But the "original sin" heresy is based on the unbiblical idea that we are born damned for the sin of the Father. We do not die for another man's sin.

Uzziah allowed pride in himself for the victories and blessings given of God, to put himself where he ought not be, and it cost him all that he had, living out his days as a leaper, being buried in the field of his father's, and not their sepulcher. When we do great things for God, and are rewarded openly, we should remember that the rewards are not primarily for our benefit. Yes God wants to bless us, yes we will see success when we set our eyes on doing His will. But the real purpose is that others may see and believe. Just as wrath against the ungodly, and chastening of backslidden believers reveals the truth of God to men. Stay humble.

The short account of Jotham, King of Judah. The Bible says he did that which is right in the sight of the Lord, but that he did not enter into the temple. And while Jotham had success, building up walls and fortifications, and defeating enemies and receiving tribute, becoming mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord during his short reign, the people were yet corrupt. Hebrews 10:23-25 Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;) And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching. A Christian may have some success in their walk with Christ, and even do mighty things. But as the day approaches, and the time of judgment draws near, by forsaking the assembly we really limit what we can accomplish. Jotham is even listed in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew as a descendant. But as the Babylonian captivity loomed in Judah 's future, that day approaching, his failure to assemble in the house of the Lord seems to have contributed to the hearts of many waxing cold. At the very least, it did nothing to slow it down. To get people saved. Jotham was a contemporary with the prophets Isaiah, Hosea, Amos, and Micah, and their preaching aided him in his reign, no doubt. But how much more had he done had he not forsaken the assembly. If he had gone to church? Now Jotham's father, Azariah, had been smitten with leprosy for his defilement of the temple. Perhaps this put off Jotham, keeping him from attending. Maybe he was like those who had a bad experience or saw a bad report from their parents, and decided that "church isn't for me." Similar today to all these "recovering fundamentalists" and other movements of people claiming "church trauma" as an excuse for their being out of church. And while Jotham still had a semi-successful spiritual walk, most of those whiners and complainers are just looking to justify their sin. Many aren't saved and reject the truth. Some are saved and backslidden. We should all seek an assembly, and do what we can to edify it. Doing the first works of soul-winning. Being a blessing one towards another. More and more as the day approaches.

Ahaz was a wicked King who walked in the ways of Israel, and did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, worshipping Baal, burning his children in sacrifice, setting up idols and images and altars, groves and high places. And led the people to sin. The Southern Kingdom had a run of 4 godly kings, who were not necessarily perfect, but mostly ruled well, giving honor and fear to the Lord. And in one generation, the wickedness of one man brought all this ruin, slaughter, captivity and spoil against those that followed. Even as Israel led away captives of their brethren, the mighty men of Ephraim heard the rebuke of the word of God from the prophet Oded, who told them of God's displeasure at what they were doing, making their kin bondmen. As far as Israel has fallen, they still retained some measure of fear of God and repented of what they were to do. Judah, which should know better, and their King, Ahaz, failed to. Despite the wrath of God being upon them. He turned to Assyria for help, yet was spoiled by them and every surrounding nation. His worship of the Assyrian gods, the people who had just invaded and betrayed him, were the ruin of him, and all Israel. A true low point in Judah, which had mostly been blessed up until this. You get real end of days vibes, and current year feels from these stories. The US seems as Judah and Europe as Israel, and God's judgment is upon us all. Evil and untoward generations rise up, disobedient to parents, filled with rebellion, rejecting the truth of God, turning towards idols, false gospels and blasphemous paganism, murdering babies, celebrating sodomy, and being spoiled and slain by strangers in the land. It is a cycle that godly nations can find themselves in quickly, within one generation. Raise godly children.

And so we have the chronicle of the reign of Hezekiah, who took the throne at the age of 25, after the death of his father, Ahaz, the wicked. Ahaz reigned for 16 years, and did much that was wicked in the eyes of the Lord. When Hezekiah is anointed King, he immediately turns to the word of God as given to David, through Nathan the prophet, and David's seers, and reinstituted the Temple worship according to the Law of Moses. The priests and Levites, again a focus of Chronicles, written to those returning from captivity to rebuild the Temple, are commissioned to sanctify themselves, the temple, altar and vessels, and then give sin offerings for the people, to seek the forgiveness of the Lord. Hezekiah recognizes the tribulation their people had suffered under the rule of Ahaz, and their own whoredoms with Baal. And all the congregation worshipped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded: and all this continued until the burnt offering was finished. The sacrifices are so great, the Levites who served the priests were called to help in administering the offerings; But the priests were too few, so that they could not flay all the burnt offerings: wherefore their brethren the Levites did help them, till the work was ended, and until the other priests had sanctified themselves: for the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests. This indicates that the sons of Aaron, who were the priests tasked with the slaughter of the offerings, were not as zealous to sanctify themselves as the rest of the Levites. That there were not a few who just didn't care enough to get right. Here you have a young king, leading a revival by turning to the word of God, and some pushback or reluctance by the priesthood is indicated. Sometimes older Christians in lukewarm or dying churches resist the zeal of the young who come into the congregation. Even the pastor and deacons may resist the sudden change in attitudes that young Christians can bring to an assembly. But they should be as the loyal priests and Levites, eager to sanctify themselves and to do the work of the Lord. Even those saints who aren't used to evangelizing, or who have little to no experience with soul-winning, have to step up and join in the service of the Gospel. An injection of youth into a church is a reason to celebrate. Even the most prayerful and spiritual group of elders need foot soldiers to do the work of the Lord.

The revival led by King Hezekiah continues, and he leads the great restoration of the Passover, the feast of unleavened bread, which is given to Israel as a picture of Christ. The King bidding all Israel to the feast of the lamb slain for their iniquity is similar to this parable told by Jesus in Matthew 22:1-10 And Jesus answered and spake unto them again by parables, and said, The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son, And sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come. Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage. But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise: And the remnant took his servants, and entreated them spitefully, and slew them. But when the king heard thereof, he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city. Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy. Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage. So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests. Just as with Hezekiah's letters to all Israel, many made excuses, or mocked the invitation. But many were compelled to come, turning their heart to the Lord. And as Jesus' parable, both bad and good came. People who were ceremonially unclean, yet sought after the Lord God of Israel. And Hezekiah begs their pardon of the Lord, and our merciful God grants it, a picture of the fact that while we were yet sinners Christ died for us. Ye children of Israel, turn again unto the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and he will return to the remnant of you, that are escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria. And be not ye like your fathers, and like your brethren, which trespassed against the Lord God of their fathers, who therefore gave them up to desolation, as ye see. Now be ye not stiffnecked, as your fathers were, but yield yourselves unto the Lord, and enter into his sanctuary, which he hath sanctified for ever: and serve the Lord your God, that the fierceness of his wrath may turn away from you. For if ye turn again unto the Lord, your brethren and your children shall find compassion before them that lead them captive, so that they shall come again into this land: for the Lord your God is gracious and merciful, and will not turn away his face from you, if ye return unto him. Hezekiah is preaching the word of God to the lost sheep of Israel. The Northern Kingdom had been made nearly desolate by the Assyrians. A remnant still remained, and Ephraim and Manasseh were yet to be wiped out. There was still time and hope for them as a nation of people who called themselves after His name. The fierceness of His wrath could still be turned away. 2 Chronicles 7:14 If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land. This is a standing promise to Christians, from a God who cannot lie. God, who is longsuffering and merciful, Who rewards those who diligently seek him. Who runs to meet the prodigals coming home to Him. Very apt timing, the day before our elections here in the United States. Not that a godly person is on the ballot. Not that our wicked nation deserves healing. But as bad as the people are, and as unclean, we are to compel them to come. To turn back to the Lord, that the fierceness of His wrath be delayed, that a remnant will hear and believe, and His children will get right and sanctify themselves, so that He may forgive us our sin and heal our land.

The Levites to whom Chronicles is primarily written for, see the era of Hezekiah as a golden age, one they sought to return to after the Babylonian captivity. You can see how in this, they were edified to do that which was right. They also sought to keep their lineage pure, to the service of God as a way of separation. Not only their sons, but their wives and children being of their patrilineal line. Not mixing their marriages, reckoning their genealogies among the Levites.

Here in 2 Chronicles 32, and we have the last chronicles of the King, Hezekiah. Sennacherib, a captain of Assyria has come to lay siege against Judah and her walled cities having already begun its conquest of Israel. Knowing the hosts of the enemy are going to surround Jerusalem, compassing it about, Hezekiah has his men stop the flow of water to the fountains without the city. He has done great public works projects, and throughout his reign in Chronicles, we see how his diligently seeking the Lord has blessed him with civil engineering marvels (later we see he turned a river to bring water closer to the city). So his order to shut up the fountains so that Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water? When Sennacherib comes, he immediately begins to profane and blaspheme God. The parallel I see to the Reprobate Doctrine, that those who do not wish to retain God in their knowledge and blaspheme and speak of the Lord God of all creation as if he were like other gods, weak and ineffectual and not to be trusted or relied on, have the waters of Life shut up from them. While all others are told by Jesus to come and drink freely, reprobates come to spoil that which is God's and to do harm to his people, because they have been denied partaking in the water of Life. And while under siege, and railing and ranting by word and epistle, taunting God, Sennacherib, like the beast surrounds Jerusalem with his armies. And King Hezekiah cries out to heaven for deliverance with faith in the Lord. And the Lord strikes down the armies slaughtering the mightiest men of valor among them and sending the Assyrian General home in disgrace. So much so that his own children slay him. There's echoes of the end times there but also of the promise that God makes to us. If we are steadfast and true he will deliver us from the evil that the sons of Belial seek to do to us. Amen.

Manasseh's story of redemption by calling upon the name of the Lord, after a life of wickedness, idolatry, leading others to sin, murdering his own children, has been an inspiration to many Christians, brought low by their life of sin. Who have done what we might think are irredeemable things. And yet God's mercy falls on them that do great evil just as much as the innocent child who takes Jesus into their heart. God's grace abounds. 2 Kings 21:10-16 And the Lord spake by his servants the prophets, saying, Because Manasseh king of Judah hath done these abominations, and hath done wickedly above all that the Amorites did, which were before him, and hath made Judah also to sin with his idols: Therefore thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Behold, I am bringing such evil upon Jerusalem and Judah, that whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle. And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down. And I will forsake the remnant of mine inheritance, and deliver them into the hand of their enemies; and they shall become a prey and a spoil to all their enemies; Because they have done that which was evil in my sight, and have provoked me to anger, since the day their fathers came forth out of Egypt, even unto this day. Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another; beside his sin wherewith he made Judah to sin, in doing that which was evil in the sight of the Lord. In the account given in Kings, the repentance of Manasseh isn't given, but we are given the judgment of God upon Judah for the sins of Manasseh, which they were led to err by. It is important to recognize this difference between the judgment of nations and the judgment of individuals. Manasseh may have come to Jesus, and been forgiven and saved, and we will meet him in the Kingdom, but meanwhile Judah is rapidly heading to judgment by the desolation of Jerusalem, and the Babylonian captivity.

2 Chronicles 34 tells the reign of Josiah, son of the repentant Manasseh, who was only 8 years old when he took the throne from his father. We can infer that he was born later in Manasseh's life, and the influence of his father's conversion had an impact on him. At 16, by faith he began to diligently seek after the things of God. And we know without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. With a heart towards God, having purged the land of the idols and high places, Josiah began the repair of the temple. Just as a Christian seeking the Lord would cast out those things in their old life, and then begin building up the temple, repairing their hearts. Seeking after the things of God. And He rewards the king with the rediscovered copy of the Law. Just as the Spirit brings all knowledge and truth, and we study the Bible. And as Josiah is read the word, he rends his clothes knowing how far from God's will the people had fallen away. Just as we are convicted of sin the more we study His word. And so the king seeks after a prophet, to learn the will of the Lord, to know what to do. As the Christian may assemble under a pastor to be preached to. Josiah makes a covenant to serve God all his days, and God brings him peace and spares the king the wrath that is due the nation. It isn't a perfect parable to the Christian life, and we all must make the decisions along the path to do as Josiah, but it is a fine model for that life. One we can choose to follow.

Good King Josiah keeps the Passover in an epic fashion, greater than all who had come before him. And the Levites perform their role and function in the manner they were meant to, and it was a great success in honoring the Lord. But when Egypt's army was traveling through Judah on its way to aid the Assyrians against Babylon, Josiah does not consult God, but rather rides out to prevent them. But the Pharaoh, Necho, (likely Necho II), tells him he is making haste at the urgency of God, Josiah does not believe him. Now Egypt will fail and be defeated in the battle against Babylon with the Assyrians, and perhaps that was God's intention. It is doubtful Necho was a believer, but God did speak to Josiah a warning through him. There are some battles God undertakes with even unsaved people, that He does not want us interfering with. Josiah not consulting the prophets or seeking God's will led to his downfall, as he is slain at the battle at Megiddo. The prophet Jeremiah laments the kings passing, as we covered in the book of Lamentations. Judah is now facing the imminent rise of Babylon, and the captivity promised by God as punishment for their ways.

Here, in the final chapter of 2 Chronicles, we see the turnover of kings, the wickedness they did in the sight of God, while they were spoiled and made desolate by the Babylonians. And as Jeremiah had prophesied, the 70 year end to their captivity through Cyrus, King of Persia. Because the land saw no rest from their abominations, the Lord forced a Sabbath upon it. He has sent his prophets, and the people mistreated his servants, even killing the messengers, even as they killed Christ. Upon the return from captivity, the 2nd Temple would be built. Ezra tells that tale. I may take a diversion through some of the prophets before picking up that chronological reading. We will see where the Spirit leads.

The book of Ezra begins with the proclamation of Cyrus, returning the Jews to Jerusalem in fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy, and the order to rebuild the house of God. As king of Persia, Cyrus says he is given his power by the Lord God of heaven, and that the Lord has charged him, a foreign potentate, with the reconstruction of the temple. As we know from Haggai and Zechariah, the work on the temple would not be completed while he was king. But the treasure sent to prepare the temple was impressive. When the Lord says in Haggai 2:8 The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, He is not only saying that all riches in the world are His, but specifically the treasure given for this purpose, which languished until Zerubbabel and Joshua heard the prophets and finished the job. But here, at the beginning of the end of exile, the Jews; Judah, Benjamin and Levites, gladly returned to the city, with the treasure of the Lord.

The account of Ezra 2 is till looking back at the time of the return, to establish some things needed to be understood for his story. The return from captivity first under Cyrus the great, and then under Darius I, when Zerubbabel and Joshua and the others returned to Jerusalem. The genealogy of the Levites who returned is given here. The timeline from Haggai and Zechariah to Esther, then to Ezra, and Nehemiah spans several decades within the Persian Empire's rule over the Jews. Haggai and Zechariah prophesied around 520 BC during the reign of Darius I, focusing on the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem. Approximately 40-50 years later, around 483-473 BC, the events of Esther unfolded under Ahasuerus (likely Xerxes I), who reigned from 486 to 465 BC. Following Xerxes I's death, his son Artaxerxes I ascended the throne around 465 BC. Ezra's mission to Jerusalem occurred around 458 BC, and Nehemiah's efforts to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem began around 445 BC, both under Artaxerxes I's rule. So we have skipped forward around 60 years in time from Zechariah to Ezra. We see Zerubbabel and Joshua (Jeshua) mentioned. Nehemiah mentioned here is likely not the same as the Governor of Judah who ruled after Ezra's time. Just as the Mordecai mentioned in Ezra 2:2 as part of the list of exiles who returned to Jerusalem around 538-520 BC, during the reign of Cyrus the Great, 65+ years before the events of Esther, make it highly unlikely he is the same guy. It is possible that Ezra is giving their names, or at least Nehemiah's, as a shorthand way to say his people returned then. The Nehemiah in Ezra 2:2 would have been part of the initial return and rebuilding efforts, whereas the later Nehemiah was a high-ranking official in the Persian court before being appointed governor to oversee the reconstruction of Jerusalem's walls. But it's more likely that these men shared a common name. We are given a genealogy for multiple clans of the Levites and the understanding that those who could not provide a patriarchal lineage were rejected as polluted, and put away from the preisthood. It is funny then that today, Jews Mark their lineage by mother, not father. A matrilineal line due to their rampant mixing, fornicating and adultery. The inverse of their supposed father's law. We are given their list of holdings they returned with, and the wealth they gave freely as an offering to the service of God. So we see the priests, Levites, the singers and porters and the Nethinims listed. What a great choir of 400 people singing Psalms and hymns! I had to look up what Nethinims meant. "The Nethinim (or Nethinims in older King James translations) were a group of temple servants in ancient Israel, meaning "given ones" or "those set apart". Primarily of foreign descent and assigned to the Levites, they performed menial, practical tasks like cutting wood and carrying water for the Tabernacle and later the Temple." They were likely either of mixed Gibionites or Midianite decent, used as slaves to the Levites under Solomon, their children returning in service as well. So Ezra gives us the background and setting for his story in the first 6 chapters. Then in Ezra 7 he tells us his tale.

Ezra 3 continues the historic narrative being given, explaining how the circumstances of the author and his time came to be. Here we flash back to 538–537 BC, and the Jews initial return under Cyrus’s decree and begin temple construction, laying the foundation for the Temple. This is roughly 17 years before Haggai and Zechariah, in 520BC. And before the full 70 years of captivity had expired. The people celebrated and cheered the laying of the foundation and the beginning of their work. Doing the feasts and offerings as best they could, singing the songs of praise and worship. Blowing the trumpets. But while the young people shouted for joy, the old men wept. They had seen the former glory and remembered what the first Temple looked like, and the Bible says the people couldn't tell the difference between the joy and weeping, it was so loud. There is a parallel with Christians today. That as a believer comes to repentance, trusting in the Lord, there is great celebration, in Heaven, in the congregation, and in the heart of the person who has accepted the truth of Christ. This laying of the foundation of Christian life. Of the Temple of God. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? When we sing together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the Lord; because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever, toward the Israel of God. But some weep, from regret or longing. We cheer the new babe in Christ and perhaps remember when the foundation was laid in our hearts, and the joy that came. Maybe they weep to remember God's mercy on us when they were saved. Psalm 51:12 Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.. Still the shouts of joy and sadness are one voice. And the glory is God's.

Ezra continues to give background to the history of rebuilding the Temple, and here he writes about the period when, under Cyrus the Jews returned to Israel, and began work on the foundation. And adversaries of Judah and Benjamin, the people who occupied the land of Israel after the Assyrian captivity, the mixed and displaced strangers that had become the Samaritans ask to help Zerubbabel and the people with the construction. They say that they too worship the Lord, and had since the days of Esarhaddon, king of Assur, which is Assyria. But, as we know they worship what they know not. 2 Kings 17:20-34 And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, and afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of spoilers, until he had cast them out of his sight. For he rent Israel from the house of David; and they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king: and Jeroboam drave Israel from following the Lord, and made them sin a great sin. For the children of Israel walked in all the sins of Jeroboam which he did; they departed not from them; Until the Lord removed Israel out of his sight, as he had said by all his servants the prophets. So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day. And the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel: and they possessed Samaria, and dwelt in the cities thereof. And so it was at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they feared not the Lord: therefore the Lord sent lions among them, which slew some of them. Wherefore they spake to the king of Assyria, saying, The nations which thou hast removed, and placed in the cities of Samaria, know not the manner of the God of the land: therefore he hath sent lions among them, and, behold, they slay them, because they know not the manner of the God of the land. Then the king of Assyria commanded, saying, Carry thither one of the priests whom ye brought from thence; and let them go and dwell there, and let him teach them the manner of the God of the land. Then one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and dwelt in Bethel, and taught them how they should fear the Lord. Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities wherein they dwelt. And the men of Babylon made Succothbenoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima, And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim. So they feared the Lord, and made unto themselves of the lowest of them priests of the high places, which sacrificed for them in the houses of the high places. They feared the Lord, and served their own gods, after the manner of the nations whom they carried away from thence. Unto this day they do after the former manners: they fear not the Lord, neither do they after their statutes, or after their ordinances, or after the law and commandment which the Lord commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel... They did not worship the Lord alone, or properly. They were worshiping in the high places, the mountains. John 4:19-23 The woman saith unto him, Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet. Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship. Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father. Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews. But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. So these Samaritans were offering an ecumenical union to build the Lord's house, similar to if a group of Catholics sought to join with a NT Baptist Church. And naturally, Zerubbabel rejected their offer as tainted. Offended, these false religions begin to petition the government of Persia to stop the rebuilding effort. Ezra 4 documents the pre-520 BC efforts by Judah's enemies to undermine the temple rebuilding that began shortly after Cyrus's decree in 538 BC, and persisting throughout his reign, through his predecessor Cambyses's rule (530-522 BC), and into Darius I's early years, circa 522 BC, resulting in halted work until Darius's second year in 520, when Haggai and Zechariah pick up. The chapter also mentions later similar oppositions during Ahasuerus's reign (likely Xerxes I, starting around 486 BC) with initial accusations, and under Artaxerxes I (465-424 BC) via detailed letters that enforced a cessation of Jerusalem's reconstruction as a threat. Ezra lists all these efforts as one long opposition campaign. How relatable this is to our modern day efforts of soul-winning and building up the house of God. How frequently do false "Christian" leaders join together to get Bible-believing church's "in trouble" with the local government? To try to stop door to door evangelism, labeling it as solicitation. To try and get churches denounced and shut down for preaching against the sodomites. When you look at the history of the Roman Catholic Church, it literally was formed by apostates working in conjunction with the government to shut down and martyr believers and good NT churches, to force them out. Declaring their pastors heretics. History is filled with these same types of people. But God had promised in the 70th year of captivity to turn towards the people if they built His house. And Darius I blessed the construction, and it resumed for a while.

Continuing the history lesson, Ezra 5 mentions the prophets sent to spur the Jews to continue the construction of the 2nd Temple, and Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest who were persuaded to finish the work. But, again, local governors of the other nations questioned their efforts, seeking to derail the construction. Tatnai asks, Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall? They also ask for the names of the construction crew, so they could inform on them to the King in Persia. But the Lord protected the Jews and gave them the response designed to bring the matter to Darius I for judgment. They answer truly, if not the answer Tatnai and his crew were looking for. That they are servants if the God of heaven and earth. That they do as He commanded and restore what was, and that the Lord destroyed by the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Further, that Cyrus the great had made a decree to build this house if God. That the king returned to them that which they had plundered under Nebuchadnezzar. The Jews tell their inquisitors to go tattle to Darius, and let the king decide the matter, trusting God will ultimately be the judge. The meekness and humility to say, "we are the servants of God," and leaving the judgment to the higher power trusting God has our backs, is a difficult thing for many believers. When we are accused by others, targeted for some kind of persecution for doing the Lord's work, we should not be afraid. We should not proudly stand up. We should show meekness and humility before God, trusting Him to deliver as He sees fit. Others may, in fear, kowtow to their accusers. Ashamed of what they are doing for the Lord, and cease their efforts hoping their accusers will leave them alone. Neither of these paths are what God calls us to do. We are to humbly and honestly stand for what we believe in, while accepting whatever judgment comes upon us for it. And if you suffer for it, give glory to God. And if He delivers you, give glory to God. Too many want to take matters into their own hands and force the issue on our terms. Pridefully. But again and again in scripture we see this isn't the way. Daniel and David, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Zerubbabel and Joshua. So when an apartment manager or homeowner threatens to call the police on soul winners, don't argue. Don't get proud. Humble yourself but stand firm, being honest that you are being a servant of the God of heaven and earth. Trust Him to deliver you. Let Him repay.

In Ezra 5, the governor Tatnai and his allies had written to Darius I, king of Persia, seeking to stop the building up of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple, which had begun under Cyrus, and was now being done in earnest by Zerubbabel, after the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah. Here, in Ezra 6, we see that Darius seeks to understand the matter, and finds the scroll of Cyrus's proclamation. The return of the treasures looted from the house of God by Nebuchadnezzar, and the gift of stones and timber ordered by the former king. Darius not only endorses the construction and decrees it is good, but calls on God to curse those who oppose it, and demands that Tatnai and the others pay a tribute in sacrifices to the effort, that the Jews may offer unto God and pray for their king and his sons. When the enemies of the people of God sought to derail His will, they not only failed, but were made to aid the effort. It may be a reach, but it seems to me to be a picture of what would come when the Jews sought to stop Jesus, to destroy Him, and instead brought the sacrifice that fulfilled God's will for man. And Jesus, the Temple was raised again on the third day, just as 3 years after the construction started, in the 3rd year of Darius, the new temple was complete. And like Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, and all the children of Israel, the priests, Levites and the rest in captivity kept the Passover with joy and the rebuilt temple, as we rejoice over the Passover Lamb, which is Christ.

Like Ezra, we are of a long line of a holy priesthood, great men of God before us, and we are ordered by the King to gather together, and carry the treasure given us, the law of our God in our hands, to go up to Jerusalem to build the church of our Lord. Today's reading is a wonderful demonstration of God equipping His men to do His work, and the application on this Saturday morning as I head out to knock doors, is clear. Tell someone about Jesus this weekend. And I was strengthened as the hand of the Lord my God was upon me, and I gathered together out of Israel chief men to go up with me. Go soul-winning!

Here in Ezra 8, he recounts the genealogy of those that came down to Jerusalem from Babylon, carrying the treasure for the house of God. It lists the key patriarchs of the lead families, each with significant roles. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, secured a priestly covenant through zeal. Ithamar, Aaron’s son, upheld temple duties. David, the iconic king, represents royal and messianic legacy. Shechaniah, meaning "YHWH dwells," ties to divine presence. Parosh ("flea") led a resilient clan. Pahath-moab ("ruler of Moab") suggests foreign integration. Joab ("YHWH is father") was a chief warrior for David's mighty men. Along with the others, each are given a pedigree to note the continuity of things, going back to Jacob, Moses and Aaron, and David. The integration of Moabites and others after the captivity, into the ranks of "Jews," is something that is often contested, and will come into play here in Ezra 9 and 10, but it's interesting. Ezra says that he refused armed escort from the king, relying on God to protect them. He proclaimed a fast of 3 days, as they prepared to make their way across the Jordan, asking the Lord to watch over them. They are traveling with an incredible amount of wealth and treasure. The offer wasn't unreasonable. But Ezra had spoken to the king saying The hand of God would protect them. It is like the old cliche about the person trapped in flood waters, refusing rescue boats and helicopters because the Lord would save him. Maybe the offer itself came from God. Not everything in the Bible is proscriptive, and in Ezra it is often just his description of events. Their faith saw them through and God did deliver them, but we shouldn't always refuse help when that help may be the means God chose to protect us. It's like when Satan is tempting Jesus in the wilderness. Matthew 4:5-7 Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple, And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone. Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. There is a fine line between faith and knowledge that God will watch out for us, and tempting God by putting ourselves in the position where He has to. Between courage and faith and testing the Lord. I think Ezra fell just on the good side of faith vs tempting God. It was God's will and plan that they rebuild His house and the situation was providentially blessed. However, it may not always be the wisest course. They arrive in Jerusalem and the sum of the treasure is weighed, and offering is made for them by the priests. Their mission accomplished. Furthering the people and the house of God. Isaiah 41:10 Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. Balancing this promise, and knowing that when we do the Lord's will we have a hedge of protection, with the understanding that sometimes we will be afflicted, suffer, be beaten, jailed, even beheaded, all for the cause of Christ, and that, even with the knowledge that both things are true, we shouldn't take needless risks to test the Lord.

Genesis 6:1-2 And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them, That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose. 2 Corinthians 6:14 Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? Ezra, having returned to Jerusalem with the treasures to aid in the building of the walls of the city, and the establishment of God's law in the rebuilt temple, faces a crisis when he sees that the Levites among the land have taken strange and outlandish women for their wives.
