He calls in prayer, recalling the words of God that Israel, upon entering Canaan would not give their daughters to the sons of the heathens, nor take their daughters in marriage. He reasons that, given God's grace in allowing the restoration and the support of kings, and the end to captivity, this affinity with abominations cannot stand. That it would be the final straw, and God would destroy them utterly, leaving not a remnant behind. He says to God, we cannot stand before you in their trespasses. Worse, the mixed marriages, the "holy seed of Israel" joining with these heathen nations had led to the men doing accord to the abominations of the Canaanites. Just as the sons of God, those of the line of Seth, Enos, believers who called upon the name of God, mixing with the daughters of man, those unbelieving and from Cain, led to the wickedness and abominations that caused God to repent of creating man. Sending the flood that only Noah, perfect in his generations, and his sons and wives escaped. Just as today, we are told not to be unequally yoked to non-believers, not just in marriage but in all spiritual enterprises. But is the sin here the mixed marriages by ethnicity or spiritually, where the women bring the men to commit idolatry and abominations? The way that Balaam caught the Israelites at Baalpeor. There are 4 outlandish women (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba—referred to as "the wife of Uriah") in the lineage of Christ. God showed grace to these mixed marriages, clearly. He used their offspring in the human genealogy of Christ. No greater honor could be given any woman. But these women had faith, making the difference. That God uses our mistakes and weaknesses to His benefit and to do His will, is a lesson found throughout scripture. A sovereign Lord that doesn't simply micromanage everything, but actually allows free will, time and chance within all of His creation to determine things, and ultimately, He uses all those things for His will regardless of how they seem to us. Having said that, many will teach that the Bible clearly paints mixed marriages as a sin. That beyond the spiritual things, being unequally yoked with unbelieving spouses, that the physical nations, races, should not marry. Others point to Moses and the Ethiopian woman he married, and say that it is fine. That Miriam's leprosy given as a curse by God when her and Aaron took the opportunity to undermine Moses, shows that God hates racism or something. But Miriam's sin was rebellion. Not "racism." In my opinion, it is less than ideal, but not always a sin. That God would prefer a nation of believers that kept marriage among themselves. That the natural consequence of mixed races are generally negative, especially when both parents are outside of the faith, and doubly so when one spouse is a believer and the other is not. He gave us the nations and bounds and habitations thereof. Every tongue and kindred can come to salvation by faith. There is no difference, Jew or Greek. But there are nations in Heaven, the Bible says. On earth, it matters. Mixed marriages are how the Assyrian empire destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel. How they became Samaritans over time. Being bred out of existence by miscegenation is a judgment of God against a nation. So, in my opinion, it is taught against, it is unwise, but it is also not the end of the world if both are saved believers and they raise their children to be. But if one isn't a believer and the other is, that sin is compounded by it being a mixed-race relationship. Especially as we see from Eve to Solomon, and even these Levites, that being spiritually mixed always takes men's hearts from God and into sin through their wives. Just to be clear, I think pastors should ALWAYS preach against spiritually mixed marriages. To tell young people in no uncertain terms that they shouldn't even date an unsaved person, especially from unsaved families that practice a different religion. I think they should counsel against ethnically and racially mixed marriages, even between believers. That it's generally not a good thing, personally and for your nation. And if done out of the wrong spirit, it is wicked. Fetishism. To spite parents. To chase the exotic. To force the issue when you lack the faith that God will provide you the appropriate partner. Self-loathing. These are all common and sinful motives behind the act. But, sometimes people do what people do. And they do it out of genuine love and things happen. So we should show grace to those in such a relationship, when they are brothers and sisters in Christ. If this seems like a compromise to some, I don't know what would please you. If this seems harsh and racist to others, I don't care. Ultimately, Ezra's concerns are both racial and spiritual. He is going to make his case in the next chapter for how this problem can be resolved. And depending upon your viewpoint, depending on your discernment.... Your opinions might differ from his.

Here in the final chapter of Ezra, we see the solution that the Jews come up with for the men who took strange wives and intermarried outside of the children of Israel. Mass divorce. The putting away of the women and even their children with them. Malachi writes, For the Lord, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away, and Jesus clearly teaches that the idea of divorce is not God's, but man's. Matthew 19:8 He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so. Divorce was never in God's plan for marriage. The children of Israel may have been commanded to not intermarry with the heathen, but He never commanded them to divorce. Ezra's emotional breakdown over the issue did not lead to God telling him to order this. A man, responding to Ezra came up with the idea. And Ezra agreed and the people went along with it. 113 men are assumed to have been unequally yoked, based on the list and names. (I didn't count it, I looked it up). They spent a considerable amount of time doing it. Ending with sacrifice for their sins. But was this God's will? Wouldn't the more prudent course of action be to do to the men who had taken strange wives as they would have done to those that didn't come down to Jerusalem to vote in the matter? And that whosoever would not come within three days, according to the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his substance should be forfeited, and himself separated from the congregation of those that had been carried away. These men could have been removed from office, having disqualified themselves. The way a pastor or Deacon would be if they divorced or committed adultery. Two wrongs don't always make a right. There should have been grave consequences for their disobedience, but not at the expense of the institution God ordained. In Nehemiah, we will see shortly that he faced a similar problem with one specific priest. And he doesn't order the priest's divorce, he removes him from office. I think Ezra was overcome and overwhelmed by the tough choice he had to make, and when the man Shechaniah the son of Jehiel came up with the idea of putting the wives away, so that the men who transgressed could eat their cake and have it too, Ezra pounced on it because it was the easier path. When we are faced with a hard choice because of our sins, and decisions of what to do about it will require self-sacrifice and dealing with unpleasant repercussions, we should wait on God's will. Do the hard things. Not latch on to man's compromise and easy way out. It is hard to put someone out of church, but it is God's prescription for certain situations. It can be hard living with a spouse who doesn't treat you right. God says stick it out. We should patiently accept the consequences of our actions. That would show true remorse and humility before God. Not doing the easy thing and then crediting yourself for it.

We are in Nehemiah 1, which continues the narrative of the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and it picks up roughly 13 years after the end of Ezra. Nearly 100yrs after Haggai and Zechariah. And we are told that the city's walls and gate remain in ruin, still fire scorched from the original invasion by Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian empire. Nehemiah, the cup bearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I, in the 10th year of his reign, laments the languished reconstruction. That now, after many divine starts and human stops, Jerusalem still is not walled. He recounts the instructions of Moses, that if the people who call themselves the children of Israel failed to keep God's commandments, and chase after other gods, they would be scattered to the ends of the earth. But if they turn back again to Him, repenting towards the God of their fathers, He will bless them and gather them again. Nehemiah's prayer is often used by dispensationalists, saying "See, this proves that God will always gather His people!" But, alas, this is the final time. The city God chose to place His name needs to be ready for the coming of the Messiah. The people have been unable and unwilling to repent. Only a remnant remain faithful. In a few centuries, Jerusalem will be under Roman control which will act as a means to protect and preserve the city until Jesus' birth. Doing what the Jews failed to do all this time. Also, we see Nehemiah lay out the condition for this gathering, that the people turn back to the Lord and obey Him. That includes being ready for the coming of Christ, with hearts ready. That if they believed Moses and the prophets, they would be prepared for Him. Modern Israel was not the result of Jews coming to repentance, and turning towards God the Father by embracing His Son. It was the result of pride, and satanic forces. They are cut off in unbelief, their covenant faded away. As Jesus cried; O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not! Behold, your house is left unto you desolate. For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.

Nehemiah recounts how he came to be in the king of Persia's presence, as cupbearer. Bringing wine to the king. And his sad countenance at the condition of his fathers' home, Jerusalem, still not finished rebuilding. The king inquires about the matter, and he agrees to give Nehemiah a time to go an do the work, letters of passage and of support to show the governors beyond the river, that they prepare timber for beams and provide materials. Unlike Ezra, Nehemiah travels with captains and horsemen. When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel. But Nehemiah continues to the city, and the gates are consumed with fire, collapsed to the point he has to enter on foot. He goes out and examines the gates and the walls without announcing himself, and afterwards he goes to the Jews and says let us build up the wall of Jerusalem that we be no more a reproach. Hearing his encouragement and that the hand of God was upon him and this goal, they rose up to join him. Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite and Geshem the Arabian scoff at Nehemiah's mission. But the cupbearer tells them they have no portion in Jerusalem. The God of heaven, he will prosper us; therefore we his servants will arise and build. Christians today have a mandate from the King of kings, Christ Jesus, to build up heavenly Jerusalem. And He will prosper us when we do. But as Peter writes, Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts... When we seek to do the works of the Lord, we will face acorn and ridicule, often from those close to us. But they have no portion or memorial in Jerusalem. We should be ready laborers and remind ourselves of this. That we please God and not men. And do the work He has commanded us to do.

Many hands make light work. Nehemiah has spurred men from all over Judah to help repair sections of the walls and fix the gates. Some working on sections near their homes, others helping out who live outside the district being surrounded. Priests from Jerusalem led repairs near the Sheep Gate and temple area; goldsmiths and apothecaries from the city handled sections by the Broad Wall; merchants from Keilah and Beth-haccerem worked on districts around the Valley Gate and Dung Gate; rulers from half the district of Jerusalem and the other half oversaw portions near the Refuse Gate; Levites from Mizpah and Gibeon, along with singers from the house of Gilgal, mended spots opposite the ascent to the armory; Tekoites from the village of Tekoa built near the great tower projecting to the wall of Ophel; and men from Jericho, Zanoah, Beth-zur, and other rural locales contributed to gates and walls in their home territories. All pitching in gladly, except some of the rulers who are mentioned derisively. All hands on deck is how we should approach the local church. If you have a talent or skill or even time, you should pitch in. The gifts you have are of God, designed to edify the church in the same way these men edified the walls of Jerusalem. Ephesians 4:11-12 And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ So, if you go to a local church, pitch in. Don't just show up for Sunday morning service and leave. Make yourself useful in whatever capacity you're asked to. If you don't belong to a church, find one and join it. It's a command of God.

And so as the construction continued, and the mockers increased their scorn and ridicule, it became apparent to the scorners, like Sanballat, a governor in Samaria, Tobiah the Ammonite, that the Jews were serious in the endeavor. The wall wasn't finished but it was getting there. In our Christian life, we may experience initial scoffing by our friends, family and neighbors. People who doubt our conversion because they know us. The old man. And those things they say may throw us off our course. Make us doubt ourselves. When Tobiah says a fox could topple their wall, it's like when a brother or parent scoffs at our faith and our attempts to get right. But we see from Nehemiah how to handle this. To turn their reproach upon their own head. To trust in the Lord. Their mocking comes not only at our expense, but it reveals in themselves to their own sin and iniquity. Proverbs 29:27 An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked. Jesus says He came into this world to divide it. Even family. John 3:19-21 And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved. But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God. So the scoffers in Nehemiah's day set their minds to violence in an effort to stop the construction. This also can be how some people will react to your sanctification, as you build upon the foundation Christ has laid in your heart. So we must stand watch, and continue building. We put on the whole armor of God. Ephesians 6:10-18 Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness; And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God: Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints The prayers of the saints are our spears, always at the ready. Pray for one another to stand strong to the mocking. Our brothers and sisters in Christ. Knowing we have each other's back, as the people of Jerusalem did against the mockers. This is another reason in a long list, as to why you need a local church. To help you edify your walls and repair your breaches, and to watch over you in prayer as you reclaim the stone from the rubble, and build anew in Christ. Go to church!

Nehemiah as governor over Judah, hears the cry of the people that they have been taxed so heavily during lean times that they had to turn to the rulers and the rich men, and borrow against their homes and property, and their sons and daughters. That their fellow tribesmen were changing brothers usury. Nehemiah makes a plea to the lenders and bankmen, that God is not pleased that they have done this to their people. And those holding the loans forgive the people their debts. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. Then Nehemiah proceeds to say that in his time, he hasn't demanded the honor or tribute of the governor's bread. Only sufficient food to feed those at his table. This is a tax on all the people, and he is entitled to it, but refused it to avoid offending God. That they did not acquire land or get rich off the position Nehemiah and his house were in. Instead he labored on the wall with them It's similar to Paul's epistles. 2 Thessalonians 3:8 Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you. 2 Corinthians 11:9 And when I was present with you, and wanted, I was chargeable to no man: for that which was lacking to me the brethren which came from Macedonia supplied Acts 20:34 Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me. Note Nehemiah did receive payment of food and lodging and was not left to starve. His house was supplied with the Ox and sheep and fouls. Similarly, a pastor is entitled to some payment for their services. 1 Timothy 5:18 For the scripture saith, thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward. It's a pretty clear line between being paid for the ministry with enough to live on, and taking advantage of the position to become rich from it. Because some have used filthy lucre to get mansions and private jets, some Christians begrudge any tithing or professional full time ministry. But the excesses of some doesn't mean that all are guilty. Tithes and supporting a pastor are a good thing. Pastors are to not take advantage of their flock.

Nehemiah bears the end of the construction of the walls and gates and his enemies still seek to destroy him. When they realize they cannot lure him out, they threaten to defame him that the authorities of the King of Persia will come and destroy him for rebellion. But he isn't tricked and he calls them out on their lies. Then they seek to have him violate the sanctity of the temple in fear, sinning. Again, his faith is in the Lord and he refuses and continues the work to completion. Then the nobles of Jerusalem, who are in league with Tobiah, and intermarrying with his family begin to tell Nehemiah what a good guy he is, and to convince Nehemiah while at the same time Tobiah is sending him threatening messages. These are common tactics of the enemies of God. Truck, threaten, betray, seek to have you sin, tell lies about you, flatter you, and get those with influence in your world to turn on you, while they try and get the powers that be against you. The Jews did it to Christ. He says, because they hated Him first, they'll do the same to us. But Nehemiah continues to the end, doing what God commands. Faithful that it will work out for good. He doesn't waste time exchanging railing for railing or fighting with them. He just does the work of the Lord. This is all we can do. Trust God. Don't fear. Isaiah 41:10 Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. Matthew 5:11-12 Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

Nehemiah 7 records a detailed genealogy of the Jewish exiles who returned to Jerusalem from Babylon, totaling 42,360 people, along with 7,337 servants and 245 singers, for a grand total of 49,942 individuals. Among them, 652 individuals from the families of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai (who took his name from marrying a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite) could not prove their lineage as part of the priesthood or Israel, as their genealogical records were missing, leading to their exclusion from the priesthood. Similar problem Ezra agonized over, and ended up compromising by ordering a mass divorce. Nehemiah just excludes them. Sometimes the simplicity of doing the right thing makes us stumble over it. We overcomplicate and make things way more difficult than it has to be. But following God's word and trusting it is so, relieves us of that burden. We can take comfort in the simplicity of obedience.

Here in Nehemiah 8, with the walls completed and the people gathered, they celebrate the feast of Tabernacles, or booths. Sukkot. First seen in Joshua 18. Commemorating their wandering in the wilderness, just as they themselves had been in captivity. And Ezra (not the prophet), reads the law and the Levites teach all the people that they have understanding. From a pulpit made of wood, that all the people could hear, reading the word of God and teaching His ways. With the people answering, Amen! Amen! It was an Independent Fundamental Baptist service. A week long conference. A revival. When you are at church this Sunday, remember that we are an unbroken line of believers, worshipping God in the Spirit and in truth. Just the way they did in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's day. And he read therein before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until midday, before the men and the women, and those that could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law. Pay attention in church, when the pastor or anyone is at the pulpit, reading and expounding on the scriptures. Sit up straight. Ears open. Receiving it gladly. Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose...And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people; (for he was above all the people;) and when he opened it, all the people stood up Here is the tradition we Baptists have, of standing out of respect for God's word as the man of God preaches from the pulpit. ...and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place. So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. This is the purpose of the called out assembly. To give understanding to the people, reading from the Law of God distinctly. And all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands: and they bowed their heads, and worshipped the Lord with their faces to the ground. This is the way to worship God in spirit and truth. Notice the people were outside. They made booths of branches. It was simple and about God and His word. The Roman Catholics would say you must have a temple to worship God. The Jews in Jerusalem had the best temple, and yet they pitched tents to hear sermons preached from an old wooden pulpit. Acts 7:48-49 Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; as saith the prophet, Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool: what house will ye build me? saith the Lord: or what is the place of my rest? Never mind those that need worldly things, carnal, idols of wood, metal and stone. Beads. Incense. Stained glass and marble. They have to have carnal and worldly things because they do not worship God in spirit and truth. They need physical relics and iconography because they lack the Spirit. Baptists follow the Bible.

The revival in Jerusalem, led by Nehemiah and the efforts of the people to rebuild the wall, as they had rebuilt the temple, leads to their confession as a people; that they and their fathers had sinned against the Almighty God. They admit their wrong doing. They admit their fathers. They take the blame for their people's repeated stiff-necked reaction to God's mercy and grace. For the blood of the prophets. For their disobedience. They say they failed to live in the laws of the Lord. That they sinned against His judgments. They acknowledge that if a man do those judgments, he shall live in them. And they acknowledge that the Lord's use of the armies and kings brought against them, from Assyrians on, the Babylonian captivity and being made a tributary to Persia, was all justified for their sin. They all repent towards God. Admitting their sin and the justice of God against them, and appeal to His grace and mercy. They seek His salvation. And so they make a covenant to keep and put their seal upon it.

When the roll is called up yonder.... Nehemiah brings revival to the people. A recommitment to the Lord, His commands, the curses and oaths. And the names of those sealed on their proclamation are recorded for eternity. Just as the names of all who are sealed by the Spirit are in the books of life.

As Nehemiah begins to wrap up, with one chapter left to go, the prophet details the disposition of the land and the people, concerning the holy city where the Lord placed His name. Set roughly 400yrs before Christ, we get the idea of who is where. Judah, Benjamin and Levites making up the bulk of what would be the Judea of Christ's time. The rest of those scattered out to Samaria and beyond, to Galilee and the coasts. Where Joseph would meet Mary. Where the bulk of the Apostles lived. Where Jesus grew in stature and wisdom. Where most of His earthly ministry would take place. Jerusalem saw converts, to be sure. But the majority of those who believed John the Baptist about the coming savior, and then Christ Himself and His disciples soul-winning efforts, came from outside the city, where a mob will soon shout "Crucify Him!" God has given us what is the most detailed and longest continual history known to man. From creation to the setting up of things for the coming of Christ. With great detail, genealogies, information about other nations and people that are lost to secular history. All with a reason and a purpose, always to His glory. Never the accomplishments of men, but what God has done for His people. It is awesome to consider.

It is amazing to read the celebration and purity of the people in thanksgiving to God, and the celebration of the restoration of the Temple and the city walls of Jerusalem, the honoring of the generations of great men that made it possible, and to know in 400 years they will turn and shout, "Crucify Him!" Yet that's what man does. We make the pure impure. We wax cold. We build ourselves up when we aren't building up the things of God. In 400 years the sons of these priests will judge Jesus Christ, the Son of God, before their high priest. Spitting in His face. Striking Him. In 400 years the people who were praising God in the streets with instruments and joy, the women and children, will be caught up in the false 2nd Temple religion of Pharisees and commandments of men. Of hypocrisy and their works without mercy and judgement. In just 400 years and a few decades, God will utterly destroy all those things they built up. That not one stone remains on another. But God raised up His Son. It is impossible that man not take pride in what we do, when we stop working for God and glorying Him only. When we begin to think the things He has blessed us with are ours by right. That we deserve it. We fall from grace. Don't take for granted anything in your Christian life. Don't complain, because everything you have is from the Lord. Don't brag, because everything you have is from the Lord. Give thanks and celebrate it and keep that spirit in your heart.

The final chapter of Nehemiah's account of the restoration of the walls in Jerusalem, and the continued efforts to cleanse the priesthood and the people of outside influence. Nehemiah writes of how, when the law of Moses was read and the truth that Ammonites and Moabites were forbidden from joining the congregation forever, by God, that the people removed them, wives and children, from the priesthood and the church. But now, years later it's still a problem for a holy people, separated unto God, but having mixed multitudes in their midst. Unequally yoked to non-believers. Tobiah was a prominent Ammonite official who vehemently opposed Nehemiah's efforts to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem and was a bitter adversary of the Jewish people. Despite this, the high priest Eliashib, who was related to Tobiah by marriage, inappropriately prepared a large room in the Temple courts for Tobiah's use. The room was storage for sacrifice and holy things, so to give it to an Ammonite, especially one who opposed the man of God, was especially galling to Nehemiah. He threw the items out, cast out the Ammonite, and had the temple priests cleanse the space. He notes that intermarriage was rampant. Mixed children unable to speak the Jewish tongue. Merchants of foreign people came and sold on the sabbath. And so the Jews worked themselves on the day of rest. Outside influence was leading the people to sin. Comparing it to Solomon, the wisest and greatest king of Israel, who was undone and led to sin by foreign wives, Nehemiah not only preaches against mixed marriages, but assaults men into agreeing to not give their daughters to foreigners. He shuts the city gates on the sabbath and appoints his own sons to keep guard. When the merchants set up shop outside the city walls, he threatens them until they never come back. Nehemiah cleans the city and people of outside influence, driving the ungodly from among them. And he prays God to remember this good he did. It is shoveling against the tide sometimes, to hold standards and expectations of God, among a stubborn and rebellious people. As a pastor or a father in a Christian home, it can seem endless, the number of times the people go out into sin always seems greater than the rebukes and restoration done to undo the last. A constant struggle against the world and the god of this world. And the lust of the eyes, the pride of life. To keep the people who you have charge over pure and separated unto God. Let alone ourselves. But it is important to be constantly diligent. Just as Moses saw the Israelites rise up to play, and to worship an idol, being gone just 40 days, and so soon removed from bondage in Egypt, Nehemiah is gone a short time and the city of Jerusalem has descended into sin. People forget the bondage and cruelty of their unregenerate pre-Christian life. They quickly forget chastisements. They soon return like a dog to its vomit. Like a pig to the mire. It takes constant vigilance, preaching and hard leadership to maintain even a bare minimum of standards. But it is a good work. And something Christian men should commit themselves to.

Beginning the book of Esther, we find it is set during the time period between Ezra and Nehemiah, under the rule of Xerxes, here rendered Ahasuerus in the Hebrew. The king of the Persian empire, where the Medes still has influence. And his empire is great encompassing lands from India to Ethiopia. Including obviously, the Kingdom of Judah. And 3 years into his reign, he orders a feast that lasts nearly half a year. And in that feast he orders the queen to appear. And she, having a feast of her own refuses. This presents a problem. The princes of the empire say to the king that her disobedience will be copied by other wives throughout the land. And that he must remove her from office and strip her of her titles. The King agrees. A new Queen will be found. Obviously, the concept of a wife submitting to their husband is biblically sound. From Eve having her desire be that of Adam, through the New Testament teachings on marriage, it is given that a wife should submit to her husband. As in much of the book of Esther, We are presented with two wrongs. Not one. Vashti should have taken heed and appeared. Her desire to stay at her own feast that she threw where she was the head of the show, led to her being made an example throughout the empire. But, Ahasuerus' example of a drunken feast where obsequious princes gathered, was a poor one to set for the kingdom as well. And it was more his embarrassment in front of his friends than doing the right thing that led to his proclamation. In a similar way to the Book of Judges, we are called upon to use discernment when reading Esther. We will see that God is not in it, literally. God isn't mentioned. And so, we are given circumstances and situations to judge. And so we shall.

And so we meet Mordecai and his cousin, Esther, of the tribe of Benjamin, in the land because of the captivity of Judah. When the king calls for the women of the land to replace the queen who had humiliated him, Mordecai tells Esther to go, and to keep her being of Israel a secret. She was well pleasing to all, and became queen. And Mordecai begins to sit near the king's gate, and overheard the doormen talking about laying hands on Ahasuerus. He informs Esther, who tells the king and the men are hanged. God commanded the children of Israel to not marry their daughters to foreigners. To not lie. To trust in Him alone for their salvation, knowing the end of captivity would come as He promised. God is not mentioned, again.

Esther 3, set after her marriage to the king, shows Haman that Agagite advanced over the other princes, to be second in the kingdom. The king commands that he be bowed to and revered for his position. Given tribute and honor as due. God commands the same for us. We are supposed to submit to the authority He places in our lives, so long as the authority doesn't ask us to violate the higher power. Bowing to the King and his chosen was custom. The servants and guards and others at the King's gate obeyed. Mordecai did not. The servants at the gate ask Mordecai the Jew, Why transgressest thou the king's commandment? He doesn't answer. And when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath. Now Haman was an Agagite, a great grandson of Agag. Agag was the king of the Amalekites when Saul as king of Israel was commanded by Samuel on behalf of the Lord to slaughter the Amalekites. Saul spared the king, and when he doesn't obey God, the Lord comes to Samuel saying He repented of choosing Saul, who did not honor His word and obey. And so the kingdom would be taken from him. Saul, in this story, is a picture of the Jews, how they waxed worse and worse in disobedience, and so had the Kingdom taken from them. Samuel himself executes Agag. But first he preaches against Saul; 1 Samuel 15:22-23 And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king. It is interesting that a Amalekite was placed in this position, and a Jew rebels against his authority. The Jews in captivity were told to get along with the powers it be. Repeated warnings like this; Jeremiah 29:4-7 Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon; Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them; Take ye wives, and beget sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; that ye may be increased there, and not diminished. And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the Lord for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace. Mordecai's plot to elevate his cousin Esther to be queen was successful, and his decision to then stalk the king's gate, paid off in the assassination plot he revealed to Esther, securing her the throne through deception. And so his rebellion against the king seems borne of arrogance and pride. Stubborn. Rebellious as Saul's rebellion against God. Haman, however, reacts to the disrespect in anger, so fierce and irrational, he calls for not only the death of Mordecai, but all the Jews in the kingdom, and spoil them for the king. And the king, as we've seen, is impulsive and easily swayed by his princes, goes along with the plot and gives his royal seal to a proclamation, setting a date, a year out, to carry out the order. And publish it in all the land. And as Haman and the king sat down to drink, the city was perplexed.

When Mordecai perceived all that was done, Mordecai...turned to the Lord? No. Begged the people to turn to the Lord? No. He rent his clothes and put on sackcloth and came before the kings gate. When offered raiment by Esther the queen, he refused. And he tells her servant all that had been decided by the king and Haman. Mordecai threatens his cousin, saying to go before the king and risk death to plead their case, because if Deliverance should arise from some other place, she'll be destroyed. The deliverance from God is never even considered. And appealed to heaven is never done. Just self-serving sackcloth and ashes. Mordecai says, Who knows if she had come into the kingdom for such a time as this? He doesn't say put you here for such a time as this. III hear a lot of preaching on this make that inference, make that leap and credit Mordecai with an appeal to God that doesn't exist in the text. So to risk death by going before the king unbidden, Esther tells everyone to fast. But again doesn't say for what. As if the works themselves will save them. Rather than the repentance towards God which could. Again, God isn't in it. I have heard multiple sermons by multiple pastors, that reference Esther 4, saying that it is a testament to the power of prayer. That Mordecai, Esther and the Jews in Shushan, by prayer and fasting, were able to find favor with Ahasuerus. But there is no prayer mentioned. There is no appeal to God to be delivered. There's fasting, with a grim acceptance of chance, rather than faith in the Lord. Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this? ...and if I perish, I perish. This isn't prescriptive.

So after 3 days of fasting, with no prayer mentioned or appeals to God or anything else, Esther dresses up in her Royal apparel in her finest, and positions herself in such a way that the king sitting upon his Royal throne in the Royal House could see her. Esther, looking beautiful is bidden by the king who holds out his golden scepter showing that she is allowed to come to him. The king offers Esther whatever her request may be up to even half of the Kingdom. And instead of frankly dealing with the issue, and confessing her ethnic origin, and pleading the case of her people, she says that she would like to invite him to a dinner with Haman the following day. And that there she will let it be known what her request is. She could have asked for up to half the kingdom, in that moment, and then given refuge to her people. But that doesn't occur to her at such a time as this. We continue to see that King Ahasuerus is weak and easily manipulated by anyone who comes before him. He has agreed to go along with his princes in chapter 1, and with Haman, and now with Esther. He's essentially a pushover. Now Haman has a joyful and glad heart at being invited to a special feast by the queen with the king. And he goes out from the palace through the king's gate, and Mordecai, rather than be humble and repentant, blocks his way. He didn't stand up or even move for him. Mordecai is determined to provoke Haman. Even in the face of genocide of his people, his pride prevents him from not only honoring the king's second man, but just being polite. And Haman develops more hatred and resentment for Mordecai. And yet refrains himself. He shows self-control. And he goes home and calls his friends and his wife and tells them of how blessed he's been as the king has promoted him and tells them the good news that he is being invited to a banquet with the queen. Haman's problem is that despite all of these blessings, rather than being grateful he allows his resentment for Mordecai the Jew to fester. His wife Zeresh and his friends suggest that he make a giant gallows, 50 cubits high, about 75 feet, with which to hang Mordecai. Haman's reaction is of course bad. He shouldn't allow it to get to him like that. And yet he does and he will be hoist on his own petard. But again we see that God is not in this. That there aren't any good people in the story. It's hard to see it any other way once you strip the tradition of men that paints Mordecai as a hero and Esther as a great woman of faith.

Esther 6 continues the story, and the king has restless sleep. He remembers that someone had tipped the palace off to an attempt on his life by his servants, and has the chronicles of the king searched to find who it was, that they may be honored. And Mordecai the Jew, who the king recognized as sitting by the kings gate, is named. The king summons his number two, Haman and asks a question; What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Haman was there to tell the king of his plan to hang Mordecai from the 75' gallows he had constructed. But when he hears the king's question, he immediately thinks it is about him. Now, Ahasuerus is easily influenced as we have seen, and Haman did not waste the opportunity to glorify himself in his heart, and suggested the honor he thought he deserved. The irony being that the king has him carry out these very things to the man he has come to kill. But, it isn't incidental to note that Haman did as he was commanded to. Haman proclaims the king's honor before the royally decked-out Mordecai, led on horseback through the city, and then runs home in mourning. His plan was undone and his humiliation was compounded. His wife and advisors try to comfort him, his wife saying that as "seed of the Jews," Haman won't prevail against him. Many will teach this and tie this to the promise of God regarding the blessing and cursing of Abraham and his seed. Which is Christ. What she actually sounds like is a modern conservative Zionist. Misapplying it. Haman is like those whose own own pride and quest for power, coupled with blind hatred, has made them susceptible to the machinations of Jews. Their power and influence really is only able to work by provoking reaction in others. In and of itself, they come off as contrary to all men. They will use a opportunistic moment to ingratiate themselves with the power structure, but in the end, their power is grown and maintained by being victims of irrational reaction, rather than their own qualities. And as Haman reaches this low point, he is summoned to Esther's feast.

The easily manipulated Ahasuerus and Haman attend the banquet of the Queen, and on the second day of the feast, the King asks again of Esther what her request for him is. She tells him, under fear of death, that she and her people were sold unto death by Haman's proclamation against the Jews. She appeals to him that had it been into bondage, she'd have remained silent, but not until death. She says that until now, she had held her tongue despite knowing that the deal Haman struck for 10,000 pieces of silver was not sufficient to offset the damage to the king of the genocide of the Jews, including his wife. Notice that she doesn't name her people and the king seems confused on this point, asking who it was that did this thing. She names the "wicked Haman," who becomes instantly terrified. The King in his anger leaves to the garden, and Haman throws himself before Esther to beg for his life. The King returns to see this and in a rage assumes Haman is actually and impudently about to rape Esther before him, in his own palace. The guards cover his face, subduing the number two man of the Kingdom. A chamberlain tells the King about the gallows 50 cubits high Haman had erected for Mordecai, and the King, remembering the honor he gave the Jew the day before orders Haman to be hoist on his own gallows. Quite an ironic turn of events. Again, it's worth noting that there was no appeal to God or fear of Him in the story. Esther still hid her race from the King, and did not take mercy on Haman, or correct the King that it was Haman's begging for his life, not attempting to lay with her in front of him. Haman got his just dessert, but he's not the only bad person in the story. There are none good. No not one.

So Esther, and really Mordecai her uncle, had gotten vengeance on Haman and his family, because of the wrath Haman had towards Mordecai's insolence. And now the King gives to them Haman's property and inheritance, And gives Mordecai haman's position in the Kingdom. Even allowing him the ring that seals the proclamations and that he could write them in the king's name. Esther asks the king to reverse the earlier order given to Haman for the destruction of the Jews throughout the empire. But because a king's proclamation cannot be reversed, he simply has them write a new one that gives the Jews the full backing of the government to kill all the people that would kill them, even the women and children of their families. How that would be determined? What were the criteria for determining that someone would have come against them? It doesn't say. I've heard it preached that they were just given the right to self-defense and that on that day people did rise up and try to kill them. But the text says that the people not only didn't rise up to try to kill them but converted to be Jews out of fear of the Jews. Not fear of God.

The final chapter of Esther, and we see the origins of the Jewish observance of Purim. On the day Haman had hoped to wipe out the Jews, the Jews had gained power instead and used it to mass murder their enemies. The rulers of the provinces of the empire, their military and officers of the King helped the Jews to find and kill those that they said hated them. Mordecai was given greater power. The king reports to Esther that Haman's sons were killed and 500 in the palace, and unknown number in the rest of the Kingdom, and the King asks his wife if she's satisfied. She isn't. They hung the sons they slew on trees. They extended the slaughter another day. They killed 300 more in Shushan. They killed another 75,000 throughout the empire, though they did not take the spoils. And the Jews declared it would be a feast day. Mordecai made it official. Because Haman had sought to cast lots on the Jews, Pur, they called the feast Purim. Again, nothing of God. They made their own holy day and feast, celebrating the slaughter they had. They did what was right in their own eyes, and proved that Haman was right to see them as a threat. Even if he went about it the wrong way. There are no heroes. It's a history of something that happened. God wanted us to know.

The Book of Job begins with the introduction of a man in the land of Uz, the titular character; Job. Uz, from the biblical clues appears to be a fertile plane in the Arabian peninsula, near where Edom would be. The time frame, many believe, is during the era of the patriarchs; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It would be good to note that, Abraham, or Abram, was a Chaldean, a nation who are mentioned here in this chapter located in what is modern Iraq. Where the seat of Babylonian power would be. And he was called out from the city of Ur there, to go unto Hebron by God. And, as mentioned throughout his story and his sons', there were people in this post flood era who feared the Lord, and offered sacrifices unto him. Of course we know about Melchizedek, King of Salem, and high priest, and the tenth of the spoils offered by Abram to Melchizedek. Many consider him to be a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus. All this to say that the idea of the worship of God originating with Abraham, and only his seed after the flesh, is incorrect. There were many following the flood and the dispersion of nations out from Babel, that called upon the name of the Lord for salvation, and sought to offer the blood as a picture of their faith in Him, as we see Job does for himself and his family. One of the conceits of modern Zionism and dispensationalism holds that only the sons of Israel after the flesh were special, and that they invented monotheism. But throughout the Bible we find people who were not of that line, and not given to idols and false gods. It's important to understand that salvation has always been by grace alone through faith in the Lord, calling upon his name. And that salvation was always offered to all people. We will see in Exodus the mixed multitudes that followed Israel into the wilderness from Egypt. We will see high priests of other nations that fear the Lord. There will be people like Ruth and Rahab and others who have the faith. The distinction for Israel was that they were given the oracles of God. That they had the prophets and the word of God delivered directly to them, and given the law of the Lord that they may be perfect, complete, and a light unto the Gentiles. The other nations. Calling all men to repentance. But we see the greatest man on Earth at this moment, according to God, who feared Him, eschewing evil, offering sacrifices to sanctify himself and his family. Without the law. Without the temple. Without a priesthood. Without the oracles of God, knowing by the faith of his fathers what was expected. And so we find Job, faithfully keeping the sanctification of sacrifices for himself and his children, and he has been blessed beyond measure by God. 10 children, seven sons and three daughters. Incredible wealth and cattle and livestock. Great land and a great house. And all his adult children successful in that they were established in their own homes to have their own feasts. Having established all of this, the Bible shifts focus to the throne of God in Heaven. Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also among them. I've covered this multiple times in other studies, but the sons of God here refers to the spirits of those saved by faith in Christ. The same as the sons of God in Genesis 6 being the children of obedience, through Seth. Because the only way to become A son of God, is by faith in THE Son of God. So, not to belabor the point, but at no time has God called angels His sons. And further evidence of this is in the text itself, in verse 6. Satan came also among them. Satan is an angel. A rebellious angel, a cherub. Perhaps a prominent angel but, an angel nonetheless. And he came among them, as a separate entity than them. Not as one of them. And God asks him where he's been, and he says going to and fro in the earth and walking up and down in it. 1 Peter 5:8 Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour Christians should remember that Satan continues this practice today. And like his appearance before God, to accuse Job, he does the same of us even now. Revelation 12:9-11 And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him. And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night. And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death. Satan is our adversary, the god of this world, and our accuser before the Lord. I sometimes wonder if he even bothers with the unsaved, beyond giving them power that they can afflict those who are saved. His resentment is in those sons of God, that God so loved us that He gave His only begotten Son for us, knowing that hell was created for him and the angels he deceived. Now God knows who Satan is and what he does and His pointing out Job is deliberate, and in so many ways this is done for our admonition, upon whom the end of the world has come. If a man as upright and perfect in his ways can be sorely tempted by the persecution of Satan against him, If the hedge of protection may be lifted, to show the glory of God for such a man as job, how can we expect the small tragedies that befall us as believers to be any less to His glory? If the Book of Job was one chapter, the lesson is present and clear. But as we'll see, there is so many more lessons to learn than simple perseverance in faith. Satan of course credits the hedge of protection God has placed around Job and his family and the blessings of the holdings that he's acquired which are gifts of God, as the only reason Job's faith is so strong. He says to God that if He put forth His hand now and touched all that he had, Job would curse Him to his face. I have seen an error among people similar to this, that says only the wicked prosper. Job shows this isn't the case and that wealth in itself is not a bad thing, but that all we have is a gift of God. Then there's the prosperity Gospel types, who falsely say that if you're not successful and you're not succeeding, that you're not right with God. But here we humbly learn that whether we are blessed or cursed, all is to His glory. As Paul writes: Philippians 4:12 I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. Whether you're in good times or bad times or the mix most of us find ourselves in, it's all to the glory of God. His grace is sufficient. Now the Lord says to Satan, behold all that he hath is in thy power but bars him from doing harm to Job physically. The prime interpretation of this is that God has granted Satan special permission to afflict Job, And that is a fair reading of the text, especially in light of the hedge of protection Satan says God has placed about Job. But, as I've mentioned, the Bible says that Satan is the god of this world, That he is the prince of the power of the air, ruler of this world. Not as God, but as having influence and power over the things of this Earth. So is the Lord reminding Satan, or enabling him? It's difficult to say. But we should keep it in mind always. Ephesians 6:12 For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. But regardless, Satan is given the power to affect all that Job has, if not his person. And in one day, he does his worst. First we see that his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine and in the eldest brother's house, this detail is given before the rest, creating tension in the reader. Then the messengers begin to arrive. One tells of the oxen and asses killed by marauding Sabeans, who are from the south, where modern Yemen is. Then another arrives to say that the fire of God reigned from Heaven on the sheep in the servants and consumed them. When God gave permission to Satan to do what he will, he gave him access to the fire of God that rains from Heaven. Revelation 13:11-13 And I beheld another beast coming up out of the earth; and he had two horns like a lamb, and he spake as a dragon. And he exerciseth all the power of the first beast before him, and causeth the earth and them which dwell therein to worship the first beast, whose deadly wound was healed. And he doeth great wonders, so that he maketh fire come down from heaven on the earth in the sight of men The false prophet of the Antichrist will have this power and ability, And it will cause the unsaved to worship the beast and his image. Before the second messenger can finish, a third arrives and says the Chaldeans made out three bands and fell upon the camels and slaying the servants. Of course this is a raiding party from the north, striking simultaneously with those from the south. Finally as the third messenger is conveying his report, A fourth arrives and says that while Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking a great wind came from the wilderness and smote the four corners of the house and it fell on them and they are all dead. Job was beset from the south, from above, from the north and from all four corners, surrounded by evil. And the devil allowed a sole survivor from each. The coordination and power and influence that the devil has where he can have two different armies attack at the same time, controlling fire from heaven, and the winds of the air, that the sole survivors of each would arrive one after the other, to absolutely devastate Job, shows Satan's cunning wickedness. Each blow would be sufficient to cripple most men. To have them come one after the other after the other after the other, in quick succession is unimaginable. And Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped. These were the manner and customs throughout the Old Testament for mourning. We see here that worship is defined as falling to your knees or bowing down. Job in absolute sorrow tears his clothes, shaves his head for the dead, and lays face first down upon the ground. And the prayer Job makes contains two statements that have both become idioms even among the secular world. Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. And despite all of this tragedy, despite all of the cause Satan gave him to sin, Job sinned not. And he didn't blame God, but rather blessed His name. Thematically, as prose, this setup creates tension in the reader. I'll probably say this multiple times throughout this study, but the Book of Job is the finest example of literature ever written. While its exact date of composition isn't known, it likely found its final form during the Babylonian captivity. Shortly thereafter, in the Hellenistic world, the Greek drama became a literary style. Acted out by people, to tell a story either from a monologue or a soliloquy or a troupe of performers. Because we are gifted with the King James version, and it's eloquent prose in what many would say is Shakespearean English, it's easy to picture the Book of Job as a play. And it is possible to perform, and many have. And it is greater than all of the plays the Bard penned. Isn't it interesting that it was put to pen under the inspiration of God, separate from and before the Greek tragedies and comedies that the world now considers classic literature? “Naked came I… naked shall I return thither” – “Thither” or shām in the Hebrew means, “to that place." Clearly Job doesn't mean the womb. The return is to what then? What is thither? The grave? "Sheol" and nothingness? We're going to see that Job's faith is redemption through the Lord. Not that empty meaning that many give in their Old Testament interpretations. Either way, Job sees life as lease, not ownership, that all is from God, Who is blessed forever. It's humbling and something we should always keep in mind. Life is a vapor. Genesis 3:19 In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.

The Book of Job continues into chapter 2. I've often thought that, had Job been confined to just the first chapter it would serve as a great lesson in patience and understanding in the faith. But in the wisdom of God it continues, bringing many other lessons to us. Again, the spirits of the righteous men in Heaven come before God, and among them the devil comes. And again he's been to and fro in the Earth, and walking up and down it. And the Lord said unto Satan hast thou considered Job? That there's none like him the perfect and upright man, who is still holding fast his integrity even though Satan had moved God to destroy him without a cause. And Satan says that a man will give up anything for his life. He calls God to afflict Job by touching his bone in flesh and says that he will curse God to His face. And so God agrees, saying only take not his life. And Satan afflicts Job with postulant boils from The souls of his feet to the crown of his head. Poor Job sits in ash, mourning, And now is taking a shard of pottery to his skin to scrape himself of the sores. Miserable, having lost everything and now afflicted with a painful and disgusting curse. His wife is disgusted with his continued faith, and says curse God and die. But he said that this is foolish. That if we receive good at the hands of God shall we not receive evil? And Job sinned not with his lips. The continued patience of Job is a testament that we should seek to emulate. As bad as things are we've all been blessed beyond anything we deserve by God's grace. His grace is sufficient. Paul, similarly had bemoaned a thorn in his flesh, appealing to God three times saying that he would be so much more useful in the cause of Christ if he had it removed. It took him a while to understand. 2 Corinthians 12:6-9 For though I would desire to glory, I shall not be a fool; for I will say the truth: but now I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth me to be, or that he heareth of me. And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Our suffering exists for many reasons, but ultimately it is to give glory to God for His grace and His mercy. That while we are weak He is strong and our strength. Even if it's just to humble us that we glory not in ourselves. And so the scene shifts as three of Job's friends arrive from far off, barely recognizing him. They enter and sit down with him on the ground, for 7 days and seven nights and none speak to him for they saw that his grief was very great. We will learn more about each as the story progresses.

In Job chapter 3, the titular character begins a monologue of absolute dejection and woe. He wishes he was never born. He wishes the day he was conceived would be stricken from time. He asked why he didn't die in the womb rather than suffer as he is. He asked why he didn't die at birth than be in the position of torment he's found himself. He wishes for death, that Kings and princes and the wicked and the weary all find rest in, from this life. That the prisoners of death escape the voice of their oppressor and the servant is free from his master. He asked why light is given to him that is in misery, why life is given to the bitter in soul, why those who long for death don't receive it. He poetically compares the digging for hidden treasure to those that can find the grave. He is miserable. But he has not sinned against God with his lips.

Job 4 will begin a dialogue between Job and the three friends who came to him to mourn. The first to reply to Job's plaintive cry, cursing the day he was born, is Eliphaz the Temanite, of Teman, a city in Edom. (Genesis 36:11, 15; Jeremiah 49:7, 20; Ezekiel 25:13). His initial argument is made in chapters 4 and 5, and offers a view of "retribution theology," the idea of karma in God's doings. That sin is the cause of suffering, and that you get what you deserve. Job’s friends defend retribution theology rigorously, and it is difficult to disagree with many of the points made, from a human perspective. Much of it sounds right in our minds. So, before we dive deeper into the text, we should keep in mind the end of the matter, where (spoilers), God addresses the men and what they say. Job 42:7-9 And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. Therefore take unto you now seven bullocks and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept: lest I deal with you after your folly, in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job. So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them: the Lord also accepted Job. The friends of Job, (and later, the young accuser Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite), are given opportunity to make multiple philosophical and theological points regarding the nature of God, His justice and their natural suspicion of those who suffer as being sinners, and worse, that those that suffer worse than they do must be greater sinners than they are. This line of thought is just as common today as it was then, and is human nature. But not God's. And while there is general wisdom to be found in their arguments, the application they choose to make is wrong. As we go, it is good to keep this in mind, especially when we read something that seems perfectly reasonable to us, and may reflect our own views that we may have held against others in our life. It should cause self-reflection. So, to recap: Job, devastated by the loss of his children, wealth and health, and wishing he was never born, while yet not sinning against God or cursing Him, sits in ash, scraping his sore-covered flesh, in agony. He had been blessed by these three well meaning friends, who traveled afar, and patiently, in love, sat mourning in silence for a week. But with the silence broken by Job's lamentation, Eliphaz the Temanite now speaks up. He starts by asking that, if they attempt to talk with him, will it offend Job? And then immediately, before Job can answer, Eliphaz gives himself permission by saying "Who can withhold themselves from speaking?" We have all likely, at one time or another been on the receiving or delivering end of this. "I know you're going through a lot, so I don't want to offend you, but I can't help myself..." As well intentioned as this sentiment can be, what follows it rarely is a help to the person hearing it. Ultimately, the motivation behind it is self-centered and doesn't come from sympathy for the aggrieved, but out of an impatient empathy, where the friend sees it from their detached view, and thinks their opinions and musing can fix what's broken, or even just make the person stop complaining. Many times, after having given our two-cents, we can feel comfortable washing our hands of any obligation to be bothered by a friend's burdens. "Well, if they'd just listen to reason...Oh well, I tried." Better to have remained silent than to do this. Eliphaz the Temanite barrels along right into it. He begins by pointing out the example Lot has been for many, that his faith and council have helped those in troubled times. Strengthening the weak. But...it is never good to follow a compliment with a "but," but now that it has come upon Job, he faints and is troubled. Rather than encouraging Job to embrace the same strength and hope that he gave others, Eliphaz uses this good quality of his friend as an indictment. As an accusation of weakness. I would doubt that any of the people Job had encouraged had gone through anything even remotely touching the tribulation that he found himself in. But even so, rather than repaying the favor and encouraging Job, Eliphaz makes an accusation out of it. Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways? He says, isn't your religion, your trust in God, your piety and righteousness, shouldn't that all be enough to console you? If all of that was sufficient for Job to preach to others in their moments of doubt and pain, why isn't it enough for him? And rather than waiting for a reply to his condescending "tough love," Eliphaz answers his own question in the least charitable way possible; by accusing Job of hidden sin. Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off? This is the crux of his argument, That Job deserves what has happened to him. That he is reaping what he has sown. Eliphaz uses the truth that God's wrath is revealed from Heaven against the ungodly, to say that this is evidence enough that so great a temptation has befallen Job, because his piety was vanity, and hid the truth of his sin. "What goes around comes around," even when true, is the last thing we should say to another when we're trying to comfort them. Especially considering the grace God has extended to us. In Luke 13, Jesus answers his disciples, who suggest that recent tragedies that happened to others was a direct result of their sin, that it was karma, by asking "Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?" Jesus says, nay, and that something evil can happen to anyone by chance, but if men don't repent, everyone will likewise perish. Stuff happens. The rain falls on the just and the unjust alike. A similar question is asked in John 9:1-3 And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man which was blind from his birth. And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him. The Truth is we cannot assume by someone suffering that they deserved it for some secret sin that we imagine they did. It may be comforting to us to think that we're safe from such tragedies, because of our innate goodness in contrast to this wretched sinner. But we are all deserving of death and hell, and it is by the grace of God that we yet live. Eliphaz continues, letting us know of a vision that he had just before sleep, of a spirit he thinks he glimpsed and a voice he heard, that asked: Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? Behold, he put no trust in his servants; and his angels he charged with folly: How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed before the moth? His private interpretation, his own inner musings that he paints as a spiritual vision, posits that since man is obviously not as holy as God, and if even the Angels were punished for their rebellion, how much more man is under judgment for our wickedness, men, whose life is but a vapor and to dust we return, crushed as easily as the moth. And it is true that God reserved punishment for the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.. 2 Peter 2:4 For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment. And in Hebrews 2:6-7 (paraphrasing Psalm 8:5) What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man that thou visitest him? Thou madest him a little lower than the angels... Again, Eliphaz uses true things to make false points. And because it is true that God punishes the wicked, that he spared not the angels that kept not their estate but sinned, and that all men die, and their bodies decay and their excellency goes away. And it happens to the wise and those without wisdom alike. Ecclesiastes 9:2 All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner; and he that sweareth, as he that feareth an oath. Many times the greatest lies are based on a misrepresentation or misapplication of the greatest truths.

Eliphaz's monologue continues, directly from chapter 4, and he continues to paint a picture blaming Job for his own suffering. Implying secret sin that has led him to his current condition. He says to call upon the righteous, and see if any man would answer him. Some Catholics use this verse as a proof text for praying to saints. Because they will strip verses from context, and ignore that God completely rebukes everything that is said by Job's friends. But Eliphaz is not encouraging Job to pray to the dead, but to appeal to the stories of the righteous to find if any ever suffered as he did, If any holy one had ever been down so low. He then begins to list off parables, about the foolish being cursed, their children killed, their harvest spoiled, their things taken by thieves. He says that this trouble doesn't come up out of nowhere, but that men are born into trouble and that it comes up like sparks flying out of a fire. As embers. That the destruction that comes naturally follows the life of a foolish man. He advises his friend to seek God and to commit his cause to God Who is mighty and punishes the wicked. But saveth the poor. He then gives the proverb that a man should be happy when God corrects him and to not despise the chastening of the Almighty. Proverbs 3:11 My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; neither be weary of his correction. So he is quoting scripture, and some of what he is saying is true. But he's misapplying it by assuming that that is the cause of his friends misery. And worse, he mentions children being crushed at the gate, knowing that Job's own sons and daughters were killed by a collapsing house. He insensitively talks about having his things spoiled and stolen. He's clearly indicating that he believes Job acted foolishly in some way and deserved everything he got. And in his own judgment he thinks he's giving good advice. It's something we should be aware of because, far too often we judge a matter by its appearance. And we have a ready verse to give. And we pride ourselves in it when we should be comforting the afflicted. Not forgiving sin, not excusing it, but when we don't know the circumstances or the situation, or even more, we know the person is honorable and upright in their ways, we shouldn't assume or presume to lecture. But you can tell Eliphaz really thought he was cooking here, giving these great words of wisdom to a man laying in ash, with a shaved head for mourning, scraping the oozing sores on his flesh. Telling him to hear it now and know that it's for thy own good, is the last thing Job needs to hear.

Job begins his reply to Eliphaz's accusations of sin being the cause of Job's woe. That he must have deserved it, and so he has to get right with God and stop complaining. Job is overcome by his faithless friend's words. He says his grief is heavier than the sands in the sea, and if measured against his lamentation, his words would be swallowed up by it. That while the poisoned arrows and terrors of God be in him and against him, Eliphaz chose to lecture Job instead of pitying him. Job asks rhetorical and obvious questions, saying that Eliphaz's argument is as obvious as these sayings. A fed animal doesn't bray and flavorless food needs seasoning and the white of an egg is flavorless, and the accusations and advice Eliphaz gave are just as unnecessary to say. They may be true, but they are obvious truths that Job is already well aware of. They aren't great insights, and they do nothing to help him in his grief. He still longs for death, and Job begs God to take him, and call him home. That he should find comfort, let God not spare him. Here, Job gives his confession of faith, his trust in the Holy One, Christ Jesus. He is his strength and his hope. If his end is heaven, why prolong his life? His faith built upon a rock, His ready help in Job, His wisdom is present, still. And so, Eliphaz's rebuke stings, rather than the comfort of pity, and Job points out this is sin, and turns the accusation back upon Eliphaz, that his erstwhile friend has forsaken the fear of God by his callousness. That his brother has dealt deceitfully, and gives an allegory of a brook, a small stream that freezes cold in the winter, undrinkable, only to vanish in the heat, dried up. It's a stinging rebuke. The brook, like his expected compassion from a brother is like its waters, the troops of Tema looked, the companies of Sheba waited for them. The water is gone, and they are left without the expected relief. Job accuses Eliphaz further, saying his holier than thou act comes from fear. If Job, who Eliphaz knows has been faithful and a good council, in the Lord, has been cast down so low, what could that mean for him? Job says, did I ask you for anything? Money? Deliverance? Redemption from captivity? He didn't ask for Eliphaz's opinion either. He continues to upbraid his friend, saying if Eliphaz has something to teach Job that he doesn't already know, Job would listen. He would gladly accept understanding, but Eliphaz's argument is insulting. Job asks what exactly is he reproving by it? Job asks did Eliphaz think he was reproving a shallow argument of the desperate. Job had wailed in his sorrow, he didn't curse God or sin with his lips. So what exactly did Eliphaz think he was rebuking? Job says it is as attacking the fatherless, as digging a pit for his friend to fall into. Iniquity and betrayal. He says, "look at me," and asks if he's lying. If there is sin in his speech. Is he saying anything against God? Job's righteousness is in it. It is sorrow that compasses him about. Job’s longing for death is not despair but a plea for release into the only comfort he still trusts: God’s final summons. “Let Him not spare me” is not suicidal rage; it is the confidence that his end is with the Holy One. Even here, in the furnace, Job confesses the rock beneath his feet, Christ Jesus, his strength and hope. The rebuke of Eliphaz therefore wounds doubly: it is not merely unfeeling; it is faithless. To kick a brother when he is down is to forsake the fear of God. The presence of faith in Job's response to this unspeakable tragedy has been consistent. The vain theology of karma that Eliphaz offers is predicated on the idea that Job deserves what's happened, while Job in his heart knows his trust is in the Holy One, his Redeemer.
