It is similar to the struggle Paul felt, as he wrote to the Philippians from his bondage in Rome, potential death by execution, certain. Philippians 1:20-24 According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour: yet what I shall choose I wot not. For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you. It can be tempting in trials for a believer to long to be called home. But, better to redeem the time while we are here. God's perfect timing is His, not ours. Many argue that Jesus wasn't known in the Old Testament, that salvation by faith didn't exist. That it is an anachronism to see Jesus in Job, and the Holy One. There is no anachronism when we see Christ in in the Old Testament. It is entirely about Him. He is the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world. The same Word who was with God and was God, Who walked in the furnace with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He was the Rock in the wilderness. Job’s cry a few chapters from now, “I know that my Redeemer liveth” being about Christ is not an anachronism or a theological reach; it is an inspired revelation. When Job clings to the Holy One as his strength and hope beyond death, he is laying hold of the same eternal Christ who is the substance of every shadow, the end of every type, the answer to every promise. The Old Testament saints were saved by the same faith, looking to the same Savior, the same redemption, if through a veil that has now been torn.

Job continues his defense following Eliphaz's unsympathetic advice. He returns to the theme of chapter 3, where his lamentations for this life are a reflection of the misery he is in. He asks, aren't all men appointed to death? Reminiscent of Hebrews 9:23, And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment. And aren't the man's days like the days of an hireling? In the Old Testament, We see that the cultural tradition of a hireling is to be taken on for the course of 3 years, and paid out a reward at the end in addition to his wages and room and board. Joe basks isn't there a time appointed or a limit to the suffering of this life? Can't he earnestly desire the relief of the shadow, shade for the laborer in the Sun, or the reward at the end of his work? Man is made to live through months of vanity and wearing some nights that are appointed to us. I think of great men like Abraham who, for 75 years toiled through his life before he committed to doing the thing God had asked him to do. Or Moses who twice spent 40 years in the wilderness, just living day to day. We all can relate, especially the older we get, to this wearisome, repetitive life. We go to sleep waiting for the day to come, waking restlessly at the dawn in anticipation for another day of toil. But worse, Job is experiencing the pain of his flesh the loss of his family and all of his goods. His wife doesn't respect him and now his friends have turned on him in his mourning. Confronted with the utter futility of life and his own suffering He says I will not refrain my mouth, I will speak in the anguish of my spirit and I will complain and the bitterness of my soul. He's saying I have a right to complain, and has an expectation of sympathy that he hasn't received since opening his mouth. And yet he has not sinned against the Lord. But when he's complaining that he needs rest and he's tired and he's beaten down by all that's happened to him, Eliphaz's "visions" are given to terrify him. To put fear in him that's unfounded, but delivered in a dream. He's now so miserable by all of this affliction and by the reproach of his friend, that he simply just wants to die. And in his anguish, Job turns to the Lord and asks what is man that thou should magnify him. The thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? As the psalmist writes; Psalm 8:4 What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him? But David is writing to glorify God, Job here is not questioning God or sending against him, But simply asking him why he must continue to live in such misery. He confesses he's a sinner. He asks what shall I do unto the preserver of men, the Lord. He asks why God is turned against him and set him so that he is a burden to himself, a burden unto death. He asks for that blessed pardon, for the forgiveness and death, that he would die that night in the flesh so that he doesn't have to live as a burden and in vanity and in weariness. How utterly defeated he is.

And so, following Job's blistering defense against Eliphaz's criticism, and Job's bemoaning his fate, now his friend, Bildad the Shuhite speaks up, in seeming exasperation, asking how long will they have to listen to Job, and insinuating he is full of hot air. He thinks Job is calling God unjust, when Job is actually confused as to why. And so Bildad lectures his pitiful friend. He says the kids must have deserved it, so Job should seek to get right with God with haste, betimes. That if the case is that the children were in sin, and Job righteous, then maybe God would deliver him. This is cruel, of course, and wrong. He's judging Job's sons and daughters without knowledge, and assuming Job himself is turned from the Lord. Bildad preaches the prosperity gospel, that if you're righteous you will be blessed and your life abundant. That God does bless Job that his latter end is better, it is for not cursing God in his tribulation. Not by any acts of righteousness, which also did not save him from this predicament to begin with. He then lays on the condescending rhetoric thicker than Eliphaz. He says, search the ways of the fathers, seeking wisdom from their lives, because our life is short. He asks rhetorical questions, about the rushes that grow in the mire, the flag being a type of riverbank rush, whose leaves mold and decay all season. He compares this to the backslidden and the hypocrite, whose hope is cut off. Whose trust is as easily destroyed as a spider's web. His house, unstable. Like those who build upon sand in Christ's parable about building upon the rock of His word. But this is done to ill effect, Bildad chastising Job for the sins he imagines brought Job to misery. Again, a holier than thou attitude, given in place of solace and mercy.

Job 8 ended with Bildad the Shuite proclaiming that God is just to punish the unrighteous, and to bless the righteous; Behold, God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will he help the evil doer. And here in chapter 9, Job again replies to the admonishment of a friend against him, saying sure, this is true, but then asking the key question; How should a man be just with God? He says, if one were to argue with God, they couldn't win one of a thousand points of contention. That His wisdom and strength is greater than all others. Against the Almighty God, none could prosper. He moves the earth, destroys mountains, set the stars in constellations in the heavens, doing things that they cannot even imagine. How can any man then be perfect before Him? Romans 3:10-12 As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one. God is Spirit, unstoppable, His wrath undeniable. His judgment, impeccable. Romans 1:20 For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power. Job says, all the proud are humbled before Him and His fierce anger. So, what can Job even say to God in his sorrow and misery, to defend himself. If God punishes the sinful, and no man is without sin, than any fate, even is extreme as what he's going through, is justified. Because God is just. So what could he say? How could he reason with God as to why he doesn't deserve what he's getting, when his friends all agree that sinners get punished while the righteous prosper, yet there are none righteous!? If you were righteous, you could appeal to the judge your righteousness, but not before God. Why would he listen to a man? Does He answer to men, or men to Him? Job bemoans his fate yet again, that he's broken and his wounds multiplied without a cause. That He won't allow job to die but filled him with bitterness. He could try to justify himself, but in doing so to a holy and perfect God would condemn him. Even his words to make known his righteousness, his filthy rags, would expose him as the sinner he is compared to God. And so, Job comes to the conclusion that God destroys the perfect and the wicked alike. Bad things happen to good people, and bad people prosper. So it cannot be as Job's friends described. And if it's not, then all the lectures against him are hypocritical and vain. He says for their sakes, he could stop complaining then try to comfort himself, because they're not comforting him. That no matter what he does they will not hold him innocent. They will say he deserves what he's getting. And good. But he ask, if he truly is wicked then why is he bothering to explain himself? That even if he washed himself in purest water of melted snow, they would still hold him guilty. But with God, there is no parity. There's no coming together and reasoning with the Lord, who knows all. There's no mediator of men between them that may lay his hand upon us both, he says. His faith is in his Redeemer, and his Lord, but the only mediator between man and God, the man Christ Jesus, isn't a man yet. And so his fear of the Lord keeps him from appealing to the Lord in his tribulation. He can't even get comfort from his friends. That his situation is such, as he seeks to remain faithful and unwilling to curse God in his integrity, he doesn't know what he's supposed to do.

Job continues his lament to God. He is weary of life, bitter of soul. He would ask of God to not condemn him for asking, but to explain why. Why create man to be miserable? Why make someone, and despise them? He never questions God Himself, but why he is made to suffer so much affliction, and to just let him die. Isaiah 45:9 Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands? Romans 9:21 Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour? Here, Job isn't speaking against God's power to shape him and use him as He sees fit, even as a vessel fitted unto destruction. He just wants to know why. Job says that God knows he's not wicked, because he is in the Lord's hands. That not only has he made him of flesh and Bones but has granted him life and favor, grace, the preservation of his spirit. Salvation. He says if it's sin, if he be wicked, God will Mark him for punishment and if he's righteous he would accept punishment and not lift up his head, knowing that his righteousness comes from God. But he's full of confusion because he can't understand what the point is. Why he is suffering the way he is. And if this is his life then why bother even being born. At this point he would welcome the darkness of nothingness rather than continue in the life or the light. He is that miserable. And that confused.

Now the third of Job's friends speaks, Zophar the Naamathite. And he has quite a bit to say along the same lines as Eliphaz and Bildad. He right away accuses Job of being full of words, full of hot air basically, and full of lies. He says that Job's mockery of the false accusations against him deserves to be answered and he's just the guy to do it, too. He mocks Job's claim to be innocent of the accusations against him. He tells a grieving man sitting in ash with his hair plucked and skin covered in boils, who's lost everything, you deserve worse than what you've gotten. That God knows Job's secret sin and that they are double to that which is! Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth. What a blow. Regardless of anything else, this is a railing accusation. And he feels comfortable doing it because the other two already have leveled the same, even if they did it in a gentler way. And isn't this kind of dog piling so typical? Especially the holier than thou hypocrisy and fake piety that comes with those that go along with the crowd on moralizing campaigns. And again he says something true, that God's ways are not our own and there are aspects to God that we can never understand. So true. But, we can know God's judgments and His word is ever nigh to us. Deuteronomy 30:11-14 For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go up for us to heaven, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? Neither is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it. See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil... God's word was there present with them that they could know it. In a similar way, as Paul writes to the Romans quoting Deuteronomy, the Word, which is Christ Jesus, also came down from heaven that we may know God's will and be circumcised of the heart. Romans 10:5-9 For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them. But the righteousness which is of faith speaketh on this wise, Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down from above:) Or, Who shall descend into the deep? (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.) But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach; That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. But the hyper spiritual hypocrites will always couch things about God's word as being unknowable. That we just can't know for sure what God wants or what He thinks is right or what He thinks is wrong. Unless it's to their advantage. They'll say you can't judge, while they judge unrighteously. And so, Zophar the Naamathite goes on a long-winded explanation about how Job just needs to repent and everything's going to be great. Prosperity gospel time.

Job responds to Zophar the Naamathite, and his assertions that none can know the ways of God, His secret things. That all that Zophar knows is that Job deserved what he received and more, God should have done worse to him. But this was pontificating nonsense. God reveals Himself to man in innumerable ways. In sundry times and diverse manners. All creation testifying, a parable of God. Romans 1:18-20 For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse. And so Job answers this claim. He says, surely they have a wisdom, as men, and as men, it will die with them, but he has understanding as well. He isn't inferior to them in knowledge, and Job says they are not giving him profound arguments, but things everyone knows. Obvious truths and natural man wisdom. Many will say banal and vain words, of basic truths and pass it off as great wisdom when they are looking to be holier than thou hypocrites. We see it all the time: "Jesus said not to judge!" they'll say, while judging the righteous for preaching the whole word of God. For preaching standards and separation. Job says he's like the upright man that is scoffed at by his neighbor for calling upon God. Peter wrote about scoffers in the last days, just as Noah was scoffed at in his day. People mocking faith is a constant in the believer's life. A man who is in tribulation is hated too. As Job describes it, a man ready to slip with his feet, being as hated as a lamp or a light to a person at ease, who is resting. People who are comfortable don't want to deal with people in need. They resent them. Those that provoke God, and mock faith may seem to get away with it and even be given abundance. But look upon creation and see the truth. Every man knows God is real and all creation testifies His wrath and nature and truth. Wisdom comes to the elderly by the exposure and experience in God's creation. Length of days leads to knowledge and wisdom, and understanding of God's counsel. God gives life and breath. He breaks things down, corrupts and decays, and nothing can bring it back. He causes drought and flood. He even gives to the deceived strong delusion. He sets up judges and deliverers and kings and princes, and leads the same to ruin. Just as long life gives wisdom, He takes away the understanding of the aged. Senility and dementia are His to give, just as the knowledge and wisdom were. God controls the fates of nations, reveals secrets. He causes the people to wander in the wilderness. To grope in the dark, all to teach us of His wonderful light.

Job continues his rebuke of the 3 friends-turned accusers. He says he heard them and understands them, he knows what they know and isn't inferior, not a novice that needs their theory that his suffering is because his sins are great. He is lamenting because he wants to reason with God, not men. He calls them liars and physicians with no value. They should be comforting the broken hearted, not castigating him. He says if they'd only remained silent, that would have been wiser than the things they had said. Proverbs 17:28 Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding. When dealing with someone in grief and inconsolably miserable, it is better to sit in silence and love them, than seek to explain away their feelings, and lecture them what to do. Many well meaning people, afraid of sitting in silence need to fill the air with words, and those overcome by sympathetic fear, seek to project those fears of their own misdeeds onto the person suffering. Like Job's friends. Job pleads to God, and says they don't have to reply for Him, especially when their entire premise is based on a lie. He lets them know in no uncertain terms that they will have to answer to God for their temerity in speaking for Him, in unrighteous judgment. Judging the appearance, not the spirit; John 7:24 Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. He puts the fear of God in them, reminding them that they are just mortal men, so they should hold their peace, shut up and let Job speak out to God, and if Job is in the wrong before the Lord, let God judge and take his life. Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him. We often quote the first half of this verse, to show our faith being absolute, especially in tribulation. But this is Job not only proclaiming his faith, but accepting God's judgement against him for asking, "Why?" To Job's understanding, he had put off the sin of his youth, and was upright and perfect in his ways, having trusted God. He isn't a hypocrite (as some are) and he reiterates his conviction that he is a saved son of God. He knows that he is justified by his faith before God, so why all this? He asks of God two things. To lift His hand from against him, to stop the mounting evil that has befallen Job, and to answer Job's question, Why? If it is sin, tell him that he may turn from it. Does God see job as an enemy? If so why, that he may get right. He compares himself to leaves in the wind, the stubble of the wheat, fanned into the air, as bitter things are against him. As of he's been put into stocks, marking his feet with their bonds. Permanently disfigured, physically and spiritually. As rotten meat or a motheaten garment. Job has humbled himself before the Lord, he just wants to know the cause.

Job in chapter 14 begins a section of the discourse between he and his erstwhile friends, that continues to show his lament against his bitterness towards life, but starts the process of his proclaiming, in chapter 19, that he knows his Redeemer liveth. He again notes the brevity of life, that the mortality of men is like a flower cut down or a fleeting shadow. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean, not one. Not man. Our days are numbered and God is appointed us the bounds that we cannot pass, a day where our flesh will die. But, job says there is hope of a tree. That even if it's branches rot and the stock die in the ground while the roots still there, there is hope. A little water can bring it to bud and bring forth boughs again. Men die and until the heavens be no more they shall not be raised out, until the judgment. Until the end of His wrath is passed. He says that if he dies, shall he live again? But all the days of his appointed time he will wait till his change comes. This is both the change of death from flesh and the change of being resurrected into eternal life. After the bounds of his life are come, God will call and he will answer and God will do the desire of the work of His hands, The promise of putting on incorruption. But he asks, if God is numbered his steps, if God has determined when he will die, then can't He also have watched over his sin? Our sins are as they were sealed up in a bag. Sewn up. And while a man may die, as God prevail so against us all, though he destroys our Hope and return our bodies to dust, although our sons may come to honor or dishonor, well after our time, in this life, his flesh shall have pain and his soul shall mourn. What's sadness he has. What wisdom he has in his sadness.

And so, Eliphaz, the first of the men to reproach Job in his sorrow, speaks again. Offended by Job's mockery of their so-called wisdom. He calls Job unwise and vain, full of hot air. That his talk is unprofitable and worse, accuses Job of attacking God by attacking them. Thy own mouth condemneth thee, and not I. But we already know this isn't true. Eliphaz goes on to ridicule the misery Job feels in his pain. The hurt of his situation, saying, you aren't the first person to suffer, and then minimizing what Job's been through, as if he could understand. He couches his critique in respect for the Lord. That Job, in reproving these men, actually is attacking God. Eliphaz says that if God doesn't put trust in His saints, in the righteous, how much worse is His wrath upon the unrighteous? And it is a true saying, as far as it goes. Men are only made righteous by the imputation of Jesus, upon those who trust in the Lord, and Him alone. But to take the liberty of God, and use it to accuse his friend of being a worse sinner than they are, deserving all that he gets, is wicked. The second half of Eliphaz's harangue is interesting, and worth noting. It shows an understanding of salvation and Hell for the unbeliever, even from the mouth of this bad friend, and even among the Gentile nations, outside of Israel, even before Jacob was likely born. Like other bits of misapplied wisdom in these men's words against Job, we shouldn't throw the baby out with the unsympathetic bathwater. Eliphaz posits that if the saints are not righteous by their own acts, how much more of an abomination are the filthy men, which drink iniquity like water. An interesting allegory, compared to those that are saved, who drink the water of life, freely. He says condescendingly to Job, let me explain this to you, this wisdom passed on from our fathers. A truth that has not been hidden, from before there were nations, among man to whom God gave the earth. This takes place within centuries of the flood, and Babel. Just a few generations. And this is what he says is that wisdom. That a the wicked are in pain, spiritually, all their lives. Knowing death is coming for them, but not knowing when. Knowledge that they will be struck down, even as they prosper. He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword. Return out of darkness, the resurrection. The eternal life granted believers. He doesn't believe, and so awaits death as a condemned man waits for the sword. He searches out for bread, for sustenance, unsure of provision, unlike the believer who trusts in the Lord for our daily bread. All the while, he knows that the day of darkness, death, is at hand. The wicked are constantly afraid, are led into temptation, unable to stand trouble and anguish for their fear, lacking the strength of the Lord. They fall to tribulation. These evil men go up against God, but their strength and buckers, their defense and their armor, all fail them. While the believer has the strength of the Lord to rely on. Psalm 18:2 The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower. Eliphaz says the wicked grow fat with gluttony, even as their cities and homes are in reality, desolate. Ready at any moment to become heaps. The unbeliever doesn't actually prosper, because their substance is earthly, fleeting, and their time on this earth is short. They can never reach perfection. Never be complete. He shall not depart out of darkness; the flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away Outer darkness and eternal hellfire will consume them. It shall be accomplished before his time, and his branch shall not be green. Unlike Job's picture of salvation in the tree that dies, even to the roots, but shoots forth new life at the rain, these men of iniquity will fall, be cast off. Never reaching perfection as the fruit of the vine, cast off as the flowers of olives. Fruitless. Vain. For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery. They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit. The congregation of hypocrites. What an accurate description of Hell. Made desolate, no fruit to their account, all they are and have is vanity. Useless. The only thing they produce is mischief and deceit.

Then Job answered and said, I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all. And isn't that the whole of the matter, the failure of Job's friends to comfort him in his affliction, rather than accuse him in their hypocrisy. He says that if the roles were reversed, he could speak as they do, shaking his head in judgement, but he wouldn't. Job would try to assuage them. He has been made weary and beaten down by such desolate company. His face and body bear record of Job's suffering and the wrath against him. He teareth me in his wrath, who hateth me: he gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me. They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me. God hath delivered me to the ungodly, and turned me over into the hands of the wicked. This is, of course, literally the feeling of Job in his wretched condition, yet he speaks in the Spirit throughout, and it is difficult not to see Jesus' suffering in this entire exchange. He cleaveth my reins asunder, and doth not spare; he poureth out my gall upon the ground. But as prophetically accurate, it still is Job's lament, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? He has mourned as a man mourns, and in sackcloth and dust. His face foul of weeping, and his eyelids darkened as it were the shadow of death. His prayers are ernest and sincere. He just wants to know why, and be comforted. And in all that, the faith of Job is clear, Also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high. This is Jesus and His wonderful advocacy for us sinners before the judgment of God. Job is certain of that, despite all else. He laments, crying out that his friends scorn him even as he calls out to God. O that one might plead for a man with God, as a man pleadeth for his neighbour! An indictment of the three, but also an appeal to Christ the mighty councilor. Psalm 22 My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? 2 O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent. 3 But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel. 4 Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them. 5 They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded. 6 But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. 7 All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, 8 He trusted on the Lord that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him. 9 But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts. 10 I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou art my God from my mother's belly. 11 Be not far from me; for trouble is near; for there is none to help. 12 Many bulls have compassed me: strong bulls of Bashan have beset me round. 13 They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion. 14 I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels. 15 My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death. 16 For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet. 17 I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me. 18 They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture. 19 But be not thou far from me, O Lord: O my strength, haste thee to help me. 20 Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. 21 Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns. 22 I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee. 23 Ye that fear the Lord, praise him; all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him; and fear him, all ye the seed of Israel. 24 For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard. 25 My praise shall be of thee in the great congregation: I will pay my vows before them that fear him. 26 The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the Lord that seek him: your heart shall live for ever. 27 All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the Lord: and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. 28 For the kingdom is the Lord's: and he is the governor among the nations. 29 All they that be fat upon earth shall eat and worship: all they that go down to the dust shall bow before him: and none can keep alive his own soul. 30 A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. 31 They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this.

Poor Job. He wants to die, he feels like he is, and he is surrounded by people he thought well of, and who thought well of him, and now they are mockers, surrounding him. He has no one to put in a surety, to enter into a deal with him by striking hands. Either due to his feelings of being betrayed by his best friends, or due to the shortness of his life as it seems, who would take a good faith payment towards any future involving Job? He cries to God that He has hidden understanding from these men, who in the past had flattered him as just. But now he is a byword, a cautionary tale in their mouths. They used to celebrate him, and his name was like a tambourine, ringing out. He, in his affliction, had hoped for comfort, and got ridiculed. They make the day dark, the light short with their gloom and railing. He wonders, where is my hope? Who shall see it? He doesn't think these three will. I am ready for the grave, he says. To go down into the pit. To be as other men in the dust. What a miserable creature he is, even more so at the turning of his friends.

Bildad, furious at the rebuke of Job against him and the other two fairweather friends, unleashes curses against Job. We must remember the context, that not only is Job broken, financially ruined by bands of robbers and spoilers, and is physically tormented by sores, he is also laying in dirt, wearing sackcloth, mourning the loss of his sons and daughters. Bildad says, you dare to accuse us of being wicked? And then lists all the curses that Job has suffered as good. As the wrath of God against Job. His light snuffed out, his paths straightened to cast him down, snared in a net, terrors on every side...It shall devour the strength of his skin: even the firstborn of death shall devour his strength. No more is it vague platitudes and misused proverbs, he is directly attacking Job, fiercely and without mercy. Telling this man who was his friend, in grief beyond comprehension, that it is good it happened, he deserves it. Imagine being the father of 10 goodly adult children, and losing them all at once, and then having the man you thought came to comfort, now berating you. His roots shall be dried up beneath, and above shall his branch be cut off. His remembrance shall perish from the earth, and he shall have no name in the street. What a wicked thing to say to anyone suffering this loss. When bad things happen to friends, it is an opportunity given by God to show His love. His light, on the darkness they are in. Matthew 5:16 Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. We are to comfort the broken hearted, with the love of God that His glory may be shown from Heaven. Not make it about ourselves. Bildad finishes his cruel screed by accusing Job of being wicked and not knowing God. Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God. All to a broken man, laying in dirt made mud by his tears.

After the merciless railing by Bildad, Job again offers his defense. He lists in all the ways that God has clearly set against him, and the reproach he has become to those around him. His friends, family, kin, wife. All are opposed to him in his sorry state. Job is destroyed on every side. He wonders how much more these three friends will continue to break him further with words. He is indignant at their attitudes, that they feel no shame in beating a man when he's down. He says, if they want to continue to pile on him, know that God has done this and more, and they aren't God. He begs his friends, "Have pity upon me, for the hand of God hath touched me." This is all he asked for from them. Not belaboring the obvious and accusing him relentlessly, rubbing his nose in his plight. And then Job makes a general plea to the Heavens, with a profession that is clear: Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book! That they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever! For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth We know his words were preserved, forever by the power of God, and his confession of Faith in his living redeemer, his Savior, Who shall stand in the latter day upon the earth. Christ Jesus. Job says, even after his corrupt flesh is destroyed, his mortal body gone, that in his flesh he shall see God. The resurrection is his hope and he knows he will see it come. His own eyes will witness the Lord in that day. The same blessed hope we share to this day. And this truth Job holds in his heart, despite all the suffering he has experienced, makes him fear for his erstwhile friends. If he suffered, be afraid. For the wrath of God is obviously real. And fear it. That rather than their cruelty, they should ask themselves why they do it, given God has done enough. They should fear the same recompense for their behavior, and repent.

Ecclesiastes 5:13-15 There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand. As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand. Psalm 49:16-17 Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him. Matthew 16:26 For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? Zophar the Naamathite joins in, again, and he says that all this back and forth with Job has triggered in him a need to interject, to speak with haste. He is going to proceed to give a recitation of wisdom, that is all undeniably true. Everything in this monologue is accepted wisdom, and reflected in other teachings throughout the Bible. However, he neglected some of God's good advice; Ecclesiastes 5:2 Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few. Despite the truth Zophar tells, the things he cannot wait to say, his timing and intent, as a reproach to Job and a counter to Job's chastisements of the froward trio, makes him a fool. A real "Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" moment. But his words are wise in the right context. God is just to reward the hypocrite and those that work iniquity, even the rich man is punished in their unrighteousness, knowing that whatever they stored up in this life will perish. It will be spoiled and robbed, frittered away by their sons, returned to the soil and the people they took it from. And they all go down to the grave, returning to dust, the same as anyone else. Matthew 6:19-21 Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. The disquiet and fear that accompanies the gathering of wealth, the love of money and the evil that springs forth from its bitter root, that darkness in his secret places, not feeling quietness in his belly, will consume him in this life. He will never know peace. Never be satisfied. Never feel sufficiency, and knowing the hands of the wicked are always at his throat. The knowledge that his increase that fills his house, is fleeting. That all his goods will do nothing to protect him when God's wrath comes upon him. This is the punishment in this life for those who oppress the poor and take advantage of the righteous. This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed unto him by God. Luke 16:19-24 There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores, And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores. And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried; And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom. And he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame. The rich man in Hell, begging for a drop of water, while the poor beggar Lazarus, in similar condition to Job, except his whole life, destitute and covered in sores, is met in Heaven by Abraham, knowing peace for eternity. This is a perfect parable for the situation described in Job 20, to show the fate of such men as Zophar the Naamathite describes. But it also reveals his own disregard for the beggar, making his lecture vanity, in hypocrisy.

Matthew 19:24 And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God. Job's reply to Zophar is softer than he deserves, and less deliberately scornful, because Job acknowledges the truth behind what he said. He points out that his complaint isn't to men, but to God, and isn't made due to his lack of understanding. Job says he understands what he looks like, and even he is astonished by the thought of himself in his current condition. But, he says, why do the wicked live, and have in their time children born and established, and grandchildren before their eyes? God's wrath isn't present on them always. They are blessed with wealth and safety. But in a moment, it's all lost as they go down into the grave. Job says they say unto God, depart from us. They, like the Romans 1 reprobate do not wish to retain God in their knowledge. Seeing no profit in prayer or gratitude. Romans 1:21 Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. Even though they may live long and prosper, God's wrath eventually comes to them in their death. Their wealth scattered. That even as they sit fat and comfortable now, they will descend into the grave, where the worm dieth not. Job talks about the judgment, reserved for the dead in that day. That the wicked is reserved to the day of destruction? they shall be brought forth to the day of wrath. Who shall declare his way to his face? and who shall repay him what he hath done? The great White Throne; Revelation 20:11-12 And I saw a great white throne, and him that sat on it, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away; and there was found no place for them. And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works. Job is stipulating that he agrees with the true sayings made by Zophar. He has no quarrel with the obvious truth. But, how is it comforting to tell him all these things he knows, about the God he fears? Because in their answer if the lie that Job is actually wicked. But he is the most faithful man alive.

Where Zophar the Naamathite kept his argument to generally true sayings, only hinting at Job's supposed guilt being the cause of his suffering, Eliphaz the Temanite, in his final outburst, lays charge to Job. He accuses him of great wickedness and infinite iniquity. Breaking pledges, and the arms of the fatherless. Stripping the poor of their garments and refusing to feed them, or give water to the thirsty, bread for the hungry. Sent widows away empty handed. He even accuses Job of engaging in the level of wickedness mankind had reached before the flood. It seems as though the railing accusations come from a resentment of Job's well-known perfection in his faith. The righteous living that made God point him out to Satan to begin with. Eliphaz claims that God is not pleased by well doing, and doesn't care if man makes his ways perfect, complete and mature. This seems like sour grapes. We know that God not only doesn't delight in the destruction of the evil, that He would that all men be saved. The Lord takes pleasure in His children's righteousness. Psalm 149:4-5 For the Lord taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation. Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds. Psalm 35:27 Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the Lord be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant. God does rejoice at men's repentance towards the truth, and our turning from sin to separate ourselves to His service. When we do well for others, we let our light so shine that He is glorified among men. Eliphaz is correct in one thing; the gospel. Receive, I pray thee, the law from his mouth, and lay up his words in thine heart. If thou return to the Almighty, thou shalt be built up, thou shalt put away iniquity far from thy tabernacles. That the humble before Him are delivered, and their needs met. But he uses this truth as an accusation against Job, presuming he has taken pride in his own righteousness, and not humbled himself as Eliphaz clearly thinks he has. He is a hypocrite, and I believe it stems from feelings of inadequacy and envy when he compares himself to Job. This also feeds his fears, that if it can happen to such a good man, how can Eliphaz avoid similar wrath in judgement? And so, Job must be the worst. The leaven of the Pharisees is the fruit of works based salvation. Hypocrisy drives feelings of being holier than others. But it also leads to envy of those more obviously righteous than the adherent. And so they love to tear these people down and delight in their shortcomings. People who trust in their own works of righteousness live in a sweet spot where they have to be less sinful than the next person. And so they have to resent anyone who upsets this equation by being better than they are.

Job again replies to his friends, and makes it clear his thoughts on God, for he is a righteous man. He says his complaints are not sufficient to convey his suffering, that he has withheld from overstating his groaning. He just wishes he could find God, and defend himself before Him. He wants to know what it was God had against him, and to understand why. And Job makes it known his Lord is merciful, because he is saved. That God's great power would not be brought against him, but His strength put in him. That before the judgment, the righteous would dispute with Him, and Job will be delivered. This is Christ, the advocate. The Righteousness of God. Councilor. Our deliverer. Job is bitter because he cannot feel the peace he felt, the joy of his salvation, in the heartache and physical pain he is in. But job is sure that his Redeemer liveth, and knows his path, and when he is tried, he shall come forth as Gold. This is the comfort of all the afflicted who are children of God. Regardless of what tribulation we have on this earth, we are tried as gold, and redeemed. We shall keep His ways, walk His paths, keep His commandments, knowing we are already His. Job says I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food. A reminder that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God. But, he wonders, if God has judged him, who can turn Him? How can God repent if it is His will that Job suffer? Therefore, Job is troubled. This is the crux of his complaints. He fears God and knows Him, and so this affliction troubles him to his soul.

Job continues to speak, having just made points about the nature of God relative to his own complaints, in the previous chapter, Job is beginning to gain understanding and perspective to his predicament. The railing and rantings of his friends against him has given him the spirit to reprove them in his own defense, and in doing so, he cuts to the heart of the truth he knows but has set aside in his mourning. Here in chapter 24, Job paints a picture and gives parables of the wicked, and both their iniquity, their seeming prosperity, and their ultimate fate. He begins by asking how those that know God don't understand their days are short. That His wrath will come on them. They brazenly remove the landmarks, the stones set as borders to a man's fields, to steal the land, and the flocks of their neighbors in doing so, to feed themselves. There is an allegory here, that can be used to take this and apply it to the false teachers of today. Vipers who "move the landmarks," the Biblical fundamentals, in order to steal away the flocks of God. To feed on them, spiritually and literally, for filthy lucre's sake. This parable was naturally relatable to agrarian era men, post flood, but also just as understandable to Americans, right through today. God's truth is eternal, not archaic. Job continues to describe the evil men do, particularly against the poor, the widows and fatherless. Having just been accused of some of these wicked sins, Job is demonstrating a keener understanding about these matters than even his friends, showing the. That he not only recognizes the sins of the wicked, but the judgment of a righteous God against these things. As he lists them, Job talks about the light and the dark, that the evil hate the light. John 3:20 For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved. Job transitions from their evil ways, hated of God and the light, to their inevitable end. The grave, worms and destruction. Consumed by death as the winter snows. As a dead tree, ready for the fire. His short, vain life, meaningless. Exalted for a little while, and brought low. Cut off. Job finishes, and asks, who will call him a liar? Do they disagree with him? Has he not shown the understanding they were accusing him of lacking?

Psalm 22 My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? 2 O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent. 3 But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel. 4 Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them. 5 They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded. 6 But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. 7 All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, 8 He trusted on the Lord that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him. 9 But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts. 10 I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou art my God from my mother's belly. 11 Be not far from me; for trouble is near; for there is none to help. 12 Many bulls have compassed me: strong bulls of Bashan have beset me round. 13 They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion. 14 I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels. 15 My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death. 16 For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet. 17 I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me. 18 They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture. 19 But be not thou far from me, O Lord: O my strength, haste thee to help me. 20 Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. 21 Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns. 22 I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee. 23 Ye that fear the Lord, praise him; all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him; and fear him, all ye the seed of Israel. 24 For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard. 25 My praise shall be of thee in the great congregation: I will pay my vows before them that fear him. 26 The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the Lord that seek him: your heart shall live for ever. 27 All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the Lord: and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. 28 For the kingdom is the Lord's: and he is the governor among the nations. 29 All they that be fat upon earth shall eat and worship: all they that go down to the dust shall bow before him: and none can keep alive his own soul. 30 A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. 31 They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this. Bildad's short response to Job is less accusatory, and more reflective after Job's previous statements on the nature of God, His wrath on the unrighteous, and the hope of salvation. He comments on the power and holiness of the Lord, His hosts of Heaven, His great light more pure than the sun and moon. His question, with a God so pure and holy, how can man be justified with God? How can any man be clean that is born of women. That men are worms before Him. But even in this rhetorical question, God shows us His plan. To be made little lower than the angels. To be born of woman and be pure. To be a son of man, a worm, bearing the reproach of men, and yet Jesus was made hope from the womb. Pierced hands and feet. Garments parted by lot. And still, raised from the dead, declaring the deliverance of the meek, those that fear Him, to all kindreds, the Governor among nations. The Lord. A generation of people who were not a people, declaring His righteousness. Hebrews 2:1-13 For unto the angels hath he not put in subjection the world to come, whereof we speak. But one in a certain place testified, saying, What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man that thou visitest him? Thou madest him a little lower than the angels; thou crownedst him with glory and honour, and didst set him over the works of thy hands: Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man. For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings. For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren, Saying, I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee.

Following Bildad's short speech on the Holiness of God compared to man, and undeserving of redemption (which had allusions to Christ, even in his doubt), Job answers. He asks how has he helped others in need? Those without power, without strength, without wisdom? A man may answer of themselves, but Job makes it clear, it is of God. Man doesn't speak things into creation, or give spirit and life. Man doesn't have the power of God, which all creation testifies. There is nothing kept from Him and yet, man is left with such little understanding of the Lord. Job says all the wonders and miracles of creation are just a glimpse, and the thunder of His power, who can understand? The dialogue has begun to transition from talking about Job as if he were a heathen, sinful, ignorant and scornful of God and His ways, to Job instructing the three men of the nature of God, salvation and creation, which is a parable offered to all men, plain to see. The stars in the heavens, the earth in space, the oceans and land that bound the waters, all speak of His power and glory. Romans 1:18-20 For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse Psalm 19:1-3 The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge.There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.

Psalm 73:3-17 For I was envious at the foolish, When I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no bands in their death: But their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men; Neither are they plagued like other men. Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; Violence covereth them as a garment. Their eyes stand out with fatness: They have more than heart could wish. They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: They speak loftily. They set their mouth against the heavens, And their tongue walketh through the earth. Therefore his people return hither: And waters of a full cup are wrung out to them. And they say, How doth God know? And is there knowledge in the most High? Behold, these are the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase in riches. Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency. For all the day long have I been plagued, And chastened every morning. If I say, I will speak thus; Behold, I should offend against the generation of thy children. When I thought to know this, It was too painful for me; Until I went into the sanctuary of God; Then understood I their end. Revelation 14:10-12 The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name. Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus. Job continues his parable, the wisdom and knowledge of God, His wrath revealed from Heaven against the ungodly. Job, like the psalmist, has seen the wicked prosper, while he himself is vexed, but despite his bitter circumstances, Job will not reject his righteousness, which is in the strength of the Lord. He details the vanity and worthlessness of the treasure built up by the wicked, knowing their end is just. While the widow of a believer can take comfort in their rest when they die, the unbeliever is going to eternal torment, their wealth motheaten and dust. This is the portion of a wicked man. For what is the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath gained, when God taketh away his soul? Mark 8:36 For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? In the past week, many have turned out to declare the false doctrine of "annihilationism," that there is no eternal torment in store for the unbeliever. But, as the psalmist went to the sanctuary of God, and understood their end, as the saints, we are patient with the tribulation of this world, knowing we have peace in death, and taking comfort in the wrath poured out on the wicked. The smoke of their torment rising forever.

Proverbs 9:10 The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding. Job describes the relative ease of finding precious stones, silver, gold, iron and brass, compared to the wisdom of God. Proverbs 8:11 For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it. Colossians 2:2-3 That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ; In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. In Christ is all God's wisdom and knowledge. Other creatures and creation is nothing compared to Him. Only in Him is understanding. Jesus is the vein of wisdom, through the fear of God. 1 Corinthians 2:7-16 But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory: Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God. For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God. Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man. For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? but we have the mind of Christ. What an awesome thing. To have the mind of Christ. But, our flesh is at enmity with the spirit, and so when we walk in the canal, we have less access to the wisdom of God. We often use 1 Corinthians 2:14 to say that unbelievers cannot understand scripture, but Paul is writing to the church at Corinth to tell them to stop being carnal. They're arguing over personalities of men, who is of Paul and who is of Apollos, and so they are natural men, and shutting themselves off from that font of wisdom in Jesus Christ. The spiritual things of God. That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nough Job understands that to even begin to grasp the unsearchable richness of the God, that fear of the Lord and departing from evil is where understanding is found. 1 Corinthians 3:18-23 Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness. And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are your's; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are your's; And ye are Christ's; and Christ is God's.

Job's monologue continues, building upon the stipulations and understanding of God and His judgment, to how it applied to Job's life. He laments again his current situation, wistfully thinking about his life before the tragedy. Job in all his ways acknowledging the Lord, and letting His light direct his ways. The secret of God, I believe is the gospel. The mystery of salvation to those that believe God and it is counted for righteousness. The Almighty was with him, Job was blessed with children and prosperity and had the respect of the men at the gate. This is the patriarchal rule of the day. The men of means and power sat in the street of the city and heard matters, and offered wisdom. They judged. The young men feared Job, the elders gave him deference. Even the princes, the governors of the city gave him his due. They listened and watched what Job would say and do. His influence was such, that he had everyone's respect and attention. Why? Job tells us. He delivered the poor and the fatherless. Those that had no man. He blessed the dying and gave to the widow in her need. Because he clothed himself in righteousness and wore judgment like a crown. This should be the goal of all Christian men. To have this mind in them as it was in Christ, to start with the Lord, and to lead others in His wisdom, for His purpose and other's profit. Job not only was as a father to the poor, seeing the hungry and feeding them, as Jesus commands us, but further seeking out causes to take up that he hadn't known yet. Going out of his way to help others. Note Job also did this soberly, with seriousness. That when he smiled upon someone in need, they couldn't believe their luck, they delighted in the light of his countenance. 1 Timothy 3:8-13 Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless. Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well. For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus Many men in Christ today say, "well I am not a pastor. I don't have to do much, I can coast on helping with chairs after the service. The deacons and elders at the church have always been there. They do the heavy lifting." Respected men of faith in the church don't put on this gravity like a coat when they get named. It isn't a longevity award. You must be these things before you are ever even considered for leadership. And it should be your guide and goal as a young man. The world has made arrested development into a virtue. Being unserious as a way to comport yourself. This retards the growth of a Christian man. We see it in ourselves, certainly. An immaturity that must be tamed and brought under control. It's fine to joke and laugh, but in its place. Sobriety and gravity are what we should strive for, coupled with grace and mercy for those who have no one to deliver them. With kindness as the goal. Not lordship. Like Job, respect that comes from putting on God's righteousness and judgment. From living out your faith. You gain respect and influence by being a doer of the word, by being a humble servant. Not a prideful boaster. In chapter 32 we will meet a young man, Elihu, who we will see is offended by Job's defense, and seeks to have respect given him, the wrong way. But for now we should reflect on Job's example, and the application for our own lives. If you are a Christian man in your middle age, and aren't contributing to the mentioning of young men in your life, especially your church, give an honest assessment between you and God as to why that is, and make a commitment to be. Some men, especially who grew up outside of the faith or backslidden and making disqualifying mistakes, don't see the point of stepping up. Many are divorced, or engaging in some kind of sin that they are ashamed of. They think they are a broken vessel, that cannot be used by God. You might never be named a deacon or a church officer. You might not hold a title or be given some kind of imprimatur, but your quiet strength and aged wisdom can still be used mightily by God. Humbly accept the grace God has given you, know you are forgiven and seek to be used in whatever capacity God has planned for you, anyway. We all have a talent to edify. Submit yourself to those with authority, and stand as an example to the young men around you.

Having established that he was respected and honored for his ways, Job says he is now the byword, the laughing stock of the young men. Not only young men, but the worst of them. The sons of base men, those that are outcasts from society. The worst people. All from the calamity allowed by God. If Job's own friends aren't willing to show him grace in his predicament, strangers certainly won't. And the pride of youth, likely full of resentments against him, glory in Job's downfall. Young people should show more honor for the elders, and respect for the hoary head should include understanding that bad things that come with age will fall on all of us, God willing. That death will come, but before that many ailments, disabilities, embarrassing conditions, circumstances that just are unavoidable. Youth often comes with lack of understanding, a lack of awareness and a back-of-the-mind fear of it happening to them, that combined makes them very unsympathetic to the old. Young Christian men especially should seek to learn from their elders, not mock them.

Job comes to the conclusion of his final defense. Having stipulated all that the friends had said about God's judgement against the ungodly, and having given a list of all the ways Job had proven himself over the years, and having admitted that his reputation is now in tatters among those young and bitter men (a backhanded insult to the quality of his friends character), Job now ends his words by again listing what he has tried to do, and what the judgment would be had he not. He says, I try to do this, and if I didn't then yeah, I deserve punishment. But these are the things I have done. Job made a vow to his own eyes, to not look at a woman with lust. He says that the inheritance of the wicked is destruction. Punishment. God sees everything, so if he has done anything vain or deceitful, then let the Lord do his worst. Let him sow and not reap the harvest. Let others eat it. If he's committed adultery, coveting his neighbor's wife, then let his own wife be a harlot. He treated his servants well, took care of the widow, the fatherless, the poor, and if he hadn't, he asks, What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him? That day of judgement, the day of the Lord, is coming for all men. How will we answer for our iniquity? Job asks how he could harm others when the same God fashioned them both in their mothers' womb. For from his youth, he says he has been as a father to the fatherless and has guided the widow, taking care of her. This reminds me of the rich young man who asked Jesus what he must do to be saved, and who claimed he had done all these things from his youth. The difference between him and Job being that Job first acknowledged God. The rich young man didn't see God sitting in front of him. But Job's wisdom came from his fear of God and the destruction and wrath to come. So he doesn't trust in himself or in gold or his wealth. He trusted in the Lord and fed the stranger and took care of the poor. Cursing no one. Helping everyone. He says, if he had done all these bad things being assumed, and had not done the good the Lord expects of us, if he had sins of commission and omission, then he would admit them. If they were written, he would wear the book of his sins upon his head as a crown. He would accept the punishment of God and the derision of men. And so in all things Job maintained his fear of God, and spoke not in sin. He maintained his integrity and did not curse God. He just wants to know, why? One of the things that we should take away from Job is his attitude towards service. Putting others first. A lot of people seem to think that Jesus introduced all of these concepts of loving your neighbor, and caring for the poor in the New Testament. But again and again we see that this is how God wants us to be. He took no pleasure in the blood of bulls and goats. He called people to mercy and judgment. To have discernment. To be so grateful for the things that we have that we have no problem sharing them with others. That we put others profit before ourselves. Especially when it comes to the fatherless, the widow, the poor and feeble-minded. James 1:27 Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. When you reach the point where you're Christianity isn't about you at all, but about God, glorifying Him in service of others, you are reaching perfection. This should be the goal of all Christians. I've talked about it before but, Jesus quoting Isaiah gives us a mission statement for our Christian walk: Luke 4:16-19 And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read. And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Let this mind be in you as it is in Christ.

An angry young man has entered the conversation, Elihu. And the Bible tells us his wrath was kindled 4 times. The young man is angry at Job, the thinking the poor man suffering before him had justified himself, rather than God. He is angry at Job's friends, who accused Job but didn't answer him when he defended himself. He says "I am young, and you are very old." Starting off with a false humility, claiming to respect his elders, that he held off from giving his opinion until they were done, but now he must share his opinions. He was chomping at the bit to tell his elders off, who are very old (not just older). Elihu is rash, while counting himself reserved. He is rude, while claiming to be patient and respectful. He is a picture of impertinent youth. Four times we are told Elihu is angry, and three times he tells the men that he is going to give his opinion. An opinion no one asked for. Young men, do not be as Elihu. He waited on the elders, it's true, but not out of respect or seeking after wisdom, but to bide his time so he could give his opinion. He is a special boy. He wants Job to know, God thrust him down. He wants the friends (who didn't hesitate to accuse Job), to know they are weak and afraid to say it. To condemn Job utterly. He describes his need to unload his opinion as wine fermented in a sealed cask, the gases exploding the seams. For I am full of the matter. He cannot wait to tell them what he thinks. He rationalizes and spiritualizes his rashness, by saying he won't give flattering titles to them, won't show them respect they are due, because his maker, the Lord, wouldn't like it. Convenient! The pride and arrogance of youth is what he is actually filled with. How often do we see this in chatrooms and even in churches? Young men with no experience, babes in Christ, convinced they know more than their elders. Who can't wait to tell them their opinions, because the older people just don't get it, in their eyes. As we will see, Elihu actually offers little to the conversation. It really is just his pride. If you are like Elihu, if you jump in to give your opinion thinking your newfound wisdom and knowledge, repeating things you recently heard, thinking you are blowing minds, stop. Consider him, and this lesson. You aren't a special boy, and you have limited understanding. Have real humility, not the fake kind Elihu shows here.

Elihu, having spent all of the previous chapter telling Job that he's heard all of the conversation, and is going to speak his opinion on the matter, and how much he is looking forward to give it, then spends another 7 verses prattling on about how he is going to speak, and Job better listen up. It is vain speech, the lips and his breath and his words and how Elihu is going to answer in God's stead, he's going to really tell Job what's up, erm actually. He gives his own recap of Job's points, he says I have heard the voice of your words, saying "I am clean, without transgression, I am innocent." This is more than Job actually said. The context is Job facing so great a trouble in his life, that Job doesn't understand what he'd done to deserve so much pain. Not that he was without sin. Elihu is giving the least charitable account. Elihu lectures the older Job for being so audacious as to ask why of God. He's lost all his wealth, his 10 children, the respect of his wife, his friends, the men of the city, even the youth who live in the wilderness because of their baser and lewd families disrespect him, holding Job as a byword and mocking him...but Elihu has decided that Job is not just to ask if the Lord, as if this young man can begin to comprehend the suffering Job's been through. Elihu begins to pontificate about how God actually speaks to men in dreams, and describes the outcome of old age as punishment to humble man. God speaks to us by inspired words, and prophets. Clear teachings. Hebrews 1:1-2 God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds Dreams may be involved, but Elihu's understanding is overly spiritual and limited, and his idea of old age being a humbling curse is a conceit based on his relative youth. How he sees his elders. Elihu sees himself as the messenger of God in v23. And that all this was God's way of giving Job Elihu's wisdom. Of bringing him the truth of God through Elihu, to spare Job from the pit, from death. To be enlightened. It is an absurdly grandiose view of himself. Hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom. Quiet Boomer, let me tell you how it is! Paul's instructions to Timothy, address his young protege's age; 1 Timothy 4:12 Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity. This isn't a command to elders to give any special honor to Timothy, to the young. It's a warning to Timothy to be an example by his behavior, that no man would see him and hold his limited years against him. To not be like Elihu. Young Christian men should keep this in mind. That if you want to gain respect of the elders in your life, let it be by your spirit, charity and purity, not puffed up vain words. Elihu's point about God speaking through dreams and visions or through pain and affliction to turn people from pride and the pit isn't entirely wrong theologically (Scripture elsewhere affirms God can use suffering redemptively Psalm 119:67, 71; Hebrews 12:5–11). But applying it directly to Job's case assumes the suffering is for specific sin or pride, which the book's prologue shows isn't the full story. Job's trials stem from a heavenly challenge, not personal wrongdoing. But Elihu's unable to hold enough grace and empathy to relate to Job in charity. In faith. Young (or any) believers gain influence through quiet godliness, love, and purity, not puffed-up words that lack empathy for profound grief. Job's story shows that suffering often defies neat explanations, and the wisest response is often humble presence rather than overconfident correction. Everyone else's misfortune isn't an opportunity to show how smart or wise or spiritual you are. No one profits from that.
