It leads to men despising your youth, not establishing you as more wise than they are I also want to point out that all the build up Elihu uses before he starts to speak directly, all his "I am going to speak, and words will come off my tongue and my lips will move and I will breathe, so listen up!" set up, and even the arrogant end to the chapter.... Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak. If thou hast anything to say, answer me: speak, for I desire to justify thee. If not, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom. ...where Elihu tells Job to hold his peace....unless he has something to say, shows the lack of conviction and confidence that betrays his own brashness. Elihu is super confident, and you better listen up, unless you don't want to. He knows he is over his head, and these slips show an insight into his character that adds depth to the story and character in a purely literary sense. Job is such an awesome study on people and how we can tend to be.

The young man, Elihu, continues on his monologue, accusing Job of being unrighteous, unwise and wicked. Repeating many of the charges leveled against Job by the three friends, while proclaiming his own wisdom, Elihu's understanding is shallow and, as the reader knows, untrue. There are some valid points made about God not being a respecter of persons, holding the kings and the common man to the same fate of death and judgment. All the accusers of Job have said some right things. What makes Elihu's portion so obnoxious is that he is regurgitating obvious points, while proclaiming his own wisdom in knowing them. A lack of humility Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar maintained. Again, for Christians, this is an example of what not to do. Even if you have knowledge, it is of the Lord. The more basic and obvious, the more humility you should have in passing it on. Assuming that commonly held wisdom is already understood by those you are dealing with. Not pontificating and acting like you invented the doctrine. That your ability to recite dogmas makes you an intellectual, rather than a parrot. Elihu haranguing Job, says that he hopes Job suffers even more than he has, that he not only deserves it, but more that Job is in rebellion against God for even questioning why this happened. The misapplication of wisdom, the lack of maturity and grace, the presumption and pride, these traits make many young people look foolish in the eyes of their elders.

Elihu continues to accuse Job, and again, builds a strawman to do it. Job never uttered the words "My righteousness is more than God's" anywhere in the book. Job repeatedly defends his own personal integrity and blamelessness before God, while fully acknowledging God's supreme righteousness and power. Job 9:2 I know it is so of a truth: but how should man be just with God? In his statements, Job repeatedly recognizes no one can claim perfect righteousness with God. But Elihu puts words and intent into Job's mouth to attack him. This is also a very common tactic online, especially with young theology bros. They learn the proof texts and apologetics for their presuppositions, and can only apply them to certain expected responses. They need the person they are "debating" to fall into the trap of defending the false representation of their own argument, so the special boy can pounce. One reason this is so common is the prefab doctrines and canned arguments work against the unstable and unlearned. Good faith Christians take the bait, and so the argument is derailed into being about what the special boy needs it to be, so that his regurgitating is effective. Which is why it is very important in these situations to know what the Bible says, and to keep the discussion focused on that. And to remember the Titus 3:10 rule; A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject. The second they enter into putting words in your mouth, or reframing what you've said in a dishonest way, they are in bad faith and cannot be reasonable. "So you're saying...." only works if it is actually an honest assessment of what was being said. Otherwise, it is an insult. Elihu's take on what does it matter to God if you sin or are righteous, overly spiritualizes God into a disinterested deity. This theory of theology then allows Elihu to twist what Job said, and for the young foolish boy to claim Job's words are vanity. Ironically.

Elihu's lecture to Job continues, and he lets Job know he is just getting warmed up. To sit back and relax, because someone with perfect knowledge, speaking on behalf of God with wisdom from afar, is present with them. Wew. And for all this boasting, Elihu talks about turning to God with humility. He gives a long-winded explanation of the prosperity gospel, repeating what the three friends had already said, and condemns Job, saying he's worse than the hypocrite. That even the wicked understand the wrath they stored up for themselves. But Job, Elihu says, has chosen this affliction. As he goes on, Elihu runs out of steam, pun intended. He starts a parable about God bringing rain, and the thunder and lightning that come with it. And by the end he's like, "um the cattle...also concerning um, the vapor..." In all ways, Elihu is an embarrassing display of youthful pride. What's interesting, as a story, is that the more Elihu speaks of the weather as allegory, as we really see in the next chapter, we come to realize as the reader he is actually seeing a storm forming around them. He unknowingly is announcing the voice of God that will be coming from a whirlwind. But it is ironic that his blustering about his wisdom is relying on just what he is seeing, and spiritualizing it. He is running out of things to say, and just starts describing the weather. It always makes me chuckle.

And, at last, young Elihu is silenced. But not before his observations of the weather, roiling around them as a storm builds, fuel his final sayings. There is a whirlwind coming. I picture the 4 men standing over pitiful Job, as Elihu calla out the ways God is like the advancing storm. The dark and heavy clouds pushing out the bright clouds, the sky becoming filled with lightening, and the voice of thunder. A cold wind blowing from the north, as the whirlwind approaches from the South. Whatsoever He commandeth them up on the face of the world in the earth. Psalm 19:1-3 The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge. There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard. Elihu is right about the power of God. But as Elijah found, God is not nature. He is the small still voice speaking to us through His creation. 1 Kings 19:11-13 And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the Lord. And, behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the Lord; but the Lord was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the Lord was not in the earthquake: And after the earthquake a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice. And it was so, when Elijah heard it, that he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out, and stood in the entering in of the cave. And, behold, there came a voice unto him, and said, What doest thou here, Elijah? I believe as the storm intensifies, Elihu's fear begins to overtake his pride. He turns to Job, the man he spent so much wind slandering, and asks; Teach us what we shall say unto him; for we cannot order our speech by reason of darkness. Shall it be told him that I speak? if a man speak, surely he shall be swallowed up. His fear of God is the beginning of wisdom. The Lord has arrived to answer Job.

Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind... The storm that gathered as Elihu spoke, which the boy used as it came to lecture Job with what he thought was profound wisdom, brings with it the voice of God. And He sets to immediately show the shallowness of Elihu and the three friends' thinking. Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge? What a terrifying moment, to know that God will demand answers of you. And this fear should grip all men, that they believe on Christ, to avoid that fierce judgment, where all will be asked of those not found in His book of Life, by the omnipotent God of all. He laid the foundations of the earth, the breadth and scope of creation was measured out by Him. The foundations of the world are set by Him, and the cornerstone thereof. Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone... 1 Peter 2:6-8 Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed. The morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy and the truth of Jesus Christ, the lamb slain before the foundation of the world. The cornerstone laid, upon Which all is built. (I believe this is a OT prophecy of Christ, Who has been since before creation, but Who IS and was born of men, to die and rise again. That the stars are the hosts of Heaven. That the sons of God are those from Adam who believed. Some think this is literally creation, and so the sons of God must be angels, to whom at no time did God call sons, according to scripture.) From the seas to the shores to the heights of the sky, to the position of the stars in the sky, God has set all things, and the paths thereof. The wonder of creation is not only in the placement of these things God created, but in their paths and purposes. Time itself is a testimony of His power. The day chasing away the darkness. The rivers carrying the floodwaters to the sea. The voice of thunder, and the rain upon the wilderness, making it spring to life. The pictures of God's mercy and wrath, revealed. Made manifest that no man has an excuse. Only God can create these things, and not as man would, even if we could. For the Lord knows the beginning from the end. The order He has made is greater than our ability to comprehend. Creation isn't like the birth of man. Flood waters are pictured in birth, but is not the birth. There is no womb that could create the frost. The hail which will be used in due time by the Lord in His wrath. Rain isn't called and lightning ordered and arrayed, but by the living God. God has even put what we call the food chain in its place, that the beasts of the world eat, even as they don't sow or reap. But that He opens death to all, that they may eat. And this same God puts wisdom in man's heart.

The Lord continues to speak to Job out of the whirlwind. Job, His servant, seeks to know why he has been afflicted. But God challenges him to see the things that His providence delivers. The grand scheme. The big picture. That for all the wisdom the Lord has given man, and the ability of man to apply it for their lives, there is so much more that is beyond our control, but not His. God asks Job to consider the wild goats, the wild ass, the unicorn - which isn't a one horned mythical beast, but the wild oxen, the strong bull or aurochs as it was known, the ostrich or the horse. The hawk and the eagle. Man doesn't control or understand the time of the goat, when they calve. Unlike the tame goats, they, without any aid or midwifery, bring forth their kids in sorrow, and cast them out to fend for themselves. And God provides. The wild ass is free. God has given it liberty in the wilderness, and a stubborn rebellion against being controlled by men. He searches the mountains for his food, and while it doesn't starve, it isn't fed as a tamed donkey would be. The unicorn, or wild bull, doesn't serve man, or tread out the corn. It doesn't reside in a stable. It can't be trusted with the work of the tamed oxen. But it lives. God gives goodly wings to the peacock, which cannot fly. And wings and feathers to the ostrich, which not only cannot fly, but runs in the wilderness, dropping her eggs to be hatched in the sand and sun. Not protected in a nest, but exposed to being crushed or broken and eaten. And yet, they don't go extinct. God provides, even as He withheld wisdom and understanding to the big dumb bird, giving her speed to outrun man, even on horseback. The ways and whys of creation don't always make sense to man, and are often well out of our control, and yet it continues on, in His ways. Like the beasts, man is a wild thing, marrying, and bringing forth children. Stubborn and strong willed. Even at liberty, prone to wander, God provides. The rain that brought forth green vegetation in the wilderness, and it becomes the food the wild beasts survive on. The horse, whose strength man has harnessed, did not gain its strength from men. It can be startled by a grasshopper, but charge into battle, the noise of armed men, and the shield and spear rattling against him, the trumpet sounding as it rides headlong towards death. The hawk flies towards the south, soaring in the warm winds, without our instruction. The eagle nests in the castles of mountains, and seeks prey afar off. Not by will of man. Her chicks go where corpses lay, and feast. In all this, man is helpless. It is all the providence of God. But we are like these same beasts. We go about our lives, having children that will grow and go off. Stubborn to instruction, refusing to be driven where we should go. Forsaking the blessings of being a servant to God, in exchange for His mercies and bare sustenance in the wilderness. All things exist as He made them. And the systems in place for a reason. Man, who is frightened of thunder and who can't be trusted to do what's right, who runs after war, who abandons their own kin to the wastes of life, who feeds on the dead, our wisdom is not sufficient to explain our nature, or how it mirrors those wild beasts we can't comprehend. But to God, and to His point of view, it is all in order. God's speech from the whirlwind is a humbling reminder of divine providence over creation, far beyond human control or full comprehension. Job 39 portrays wild creatures thriving under God's care, even in ways that seem precarious or counterintuitive to us, underscoring His sovereignty while highlighting our own limitations and rebellious tendencies. Like these wild creatures, we often wander in stubborn liberty, forsaking full submission, yet God sustains us in mercy. We behave in ways that should result in our extinction. And yet, God's mercies are extended to us in ways we don't even notice or comprehend. In all these, suffering, danger, apparent neglect, and death are woven into the fabric of life, yet the creatures flourish under God's hand. None of it is explained to them. None of it is micromanaged by man. And none of it indicates that God has abandoned His creation. Job is asking "why?" But God is showing him "Who." By enlarging Job's view of God, and the order He created, He is answering Job, just not in the way Job intended.

Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth. In the face of the living God, righteous Job faced with the holiness that is the Lord, is speechless. The Lord asks from the whirlwind if any contend with Him, do so. If any seek to instruct Him. Job has no answer. His friends are silent. God responds to meek Job rhetorically;, telling him to find his loins, to stand up and go against Him. To condemn Him and declare himself righteous. That if Job is strong, having a mighty arm, a voice like thunder, decked in the majesty and glory like God, and if Job can abase the proud in their wrath, go on and stand against God. Now, as we know from the beginning and the end, Job maintained his integrity and his faith. He did not stand to correct God. But God says he couldn't of he wanted to. He isn't like unto man. And our own right hand cannot save us. Only His. Hebrews 12:2 Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. Having made clear the lowliness of man, God again points to His creation, how can man ever comprehend the wonder and glory of God and His divine will, when they can't even comprehend the creatures and their ways He created. He describes the behemoth, a creature like we are, whose great size and stature is achieved, while eating grass as an ox. But its strength and power is overwhelming. A tail like a cedar. His hide, even around its privates, is strong, bones like brass, like bars of iron. There is discussion about what this creature is. A hippo, rhino, an elephant, a brontosaurus. But the number of beasts throughout the time since creation it could apply to, points to a real animal, one Job would know. Irrelevant to the main point, that only God could make it, fell it, feed it. To God, this creature is nothing, while it is a behemoth to man.

Psalm 104:25-26 So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts. There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein. Psalm 74:13-14 Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces, and gavest him to be meat to the people inhabiting the wilderness. Isaiah 27:1-2 In that day the Lord with his sore and great and strong sword shall punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea. In that day sing ye unto her, A vineyard of red wine. Revelation 12:3-9 And there appeared another wonder in heaven; and behold a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and seven crowns upon his heads. And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth: and the dragon stood before the woman which was ready to be delivered, for to devour her child as soon as it was born. And she brought forth a man child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron: and her child was caught up unto God, and to his throne. And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days. And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven. And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him. Revelation 13:4 And they worshipped the dragon which gave power unto the beast: and they worshipped the beast, saying, Who is like unto the beast? who is able to make war with him? Revelation 20:1-2 And I saw an angel come down from heaven, having the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain in his hand. And he laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years Revelation 20:10 And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever. God again humbles Job. The great leviathan, that dragon of many heads, whose size and power make him impossible to catch, his scales like armor, his breath as fire that even his sneezing brings forth light (By his neesings a light doth shine...) Again, like the behemoth, there is much debate over what animal the leviathan is, a whale, a crocodile, some other mythic beast. But the use of the term, interchangeable with dragon throughout scripture, makes a compelling case that it is that old serpent... he is a king over all the children of pride. But, regardless if it is a real beast, a figure for Satan, both...the insignificant Job is powerless before it. Man cannot contain it. Only God can break its heads and slay it. Man is finite. God, infinite. And before Him who can stand? In Job 41, God illustrates human inability to subdue the leviathan. No one can catch it like a small fish using a hook, line, or thorn through its gills. It will not plead for mercy or agree to serve as a captive. It cannot be tamed or confined like a pet bird for amusement. Its flesh is not suitable for food, and it cannot be caught and divided as spoils among merchants. Any hope of capturing it is vain; the mere sight of it overwhelms even brave men, causing them to faint. Attempting to lay a hand on it is futile—remember the battle and the impossibility of prevailing against such power. If the leviathan is a picture (real or spiritually, or again, both) of Satan and of the sin of this world, isn't it a fitting analogy? Man is helpless against sin on our own. We can't subdue it, reason with it, enter into a covenant to make peace with it, control it, enslave it, or truly make profit from it. It produces fire that burns all in its path, leaving behind it a trail that shines behind it. Even air cannot slip between its scales. Its armor is impenetrable. Iron and brass are nothing to it. The mighty fall as it rears up. Satan himself initiated the trial of Job, that the old serpent could accuse the man God described as perfect in his ways. And since the destruction of Job's life, his wealth, posterity and health, the Devil is noticeably absent afterwards. There is a kind of closure to the story here, in the penultimate chapter, to see God describe a beast too fierce for man to handle, yet nothing to Him. Just as man is incapable of destroying sin and death and the fires of Hell, himself. Job isn't restored by his own wisdom, his works, by proving his own righteousness before God. When the Lord offered Job to gird up his loins and confront Him, Job could only cover his mouth and sit in silence. So, it is God who restores Job. Only by God's grace do we find a way to overcome the world, death and Hell, by the blood of the atonement shed by Jesus, and everlasting glory by His life, risen in triumph. Only God can subdue the dragon. Man is helpless against it.

Job, having seen the glory of God, His power and might, he says he has uttered what he understood not. In ignorance, he demanded of God the "why" to his predicament, and now sees the Who behind all things. He has gained understanding and repented towards the truth of the power of God. Left humbled in the dust and ash of his mourning. This settled, Job has gained the the understanding that God does what He does, at a higher purpose and longer view than His creation can even comprehend. The Lord then turns to Eliphaz and the two friends, saying they kindled His wrath, having spoken falsely about Him. Things that aren't right. Their prosperity gospel theology and their standing in judgment as if they were God Himself against Job was wrong. And He tells them to make sacrifices and offer burnt offerings, and Job's prayers for forgiveness for them He will accept. This act of humiliation, seeking forgiveness through the man they had slandered, is done according to God's word, and the Lord accepted Job. This, in a way is symbolic of Christ as the mediator between God and man, as Job is the mediator here for his friends. And when Job prayed for his friends, the Lord turned the captivity of Job, the allowances of the devil to control his fate, and restored Job twice as much as he had. In all these things Job never spoke improperly, but in ignorance demanded of God. But it was Job's forgiveness of others who had wronged him that led God to restore him, and bless him with more than he had. Job reached peace with God just by his understanding and faith. But it was forgiveness of others that restored him. This is such an important point to remember. Job first receives the comforting and support, from family and friends, that he needed. And their financial support to him that was without, allowed Job to restore his wealth. The love and respect Job had shown others paid off, as they loved on him with emotional support and alms. Gold and riches he used to make his flocks great again. And God blessed him with 10 children, seven sons and 3 daughters. And Jobs delight in his daughters, naming them for peace, and fragrant spice and beauty, led him to make them co-heirs as their brothers. The Lord gave Job a long life, to see four generations come from these children. And so Job died, being old and full of days. Quite a ways away from his lamenting his own birth. Our struggles and temptations may never be as horrific and total as Job's test. We may seek to know why from the Lord. We may be tempted to blame Him, to curse God and die, as Job's wife said. Others may use the occasion to imply we deserve it. But we should see the opportunity to better know God. To grow our faith, and our understanding of Him. To know that here, or in the resurrection, we shall overcome. The Lord will deliver us, He has turned the captivity, the bondage of sin we are all under, to liberty in Christ. We have the Comforter sent by Him. Our later end will always be greater than our former, because we are all heirs in Jesus. But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. Amen. A reflection on Job and his later end being better than his first, and the salvation of his (and our) Redeemer: Like Job, we are born of woman and blessed by God to an abundant life, no matter our station, having life. When temptation comes, and the law enters, and sin slays us, the Accuser, Satan, does his worst to us (tempered by God's mercy). We have trials, and tribulations. But, entering into grace by faith, we have the hope and promise of God in Christ that our end will be better than our beginning. That at the adoption, when we put on immortality and shed corruption, when we are redeemed, our end will be glorious, as we will be like Him. And like Lot's children, male or female, we are made joint heirs with Christ.

The book of Psalms, songs sung by the congregation, musicians and singers, in the called out assembly. Most are attributed to King David, whose playing of the harp soothe his predecessor, King Saul, and while Psalm 1 isn't clearly introduced as David's, it follows his patterns of praise and doctrine, and generally is believed to be his. But more importantly, they are of the Spirit, like all scripture, and profitable for learning and reproof. And much like the poetic wisdom of Solomon, we find the gospel of Christ throughout. Verse 1 opens with a standard refrain found in Psalms; the blessedness of the man, and the understanding that it is by God's grace and mercy all blessings flow, Whose promises are sure. Here, the promise to bless those who do not listen to the ungodly, the wisdom of this world. Blessing those who do not go the way of sinners, or the scorners. In many ways, the Psalms reflect the wisdom of the Lord found in Proverbs, and give an insight to the mind and heart of the King, a man after God's own heart. David contrasts the ungodly sinners and scorners with the man who delights in the law of God. Who meditates upon the word day and night. This too is a frequent theme found in Psalms, and it shows the importance of scripture, and its role in the Christian life. Too often we see those opposed to Christ attacking the inerrant, inspired and preserved word of God. As Satan tempted Eve in the garden, saying "Yea, hath God said?" enemies of God attack His word, because it is the easiest way to cast doubt, or to put false doctrine, vain traditions and damnable heresy in place of the rock which Jesus tells us to build upon; these sayings of His. Even so-called professing Christian sects and denominations, that make their history, mythology and traditions the focal point of their faith will downplay and minimize the importance of scripture, mocking Bible believing Christians for making it the sole authority in our faith and practices. But what sayeth the scripture? Those that walk in the Spirit, seeking the blessings of God, meditate in His word day and night. By doing so, we become as a tree planted by the river, constantly fed and nourished. Bearing fruit for God. Not withering and being cut off, as the unfruitful. Prospering in all our ways. The ungodly have no fruit. They are compared to the chaff of wheat, that blows away in the wind on the threshing floor. Insubstantial. Unfruitful. Hollow husks with no purpose other than to be burned up in fire. The distinction between the two types of men, the saved believers, the righteous by faith and the ungodly, who do not walk in faith, is made clear. We will sit in judgment with Christ. We shall be the church of the righteous, the congregation of the elect in Jesus. But the ungodly will not. For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish. Just as Jesus asks Martha after the death of her brother, Lazarus: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this? David clearly did. The sinners perish. But the righteous in Christ are with the Lord, always.

Why do the heathen rage? Why do people think they can go against God? Kings and rulers, presidents and prime ministers, popes and priests, all seek to be freed from the ways of the Lord, to do what they will. Especially the religious and political leaders in the time of Jesus. Acts 4:27 For of a truth against thy holy child Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together. They believed if they killed the Son, they would break the bands, Their bonds, and be free of God. Jesus addressed this in a parable, about a Lord who planted a vineyard and lent it out to husbandmen to dress and keep it. And when the Lord sent servants to gather the harvest, the stewards beat and killed them. So finally, the Lord sends his son; Matthew 21:38 But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance. David prophetically writes of this here in Psalm 2. But, it is folly. The Lord holds them in derision. He laughs at their vain efforts, because Christ, His anointed, rose again. He set His Son upon Zion, and upon the throne. Acts 13:32–33 And we declare unto you glad tidings, how that the promise which was made unto the fathers, God hath fulfilled the same unto us their children, in that he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. Jesus' inheritance are all the nations of the world, and possession of the uttermost parts of the world. And as Lord of lords and King of kings, He will rule them. Revelation 2:26–27 And he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him will I give power over the nations: And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father. This prophetic Psalm gives warning to the rulers of this world, reminding them of their place. That they serve at the pleasure of the Lord, and He will deliver vengeance. It's an amazing and consistent message, across the entire Bible; The Christ is God's anointed, and Jesus is the Christ. All who believe on Christ Jesus shall be saved. His grace and mercy giving us the chance to serve Him in righteousness. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him. Amen

When the world seems against you, and the wicked seem to prosper, and scoffers mock your trust in the Lord, we can grow weary and discouraged. Knowing there are others who share this feeling, and have experienced similar despair, but found comfort and solace in prayer, as David does here, is such a blessing. And it is part of what makes the Bible so different from other religious texts. The Lord is our shield. He does lift up our heads when we are feeling down. When everything feels lost, and we don't have the strength to continue we can cry out to the Lord, and He will hear us. The same Lord over all that gives us life, and a new day and another chance, is the same Lord Who protects us from all evil. Vengeance is His. And He is faithful to answer our plea for it. Turn to the Lord rather than wrath or despair, and see His faithful love for us. Knowing that Salvation belongeth unto the LORD: thy blessing is upon thy people.

Psalms of prayer are the most common. The cries to the Lord to save us from affliction and thanksgiving for having delivered us. We often don't know how to pray, let alone in the midst of trouble. We often don't take our troubles directly to God. And when we do, we do, are at a loss for what to say. Romans 8:26 Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered But the Psalms are given as a foundation of prayer, to know we have a strong deliverer, a Lord that hears us, Who has given us help in our distress and Who grants mercy to His people. David calls out to the Lord, O God of my righteousness, not telling God of his own righteousness, but the knowledge that whatever righteousness we have, is His. David acknowledges that the Lord has delivered him in the past, and is asking to be heard to do it again. Praise and gratitude. Humility. These are the foundations of an effective prayer. Lamenting the ways of those who trouble us, the sons of men who vex the righteous with their filthy conversation. They scoff at the faithful. They love vain things, worldly ideas that profit nothing. They seek after leasing, which means to pursue lies, falsehoods, or deceit. But we are not like they are. Or at least we shouldn't be. The Lord has set us apart, His holy people. And He will hear when we reach out to Him. Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah. How often do we lay awake in prayer. Pondering our own sins, and seeking the Lord? How often do we wake in the morning, and praise God for His mercy, asking to be used by Him today? We have the power given us by Christ, to be sons of God. To boldly go before the throne. Stand in awe, and sin not. Make yourselves a living sacrifice, in all you do. Put your trust in the Lord. Comfort yourself with this relationship with Him, that He has mercifully granted to us. David writes of the many who have no hope, who don't know the Lord is good to those that love Him. Don't despair as they do. Ask Him for His grace, to shine His light upon us. To look your way. Going to Him in confidence that whatever is His will, it shall be done. Those that trust in the Lord shall not be ashamed. Let His light fill you, rejoice. We are more blessed than those of the world. More blessed than those in time of bounty. He has made us His children. He has given us eternal life. Rejoice in that. Be still and know He is faithful. I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety. Amen! And in the dark night, when you call out to Him in prayer, know He is with you, even His Spirit that dwells within you.

The song of Psalm 5 opens again with prayer, asking the Lord to hear and harken to the singer. David, the psalmist, King of Israel calls out to his King and his God. Many of the Psalms open with this plea, and serve as a model for prayer. "Lord, my God, hear me" is an excellent start any time you go boldly before the Throne. Unto Thee will I pray. And as Psalm 4 was about praying in the night before sleeping, here in Psalm 5 it is prayer to start the morning. Day and night, we should be in prayer to our Father. Directing our prayer to Him. Matthew 6:9–10 After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Hallowed be His name. He is holy, and hates the wicked, the foolish, the workers of iniquity. We see imprecatory cursing of the liars and the bloody deceitful men, followed by the pledge to submit to God's mercy, and in fear worship Him in His house. Then, the plea to show us His will, that the Lord's paths be made known to us, by His righteousness and in the face of our enemies seeking to destroy us, asking that God's will be done. The enemies of God are wicked, and their throat, an open sepulchre, an open grave, giving off the stench of their own corruption. Jesus uses this term so effectively in Matthew 23 against the Pharisees. Matthew 23:27–28 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness. Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. He curses these workers of iniquity, in terms they know from scripture. The death their words bring forth to those that follow them and their lies, Jesus will say to them, begone, I never knew you. The Psalmist asks God to destroy these people that rise against the Lord and against truth. To bring them down by their own wicked plans, to cast them out in their rebellion against God. But, for those that trust in the Lord, rejoice. Shout for joy! Let those that love His precious name, who love Jesus, forever shout for joy, because the Lord defends us from the wicked. And redeemed us from our sin in His mercy and grace. For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield. Amen.

Psalm 6 continues the prayer and plea theme, with David now up all night with sweat and tears and crying out to the Lord for mercy and for the destruction of his enemies. Appealing to the mercies of the Lord, to not rebuke us in anger, to not chasten us while He is hot and fiery in His wrath, is wisdom that all Christians should take heed of. When we sin, when we have been goaded into a reaction by the temptations in our lives, our first instinct should be to ask God to forgive us. The Devil knows our weaknesses. Our enemies know what buttons to push. How to frustrate us and to get us to react. We are weak. We need God to heal us. David is crying out that his body and soul are vexed and he is in real pain, and only the Lord can heal him. Before anything else, the Psalmist has prioritized calling out to God, humbling himself spiritually, physically and mentally, admitting fault and decency on God. This should be our starting position in prayer. Praise, humility, mercy, then judgment. Jesus taught us to pray; lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. To bring an end to the tests and trials, and deliver us from the evil set against us. Many of us may use prayer as a means of complaining, to gripe to God for whatever trouble there is in our life, and to whine about it being unfair that we are suffering at all. I think all Christians can fall into that during our despair. But the problem with this is it lacks the self-reflection and humility, and acknowledgement that we are to blame for many of our own problems. Begging for forgiveness, and forgiving others, recognizing our sin before God, and then asking for relief from His chastening puts the matter right in our heart. And so, settling this, David transitions to judgment, asking how long will the Lord allow David's enemies to vex him? How long will the trials and temptations continue? One of the effective means of prayer taught in Psalms, and reinforced by Jesus, is importunity. Persistent prayer. David will frequently ask the Lord to deliver his enemies and ask how long must he suffer the affliction in his life. There is nothing wrong with persistently going to God and asking for His resolution to the matter to come quickly. Luke 18:1–8 And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint; Saying, There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me. And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith. And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? We should not be afraid to bother the Lord with long-standing issues, be it health, or work, or enemies or anything else. Praying for resolution of a matter, while understanding that His will be done, and resigning yourself for whatever the end of the matter is, is crucial in the Christian prayer life. And often, settling it in your heart to be glad with whatever God has given you in terms of an answer will lead to Him blessing you with yet a better alternative or outcome. I have personally experienced this. I have witnessed it in others. Persistent prayer and genuine gratitude for whatever His will is, can often work miracles and bring the Lord to not only give you mercy, but shower you with His grace. Return, O LORD, deliver my soul: oh save me for thy mercies’ sake. For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks? Here, David appeals to the promise of God to save us. To remind God of His word shows you actually know it, and trust in it. I think this is pleasing to the Lord. He means the physical death here, but it has the same application spiritually. How are we to praise Him, if we are dead? How can we show the world His mercies if His promises aren't kept. I wonder how many appeals to the throne David sat though, that showed him this pattern of petition. Letting God know how weary it has become, how the vexation has worn you down, is also an effective means of working it through yourself. David says he is weary with his groaning. He's sick of hearing his own laments. It's all he thinks about, and it is destroying him. The desperate plea to God appeals to His love for us. He finishes this Psalm as he has others, letting his enemies know his faith in the Lord is unwavering and his confidence in God is strong. No matter how weary we are, no matter how long we are vexed, no matter how long our temptations, we know we have already overcome in Christ. The Lord has heard our plea. He promised, and so we know He has. He will receive our prayers. Our enemies will know He is with us, when we keep these models of prayer in mind, and humble ourselves to God's will. He will not make us ashamed.

Again, David writes a playful song of faith in God to deliver him from evil. And again, the pattern of praise, plea, confession, and confidence in the Lord is present. Because of their nature, the Psalms are dripping with doctrine. Here we see the faith and confidence in God lends itself to appealing to His mercy and holiness. We learn that we should ask Him to search us. To show us what sins we have in our life, that we may be cleansed and pleasing to Him. David sings out to the Lord to allow the enemies that compass him about to destroy him, if there is anything he had done to deserve this. When we are being persecuted or falling into diverse temptations, tests and trials, self-examination should be on our mind. Dealing honestly with ourselves and with God, that maybe it is the result of something we have done. Chastening of the Lord for iniquity in our dealings with others. Sins against the Father. Confession is rewarded by God. He loves an honest soul, humbly seeking Him for forgiveness. So, like David, call out in crisis, but be willing to accept our role in our calamity, and have a clean conscience towards God. Ask Him to judge you according to your integrity and righteousness, that we don't deceive ourselves. That we don't fall into a victim mentality. Pray for God's judgment, not only upon you, but your enemies. That His will be done on earth, and upon all people, that He will stand up the righteous and lay low the wicked. Knowing that our defense is of God. God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day. This important doctrine is a necessary one, to develop a healthy fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom. The same wisdom here that we find so often in David's son, Solomon and his Proverbs. That those that deal in iniquity will fall victim to their own mischief. The pits they dig for others to fall in will swallow them up. His violence come back upon his own head. This expectation of God's judgment is a key portion of our faith. Not only the Lord's mercy upon His children, but His wrath on evil-doers. God is love. But God is also burning vengeance. His anger is kindled and wrath is stored against the wicked. Romans 2:2–6 But we are sure that the judgment of God is according to truth against them which commit such things. And thinkest thou this, O man, that judgest them which do such things, and doest the same, that thou shalt escape the judgment of God? Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; Who will render to every man according to his deeds This truth is as important for understanding God as His love. And is why He deserves our praise as we petition Him for our deliverance. I will praise the LORD according to his righteousness: and will sing praise to the name of the LORD most high. Amen Psalms 7:6–9 Arise, O LORD, in thine anger, lift up thyself because of the rage of mine enemies: and awake for me to the judgment that thou hast commanded. So shall the congregation of the people compass thee about: for their sakes therefore return thou on high. The LORD shall judge the people: judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me. Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end; but establish the just: for the righteous God trieth the hearts and reins. This passage in Psalms 7 is prophetic to the day of the Lord, Jesus' second coming, the rapture and the wrath. The congregation of the people, the resurrection of the saints, gathered together in the air to meet Him at His glorious coming. Matthew 24:27–31 For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be. For wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together. Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken: And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. As eagles, carrion birds, circle a carcass, so will the risen saints "compass about" Jesus, as we meet Him in the air. When He returns with His own, the spirits of the dead, raising them first, and then those which are alive and remain: 1 Thessalonians 4:14–17 For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him. For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep. For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord. David looked forward to this day of judgement, the day of the Lord. The day of redemption. The pre-trib rapture is so clearly false that it is a wonder it has persisted all this time. "Jesus came to His own. Jesus will come for His own and then Jesus will come with His own!" literally describes 3 comings, yet those who use this will look you in the eye and say that it only describes two.

O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the Lord our maker. For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Matthew 1:18-25 Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost. Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a public example, was minded to put her away privily. But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus: for he shall save his people from their sins. Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us. Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name Jesus. The excellent name of our Lord is Jesus. Psalm 8 is a song of praise for the Christ. The name of the Lord, who has been set by the LORD, God the Father, over all things. Who also is God. Jesus is the anointed, Who is ordained to strength, and mighty. Hebrews 2:4–9 God also bearing them witness, both with signs and wonders, and with divers miracles, and gifts of the Holy Ghost, according to his own will? For unto the angels hath he not put in subjection the world to come, whereof we speak. But one in a certain place testified, saying, What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man, that thou visitest him? Thou madest him a little lower than the angels; thou crownedst him with glory and honour, and didst set him over the works of thy hands: Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man. The New Testament reveals the intent and interpretation of the Old. We see Jesus using Psalm 8:2 against the Pharisees, showing that He is the name of God; Matthew 21:15–17 And when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying in the temple, and saying, Hosanna to the son of David; they were sore displeased, And said unto him, Hearest thou what these say? And Jesus saith unto them, Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise? And he left them, and went out of the city into Bethany; and he lodged there. Through His name was all creation made: Colossians 1:16–17 For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: And he is before all things, and by him all things consist. John 1:1–3 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. The same was in the beginning, when men first called upon the name of the Lord. Genesis 4:25–26 And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son, and called his name Seth: For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew. And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD. Jesus has been made to have dominion over all things, that the glory and honor be given to Him. Ephesians 1:9–10 Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself: That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him And the excellency of His name is revealed in Christ Jesus. Philippians 2:9–11 Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Jesus is the name of the Lord. Of the great I Am. John 8:56–58 Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad. Then said the Jews unto him, Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast thou seen Abraham? Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am. No other name is given by God to be worshipped as God. Acts 4:12 Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. Jerusalem, was chosen by God to "place His name"; Deuteronomy 12:5, 11 But unto the place which the LORD your God shall choose out of all your tribes to put his name there, even unto his habitation shall ye seek, and thither thou shalt come...Then there shall be a place which the LORD your God shall choose to cause his name to dwell there; thither shall ye bring all that I command you; your burnt offerings, and your sacrifices, your tithes, and the heave offering of your hand, and all your choice vows which ye vow unto the LORD The OT scriptures repeatedly say that Jerusalem is where God chose to place His name. Where the Son of God would be revealed. Where His name would be killed for our transgressions: Isaiah 53:3–5 He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. The same place Abraham was told to bring Isaac, at Mount Moriah, Zion: Genesis 22:2 And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of. But God did not require the sacrifice of man, but rather gave His only begotten Son: Genesis 22:8 And Abraham said, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together. In this place, where the altar was made, and the son was to be sacrificed, where a ram without blemish was caught in the thick of thorns was provided, Abraham recognized it for what it was: Genesis 22:14 And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen. The place where the temple would be, pointing to the Messiah: 1 Kings 8:28–29 Yet have thou respect unto the prayer of thy servant, and to his supplication, O LORD my God, to hearken unto the cry and to the prayer, which thy servant prayeth before thee to day: That thine eyes may be open toward this house night and day, even toward the place of which thou hast said, My name shall be there: that thou mayest hearken unto the prayer which thy servant shall make toward this place. God says that His promise to David that the anointed one would come from his line, and His determined use of Jerusalem as the city where He would place His name, is the only reason He did not wipe out Judah as He did Israel. Isaiah 37:34–35 By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the LORD. For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake. Zechariah 9:9 Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. There, in Jerusalem would He place His name, Christ Jesus. The Alpha and Omega. The Lord of lords and King of kings. Isaiah 9:6 For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. The entire Old Testament is about Jesus, the Name of the Lord. And so when we see in Moses and the prophets and the Psalms, when they speak of the name of the Lord, we know that it is Jesus. Luke 24:44–45 And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me. Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures Acts 10:43 To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins. This witness is true, and revealed now, in the last times. That the name of the Lord is Jesus. Amen Psalm 8 as a song of praise and worship for the Christ, the Messiah, Who was made a little lower than the angels, and was raised into glory, is a beautiful and heartfelt prayer. When we consider all that the Lord has created and look upon ourselves, we stand in awe that God's grace would ever extend to us. That He would visit us at all, let alone become man and die for our sins. Hebrews 12:2–3 Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. The awe we should feel in consideration of His grace and mercy - that He became as man, lived, tempted at all points as we are yet without sin, and then despised and brutalized for our sins, and raised again onto glory, that His name be exalted above all - is beautifully summarized in this brief song. O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!

Psalm 9 continues the prayerful praise of the Lord, the call for His righteous judgment, destruction of enemies, rebuke of the heathen, and the eternal salvation to come. The first of the two great commandments, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, is reflected in the praise and worship of David's song. Praising God with our whole heart, acknowledging all His wonderful and marvelous works, rejoicing in them. Note, David is beset by enemies, his cause is right, yet many are against him, he is oppressed, and yet, David begins with praise and rejoicing. It's been said before, but Jesus does not take away our burdens and cares, He simply makes those burdens light. His yoke is easy. When we are buffeted by the cares and worries of this world, we should stop and praise God for all He has done. Gratitude and praise should be in the front of our minds and love for Him in our hearts, because in the end, His grace, His saving us is sufficient. We are on the winning side. We have overcome the world in Jesus. So sing praise to His name, O Thou most High. When mine enemies are turned back, not if, but when, when they are destroyed by His presence, it is because His enemies are ours. Matthew 5:43–44 Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you We are called to love our personal enemies. David had multiple opportunities to kill Saul, yet he spared him, and appealed to the King in love. But those that oppress the righteous, and the wicked full of iniquity, God will judge. And we can absolutely pray imprecatory prayers against them, that God will repay. That His vengeance be done, knowing that in the end, there is no escape for the wicked. Their cities will burn, their line will be cut off, there will be no memory of them, and their soul will be in flames of eternal torment. What little we can do in our wrath? Better to rejoice in the wrath of God, knowing He will handle it. His throne is established forever in righteousness. He will judge. He will take up the cause of the poor and oppressed. Even in great tribulation, it shall be cut short for the elects' sake. Because we have placed our trust in His holy name, the Lord Jesus, Who will not forsake those that seek Him. He hears the cry of the humble. There are so many problems we will have in our life, as men on the earth, and persecutions and attacks added on top of them for believers, if we do the works of God. If we serve Him, we will see trouble. How often do we experience or witness the attacks of the devil on believers who turn to God, and do His work? I was talking with a younger sister in Christ who just won someone to the Lord, and how awesome that was. Within a few days, she was being afflicted from all sides by multiple travails and trials. It was good to be able to give her this perspective. To know to patiently endure it, and see her faith grow. To turn to trusting the Lord to see her through it, and to love on those around her so that they will see her light so shine, that they'll praise God in Heaven. That the unsaved might be persuaded by her chaste conversation. Her behavior in the face of adversity. David's story is a wonderful example of how we should view things. His Psalms help sharpen that focus on God when we are really going through it. We can humbly ask God for His mercy, and know that He who has lifted us up from the gates of death will save us, while the heathen and enemies of God will be snared by their own sin and turned into Hell. Amen Brief note on "Higgaion. Selah." Higgaion is a Hebrew word that means 'meditation,' or something like it, and seems to be a cue for a musical break, heavy harp, where the singers and congregation considered the words just said. It is used just a couple of times in the Psalms. Selah, which is used much more frequently, seems to serve as a pause, perhaps for a musical bridge. The definitions are somewhat educated guess, and opinion. I feel that 'selah' is a bit of a 'think about that,' and 'amen' combined. But I am not a musician, and it may seem more of a way to bring the music back around to those that are. I think it is more important to look at what's being said, and not get caught up in the pedantic. Selah. And he shall judge the world in righteousness, he shall minister judgment to the people in uprightness. The Apostle Paul quotes Psalm 9:8 during the Sermon at Mars Hill, where Paul preaches Christ to the heathen. Acts 17:22–31 Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars’ hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; Neither is worshipped with men’s hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things; And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man’s device. And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent: Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead. The cry of David against the heathen, that those who don't believe in the power of the Lord be destroyed, is turned into a warning by Paul to the heathen of Athens. The time of God winking at their pagan idolatry is over. The judgment is here, because in Christ there is no excuse. God was made flesh, died for all men and rose again. That assurance is sure, and every man must come to repentance, trusting on the name of Jesus.

Psalm 10 acts as a pair to Psalm 9, and a meditation on the wicked, against who David is seeking God's judgment. David opens the Psalm feeling like God's delay in judgment is His hiding Himself, standing afar off, allowing it to continue. We may all feel this way at times. We know God hears us, we have experienced His mercy and blessings and seen His wrath revealed from Heaven, that no man has any excuse to not fear Him...yet, His perfect timing can make us impatient. Even as the saints in Heaven, martyred in tribulation cry out; Revelation 6:10 And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth? Obviously, the wrath of God pours out soon after, His vengeance is sure. We can trust it will come. But it is hard for our human minds to wait. The wicked, through pride, do not seek God. They boast of their wicked desires, and bless those that join in their covetousness. They persecute the poor with their evil devices. Set snares and nets, dig pits, and scheme mischief against the fatherless and the poor. Their iniquity knows no limit. While their murder and violence is obvious, some of the ways of their deceit is less so. He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net. The subtle ways of the wicked, the nets they spread, are not only to blatantly rob the poor of whatever meager wealth they have, but to trap them in temptation. They are the drug dealers, booze peddlers, pimps and whoremongers, pornographers, bookies running gambling parlors, scam artists with get rich quick schemes...all of the ways, big and small that evil men seek to take advantage of those who are struggling, who have no father to guide them, who are desperate to escape their poverty, who are not strong in faith and so are easily caught up in vice. The description of these men in verse 9 echos the description of their father, the devil. 1 Peter 5:8 Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. These men are as the devil, seeking to take men into their maw, and to bring the righteous to falling, that the adversary can accuse the brethren before God. David, praying to spur action against these men, reminds God of their pride and arrogant way, dismissing any thought of God making recompense against them. They say that He will not require it, He won't make them pay the wages of their sin. That they mock God, so they deserve swift and immediate recompense. David often uses these formulas for the Psalms, praising God, reminding Him Who He is, what He's promised, who the enemy are, what the Lord has done against them in the past, what they deserve now, faith in what He will do to them in the future. Because, God is the judge to the fatherless and defender of the oppressed. The reoccurring theme of the Lord defending the widow, the fatherless and the poor, and our role in carrying out righteous judgment for them, is probably the most talked about doctrine outside of Who God is, and the doctrines of salvation in Christ. More than anything else, we are to clothe and feed the truly needy, to make sure people don't take advantage of those who have no one to defend them. No husband, no father. To do unto the least of these, and in doing so, doing it for Jesus. James 1:27 Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. This is the ultimate expression of our faith. The outward practice God expects. Self-sacrifice for others, not the selfish sacrifice of the works-based religions of the world. Hosea 6:6 For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings All the penance and "Eucharist" sacrifices, and all the other rites and rituals men do to get the Lord to be pleased with them are vain. God wants us to exercise mercy and judgment. Proverbs 21:3 To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. Jesus, reading Isaiah, gives us the mission statement for Christians; Luke 4:18–19 The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Amen

Psalm 11 is a short song addressing a doubtful disputation of an unknown interlocer, someone who may say our faith in the Lord is insufficient to save us from our enemies. Our trust is in the Lord. We have no need to fear. To flee. Especially in the end times this Psalm's dual-fulfillment of prophecy, portends. I think of all the fairweather Christians who spend their days in fear, prepping to flee to the mountains in the Tribulation. Who plan to flee as a bird to their mountain. The wicked seek to shoot their arrows at the hearts of the upright, even now. In the Tribulation, they won't need to do it privily, but will openly seek the lives of the children of God. David asks, rhetorically, If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do? If the Lord isn't true to save us, if the foundation of our faith is destroyed, we would of all men be most miserable. 1 Corinthians 15:13–17 But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain. Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God; because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ: whom he raised not up, if so be that the dead rise not. For if the dead rise not, then is not Christ raised: And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins. Because there is no other foundation upon which we may trust; 1 Corinthians 3:11 For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Knowing this sure foundation, and knowing He is risen, we can place our trust in Him. We know with certainty the Lord is in His holy Temple, the Lord is on His throne. We know He is the omnipotent judge of men. He tries, or tests the righteous to increase our faith. He hates the wicked and the violent, and shall rain down His wrath upon them. This is the portion of their cup. This is a promise of God. Revelation 14:10–11 The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name. But the righteous are before the face of the Lord, always. I want to take the opportunity here, with such a short and concise Psalm, to deal with the way many modern "theologians" approach the Old Testament, and the Psalms in particular. When I read and react to the text, all I see is Jesus, the gospel, and the clear and present application of worship in our lives, and the prophetic nature, which clearly is reflected in New Testament end times scripture. Nearly every Psalm is an uplifting song of praise, worship and trust, with the warnings against the wicked and promises of deliverance from their evil, and God's wrath upon them. Meanwhile, most studies become hyper fixated on the context David wrote them in, the situation he was facing. Often totally invented by the author (or parroting an earlier study of another man). Seeking to be wise, they become fools. They want to impress the reader with how clever they are and how their "knowledge of the Hebrew" and extrabiblical sources puts them above the normal believer, who may read the plain text and see themselves, and the future promises of God, as the primary application today. A typical example; "Actually, Psalm 11 is best understood as David’s response to well-meaning but fearful advisers during a time of personal danger, most likely when political enemies or rebellious forces threatened the stability of his rule. The opening dialogue (“Flee as a bird to your mountain”) reflects counsel to seek temporary physical safety amid apparent societal collapse, while David’s reply anchors his confidence in Yahweh’s unchanging character: the Lord remains in His holy temple and on His heavenly throne, testing the righteous and preparing judgment for the wicked. This likely was written during one of the many crises King David faced. Notably, the Hebrew of verse 3—kî haššātôṯ yēhārēsûn (“for the foundations are being destroyed”)—employs a rare plural form of šātâ that some scholars conjecture may allude to the subterranean pillars of cosmic order rather than mere institutional collapse, thereby elevating the crisis from the merely political to the ontological; yet even this linguistic subtlety serves primarily to underscore David’s immediate existential plight rather than any distant eschatological horizon." These men miss the forest for the trees, and create this sterile and unrelatable version of the word, buried under jargon, and with little to no edification or doctrine. I don't claim to ever exhaust the full meaning and layers of the text in my morning studies. God's word is deep and there are passages that carry a meaning and purpose today, and then read later, convey something totally different. Where the Spirit leads. But when a study becomes an exercise in dazzling the reader with theology, vain philosophy, jargon and concepts that come more from linguistics, semantics and traditions, than the Spirit, I recommend they be avoided.

Psalm 12 opens with the most plaintive cry, yet. Calling upon the Lord, "Help." That simple prayer, asking for help during our trials, is perhaps the most often prayed. "Help, Lord" because the circumstances have led to humble ourselves before Him. Our admission of weakness allows God to be our strength, and glorifies Him that deserves all glory. Even the erstwhile atheist, the fool who says in their heart, "there is no God," cries out for help from the deity they profess doesn't exist. We often will ask someone we give the gospel to, have you ever called out to the Lord for help? Because of health, or the health of another. Cry out in fear, because of a crisis or an emergency need has left them no other way to turn, except towards the Lord and His mercy. Or something as simple as a job, or test. Nearly all will say "Yes" if they're being honest. From there, it becomes easier to lead them to the truth that they need to call upon the name of the Lord specifically to save them, eternally. To receive forgiveness of sin and everlasting life. If man struggles with the things of this world on his own, how much more do we need help for the spiritual things of God? Have you cried out to the Lord? Have you come before God, unable to go on, let alone articulate the need you are petitioning, beyond a simple "Help?" Have you called upon the Lord for salvation? David's plea for help, like many of the Psalms, comes from the vexation of spirit in dealing with the wicked of this world. That in a world where believers, Christians, are called to be separated and holy as He is holy, the fallen world full of the iniquity of man troubles us. It is the lot, no pun intended, of the believer. 2 Peter 2:6–9 And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly; And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;) The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished This is a feeling we can all relate to, if you walk in the Spirit. The vexation is not just bearing witness to the unlawful deeds of the wicked, but in hearing them as well. David says they speak vanity to each other, and flatter, and with a double-heart, speak lies. They pridefully boast. It is the wickedness of words that sees David cry out. Matthew 12:34–37 O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh. A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things. But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned. Jesus shows us that words are the window to the heart of a man. An evil heart brings forth evil words, and it is those words that condemn them. Matthew 15:10–11 And he called the multitude, and said unto them, Hear, and understand: Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man. This understanding, that it wasn't the ritual washings and dietary laws, cleaning the outside of the cup -but the heart, and what proceeds out from it though the mouth, that makes a man unclean, is often neglected by Christians, today. But one of the most repeated commands in scripture is to watch what you say. Proverbs is full of advice to remain silent, to not speak like the fool or the froward. To speak truth in all things.
