To refrain from vain, useless speech. But the wicked refuse to hear God's word and follow His way. Men Who have said, With our tongue will we prevail; our lips are our own: who is lord over us? Of course, by admitting they have power over their own tongue, they condemn themselves. James, the half-brother of Christ, writes in his epistle, about the importance of controlling your tongue. James 3:2–8 For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body. Behold, we put bits in the horses’ mouths, that they may obey us; and we turn about their whole body. Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth. Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth! And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell. For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. Controlling your speech will go far in controlling your body. We talk ourselves into a multitude of sins. We give cause for the enemies of Christ to blaspheme by our publicly spoken words, far more than our sins done in secret. When we curse, profane and use vulgarity, when we lie and double-deal. When we oppress and offend others. When we puff up with vain words and flattering lips. We defile the whole body by that tiny member, the tongue. For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him. This is a promise from God Himself. These are His words. 2 Peter 1:20–21 Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. The psalmist was moved by the holy Ghost to pen the words of the Lord. His promises are our sure foundation. His word settled forever in Heaven. Jesus is the Word made flesh. The promise fulfilled. Faith cometh by hearing the word of God. Those that hear and do the things the Lord says are built upon a rock. We live by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. All scripture is given by inspiration of God. It is the source of all our knowledge and understanding. His precepts give us understanding. We are told to meditate in His word day and night. To bind His words upon our heart. His words are powerful; Hebrews 1:1–3 God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds; Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high The word which we preach is the power to save men's souls to all who trust His word: Ephesians 1:12–14 That we should be to the praise of his glory, who first trusted in Christ. In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory. And so, the preservation of God's word for all generations is a divine role. God supernaturally has revealed His word to man in sundry times and diverse manners, and He keeps His word pure. The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. Thou shalt keep them, O LORD, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever. If man needs every word of God to live, as much as bread, man needs access to every word He has given us. The blessing of having a consolidated, complete, incorruptible source, an every-word Bible, cannot be overstated. The King James Bible is the every-word source, in English, without error. The 6 earlier English attempts, like a refiner's fire. We have the purified silver of the Authorized version. We can know the Lord has preserved His word. We can trust and build upon that sure foundation. Speaking of the sure word, preserved, modern versions change and corrupt this text. Rather than the promise to keep His words for all generations, they make it about preserving man; The ESV: You, O Lord, will keep them; you will guard us[a] from this generation forever. The footnotes cast doubt. The changes remove the Psalm's comparison of the vain words of the wicked with certainty of God's word of promise. The Lord promises to hear the sighing of the needy, and to arise to set them that call upon Him in safety. It is that promise that is preserved. And must be, or God is a liar. The first thing modern versions do is create doubt and deny the preservation of the inspired word. Just as Satan tempted Eve in the garden, asking "Yea, hath God said?" The wicked walk on every side, when the vilest men are exalted. But the hope is in the help of the Lord, promised to us before the foundation of the world.

One of the shortest Psalms, the theme is entirely about words, the wickeds' and God's. There is a lack of godly men and a fall of the faithful, because they speak vanity, flattery, and lies (a double heart). The Lord shall cut off all the lips and tongues doing this, speaking proud things. Quoting the proud and wicked "With our tongue will we prevail; our lips are our own: who is lord over us?" The wicked and their Talmudic reasoning, pilpul, theologies of men, their vain and foolish ideas believe they are triumphant over God. But David, writing in the Spirit says that the Lord shall reprove them. Expose them. Because the words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. (BTW, the KJV is the 7th of the major translations into English, and considered the best) Thou shall keep them, o Lord, thou shall preserve them. From this generation for ever. It's God's word. Perfect and inspired and preserved. That's what cuts off the lips and tongues of the wicked. The liars. The proud. Those speaking vanities. And praise God we have His preserved word, because the wicked walk in every side when the vilest men are exalted. The word of God is the rock. It is the foundation. It is unchanging and pure. That is why Satan and his sons attack it, cast doubt on it. It is His promise and our shield. This is why fake Christians and perverted modern versions insist on twisting Psalm 12, into saying that it's about preserving His "people" (((Jews))) forever. But we see in context, using the KJV, that's foolish. Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar. Just look at this jumbled mess, casting doubts and changing entire meaning, and compare it to the KJV which is strong and clear. The footnotes alone are sufficient to see how modern versions pervert the word of God by casting doubt, if it even says what it says...it's wicked as Hell. Lacking all discernment. James 1:5 - If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him. 1 Kings 3:9 - Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people? Matthew 10:16 - Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves. Romans 12:2 - And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 - Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

Psalm 13 beautifully captures a very real feeling of the Christian life, the impatient waiting for God's perfect timing, turning into an acknowledgement that He has dealt bountifully with us. It can be easy to slip into despair when facing trials. It can be easy for us as humans, weak in the flesh, to see the enemy seemingly triumph. To pray and wait upon the Lord, but feel like He may have forgotten you in regards to your trouble. We've discussed the idea that even as martyred saints in Heaven, this impatient call for the Lord to hurry and fulfill His judgment, occurs. How much more can this take hold in our finite flesh? As Peter reminds us; 2 Peter 3:8–9 But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. God calls upon His faithful to wait. And in that waiting, there is promise as well. Isaiah 40:31 But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint. In our patience, God gives us added strength. It is part of a ladder of virtue in the Christian life, elevating us to godliness. 2 Peter 1:5–8 And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity. For if these things be in you, and abound, they make you that ye shall neither be barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the end, our prayers for God to act, and reminders that He has promised to tend to our welfare, and bring us peace from our enemies must inevitably lead to our recognition of His mercies and blessings. Of His salvation. Because, as we call out to Him, it is impossible to not remember the very reason we are trusting in Him, beginning with eternal life granted through Jesus. And with the heavenly perspective of God's grace, it is incredibly difficult to continue in complaint. Because he hath dealt bountifully with us. We've already received more than we could ever deserve. 2 Corinthians 12:7–11 And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong. I am become a fool in glorying; ye have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended of you: for in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing. It's also good to remember that, if a prayer remains "unanswered" by our measure, it very well may be answered in His. That His grace is sufficient. We've already been spared, hell and deaf, and given the glory of eternal life in Christ. Remember the Israelites, who when delivered out of Egypt and bondage, complained incessantly in the wilderness. They complained about a lack of water. They complained about the daunting task of taking the land, despite God promising to drive the inhabitants out before them. They believed the bad spies report, and ignored Joshua and Caleb. They complained about mana, and they complained about quail. And God had to constantly remind them that He had delivered them in the first place. Sometimes if we feel the need to complain to God, we should remember that he's delivered us in the first place. That His grace is sufficient. Reminding ourselves of what we're going through currently is nothing in comparison to the abundance we've already received. Romans 8:14–18 For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. Keeping that eternal perspective gives us faith in the Lord's of ability to deliver us. The suffering of this present time is nothing. Life is but a vapor. So, having persistent prayer and letting God know how you feel while waiting for His perfect timing to occur is fine. But keep that perspective in mind. And understand that patience builds godliness. And everything to His glory, amen.

The opening 3 verses of Psalm 14 stand as the definitive and true statements of the doctrine that all men have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. Quoted in part by Paul in Romans 3:10–12 As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one. It serves as a universal appeal to the need for the gospel, and the reconciliation of fallen men with a holy God. There is none good but God. All have gone astray. The opening verse is an even deeper truth, showing the self-deception that leads fools to claim there is no God. They may say this, but ultimately every man knows that God is, and the judge of all things. Like the scribes and Pharisees that Jesus preaches against in Matthew 23, these fools, the workers of iniquity, devour the poor. They eat up the people as bread. They call not upon the Lord. They shame the counsel of the poor, they profane the hope of the righteous, they deny the Lord that bought them. Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! when the LORD bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad. Again, the eschatological application is clearly seen in the text, and the prophetic words of David's prayer is ultimately about Jesus. He is the salvation come out of Zion, and at His coming, Jesus brings all the risen saints, death and Hell defeated. This was the hope David had. And the hope that God's judgment and resurrection of the righteous and wrath to the wicked, was the refuge of the poor and the oppressed. This is our future, rejoice.

The Christian life is one of separation. Of leaving behind the things of this world, and the wickedness men do, separated unto His gospel, and proclaiming His truth. Epistles in the New Testament show us examples of godly living. Admonishments against the behavior that the lost may do, but we should strive to reject even the company of those that behave as the heathen. 1 Corinthians 5:11 But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat. 2 Corinthians 12:19–21 Again, think ye that we excuse ourselves unto you? we speak before God in Christ: but we do all things, dearly beloved, for your edifying. For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults: And lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed. Here, David gives a similar refrain. Against backbiting, talking behind someone's back, railing and gossiping. Against evil done to your neighbor. The very traits David spends multiple Psalms praying imprecatory prayers against workers of iniquity for doing, should not be spoken of among God's children. We should condemn vile persons, not partake in promoting them, or their pride in sin. We should honor and fear the Lord. In all our ways, acknowledging Him. We should keep our vows and promises, especially when it is not to our favor. Where we suffer loss for our honesty's sake. We should avoid usury, and taking advantage of the poor and desperate. Instead, with gratitude to the Lord, lend freely. By our actions we establish ourselves in truth. Building upon the rock, by being doers of the word. We shall do these things and shall never be moved. Imagine you are a King, and powerful among the people, yet your empathy and thoughts are for justice and the poor, widows, fatherless. Making your priorities about others. David, far from being sinless, yet this was the mind within him. His power wasn't for him, but from God to help the helpless. This is what made him the apple of God's eye. And it is the calling we are to answer, as princes of the Kingdom. The same instructions in humility and decency that Solomon, David's heir, taught in Proverbs. The same as the teachings and example of Christ Jesus in His ministry as a Servant. May this be our starting position, every morning. In our prayers and supplication before the throne, seeking the benefit of others and the glorification of God.

Psalm 16 presents another sacred hymn celebrating the Lord's salvation, the eternal security of the believer, and the promise of the risen Christ. The preservation of the saints is the hope of all who place their trust in God. Our very being cries out to Him for salvation, recognizing He is Lord. Note here that this isn't "Lordship salvation," a false gospel that says you must "make Jesus the Lord of your life" to be saved. It is saved believers, already trusting Him to save us, recognizing that He IS the Lord, as a statement of fact. David writes, Thou art my Lord: my goodness extendeth not to thee; But to the saints that are in the earth, and to the excellent, in whom is all my delight. The good that we do isn't for Him, it adds nothing to the holy and perfect God. The idea that Jesus needs us to make Him Lord, that by our "turning from sin," we justify ourselves before God, is hubris. It's a false gospel. The good we do comes from Him, and is poured out to the brothers and sisters, the saints. We benefit others, and they glorify God. We obey His judgements, to one another's profit. Matthew 5:16 Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. We submit ourselves to the righteousness of God. We do not seek to establish our own righteousness, but to magnify His. Romans 10:3–4 For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. David's burden is for the saints in the earth, his delight is to the excellent of God. Just as we are commanded to. John 13:34–35 A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another. While we should seek to live peaceably with all men, we should especially look with love upon our fellow believers. Galatians 6:9–10 And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith. This is the message that we have heard from the beginning. It is our job as Christians. It is how we are to know one another. Not keeping to ourselves or seeking out own profit. Certainly not by hating our brothers. 1 John 3:10–11 In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God, neither he that loveth not his brother. For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another. This is the mind of Christ, to be servants, one to another. To delight in others. The ultimate expression of humility isn't thinking less of yourself, but not thinking of yourself at all. And the humbleness of submission to God's righteousness should naturally turn to our service for others. Not to add to God's goodness our filthy rags, but to glorify His goodness in us. Continuing in Psalm 16, David calls out the vanity and ultimate end of those that call not upon the Lord for salvation. Who go after another god. They make drink offerings of blood, and speak other names in their prayers. The most prominent example of this today is Roman Catholicism. They make drink offerings, claiming it to be the blood of Christ, profaning His name, and bow to and serve idols representing their own gods. But for the saved, the Lord is our inheritance, we are co-heirs with Christ the Bible says, and He is our cup, the blood shed for us on the cross: Luke 22:20 Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you. The very new testament which we preach is founded upon the blood shed by Jesus. Not a chalice of gold held up by a priest to an image, sacrificing Jesus daily, as if that were possible or necessary, to call Him down from heaven again. And it is God that maintains our lot. Who holds us by His power. Not carnal sacrifices made over and over again. Hebrews 10:10–14 By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God; From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool. For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. This is our goodly heritage. This is the promise of God. The Son at the right hand of the Father. We shall not be moved. And so we rejoice. We rest in hope. For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. The Psalm is quoted in the preaching of Peter before the crowds at Pentecost. Acts 2:25–28 For David speaketh concerning him, I foresaw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved: Therefore did my heart rejoice, and my tongue was glad; moreover also my flesh shall rest in hope: Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. Thou hast made known to me the ways of life; thou shalt make me full of joy with thy countenance. The New Testament gives context to the Old, If it wasn't obvious already, the meaning in the psalm. We know David was speaking of Jesus. David, looking forward to the Christ, his savior and Lord. Seeing Jesus in all things, that blessed hope we rest in. And because Jesus was not left in hell and His Holy One did not see corruption, we have the promise of eternal life, by His resurrection. So neither will we be left to Hell. We can rejoice knowing that He will forever be before us. Amen

Psalm 17 again shows us the model of importunity in prayer. Importunity is a noun that means asking for something over and over again in a strong, pushy, or annoying way. It is the act of persistent begging or making urgent demands that wear people down. David utilizes this in Psalms to great effect. Pursuing an answer from the throne of God, with repeated supplication. It may seem contrary to the fear of the Lord and humility before Him, but scripture shows it is effective. Jesus taught us this as well. Luke 18:1–8 And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint; Saying, There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me. And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith. And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? We often find ourselves in difficult situations, where we have not because we ask not. We also tend to move on, rather than "bother God" with whatever it is we need of Him. Praying without ceasing, staying strong in prayer because we are weak, this is pleasing to the Lord. So we should pray without fainting, and in doing so, exercise our faith that should Christ return in our time, He finds that faith upon the earth. Notice too, that the woman before the unjust judge is pleading for vengeance against her adversary, just as David is here in this psalm. Just as the martyred under the throne in Heaven plead with God for His wrath to pour out. Imprecatory prayers are Biblical. Acknowledging God's ownership of vengeance, while suffering for His sake, is an act of great faith. And as we have seen previously in Psalms, patience is a virtue that leads us to godliness. Importunity in prayer, and imprecatory prayer feels wrong to many. I have seen supposed Christian teachers make the claim that there is no room for this in the New Testament. But they are a mighty tool in our arsenal of faith. The psalmist calls for the Lord's judgment, that His sentence be given against the wicked. But it is foolish to cry out for God's perfect justice to be administered, while you yourself are guilty. It is like a thief going to the police because his partners robbed him of his share of their stolen things. Of a drug dealer complaining about being ripped off in a deal gone wrong. And so, David wisely shows us the pattern of praying imprecatory prayers includes self-examination and willingness for God to judge him the same way he is judging others. Thou hast proved mine heart; thou hast visited me in the night; thou hast tried me, and shalt find nothing; I am purposed that my mouth shall not transgress. David credits God's word to keep him from the paths of the destroyer. A key doctrine, that it is God's word that we judge ourselves and others by, not our own feelings or desires. We judge righteously when we allow God to tell us good from evil. David then calls for the Lord to hold up his goings, to keep him on the right path. So we see that it isn't simply cursing your enemies and expecting God to overlook your sin. But praying for God's judgement, knowing He is just and seeking His confirmation that you are blameless in the matter. Also, praising Him for keeping you from sin in the first place. All glory goes to God. Having the faith to be judged fairly by God, knowing that because of God you have walked in His ways, but accepting any fault of your own that He may find...this humility should be at the heart of your prayer life. Continuing in Psalms 17, we see that David's importunity comes from his faith in God to hear those who call upon Him. That we may go boldly before the throne of grace, because He has shown us that He listens to our cries. The initial call for salvation in the Lord's name gives us the hope that He listens to us for far less important matters, such as our suffering in this life. The Lord's lovingkindness is already apparent to those that put their trust in Him, that have been saved by His strong right-hand. Christ Jesus. We know that our Savior is at the right hand of the Father. The New Testament is clear on this. But David is writing hundreds of years earlier, showing that Old Testament saints knew and understood the concept, even if they didn't have the full revelation and details. Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings, From the wicked that oppress me, from my deadly enemies, who compass me about. Keep me, o Lord. It is His power that keeps the children of God under His protection and secure in His promises. We shall not fear, because we are under His mighty wing, as a mother hen keeps her chicks. Jesus laments the unfaithful Jews for refusing to be gathered thus. Matthew 23:37–39 O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not! Behold, your house is left unto you desolate. For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord. And His protection is needed in this world, where they hate us for His holy name. Where we are often at the mercy of forces beyond our reckoning. Where the judgment of God against our nation is executed by the hands of the wicked. They are His sword. They may profit in this life. They may have riches, while we are poor. They may have children and an inheritance. But we have the eternal promise of Christ, which is far more precious than any treasure of this life. As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness. This is the eternal perspective that Christians should seek. That our satisfaction is in the resurrection, and the current, temporal troubles are nothing compared to the everlasting. When we awake, when we are raised up, we will see Jesus, the express likeness of God. But, maybe David is also speaking of the glorified body we will receive in His likeness. 1 John 3:1–2 Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God: therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not. Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is. This is our blessed hope. To awake into glory with Him. When we see Jesus as sons of God. Gathered up to the Lord, and with Him shall we ever be. Ultimately, this is the only satisfaction we need. If our enemies prosper, if God allows them to have advantage over us, while we suffer them, we know His grace is sufficient. That ultimately, vengeance will be His. That in the Lord's love for us, we will see Him as He is, and be like Him. That no matter what may come in this life, we have peace in the next. Amen

Psalm 18 is one of the first long-form songs of David, and it reflects his own experience with the Lord, his trust in God, and deliverance from his enemies, while weaving together prophetic views of Jesus, the doctrines of salvation, the end times wrath and Kingdom of God. Ultimately, the Psalm gives us understanding of Who the Lord is and why He is worthy of our trust, today. The Lord is our strength. Our rock. Our fortress. Our deliverer. Our strength. Trustworthy. Our buckler, the horn of our salvation, our high tower. He is worthy to be praised. He is merciful to those that are merciful. Upright in all His ways to those that walk in them. Pure to the pure and froward to the froward. His way is perfect, His word is tried and trusted, and the strength and shield of those that place that trust in Him. For who is God save the LORD? or who is a rock save our God? There is no other rock than the Lord. There is no other name given but Jesus. He is the fulfillment of the word, the word made flesh, the promise of God come down from Heaven. The Christ. And He liveth. The shield of salvation is given, by the right-hand of God. His gentleness has made those who trust Him great. The LORD liveth; and blessed be my rock; and let the God of my salvation be exalted. The Lord is praised among the heathen. The strangers hear and obey. The people who were not a people are come, and are subdued under the throne of David, to his Seed. To His anointed, evermore. The enemies of David, like the enemies of Christ, are crushed before them by the fiery and fierce judgment of God. Rains of fire and brimstone, hail and lightenings, leading the wicked to cry out, and hide themselves from His fury. And ultimately be destroyed by His coming. The Lord then is a rewarder of those that trust in Him, who diligently seek Him. Who follow His ways and obey His statutes. He will reward us for the righteousness we have shown, and the recompense for our cleanliness in His sight. The righteousness of Christ imputed on His children. The gold, silver and precious stones we build upon that foundation. He lifts us up, strengthening us to do great deeds in His name. He fills us with His light. He hears our cries. He comes to our aid. He destroys the wicked for our sake, in the anger kindled by their sin against Him and their treatment of His children. Therefore will I give thanks unto thee, O LORD, among the heathen, and sing praises unto thy name. Amen Songs of deliverance and praise, with the appearance of the Lord as a consuming fire, yet displaying tender mercies to His beloved, those that place their trust in Him, and who call upon the Lord, are found throughout the book of Psalms. The reassurance to believers that what God has done for David will be done for us, His name and word are worthy, and are to be trusted. The picture of salvation and judgment. All are detailed repeatedly, just as much as songs of despair and pleas for God's intervention. But both styles of song contain thanksgiving and praise for His grace and mercy, and all the blessings He has already provided those that love Him. Taken as a whole, Psalms gives us the complete picture of the Christian life. They give us a model of prayer and praise that fits every stage of our growth and development, while also dripping with doctrine, teaching us the truth of God.

Psalm 19 is fairly short, yet packed with doctrine, teaching the purpose of creation, the testimony of God to all creatures, the picture of Christ, and the establishment of the law of the Lord in nature itself, that there is no excuse, while the believer is given constant reminders of His judgements. Romans 1:18–20 For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse The heavens declare the glory of God. Looking upon the night sky we see His precision and power. And as the day follows day and night follows night, each with the passing of the sun and the stars, we are given evidence of His might. The things of creation speak without words, that all man may understand. They don't need a language. They don't need to be explained. Man sees the passage of time, seasons, years, decades even, in heavenly bodies. The vain hypothetical of a savage on a remote island, never hearing the gospel, is undone by the understanding that all nature is a parable and a testament of God, showing men truth. The boldness of the sun breaking forth in the morning is as the risen Christ, returning in glory, a picture of the Creator Who is blessed forever, amen. Nature teaches us God's law. His ways. 1 Corinthians 11:14 Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him? His wrath is revealed against those who sin, even without the oracles of God documenting His commandments. The Spirit showing mankind the results of their transgressions. The understanding that murder, adultery, lying, stealing, all of these things that do harm to your neighbor and are a shame before God, are known. Romans 2:11–16 For there is no respect of persons with God. For as many as have sinned without law shall also perish without law: and as many as have sinned in the law shall be judged by the law; (For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified. For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;) In the day when God shall judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ according to my gospel. Man can see the law of God, know it written in their hearts, watch the outcome of their behavior and the wrath upon those who sin, and know they are guilty before the consuming fire which is God. How much more are we who have His statutes and commandments by the oracles of God? Romans 3:1–2 What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God. The advantage given Israel, and held by the Jews in Paul's day, is now given to the world. That everyone may know His word. The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple. If the day declares His righteousness and the night His knowledge, and the very nature of things speaks to His wrath, then the oracles of God give us the hope of His mercy. God is a rewarder to those that diligently seek Him. The fear of the Lord is clean, and known to all men. The fool may say in their heart there is no God, but the wise fear Him, even if they don't know scripture. The truth is more desirable than gold, sweeter than honey. Its pursuit is its own reward, spurring us to seek Him. The warnings and rewards, motivation to learn His ways. And, in that knowledge, we find His word, and from that word, salvation. In Him we are cleansed from our iniquity. In Him we are conformed to His image, kept back from presumptuous sin. Made upright. His righteousness imputed on us that we may be transformed. To be our strength and the Lord our Redeemer. We are blessed to have the knowledge of the truth before us. His inspired and preserved word, that we may know Him. And God does not leave those without the oracles lacking. But for the children of God, creation gives us reassurance and opportunities to worship Him for His might and glory. To have reminders that He loves us. To every seed we sow that comes to fruition. To every shooting star, or bird in flight, or wave crashing on the shore, we are able to look at the Lord in awe. Babies born to the death of the elderly, spring following winter, the setting sun and darkest night...all creation is a parable to those with ears to hear and eyes to see. To know God loves us. And His mercy upon us is evidence to others seeking truth. The light in us shines that others may see and glorify God. We are to be as the firmament, as the rising sun and the crashing wave. His children are meant to teach the heathen who seeks the Lord, as much as anything in creation. Because we are new creatures in Christ, brought forth as a testimony to God's greatness. Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer. Amen

Psalm 20 is yet another song of praise and worship for the salvation that is in Christ Jesus. The name of the God of Jacob. The Lord that strengthens us out of Zion. The one offering forever, the burnt sacrifice. Christ Jesus. The love of God has been granted to us in his grace, and his counsel is wisdom; trust in the Lord. We will rejoice in the salvation given to us in the name of our God. We will set up banners in His holy name. He is Christ Jesus, and God hears all our petitions, lifted up in His name. The Lord saves His anointed. He did not leave his soul to see corruption. His anointed was not left in hell. The saving strength of His right hand. Christ Jesus. Some trust in the power of this world, their own strength, their own works. And they will be brought down low. He will say depart from me. I never knew you. But to those of us who trust in the name of the Lord, our God, we are risen and made to stand upright. In Christ Jesus. Save, Lord. In the name of the King of Kings and the Lord of lords, Christ Jesus. Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God. This verse is often quoted, and has inspired generations of believers. But in practice it can be difficult. We often seek reassurance from our material, wealth and position. David, writing this. Psalm with dual purpose (at least), the prophetic imagery of Christ Jesus and the surety of his salvation, but also as an intercessional prayer before a battle against a well-armed and equipped foe. David's showing us that it is better to trust in the Lord than all the horses and chariots in the world. That in our battles, even if we are seemingly overmatched by our enemy, we are still victorious in God. What a comfort. What a blessing. That we can stand fast, and be sure of our deliverance. That we can trust in the Lord in all things, because we've first trusted in Him, our eternal security. When we are weak we are made strong. God uses us to confound the wise. We have already overcome in Christ. And we should rejoice in our salvation.

The dominant theme of the book of Psalms is placing all your faith in God alone, to redeem, to save from danger, to exact vengeance and recompense, to be the strong tower and shield, a ready comfort, faithful to His promises, generous with His mercy and gracious in His gifts. Trusting in the Lord for every category, especially for our eternal life. He asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever. Those that have called upon the name of the Lord for salvation, who trust in His promises, are given eternal life. Forever. This is the confidence we have. The sure hope that we place our trust in. And we trust that the wicked will be dealt with according to His perfect and holy judgment. Just as sure as our exaltation and glory is guaranteed, that through the Lord's mercy we shall not be moved, we can know the wicked who reject Him will be swallowed up in His wrath. That His fire shall devour them, as the smoke of their torment rises forever. Eternal life and salvation, contrasted with eternal wrath and fire. We who trusted in Him, sing praises and worship Him. We exalt the Lord, we sing praise to His power. Amen It is amazing that people deny the idea of "faith alone," and claim it is absent from scripture, when the book of Psalms exists. (It is equally amazing that they'll deny the idea of trusting and scripture alone when Psalm 119 exists)

And at around this time, Jesus shouted out in Aramaic, the language he spoke the words echoed by David in prophetic psalms, written in Hebrew a millennia earlier, and gave up the ghost. Mark 15 33 And when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. 34 And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? 35 And some of them that stood by, when they heard it, said, Behold, he calleth Elias. 36 And one ran and filled a spunge full of vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink, saying, Let alone; let us see whether Elias will come to take him down. 37 And Jesus cried with a loud voice, and gave up the ghost. 38 And the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom. 39 And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God. Minor quibble, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? Is actually not Hebrew it's Aramaic and most likely the language Jesus spoke from his youth, obviously as God he could speak any language but, Aramaic was the language of Galilee in Samaria. He clearly could speak Hebrew, but it wasn't his first language so to speak. What's interesting is David the psalmist writing in Hebrew the same phrase as a kind of backwards echo, of the Spirit moving through David telling him the words Jesus spoke. Of course this is semantics. Pun intended. The message of that VM is dead on, at that moment on the cross Jesus became all sin and was cut off completely from God. 2 Corinthians 5:21 “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? In the 9th hour, Jesus cried out from the cross the words of the Psalm, the opening line of a song of desperation, penned by David centuries earlier. An event recorded twice in the gospels: Matthew 27:46 And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Mark 15:34 And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? The man Christ Jesus, after a day of betrayal, abuse, beaten beyond human recognition, scourged, shamed and mocked, cursed, hung on the tree, and become sin for all mankind, acknowledging in death that, by taking on all of the sin in all of creation, He is, in that moment, no longer looked upon by the Father Whom He has been with, and a part of, since everlasting. The prophetic words of the Psalm, Christ's words echoed through time to the psalmist, words Jesus Himself knew from before the foundation of the world, conveying the heartbreaking moments before the perfect and holy Lord would willingly give His life that we may live. Jesus cried out in Aramaic, the daily language of the people, the language He grew up in life speaking, conveying His humanity in that moment. The Hebrew words, long sung by Israel in the congregation, translated, and again, interpreted into Greek, and given to us in English, never losing a scintilla of power. Given to us as the blessed hope, an example of the endurance and steadfastness we should look to: Hebrews 12:2-3 Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. Jesus, our scapegoat, receiving our sin in atonement, without the camp. Taking them utterly away. Not as the blood of bulls and goats, offered yearly for sanctification by the High Priest of the Tabernacle, but once and for all, shed for man. And He, as THE High Priest, entered into the Heavenly Tabernacle, and applied His own precious blood upon the mercy seat in Heaven. No greater love than this has ever been shed towards us, that God became flesh, and lived among us, sinless and perfect, that He might drink of this cup. Going to the cross that we might live. The tragic nature of these words reveals the depth of the love of God. That while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Psalm 22 continues from its powerful open, to convey the desperation that Jesus' flesh must have felt in that moment, which is felt by everyone of us at times in our life. Certainly, it was David's own state of mind when the Spirit led him to compose it. That we cry out to God, and feel like He is far from us. That He doesn't hear. That He may have abandoned us to our plight. But there is always the hope of faith, and trust in the holy God, Who has kept His promises and delivers those who trust in Him. The promises made to the fathers, kept. He heard the cries in Egypt, and brought them out of the land. He heard their cries during the time in the wilderness. He delivered their children to the promised land. He heard them in the days of judges, where their own sin brought them low, sending men to raise them up and bring them out of evil. Those that trusted Him were not confounded. Hebrews 12:1 Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us We know that God is good, and cannot lie. And so our deliverance is assured, even when our flesh is weak and we feel abandoned. The almighty God's consistent faithfulness in keeping his word to those he foreknew, gives us confidence and strength. These things were written for our admonition. That we may know Him as a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him. Romans 15:4 For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope. We are given that knowledge of the past that we might have the surety of the future. The prophetic nature of the God-inspired Psalm of David continues, showing the children of Israel the truth of Christ, through a glass darkly. In David's personal pain, we see a shadow of the suffering of Jesus, a reproach of men, despised of the people, laughed to scorn. Matthew 27:39–43 And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads, And saying, Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, save thyself. If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross. Likewise also the chief priests mocking him, with the scribes and elders, said, He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God. Compassed about by bulls, by dogs, men like lions, surrounded by the Roman soldiers doing the work of the Jews, piercing Jesus' hands and feet with nails. Splayed out upon the cross, His joints distended and twisted to support the weight of His body. The sinking feeling of death settling in His guts, as He struggled to breathe. His bones in sharp relief to His stretched out skin. Crying out for water, Jesus is given vinegar to drink, raised up on hyssop, a bitter gall that could not quench His overwhelming thirst. The soldiers then parted His garments by lot: Matthew 27:34–35 They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink. And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots. The desperation and loneliness, the mental anguish Jesus suffered on the cross, He had also carried with Him for 33 years. Understanding the suffering that awaited Him at Calvary, knowing His anointed part in the great redemptive plan, while at all points being touched by the infirmity of the flesh, and tempted as we are. His prayers at Gethsemane, Son to the Father, that if it were possible to take this cup from Him, please let it be so. But steadfast to do the will of the Father, even knowing the physical and emotional pain He would endure. These stanzas in this psalm tragically capture it all, before transitioning to the joyful hope found in every tribulation those who love God can take comfort in: Romans 8:28 And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. Psalm 22 continues. The desperate plea of the condemned man, compassed by dogs, scorned and ridiculed, pierced and heartbroken, feeling abandoned by God, turns to a prayer of certain hope. We know God has delivered every promise He has made. He has heard the cries of His people and, in due season, saved them. We may persist in our prayers, reminding God, and ourselves, of His faithfulness, as we ask for more immediate relief. His perfect timing may not be ours, but at our weakest He shows His strength. Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns. From the proverbial horns of a dilemma, from the immediate threat, we call upon the name of the Lord. Not only the saved, His darling, but the lost often find His strength in their time of trial. Foxhole converts. The Potter often moves the clay in such a way, that we finally see our shortcomings and impotency, and need His hand to lift us up, that we may be what He has planned for us to become. If even Jesus Christ was to be made a reproach and murdered by bloody men in a wicked act, that we may know eternal life, as the risen and triumphant Son of God, then our trials are an opportunity to overcome by His power and to give the Lord the glory. I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee. In the midst of tribulation, we shall praise Him. That is the mind of a mature Christian. It is difficult to see, sometimes, and we may feel isolated, alone, but in our most desperate hour, we praise Him. We declare His holy name to our brethren, in the congregation we hold up His excellence. (It may not be a primary (or even secondary) application of this psalm, but it strikes me that we cannot lift up our voice in praise to the congregation, to declare His name unto the brethren, if we avoid church. If we forsake the assembly. Go to church!) Ye that fear the LORD, praise him; all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him; and fear him, all ye the seed of Israel. The praise and glory and fear of the Lord comes from knowledge of the doctrines of God. The understanding of His ways, the past performance of His promise, the teachings of the fathers through the inspired and preserved word of God. Faith cometh by hearing. In the midst of the congregation, among those that fear the Lord and sing His glory, blessing God and His holy name, we are not only given the opportunity to give testimony of what He has done for us, but hear what He has done for others. To learn doctrine and see that He has heard those who call out to Him. We can know, as Elijah on the mountain, alone, that there are a remnant of believers. Romans 11:3–4 Lord, they have killed thy prophets, and digged down thine altars; and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what saith the answer of God unto him? I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal. We have fellowship in our gatherings with the brethren. We have understanding from preaching and support of prayer, and the opportunity to worship God with those who have gone through what we have. To edify those going through things we have endured. Hebrews 10:23–25 Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;) And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching. That communal exhortation is invaluable to a believer in tribulation. Going through a personal trial. Hearing the victory Jesus has given others provides the strength to go on. To know the meek shall eat and be satisfied, seeking the Lord and finding Him, unto eternal life. John 6:35–37 And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst. But I said unto you, That ye also have seen me, and believe not. All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. This is the meat we eat, and are satisfied, never to hunger again. Complete in Christ, and having eternal life. The truth of this gospel goes out to the ends of the world. And every knee shall bow. For the kingdom is the LORD’s: and he is the governor among the nations. Ultimately, our hope rests on the truth that what God has promised to deliver, He will. And the present suffering pales in comparison for what will come. Romans 8:18 For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this. Our suffering is cause to praise the Lord to the brethren, to being others to the knowledge of Christ, to proclaim His power and promise, and to partake in the spreading of His gospel to all people, that every tongue shall confess that He hath done this. Amen

Psalm 23 is perhaps the second most famous passage of scripture, behind John 3:16, and like it, contains the gospel promise, the good news of the Lord towards believers. The world knows the Psalm because it has become the standard go to, in fiction and in real life, recited at funerals by priests and reverends, in every religion that claims the name of Christ. Sadly, for most, the departed have no idea that the promises are not automatic, and aren't achieved by their works, their character or how "good" they are. They are by faith in the Good Shepherd, alone. Of course, Jesus is that shepherd. John 10:11 I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. He gave His life that we may be forgiven, and rose again that we may have eternal life. He did this for those that follow Him, and who have been entrusted to Him by the Father. Believers are His flock. And because He is our shepherd, we shall not want. What an amazing promise, which God Who cannot lie has given us. We shall not want. He provides all things: Philippians 4:19 But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus. Not riches as this world judges, necessarily, but all our needs are met by Him by Christ Jesus. 2 Peter 1:3 According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue. You may feel financially burdened, or pressed by health concerns. You might be struggling in your faith, to live by trust in God to deliver. But ultimately, the truth is that all we need, everything that pertains to life and godliness, is given freely, that we may have life and more abundantly in His name. The green pastures and still waters are generally equated to Heaven in the way the world uses Psalm 23, and certainly, what little we know of Paradise is the peace of being in the presence of the Lord. But this stillness is a promise of this life, for a believer. Philippians 4:7 And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. Our burdens aren't removed, but the yoke of carrying them is made light by His grace. Because in the end, whatever we are going through will be for our good. Romans 8:28 And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. We are renewed in Him, and regenerated by the Spirit in faith, our soul restored. We are led in His ways, and shown the truth from His word, for His name's sake. In Jesus we are made whole, and by His power revealed in us, by His word, we are shown the deeper things of God. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. This allegory is considered death itself by the secular world, but note the imagery of a shadow. The Bible says a shadow is not the very image of the things that cast it. We may be in a low point in our lives, a valley, and maybe even feel the shadow of death on our flesh as we endure this season in our lives, but the strength to fear no evil, to glory in our tribulation, comes from knowing the good Shepherd is with us. His rod and staff, our comfort. The rod of correction, the staff that guides us as we go astray. His protection, our safety. Knowing He laid down His life for us. That He will seek and save His lost sheep, and bring us home by His power. What the unsaved world uses as a false comfort in death should be a comfort in this life for saved believers. The table He has set for us, the bounty of His blessings, the deliverance from those who seek to destroy us, that they may know we fear the Lord, and glorify Him, is in this life. In the presence of our enemies. Yes, there is the idea of a feast set for us in the end times prophecy, a wedding feast for the Bridegroom. Served by Christ Jesus: Isaiah 25:6 And in this mountain shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined. Luke 12:37 Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them. ...but the primary application in Psalm 23 is the peace found in this life. At this time. Our cup runneth over with His grace, even now. The table has been set in Heaven, but the bounty we are given starts the moment you call upon His name in faith. The final verse places this context firmly in the "now" of the believer: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever. Goodness and mercy follow us, today. We can rest assured that He has delivered us, and be blessed in this life, knowing we have eternity with Him in the next. We shall fear no evil, because we have eternal life and shall never perish. We will dwell in the house of the Lord forever, so rejoice even in perils and trials. Rest in the green pastures by the still waters. We have a good Shepherd Who loves us. Amen

Psalm 24 is a meditation on the truth of the Christ, the Lord, King of Hosts. Creator of all things, and the truth of the way of righteousness for those that trust in Him. The gospel message of the Psalms, sung in the Temple, performed by the chief musicians and the congregation is the inspired doctrines of God, and the focus is entirely Jesus. They may have looked through a glass darkly, but the concepts of Christ are hammered home, in verse after verse, chorus and stanzas of praise for the name of God, the Holy One, the Lord. Here in the 24th Psalm, David asks Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? Those with clean hands and pure hearts, who hasn't put their trust in vanity or lying lips, but who trusted the God of their salvation. He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation. We are made clean of our sins, our hearts purified by the imputed righteousness of God. We receive these blessings by grace through faith, and access to the Kingdom, not by our own righteousness but by submitting to the righteousness that is God's. Romans 4:5–8 But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. There are false religions that deny the imputation of righteousness by faith in Christ. They say that imputation is not taught in scripture. This is a lie. 2 Corinthians 5:21 For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Our righteousness is as a filthy rag, our works could never justify us before a holy and perfect God. But these men believing vanity, and swearing deceitfully, teach that man needs to establish their own righteousness through works of the law, and many are misled by this lie. Romans 10:2–4 For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. Roman Catholicism rejects the idea that we are made righteous by receiving righteousness from the God of our salvation. The Council of Trent (Canon 11 on Justification) anathematized the idea that people are justified “by the sole imputation of the justice of Christ, or by the sole remission of sins” and that righteousness is "infused" by works, sacraments and "grace transforming a person," so that their own righteousness is established, rather than submitting to the righteousness of God. But let God be true, and every man a liar. The generation of them that seek His face shall not be ashamed. All who come to the saving knowledge of Christ are made pure, in Him. Righteous, in Him. Titus 3:5–7 Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost; Which he shed on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour; That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life. The truth of imputed righteousness of God being given the believer is found throughout scripture. And thank God for His grace and mercy. That our sins are washed clean, justified by the blood, and remembered no more. The final verses of Psalm 24 are pure prophecy, the adoration and glory of the King. The opening of the gates to receive Him. The Lord strong and mighty. Who is the King of glory? We know His name is Jesus. King of kings, Lord of Hosts. The everlasting doors of the Kingdom of God open, and receive Him. All glory is given to Him. The Creator Who is blessed forever, amen.

The powerful prayer of Psalm 25 is a model for all that trust in the Lord, and a doctrinally-rich reminder of why we should. That we who wait on the Lord will not be ashamed. Verse after verse, the psalmist has us call upon the name of the Lord, as we read or sing through the Psalm. And verse after verse we are reminded of His mercy and faithfulness. We lift up our souls, every fiber of our being, unto the Lord, and He delivers us from our enemies. Those that trust in Him are never ashamed, but those that reject His truth are. We are shown His ways, taught His statutes, walk His paths, and we are preserved in this life, and established in the next. The meek and his seed shall inherit the earth, and in meekness we humbly admit our sins and ask for God's mercy, to forget them. His lovingkindness is established from old, and the God of our salvation keeps us by His power, unto redemption. What an amazing God we have. How can we not serve Him in truth. Truth of Who He is, who we are, and the reconciliation we have with and in Him, despite our sins. The Lord teaches sinners like us in His way, and the meek share this truth with the world. His secret, His covenant, is shown to us. And that good news is spread abroad by those that fear Him, that others may know the mystery of the gospel, and be saved. Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net. Proverbs 3:6 In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. Galatians 5:16 This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. Looking to Jesus the author and finisher of our salvation, we are lifted from the nets, the snares of sin set for us by the wicked. Walking in the Spirit. Acknowledging the ways of the Lord. With importunity and persistent prayer, we remind Him of the goodness He has shown us, and ourselves of the grace we have found in Him. Our troubles become lighter, as His yoke is easy. He brings us out of our distress. The pain we feel, He understands. The affliction that besets us is often due to sin. Seeking forgiveness, because our troubles may be chastening by a loving Father. Getting right so we may be lifted up by Him. Delivered, because we put our trust in Him. Never ashamed, because His word is true. Waiting on the day of the Lord, and the redemption of all Israel. All His people who trusted in the Lord. Amen In the original Hebrew, David used the format of an "alphabetic acrostic psalm," where stanzas begin with consecutive letters, to act as an mnemonic device, and form of poetry, that David uses multiple times in Psalms. This stylized form of writing is "lost" in translation, some textual critics may say, but the strained gnat of it all makes them miss the power of what we have in English. The repeated calls to trust the Lord, seek forgiveness, humbly petition and wait with patience is all beautifully expressed in Psalm 25 as we read it here. The prose of the Authorized English loses nothing to the power of God's word. So, while it is interesting to note the format, and discuss the ways it was used (here, imperfectly with missing and skipped letters) it isn't necessary for the truth to prick our hearts and give us comfort. However, recognizing Psalm 25 as an attempted alphabetic acrostic in the original Hebrew, intended to run through the 22 letters of the alphabet, does give us the opportunity to see something of ourselves in it. In this Psalm, the alphabetic pattern is incomplete, the letter vav is missing, resh appears twice, and the final verse falls outside the sequence. The broken acrostic still carries the psalm’s prayer, and focuses on the Lord's mercy and power. Could the broken format look to the broken-hearted sinner, imperfectly calling upon a perfect God? Could it be that by breaking the expected format, David shows the same brokenness of spirit we have in this life as we wait upon the redemption of Christ in the end? I don't know. But it sounds good. Selah.

Matthew 7:1–2 Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again. Jesus' words are often twisted by others to mean a Christian should never judge another person, no matter how wicked they are or what sins they do. But, we know the warning is against hypocrisy, not right judgment. Psalm 26 gives us a picture of what Jesus is actually teaching, where David asks the Lord to judge him by his doings, according to his faith, in comparison to the wicked around him. The understanding of proper judgement is key to good Christian living. It allows us to be separated, to be holy as God is holy, to put away the filth of the flesh and walk in the Spirit. To seek to be a disciplined servant of the Lord. We walk in integrity, and trust in the Lord alone, that we shall not slide. Firmly on His rock, not backsliding to live as the world does. It is not an automatic transformation. We are sanctified by the Spirit by the inward man, the new man, but our flesh is still prone to lusts of the eyes and the pride of life and we can stumble and fall. But if we seek the judgment of God, asking Him to try us and see that our heart is right, we are opening ourselves to correction and refinement, to better be used by God. Walking in His truth, keeping ourselves pure and humble, seeing others in the way God does, with grace and mercy and lovingkindness, we can make our case to the Lord, and compare ourselves to the wicked without the leaven of the Pharisees, hypocrisy. David lists the things he has not done, to separate himself towards God. He has not sat with vain persons, false believers. He has not had ecumenical fellowship with the dissemblers, the false prophets who teach lies. He has avoided the congregation of evil doers. The bitter fruit of the false religions of this world. He has not yoked with unbelievers. Instead, knowing he is innocent of these things, and sanctified, he is able to come before the altar of the Lord. To gather with the assembly of God's people. To walk into church without the burden of unresolved sin, with a good conscience towards God. He doesn't do this to be haughty, or to puff up himself in comparison to the wicked, but that he may proclaim the goodness of the Lord in the midst of the congregation, without hypocrisy. Meekly seeking God's judgment in our lives that we may be a better testimony is a good thing. Judgment that leads to repentance and forgiveness of others, that we may love the habitation of His house, that we may know how to behave in the church, as a pillar and foundation of truth, is a good thing. Asking the Lord to remember us, that we aren't caught up in His judgment of the wicked, but rather walk in our integrity, waiting for His redemption out of His wrath, seeking His mercy in our obedience. My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the LORD. This should be our guiding principle. To rightly judge, beginning with ourselves that we may purge ourselves, be separated unto the Lord that we may boldly proclaim His mercy and bless the Lord in the congregation. Amen. Fundamentally, Psalm 26 is an encouragement to purify ourselves and avoid hypocrisy while recognizing the evil of men, that we may go into the assembly sanctified. But this also presupposes that we are to go into the assembly. That we are not to forsake the assembly. That we go to church! We have an obligation to bless the Lord among the brethren. To gather and sing praises towards Him. Because He has judged us, found us wanting, and yet while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. That in God's lovingkindness, He made provisions of grace to redeem and reconcile us. For this we should want to sing His praises. But often, if we don't allow God judgment willingly, if we don't purify ourselves, if we gather with dissemblers, and allow our own hearts to mislead us, and justify ourselves despite our sin, we may find ourselves forsaking the assembly, not going in to the congregation, skipping church. Our conscience may be pricked, and there will be preaching against sin. It is easier to backslide when you do. And the feedback loop compounds, until you are among the vain persons. If you don't willfully seek the judgment of God in your life, He will still judge you. And in a backslidden state, a Christian can be caught up with the bloody men, and lose their life. Not their eternal life, certainly, but cut short in this one. Seeking to avoid the refiner's fire of God's judgment can result in far greater pain and loss in His chastening than in the embarrassment and humbling of ourselves when we get right and submit ourselves to His ways. Be ready daily to submit to His judgment. His mercies are new each morning. It's never too late to get right while you're on this side of Heaven. Allow God to judge your walk, and stand in your integrity, that you may enter gleefully into the congregation. That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works.

Psalm 27 continues the pattern of praise for the salvation found in the Lord, by faith. The Lord is our light and salvation. Jesus is the way, the truth and the light. We who have trusted in Him, are kept by the power of God unto salvation. What do we have to fear from men? Luke 12:4–5 And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him. The wicked who may seek your life cannot do anything but threaten you with Heaven. Whatever battle we face, we are already on the winning side. All in Christ have overcome this world. We can be confident in this, unto death. And praise God we aren't in a time where we face constant war and battles. That our greatest fight is spiritual. And against our own flesh. But there are those in the mission field, in countries where you can be beaten, imprisoned and killed for the cause of Christ. Meek and humble men and women who do great things for the Lord, daily. Winning souls and spreading the word of God in the face of persecution, without fear. Many Christians today won't even venture into safe suburban neighborhoods once a week to do the same. Often, out of fear. The fear of being a peculiar person. Of being socially rejected for the audacity of preaching Jesus to strangers. Of the "danger" of someone mocking you, or shutting the door in your face. David believed, and it was sufficient to face legions of enemies. To face a giant with a sling. Missionaries and their converts face arrest and imprisonment, beatings and death. American Christians wear "Faith Over Fear" graphic tees to the gym and think they are making a bold stand for Christ. We should be boldly proclaiming the trust we have in a mighty God and the reward He has promised through the Son. Though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident. Continuing Psalm 27, after establishing the faith on which he stands, and the confidence he has on the promises of God, David as psalmist cries out to the Lord for His mercy, to hear his prayer. As these are meant to be sung or said, as model prayers or devotional worship, we are called to do the same. To call upon the mercy of the Lord. To bless His longsuffering and grace towards us, and petition the Lord with prayer. Hebrews 11:6 But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. When we seek the Lord, it is obedience to His command to seek His face. To search for Him. As individuals and as a nation of believers. 2 Chronicles 7:14 If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land. Seek and ye shall find, the Bible says. Our God is merciful to hear our prayers and to reward those that in faith, have sought Him out. What a humbling and amazing thing to be considered worthy of attention by our Creator. David continues, meekly asking for forgiveness if there are any transgressions that may have displeased the Lord. Asking for His favor, to not forsake us in times of trouble, yet having the understanding that our trouble may be due to our own unresolved sin. Either way, O God of our salvation, hear our prayers. In the very next breath, David affirms the steadfast faithfulness of the Lord, that even if our own parents forsake us, He remains true. Expressing fear and doubt while recognizing the truth of the promises of God is a human thing, and we see this play out on our own minds, even as it does David's. We are a weak and needy people, and we need God involved in every aspect of our lives. Remember this, and be open to His teaching. Be open to hearing His voice in scripture, recognizing the chastening in our life, seeing His mercy towards us, and wrath revealed from Heaven, and fearing Him, always. He shows us the path.
