There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness. There is a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up. There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men. Many are always quick to apply this to "kids today," or to Baby Boomers, and arguments can be made to support this, but it's a mistake to isolate this as purely prophetic of specific cohorts united only by age, and attribute to them all these evils. The generation is always with us. There IS a generation like this, the Bible says. There are always evil people, who curse their father and do not bless their mother. Who reject the instruction of their parents and do not honor them. Disobedient to parents. There are always segments of the population who are pure in their own eyes, justifying the filth of their flesh and the lust in their hearts. There are always prideful and arrogant people, who see themselves as above the righteous, while they live in the gutter. Who reject the ways of the Lord, to walk the paths of folly. People who use words as weapons, inventors of evil, who use and exploitation and extortion, usury and inequity to destroy others. There are always reprobates among us. Romans 1:29-32 Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers, Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents, Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful: Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them. Proverbs 30:15-16 The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough:The grave; and the barren womb; the earth that is not filled with water; and the fire that saith not, It is enough. The proverb compares a bloodsucking leach, whose daughters cry "give, give," never satisfied, implacable, always wanting more, to four things in life; the grave (death), a barren womb, dry earth, and consuming fire. Death is inevitable, and decay and entropy the nature of the fallen world. There's always more graves needed, as there is always death. A barren womb is filled with the desperation of the woman, and never satisfied. Waters flood the dry earth, and still it will absorb it, and not be full. And fire cannot be quenched so long as there's something to consume. V17 The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it. This curse against disobedient and dishonorable children shows the spiritual blindness that comes inevitably to those that will not honor their parents. v18-19 Agur compares the seemingly random ways of an eagle soaring in the winds, a serpent moving upon a rock, and a ship cast to and fro on the sea to the understanding of a man with a woman. A beautiful picture of the ebbs and flows, the listing and sway of nature, to the romance and subtle grace of a man with a maid. Verse 20 tells us of the false justification that adulterous women delude themselves with. As someone cleans their mouth from eating, they think they can dismiss their sin with a hand wave. Rationalizing it away. v21-23 presents another "3 things/even 4" formula, this list of things that the earth is disquieted by, things that just aren't right; a servant put in charge, a fool who is filled with meat, an odious woman when she is married, and a handmaid that is heir to her mistress. The general idea is that all four lead to the person to think more highly of themselves than they ought to. It gives a false confidence to them that is troublesome to others. A servant put in a position of power they haven't earned, a maid given the inheritance of the household she served, a full fool who thinks he deserved the bounty he's received (and that it will continue), and an odious, obnoxious woman who has managed to find a husband just as she is. v24-28, another list of four. This time observation of animals and the wisdom that they provide; despite their relative weakness to man, ants still prepare for winter, storing their food in the summer. Foresight and patience, diligence and delaying gratification. The conies, the Syrian hyrax, a small, rabbit-like mammal found in Africa and the Middle East, often called rock badgers, are small, defenseless but place their dens in the rock of the mountainside. They wisely seek shelter that protects them. (There are spiritual applications to this as well, both the believer taking refuge in the Rock, Christ Jesus, and the sinners asking the rocks to fall on them to try to avoid the wrath of God). The locust swarm moves together as an army, without any king directing them. They work together. Cooperative achievement. The tiny spider weaving its way into palaces, a reminder that diligence can bring even the weak to places of strength. v29-31, yet another list of 3/4; the opposite of v21-23, which were disturbing things. This list are pleasant to the observer. A strong lion that fears no one, a greyhound's speed, and a goats agility, are all like a king who is secure in his throne. Untouchable. v32 reminds us of we've done foolishly, lifting ourselves up in undeserved and even embarrassing shows of pride, or has thoughts of evil, intrusive or perhaps something we've ruminated in but caught ourselves, lay your hand over your mouth. Be silent and humble yourself. Don't dig the hole deeper with words that betray your foolish thoughts. Finally, v33 warns against anger leading to strife. Stirring up milk to butter, or a punch in the nose brings blood, forcing your wrath will cause conflict.

The final chapter of Proverbs, attributed to the mother of King Lemuel, which is considered a pseudonym or pet name for King Solomon (meaning "devoted to God"), and possibly what Bathsheba called her son. This wisdom is a mother's, and as impactful as any given by a father. As we know, we should not forsake the law, or instruction of our parents. Proverbs 1:8-9 My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother: For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck. And so here, we are privy to some of the sayings given a king by his mother. It begins with the loving devotion a mother has for her son, born of her womb, the fruit of her vows. A special relationship that fathers are blessed to witness and to share with their own mother, unique in the bond shared. Regardless of her identity, or his, we have the Spirit inspired wisdom given to us. Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings. Women and being given to many wives were not just problems Solomon carried, but they were a downfall for his father David, as well. King David had eight named wives and an unspecified number of additional wives and concubines taken after he moved from Hebron to Jerusalem. Michal, his first, King Saul's daughter, who became bitter against him and had no children by him. Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, mother of Absalom, the son who rebelled against David, and of their daughter, Tamar. Ahinoam, the Jezreelitess, mother of Amnon, whose rape of his half-sister Tamar led Absalom to be bitter against David. During the rebellion of Absalom, he "went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel" on the roof of the palace, using them to humiliate David, and to make his claim to the throne through them. David's lust for Bathsheba, which led to the murder of Uriah the Hittite, her husband, the death of David's first son with her, as punishment from the Lord. All these things, and more, made David a bloody man, whose life was filled with strife and death. Thus, despite his desire to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, he was told he would not be allowed to; 1 Chronicles 22:8 But the word of the Lord came to me, saying, Thou hast shed blood abundantly, and hast made great wars: thou shalt not build an house unto my name, because thou hast shed much blood upon the earth in my sight. Bathsheba, having been witness to all these things, may well have imparted this wisdom of experience to her Lemuel. To her second son and living heir of David, in hopes that he would not forsake the law of his mother, and suffer the same as her husband. But in the end, we all fall short of the glory of God. Solomon was given the blessing of God to build the temple, which David had provisioned for. But his heart was not always right with God, for he gave his strength to women, and his ways to that which destroyeth kings. Continuing; Of the things that destroyeth kings, given as the law of a mother to her son; Alcohol. It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink. This should be the end of the matter for saved believers. We are princes and heirs, co-heirs with Christ. We rule in the matters God has given us in this life, we are to rule the world with Him in the next. It is not for us to drink wine or strong drink. The only allowance for drinking alcohol is medicinally, for the perishing. For the dying. And for those with no hope, for the miserable. But we have the hope of Jesus. We are poor in spirit, and content with whatever state we are in. Those without, who don't know Christ, they drink to forget. God's word warns us that forgetfulness that comes from a drunken stupor leads to forgetting the law and perverting judgment. It is unbecoming of the princes of God to drink. We've been instructed to not even look upon it; Proverbs 23:31-33 Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder. Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things. Without getting into the cope many professing Christians use to justify their drinking; that Jesus led the wedding party in Canna to drunkenness, giving them that had already been well-drunk to further drunkenness. Or that He used alcoholic wine at the last supper, rather than juice of the vine, new, as Jesus describes, or the various means of preparation and preservation used in ancient times to keep unfermented and low-fermented juice, watered down for consumption; the plain meaning of the text is undeniable. We may have liberty in Christ, and all things may be lawful, but all things do not edify. All things are not convenient. We should strive to be men of God, blameless. 1 Timothy 3:2-4 A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous; One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity. These standards for the pastors of a church exist to be the example for all young men. And women as well, Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. This is a true saying, if a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. We should all desire to be overseers and stewards of God's ministry of reconciliation that He has given us. Princes of the Kingdom. That means not being inebriated and forgetting the law. Not being led away by strange women in our alcoholic haze. Not uttering perverse things. Certainly not profaning Christ Jesus to justify our sinful habits. Vs 8-9 Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy. The call to be a voice for the condemned without a voice, for the poor and needy, is the way of Kings and pleasing to God. Jesus, appearing before the judgment spoke not at all. Matthew 27:12-14 And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then said Pilate unto him, Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee? And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly. Jesus, appointed for destruction and mute to give His cause, directly exemplifies this saying. While Pilate could be excused for not knowing the proverbs (or the prophecy; Isaiah 53:7 He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.) Herod, King of the Jews, and the priests and scribes should have. Luke 23:8-9 And when Herod saw Jesus, he was exceeding glad: for he was desirous to see him of a long season, because he had heard many things of him; and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him. Then he questioned with him in many words; but he answered him nothing. A fit ruler should speak for the condemned, to ensure justice. To consider the judgment. To plead the cause of those brought before them by the powerful, to ensure the poor and powerless aren't being falsely accused. The knowledge given to Lemuel by his mother was certainly heard by those princes of Judea, by their King, and ignored. What should have convicted them in the heart, witnessing Jesus, silent before them, instead was an indictment, that they had no excuse. One thing that we see again and again in Proverbs is a call for God's justice. Righteous judgment. Equity for the poor and oppressed. These are Christian virtues and values. But when a Christian Nation abandons them, when they hold vengeance and disdain for the poor as respecters of persons, then these ideas are hijacked by those seeking to defend the guilty. They are used as rhetorical cover for perverting Justice, by those who call evil good and good evil. Right judgment doesn't mean weak judgment. Or lack of judgment. We should consider the poor with the understanding that it's often sin that brings them to poverty. That we should provide the opportunity for gleaning our fields. To be generous and hospitable, while maintaining the biblical truth; that if any would not work, neither should he eat. We should plead for the fatherless, explicitly standing against the causes of fatherlessness, such as fornication and adultery and divorce. Feeding and clothing the needy is an opportunity to do unto them and by doing so, doing it unto God. What we do to the least of our brothers, we are doing to the Lord. Therefore, it should be personal and local. Acts of charity and alms done discreetly, or by our churches. Not given off to the government to do for us. Biblical Christianity, not "social justice." Ruth 3:10-11 And he said, Blessed be thou of the Lord, my daughter: for thou hast shewed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning, inasmuch as thou followedst not young men, whether poor or rich. And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman. Proverbs 31:10 asks the rhetorical question; Who can find a virtuous woman? Boaz, in the story of Ruth certainly does. A wife is a gift of God. Proverbs 18:22 Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the Lord. A virtuous wife? Their price is far above rubies. More valuable than gold. A gift from God Proverbs has instructed women not to be contentious, loud, not striving with their husbands. Not driving their man to the corner of the rooftop, or out into the wilderness by being a nagging continuous dropping, like heavy rain. But here, in the final chapter of the sayings of Lemuel's mother, we find God's ideal for a woman. She is trustworthy, that her husband never has to worry about adultery. He can safely trust she won't be spoiled by another. She does him good and not evil, every day. She is diligent in her ways, seeking materials and food for her family, working with what she's given to provide for them. Rising early, while it's still dark to cook for them. A hard worker, who manages a household, starts small businesses, buys land, makes it fruitful and profitable by the strength of her arms. She uses her talents to supplement the household income, selling her wares, knowing her own family is taken care of first, seeing them clothed against winter. She helps the poor, is generous and hospitable. 1 Timothy 3:11 Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Like the pastor's wife, her temperance and chaste behavior is a crown for her husband, increasing his reputation, not shaming him. The work of her hands is valued and valuable. She is known by her strength and honor. Her patient attention to these virtues ensure her long-term joy. She speaks wisdom and kindness. A blessing to those that hear her. Her children learn her law and the fear of God at her feet. She isn't lazy, or idle. Paul warns against this tendency in young widows, but it applies to far too many wives; 1 Timothy 5:13 And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not. This is in stark contrast with the hard working, wise and kind virtuous woman. Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her. Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all. The mother and wife who is the joy of her children and husband doesn't become this way by accident or by virtue of being married and having children, but by her following the way of the Lord in all things. Favor is deceitful; by vain words and flattery, she may seem to be virtuous, because of her beauty in her youth, be attractive and alluring. But these things don't last. But a woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised. Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates. Allow a virtuous woman to be rewarded for her enterprise and let her be praised among men for her value. Proverbs 19:14 House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the LORD.

Following Proverbs, the collected wise sayings and instructions of Solomon, the wisest man in history, we have Ecclesiastes, the preaching of the King that collects his life observations that fortified that wisdom. Solomon identifies himself as the author, and the thesis of his sermon is given in the 2nd verse. Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. I picture Solomon preaching this to the court, or perhaps the congregation from his eponymous porch, located at the Temple he had built. A crowd convicted by his words, and the Spirit behind them. Shouts of "Amen!" throughout. King Solomon's reign is traditionally dated to the 10th century BC, 4-500 years before Greek and ancient Chinese philosophy is recorded, and this extended sermon on the vanity of life, (and its ultimate purpose), is clearer, and more wise than all of the vain philosophy of men put together. The preacher asks, What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun? Men die. Men are born. The earth abides. The sun rises and sets. The wind comes and goes, from the North and the South, changing with the seasons. Everything runs in these cycles, he says. The rivers run to the sea, yet the sea is never filled. The water, returning to the place where the rivers come from. (This understanding of the water cycle predates scientific explanation of it by nearly 2,500 years. The sharpest Greek minds thought there were springs underground, carrying the water back to the source.) All is vanity. All things are full of labor, work is never done. The eye doesn't stop seeing, ear hearing. The senses never are filled. The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: Nothing ever happens. All things have already been, and things that will be have already been. A truth that even the secular world will cite; There is no new thing under the sun. Every "new" thing a man discovers was old, and done before. We forget, and rediscover. Things we discovered will be forgotten. The cycle will continue. And so, Solomon, the Preacher, as King of Israel sought out the wisdom of all things done under Heaven. The sore travail God has given to men in this life. Having established there is nothing new under the sun, nor will there ever be, and having observed all these things, he came to a conclusion; ...all is vanity and vexation of spirit. That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered. The travails of life are fed by this truth. And so, all is vanity. Solomon says, he gave his full heart to experience all things, to feed the wisdom God gave him, to increase his knowledge more than any man before him. And I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also is vexation of spirit. He says that even this quest to know all things is vanity, since all things that can be known are part of this endless cycle, that ran before he ever came, and continues now, long after he departed the earth. And this has brought him much grief; he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow. Now, we are called to pursue wisdom, to gain understanding, to know the ways of the Lord and to follow His paths, rather than following after folly. But the accumulation of much knowledge of the things of this world, in the eyes of finite man, the entropy and atrophy of a fallen world, and endless labor, only to die; increases our sorrow. The seeming futility of it all, reinforced by observation. A feeling even the simple who has noticed life in their limited experience can relate to. The opening of the sermon as a depressing hook that captures that feeling of vexation, which Solomon will use to bring us to the truth.

Psalm 51:12-15 Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; And uphold me with thy free spirit. Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; And sinners shall be converted unto thee. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: And my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness. O Lord, open thou my lips; And my mouth shall shew forth thy praise. Proverbs 3:13 Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding. Proverbs 2:6 For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding. James 3 But if ye have bitter envying and strife in your hearts, glory not, and lie not against the truth. This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish. For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. John 14:26 But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you. 1 Corinthians 1 20 Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? 21 For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe. 22 For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: 23 But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; 24 But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. 25 Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men. 26 For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: 27 But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; 28 And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are: 29 That no flesh should glory in his presence. 30 But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: 31 That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. The things of this world are vanity and vexation. The wisdom of this world is foolishness. But the joy of our salvation and the praise of God's name is joy, and the knowledge given each of us who is saved, by measure of the Holy Spirit, is wisdom and life. Foolishness to the wisdom of this world, but righteousness and power unto salvation for those who believe. Rejoice then, and glory in the Lord So, heading towards Easter I plan on picking up Luke, to finish off the Gospels and pretty much the entire NT. We are almost there, and God willing we will be by then. But over the next week or so, I am going to try and go through several doctrines in light of the Bible with the intention of providing insight and uplifting application of God's word. See where it takes us. Today, the wisdom of man and the vain things of this world that bring vexation vs the wisdom of God and the joy it brings for those who believe. I pray that it helps build my own faith and understanding and that others get something out of it in the process. The despondency of the natural man is manifest in how we react to the wisdom of this world. To the toil and drudgery that is a life without meaning. The same folly that our fathers endured and that our children will face. The wickedness and sin throughout the world. Evil called good and good, evil. The weakness of others and the burdens they become on our shoulders. A yoke that leads to bitterness, resentment, wrath, covetousness and a host of other sins and the vices that we take up to fill the time and dull the pain. Even a "good man" has their patience stretched thin and feels the despair more acutely it seems. But then there's the wisdom of God, which makes the weak strong and brings forth the truth of the things the world hates to bring to nought that which they love. And the foolishness of the Gospel is the power unto salvation. That God became man, dwelled among us, sinless, to do the will of God unto death that we who deserve Hell are made righteous in His blood. And the resurrection of Christ giving us the hope of our faith, that we have eternal life through the grace and mercy of God the Father. And by that faith, we are given wisdom and knowledge and strength. The power of sanctification and redemption in the day of judgment that all men are appointed to. And so, we rejoice. We rejoice in tribulation knowing we have triumphed. We give glory to God in suffering and in blessings. We patiently wait for His return, while being a light to those still in darkness. If you're not 100% certain, today, right now, that if you died today you would go to Heaven. If you're scared and alone and feel hopeless. If you're carrying guilt and trauma and regrets that are tearing you up inside. If you're seeking answers and wisdom, but only finding despair and vexation. If you're struggling to find an identity, a place in a world that makes no sense to you at times. If you have been laboring to be righteous, to cleanse your sins by your own works, and frustrated with how fruitless it is to obtain righteousness on your own, please consider this presentation of the Bible way to Heaven. You don't have to carry the burden. Jesus already has done it for you. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

In Ecclesiastes 1, Solomon established his underlying idea, that all of life is vain, meaningless, full of travails, trials and hardships, that every life is full of tribulation, a cycle of never-ending labor. Now, the preacher begins to expound. He starts chapter 2 by explaining how he, to test all things, gave in to the pleasures of the heart; mirth, laughter. Wine and merrymaking. Partying, as we would say today. And he found it wanting. He continued in wisdom, while allowing himself folly, testing all things to see what was good that man should do. A scientific approach that rationalizes sin in the name of gained knowledge. Solomon, a King gifted with supernatural wisdom sought pleasures for a season, to prove wisdom. Yet, this approach to life is honestly all too typical for man. We sow our wild oats. We all have our time of life where we question the wisdom of our parents, the law and ways of God, the judgment of our conscience, to see what good can be found in the ways of the world. And, for most of us, we grow out of it. God's chastening and the reality of the wages of sin, bringing us back from folly, to see these things as vain. Ineffectual and worthless. Wisdom teaches better, but folly is doing what you know you shouldn't, and expecting a better result than doing the right thing. Reality is a harsh tutor, and when it comes to the party lifestyle, you don't have to be the wisest man ever to live to see it is folly. Yet many fools continue to chase after mirth, drunken merrymaking, long after it has cost them everything and brutally affected the lives of those around them. Solomon then talks of the great works he undertook, to redeem the time in more constructive ways. Building houses, planting vineyards, gardens and orchards and every kind of budding fruit trees. He made pools of water to irrigate his great gardens. He had many servants, even generational, born in his house, all to staff his households and agricultural enterprises. He owned much cattle, great and small, livestock more than any other before him. The accumulation of wealth, the peculiar treasures of kings, unique offerings and crafts made of precious stones. He gathered unto himself silver and gold in abundance. The description of Solomon's possessions, the magnitude of his wealth, seem at first blush to be beyond our ability to understand or relate to. But, within these pursuits we should find familiarity. We all seek to build out our home. We plant our gardens, both literally and metaphorically, utilizing what we have to build something more. We all have projects and plans we devote time and resources to. We may lack servants and palaces and peculiar riches, but we all strive to have more. Solomon used his position to have multiple singers, male and female, musicians and the delight of music to entertain him. Again, we may see this and think, "he is a king, of course he can command this, I can't relate." But today, even the most poor among us has instant access to the greatest singers and musicians of the past century, to listen to the delights of the sons of men greater than even Solomon at his height could ever hear. The Preacher says So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me. And in that wisdom, these pursuits, as cyclical and vain as they were, did produce joy. He says he withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour. The brief moments of joy all of this brought him, he considered his reward. But, beyond the temporary rejoicing, he perceived the underlying problem; death. Looking at all he worked for, all he gained, and the fruit of that labor, and he sees the same end as the mirth and laughter. ...behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun. All the things that man could do, under the Sun, had been done before. Even by a King who could do more, and more abundantly than any other man, and it was all in vain, without lasting meaning. Even his son, Rehoboam would be unable to achieve anything new; Solomon had exhausted the most extreme versions of all that existed and was known to man under the Sun. But his wisdom remained; Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness. The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all. Death. The end comes for the fool and the wise alike. And the depressingg notion came to him, thinking, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity. What good is wisdom, if like the pleasures and labors of life, it all ends in vanity? What good is the pursuit of discernment and knowledge, to know the ways of the world and gather wisdom from experiencing all that life has to offer, if in the end it dies with you, as the folly of a fool dies with him? If this is all that life has, if the meaning of it is to toil, travail, and then die, then all is vanity and vexation of spirit. Solomon says he hated the vanity of life, hated all his worthless labor, which in the end would be left to an heir who may or may not value it, who may or may not be wise, or a fool, and squander whatever inheritance there may be. The projects and planning and pleasures, and treasure and toil, all are vanity. The works of wisdom and in knowledge and equity, fair dealings and not being a respecter of persons, the wisdom we saw again and again in Proverbs, is the same portion as those that did not pursue wisdom. This also is vanity and a great evil. If our labor is in vain, and the days full of sorrows, and our works and plans lead to sleepless nights and grief, leaving behind little lasting legacy, what is the point? There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This is a repeated idea throughout Ecclesiastes, and in Scripture; if all is vanity, and nothing matters, better to eat, drink and be merry. Isaiah 22:13 And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die. As Jesus says of the rich man, who like Solomon had stored up riches; Luke 12:16-19 And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully: And he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. If the only reward that man may have for all our toil in this life, for worldly things, is the brief joy that comes from resting in the fruit of our labor, then perhaps, Solomon reasons, this is something to offset the vexation, the depression that comes from seeing all things as vanity. The wisdom of Solomon gives us the first glimpse of hope and purpose; This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God. The gift of those moments where we enjoy the good of our labors, is from God. For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy. The virtue of wisdom and walking in the ways of the Lord is superior to the ways of the fool, the sinner, who has greater travails and endless labor as their reward, which is again vain and vexing. At the first mention of God in this sermon, we can start to see a glimpse into the everlasting. To see life's meaning and purpose. If the fool labors more, heaping up and gathering what the wise will ultimately gain, to be given to him that is good before God (as echoed in Proverbs 13:22 A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.) and not enjoying the God given gifts of their labor, then all their efforts are vain. The Preacher is building a case, and the answer to vanity and vexation of spirit, and we see here the first hint of what the answer is, by the grace of God towards the just.

To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven. This biblical truth has influenced all of mankind. Even those that reject the word of God accept this philosophy of time and discernment as wisdom. Solomon the Preacher has been making the case of futility in life. That the cyclical nature of things, the endless travails, trials and tribulation man goes through, only to die and be forgotten, regardless of how he lives, is vanity and vexation of spirit. In Ecclesiastes 2, he drew a distinction, the first glimmer of hope, by the acknowledgement that the fruit of our labors, the food and drink God blesses man with, is good. That the treasure the wicked heap up for themselves is destined for the righteous. Here, in chapter 3, Solomon continues the sermon, opening with the understanding that there are appropriate times for everything, seasons of life; birth and death. Sowing and reaping. Killing and healing. Destruction and construction. Life has moments of joy and despair. Hatred and forgiveness. Economic ups and downs. Purging and gathering. War and peace. To everything, in its season, to every purpose, in every life, these truths apply. And the wisdom of knowing what season you're in, or observing their change, and doing the appropriate thing, is discernment. Having the understanding that in the midst of triumph, there are seeds of destruction, and in mourning, joy, is a gift of God. But, again, life is a cycle. These things are necessary, but they too are vanity. What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboureth? What's the point of all this labor and toil? The empty exercise of taking land that turns back again to wilderness, the things built up and eventually torn down. The embrace that ends in rejection. The shortsighted nature of man, with the world in our heart, makes us unable to know the beginning from the end as God does. So our labors match the fleeting vapor which is our life. If the only blessing to all of it is to enjoy the fruits of your labor, the sustenance and riches, our families and relationships, to eat and drink what we have tilled and toiled, then man should enjoy this good. It is the gift of God. There are generations and nations where the labor of man is more fruitless, and life is brutal and short. If God has blessed you with food and raiment, peace, a time to dance, a time to love, enjoy it, knowing that it is from God. I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth it, that men should fear before him. Solomon is again hinting at the purpose of the cycle of life. That the same God that blesses us, and punishes the wicked, has a purpose that we cannot fathom. His ways are eternal, ours worldly and come to an end. Hebrews 9:27 And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment... And while, under the sun, in our fallen world, the seats of judgment and the places of righteousness may have wickedness and iniquity, God's judgment is just, and it is coming on everyone. Because there is a time for every purpose and for every work. Solomon says that the manifestation of our status before God, the reality of our limited consciousness, is as the lowly beast, the creatures of creation. We live and breathe. We fall and die. We die as they die. From dust, we are formed. To dust we return. In the end we are appointed to the same end as the beasts. In the end, the life of man is vanity. Other than the brief joy we get as the gift of God. This is the subtle difference between beast and man; we are given the ability to rejoice in the portion He has provided us, in this life. So, Solomon concludes we should eat, drink and be merry, for who can show us what should come after? Although the conclusion that we are temporal beings, gifted with the fruit of our toil by the eternal Lord, we see more glimpses of something more. The sure divine judgment, in due time. The spirit of man, ascending. Perhaps all is not vain.

The chapter opens with an observation of the oppressed and the oppressors. Solomon the Preacher says he began to consider oppression, and noted that despite the tears of the oppressed, they have no comforter. They cry alone in their tribulation. But, he also takes notice that the oppressors, despite their power, also lack a comforter. That, since all of life is travail, and the endless work, vanity, there is no difference between the oppressed and their oppressor, fundamentally. They lack a comforter, someone to share the burden and lift them up against the vexation of spirit, of being ground down by the cycle of life. Yet, Jesus has promised us all a Comforter. John 14:16-20 And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you. Yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also. At that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you. With Christ, we are never alone. We are never without God. We have this blessed assurance and indwelling of the Spirit, as temples of God. But, the Preacher is preaching to the world, who do not know the good news, and in a time when the Holy Spirit only came upon man for a brief time to do the works of God through them. And so, to the world he declared it is better for the dead than the living, because it is better to be free from the lonely vexation of the troubles and tribulations of the world. Where the right works of one man lead his neighbor to covet the results of a man's travail, but it is all vanity. The fool foldeth his hands, the same sluggard analogy from Solomon's Proverbs, and in their laziness, they eat their own flesh, they destroy themselves. Better to have little and have peace, than much from vain works and the vexation of spirit that comes with it. This is not prescriptive, but descriptive. If the works of life are almost meaningless, except the brief moments of joy from the fruit of the labor, then why strive for more? Solomon is building a case of hope, by challenging the futility of the worldly outlook of life. He turns his attention to the empty works of toiling without an heir. Neither son nor brother. For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail. He proclaims the truth that two, working together, are better than one. They have more reward for their labor, lifting one another up as they go. Again, as we with the Comforter can attest, those in Christ never walk alone. But for man, striving to toil under the Sun, it is better to do so with others. Solomon compares it to the difference between sleeping alone and cold in the night, and the warmth of shared body heat by being with another. Alone, we feel the biting cold, but together, somehow, our combined body heat is a comfort to the cold. That together, if in a one on one fight, you may lose, with another, you win. If two attack, you can withstand them. If three, by two you can hold them off for a while. The importance of having another to share the load is the point, and again this points to Jesus, Who not only helps shoulder the load, but bears it all on Himself. He carries us in Him, and gives us rest. And nothing shall overcome us. Isaiah 46:4 And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you Matthew 11:28 Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. The chapter finishes with a rumination on rulers and kings. That a poor but wise child is in a better position than an old, foolish King. They may rise up from obscurity, as David, Solomon's father had, and take the throne, while the old, foolish King becomes poor, removed from power as was Saul. All the living go to support the second child, the new King, and they will also rejoice in the ruler who comes after the new King. This cycle of leadership, this too is vain and vexing. This week in heresy: we have evangelicals learning the lesson of the reprobate doctrine. We have orthos putting sainthood on a reprobate who taught ridiculous false doctrine and damnable heresies. We have an ortho claiming in a debate that the Bible is not divine. Now we are having people deny Jesus went to hell, for 3 days and three nights and a resurgence of the idiotic Abraham's bosom heresy. And it's only Wednesday!

Ecclesiastes 5 sees a brief detour in the sermon, a rabbit trail of wisdom stemming from Solomon's preaching. Verse 1 is an oft-quoted favorite of pastors; a reminder to take church seriously, to come to hear and learn in the house of God, which Paul tells Timothy in 1 Timothy 3:15, is the pillar and ground of the truth. He warns against the fool's sacrifices, his offerings and his words, not considering God's holiness and His word, uttering long prayers and excuses, a multitude of words, to make up for the lack of sincerity and humility. Solomon compares the restless dream-filled sleep of those stressed out by their busy lives to the fool's prattling speech. Just as dreams are nonsense, so too are the fools vows; For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God. And so, we are given another proverb against vowing vows to God that you don't mean, or are beyond your ability to keep. Fools do this, promising God a multitude of promises; turning from this sin or that, promises that for God's favor the fool will do something or give an offering for it, that is never paid. When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay. Jesus teaches this. Matthew 5:34-37 But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. James repeats the doctrine. James 5:12 But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation. God takes vows seriously. He doesn't care for excuses, long public prayers, vain repetitive prayers. He wants sincere prayers and humble servants. Better to say nothing than to be a fools. Proverbs 10:19 In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps his mouth shut. Proverbs 17:28 Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding There are blowhards in every church in the world. Professing Christians who cannot help but make themselves known, and promote the things they do. Who make grand promises to help the church, or make this offering or that, to do works for the Lord, all to be seen by men. It's foolishness. And vanity. Verse 6 warns against the foolishness of talking yourself into sin, or excusing your sin as being done ignorantly. God hates this. The angel here, I believe, is the human messenger, the Levitical priest where the sacrifice is being made. But the principle remains, even now before God and His judgements. A humble and contrite heart, this pleases God. If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they. This proverb acknowledges that even the most high rulers have bias and favoritism. That the oppression of the poor and unfair judgment that we witness is unsurprising, but to know that there is one higher still; God. And God is not a respecter of persons. And God gives provision to all men, even the king eats of the same earth as the poor. The love of money is the root of evil, and those with this covetous heart are never satisfied. They seek increase for increase's sake, and this is vanity. With more substance comes more mouths to feed. More bills to pay. More work to do. Solomon asks, what good does chasing after more and more wealth provide, other than to look at it and see you have gained, especially if it doesn't satisfy. The sleep of a working man, though he has little, is sweet. But those restless nights of dreams come with the business of the rich. Coming back around to his main theme, the vanity and vexation of spirit that this life and the cares of the world that beset us all, Solomon addresses those that horde wealth. Who greedily gathers increase to themselves. He says the riches they keep are to their own hurt. That their heir is born without, and will die as all men, without. You can't take it with you. Even in an inheritance, is vanity. It is a sore evil, the preacher says, that the profit of excessive gain is like the wind. The man labors for more and more, yet will have nothing in death. Jesus teaches on this, as well. Luke 12:16-21 And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully: And he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. It is vanity. And so, Solomon brings it back around to the one good thing he has found under the Sun; the blessing of God that a man may enjoy the good of his labor in this life. That the portion of the rich man, as it is for the poor, is to take and rejoice in the fruit of their works. That this is a gift from God.

Ecclesiastes 6 continues the Preacher's lament on the vanity of wealth and increase in a fleeting human life, but that the gift of God is the good of enjoying the fruits of that labor, in this life. The evil Solomon sees all too often is this; that for all a man gains, ultimately it goes to others. And so, if God gifts a man riches, wealth and honor, having everything he ever could want, what good is it if that same man was not given by the Lord the ability to enjoy it? Solomon reasons, If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he. He says that if a man were not blessed to enjoy the good life that his efforts earned, living long with many children, if he die alone and in darkness, without even a proper burial despite his 100 children, he is worse off than a stillborn child. That the soul that never saw the sun, nor known anything of this world is better off than to have the vanity of travails and not be able to enjoy what comes of it. All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled. We are never satisfied, but must work to feed ourselves. Writing to the Thessalonians, Paul commands that if any would not work, neither should he eat. This is not only a maxim of truth, warning against idleness and sluggards taking advantage of the more enterprising in the church, but hunger is a reminder of the curse upon man that came from Adam's fall. Genesis 3:17-19 And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field; In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return. The vanity of life, the endless labor and the vexation of spirit, knowing that ultimately, other than the portion we are given to enjoy by God, is gone when we return to dust, is a direct result of sin. Knowing that the endless cycle of work and the certainty of death is vain, yet necessary, what is the point without the blessings of God, that we may at least eat and drink and enjoy what we earn? So he asks rhetorically, what advantage does the wise have over the fool? Or the poor that walks in the Lord's paths? It is that reward and blessing that comes from God for doing well. Better to keep in mind that which is set before you, the sight of the eyes, to do what you can and let God bring the increase, than to give in to covetousness and greed, the wandering of desire. Because that need to seek ever more, rather than being grateful for what you have, is vanity and vexation of spirit. 2 Chronicles 9:13-22 Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred and threescore and six talents of gold; Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon. And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of beaten gold went to one target. And three hundred shields made he of beaten gold: three hundred shekels of gold went to one shield. And the king put them in the house of the forest of Lebanon. Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with pure gold. And there were six steps to the throne, with a footstool of gold, which were fastened to the throne, and stays on each side of the sitting place, and two lions standing by the stays: And twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other upon the six steps. There was not the like made in any kingdom. And all the drinking vessels of king Solomon were of gold, and all the vessels of the house of the forest of Lebanon were of pure gold: none were of silver; it was not any thing accounted of in the days of Solomon. For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Huram: every three years once came the ships of Tarshish bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks. And king Solomon passed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. Solomon was possibly the richest man to ever have lived. He knew the truth firsthand that more money created more problems. That every increase he sought by the desire of his wandering eyes, came with it the vexation of knowing it would be eventually taken from him in death. That even his heirs would not be able to maintain it. That strangers would profit from his mighty works. His restless dream-filled sleep that comes from a man with much business, greater than all before him. The understanding of great wisdom, showed him greater evil under the Sun. If any man were able to appreciate the woefully brutal and short life of mankind, even with every advantage, it was Solomon. Seeing there be many things that increase vanity, what is man the better? If his lament ended here, we could easily resent the idea of the richest man in history crying "poor me!" But he is leading somewhere. For who knoweth what is good for man in this life, all the days of his vain life which he spendeth as a shadow? for who can tell a man what shall be after him under the sun? Who indeed? The same God Who judges our works, who rewards the righteous, Who gives them their due portion, and withholds it from the foolish and froward and the wicked.

Ecclesiastes 7 is the true beginning of the culmination of the Preacher's sermon, where the wisdom gained by observation of all things under the Sun, and the ways of man and God, leads Solomon to many conclusions regarding life. It is deep, and full of truth that is both particular to King Solomon, and broadly applicable to all people. In chapter 6, Solomon compared the relative benefit of the stillborn over the man of toil, who lived long and labored much, but enjoyed none of the fruits of his hands. This was to add to his argument that the blessings of God towards us, that while we are cursed through Adam to travails, God's mercy is that we get to enjoy the results. He made the case that it is better to walk upright, and gain increase through the blessings of God, than to seek wealth greedily. To be wise rather than a fool. Because ultimately, the sluggard and the foolish gain little, and see what little they have given to others. Here, in chapter 7, Solomon posits a different argument; that the end is better than the beginning. That the day of death, for some, is better than their birth. That a good name is better than precious ointment. People will remember you in a better light than the fool. He says, It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart. Our time with death better prepares us for life. We can appreciate the mirth and feasting all the more, having an appreciation for the end that comes to all of us. Sorrow heals us, more than vain laughter. The wise go into the house of mourning, giving comfort to the broken hearted, and taking from the truth of death, seek more of God and eternity. The fool seeks pleasure, and forgoes the pain that brings experience. They sing songs of shallow happiness, like the crackling of thorns, green briars used to kindle, and their laughter is vexing to the wise. Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart. This aside, noting that under stress and oppression a wise man may be driven to madness and in wrath, commit sin, or by bribery, brought to do wrong, sets up a subtle transition. Testing his thesis, the idea that the end is better than the beginning, Solomon notes the human limits of wisdom and righteousness. Things which may make it appear that all things under the Sun grow progressively worse. The proverb of v9-10 warns against the tendency to see things this way; Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools. Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this. This tendency, especially among the righteous who walk in the ways of God as much as lies within them, is a snare. It leads to sin that we are all guilty of at times. "Make America Great, Again," and calls to RETVRN! and other appeals to the "better days" of the past prey upon the inclination to see the former days as better, especially given the evil we see all around us. For we all feel like Lot at times. 2 Peter 2:7-8 And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;) But coveting the past takes us away from doing what we are supposed to in the present. There is no political solution to a spiritual problem. Revival is a continuous process. The need for revival is never greater than now. No matter when "now" is. To enquirer wisely, it is better to ask God to straighten that which He has made crooked. To seek God to make the hardships given to teach us wisdom worthwhile. Rather than curse that things are the way they are, which is vanity. If we seek His wisdom from adversity, we gain. We gain understanding and, by our diligence in tribulation, wealth. And both serve as an inheritance to our children, a defense, Solomon writes. It is profitable to our future to redeem the time in the present, rather than getting angry about a past we cannot change. The excellency of knowledge is the wisdom that giveth life. This is what we should consider. Giving to our children the understanding of God. Solomon reiterates the understanding that we should rejoice in the good days, for the prosperity God grants, while also considering that God gives adversity as well, and for our own good. He sets the two against each other, that we find nothing after Him. Continuing in Ecclesiastes 7, where Solomon the Preacher has built upon the truth that the toil and tribulation of life is vain and vexing, his observation that despite this, God has blessed men to enjoy the fruits of that labor. He has shown that it is better to be reminded of the short span man's life is, that death comes for us all, wise or fool, rich or poor. That, despite the seeming vanity of life, the pointlessness of endless striving, that the blessing of God makes it bearable and that this blessing comes on the righteous and the wise, while the foolish and froward, greedy and lazy see their efforts come to nothing in the end. And so, picking up in v15, the Preacher concedes that he has seen the wicked prosper and the righteous perish. That there are other factors that determine the outcome. That the just man may see a short life, while the unrighteous may prolong their time under the Sun. But generally speaking, the just and wise are blessed more than the fool and the wicked. From this he argues temperance, and against self-righteous displays of piety, or becoming self-important in your wisdom. Why tempt God? And don't be wicked or foolish, because again, God will repay. It isn't the appearance that brings life, but the genuine fear of God. The key understanding is sincere and humble respect for the Lord. The rest takes care of itself. The strength of wisdom is true, and can be relied on, but the truth of the matter is we all fall short. For all have sinned. v20 For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not. This wisdom is the foundation of the gospel. We are all sinners before a holy God. So even in appearance of righteousness, we have sin. Even in the strength of wisdom, we've all done foolishly. Thus, what the Lord decides is just, is just. It is hypocrisy to think more of ourselves than we should. An honest inventory, examining ourselves as we are instructed to do, reveals that we too have fallen short. We have cursed others. We have held hatred in our hearts. We have dealt unfairly, the iniquity we see in the wicked has had a home in our hearts. Fear of God humbles us to know our own heart. Acknowledging this truth of ourselves, the course of the wicked and the just, revealed by the wrath of God from heaven, and His mercy and longsuffering towards us, we should humbly seek His grace. Finishing up on Ecclesiastes 7, the Preacher explains that, even as he proved his argument from wisdom, and sought understanding, there are still things he fails to know. He has seen the vanity and folly of life, the endless cycles where there is a time for every purpose under Heaven. That there is nothing new under the Sun. That man's labors are endless, the travails of life grinding, that death comes for us all. He has learned that God blesses man to enjoy what we have, but that seeking much increase leads to more trouble. Not necessarily more blessings. He has found that the lazy, unjust and wicked receive His wrath in due time, but even the just man may come to an early end, while the wicked continues on. That the lessons learned in mourning, the inevitable death of all men, are more valuable than the mirth and enjoyment of our labors. He has sought wisdom and been given understanding from God that all have sinned and fallen short of His glory. That even as we judge the fool and the iniquity of others, waiting for their recompense and fall, we have our own account of sin. That judgement comes for us all. All this have I proved by wisdom: I said, I will be wise; but it was far from me. The wisest man to ever live still falls short of the depth and riches of the Lord. Romans 11:33-36 O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen. Solomon applied his heart to know and search and seek wisdom, to know the reason of things. The wickedness of folly, foolishness and madness. He considered all things under the Sun and burdened himself with much knowledge. And from it all, even the understanding of death and the bitter end we all face, he could not comprehend the ways of women. We all know Solomon's weakness was the women he married, the concubines he kept. That by going after their strange gods to please them, he brought curses upon his kingdom. He says, in his experience, that women have a heart full of snares and nets. The allegory in Proverbs of the strange woman of folly, who takes in the young and simple, bringing them to their death echoes his words here. But more, he says that while only one in a thousand men he has found to be upright, he has yet to find an upright woman. We know by Proverbs 31 that such a virtuous woman may exist, but is rarer than rubies. Solomon sees that those that please God may escape from the snare of the woman, the strange woman, but the sinner is taken by her. As Adam was by Eve. 1 Timothy 2:8-14 I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting. In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works. Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence. For Adam was first formed, then Eve. And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression. The view of women as more mercurial and prone to follow their volatile emotions, doesn't discount their ability to continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety. To strive to be that virtuous woman. To be as lady wisdom. To be blessed with children. To be equal in Christ while subject to her husband. It is just acknowledging the nature of the female, as much as the nature of man to sin. Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions. As rare as a good man, made upright by God, may be, the inventions of evil in a man's heart are still our nature.

The Preacher continues his sermon. Having said he has searched for wisdom by observation of all things under the Sun, and having found all have sinned and fallen short. That the wise and the fool, the rich and the poor, all are appointed to die, and after this, judged and found wanting, that then the only way is God's. That fear of Him and seeking His favor is the only alternative to the vanity and vexation of spirit that man travails in. Solomon begins Ecclesiastes 8 praising the effect that seeking God's wisdom has on us. That it makes the face to shine, and to speak boldly His truth. That it changes the countenance of a person to walk with God. Exodus 34:29-30 And it came to pass, when Moses came down from mount Sinai with the two tables of testimony in Moses' hand, when he came down from the mount, that Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him. And when Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come nigh him. Moses had to cover his face from the people, it disturbed them so much to see the radiance coming from his time with God. Psalm 104:15 And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart. The Spirit is described as oil, which anoints us as we walk in Him. The bread, His word. Our heart, merry from the juice of the vine, which is Christ. He does make our faces shine. His light magnified through us, that men see us and know, we have been with Jesus. And the boldness of our wisdom comes from the confidence we have in Him and His word. The Spirit filled the disciples of Christ, gathered in the upper room on Pentecost, and having His anointing, they went out among the multitudes gathered for the feast in Jerusalem, and preached with boldness. Acts 2:1-4 And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. The men, hearing the miracle of preaching Christ from scripture, in their own tongues, languages from around the known world, they wondered; Behold, are not all these which speak Galilaeans? But the disciples had been changed by their time with God. The boldness to preach Christ from scripture, and 3,000 souls came to repentance. Just as when Peter and John were brought before the religious leaders of the Jews for preaching Christ, these lowly fishermen gave witness that they had been with Christ by their boldness. Acts 4:13 Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus. Their light so shined, that others saw and praised God. The anointing of the Spirit, the truth of God's word, the wisdom they trusted, gave them boldness to preach the truth. They were changed. The understanding that man's countenance gives away their time with God to others, has a counterpoint in scripture. That the reprobate, those that hold the truth in unrighteousness, have a similar change; Isaiah 3:9 The shew of their countenance doth witness against them; and they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not. Woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves. We should seek to walk with God, to be anointed with the Spirit, that men look upon us and take note that we have been with Jesus. To speak boldly the wisdom of the gospel. To make known the truth of His way. Ecclesiastes 8 sees the Preaching of Solomon shift from building his premise to the application of it. The wisdom he has gathered has led him to be persuaded of certain truths regarding man and God. That to be wise is to recognize the commandments of those who rule over you, and to keep the oath of God. Obviously, the Lord's commandments being the higher authority. This obedience is that it be well with you. In a world of toil and tribulation, where vanity and vexation of spirit, being worn down by the nature of the fallen world, this truth is designed to keep a man from evil. The word of the king is power. The Word of the King is the ultimate power. Consider your ways, don't be hasty to leave the commandments of God or to stand in evil, least you be judged. Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him. This is true in life, before the authority of men, God's anointed. And it is true that in death comes judgment. Because man cannot know the future, this burden of knowledge can bring misery. Man cannot stay his date with judgment. He can't keep his spirit alive in himself, or stop the inevitable end we all will face. There is no deliverance in wickedness, only a more sure recompense for the evil we do. It is a gospel message at its heart. Solomon has seen that in the purpose of time, there is always a point where a man is brought to judgment for the things they have done. One way or the other, in life or in death, a man ruling over another, or God, in death. We will feel the pain of our sin. He says he has seen the wicked come and go, and go down to the grave and are forgotten. The vanity of life, evidenced in death. Finishing Ecclesiastes 8, Solomon again comes back to his observation that, with all things considered, the blessing to enjoy life's good things by our labors is a gift of God; Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be merry: for that shall abide with him of his labour the days of his life, which God giveth him under the sun. The Preacher has applied his heart, put in the effort to see all the business that is done in the earth, kept up at night by searching out all things. The wisdom of Solomon, applied in the tireless search of all he surveyed under the Sun, and his conclusion to the matter is that God has blessed those that work diligently in fear of the Lord, are blessed to enjoy the fruit of their labor. But more, the King's search for understanding has led him to recognize that despite all his knowledge and wisdom, the ways of God are still far above him. 1 Kings 4:29-30 And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore. And Solomon's wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east country, and all the wisdom of Egypt. He composed 3,000 proverbs and wrote 1,005 songs during his lifetime. In addition to his literary achievements, Solomon held an extensive knowledge of botany and zoology, speaking authoritatively about flora and fauna ranging from the massive cedar trees of Lebanon to the tiny hyssop growing out of the wall. His scientific observations also encompassed the animal kingdom, as he classified and described various beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. And yet, though Man's wisdom, no matter how diligently he may apply his labors to seek it, man shall not be able to find out all the ways of God. But we have access to His wisdom by other means. As a gift to those who diligently seek Him. 1 Corinthians 2:12-14 Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. Not by man's wisdom. But by His Spirit. Proverbs 2:6 For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding. Solomon has reached the limit of his understanding, and now is leaning upon the Lord's.

The preaching of Solomon continues. He has considered all things under the sun, mirth and madness. Labor and travail. The vanity of life. He has sought the wisdom of God, and come away with fear, that the ways of the Lord are past finding out. That the only thing that makes a life of vanity worthwhile are those things God has blessed us with. The righteous and the wise and their works are of God. Our understanding comes from Him. We who walk in faith are in His hands. But the fact of death is inevitable, and to every man the same event comes. To the righteous and clean, to the wicked and unclean. As is the good, so is the sinner. Only God is good, as Jesus tells us. And so any righteousness we have is His. Ours is as filthy rags, the Bible says. Our works that aren't built upon Christ are wood, hay and stubble. Fit to be burned and remembered no more. Only the silver, gold and precious stones, refined by fire, will remain. Solomon laments this truth. That the wickedness and evil of a man's heart dies with him. That the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. The things that last, are from God. Our children will live out their life of vanity. The inheritance we leave them will eventually be gone and forgotten. But the good works done for the Lord will last, and be rewarded. And those works, especially leading others to Christ, will ripple throughout time. The Bible says in Hebrews 9:27 And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment. The righteous and the wicked alike are judged by a holy and just God. Romans 14:12 So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God. For the unsaved, this judgment occurs at the great White Throne of God, where the dead are judged against the books of the law, and cast into the lake of fire, which is the second death. But for the saved, clothed in the righteousness of Christ, we are judged by Jesus, for reward. 1 Corinthians 3:10-15 According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble; Every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is. If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. After we die, there is no more chance to get right. No more opportunities to seek the grace of God. No more works we can do to earn reward. No more memory of our life's wood, hay and stubble. Our love, hatred and envy will perish. There is no more portion to be blessed with for our labors. So live your life to the fullest with eternity in mind. Life is but a vapor, our time is short. Redeem the time. Set your heart on the treasure above. Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works. Let thy garments be always white; and let thy head lack no ointment. Solomon's preaching on the vanity of life leads us inevitably to consider the works done for the Lord, which are never in vain. 1 Corinthians 15:58 Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. We have to understand that the preacher is appealing to the life of man, which is short and brutal. But spiritually, those that are wise fear the Lord. And those works that we do have lasting impact. And the rewards we receive, they are blessings from God. We only know love because He so loved us. 1 John 4:7-8 Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God.He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love. We know a wife is a gift from God. We know the fruit of our labors in being able to enjoy it comes from Him. We know the sweet things of life, to eat, drink and be merry, is of God. All good things are of God. And it's okay to enjoy those things. They are a gift. They are examples of His grace.
