Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun. Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest. The Preacher, having established the goodness of the portion we receive in this life, that it is from God and should be enjoyed, continues to bring sobering truth to the purpose of life. The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all. There are things beyond our control. The swift and strong do not always persevere. Wealth and sustenance don't always go to the wise and understanding. Skill isn't a guarantee. Time and chance, opportunity and luck, play a role in the outcome. Just as the traps and snares of men catch the unlucky fish or fowl, a man may be taken out before his time. He may lose everything including his life to chance. Bad luck. It rains on the just and unjust alike. He gives a parable of a little city with few men delivered out of the hand of a great king and his siege of it by the wisdom of a poor man, forgotten afterwards despite it. Wisdom is ultimately despised, despite being greater than strength. People remember the mighty men and often remember foolish men, far after the memory of the wise has faded. Wisdom is better than weapons of war, and yet men place their trust in chariots and swords. A lowly wise man may save a city, but a single sinner can destroy more than the wise saves. The impact we have in this life may not reflect in our monetary situation, or our glory among men, or in lasting memory after we die. Time and chance may take us out. But better to be wise than not, either way. Wisdom is its own reward and the desire of the Lord for us. Fear Him and in all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct thy paths.

Chapter 10 sees a familiar format, where the wise Preacher goes down some rabbit-trails with proverbs. We've obviously seen some scattered throughout the book, and so it isn't surprising. Holy men moved by the Spirit gave utterance to truth, because the word of God is truth. Vs 1, continues from the final verse of Ecclesiastes 9:18, that wisdom is better than weapons, but one sinner destroys much good. Here, Solomon compares how one dead fly ruins a sweet savoy ointment, the same as a little folly ruins a wise man's reputation. Recall Ecclesiastes 7:1 A good name is better than precious ointment... It is difficult to build a good reputation, it takes time, understanding; walking in the fear of the Lord. And it can all be thrown away by one act of sin. Think of all the great preachers brought low by their sin. (And as children of God, when we sin in secret without repentance, one of the ways God will chasten you is to make sure your sin is found out) David, a man after God's own heart, sinned greatly in secret, but Nathan reminded him that the Lord knew, and so David suffered for his sin. We always talk about Solomon's wisdom, but temper it with the understanding that he was backslidden and allowed his strange wives to worship false gods. Of course He knew better and believed the truth, but he succumbed to the same temptation as Adam. Pleasing the wife, rather than God. It is a sobering reminder that our heart is in our hands. Wise man's heart is in his right, but the fool's is in treachery, in his left. And a wise man can become a fool in a single act. And when a fool walks in his way, his folly will always reveal itself to others. In deed or in word, it becomes obvious that they are fools. Vs 4, he transitions to a Biblical truth, that if a ruler comes against you, justly or unjustly, it is better to yield than to flee or fight. We see it time and again, the greatest example being Jesus of course. But the apostles who willingly went to judgment to further the cause of Christ, even in death. We see it in the Old Testament where Jeremiah warns the people of Judah to stay put and trust the Lord. Those that fled to Egypt were slain in the way. Those that rebelled were put down. We see the example of Daniel and his friends, Joseph in Egypt, David while being pursued by Saul, had opportunity to kill the king, and refused and continued to appeal to his reason. Vs5-7 Solomon recalls an evil he has witnessed where rulers give honor to fools, and treat servants as princes. While we are not to be respecters of persons, we shouldn't give dignity to full of foolishness or rebellion. Tying vs 4 with 5-7, I can't help but think of Mordecai from the book of Esther. Where rather than yield to the king's prince, Haman, he continued to disrespect him...even as the plot to kill the Jews was known to him. Jesus says in Matthew 5:25 Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison. We are to give honor and tribute to whom it is due. The entire affair that led to the slaughter of 75,000 people could have been avoided by simply and meekly apologizing, and bowing. And the King put Mordecai on a horse, and rewarded him, despite his unwillingness to yield to authority. Haman reacted with evil, but there are no good guys in the story. Vs 8 and 9 reflect the understanding that we saw in Proverbs; that treachery and iniquity will come back to bite you. It echoes the proverbs against moving landmarks, or setting traps for others, that God's justice will see to it that you will receive the recompense for the evil you do to others. He then compares wisdom to the sharpening of a blade, noting the dull blade makes work harder. Wisdom sharpens, making work easier. And we can make each other wiser, sharper, with advice and counsel. Proverbs 27:17 Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend. Of course the sharpest sword is the word of God. Hebrews 4:12 For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. For wisdom and spiritual things, there is no greater tool than the Bible. Ecclesiastes 10 continues with Solomon's proverbs against the fool. He repeats the theme from his broader book of Proverbs. That a fool's lips, his words, lead to his own destruction. They begin with foolish nonsense and end in mischievous madness. The further from obeying wisdom a fool gets, the greater their distance from God's path, we see that their folly becomes insanity. We witness this today, where the foolishness and abomination of allowing sodomites led to they/them pronouns and transvestites being held up as role models. When there is no bulwark of truth from fear of the Lord, then evil runs rampant. The fool is full of words, bold predictions based on their own inane blabbering, while they don't consider the likely consequences of their actions. If a normal man is already blind to the future, who can tell the fool? The humility to know you can't control the future is lost to him. Even the work of the fool is tiresome. They don't have common sense. The city would have broad ways towards it and normal people have a clear understanding of how to get there. These fools can't see the obvious path before them. We have cruder terms about not knowing one body part from another. The Preacher preaches woe to the land ruled by children, where judgment is deferred for their own bellies, their own selfish interests. But, being under a king raised to rule, who understands judgment, is a blessing. Where the leadership delays their own gratification to do right by the people, and feasts for strength, not drunkenness. By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through. It takes work to maintain anything. Especially a home or other building. But it is the laziness of man that sees it decay. A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh merry: but money answereth all things. The appropriate thing for the appropriate thing, but at the end of the day it is money that solves the problem, moves the man, satisfies an accuser, and gets things done. Finally, Solomon warns against gossip and backbiting, especially against the king. "A little bird told me..." The things we think we say in secret and in confidence have a way of getting back to those we are cursing in secret. Even in our own thoughts. The rabbit trails of King Solomon's sermon continue into chapter 11, as he comes to the end of his preaching on the vanity and vexation of life. The benefit of Wisdom, and seeking the blessings of God.

The Preacher, Solomon, is beginning to wrap up his homily. He has built his case, that while life is vain, and full of vexing things, toil and tribulation, that God blesses us to enjoy the fruits of our labor. And that God blesses the wise and prudent more than the wicked and fools. The chapter begins with an appeal to generosity. Casting your bread on the waters. Giving liberally to others, and guarding against an uncertain future. It will return to you in like measure. And you can't take it with you. Who knows what tomorrow may bring? Whatever will be will be. If the clouds bring rain, or a tree falls in the forest with no one to see, it still is what it is. And so is life. Natural events occur without our ability to predict or change. James 4:13-15 Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain: Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. We should then make the most of it, and God willing, enjoy the blessings He provides with thanksgiving. Hospitality. Generosity. Charity towards all, regardless of the conditions we find ourselves in. Don't wait for a perfect opportunity to do right and live well. He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap. Take what you are given and act. We don't understand the miracle of life, the ways of God, let alone the ideal circumstances for our best laid plans. Remember, time and chance happen to us all. Death comes for us all. Sow your seed in the morning and evening and at every opportunity, and give the rest to God. Spiritually, this includes the seed that is the word, and laying up treasure in Heaven. Be ready at any opportunity to give the gospel. Isaiah 55:11 So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it. Jesus is the bread of life. Cast His word on many waters, and see it return again unto you. Boldly preach salvation in the name of Jesus Christ. Be a cheerful giver with what you have in this world. Be it food or wealth or the truth of Christ. The light is sweet. We glory in the sun. The warmth of Summer. The time of sowing. The joy of our lives is like a sunny day. It is welcome and refreshing, but we should remember the darkness, the Preacher says; for they shall be many. In every life, there are periods of darkness. There are more winter days, and cloudy days than there are joyous ones. All that cometh is vanity. Keeping this perspective in mind makes the sunny, joyous days more precious. We tend to lose sight of this perspective, especially in our youth. When time seems abundant and the promise of tomorrow makes the cares of today seem insignificant. Solomon says to the young; enjoy it now. Be cheerful. Let your heart be merry, and walk in your ways, but, he cautions, know that for all that we do, God will bring us to judgment. Youth is vanity. It is fleeting, like beauty on a woman or the warm sunny days of Summer. What we sow comes back to us. Be it charity or God's word, or our sin. The blessings of God upon us is all that makes the vanity of life worthwhile. Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity.

The end of Solomon's sermon, the preacher has spoken. Life is vanity and vexation of spirit, man toils and dies. There is iniquity and wickedness. Time and chance. A time for every purpose under Heaven. No guarantee of tomorrow. Only fleeting moments of joy where God has blessed us to enjoy the fruits of our labor. We should rejoice in our youth and remember the darkness, reflecting in mourning more than reveling in mirth. We should seek wisdom and reject foolishness, and in all things remember that there is a God, and He is just in His judgment. And so, Solomon the king and preacher, with his thousands of proverbs, songs and sayings (and wives), sums up the end of the matter. Remember thy Creator. Remember Him in your youth, while it is still light. Before the darkness of this life or the time to come, when it is too late and tribulations and tragedies bring grief and sorrow. Before you die, and it's too late. Before the day of the Lord. The sun and the moon and the stars darkening is always a sign of the end, and the 2nd coming of Christ. Matthew 24:29-32 Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken: And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. Joel 2:31 The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord come. There is a time it is too late to fear the Lord, to get right with Him, to remember our Creator. 2 Corinthians 6:2 (For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.) The day of the Lord will see the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men bow, every knee shall bow and tongue confess. The rich men and rulers will beg the rocks and mountains to fall upon them. They shall have their fear come upon them. The music will cease. The streets full of mourning. Revelation 6:17 For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand? The grinders shall cease, for there are few... Matthew 24:41-42 Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left. Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come. The day of our death or the day of the Lord, the end comes for all men. Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. If our bodies are broken, our spine snapped, our skull cracked, our heart stops and we bleed out, if our body can no longer move...And ever the curse of Adam is upon us; Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it. Genesis 3:19 In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return. ...All things considered, this is the ultimate vanity. Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher; all is vanity. The preacher is wise. The wisest man in history, filled with the Spirit of God to know things and the time and treasure to consider all the ways of man under the Sun. He sought understanding and set in order many proverbs, and taught the people knowledge. Seeking truth. Instruction in uprightness. Righteousness. The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd. All wisdom comes from the Lord. Jesus is that good shepherd. His words are as goads to cattle, the sharp and pronged sticks used to guide the herd. As nails of a master builder, sure and true. Holding the whole house together. Built upon the rock, which Jesus likes His sayings. The word of God is sufficient to admonish, to guide and be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works. We may write and study an infinite number of books by men, the ways of this world. But the only way we need is God's. Studying to be approved by Him. Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man. Having considered all these things and having observed all he could, knowing there is nothing new under the Sun, and that what is discovered today was known before and will be forgotten and known again in the future, Solomon the Wise comes to the ultimate conclusion that the purpose of life isn't gathering riches, or pleasure or mirth. It is not toil and working endlessly, only to be forgotten. It is only to fear God and keep His commandments. This is the whole duty of man. Hebrews 9:27 And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment Luke 8:17 For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad. We all have an appointment with death. And a time of judgment before the Lord, Who will render to every man according to his deeds. For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil. Vanity, vanity, all is vanity. But faith in the Lord, fearing Him only and keeping His ways and wisdom, in all our ways acknowledging Him that He may direct our paths...this is the secret to life. As Jesus says in John 10:10 ...I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly. With this, the sermon ends. The matter is settled. Life is a gift from God, and an abundant life is in service of Him. The true meaning of it all is to give Him glory. Our purpose is to be known of Him that we may know Christ. Amen

We are in the penultimate book of the Bible for the purposes of my goal to write out studies of every book of the Bible. Only Song of Songs and Psalms remain. Here in the first chapter of Solomon's ode to his love, we can observe why it is in scripture; the clear allegory of Christ and His beloved, the saved. The poetic language used, going back and forth between the woman and the man, is beautiful prose in itself. Begging for kisses from one whose love is better than wine. Whose savour is as good ointments. The use of ointment and fine, perfumed oils as a representation of the Spirit, is found throughout the Bible. Her saying that even the king's name is as an ointment poured forth, that the virgins, or the innocent ladies in wait, do love him. Just as the righteous in Christ love even the name of Jesus. She says to draw them, the damsels, to call them. And they will run after him. Just as the Spirit calls us, as a sweet savour to those that seek Him, calls us, and we willingly respond. We will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee. The upright, like virgin, indicates the quality of the saved. We are the righteousness of God. We have Jesus imputed righteousness upon us and a new man within, making us as virgins in His eyes. The forgiveness of the Father. We are upright because He is upright, and we are His. I am black, but comely...the woman isn't referring to race here, but the darkness of her skin from the sun. Her mother's children were angry with her, forcing her to keep their vineyards and to feed the sheep. But the blackness is also sin, what it does to our heart. And the daughters are unbelieving Israel. They who persecuted the prophets and would crucify Christ. The world hates believers, because of His love for us. That despite our sin and being made their servants to do the work of the field, He so loves us. The bride, having spoken of her love, and having told the daughters of Jerusalem her unworthiness, and having sought to find the king, hears back from him. She seeks out his flocks, to be with him, and Solomon responds to her in verse 8. If thou know not, O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents. He praises her, after her own shameful confession. She calls herself black from the work of being a servant. He calls her most fair among women. This is how Christ views His own. Solomon says, follow the footsteps of the flock. Find the shepherds. We are Jesus' sheep. He is our Good Shepherd. We may find Him where the other sheep are, and follow in their footsteps that we may know Him. Solomon goes on to describe his beloved in epic terms, and the chorus of the daughters of Jerusalem tells of how they will dress her in fine jewels and ornaments of fine gold and silver as the King's desire. Where before the children of Israel had despised her, the fair daughters of Jerusalem follow the lead of the King, and honor who he has chosen. Verse 12 sees the woman at the King's table. In his court. The spiced wine calls him. She compares her attraction to him as the pleasant smell of myrrh, and her desire is for him to lay upon her bosom all night. He is like a cluster of henna flowers, or camphire, alluring, heavily scented clusters of small white and yellow flowers used as perfume. She longs for him, his eyes like a doves. Their bed green. The beams cedar and rafters fir. The finest materials build their house, and she wishes to live with him forever.

Chapter 2 contains a poetic back and forth dialogue between the woman and the man, the rose of Sharon and her beloved, an apple tree among the trees of the wood. He compares other women to thorns, but she is a lily, a beautiful flower among them. The woman delights in his shade, his protection, and in his fruit, which is sweet to her taste. He calls her to his banquet, under the banner of love. Again, we see the gospel. He is the tree of life, over a precious flower among the thorns. Invited to the banquet house of the Lord. The wedding supper of the Lamb. She is overcome by his love, she longs for him as we long for Jesus, and His embrace in that great day of redemption. I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please. The timing of the Lord's return is at God's pleasure. Just as she waits for her love to awake, we patiently wait for Him to return. The roes, the hinds of the field are the wild deer that play in the pastures and roam the hills and mountains. She hears the voice of her beloved, and compares him to the roebuck leaping and skipping on mountains and hills. She sees him through the lattice of the window, just beyond her walls, and he speaks to her, calling her to rise up and come with him. This pictures the return of Christ, gathering the elect from the four corners of the world. Jesus descends with a shout. We who are His hear His voice, and Rise up, and come away with Him. For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; it is spring. The rains fall and the flowers burst forth, and a time of peace is at hand. The signs of the season are showing. The fig tree puts forth her green figs. Matthew 24:32–33 Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When his branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is nigh: So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors. She begs to see her love, he is among the clefts of the rock, the stairs of the mountains, as a dove, his face is upon those that take shelter from His wrath there. They fear him. But she longs to see him. Revelation 6:15–17 And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand? Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes. The wrath is upon these "little foxes," the wicked, those that spoil and corrupt the tender grapes. The wicked that seek to destroy the believers, especially during the great tribulation. Her certainty of their love, that he is hers and she is his, even as he waits for his time, reflects the eternal security we have as believers in Christ. Waiting patiently for His return, when the day breaks and the shadows flee the light.

Chapter 3 begins with the woman waking to a desolate bed, unable to find her beloved. Seeking him, she desperately searches in the night, throughout the city streets. She repeats the refrain that she sought him, but I found him not. She then encounters the night watch, and enquires of them if they had seen him, whom my soul loveth. This passage beautifully reflects the death of Christ, picturing the panicked feeling of believers at His death, and at the empty tomb. The watchmen, the religious leaders who crucified Him, unable to give an answer, but then, in her search, she finds him. Him whom my soul loveth. And she holds him and will not let him go, bringing him into her mother's house, even to the bed chamber she was conceived in. As Jesus comes into us, and is held in the most intimate chamber of our hearts. For the second time in the song, the chorus in verse 5, also found in chapter 2:7 is repeated: I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please. It is repeated again in chapter 8, and the verse is used as transition in the structure of the song. While it may picture the current time, where we wait for our beloved, the Lord Jesus to return, it also serves as an oath, asking the daughters of Jerusalem to swear by the roes and hinds, the graceful and skittish deer of the land, to not stir the Beloved too early. To let him sleep as late as he pleases. The immediate application speaks to the delicate nature of love, especially in its earliest stages, where you almost feel a surreal and magical experience and are afraid it could burst like a bubble at any time. You don't want to lose that joyous state. You don't want it to be disturbed, like the gazelles of the mountains startled at a sudden movement or sound. She has found her beloved and taken him into her heart, and wants that joy of her salvation to last. The chorus serves to transition the narrative to an epic description of the King, and his entourage, emerging from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, an endless caravan. Perfumed and decked out in fine clothes for the wedding. This pictures the return of Christ, after the wrath, on a white horse with ten thousands of His saints, wearing their wedding clothes, prepared for the marriage supper of the Lamb. The bed of the King, his chariot, surrounded by threescore valiant men, the valiant of Israel. The soldiers with swords at their hip, like the prophets armed with the word of God. King Solomon's chariot, made of the finest wood, decked in silver and gold, covered in royal purple, and as it goes, paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem. This is the interior of the royal chariot, embroidery made by the daughters of the land with love, the inner bed, where the King and his bride would recline. The purity of God in the silver pillars, His grace, the gold that surrounds us. The purple of His majesty as Lord, and the interior, the soft comfort of His love for us. The bride of the song calls out for the daughters of Zion, Jerusalem, to go out and welcome the King. To examine his wedding crown, to celebrate the betrothal and his gladness. The tradition of the people is that the mother of the bridegroom crafts a crown to celebrate the nuptials. Not a crown of royalty, but of love. In Revelation 19:12, as Christ rides forth to claim ultimate victory and gather His people, the text says, on his head were many crowns. The crowns of Christ at His triumphant arrival to meet the descending New Jerusalem, adorned as a bride, are the diadem of His love for His beloved, just as Solomon's love for his bride. As John writes in Revelation 21:2: And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The allegory and picture of the King of Kings arriving at His wedding feast, at the culmination of history, to usher in His millennial Kingdom, reflected in the prophetic love song written by Solomon.

Chapter 4 opens with an ode to the beloved bride by her lover, the bridegroom. When he looks upon her he sees her fair beauty, her eyes as doves', her hair as the flocks of wild mountain goats. Picturing her black, flowing locks as the long, black, silky hair the goats have. When a herd of these dark goats grazes and moves down a steep mountain from a distance, the flowing movement creates a visual illusion of cascading hair. He compares her teeth to the whitest of sheep, shorn and clean and notes there are none missing, a rarity to be sure in the ancient world. Her lips, red as scarlet thread and her speech comely. Her temples and neck and breasts and scent, perfect and without blemish. Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee. The poetic nature of the song, romanticizing the couples love, could be seen as hyperbole. The aura of beauty that comes with infatuation. The perfection we see when we are caught up in our love for the other. But, as a spiritual allegory, we see the woman, who works the field and vineyard, black skinned, is without blemish when the King looks upon her. Just as we who are saved and sanctified by faith in Christ are pure when the Lord looks upon us. Clothed in righteousness. No sin imputed upon our new man. 2 Corinthians 5:21 For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. He has made us without blemish; Colossians 1:21–22 And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight Solomon's King sings passionately about his beloved; How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! A sister of Israel, his spouse through their betrothal and marriage. This is also how Jesus sees us, His beloved. We are His brothers and sisters, and spouse as a collective. Made one within the body of Christ. Matthew 12:50 For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother. His idealized view of us, despite our sin and despite our falling short of the glory of God, comes entirely by His love for us. That while we were sinners, Christ died for us. That He justifies the ungodly. That the Spirit quickens and seals us unto redemption. So when Solomon compares his love to an inclosed garden, walled off, a spring shut up, barred from use by others. A fountain sealed, carrying the seal of the King, and so kept pure from pollution. In this allegory we see the promise of eternal security in Christ. We are eternally His. The fruits of the garden are orchards, even pomegranates, and pleasant fruits, and flowers and spices used in ointments and perfume. Spikenard, the precious Himalayan plant, used to anoint Christ; Mark 14:3 And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head. The odors of her garden are pleasing. Precious to the King. Just as our fruit, our good works in Christ, are pleasing to Him. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon. He views us and the works we do for Him the same way, and we issue forth the living waters of the Spirit when we walk in His ways. The chapter ends shifting to the beloved woman, the bride, calling upon her lord to enter her garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Spiritually, calling upon the name of the Lord, that one may be saved, that God may eat His pleasant fruits.

Chapter 5 opens with the aftermath of the close of the previous chapter, which ended with the woman calling upon her bridegroom, her lord. The spiritual moment of acceptance and humility, asking Him for salvation. Opening yourself to be intimately known of God. Verse 1 gives the bridegroom's POV. Having entered the garden, come unto his dearest sister, his spouse, gathered the spices and ointments of myrrh, eaten the sweet of the honeycomb, drunk the wine and milk, and calling those at the wedding feast, and his bride, to eat and drink, abundantly. Revelation 22:17 And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely. This picture of salvation, the immediate joy and celebration, the call to get your fill of an abundance of the sweet and precious food and anointing oils, wine and milk, to drink abundantly, is God's call to us to now walk in His Spirit. To take full advantage of the relationship His children have with the Father in Christ, the true King. The Shepherd. The Bridegroom. Not a thief, but our Savior. John 10:10 The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly. We are called to walk in the Spirit and receive the fruit thereof; Galatians 5:22–25 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit. This initial feeling of having come to a feast and being overwhelmed with the love of God towards us, His blessings and rest, is marvelous. But we may tire and sleep in that contentment. The bride sleeps, but her heart wakes. She hears a knock. A voice. It is her beloved, calling to her to let him in. He asks her to open to him, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled. He has come, his hair wet with the dew of the night to see her. He is Christ come to give His bride a blessing, but she doesn't leap to open the door. She makes excuses; I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? Rather than hear His voice and do His will, that we may be blessed, a believer may see their contentment and undefiled spirit as a bed to rest upon. When God asks so little of us whom He has saved, to open when He knocks, will we respond? Revelation 3:20 Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me. In the Christian life, God gives us works to do. Poor to be fed. A gospel to be preached. Divine appointments to be kept. His burden is light. He wants so little from us, yet in our own selfish interests, we make excuses. Taking for granted all He has given us. And, even as the beloved reaches his hand in through the door, making that extra effort to stir his bride, God will try and overcome our hesitation, moving in our lives. His effort stirs her. She rises but too late. She feels the sweet smelling myrrh, the holiness of Christ, upon the lock. But, He has withdrawn. When we don't respond to God's callings, and hesitate to do His will, He will give us a taste of life without Him. He will lift His hedge of protection. He will let us suffer consequences He has spared us from. He will chasten every son. The bride's soul fails, knowing she did wrong and desperately she seeks her beloved, in the very manner she once sought him. Wandering in the dark streets, calling for him. Trying to find her own way. This time, the watchmen find her and persecute her. The smote her and wound her and remove her veil of purity. She suffers for her love's sake. The watchmen who could not tell her the way to her love in chapter 3, now treat her wickedly. This could be false teachers, those religious leaders who were not able to give her the gospel, now kicking her when she's down, to try and spoil her faith. We may backslide. We may become complacent. We may try to avoid doing His work. We may ignore His calling and then, when tribulation comes, look for Him where He is not, seeking answers. And we may be subject to tribulation, to remind us that we need Him, to remind us we are His. Just as Jonah was brought to Nineveh in the whale. Just as the church in Jerusalem, ordained to spread the gospel to the four corners of the world, stayed in Judea until the persecution against them scattered many. Just like Paul's repeated attempts to win his countrymen led him again and again to Jerusalem, finally being brought out and delivered to Rome in chains. It's hard to kick against the pricks. And so beaten and bloody, the bride charges an oath to the daughters of Jerusalem; if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love. To our modern years this sounds bad, but what's being said is that she is sick from love, overwhelmed by her feelings. Lovesick for her beloved. Despite persecution, she will not renounce him. Despite tribulation for his sake, she still longs for him. And she tells others who may be seeking him to give him her message of love. The daughters of Jerusalem answer her refrain; What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us? She has been backslidden, treated horribly by the authorities, bloody, aiming to destroy her remaining faith and strip away her public testimony (the veil), and yet her love is true. The daughters cannot understand what makes her beloved so special, above all others, that she would still call to him after all she's suffered. Unsaved people who see Christians suffer for Christ and still preach His love, often are baffled, but sometimes are moved. When the churches have been persecuted, traditionally we have seen exponential growth. Men are persuaded to willingly go to their death for the cause of Christ, and this testimony brings others to the faith. Why is your beloved more than others? Why is your God over the gods of men? And she answers. He is white, with purity, sinless. Divine. Ruddy, a red complexion picturing the humanity of Jesus and blood shed for us. The chiefest among ten those, the Lord of hosts. King of kings. Crowned of gold, sovereign above all. His locks, eternally young, everlasting. His eyes, full of grace and compassion for His beloved. Kissing His cheeks, like a bed of spices. Sweet flowers. His kiss, soft like the petals of the lily, dripping with precious oils. His love and our love for Him. The strength of His hands, the purity of His works, the gold and precious stones of all that He does. The inward parts of Christ are strong and pure as ivory, with heavenly blue sapphires the eternal Godhead in Him. His legs, a picture of Jesus' unmoving and unswerving strength. He supports us and His ways are golden. Pure. His face, chiseled as the great cedars. His mouth is sweet, all that He says is true. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem. Oh what a friend we have in Jesus!

The daughters of Jerusalem chorus in chapter 5 asked of the woman; What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? The chapter ends with the woman, battered and bloody from the world's treatment of her for his sake, extolling his virtues and singing praise to his perfection. The character arc from the ecstatic bride at the feast to the complacent woman, making excuses to avoid her love, then realizing and searching him out again, only to be mistreated by the watchmen and questioned by the daughters, and ultimately to still profess her love and devotion for Jesus, is a wonderful picture of things that can and do happen in the Christian life. And her faith through the trials leads others to seek Him. Chapter 6 opens with the same chorus of daughters, and they have changed their tune. Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among women? whither is thy beloved turned aside? that we may seek him with thee. Our testimony, especially in persecution, not only reestablishes our faith, but leads others to seek Jesus. We can often feel adrift. We may realize we should do more for the cause of Christ. We may have a sense of separation from Him. We may call out in prayer as David did: Psalms 51:12 Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit. But we should be aware that as saved Christians, seeking to get back on the right path, we will see persecution. The devil will attempt to sift us like wheat. Satan doesn't need much to keep the unsaved from seeking truth, but he works overtime to keep Christians from being fruitful. So, having persuaded the daughters, the woman answers them; that she knows where her beloved has gone. He is down in His garden, to feed the garden and gather lilies. A picture of the gospel light, the harvest of believers, the fruit of His good pleasure. She affirms her faith; I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies, and then the narrator shifts again to the King. He praises his beloved, comparing her beauty to Tirzah, a city known for its natural beauty, and even as Jerusalem, ready for war, filled with bannermen, armies ready to march. He is overwhelmed with her beauty, repeating the verses poetically comparing her hair and teeth to goats and sheep as the lyrics from chapter 4. He numbers her among 60 queens and 80 concubines and countless virgins, a royal harem, and says she alone is above them all. Undefiled. The choice daughter, whom all the other women blessed and praised. Beloved above them all. Verse 10, the daughters of Jerusalem, the very courtesans the King compared his beloved to, sing her praises. Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners? We are His beloved. We are the light of the world. We shine forth to all nations, calling them to Christ. Provoking them to envy, that they may seek to be His bride. The woman sings in verse 11, that she has gone down to her beloved's garden. To see the fruit of the garden, and if the vine flourished, Jesus is the true vine. She's returned to His rest, as quickly as the chariots, to her beloved, upon seeing the bounty of his garden. The daughters encourage her, Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee. And her beloved asks them What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies. A refrain answered in the next chapter. It is worth noting that the woman of the Song of Solomon is often referred to as the "Shulamite Woman" based on verse 13. There are conflicting theories as to what that means; is it a region, a nation, a family name? Some believe it is a feminine form of Solomon. The evidence for any of these ideas is scant, and I have purposefully refrained from calling the woman a Shulamite because, in my opinion, in the end it doesn't matter to understand the context and subtext of the Song. You may disagree, and that's ok.

Song of Solomon 7 opens with the King, having called his beloved Shulamite woman to return to him that he may look upon her at the end of chapter 6, now detailing what he sees of his beloved. He describes her beauty and the perfect symmetry of her body. How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights! Everything he sees of her is good. Just as we are seen as perfect and without spot when God looks upon us, clothed in the righteousness of Christ. 2 Corinthians 11:2 For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. Colossians 1:22 In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight Jude 1:24–25 Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, To the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen. The woman responds to her husband, her brother, her spouse with unwavering confidence; I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me. We are Christ's, and His desire is for us. Beginning there in verse 10, she responds to her beloved, knowing she is his, and inviting him to go forth with her, to live with her. To get up early to the vineyards, to see the vine flourish and come to fruition, where she will give him her love. The spiritual application here; She has gone from her initial humble acceptance of his love, to the joy of the wedding feast, to her period of complacency, persecution, profession of faith and renewal, to now making the decision to plan her day and life around him, is a beautiful picture of the Christian life. A believer makes the conscious decision to make Jesus their companion. To go forth with Him and to reside with Him. To wake early in the morning, starting the day with Christ, and His word. In prayer. This intentionality is contrasted with the bride laying in bed, hesitant to wake, making excuses to avoid letting in her beloved. As mature Christians, in it for the long haul, we seek Him first. We work with Him to tend the vine, which is His church, bringing forth fruit which are new believers. Planting the seed of His word. Watering and nurturing. Tending to them, the babes in Christ, and helping them grow to maturity. Through it all, giving Him all our love. We lay up our fruit, those people we have given the gospel to, the needy to whom we give comfort. The broken hearted we have consoled. This treasure we have laid up for Heaven, but to Him is the increase. We give Him our all because He is our beloved.

We are in the final chapter of the Song of Solomon, and the opening verses are the woman, longing to openly display affection for her beloved, the way a sister and brother as family could, without being despised. Without the judgment that would come for a maiden to kiss and embrace a lover, even betrothed, in public. We seem to have come full circle to the beginning of the song. The wedding hasn't happened, the separation and then regained relationship. It is as if she's been dreaming the experience from courtship to maturity, as told in chapters 2-7. There are repeated stanzas, ideas and the chorus again in verse 4; I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please. The longing to be with him, and to experience his love, to be in his embrace, echos her plaintive desires in the first few chapters. But here, after charging the daughters of Jerusalem again, they sing; Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? They see the love-changed woman, who was the girl they had watched grow. The woman professes her love; Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame. The eternal and unbreakable seal of the Spirit, set upon our hearts, once we know Him and are known of Him. The love of Christ is like an unquenchable fire, the floods cannot drown it. Noah found grace in the eyes of God. His love for man endured, despite the flood. The love of God could not be purchased, even if a rich man sold all his substance for love, he would be despised. It is not found in riches and cannot be bought by our works. It is unmerited. Freely given. The woman's brothers join the choir, seeing their sister still as the immature girl they have known. Wondering what they shall do for her now, at her betrothal. A reality that big brothers and parents face, when their daughter has matured. They contemplate what they'd do metaphorically, if she were a foundational wall or a door in need of a frame. But she states that she is fully grown. She is a wall and the breasts of her maturity are towers. An allegory for the maturity to come to the Lord, and find His grace. Then a parable of her beloved, the lord Solomon, and his vineyard. He let, or leased it out to keepers, to be dressed. And their charge was a thousand pieces of silver, purchased by the fruit they would harvest. The same is the vineyards of Christ's parables. The talents of silver. The harvest and the increase. The unprofitable servants of Israel, the wicked keepers who slew the prophets and even the Son of the Lord. The spiritual understanding that comes from knowing this first; the Lord planted a vineyard; Isaiah 5:1–7 Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes. And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes? And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down: And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry. The woman offers her vineyard to Solomon, pledging the tribute of a thousand, and even the keepers, a wage of two hundred. Pledging her fruit to her Lord. The Lord planted and cultivated a vineyard with Israel, and the husband men betrayed Him. But the woman, as the faithful believer willingly offers herself as a vineyard, and freely gives the Lord His tribute. The fruit we gather. The works we do for the cause of the gospel. She gladly pays the workers a wage. Just as we do with tithes and offerings to sustain our pastors, our churches, ministries and missionaries, that work in the fields for God. The Song of Solomon ends with prayer. She calls upon the Lord, acknowledging that the companions of God hear His voice. His sheep. She asks, humbly, to hear His voice as He calls. We should always listen for that still, small voice. We should pray that God gives us ears to hear His will. Her final prayer is that her love come quickly. To make haste in His return, to come down upon the mountains, as a roe or young hart, gazelle among the spices. The prayer for Thy Kingdom, come. Or Even so, come, Lord Jesus, is found throughout scripture. Maranatha, come quickly. 2 Peter 3:12 Looking for and hastening unto the coming of the day of God, wherein the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat? This is our hope, for the day of the Lord. His gathering of His people, the resurrection of the saints into glory. His terrible and fearful wrath on the ungodly. As mature Christians, we should be as the woman, gladly giving ourselves to the Lord, and praying to hear His voice, praying for His return. She has come to understand love, through Him. And has gladly given herself to Him. The spiritual journey that the believer takes, is beautifully captured in the Song of Solomon. From the first glimpse of love, to the calling upon the Lord, the ups and downs, and final devotional surrender, is breathtaking in its beauty and the prophetic power of the song. Believers are His beloved. When, in verse 5, the daughters of Jerusalem sing Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? It is such a fitting picture of our salvation. How the believer emerges from the wilderness, not walking on her own strength, but "leaning upon her beloved." She is changed, sealed by the Holy Spirit. Eternally His. Amen.

Beginning in Isaiah 1, the major prophecy set in pre-captivity Judea, the Southern Kingdom, Isaiah preached in the 8th century BC, in a similar timeframe as the minor prophets and Kings and Chronicles we have recently covered, and so the themes are familiar. Israel is gone astray, into adultery with foreign gods, idols, and wickedness. Blood of the innocent shed, the poor defrauded, the widow uncared-for. The sickness of the rulers, even in Judah, has corrupted the Temple as well. God is displeased, and is warning of His coming judgment. Here, in Isaiah, God is pleading with the people, Let us reason together. The Lord has made it clear, from Moses to their present that if they walked in His commandments, they would be His people, and He would be their Lord and the land would be theirs and be blessed. And yet they fall short, and worse, commit iniquity. Unrighteous judgment. He cannot abide it any longer. Except the Lord of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah. This calls back to the pleading of Abraham before Sodom's destruction, that if there were yet ten righteous men, God would spare the city. But it also points to our own time, and the coming judgment. Matthew 5:13 Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men. We are the righteous remnant. Believers are the salt that preserves the earth and withholds God's judgment. We are called to retain that savour, to be faithful and to obey the Lord's commandments, being a light unto the world. And when the fullness of the nations comes, and the salt loses its savour, a falling away, the small remnant will be taken like Lot, spirited away by the angels of God at Jesus coming. And His wrath will pour out on the unrighteous. But, as always, God's refining judgment will lead to the redemption of those who trust in Him. The city of righteousness will be ours. That faithful city, Jerusalem the mother of us all. Isaiah 1:16-20 Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool. If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land: But if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured with the sword: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it. By faith, we are washed of our sins. By being willing and obedient, we shall eat of the good of the land, and not be devoured of the sword. God is laying out a reasonable offer of His grace and mercy. He's promised us eternal life. But if we want this life to be long and blessed, obey Him seek mercy for others, and judgment. Plead for the widow and judge the fatherless. Love one another as He has so loved us.

Isaiah 2 continues the clear teaching of the Lord, and the futility of those who trust in men, things of men like riches and chariots, and especially idols made with hands. We know in Christ's wrath, on that great and terrible day, that the proud and haughty men will be brought low, and attempt to hide from His wrath: Revelation 6:15-17 And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand? They will be brought low and flee to the mountains and the caves and their bunkers and pray for the rocks to cover them, and there will be nowhere left to hide. But the meek shall inherit the earth. The humble and poor of spirit are blessed by God through Christ. And all nations will be under the King of kings. And be taught by Him, and walk in His paths. Knowing this, Isaiah appeals to Judah, the house of Jacob. Why trust they in men? In the power of other nations to save them? In idols of gods made by hands? Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of? O house of Jacob, come ye, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. Disobedient Judah, having the oracles of God, knowing the redemption of Christ to come, and the day of judgment to follow, and yet still they trusted in vanity. As so many do today. In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made each one for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats; To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the Lord, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth. During the wrath and after, in the Millennial Reign, all of the blasphemous and profane images and idols of man will be destroyed. Even those that trusted in them, shall cast them into caves and clefts in the earth, for fear of the Lord. Every bathtub Mary. Every crucifix carried by Catholics. Every Hindu statue. Every pagan artifice will be destroyed, either by their fear or by the rod of iron Christ rules by. Amen

Moreover, the Lord says, His judgment is upon Judah for the behavior of her daughters, the women of the land being haughty, proud, not meek and gentle but wearing opulent clothing and jewelry, rings in their fingers, jewels in their nose, bells on their toes. Carrying themselves like they are special, mincing or gliding along. God says they will receive scabs upon their heads, baldness, and be smitten with stink and burning, STDs and worse. They will be made to wear sackcloth, and they will mourn in the streets for their men, slain by the sword. While the primary blame for the fall of a nation into judgment is upon the men who abdicate their roles and responsibilities, and chase pleasure and sin, defrauding the poor and afflicting the weak, the women play a part in it as well. Their lack of virtue, and pursuit of vanity bring about their own judgment against them. God hates a haughty spirit. This is why Christian women are called to modesty and meekness. 1 Timothy 2:9-14 In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works. Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence. For Adam was first formed, then Eve. And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression.

There is a commonly held theory that the book of Isaiah is connected to each book in the Bible by chapter, chronologically and is sometimes called a "miniature Bible" by theologians. Here in Isaiah 4, the corresponding book is Numbers. While the text begins with a continuation of Isaiah 3, and the women of Judah, lamenting their poverty and curses, the slaughter of their men by the sword, turn 7 to one to find a husband. To make right their whoredoms, even as they pledge to support themselves. Then Isaiah's prophecy turns to the holiness of those in Zion; When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning. Numbers 11:1 And when the people complained, it displeased the Lord: and the Lord heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the Lord burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp. ...and the cloud by day, the fire by night and the Tabernacle for shelter. And the Lord will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night: for upon all the glory shall be a defence. And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the day time from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain. Numbers 9:16 So it was alway: the cloud covered it by day, and the appearance of fire by night.

Isaiah 5 gives us a clear glimpse into the judgment of God and how He sees Israel, and especially Judah. The length and breadth of His vision, being able to see all things from beginning to end. People today act as if they understand the long view of time, and they really have no idea. The Lord planted a vineyard, the root and the vine. Israel was given everything, a hedge of protection, a tower of strength, and yet it didn't produce the fine fruits expected. Deuteronomy 32:32-33 For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah: their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter: Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps. And so, the Lord will take away all the advantages given his people, the vine he cultivated. Taking down the hedge of protection and the wall thereof. And it shall be trodden down. The Lord called forth the armies of the other nations to come and destroy it. The people drunk on wine and strong drink, oblivious to the destruction. The oracles of God ignored. In the midst of the hard preaching, Isaiah gives this faithful prayer; That say, Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know it! Just as we pray for His return, they prayed for Christ to come. Revelation 22:20 He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus. This prayer is followed by three woes, which echoes the end times as well; Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil...Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight! ...Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink: Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him! The three woes of the wrath to come are a recompense for these same iniquities listed here. The bitter fruit of unrighteousness. Deuteronomy 28:15-28 But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee: Cursed shalt thou be in the city, and cursed shalt thou be in the field. Cursed shall be thy basket and thy store. Cursed shall be the fruit of thy body, and the fruit of thy land, the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep. Cursed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and cursed shalt thou be when thou goest out. The Lord shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke, in all that thou settest thine hand unto for to do, until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly; because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me. The Lord shall make the pestilence cleave unto thee, until he have consumed thee from off the land, whither thou goest to possess it. The Lord shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish. And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron. The Lord shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust: from heaven shall it come down upon thee, until thou be destroyed. The Lord shall cause thee to be smitten before thine enemies: thou shalt go out one way against them, and flee seven ways before them: and shalt be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth. And thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away. The Lord will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods, and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed. The Lord shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart: And thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness, and thou shalt not prosper in thy ways: and thou shalt be only oppressed and spoiled evermore, and no man shall save thee. There's more to the curses promised against Israel if they failed to live up to their end of the covenant, but we can see the same curses prophesied in Isaiah 5. Conquerors. War. Famine. Pestilence and death. Darkness. Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. The same destruction and wrath promised to those in the end times.

Revelation 4:8-11 And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come. And when those beasts give glory and honour and thanks to him that sat on the throne, who liveth for ever and ever, the four and twenty elders fall down before him that sat on the throne, and worship him that liveth for ever and ever, and cast their crowns before the throne, saying, Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created. Isaiah 6 opens with a vision of the Lord on His throne in Heaven, and the Seraphim, 6-winged beasts, singing continuously His praise. It is identical to the vision of John in Revelation, and a glimpse into the glory of Heaven and God's magnificence and majesty. Isaiah says Here am I, when called by God to preach to the people of Israel, in the holy city of Jerusalem, where He had chosen to place His name. And the people would be deaf to the preaching, hearts hardened to the message, and blind to the truth so that they would not believe and be healed. As Jesus said, quoting the prophecy; Matthew 13:15 For this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and should understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them. The Lord tells Isaiah to preach until the land is desolate. But promises a tenth as a remnant, to return to the land. This after the Babylonian captivity of 70 years. So the holy seed shall be the substance thereof. The lineage leading to Christ. The sixth chapter of Isaiah is matched with the book of Joshua, both called to a mission of utter destruction; Isaiah as a witness and prophet, Joshua to destroy the kings and people of the land. Joshua 11:8-14 And the Lord delivered them into the hand of Israel, who smote them, and chased them unto great Zidon, and unto Misrephothmaim, and unto the valley of Mizpeh eastward; and they smote them, until they left them none remaining. And Joshua did unto them as the Lord bade him: he houghed their horses, and burnt their chariots with fire. And Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms. And they smote all the souls that were therein with the edge of the sword, utterly destroying them: there was not any left to breathe: and he burnt Hazor with fire. And all the cities of those kings, and all the kings of them, did Joshua take, and smote them with the edge of the sword, and he utterly destroyed them, as Moses the servant of the Lord commanded. But as for the cities that stood still in their strength, Israel burned none of them, save Hazor only; that did Joshua burn. And all the spoil of these cities, and the cattle, the children of Israel took for a prey unto themselves; but every man they smote with the edge of the sword, until they had destroyed them, neither left they any to breathe.

Here in Isaiah 7, we jump ahead in time to the reign of the wicked King Ahaz, who ruled for 4 years and did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, and didn't follow the ways of David. As punishment, the Lord had set Israel and Syria together against the Southern Kingdom, and they waged war on all Judah. According to Isaiah, this fear of destruction moved the heart of Azah and the people in Jerusalem, and so God sent the prophet to preach to the King. Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah. This ties in with Judges, the 7th book of the Bible; Judges 15:4-5 And Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took firebrands, and turned tail to tail, and put a firebrand in the midst between two tails. And when he had set the brands on fire, he let them go into the standing corn of the Philistines, and burnt up both the shocks, and also the standing corn, with the vineyards and olives. So, Jerusalem seemed caught between the firebrands tied to these two foxes, Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel. The Lord God tells the king this shall not come to pass. Rezin would be slain and within 65yrs, Ephraim, that is the Northern Kingdom of Israel, called Samaria, would be no more. To prove the prophecy, Isaiah tells the king he can ask anything of the Lord for a sign. But Ahaz refuses, saying he would not test the Lord, but he ultimately will turn to other gods, and to protection from Assyria, and see his people slain and carried away. 2 Chronicles 28:22-23 And in the time of his distress did he trespass yet more against the Lord: this is that king Ahaz. For he sacrificed unto the gods of Damascus, which smote him: and he said, Because the gods of the kings of Syria help them, therefore will I sacrifice to them, that they may help me. But they were the ruin of him, and of all Israel. And because Ahaz refused a sign, Isaiah tells him the Lord shall give a sign, a wonderful promise; And he said, Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good. The wonderful promise of Christ Jesus, born of a virgin, years after Israel, and Syria would long be dust. Overgrown with briars. Home to strange cattle, as men from many nations would be sent among Samaria. For God would send Egypt and Assyria to destroy Israel and Syria. To shave off them like a beard. With arrows and with bows shall men come thither; because all the land shall become briers and thorns. God's promises are true. Those with ears to hear at the time of Isaiah could be assured that just as assuredly Ephraim and Syria would be destroyed, Emmanuel would come. Amen

Continuing the prophecy against Israel and Syria, and the future of Judah, Isaiah 8 opens with another birth as a sign, this one immediate. Mahershalalhashbaz, meaning "quick to the spoil," is a child that was born to he and the prophetess, under witness, that when the child was born, before he learned to speak, Damascus and Samaria, the capital of Syria and Israel, would be destroyed and spoiled by the Assyrians. Because the people of Israel rejected the waters of Shiloh, the figure of the peace in the Lord, the Christ, and instead preferred Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Syria, God was destroying them with the Assyrians. And because of the comparison to a river, the Assyrian army is a river that overruns its banks, and some of the flood waters would take out parts of Judah. The Lord warns them not to take council or confederacy with Ephraim or Syria, to spare Judah. That the Lord was with them, O Immanuel. To sanctify the Lord of hosts, to hold Him holy and let Him alone be your fear and dread. The Christ to come. The stone of stumbling and rock of offense to those that would not believe. But a sanctuary to all who come to Him. This is prophecy to both Israel and Judah. The snare set for those in Jerusalem who would refuse Jesus in their midst. Emmanuel. Who crucified our Lord. And I will wait upon the Lord, that hideth his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him. When you consider that the believers in the OT were waiting for the Lord to come, as are we, there is little difference in the faith. Amen. What more can be said? 2 Kings 19:19 Now therefore, O Lord our God, I beseech thee, save thou us out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the Lord God, even thou only. The 12th book of the Bible.

The burden of the Lord comes upon Isaiah, a phrase familiar from Jeremiah, the word of God given a prophet that he must preach to the people. This is a prophetic vision of Babylon, the empire, and the spirit of Babylon in the end times. The great and terrible day of the Lord. The day of the Lord, Lord of hosts, is used to describe the days of vengeance and wrath against a people. Here, the destruction of Babylon by the Medes in 539BC is foretold by Isaiah in approximately 700BC. And it came to pass swiftly, as we see in Daniel 5:22-31; And thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this; But hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before thee, and thou, and thy lords, thy wives, and thy concubines, have drunk wine in them; and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which see not, nor hear, nor know: and the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified: Then was the part of the hand sent from him; and this writing was written. And this is the writing that was written, Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin. This is the interpretation of the thing: Mene; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it. Tekel; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. Peres; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians. Then commanded Belshazzar, and they clothed Daniel with scarlet, and put a chain of gold about his neck, and made a proclamation concerning him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom. In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. And Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old. Isaiah preached against Babylon, which has yet to carry away Judah into a 70 year captivity, the sure destruction of their empire, as the Lord says Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them... The sure word of prophecy, as spoken by the prophets in the Spirit is an amazing thing. Isaiah continues to deliver predictions he could have no way of knowing other than the Spirit of the Lord coming to him. The faith that comes by hearing the word should be strengthened by this, that when the Bible speaks of the end times, we should listen. Joel 2:10-11 The earth shall quake before them; the heavens shall tremble: the sun and the moon shall be dark, and the stars shall withdraw their shining. And the Lord shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great: for he is strong that executeth his word: for the day of the Lord is great and very terrible; and who can abide it? Acts 2:16-21 But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams: And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy: And I will shew wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and notable day of the Lord come: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved. Matthew 24:29-31 Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken: and then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. Revelation 18:1-2 And after these things I saw another angel come down from heaven, having great power; and the earth was lightened with his glory. And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird. The prophecy of Isaiah against Babylon, they the day of the Lord is at hand, clearly has dual fulfillment. It speaks not only of the destruction of Babylonian empire, which had only risen to prominence in the days of Isaiah, but that same spirit of Babylon which will be destroyed in the wrath to come. ...cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it. For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine. And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible. Malachi 3:2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? Zephaniah 1:18 Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the Lord's wrath; but the whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy: for he shall make even a speedy riddance of all them that dwell in the land. Revelation 6:17 For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?
