Another chapter of Matthew, another multitude seeking Jesus to heal them, another instance of the Pharisees come to trip up or trick Jesus into saying something they could use against him, and another time Jesus, using scripture that they should know, makes fools of them. They ask about divorce, which under Roman law was allowed for any reason at any time, and simply required one party to leave a marriage. Jewish law, given under Moses set certain conditions to be met, and obligations to be had. It is often this conflict between Roman law and Jewish tradition that the Pharisees sought to exploit, making Jesus say something that would either put Him in trouble with the government or to offend the people and give them cause to rebuke. And just as He does in other instances, Jesus uses the word of God to show that they offer a false choice, that God's way is perfect and without error, placing the shame of rebuke upon them. Again we see the mistaken impression that the Pharisees were legalistic and strict, when in reality, they sought loopholes from God's law and Jesus teaches a stricter interpretation. The false idea that Jesus came to liberalize the law rather than liberate us from the law is part and parcel to the works crowd's self-righteous theology. And so Jesus reminds the Pharisees that Moses compromise on divorce came from the failures and weaknesses of men, not a contradiction of God's intent, that what he joined together no man can tear us under. That divorce is adultery. That other than putting away a betrothed before the consummation due to her or her parents lying about her chastity, that she had fornicated, there was no sufficient reason to not marry the woman to whom you'd pledged yourself, and cleaved unto. In cases of premarital fornication, the male partner was meant to pay a dowry and make her his wife, having taken her honor. Note that fornication, a grievous sin, has remedy under God's perfect law that satisfies all parties involved, while discouraging the practice. Whereas adultery is met with a death sentence, it's being a crime. And Jesus perfect understanding of the law, for he was the word made flesh, once again turned away the Pharisees in their temptation of Him. Faced with the truth of this doctrine, and the gravity of the concept of marriage, some of his disciples questioned whether or not marriage as it's laid out under God's law is profitable to a man. The responsibilities and obligations outweighing The virtue and benefit. But Jesus corrects them, that while there are eunuchs, or today we might say incels, who have been gilded from birth, or by man, or to achieve the kingdom of heaven without temptation of the flesh, there are still those who marry which is the norm and his instruction is to them. I will say God wishes us to mary, become one flesh, and be fruitful and multiply. For the law of God is Not grievous to those that love Him. And again, as in previous chapters, the crowds that have gathered to see Jesus bring their children before Him to be blessed. And again Jesus compares the humility of a child to what is necessary to enter the kingdom of heaven, to received salvation. To suffer the children and despise them not, for their angels are before God always. And that offending one of these little ones, that is spoiling them from being able to receive the Gospel or misleading them to some other truth, or abusing them into reprobation - is a great sin that is punished in Hell exceedingly. That it's better to tie a millstone around your neck and cast yourself into the ocean if you are a "MAP," for example, for at least you'll avoid a worse damnation than that which already awaits. Next we see another telling of the Rich Young Man who claims righteousness by the law, saying that he has obeyed all the commandments since his youth, but what more must he do to be saved? He calls Jesus good master, in an act of flattery that Jesus turns around on him handing him a softball on a tee. If only God is good why call me good, Jesus asks. He's taking the compliment and giving a subtle opportunity for the Rich Young Man to say "Because thou art God," which of course will not say, it having been an insincere platitude. Running through the list of commandments, Jesus asks if he follows them all to which the Rich Young Man assures him that he has his whole life, but when Jesus suggests he sell all that he have giving up everything to follow Him, which would give action to his claim of righteousness, the Rich Young Man balks and departs. It's this pride and arrogance that Jesus is preaching against throughout the past few chapters. It is more difficult for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven than it is for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, because they're carrying that pride with them, their love of the material wealth that they've accumulated, their self-righteousness in thinking that they have adhered to the whole of the law, not just by letter but in spirit, when in truth they're as much a sinner as the beggar, who in faith, inherits the kingdom of God through Christ Jesus. Had he recognized Jesus as Christ, the son of God, and truly sought the kingdom of Heaven by faith, he would have abandoned his riches and followed Christ, when asked, and in that faith, been saved. We see then that the disciples were amazed at this doctrine, questioning then who can inherit the kingdom of God, if that is the level of adherence to the law one would need to achieve. Jesus answers "With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible." Again, we are saved by grace through faith, a gift of God, through the blood of His Son, Christ Jesus. It is impossible for us to achieve any righteousness sufficient through our works. You cannot repent of enough sin to enter into the kingdom of Heaven. No amount of self-righteous acts can ever be sufficient. Finally we see peter, always ready to ask a question whether it is prudent or not, asking what reward then do they have, having already renounced all of their worldly goods to follow Him, having already received an inheritance in the kingdom of God for their faith that He was the Christ. And Jesus responds that they will have seats of judgment, over the 12 tribes of Israel in his kingdom when it comes. And that all who forsake or lose anything in his name, suffering tribulation, or division from family and friends, being maligned for our faith, persecuted, led to martyrdom even, that these will rule over the Kingdom of Heaven with him. So many Christians today seek to avoid tribulation, when it's that very tribulation that gives us rewards in heaven. They do fruitless works of self-righteousness, a thinking that by them they will achieve salvation. Meanwhile it is the meek, and the humble who inherit the kingdom of heaven, the poor in spirit. And they who suffering tribulation, keep the faith holding on knowing that a reward not made of hands, but of God, awaits them.

³⁴So Jesus had compassion on them, and touched their eyes: and immediately their eyes received sight, and they followed him. The Gospels shows that even among Christ's staunchest followers, there was competition between some of the Apostles. Who will be greater in the Kingdom of Heaven? What reward will they receive for their devotion? Even John telling of the footrace he won with Peter to Christ's empty tomb. This continued even after the day of Pentecost, and the contentions between Peter and Paul. These human traits of pride and expectation are laid bare by God in His word, just as the great men of the OT, patriarchs, prophets and kings, are all shown to be flawed humans. Prone to sin. Often prideful. Sometimes foolish. The Apostles are no different, and suffer more for comparison to Jesus, who is perfect, the only truly perfect man in scripture, being God in the flesh. It is fascinating from a literary sense, how consistently and fully fleshed out most of those who appear in the Bible are, as characters. And the spiritual aspect, a constant reminder of who we are, and who God uses for His purposes on Earth. It is encouraging and yet humbling that these great men and women, human, do mighty works and yet are as weak as we are. Great in faith, but with moments of doubt. Great in the spirit of righteousness, but still sinners and weak in the flesh. Serving as examples, like Peter often does, with his well intentioned rock-headedness. In chapter 18, they asked who would be greatest in the Kingdom, to which Jesus used a humble child to illustrate the humility that it would require. A similar dispute occurs both in Luke 9 and Luke 22, where the Apostles are said to have had strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest. Here, in Matthew 20, is the direct continuation of the end of 19, where Jesus had just illustrated the problem with the self-righteous and rich with humbling themselves sufficiently to enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, unable to accept the simple salvation of faith, and unwilling to give up everything in this life, for the eternal. Peter had asked what will their reward be, having done just that. Walking away from their profession, their income, their families, wives and children to follow Jesus. And Jesus taught them they have their reward, but cautions them to remember the lesson of humility, suffering the children, and many that are first shall be last in His kingdom. And so we are here in Matthew 20, and Jesus tells His disciples a parable. Of a man, hiring hands for the harvest, where each is given the agreed upon wage, a penny for a day's work. Those that labored from the start, and even those who labored but a short time. And the longest among them grumbled that they should receive the same reward. But entrance to the Kingdom of Heaven is the reward itself, agreed upon in faith, and contentions of who will be greatest therein is up to the judgment of God the Father, and our own judgment of our own works does not give us the right to question this. Believing Jews in the newly forming churches saw themselves as "first," the Gentiles, "last." Often prideful and puffed-up Christians, having been born to believers and raised in a church will look down on babes in Christ, coming from a sinful past and yet to get right in all things. Those who volunteer at church, and attend 3 times a week. Who carry all the chairs and make the largest pot luck. Who show for soul winning times, and go on mission trips, spreading the Gospel, but not out of humility of being a servant. Not out of satisfaction of being least, and thus, doing all things from that meek humility of the recognition of their retched state, but instead out of striving and contention. Pride. Good works done, and some reward had, for certain, when the fire burns away the wood, hay and stubble, some diamonds will surely remain. But yet, how much the greater their reward if they had become like unto children? Had been ministers to others. Willing and happy servants? This is the lesson Jesus tries to teach His disciples, and was preparing them to see Him live out, in Jerusalem. Now the sons of Zebedee, James and John (whom Jesus nicknames 'Boanerges,' which means "Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17) were part of His core inner circle, along with Peter. They witnessed the transfiguration on the mount. James was the first to follow Christ's example of being willing to die for Him, and was first of them to be martyred. John, living the longest, writing His gospel, the revelation of Jesus, and passing from old age, the only one of the original 12 to do so. Truly they were great men of God. Here, in this context of the last and the first, the martyrs and servants, those who lose everything to gain Christ, and His impending sacrifice, that their mother comes asking, "Grant that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on the left, in thy kingdom." And Jesus replies that she doesn't understand what she is asking for them. That to obtain such position isn't His to give, but the price is higher than perhaps a mother could ever grieve for their sons. "Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?" Jesus asks them, signifying the manner of death that awaited Him. And, the Bible says, they replied, "We are able." Perhaps it is out of mercy that God only held one brother to that fate, and used the other for some of His greatest work on earth, writing the definitive Gospel of faith that unbelievers should know salvation, and revealing to John the manner of the end of the world, in his old age. James however wasn't spared. One wonders if his mother was alive to see it, and if she made peace, knowing finally what it was she had asked. Now this exchange causes the other 10 to strive with the 2 brothers. Jesus pleas with them to not engage in that kind of dispute over who is greater. He says that the princes of this world exercise authority by who is greater, who has the most, commands the most. But that in His kingdom it isn't so. "Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." This still applies today. Jesus did not come here to bring peace, but division. Separation. Among family. Among friends. From wealth and personal comfort. That we will see tribulations and persecution. And to be hated by man for His name. The promise is that every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold. That tribulation in this world is glory in the next. That being meek, poor in spirit, but great in faith, willing to suffer that others may gain, is how we are to live, and great is the reward for those of us who may. To be servants. To wash the feet of others. To be ministers. Not puffed up. But as like unto a child. To show mercy for others, not being proud of our own righteousness but a reflection of Christ's. And as they pass two blind beggars, persistent in their faith, Jesus has mercy upon them, and they are given their sight. The blind made to see. If you, like I, struggle occasionally on this lesson, how to be humble. How not to resent our status, position, wealth and comfort. How to live for Christ as a minister to the weak, with no expectations for added reward, but happy with the gift of eternal life we have hope on, listening to the Spirit with the new man inside, pray. Pray and worship, persistently. Asking Jesus to be able to see.

Approaching the finish of His work on earth, Jesus arrives in Jerusalem, meekly riding an ass, triumphantly received by the people, all in accordance with scripture. The prophets who spoke of Him signifying Jesus was the Christ. The people hailed Him with hosannas, "This is Jesus the prophet of Nazareth of Galilee" and calling Him the son of David, indicating they saw Him as heir to the kingdom. And He again chased the moneychangers out of His Father's house, who had made the house of worship into one of merchandise. And again, the Scribes and Pharisees, high priests of the temple, were threatened by His presence and sought to do evil towards Jesus. And hearing the throng of children in the temple, witness to Jesus' miraculous teaching and healing, crying out "Hosanna to the son of David!" the Bible says these supposed "men of God" were sore displeased. They confront Jesus, questioning if He hears what they are shouting out, hoping to trap Him in a blasphemy. Jesus instead replies, again with scripture, Psalms 8:2, giving the vipers nothing to accuse Him of, but God's word. Matthew continues the narrative the next day, with Jesus returning to the temple, hungry. (A reminder that in all things, Jesus was fully human as well as fully God, and aware of our condition). Approaching a fig tree, barren of fruit, Jesus says "let no fruit grow on thee, henceforth and forever," and the tree withered on the spot. This is both literal and allegory for the Jews who were to reject Him. The Apostles seeing this sign, marveled. And Jesus teaches them, had they faith enough they could do this and more. That they could move mountains. That all things asked of in prayer can be delivered unto us, we simply must have faith enough. All things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive. This is a promise from God Himself, in the flesh. Don't treat it lightly or as some kind of daily affirmation, but as literally true. Grow in faith, living faith to faith, building upon it, and witness it in your own life. God is not slack concerning His promises. Next Jesus is again tempted by the Pharisees, asking "By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority?" And again, Jesus confounds them by asking them to answer by what authority do they say came John the Baptist. If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why did ye not then believe him? But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the people; for all hold John as a prophet. And they answered Jesus, and said, We cannot tell. And he said unto them, Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things. Then Jesus questions them by way of a parable. A certain man with two sons, orders them to work his vineyard. One refuses, but changes his mind and goes to work. The other days yes, but doesn't do it. Which did the the will of the father? They rightly say the first, not seeing the meaning and Jesus readily gives it to them, but good. Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him. We see again, Biblical repentance is a turning towards belief in what God tells us is His will. Faith in His word. Jesus tells these self-righteousness holy men that the worst sinners who believed John that the kingdom of God was at hand are the first son, and they the second, claiming they do the will of the Father but did it not, not believing him who He sent. And to drive the point home even further, Jesus tells them another parable, of the certain householder, who doing all the work, created a great vineyard, and hired husbandmen to tend it and left it to them to bring in the harvest to him. And when time came, the man sent his servants to collect the increase from the husbandmen, and they beat them, killed them. Stoned them. And more servants were sent, and they did likewise. Finally, the man sent his son, that they would receive him with due reverence. But, seeking to steal his inheritance and keep it for themselves, cast out the son and slew him. Jesus asks them what should this lord do to the traitorous husbandmen, and they destroy them and hire those who will render what's due, the fruits of the field. And so, condemned by their own words, unable to come to repentance, having beaten and slain the prophets, and soon to have taken the Son to do the same, Jesus upbraided these vipers. Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes? Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof. And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder. And finally understanding He was speaking of them, they wanted to seize Jesus and kill Him, but were afraid of the crowd that had been singing hosannas to Him, calling Him a prophet. The very thing they sought to accuse Jesus with in the beginning, now what held them back at this time. Jesus says it's not that they heard John the Baptist preach and didn't believe him, but that they saw how it worked on the publicans and harlots and still didn't believe.

Matthew 22 And Jesus answered and spake unto them again by parables, and said, 2 The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son, 3 And sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come. 4 Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage. 5 But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise: 6 And the remnant took his servants, and entreated them spitefully, and slew them. 7 But when the king heard thereof, he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city. 8 Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy. 9 Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage. 10 So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests. 11 And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: 12 And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless. 13 Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness, there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. How does one get a wedding garment? Revelation 3:5 He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels. Revelation 2 7 He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God. 11 He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death. 17 He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it. 26 And he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him will I give power over the nations: 27 And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father. 28 And I will give him the morning star. 29 He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches. Revelation 3:12 Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name Revelation 21:7 He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. That sounds awesome but "Overcome?" what does that mean? How do I overcome? 1 John 5 4 For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith. 5 Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God? 6 This is he that came by water and blood, even Jesus Christ; not by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit that beareth witness, because the Spirit is truth. 7 For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. 8 And there are three that bear witness in earth, the Spirit, and the water, and the blood: and these three agree in one. 9 If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater: for this is the witness of God which he hath testified of his Son. 10 He that believeth on the Son of God hath the witness in himself: he that believeth not God hath made him a liar; because he believeth not the record that God gave of his Son. 11 And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. 12 He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life. 13 These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God. So we have overcome if we believe Jesus is the Son of God and that we believe God's word that in Christ Jesus we have eternal life, because Jesus has overcome the world: John 16 33 These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world. So, if we believe the record, we are invited to the Kingdom of Heaven, clothed in white by Jesus, given gifts of eternal life, our name not blotted from the book of life, eat of the tree of life, given a name, and if we having received all this, continue in God's work, we are given authority to judge nations under His reign. Amen! So, we who believe the servants' report are dressed in a wedding garment, clothed by Christ's righteousness, and attend the wedding of the Son. But those who try to come to the wedding in their own clothes, their own righteousness? Isaiah 64:6 But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away Oof. Who would show up to a wedding in filthy rags? Matthew 7 21 Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. 22 Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? 23 And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity. But what about the wedding? Revelation 19 5 And a voice came out of the throne, saying, Praise our God, all ye his servants, and ye that fear him, both small and great. 6 And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. 7 Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready. 8 And to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints. 9 And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God. 10 And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. 11 And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war. 12 His eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many crowns; and he had a name written, that no man knew, but he himself. 13 And he was clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God. 14 And the armies which were in heaven followed him upon white horses, clothed in fine linen, white and clean. 15 And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God. 16 And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, King Of Kings, And Lord Of Lords. 17 And I saw an angel standing in the sun; and he cried with a loud voice, saying to all the fowls that fly in the midst of heaven, Come and gather yourselves together unto the supper of the great God And the Bride? Revelation 21 9 And there came unto me one of the seven angels which had the seven vials full of the seven last plagues, and talked with me, saying, Come hither, I will shew thee the bride, the Lamb's wife. 10 And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and shewed me that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, 11 Having the glory of God: and her light was like unto a stone most precious, even like a jasper stone, clear as crystal; 12 And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel: 13 On the east three gates; on the north three gates; on the south three gates; and on the west three gates. 14 And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. 15 And he that talked with me had a golden reed to measure the city, and the gates thereof, and the wall thereof. 16 And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal. 17 And he measured the wall thereof, an hundred and forty and four cubits, according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel. 18 And the building of the wall of it was of jasper: and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass. 19 And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald; 20 The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolyte; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst. 21 And the twelve gates were twelve pearls: every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass. 22 And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it. 23 And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof. 24 And the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it: and the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honour into it. 25 And the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there. 26 And they shall bring the glory and honour of the nations into it. 27 And there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth, neither whatsoever worketh abomination, or maketh a lie: but they which are written in the Lamb's book of life. So we who are believers, as servants of God, must go out into the highways and bid as many as we find to come to the wedding feast of the Son. And as many as they found, both bad and good, are allowed to attend, who believe the report, and overcome the world in the Son, and be clothed in white garments, provided by the righteousness imputed on them by He who hath overcometh the world. We have begun the series of chapters in Matthew, (starting in 21 which we covered yesterday, and continuing in 22-25), of nonstop preaching by Jesus. In parables, in scriptures, in harsh rebuke, and revelation, leading up to His crucifixion. Where the scribes, lawyers, Pharisees and Sadducees come to tempt Jesus, to test His doctrine and find fault with Him, that they may accuse Him. But having not understanding of the word, they each fail to Christ's perfect understanding, as the word made flesh. Today's reading opens with Jesus continuing in parables to convict the so-called holy men of Jerusalem for their dereliction and disobedience to God. He has described them as the son who agreed to work the fields for their father, but did not go. To being the husbandmen of the vineyard, who rather than giving of the fruits of the harvest to the lord, beat and slay his servants, and betray and kill his son in an attempt to steal his inheritance and deny their lord his increase. Jesus has revealed to the crowd, hailing Him as a prophet of God, the hypocrisy of their religious leaders, and if it were not for fear of that crowd, the high priests would have seized Jesus there at the temple. Jesus now boldly preaches on the Kingdom of Heaven, His Father's Kingdom, likening it unto a wedding feast for the Son. And the King sends forth servants to bid all to come to the wedding, and none would. He instructs his servants to tell all that that they bid to the feast that the work is done, the meal is ready, the meat slain and prepared, and so come, and yet those bidden scoff and make light of it, and returned to their merchandise, to their money, to their land and material goods and wealth. And some took the King's servants, treated them spitefully and murdered them. And so the King in his wrath sends armies to destroy the people whom he had invited. Whom he had assured all was ready. Who refused to believe him and come. Who killed those who came to invite them. He destroyed them utterly. And now, still requiring guests for the feast prepared, to share in the work the King had done, he tells his servants to go out, to the highways, throughout the land, and as many as they find, bid to the feast. God had promised this wedding, this celebration of His righteousness and love, His creation, to mankind from Adam, and was rejected by most. He gave a select people the details, written in His law and spoken to of the prophets that they may be a light to the nations, bringing the world to the feast. And they rejected His word and slew His prophets. And so, God destroying them, sends His servants to bid all to salvation. Both bad and good. Whomever will come. And as the parable continues, the King sees a guest arrive, without a garment fit for the feast. In his own filthy rags, his own righteousness, representing those who believe they can enter the Kingdom by their own works. The King has him bound and removed, cast into the outer darkness. The lake of fire that is the fate of all who do not have the spotless white garment given to believers by the lamb of God. The imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ which covers all our sin. For many are called, but few are chosen, for they rejected the invitation. Didn't believe the report. Didn't arrive dressed for the feast. Make no mistake, as servants of God, this is our role. We are the sons who do labor in the field for the harvest. We are the loyal husbandmen, tending the Lord's vineyard, and bringing to Him the fruit of the harvest. We are the servants bidding all to come to the wedding feast of the Son. We are commanded to win souls to Christ. To go out along the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage. Both bad and good. That they may attend in the raiment fit for a wedding feast. Revelation 3:5 “He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.” Our role as those obedient to the Gospel is to go out to give the same Gospel that saved us to every creature, and compel them to come in, that God's house may be filled. Now, offended by His preaching, the Pharisees attempt to trap Jesus in sedition against Rome. They send their disciples and the Hellenistic Jews, the Herodians, who with flattery ask Jesus to judge whether it is right under the law to give tribute to Caesar. For Jews to pay taxes to the empire that occupied them. Jesus annoyed at their deception, knowing the wickedness they sought to do, says; Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites? Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny. And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription? They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's. Often the focus here is mistakenly on Jesus saying to render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, which is true. We should, as much as possible, live peaceably with all men, giving tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom is due. Materialistic things are the provence of the world. But Jesus is turning the question around on those tempting Him, that their focus should be on the spiritual. That they do not pay tribute to God as they should. They do not render unto God that which is His due. This exchange can serve almost as a Rorschach test, where the more worldly a person, the more they focus on what Christ says about the things of Caesar, debating taxes and obedience to earthly law, tributes and custom, be they worldly liberals talking about social contracts and socialism, or worldly "sovereign citizens," and their false gospel of libertarianism and sedition. Those who are more spiritual, looking to the Kingdom, see the focus on giving God His due, which the Pharisees and their disciples were slacking, as so many calling themselves Christian today are, too. Having struck out with the Pharisees, next come the Sadducees, worldly Jews who denied the spiritual things of God, the resurrection, Heaven and Hell, trying to trip Jesus up with a foolish hypothetical that they thought would expose Him to ridicule and show, using the logic of the natural man, the folly and contradictions they thought existed in God's word. In the hypothetical of the woman married to seven brothers, in keeping with the law of Moses, they ask to whom she would be married to in the Resurrection (which they didn't believe in). And Jesus answers their bad faith question in a familiar way. As He has repeatedly said to the other's attempts to trap Him, they don't know the scriptures or they wouldn't ask such foolishness; Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven. But as touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. Whether it was Satan tempting Him in the wilderness, His disciples and their misunderstanding, the Pharisees and Sadducees and their rhetorical traps, Jesus most common rebuke is that they know not the scriptures. "Have you not read...?" The answer to all our questions are found in God's word. If we read it in faith, the Spirit gives us understanding. All knowledge and wisdom come from God, and His complete, inspired and preserved word available to all who seek it. Those who claim we don't have access to the perfect and preserved word of God, who cast doubts on its veracity, its origins, its content, who add or remove whole verses, change doctrine, introduce contradictions and sow confusion, are doing the work of Satan, whose first act against man, enticing Eve to sin, was casting doubt on God's word. For where there is doubt or uncertainty, there is no power. And without the power, there is no salvation. And so Lucifer's goal of damning man is reached. This is why we are instructed to study all things, seeking to be approved unto God, not man. Comparing spiritual with spiritual. Proving all things whether they be true. And believing that God - who cannot lie, who is not the author of confusion, who promises that it is His job to keep His word preserved for all time, is true and to be believed when He promises us eternal life in His Son. And so then come the lawyers, masters of the law of Moses, who with the scribes and Pharisees minister the loopholes and rhetoric used to circumvent adherence to God's law. And they take their swing at Jesus, asking which is the greatest commandment in the law. Think about how the talmudic Jews rationalize things like placing a copper wire around Manhattan, so they can go outside on their false Sabbath. How they excuse molestation, rapes, murder, lies, broken oaths and dirty deals with doublespeak and pilpul. So to, the lawyers of Jesus' day see the law, and they believe that they can twist whatever Jesus answers as the great commandment into being the "wrong" answer. But, because they have not the truth in them, He easily breaks it down; Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. There are no loopholes to this. No way to invoke the letter of the law but avoid the spirit. No legalistic twisting, no Talmudic reasoning to get out of it. Jesus lays bare the hypocrisy and wickedness of what is to eventually become Judaism, simply by the word of God. Having 3 tries at Him, and failing, Jesus turns the tables in the Pharisees who had gathered, hoping to see Him fail, and questions them. What think ye of Christ? whose son is he? He asks. The son of David, they reply. And proving again that they do not know or understand the scriptures, Jesus reveals their ignorance with a question from the word; How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying, The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool? If David then call him Lord, how is he his son? How does David, writing in the Spirit, (for even these vipers would say that scripture was inspired of God), how could David refer to his offspring, his seed, as "Lord," giving the deference of God to whom should be the lesser, his son? And unable to answer truthfully, be it by their spiritual blindness, ignorance or understanding that the answer would require their admission of who Jesus truly is, the Christ, the Son of God, they give up on trying to trap Jesus with words. Now turning their machinations on deceiving and manipulating men to slay Him. Tomorrow is my possibly my favorite chapter in the Gospels, Jesus hard preaching against these wicked Jews who sought to trap him with bad faith questions. Slightly behind the teaching of salvation by faith alone, in grace alone given in John 3. Very excited. It's easy to understand, by looking at verses commonly cited as supporting the false damnable heresy of repentance of sin for salvation, to see precisely what is being repented of in each. Ezekiel 14:6 Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Repent, and turn yourselves from your idols; and turn away your faces from all your abominations. First, let us rightly divide the word of God here, it isn't regarding salvation of a person's soul, rather this is directed at the nation of Israel which had put their faith in idols, facing the abominations set before them in service to false gods. God speaking through the prophet is telling them that they will be judged as a nation if they do not repent of false belief in idols. Or Luke 13 There were present at that season some that told him of the Galilaeans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. 2 And Jesus answering said unto them, Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? 3 I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. 4 Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? 5 I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. 6 He spake also this parable; A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and he came and sought fruit thereon, and found none. 7 Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground? 8 And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it: 9 And if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down. Jesus isn't telling them to repent of their sins, he's reminding them that they are as sinful as those they are judging. That people who have suffered a bitter end, in this case being killed by Pilate or in a construction accident were no more or less sinners than they were. And they need to repent of that misunderstanding of how things work, because it is a stumbling block to their acceptance of salvation. Revelation 9 20 And the rest of the men which were not killed by these plagues yet repented not of the works of their hands, that they should not worship devils, and idols of gold, and silver, and brass, and stone, and of wood: which neither can see, nor hear, nor walk: 21 Neither repented they of their murders, nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts. Again, this verse isn't about individual soul salvation. What we are witnessing is God's wrath pouring out on the unbelievers that remained on the Earth, and that despite all the horrors being poured out upon them, including the plague of hellish locust creatures, the unbelieving didn't repent of their unbelief, they didn't turn from their idols or their wickedness to be saved, physically from the wrath. Using these three instances as an example of repenting of your sins to be born again, shows a lack of spiritual discernment and understanding of scripture. Don't be fooled. How can you change your mind about sin when we all know, from the law written in our hearts, from our conscience, from the rebuke and reproach of the Holy Ghost that all unsaved men feel, having the knowledge of right and wrong. Being past any age of accountability. I didn't repent of sin to be saved because I've never thought sin was good or right. I've never changed my mind about that, I've always known it's wrong. But thank God and praise Jesus, I changed my mind about what I needed to do to be saved, and believed on the blood of the Lamb that washes away sins, and the gift of eternal life. That's real repentance in order to be born again. Least ye be Reprobate concerning the faith, unless you've had your conscience seared, (or are an innocent child) you should already believe you're a sinner and have the knowledge of right and wrong. You should never change your mind about that. Repentance as preached by John the Baptist, Jesus Christ and the Apostles was not an act or work. It was not about behavior or feelings. Neither a prerequisite to nor a consequence of salvation. but was actually the very expression of faith in Jesus Christ and bringing salvation to those who have thus repented. John 3:16 says For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. If you don't believe this, repent. When you do you're saved. Acts 8 26 And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert. 27 And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship, 28 Was returning, and sitting in his chariot read Esaias the prophet. 29 Then the Spirit said unto Philip, Go near, and join thyself to this chariot. 30 And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? 31 And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him. 32 The place of the scripture which he read was this, He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth: 33 In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth. 34 And the eunuch answered Philip, and said, I pray thee, of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man? 35 Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus. 36 And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized? 37 And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. 38 And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him. 39 And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way rejoicing. The Ethiopian eunuch repented, going from not knowing Jesus or understanding the scriptures about Him, to believing that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God, and so, he was saved and then baptized. If you don't believe the Gospel of reconciliation given by the grace of God, paid for by Jesus, then you're an unrepentant sinner. If you do, you're still a sinner, but with eternal life, a quickened spirit, the Holy Spirit within you, saved by the blood, spared Hell and heir to the Kingdom of Heaven. Is there a biblical example of repentance from sin? Of turning from, with fresh information changing ones mind, turning towards the correct action in regards to stopping sinful behavior? Yes. But it's not regarding getting saved (not directly), but of those who had already believed getting right. In 1 Corinthians, Paul wrote to the saints in Corinth regarding the open fornication among them, and their taking one another to court for petty disputes, among other things. He ripped into them, that they ought to know better and to repent of it, to think better of it. To come to the realization that it is wrong and hurt their ability to do God's will in sharing the gospel, while they had such sin among them. And in 2 Corinthians, written a year or so later, Paul tells us by way of praising them, that they had repented of it. 2 Corinthians 7 4 Great is my boldness of speech toward you, great is my glorying of you: I am filled with comfort, I am exceeding joyful in all our tribulation. 5 For, when we were come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears. 6 Nevertheless God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus; 7 And not by his coming only, but by the consolation wherewith he was comforted in you, when he told us your earnest desire, your mourning, your fervent mind toward me; so that I rejoiced the more. 8 For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season. 9 Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing. 10 For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. 11 For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter. 12 Wherefore, though I wrote unto you, I did it not for his cause that had done the wrong, nor for his cause that suffered wrong, but that our care for you in the sight of God might appear unto you. 13 Therefore we were comforted in your comfort: yea, and exceedingly the more joyed we for the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all. Note in verse 10, Paul is giving us a general rule, that godly sorrow, that is sincerely being sorry at a wrong you've done, leads many to the repentance of belief that is salvation, while the sorrow of this world to death. In other words, being sorry you were caught, sorry you're in trouble, sorry you're paying a price for it, sorry that God has chastised you, this is worldly sorrow, and in it is death, because it isn't genuine, it's selfish. Paul says, godly sorrow, truly understanding the harm done to others or to God by our transgressions, can lead to repentance towards salvation, a change of mind that cannot be repented of. Faith in Christ, that cannot be lost once gained. Once saved, always saved. But to the Corinthians, who had already tasted the good word of God, tasted the heavenly gift, and the powers of the world to come, partakers of the Holy Ghost, as they'd already come to repentance unto salvation. The Bible says, it is impossible...to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame. So Paul isn't telling the Corinthians that their turning from the sin he pointed out among them is how they were saved, for they were already, but makes this comment as a part of a larger point, regarding their acceptance of his rebuke. But to focus on this a moment, as it is the only clear verse on the matter of "repenting of sin" in regards to salvation, note that this sincere sorrow for sin is not itself repentance, but rather, repentance is the work of that sorrow. That some may come to understanding of the faith by which we must believe to be justified by the sorrow for those they have wronged and the life that they've led. The regret. The penitent believer. Because, the Bible says of some, we save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh. Amen, this is the case of many, brought to repent unto Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and relief from the godly sorrow and guilt weighing their conscience, lifted up by the Holy Spirit and the surety of the promise. But again, that's not the only thing that worketh repentance. For some have compassion, making a difference, our caring and meekness, our ready answer for our hope, our chaste conversation, our example, the light of Jesus Christ shining through us, bring many to repentance as well. As many receive it in tears, many still receive the truth in joy. The circumstance and situation, the seed planted, the watering, the harvesting, the condition of the soil and the time of the season varies. But the repentance, the acceptance of the truth and the salvation earned remains the same, in sorrow and tears, or in laughter and joy. There is more valuable doctrine on repentance of sin to be had in this chapter, the change of mind with new information from Paul's first epistle and realization by the Corinthians, that what were doing that was wrong. Their godly sorrow leading to their getting right with God. The accompanying signs of genuinely changing their minds. In chapter 11, Paul lists the ways by which he knows they truly were sorry. Paul writes; For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter. He says this selfsame thing, this godly sorrow that may led one to salvation, is evident in them. He determines that they took his rebuke in the spirit it was intended and it manifested in their change of heart, which he sees (through the report of Titus), in that the rebuke and the sincere sorrow it caused led them to be careful; to take care and paying attention to the matter and the implications there of. To a clearing of themselves, that is getting right, to strive for being blameless, in this and in other possible sin. The indignation they felt towards themselves, the outrage at their own failings. The fear, of the chastisement from God, and the natural repercussions of their actions. The zeal, the vehement desire, by which they sought to get right, the revenge they took upon themselves, making good on the restitution of their error. These signs by which Paul acquits them, that ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter. This is a helpful list, both for those us us seeking to get right with God regarding sin in our life, and how we should act, and for judging rightly the sincerity, be it godly or earthly sorrow, of those who have wronged us and are seeking forgiveness and claim to be making amends. Genuine godly sorrow and a turning from a sin, or sins should produce a carefulness surrounding the behavior, an understanding of what it is you've done, how it affects others, the ripple effects and implications for the harm you've caused, and the things that lead you to the sin, whatever it may be. Not giving occasion to the flesh. It should lead to a clearing of yourself. An assessment of not just this particular sin, but of how you may be perceived by those around you, to whom you need make restitution, and others caught up in the wake of our iniquities. To make yourself as blameless as possible going forward, in careful consideration. You should be indignant at what you've done. Outraged at yourself. Embarrassed by the shame, hating even the garment spotted by the flesh. Despising that about you that led to your sin. And having a vehement desire and zeal for reformation, taking revenge against yourself, which here means making an honest retribution for the harm caused, not begrudgingly, but with zeal. Willingly and needfully making things right, as your vehement desire. Now note again, these all are the fruits of godly sorrow, just as repentance is the coming to understanding, in this case through that sorrow. They are not the same thing. It is the conflating of regret/godly sorrow/understanding of our sinful nature and the wages of death earned by it, with the actual change of mind, turning to faith in God, in Christ for our salvation, upon which bad doctrine and damnable heresies are founded. "What must I do to be saved?" Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shall be saved. That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. This is what we must repent towards, to believe to be saved. Regardless of how we get to the point of repentance, of taking the truth we hear and believing it, in our heart, turning towards God. Not of sin, though godly sorrow for sin may lead us there. Not of any works, or deeds of the law. Not of our sincere, careful, vehement desire to make right what we've done wrong in godly sorrow. These may work us to the change of heart and towards faith, but they aren't requirements for salvation, which is to believe on Jesus Christ, that He was raised from the dead. Some call upon the name of the Lord while in tribulation, being beset by the wicked and surrounded by enemies. In desperation, stricken by poor health, or in mourning for a loved one. By example of the righteous being kind and compassionate to them in their hour of need. Of being fed and clothed by believers, when they had nothing and hungered. Of seeing God's light magnified in the kindness and charity, mercy and faith of we who believe. The Bible tells us of many circumstance that brings a sinner to repentance towards God. It is not always of guilt and shame. Making it so excludes many from receiving the Gospel, and the prominence of this doctrine, making repentance of sin the way to be born again, places the onus of salvation, of being justified, upon the would-be believers to clean up their act. It implies that this is the means of salvation, their ability to do the works of the law. It becomes works salvation, either before the fact, or after, to show "genuine repentance," to maintain salvation, or as proof it was real. To both backslidden believers and the unregenerate sinner who had already 'cleaned up their life,' and had genuine sorrow and repented of their sins, but not believed on Christ, it places a stumbling block. It is a wicked heresy for this very reason. And that is why Satan pushes it so hard. I think one of the stumbling blocks for those who have come to repentance via their genuine sorrow for sins, those that hit bottom, so to speak, seeing their lives and relationships destroyed by their own selfish and destructive behavior, and having a rocky path to making things right, is that there are resentments for those who come to the faith by other means. There are many who are raised Christian, in godly homes, and can't even tell you when they believed. There are many who, when they heard the truth, accepted it. Absent trauma or drama, and yet saved. There are those who had long ago cleaned up their act, dealt with their addictions, or put away the anger and hurt at being victimized, say by abuse, physical, sexual or emotional. That turned over a new leaf, and yet only believed on the Gospel years after. And there are those, caught in the jaws of addiction, struggling to get out, long after repenting of what led them there, but unable to break free, who are comforted by a believer, and asking them, are given the Gospel and while yet, still sinners, in a moment of clarity, believe. People who crawled through whatever hell on earth to come to salvation, by sorrow for their sin, can look at these disparate cases, and others like them, and think "that person is not really saved, like I am." And the promotion of the idea that we must repent of our sins to be saved feeds that resentment, and can make a repentant heart grow bitter over time. This resentment is similar to the workers who labored all day for the same penny that those late arrivals collected in the parable Jesus tells in Matthew 20. It's sort of the inverse reaction of the good son in the parable of the prodigal son. It's this attitude that leads to holier than thou fruit inspectors, judging others salvation by their works, being a respecter of persons regarding testimonials, etc. Before heading in to Matthew chapter 23, it's a good idea to consider how hypocrisy flourishes from the idea of salvation by repentance from sin, rather than repentance towards God and faith in Christ. By placing the emphasis on what was turned from, rather than the testimony of what is turned to, what the changing of mind has wrought through faith, it creates an almost inevitable form of a caste system within a church. Of respecters of persons, who in hypocrisy see themselves as more saved than others. Just as the apostles asking Jesus of whose sin was responsible for the man blind from birth, or those questioning him about the men killed by Pilate, are those who had a wall fall on them killing them, the tendency and inclination to place the path to righteousness some take over the experience of others is the same form of hypocrisy which Jesus warns us against. For all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. For all were perishing before repenting to believe on Christ. For all are deserving of hell, and none are justified by their works of the law. We are all in the same boat and there but for the grace of God go each and every one of us. Regardless of how relatively easy we came to salvation, and regardless of how we struggle to pick up our cross daily and follow him. And losing sight of that leads to our focusing on the mote of our neighbor's eye. Of neglecting the beam in our own. Of judging in hypocrisy the Christian walk of others, while neglecting to work out our own salvation in fear and trembling. This is one reason why I dislike so-called testimonial preaching. Not the testimony of Jesus Christ and the saving power of faith, but the long winded testimonials, almost reveling in past sin, showing you just how down low someone was before receiving the gospel, almost a point of pride of how much they had to dig themselves out to get to where others are mercifully, by the grace of God. And I have been in churches where this becomes almost a competition of sorts. And where people blessed to have been born into a Godly family, and whose sowing of wild oats was almost incidental, making it out to be that they were low down wretched creatures, by way of showing just how really super duper saved they are, through their "struggle." Who haven't been blessed by God's grace and mercy, are embarrassed by it, for the glory that is heaped upon those with a testimony of a life of sin, turned around. This is yet another reason why Satan has painstakingly and methodically brainwashed everyone into adding "...of sin" to repentance. It's another way this becomes toxic in even good churches, with the right Gospel. We should not glory in the fact that those more sinful than we were saved. We should glory in God that he would save any of us. We were all equally damned. We all had to turn to believe the same thing to gain life. One sin or millions. A degenerate life in the swineherd, for a life of ease and comfort of our father's estate. For all have fallen short of the glory of God and deserve death and Hell. But God has sent his servants to invite us to his Son's wedding feast, both good and bad, called to repentance. Amen Thank you for bearing with me through this study of the concept of repentance in the Bible. It has helped sharpen my understanding, as iron sharpens iron. And as proving all things by comparing scripture with scripture, it has sincerely helped me gain understanding, and hopefully my sharing it with the channel has helped others too. I would ask that, if you haven't seen it already, you check out the posts I made early this morning, because it contains some of the insights that God has revealed in His word through this study. It's really helped me and put some things in perspective, and I would hope it would you as well.

I owe a study on Matthew 24, but I intend to make it more extensive than normally, to include Luke 12, 2 Thessalonians, Daniel and Revelation. End times Bible prophecy is a big subject and has a lot of confusion and misinformation that has seeped into the collective consciousness of the public, even Christians. Especially those taken in by the pre-trib rapture heresy and the unbelieving preterists. I had timed this for a weekend, and like most plans of man, stumble into it on a Wednesday morning before work, where I got a bee in my bonnet over stupid nazbols. I will get to it even if I have to spread it out over a few days. Meanwhile, that's the reading list above. Don't wait in me, let God tell you directly from the word. This is the beginning of the Olivet Discourse, the final big sermon to the disciples prior to the events of the cross. It is reflected in Luke 21 and Mark 13. John leaves it out of his Gospel, but then covers these end times events in Revelation. Jesus begins by giving an overview of the times and timing of things to come, the chronology of which lines up with Revelation 6. A man, as antichrist comes to make war among nations, to conquering and to conquer proclaiming himself eventually to be God. To this end, the second beast rides out to take peace from the earth, nation shall rise against nation. Wars and rumors of wars. The third beast, famine just as Jesus says, and pestilence, coming on the pale horse, bringing death. This and upheaval on the earth, disasters in diverse places, all mark the beginning of sorrows, the start of the great tribulation. Continuing, Jesus says, then shall they deliver you up to be afflicted, to be killed, hated for His name's sake. Although He is speaking to the disciples of their fate, remember that the context of this preaching is of the end times. Most Biblical prophecy has at least a double meaning, dual fulfillment. What many do is take the single application they want from it, out of the larger context to make the verses fit their preferred meaning. And so, like with the beginning of sorrows we see the persecution of the saints spoken of by Jesus reflected in Revelation 6:9 and the souls of them that were slain for the word of God. Jesus gives detail to the earthly experience of the martyrs and saints' persecution, where John gives us the Heavenly POV. Christians will be hated by the world, even by family. False prophets will lead pogroms against us. Sin will run rampant, and many believers will fall away to avoid persecution, still saved but their love waxed cold. But we are encouraged to persevere through this tribulation, for in the end Jesus coming on the day of the Lord will save us from it. This is, in context, physical salvation from the tribulation, not spiritual salvation. The false doctrine that claims only those who persevere are saved in a spiritual sense contradicts the context given. The idea of dual fulfillment, and a definitions of what constitutes the end times has long been a contentious point. 2 Peter 3 addresses this, that even in that first century: Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts,And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation. Peter goes on to warn against those casting doubts regarding the kingdom to come and the resurrection, who took prophecy as singular, and allegorical, and used that point of view to undermine the faith in the Kingdom promised us in Christ. According to Colossians 1:5-6, the gospel has been preached to the whole world, even at that time. And as Peter notes, and is referenced in other Epistles, the last days have come following the Ascension of Christ. We are living in the end times, and have for 2,000 years if the calendar is to be believed. What triggered Jesus' discourse was the Apostles wondering at the buildings of the temple, and Jesus prophesying that it would be destroyed, not one stone left upon another. It is after this that they privately ask Jesus, "Tell us, when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world?" Dispensationalists and others will take the destruction of the temple and add it to the prophecy that follows regarding His second coming and the end of the world, when it is a separate prophecy that spurred the broader discussion. Preterists will take the same approach, but say all things were fulfilled in 70AD with its destruction. But fundamentalists, reading in the spirit can see the order of how this is presented in Matthew 24. Rightly dividing the word of God. So continuing on with His prophecy, Jesus talks about "they" and "them" in Judea, fleeing what is called the "days of vengeance" in the parallel passage in Luke 21. It appears throughout the matching Gospel accounts that this is not referring to Christian believers but the Jews, as it's consistently othering pronouns. However, when talking about travel on the sabbath, He switches to "ye," the personal form, indicating the disciples and believers. I lean towards that the days of vengeance reflect both what happens to the unbelieving Jews in 70AD as well as their destruction in the end times of revelation, both. Regardless, it was also a time of tribulation for believers in Judea, and would be again when the beast turns his armies to betray the Jews, and take up his spot in Jerusalem, proclaiming himself God. Jesus tells us this is the days of great tribulation, where He has not returned as yet, and the resurrection and rapture has yet to take place. Dispensationalists insist the Great Tribulation occurs after a secret second coming and rapture, despite these clear verses giving the order of things. For then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be. And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened. Again we see that this will be worse than anything that has ever occurred, and we have witnessed world wars with the deaths of tens of millions. The starvation and execution of tens of millions under Stalin and Mao. Greater than that. It's gonna be bad, and believers alive during this time will be mercifully saved by the shortening the time, 3 and a half years rather than 7. It is at this midpoint that the abomination of desolation occurs, whatever that may finally look like. We the believers will recognize it, but it has yet to come. Jesus warns that during this time many false Christs and reports of His return will be made, but not be be fooled. That His coming will be like lightening that fills the entire sky. That it will be with a shout that is heard throughout the world. Every eye will see and ear hear His presence in the sky. He won't be in a hidden place, a cave, the wilderness. That His presence in the heavens will be like a carcass surrounded by carrion birds, as eagles, because He will be surrounded by the hosts of the saints caught up with Him in the clouds. (Rapture is just a Latin term meaning 'caught up,' for those special boys who say 'acctuuuually, rapture doesn't appear in the Bible!") Now with these caveats, Jesus begins to reveal what will happen on the Day of the Lord. Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken. Note the timing is AFTER THE TRIBULATION. Not before. Pre-trib rapture heresy BTFO with one verse, straight from Christ's mouth. We see the parallel in Revelation 6: And I beheld when he had opened the sixth seal, and, lo, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood; And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind. And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places. The sun and moon darkened is a common theme throughout the end times Bible prophecy, it is the common feature of all mentions of the Day of the Lord, second coming. It is an unmistakable sign that cannot be faked, and has not taken place in history of creation. Those claiming that the prophecy is past, that the resurrection has already taken place, that Jesus has already returned and we are in the millennium now, or had been, are all dependant on ignoring this incredible occurrence. Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken: And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. ... For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand? ... Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light. Shall not the day of the LORD be darkness, and not light? even very dark, and no brightness in it? ... For this is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge him of his adversaries: and the sword shall devour, and it shall be satiate and made drunk with their blood ... Alas for the day! for the day of the LORD is at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come. ... Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand; and the LORD shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great: for he is strong that executeth his word: for the day of the LORD is great and very terrible; and who can abide it? The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come. ... In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened ... For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine. ... The sun and the moon shall be darkened, and the stars shall withdraw their shining. Scripture is consistent on what to expect on the great day of the Lord.

Matthew 25 continues the Olivet Discourse between Jesus and His disciples, where in the previous chapter He had laid out much of end times prophecy, and His warning and instruction to be watchful and mindful, like a good servant keeping the house while the Lord was away, so as to not be taken unawares at His return. And so, by way of parable, Jesus expounds on this doctrine. The first, the parable of the 10 virgins, 5 wise, 5 foolish, awaiting the bridegroom, with their lamps. The 5 wise have lamps filled with oil, the 5 fools never bothered, and caught unawares are shut out of the marriage. And in their pleading the Lord says, "Verily I say unto you, I know you not." The oil is the Holy Spirit, the lamps, our hearts. The foolish virgins, the unsaved who, knowing full well of the bridegroom's pending return were lazy, slumbering. At His return, the foolish virgins beg the wise for some of their oil, for shared righteousness, but it is not the wise's to give or share. Each must get their own from Christ. And so, the foolish were locked out in the darkness, wailing. There are many calling themselves Christian who never received the oil, never accepted the Spirit, and tarried and slept while the master is away. Like the virgins, they may well have lived chaste lives, turning from sin, present in the chambers, but never coming to the truth and repentance to be saved. They believed they could purchase the oil, and return. Be given another chance. But once the wedding feast starts, it's too late. The next is the parable of the good and faithful servants, and the unprofitable one. In this familiar story, Jesus tells us of a wealth man, gone on a journey, leaving to each of his servants his goods to watch over. Divided according to their ability. Given talents according to their talent. The one who received 5 talents doubled it, and he who received 2 did the same. But the one to whom the lord offered one, took it and buried it and had no use of it at all. When the master returns, after a long time Jesus emphasizes, each gives an account. The 2 servants who have used what was given unto them to increase the master's wealth, and are rewarded for their efforts. To each, he says "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord." Note that to both is given the same reward, though what each is made ruler over may differ. Jesus uses the same wording for both in this teaching of the Kingdom of Heaven for a reason. While we may be given responsibility based on our talents, our salvation, entering I to the joy of the Lord is the same. And so, while one may do great things for the Lord and be given greater responsibility in the Kingdom, and another given less, but just as faithful, is given less responsibility, both are entered into the Kingdom. Both are given to the joy of the Lord having accepted the responsibility while He was away. And to the unprofitable servant, who didn't take the responsibility, but despised it.
