Here in Luke chapter 3, we find his goal, stated in the opening of his Gospel to "set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us," being met, giving precise details to the time in which John the Baptist, followed by Jesus, began their ministry. Luke establishes who was in charge, and where, pinpointing for readers the time and place of this happening, with familiar figures of their recent past; That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed. And so we find John, born roughly 6 months ahead of Jesus, has fulfilled the prophecy given his father by Gabriel, to be the answer to the prophecy given Isaiah; the voice in the wilderness making straight the paths of the Lord. In the times before modernity, when the lords and kings would travel abroad, often in caravans, taking weeks or months to get where they were going, a group of their servants would run ahead, both to herald their lord's passing to prepare those in the path chosen to receive their king, and to make certain the road was clear. That the way was smooth. Harbingers and workmen. So too, Christ the Lord was coming and the paths were to be made straight for Him. In scripture, we often see the idea of walking in God's statutes, following His wisdom, being righteous by obeying His sayings, is compared to walking a path. Turning neither to the left not right. But following the narrow way of the Lord. John, the harbinger of the Lord is sent by God to spiritually make straight the paths, to bring the people to repentance, turning towards His Son. Baptizing those who believed, a picture of Christ's crucifixion, burial and resurrection, and a symbol of their being washed clean by the remission of sins. Preparing them that shall see the salvation of God among them. Exhorting those who were saved to now do the works meet for repentance. Charity. Proper living. Changed as those who are free from the wrath should live. John is filled with the Holy Ghost, as promised, and speaks boldly and with authority the words of God. He is the first prophet of the Lord to have the Holy Ghost upon him in 400 years. His hard preaching against sin and of the word of God, scripture, draws people from all over the region. We see the lands mentioned by ruler, and it encompasses all of Judea, up into Samaria and the provinces from the sea and in and around Jordan, and it is from these places that multitudes come to hear John preach and to be baptized. In Matthew 3 we see that this draws attention of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and that the preaching he does, also shown in Luke 3, is an indictment of the Jews, especially their religious leaders. O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance: And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham. John speaking in the Spirit says that if they are truly there repentant of their false ways, show the fruit of it. Especially the religious leaders who have not the fruits, the souls prepared to repent towards God. They've failed the people. They have rested on the fact that they are God's "chosen." They haven't prepared anyone for the salvation to come. This generation of vipers has believed that by the nature of their lineage they would be saved. This is the same mistaken idea behind dispensationalism and the "God's not done with the Jews!" mentality among so many misguided and judaized Christians today. But John repudiates the idea of special treatment for the Jews. He says God could raise up Israelites from rocks if He so chose. They aren't special boys. And they certainly aren't living in a manner that shows God-fearing reverence for Him and His laws. The people ask themselves if he is the Christ, and he responds that one greater than him comes, who he isn't fit to untie His shoes. That the savior to come will not baptize with water, but with the Holy Ghost, and with fire, burning the chaff and gathering the wheat. And so, Jesus comes to be baptized, to do the will of His Father. And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased. Amen. But John's preaching against sin, especially of the political and religious leaders of that day, leads him to conflict with Herod, who had taken his brother's wife, among other evils, and so John is locked up in prison. It is at this time where Jesus, being around 30 years of age, begins His earthly ministry. Luke, having established the time and circumstances surrounding these events, then gives his version of the generations of Jesus, going from his stepfather Joseph's lineage. Perfect in his generations, all the way back to Adam, who we are reminded, was begat of God. Being the son of Joseph, even adopted, places Jesus in line for the throne of David, fulfilling the prophets sayings that there will be a King from the root of Jesse, a descendant of David, who would rule and reign forever. The Son of David. To the more secular, this places Jesus in line to be an earthly king. To make the Christ the physical deliverer of Israel. But to those called by the Spirit, and given understanding of scripture, the savior of their souls and heir to the Heavenly Kingdom. The Son of God. It is these two sonships that Jesus was born into. Fully God. Fully man. And the conflict in the hearts of those who hear of Him, even those who directly saw Him walk among them performing miracles and preaching on the Kingdom of God, would set the stage for His ministry. Psalm 86 Bow down thine ear, O Lord, hear me: for I am poor and needy. 2 Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee. 3 Be merciful unto me, O Lord: for I cry unto thee daily. 4 Rejoice the soul of thy servant: for unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul. 5 For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee. 6 Give ear, O Lord, unto my prayer; and attend to the voice of my supplications. 7 In the day of my trouble I will call upon thee: for thou wilt answer me. 8 Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works. 9 All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name. 10 For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone. 11 Teach me thy way, O Lord; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name. 12 I will praise thee, O Lord my God, with all my heart: and I will glorify thy name for evermore. 13 For great is thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell. 14 O God, the proud are risen against me, and the assemblies of violent men have sought after my soul; and have not set thee before them. 15 But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, long suffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth. 16 O turn unto me, and have mercy upon me; give thy strength unto thy servant, and save the son of thine handmaid. 17 Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, Lord, hast holpen me, and comforted me. Just a real quick application to today's study on Luke 3, something I didn't really get into this morning, but is very important. Luke 3:9-14 And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: every tree therefore which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. And the people asked him, saying, What shall we do then? He answereth and saith unto them, He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise. Then came also publicans to be baptized, and said unto him, Master, what shall we do? And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you. And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages. John the Baptist is in the wilderness, preaching to the masses of people from all around Judea and the surrounding countries, who have come to hear the word of God preached, under the power of the Holy Ghost. Many repent and believe and are baptized in expectation of the Christ. But they, as babes, don't know what to do, now that they are saved. What does this mean in practice? How is it applied in their lives. John says that dead trees will be hewn down and burned. Like the vipers of the Pharisees and Sadducees who do not produce any fruit, they're not bringing people to turn towards God. They aren't doing works of charity. As Jesus will later preach, they are hypocrites and worse. But those who by hearing the word of God come to faith, not wanting to be as the vipers, the fruitless, pricked in their conscience by the word, not wanting to be hewn down, they ask "What shall we do?" And to the publicans, who were tax collectors, a group known for their overcharging, abusing their office and taking bribes, he says take no more than you're appointed to, basically to be honest in your dealings. To the soldiers, he answers in a similar manner. He says not to commit violence, or falsely accuse or to covet more than his wages. Basically, don't abuse your position of power. Of course, all of this can be boiled down to "Love thy neighbor," which many of us overlook because it is such a basic teaching. Even unbelieving unregenerate man know the golden rule. And they knew it then, too. It was part of the law. God commanded it of them in Leviticus 19:18 Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord. But what does that look like in practice? How do we as saved Christians, at liberty in Christ, having repented of our past beliefs and acknowledged we are sinners destined to Hell but for the grace of God and are now saved, what do we do now? And John's answer to these people, 2000 years ago, remains the answer today. In your daily life, don't defraud people. Don't steal. Don't abuse whatever authority you have, at work or at home. Don't lie. Don't behave as the vipers, hypocrites and unbelievers. Love others the way you want to be loved. The way you trust in Christ to love you. And so, at work, do you slack? Steal time from the boss? Take advantage of your position? Lie to others? Gossip? Covet the status of wealth of others? Commit adultery? Not even that adultery of the heart Jesus warned us of? At home, do you love your spouse as Christ loves the church? Jealously and putting their well being before your own? Honoring your parents? Not coveting your neighbors possessions? Are you a blessing to your community? To your church family? To strangers? Are you a light that shines, magnifying God's love for you that others may come to ask you why you're full of love and hope? 1 Peter 3:15-16 but sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear: having a good conscience; that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evildoers, they may be ashamed that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ. So, ask yourself, what do we do? What fruit can we produce? How can our faith be made to benefit others? To yield an increase for the Lord?

Luke chapter 4 picks up with Jesus after His baptism in the Jordan and by the Holy Spirit, having been proclaimed by the Father "His Son, in whom Im well pleased." The Gospel says, Jesus was led of the Spirit to the wilderness, and there to fast and be tempted by Satan, 40 days. It is often overlooked that the three instances given here and in the other Gospels are not the only tests of the devil Jesus suffered. He was tempted 40 days. Jesus hungered. He thirst. He was weary. He was alone. Without shelter. Cold at night. Hot in the sun of the day. In all ways tempted as we are. But without sin. And Jesus was led of the Spirit to this temptation, He was not given a pass, was not brought to the temple in Jerusalem to preach the Gospel to an adoring throng of people. He was brought to desolate places where the prince of this world would tempt Him. Satan, the accuser of the brethren, seeking to corrupt the Christ, and derail God's plan of salvation for the world, tested and tried Jesus that he may go before the Father and say, "your Son is not worthy to be a sacrifice. He is not without blemish." But Jesus withstood Satan, and in doing so, gave us the pattern for dealing with temptation in our lives. 1 Corinthians 10:13 There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. The Bible says Jesus was tempted as we are. Knows our infirmities and understanding, shows mercy on us. We are not given more than we can handle. If we reject Satan, God will provide us a way. That way is found in what Jesus used to resist Satan. The word of God. So understanding that Jesus did not have some special means to supernaturally avoid succumbing to sin, it wasn't His divine nature that saved His human flesh from falling, but His doing His Father's will, and clinging to the word. Jesus was hungry and weak, and the devil said to turn a stone to bread. A temptation of the flesh. To satisfy the immediate need to please ourselves physically. And Jesus replied It is written, That man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God. Note His use of "it is written." That man loves not by bread. Not by the needs of the flesh. That there is more to this than satisfying our physical desires but that we live by every word of God. He quotes scripture to put of the devil from Him. Every word of God is all we need to live. (The presupposition is that, in order to be true, we have access to every word of God. Thus the preservation of His word). This having double meaning, as the manna in the desert was a picture of Christ, Jesus who is the bread of life come down from Heaven, and He is the Word of God made flesh, through whom eternal life is given to all who believe. And Jesus, using God's word, rebukes Satan. Then, tempting Jesus with power, Satan offers Him the thrones of this world, of whom Satan is god. Given power to influence kings and regents. The spirits that bring wickedness to high places. Overseeing the principalities of the rulers of the darkness of this world. By supernatural means, he takes Jesus to the top of a mountain and shows Him all the lands of man in the world. The devil says to Jesus, worship me and I will give you an earthly kingdom, ultimate power. And Jesus, again citing scripture rejects him; for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve. And again the power of the knowledge of God's word saves Jesus from temptation. Finally, frustrated, Satan places Jesus upon the spire of the temple in Jerusalem. Hundreds of feet in the air. And says to jump, because the scriptures say that God the Father would not suffer to see even His foot dash against the rocks. That God would send angels to stop Jesus from even stubbing His toe, so surely they would catch Him. And Jesus answering said unto him, It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. Again, using scripture, Jesus turns aside Satan and his temptations. And the devil departs having failed to stand against the word of God. In Matthew we read; Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him. By faith of this Jesus endured, that God the Father would provide. That He loved Him and was true. Not slack in His promise. By turning to scripture, Jesus resisted sin, and was rewarded for His trust. This is the pattern for our lives. The path we follow, led by Christ. When the Spirit leads us into the wilderness. When we are weak, and tired and hungry. When we are in peril, as Jesus upon the steeples of the Temple. When we are at our lowest physically and mentally, Satan will come to tempt us. And when he does, we can know that none of what he offers us to sin, none of the temporary satisfactions of the flesh, are beyond our means to resist as long as we turn to God, stay in His word, and have faith that our needs will be met by Him Who loves us. It is our daily walk with God that protects us. We ask Him to provide our daily bread, not just physical need for food, but spiritually, studying the word of God. We start our day in prayer, taking to God, and reading His word that His will be made known to us. His promises made clear that we may grow in faith. This is how we resist temptation. This is how we keep Satan at bay. We are weak in the flesh, but if we feed the spirit, the "new man," as Paul describes it, that quickened spirit that is the surety of our eternal life, we shall overcome as Jesus has overcome. And when we walk after the flesh, and neglect our prayers and our reading of the word, and we get caught up in the cares of this world, the way Satan caught up Jesus to the top of that mountain, to the heights of the temple, and we fear, and lust, feel wrath, covet and put ourselves at risk tempting God, and have not the means to escape though God has given them to us. His word; The pattern made by Christ to follow. It should be mentioned that before beginning His earthly ministry, Jesus sought to purify himself with prayer and fasting. Legitimate fasting, denying Himself not personal taste and treats, preference and privilege, but actually sacrificing physical necessity that He may focus on the things of God. The word. In prayer and supplication. How can those who deny that we have "every word of God" and that don't read it daily, allowing other men to be an intermediary, how can they resist temptation? If their prayers are to other men, not boldly going before God the Father with supplication? They can't. That's why they often seek worldly power. It's why they fast and pray to be seen of men, and not locked away as God commands. Not going into the wilderness but proclaiming their "sacrifice" to the world. It's why they tempt God. I will continue the rest of the chapter later. The chapters in Luke are long and cover multiple stories of Christ. We will see later in this chapter that Jesus again quotes scripture to the people and we should note that already in the past 3 chapters, and all through the book, the scriptures are referenced constantly. The law and Psalms and words of the prophets. Because, All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works. Man lives by every word of God. Biblical fundamentalism. That God's word is the only and final authority. All we need for doctrine that we may be perfect, whole, complete. It was good enough for Jesus in the desert against Satan. It is good enough for us today who follow Him. 1 Peter 5:8 Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour Deuteronomy 8:3 And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the Lord doth man live. 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them. Ephesians 6:12 For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Deuteronomy 6:13 Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name. 1 Samuel 7:3 And Samuel spake unto all the house of Israel, saying, If ye do return unto the Lord with all your hearts, then put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, and prepare your hearts unto the Lord, and serve him only: and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines. Deuteronomy 6:16 Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah. 1 Corinthians 10:9 Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents. Hebrews 4:15 For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Isaiah 61:1-2 The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound. To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn Picking up where we left off in Luke 4 yesterday, we find Jesus at the start of His earthly ministry. Having just been baptized and anointed by the Spirit, and proclaimed by the Father as His Son, and having fasted, prayed and withstanding the devil in the wilderness for 40 days, the Bible says Jesus was full of the power of the Spirit, and returned to His home province of Galilee, where He taught in the synagogues of God, gaining fame and renown throughout the area. We see that Jesus ministry begins in the remnant of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, outside of Judea, but preaching to the lost sheep of Israel. In these times, synagogues were the local churches of those who worshipped God. Where they would go, not only weekly on the Sabbath but throughout the week, to hear God's word read from scriptures, to pray and to learn about God's word. The Temple in Jerusalem was for feasts and sacrifices and pilgrims, but the communities abroad had independent, fundamentalist gatherings, or churches that people attended. Psalms 74:8 They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land. Note the Bible says there was a time synagogues were of God. It wasn't until after Christ where the unrepentant Jews were made a synagogue of Satan by the Lord, rejected. Reprobate. And Luke tells us that going to these houses of worship was Jesus' custom. It was His routine. Oh to be like Jesus and make going to church to read, hear and learn the word of God as part of our custom. To be our routine. And of course, just as churches are today, the synagogues were likely hit or miss in regards to what they taught, how they acted, if they produced fruit meet for repentance, if they were ice cold or lukewarm or red hot for the Lord. I am sure Jesus Christ Himself sat through boring sermons, by dull preachers who were wrong on doctrine, in congregations of people who were sinners and hypocrites or holier than thous. But it was Jesus' custom. And so, to begin His work, Jesus went to church. We should too. Now having established somewhat of a following throughout Galilee, Jesus returns to Nazareth, the town He grew up in. Where He lived as a child with Mary and Joseph, His half brothers and sisters. Where He developed the habit of going to synagogue. He returns full of the Spirit, and is called to read, and He preaches the prophecy of Christ from Isaiah 61:1-2 The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound; To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn; Note He leaves off the day of vengeance. That is His second coming. Here He is at His first. John 3:17 For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved. And so, Jesus reads this scripture foretelling His coming, and says, with every eye on Him; This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears. For those who doubt that Jesus ever proclaimed Himself to be the Christ, here He is saying precisely that. From the beginning. In no uncertain terms. And the crowd becomes incredulous. "Is this not the Son of Joseph?" They knew Him, watched Him grow, saw Him in synagogue. In response we are given the first record of Jesus preaching in Luke; Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country. And he said, Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country. In Mark 6, we get more detail of this part; A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house. Basically, those who know us best, whose familiarity has them over comfortable in their understanding. Many Christians can relate to this, where after being born again we try to share the good news with relatives or friends, and they, knowing us intimately, scoff. "You? I saw you that one time..." Or even just see us as the child they watched grow and can't accept that you've got something to offer them in your youth. It's why it can be difficult for a Christian to get members of his own family saved. And so, being rejected of His hometown crowd, Jesus doubles down and preaches even harder, using scripture. He says, citing 1 Kings 17, you remember Elijah, how he was rejected and shut up the heavens that it didn't rain for 3 and a half years? That in Israel was great famine? The Spirit led the prophet to a Gentile widow in the land of Zidon who, along with her son was about to die of hunger, having only one meager meal left between them. God sent Elijah there because of her faith. In the story she offers the food to the prophet in faith, even though it was all she had. And God works a miracle where they are all fed and sustained with what little she had until the time of famine was over. Jesus says, I bet there were many widows starving in Israel. But it was a Gentile woman who He saved. Then, Jesus mentions 2 Kings 5, and the prophet Elisha, where a Syrian, the captain of the hosts of the army of the king, suffered leprosy. Jesus says that many lepers were in Israel in the time, but it was this Gentile that God sent His prophet to heal. That the prophets were rejected of their own, and so the healing power of God, His blessings and promises went to others. To Gentiles. John 1:11 He came unto his own, and his own received him not. Jesus spitting fire, using scripture, He rebukes and reproaches His countrymen for their rejection of the word of God, the Gospel of truth He's brought to them, in a prefigure of the rejection He would face of the Jews at large, and prophesying God's turn to the Gentiles that would receive Him. And in a like manner, the crowd engaged at their own sin being pointed out, gathered to kill Jesus. They bring Him to the top of a hill, looking to cast Him off headlong. But Jesus, as He will do throughout His ministry after crowds of Jews offended by His hard preaching turn on Him, supernaturally passed by out of the crowd. His time having not yet come. Afterwards, we are told, Jesus came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them on the sabbath days. And they were astonished at his doctrine: for his word was with power. It was more fruitful here. And while He could not perform miracles in Nazareth by their lack of faith, here Jesus begins to heal multitudes. Luke being a physician focuses often on the healing power of Christ during his Gospel. A man possessed by an unclean devil is exercised, the demon recognizing Jesus as the Christ. Let us alone; what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art; the Holy One of God. And the people are amazed; with authority and power he commandeth the unclean spirits, and they come out. Luke tells us that Jesus heals Simon's mother, rebuking the fever she had, and being healed, she set about serving them food. Because of these miracles, a multitude brought their sick or possessed loved ones to be healed. And devils also came out of many, crying out, and saying, Thou art Christ the Son of God. And he rebuking them suffered them not to speak: for they knew that he was Christ. His time not yet come, and relying on the people to repent by faith, seen by the signs and hearing of the word, Jesus repeatedly tells the unclean spirits to be silent about who He is. And even when Jesus had left the city for the wilderness, to travel to other places with the word, the people followed Him. He gently reproaches them that He must go to others too. And so, His ministry grows throughout the land of Galilee. Now, one last thing. I wrote about this last night and want to reemphasize the point. The first public preaching of Jesus we are given in Luke is Jesus reading Isaiah's prophecy of His (first and second) coming; The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. As I point out in the linked post, this serves as a mission statement, the founding and guiding principle of Jesus ministry on earth. The same ministry we who are saved are called to continue, until He returns. Really ruminate on this verse. It is what we are appointed to do if we are following Christ. The application of this concept can change our lives as Christians. Don't miss it.

So we are there in Luke chapter 5, and we find Jesus ministry in Galilee is thriving. Multitudes are coming out to hear His preaching and to be healed of infirmities, cleansed of evil spirits and many who end up getting saved. One such is Simon, who we are told in the Gospel of John Jesus dubs Peter, or stone. Peter's brother Andrew, a follower of John the Baptist, tells his sibling "We have found the Messias," the Christ. The sons of Jonah were faithful to the coming of Christ. Peter was meet for repentance. It's in this context we see Jesus used Simon to enable Him to preach to the throng pressing Jesus up to the waters edge along the shore, by using his fishing boat which Peter, still Simon at this point, willingly allows Him to do. In recompense, Jesus performs a miracle, filling their nets to overflowing with fish after a night of fishing with no bites. When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord. It is in this manner we all come before Jesus for salvation. Calling upon the name of the Lord, in acknowledgement we are sinners and not worthy of Him. And Jesus tells Peter, Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee, James and John to follow Him, and become fishers of men. Just as we who seek to follow Jesus are called to do. Next Luke gives us an example of the healing that is a theme of his gospel, being a physician, in this the healing of a leaper who shows great faith and humility "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Again, a picture of the manner in which we are saved. Calling upon the mercy of the Lord to make us clean, with the faith to know He is able to. Jesus heals him, and cautions him to keep the manner of it to himself, but to go to the temple and offer the sacrifice for cleansing from leprosy given of Moses, found in Leviticus 14. It is a complicated ritual, one that must have seen little use in the times it was given in the law, as leprosy is untreatable and the healing from it coming only from a miracle. Yet Moses in the Spirit gives the process in the law, with specificity. I quoted only the first part of the ceremonial sacrifices, but it takes up basically an entire chapter. But nothing in the Bible is accidental, coincidental or incidental. First the leper goes to the priests who will send one out of the camp, out to the wilderness, to check the man and confirm they are healed. A testimony given, as Jesus says here. Then the priest must take two birds alive and clean, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop, and place one of the birds in an earthen vessel, and kill it, sprinkling the blood of the dead bird on the living bird, the wood, the scarlet cloth and the hyssop, and then sprinkle the blood from these items and the living bird on the healed man, 7 times, proclaiming him clean, and releasing the second bird to the wild. The bird in the earthen vessel, the clay that man is made from, as a substitutionary sacrifice, its blood upon wood, like the wood of the cross. On the scarlet, as the garments of Christ were so stained. On the hyssop, like the sprig dipped in vinegar, given to Jesus on the cross. And this blood of atonement then cleanses the man, and the living bird, like the risen Christ ascends to the heavens. The other sacrifices require lambs without blemish, etc, and are equally pictures of Christ Jesus. It's a fascinating chapter to read and study on. Placed in the OT that a testimony of Jesus could be made when he healed this man. We see a pattern in the Gospels, especially of Luke, where after successful outings in His ministry, Jesus would often go to the wilderness by Himself to pray and rest. This he does here and then, we pick up later He is gathering fame and multitudes are coming to see Him, especially that the sick may be healed. And so, the crowd surrounds a house where Jesus is teaching and healing, and in the crowd came Pharisees and scribes, "doctors of the law," come to see Jesus. A lame man, bedridden, is taken by 4 friends to be healed of Jesus, but they cannot find a way to get him through the crowd. But, so great is their faith that this miracle could be done, they devise a plan and climbing the building, lower their friend through the roof, down before Jesus. And Jesus, amazed at the faith and loyalty of him and his friends, says to the man "thy sins are forgiven thee." Not that he was healed physically, but by faith brought to forgiveness. Just as we are often brought to Jesus by our friends. Carried to this justification in faith by the faith of others. Just as we are to carry our own friends to the presence of the Lord. What love that is! And the Pharisees and lawyers wonder to themselves, "Who but God can forgive sin?" And Jesus knowing their hearts, answers; What reason ye in your hearts? Whether it is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Rise up and walk? But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power upon earth to forgive sins, (he said unto the sick of the palsy,) I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house. And the man, healed, leaps up and carrying his cot, leaves rejoicing and praising God. Everyone present is amazed. Many praise God for what they've witnessed. Some, filled with fear. Even the miracles and signs and wonders were not enough for them to believe. Only to say "We have seen strange things to day." Returning to Luke 5, we pick up with Jesus calling a publican named Levi, who we know as Matthew, who we're told, left all, rose up, and followed Jesus. Now publicans, who worked for the occupational governments of the Roman empire collecting duties and taxes, were looked down upon by the the people under their jurisdiction, who naturally resent their fellow countrymen serving the foreign state against them, and were often as corrupt and crooked as they still are today. Further, Matthew was of the tribe of Levi, who were called to be the priesthood under the Old Testament, and so must have been particularly a pariah in these times. But by faith he answers the call and leaves all to follow Christ. And for him, as it is for us, his salvation is a cause for celebration. He has wealth and status among others in his profession, and calls those he knows together a feast, inviting Jesus and His disciples. To this, as is often the case throughout the Gospels, the envious and bitter Jews, in this case the Pharisees, see the opportunity to criticize Jesus, asking why he is hanging out with sinners like Levi/Matthew. To which, Jesus replies "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." This is the purpose of Christ's ministry and our commission to give the Gospel to the poor. To the heartbroken. To those in bondage to sin. To set them at liberty with the good news of salvation. Just as Jesus stated in His reading of Isaiah 61 that we just covered; It is the mission statement of the Lord. Also detect a hint of rebuke, in that Jesus mentions the righteous in this saying somewhat sarcastically to give a ribbing to the self-righteous Pharisees. They, of course respond with another accusation, questioning why Jesus' disciples don't routinely fast as they do. (They lump John the Baptist's followers in there to lend themselves some of his credibility.) But, Jesus knows their hearts, that they are vipers. Hypocrites. As He tells in a parable later on in Luke 18 that seems based on exactly this encounter: Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted. Note that the Pharisees took pride in their ritual fasting, as well as their tithing and temple attendance and all the rest. They saw themselves as righteous by their works and better than, holier than, the humble publican, a sinner who may not have done these rituals and rites but who understands his place and the undeserved mercy and grace of the Lord. There are commandments of the Lord that we are given, things He tells us we must do. We must believe the Gospel. We must share it with others, for example. Then there are things we are expected to do, but not commanded as such. We are not told we must fast, but Jesus tells us how to when we do; Matthew 6:16-18 Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. Notice He says "when you fast." It is assumed we will fast, at the appropriate time, called by the Spirit, when we have a need to align ourselves to God's will and build our faith. Fasting in the Bible wasn't a sign of righteousness or a way to get God to do our will, but usually done at a sign of trouble or turmoil in the person's life. A death in the family, a tough or perilous time. At the beginning of a trial. Like Jesus in the wilderness before beginning His ministry. A way to align ourselves with the will of God that we may better understand and come to peace with it. That the Spirit may move in us and increase our faith as we deny our flesh. Fasting isn't to earn brownie points with God, to get him to do our will. It most certainly isn't done in an outward sign to earn the approval of men. Understanding this, and that the Pharisees had the wrong idea about what fasting's purpose is, and how righteousness is achieved, Jesus replies to their accusation; Can ye make the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days. He says, do you make people who are celebrating to fast? Is that the time or place for it? Each of us may be called to fast, in our own time and need by the Spirit. But that's not something to judge another by, if your time is now and theirs isn't. You aren't better than they are, or more righteous or spiritual because you've given yourself to fast. And if you're doing it in the correct spirit, you'd know it. But further, Jesus is saying His time is short. That He will be gone from their presence and they will have time appointed to them for fasting then. Not content with that upbraiding of these hypocrites, He continues with another parable. Parables are common examples that may be understood on their own, to better illustrate a more difficult concept. Jesus says, if you have an old garment to mend, you don't sew a new cloth to patch it. Because the new cloth will shrink, it will pull the stitching ripping it worse than it was. That the new isn't in agreement with the old. It doesn't match. It will wear differently. And in a like manner, newly squeezed juice isn't put into old wine bottles. (Bottles being leather casks, designed to be water-tight to store liquids). Wine in the Bible means all juices, fresh or fermented, and I won't get into that but the drunkards seethe at this when it is pointed out. And new wine, fresh juice, of put into an old, dried out and worn cask, an old bottle, as it begins to ferment will give off gasses, expanding inside the bottle, causing it to be ruined and the wine to spill out. (While they had ways to preserve juice to prevent fermentation into alcohol, for longer term storage, most was pressed and bottled to be consumed before it could naturally occur). These two examples of things common to that day, before modern mass consumerism gave us plastic bottles and eliminated the need to patch clothing, were things people could understand. And Jesus used it to make a point to the Pharisees who were touting their own righteousness. They are the torn and ratty clothes. They are the warn and old bottles. What Jesus was bringing was new. A new and better testament. A new and better covenant. He wasn't there to fix the tear they'd made in their disobedience. He was going to replace it. He wasn't there to refill their old, dried and cracked bottles, but to give new wine in bottles fit to hold it. He says "No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better." He is calling them out and saying why they cannot understand Him or His preaching, or the behavior of those who desired this new thing. He's saying no wonder you don't get it. They are drunk on old wine. They can't understand the new thing He is replacing the old with. It is this same point we just studied in Hebrews 8; But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second. For finding fault with them, he saith, Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord. This is the "replacement theology" that Zionists deny. Jesus is proclaiming a more excellent ministry, the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises. It doesn't say Except for the Jews. Hebrews is literally written to them. It doesn't say the Old Testament and New are coequal. The old covenant was glorious, but the fault was in the people to keep it. And so God regards them not. But in Christ, a new testament, a better covenant with better promises, one that has no fault because it doesn't require our perfection, only His. And those still caught up in the old ways, thinking their righteousness before man was the same as righteousness before God, they refused to see it and took no heed to the parables of Jesus.

In chapter 5, and now again in Luke chapter 6, we see the Pharisees seeking to accuse Jesus, that they may discredit Him and His growing ministry. Particularly, they are seeking to shame Him and His disciples for their failure to keep certain ordinances, carnal ceremony, given both by tradition and under the law of Moses, among these ordinances are things like the fasting of meats(food), ceremonial washings(Matthew 15:12) and the keeping of the sabbath, the day of rest, as we see here. The Bible says these ordinances were given in the OT as a picture, a shadow, to remind the people of the promise of the coming Christ, that they not forget and hold fast to the faith preached unto them, until the day of reformation. That is, until the things they are foreshadowing come true. Until Christ comes. At that time Jesus figuratively nails them to the cross with Himself. They are over and done, having served their purpose. And, with the ordinances ended, the Bible says, so too was the regard God had for the nation of Israel. They were to either believe or perish, the same as the Gentiles. Thus the destruction of the Temple in 70AD, least any confusion remain. And of these ordinances, the keeping of the sabbath was probably the most important, that the people would enter into God's rest, understanding that His work was finished at the time of creation. A picture man could understand, working 6 days and resting the 7th as God did. Forbidden work, because God did it all in regards to salvation. It is a picture of salvation by faith alone in His perfect, meaning complete, works, finished by the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world. But man is simple, and foolish and superstitious. The things of God that are a physical picture of the spiritual application He seeks to teach us, becomes an end unto itself in vain tradition. Many, with an autistically literal approach, put the power in the picture, not the things that are being pictured. And example is given in the OT, in Numbers 21 where by unbelief the Hebrews in the desert were beset by poisonous snakes, fiery serpents. Many were bit and were dying in agony. God, as an object lesson in the Christ to come, had Moses lift up a brazen snake, made of molten brass and formed, upon a tall wooden pole. This represented Christ and the crucifixion, where Jesus became all sin for us. He said to the people if you look up on this picture of salvation you'll be healed. Lesson learned. We know this was a picture of Jesus, because it was explained in John 3: And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. But we are told that hundreds of years later, the Israelites had lost the purpose and understanding that this picture served. In 2 Kings 4 Hezekiah became king and had to right many of the wrongs in the land; He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan. The picture of the spiritual became a physical idol. The Heavenly lesson became bonds of the carnal. This is where the Pharisees, Sadducees and scribes are at in the time of Christ. They have lost sight of the spiritual application for these things, and worship the symbol instead. And so the carnal ordinances were to them an idol. And the work of their flesh in keeping these things replaced their faith in the Lord. They became self-righteous. They used the keeping of these ordinances as how one becomes righteous, rather than faith in what it represents, the Christ to come. And so, they become holier than thou hypocrites. And later, Judaizers seeking to impose their vain traditions on the newly born again Gentiles. Circumcision, sacrifices, and the keeping of holy days such as the sabbath. And as we see here in the first part of chapter 6, Jesus and His disciples are out on a sabbath, doing the work of the Lord, and being hungry, gleaned a field of corn to eat. And the Pharisees seeking to accuse Him, (doing the work of their father the devil, Satan the accuser) call them out for doing work on the sabbath. And Jesus reminds them, again using scripture, that David and his men when they were about the king's business on the Sabbath, ate the ceremonial shewbread of the tabernacle. He says "the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath." Doing the business of the Lord is greater than these ordinances given for man's benefit, in other words. The same incident recorded in Mark 2:27, He adds "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." In a like manner, when Jesus heals a man on the sabbath, earlier casting out a devil, here, healing the withered hand. Before doing it He says to the Jews who were waiting to accuse Him, "Is it lawful on the sabbath days to do good, or to do evil? to save life, or to destroy it?" knowing there are always exceptions given to the keeping of the ordinances in the Law for things like helping someone, rescuing livestock, etc. And so Jesus heals the man defiantly, fully justified. This sends the Jews into a rage, and they begin to plot against Him. Finishing this section, and the understanding of ordinances and their proper place in our faith, it is important to note that while the ordinances of the Old Testament were done away with in Christ, there are two new ordinances made to which we should adhere. Baptism and the common blessing and eating of bread and drink, communion, what we call the Lord's supper. Just as the ordinances of the OT held no actual power to forgive sin or earn grace, but were a picture of the Christ to come, so too the ordinances we are told to keep are an image of Christ, a long shadow cast that we remember Him, and the faith we share as saved believers. In baptism, the believer is immersed in water, dead, buried and risen in the manner reminiscent of Jesus. Going down into death symbolically, and rising up out of the water, born again. The Lord's supper, likewise, where we are asked by Jesus to remember what He has done for us, the breaking of His body and the spilling of His blood that we may be saved. To recall this when we gather together in an assembly of believers to eat. Not just blessing the food in His name, but seeing the picture of His sacrifice in the breaking of bread and sharing of the wine (juice, not booze). "Do this in remembrance of Me." This is the purpose of these ordinances, just as the numerous ordinances of the old covenant were. But, like the Jews at the time of Jesus, the ordinance of the flesh representing the spiritual, become an idol unto themselves, and mistakenly transformed into a work of righteousness. A means of salvation. A means of obtaining grace, (which is an oxymoron). Some heretical and judaized churches even place keeping of the sabbath as an ordinance, and a work required for salvation, despite the clear teaching that this was a picture, and done away with in the new covenant. And just like the Pharisees, many have replaced ordinances made for man with requiring the man be made for the ordinance. And just as the Pharisees' approach led to hypocrisy and their inability to produce fruit, men ripe for repentance, create with their false gospel proselytes twofold more the child of hell than themselves. Damnable heresy. And so, to sum up if it wasn't clear enough already, things like circumcision, keeping the sabbath, blood sacrifice, ritual washings, dietary requirements, all were always a picture of Christ and had no power to save anyone, cleanse sin or earn grace. And the ordinances we keep today are the same, a picture of Christ, not a means to salvation. Not a way to gain favor or mercy, but a reminder of the faith we share as Christians, in appreciation for the Lord's perfect work. This study is the meat of the word, it's hard for many to digest. The vain traditions of those who claim Christ but teach their own wisdom, rejecting the word of God as the only authority and twisting scripture to defend their doctrines of devils, has beguiled many. And so we are warned; Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind. (BTW, that goes for praying to dead "saints," as angels) People take doctrine from out of context verses, or partial text, and using the logic of man, puffed up in their fleshly mind, work out by fallacious implications that their heretical doctrines are actually Biblical. They fail to square plainly stated and often repeated clear doctrines that directly contradict their own. They take literal readings of parables that they don't understand, and apply their carnal mind to the Spirit. They are like Nicodemus, the Pharisee who questioned Jesus in John 3, unable to understand the parables about being born twice, once of water from the womb, again in Spirit, reborn by faith. They become like the disciples offended by His parable in John 6, where He compares Himself to manna, bread come down from Heaven that we must "eat." They thought this was some sort of cannibalistic blasphemy, despite Jesus explaining "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life." Even today, many take parables and metaphors, pictures of the spiritual and make for themselves a physical idol of it. Missing the point. And so you have denominations claiming to believe that salvation is by faith alone, still maintaining that sprinkling of infants and ritualistic eating of bread and drinking of wine bestows salvation, or keeps it. That works must be done to shore up that which is by faith alone. The contradictions lost on them, as is salvation. Mark 1:35 And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed Matthew 26:39 And he went a little farther, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt Hebrews 5:7 Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared. Luke 3:21 Now when all the people were baptized, it came to pass, that Jesus also being baptized, and praying, the heaven was opened. Luke 11:1 And it came to pass, that, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said unto him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples Luke 5:16 And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed Luke 6:12-19 And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God. And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples: and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles; Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon called Zelotes, And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor. And he came down with them, and stood in the plain, and the company of his disciples, and a great multitude of people out of all Judaea and Jerusalem, and from the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, which came to hear him, and to be healed of their diseases; And they that were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed. And the whole multitude sought to touch him: for there went virtue out of him, and healed them all. Jesus prayed. He who was God made flesh, repeatedly and habitually withdraws Himself to prayer. He prays to God at the start of His ministry. He prays during the highs and lows. He diligently seeks God the Father as He prepared to make important decisions, such as appointing apostles from His disciples. He prayed before giving up His life that we may be saved. Jesus, who knows God the Father in a way none of us alive in the flesh can possibly even comprehend, went to His knees in prayer to talk to the Father and seek His will that it may be done in service of what the Lord God wanted. Jesus prayed. And when asked to give a model of prayer, an example, He said: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen. (Note He says "after this manner," not to take it and mindlessly repeat it, in vain repetition as the heathen do, believing they will be heard for much speaking. It's a model to follow) What Jesus shows us in this model of prayer is that first we praise God. We aren't worthy but come before Him in supplication in Christ's name. All glory is given the Father. His will be done. That is the first thing we must ask for, because in it is everything we need. If God's will is revealed to us and being done, our basic and banal needs will be taken care of. God who loves us already knows those. But it is our conforming ourselves to His will that is the primary purpose of prayer. We should ask for forgiveness, and the mercy that we can likewise forgive. This is gratitude. Protection from sin, from our flesh, the desires of this world. And all this because He is deserving all the glory and praise. And so Jesus prayed. The Bible tells us repeatedly, throughout scripture that those seeking to succeed sought God's will. Those making decisions and setting out on missions, facing persecution, dealing with grief and heartache, struggling in sin...Sought God in prayer that His will be done and that they who sought Him could come to see it His way. Not my will, but yours, o Lord. And if even Jesus prayed frequently, often all night, praying without ceasing, so should we who are following in His name. Here in Luke 6, before selecting the 12 who would be the main Apostles, "ones who are sent forth," the leaders of the evangelists Jesus was appointing to help in His growing ministry, drawn from His hundreds of disciples we are told that Jesus prayed all night. And in His desire to do the Father's will, made the choice of the 12, knowing one was a traitor. A viper from the beginning. But it was the will of God that He be betrayed, that the promise of God could be kept and salvation come into the world by that betrayal. By knowing the formula for prayer given by Christ, and as perfectly exemplified by His tearful prayers in the garden of Gethsemane before His trials and crucifixion, Jesus didn't seek to get God to bend to His will, which was to have the cup pass from Him, but to do that will of He Who sent Him. This is something we should keep in mind. Seek first the kingdom of God. He will see to our needs, that we can rely on. But doing His will and being at peace with it, is something we must constantly pray for. For those that may have missed it, this weekend we went over the first two sections of Luke 6, scroll up if you missed it, they are important studies on the sabbath and other ordinances of the old and new covenant, and how Jesus' prayer life can inspire us to be more diligent in prayer to ascertain God's will. Here in the last 30 verses of Luke 6, we are given a lot of red-letter preaching from Jesus, and it's all important, and much of it is self explanatory. Jesus is the truth and speaks it here without using dark sayings and parables, as He begins addressing His disciples directly. You'll notice the section begins with the masses, the multitudes, coming to Jesus to be healed. His fame has grown, the miraculous events being even more people who seek to be made whole of their infirmities, and the "virtue flowed out" of Jesus to heal them. Again, a focus of Luke, being a physician, is the nature of Jesus as a healer. Note what the Bible says; And he came down with them, and stood in the plain, and the company of his disciples, and a great multitude of people out of all Judaea and Jerusalem, and from the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, which came to hear him, and to be healed of their diseases; And they that were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed. And the whole multitude sought to touch him: for there went virtue out of him, and healed them all.And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said... Now, to increase the reach of His ministry and to serve those He can with the multitudes coming, Jesus had prayed and appointed of His disciples 12 Apostles, ordained of the ministry He was about, finding the lost sheep of Israel. Disciples, those who followed Him to learn, many who were saved believers, some were not (Judas for example). The 12 Apostles would be joined by 70 or so more at a later point in His earthly ministry, were those qualified to be sent out, to the highways and hedges, to preach and heal in His name. These disciples had left their lives and professions behind to follow Christ. They were poor, often hungry (earlier they were gleaning a field for some corn to eat), they moved about with His ministry, walking the wastes between towns and cities. God provides, but they were sacrificing to be Jesus' students. But the multitudes, we are told repeatedly, flocked to see Jesus that they may be healed by proximity, to take the virtue that came out of Him. To witness a miracle or to see a sign. Of these mobs, most didn't come to a saving faith, despite what they witnessed, even those affected first hand. Some did to be sure, but most didn't as we are reminded at the crucifixion where the same people who lauded the coming of the son of David with palm fans and hosannas, days later called for His blood. They were there, like many transient "Christians" today, just there for the show. In this context, the transition here in Luke chapter 6 is interesting. The mob presses on Jesus to be healed of their ailments, but Jesus looks from His work to address directly His disciples with this sermon, and the first topic is on humility. He says blessed are you who are poor, hungry, in tears now, because you will be inheriting the Kingdom of God, your needs will be met. This application is not only for them that followed Christ then, but a comfort to us as well, today. And with that comfort, comes a warning. He says to His disciples that they will also receive persecution, just as the prophets did, and from the very people that surrounded them as Jesus healed. The Jews' fathers treated the prophets like criminals and often killed them for the truth they preached. In a like manner they will be persecuted, but, Jesus say "Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy," when this happens to you. It's a blessing to be persecuted for His name's sake. And you can sense that Jesus then begins speaking loudly, turning His voice to the crowds. Still talking to His disciples, but addressing those surrounding them: But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep. Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets. Hard preaching, fire-breathing. Jesus wasn't a dainty and soft man. His preaching went hard, the Bible says He spoke with authority. Boldness. He never hesitated to put on blast those who needed to be reproached. Fire and brimstone. Out of His mouth proceeded a two-edged sword. The word of God. And again, He turns to His disciples and gives them a practical application for what He has given them. That these people who praised the false prophets while killing the messengers of God, and will likewise persecute those who do good in His name may be your enemies for the Gospel's sake, but that doesn't mean to hate them, but rather: I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you. And unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other... This is the part of the preaching of Christ that those who don't know or understand call "weak." They remove the context to make Jesus sound like he only taught love and peace, like a hippy. But we have the context. He's just ripped face to condemn the very masses He is serving with healing and casting out unclean spirits, for their fickleness and worldly lusts. Verily they have their reward...but blessed are those who have the Kingdom of Heaven. He says love them, turn the other cheek, if they defraud you or spoil you (meaning to take your stuff), let them. If they persecute you, rejoice. Pity your enemies. They don't have what you got. He's saying you have it better than them and it's true. It may not seem like it in the moment. You may be hungry. You may be without, poor. You may be hated of your own family for the preaching of the Gospel. But you're blessed. And woe to the rich, and woe to the satisfied. Woe to those that curse the blessed, who spoil the meek, who, like their fathers, kill the prophets and reject the word of truth. Pity them. They are perishing. They will have their reward. Eternal fire and torment without end. But we have a different fate. We have been saved by grace, a gift we didn't deserve, given by the mercy of God despite our being just as these others were. Perishing. Pulled out of the fire by His blood, and called by the Spirit that we may believe, and in faith be made heirs with Him in the Kingdom of God. And so, love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful. We were that unthankful and evil. Sure we love those who love us, and do good to them, and lend to others. But sinners do all that too. That's easy. But we have an unearned gift, made sons of the Most High. And to whom much is given, much is expected. Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven: Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again. Some of the most misunderstood and misused scripture in the entire Bible. But in context we see what Jesus is saying to us. He isn't saying to simply stand for evil, not judging the actions of others, but to put in perspective their condition with the understanding of our own. We who are saved have been judged. We know we have fallen short. We know we needed mercy and the longsuffering of God to come to where we are. Not of ourselves. Humbled by it, we are called to be merciful as God is merciful. That's the context here. God hates evil and gives wrath as recompense for those who hate Him. Vengeance is His. And so, we are called to consider the beam in our own eye, that we may help our neighbors with the mote in theirs. To not be as the half blind, stumbling in the darkness. To be a light that leads others to the truth. To reflect the love and mercy that God gave us, that others may be saved, drawn to the truth by our conversation. Thou hypocrite, cast out first the beam out of thine own eye, and then shalt thou see clearly to pull out the mote that is in thy brother's eye. Jesus doesn't say do nothing about the mote in your brother's eye. He says be in a condition where you can see clearly to help them. By living the faith we share, blessed, and knowing the woe that is upon them. For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit; neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: True servants of God bring forth good fruit. Others brought to salvation. False prophets, bad fruit. Damned. What is it your heart treasures? The mercy and grace of God? Or your petty resentments and grudges? What does what you say and what you do speak of you? ...for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh. What do you treasure in your heart? It is revealed to all by your behavior. By what you say. By our grace and love to others, and our patience having faith in our reward. Or by our petty hypocrisy. Our wrath and fear and envy. Do we produce good fruit, or cultivate evil around us? Finally, Jesus challenges His disciples, and by extension those of us who call ourselves His followers. He asks pointedly: And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say? He is giving us the truth. The word of God. But are we hearers of the word, or doers? Do we, in pride, in shortsightedness, despise the gift we've been given, or look to live like we understand the blessing it is? God has given us His word that we may know His will. Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them, I will shew you to whom he is like: He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock. But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great. This is a promise. One we can count on, if we do it. If we live by His word, which is like a foundation of rock, we will not be moved. If we don't, but lean into our own understanding, we are building on shifting sands. To be washed away. Therefore let us build on that rock. Luke 6:17-38 And he came down with them, and stood in the plain, and the company of his disciples, and a great multitude of people out of all Judaea and Jerusalem, and from the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, which came to hear him, and to be healed of their diseases; And they that were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed. And the whole multitude sought to touch him: for there went virtue out of him, and healed them all. And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said, Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh. Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man's sake. Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets. But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you. For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.
