Hebrews 11:1-2 Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. For by it the elders obtained a good report. Luke chapter 7 is a study on faith. The faith of the Roman centurion. The faith of John the Baptist. The faith of those who follow him and Jesus. The faith of the Pharisees. And the faith of the woman who washed Jesus' feet. Rich in faith, and poor in faith. Unquestioning, lacking and unsure. The chapter opens after Jesus' sermon on the plain in Chapter 6. After he'd finished speaking, we learn of a certain centurion's servant, who was dear unto him, was sick, and ready to die. And when he heard of Jesus, he sent unto him the elders of the Jews, beseeching him that he would come and heal his servant. So we get the picture. A Roman centurion, a Gentile, stationed in the region, who commanded as an officer of the empire, one hundred men. A man of power and prestige, who has a servant he loves. A slave, for Roman citizens' servants were slaves. But a person he cared for dearly, who is near death. And hearing of Jesus and the miracles and signs and wonders He had done reported throughout the region, the Centurion sees hope for his friend whom he loves. In his heart, the Centurion sees the evidence of something not seen. And his faith hangs on the substance of his hope in Jesus. And it is in this manner he uses his influence to call in a favor. He asks prominent Jews to approach Jesus and ask Him for help. Jews who he had authority over, but who the Centurion had treated well, even building for them a synagogue. And they come and testify to Jesus that this man is a good man, and worthy of His aid. And so Jesus goes with the Jews to the centurion's home. Before getting there, again the Centurion has sent proxies, this time to say "Lord, trouble not thyself: for I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof." The man to whom others testified that he was worthy. Who we see is a loving and just man. A man of faith. Who does for others, even the lowliest of his house, a slave. This great man that others testified was worthy and just and good says, ashamed to even be in the presence of the Son of God, "I am not worthy of you, but only say the word and my servant will be healed." Because the Centurion is familiar with power and authority. How it works, how it flows. That even by faith, power moves to achieve what his will is, that if he order men to do this or that, it is done. He can know it will be so. And so he understands by this that Jesus, who he believes has this power, has this authority, needn't come to him to save his servant. He has faith of Jesus commands that he be healed, he will be made whole. And Jesus, moved with compassion and wonder at his faith, turns to the Jews and others round about, and says "I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel." And they return to the house to find the servant healed. The humility and love that this man, a Gentile, showed others gave to him the understanding of who Jesus was. And the faith that such a thing would be possible led him to humbly ask for this miracle, for the good of another. To have faith in God as strong as this, we see, comes with compassion, humility, love for others. And the Centurion's faith is a model for ours. We come to repentance, to turn towards God in humility. With faith like a child's. Knowing that we will be healed. That faith grows in our service for others. Where we magnify the faith that saved us by doing the will of God, in service to those that are sick. Not sick of the flesh, though we are led to comfort them, but sick in the spirit. To hold others as dear to us. Not because of status or what they can do for us, but selflessly, genuinely caring for others. In that way we work out our faith that it benefiting others, may grow, and spread to them. That they may be healed as we were. By faith. Next, we are given an example of the compassion of Christ. Almost as an aside, an interlude to the events of the chapter, we are given one of the greatest miracles of Jesus' ministry. Jesus comes to a city with an entourage. His disciples and those who were following just to witness the wonders and signs, healing and casting out of devils. Spectators and believers alike. And here they find a funeral procession, a bereaved mother burying her son who is being carried by pallbearers to the grave. And the Bible says, Jesus moved with compassion for the mother approaches and touches the body and resurrects her son. In the witness of many, the Bible says Jesus raised the dead. Many wonder at the sight, praising God. It's an unimaginable event to witness. But what strikes me every time I read it is the compassion shown of Jesus. He sees a mother heartbroken and grieving, a stranger. A woman he doesn't know. No one has sought him to intervene. No one like the centurion humbly coming before Hm. But Jesus moved with compassion does what he can to comfort the brokenhearted. And with the power He has, He raises the boy from the dead. This brings to mind the verse from Isaiah that Jesus read at the beginning of His ministry. What I have been calling His mission statement; The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. And this is our mission statement too. Those who seek to follow Christ. The Bible tells us in James 1:27: Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. Love one another. Our neighbors. Our enemies. To entertain the stranger, because in doing so we may be entertaining the angels of God. To be, like the Centurion, someone who cares about others and uses his power that others may profit. To have compassion for the brokenhearted, and like Jesus, do what we can to comfort them. And so this act, and others like it, begin to be spread throughout the land. All of Judea hears the rumors of Christ; That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his people. And hearing this word go out, many come to faith. Yet others find their faith shaken and tested. John the Baptist, in prison for his preaching of repentance at the coming of Christ, hearing these things. In bonds, separated from the outside world, probably feeling occasional despair. Doubt. And so hearing of these signs and wonders, John seeks to know; is Jesus the Christ as he believed? Is it his faith confirmed? Is it too good to be true? And so, he sends disciples to ask Jesus, directly. Art thou he that should come? or look we for another? The Bible doesn't give us an immediate answer from Jesus. He doesn't tell them, He shows. That very hour Jesus heals infirmities and casts out spirits. Restoring sight to the blind. Then Jesus answered. He says tell John what you have seen. Jesus doesn't argue His divinity or that He is the Christ. He lets His actions justify Him before man, that they may know and believe, and bring this good news to John. How that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached. His mission statement. The prophecy of Isaiah made real. James 2:22 Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect? We are saved by faith alone. Justified before God in Christ. Not of our dead works. In much the same way, John's faith in Jesus being the Christ that he hoped for, that he believed in, is made perfect by the work Jesus did. By the witness and testimony of what those disciples had seen. His doubt assuaged, I am sure. And Jesus adds; And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me. Offended in the Gospels means shaken of faith. Turned aside from the correct path by shame or doubt or the behavior of another. By false teachings. And here Jesus is saying that we who aren't shaken, who are not ashamed of the Gospel, who aren't troubled by the truth of who Christ is and what He has done for us, are blessed. The antithesis of Mark 8:38: Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels. It is ok to have doubts. To seek a confirmation for the hope we have, but at the end of the day we are to believe the report. To trust God and His promises. To believe the witness of others, and to hear His word and have faith, unashamed. For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth... And when the messengers of John departed, Jesus begins to preach to the crowds about John the Baptist. Praising him, but reminding them that to be saved, in Heaven is an even greater thing than even being the greatest prophet among men that ever lived. I get the sense that what Jesus is doing is shoring up John's reputation least any think his doubt was an indictment of the Gospel he had preached. And the crowd responds. The Bible says: And all the people that heard him, and the publicans, justified God, being baptized with the baptism of John. Now note the word choice here. Most times when we read "justified" we think of being absolved, the remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment by grace through faith in Christ. But note here Luke says the people who heard Jesus, including the sinners like the publicans (who Luke uses often to contrast with the Pharisees, both men of power, secular and sinful vs who are supposed to be holy and righteous), but he writes these people who heard Jesus preach and His praise of John and his ministry JUSTIFIED GOD, being baptized in the baptism of John. I think this is a key point we shouldn't miss. Clearly God is not being absolved of sin here. Justified is also used in a legal sense, meaning vindication. That the evidence is sufficient to prove the argument being made. To show that they believed the report, accepted the witness, agreed with the argument, they were baptized, justifying God. But the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, being not baptized of him. You see how the act of baptism by believers justifies God, while the rejection of His counsel, not believing Him, not having that faith, is evidenced by their not being baptized. How faith is made perfect, complete, by an action that is an outward sign to man of the heart of the person, just as the refusal to act shows the abundance of the heart of those who didn't believe. Baptism itself doesn't save. It is a manifestation of the faith, the substance of things not seen, that can be seen of men. And by not justifying God, the Pharisees show they do not believe. Finishing up Luke chapter 7, Jesus had just dealt with the doubting of John the Baptist by proxy, the disciples of John sent away having seen the signs and wonders of Jesus, after asking for confirmation that He was who John, sitting in prison, believed. Having heard rumors and gossip, and tales of extraordinary miracles, even the raising of the dead, John's faith had been tested. Was it too good to be true? And Jesus gives a sermon to those there to reaffirm that John was the greatest prophet born of men. Not a reed bent by the wind. Not as the Pharisees and Sadducees, decked in fine and comfortable clothes. He came to the wilderness wearing sackcloth and preaching repentance unto salvation, by faith in the coming Christ. And by this, even more sinners believed and we're baptized, justifying God. But the Pharisees didn't believe and rejected the counsel of God. And so Jesus, preaching to the crowd but referring to the "holy men," asks rhetorically, what can He compare them to? He says they are like children at play. Kids playing a game, where they pretend to be at a feast, or playact a funeral march, and who are angry when prophets like John or Jesus do not act in the manner they think they should. "We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned to you, and ye have not wept." It's a deeply insulting comparison. Jesus is pointing out their childishness. Their spiritual immaturity and petulance. That they expect the prophets of God to play the same game of hypocrisy and pretend that they call holy and righteous, with flowing robes of comfortable and rich clothing, sitting in sanctimonious judgment of others, while, as Jesus says elsewhere, they are actually vipers. Frauds. Playacting. But wisdom is justified of all her children. That is, again using justified in the same manner as earlier in the chapter, it is evidenced. Validated. The children of wisdom here is the fruit of the judgment of these men. Their earthly wisdom is seen by the fruit it has produced. Jesus is saying basically, you've rejected the counsel of God, had poor judgment of John, and now of me, and your wisdom, or lack thereof, is evidenced by the children it has produced. People unable to come to the knowledge of the truth, and who will be gathered and burned like chaff. Finally, we see Jesus invited to dinner at the home of a Pharisee named Simon. He goes and as they are reclined at supper, a woman, identified only as a sinner, arrives and in humility and sorrowful thanks, washes Jesus feet with her tears, wiping them with her hair, and anointing them with expensive perfumed oils. The hypocritical Simon, outwardly righteous in his ways, separated and sanctified to himself by his own works and station, thinks to himself that if Jesus were actually a prophet, He would know she's a wicked sinner and not allow her to touch Him. And sensing this, Jesus tells a parable of a man forgiven little and another forgiven much. And He asks Simon which would be more appreciative to the creditor who forgave these debts? Simon rightly answers, the one forgiven much would show more love to the creditor. Because as a Pharisee, he would keep the law, maintain outward appearances, sin little, but this woman was openly known for sin. Maybe fornication. Maybe whoredoms. It doesn't say, but the hypocrisy of Simon is laid bare. Jesus says to him, Simon, you see this woman? This woman you judged as more sinful than you? Unlike you, my supposed host, who is supposed to be a loving and caring man of God, who may be a debtor of a little, as far as the Pharisees judgement goes, didn't offer Me water to wash my feet. Didn't welcome me affectionately. Didn't anoint Me with oil, or any hospitality expected by a righteous man of God, who in his gratitude for being forgiven would extend love to a guest, especially a prophet, especially the Son of God. Jesus is pointing out the lack of judgment and discernment, that Simon's priorities are backwards and hypocritical. Because this woman whom he judged unworthy, in tears and humility, did what she could to honor Him, who she believed had the power to forgive her sins. And Jesus says Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little. And to her, Thy sins are forgiven. The guests at the table question in their hearts who is Jesus to forgive sin? Only God is able to. He is all but telling them directly who He is, and they still don't see it. Yet this woman they look down on understood completely. And Jesus looks on the woman and says "Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace." BTW there is the proof text from Jesus own mouth, red-lettered, the woman who is a great sinner is saved by faith alone. That faith in Christ, her salvation, means she is forgiven her debt, and she shows great love and gratitude in return. He didn't say your works have saved you. Jesus flat out says her love for Him is due to her having been forgiven already. She isn't saved because she showed Him love and hospitality, with humility and sorrow for the sins she's done. Her faith saved her. The love she showed Him followed. In contrast, Simon the Pharisee, who believed he was righteous by his works, his keeping the vain traditions and ceremony of men, along with the letter of the law, couldn't come to be saved, lacking the faith. Despite owing little, he couldn't see the Christ, the redeemer sitting in his own house. His judgment, his wisdom, justified by its children. Revealed by its fruits, and found wanting. Another "Lenten" reminder that the concept of penance for sin is in direct contradiction with salvation by grace, and a slap in the face to the finished work of Jesus Christ, who died and suffered Hell for our sins that we may be forgiven. Fasting is meant to help a saved Christian better understand the will of God that their faith grows, that they may accept it and do that will, to the benefit of others. To feed the spiritual new man by neglecting the old man of the flesh. It is not to give "penance" for the sins Jesus already paid the price for, in a selfish effort to obtain forgiveness which is given to us freely by the grace of God. The Bible says telling people to abstain from certain foods as a means of holiness is a doctrine of devils. The idea of penance doesn't exist in scripture. In fact, it is an affront to the Gospel of grace. Reject these doctrines of devils and rely on the perfect work of Christ alone as the propitiation for your sin. Isaiah 58 Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins. 2 Yet they seek me daily, and delight to know my ways, as a nation that did righteousness, and forsook not the ordinance of their God: they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in approaching to God. 3 Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge? Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours. 4 Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high. 5 Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord? 6 Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? 7 Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh? 8 Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the Lord shall be thy reward. 9 Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity; 10 And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noon day: 11 And the Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not. 12 And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in. 13 If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words: 14 Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it. This chapter of Isaiah is incredibly relevant here. The opening verse, one of the most famous lines used by preachers for millennia. The LORD tells the prophet Isaiah, preaching in the Spirit to cry aloud, to tell His people, the house of Jacob of their inequities. To reprove them of their sins. God, anticipating the protests of the people who may resist the idea that they are guilty before Him, says yet they seek Me daily and delight in my ways, they do the ordinances of the law, the works. The sacrifices and the offerings and the dietary laws and carnal ordinances. They delight in doing these things. They may say, Didn't we fast? Lord didn't you notice? We afflicted ourselves, and you didn't see? Didn't we fast on your day, Lord? And God answers this rhetorical question for us; He doesn't regard their fasting and self affliction, because they are doing it for themselves selfishly, while they are openly oppressing others. It's not a spiritual act of humility, but arrogant and prideful. God says to them that they fast for strife and debate. To hold it over others. To judge the righteousness of others. To hold the people bound to a yoke of works-based self-righteousness, not the liberty found in faith. God asks, is this a fast I have chosen? Did He order them to do these acts of penance on the Sabbath? Is it part of the ordinances given in the Old Testament, the covenant in effect at this time? He asks incredulously, "a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord?" Basically God is saying, is that what the Sabbath was made for? To afflict yourselves with fasting and ashes and sackcloth? To burden the people? Is this what you call an acceptable day to the Lord? God continues to berate them, again asking rhetorically, "Isn't the fast I chose to loose the bands of wickedness? To undo the heavy burdens? To let the oppressed go free? "And that ye break every yoke?" The Sabbath was to be a day of rest, that pictured the rest found in Christ. A day without labor, that people could understand that God did all the work so that they could share in His rest. A picture of salvation. Not to bind people to doctrines of devils, abstaining and fasting and weeping and wailing in sackcloth, covered in ashes. God is like I never told you to do any of this. It is sin. God continues, saying He gave us the Sabbath that we may do things that a workday prohibits getting done. Feeding the poor, going out and finding them that you may give them shelter in your home. To see the naked and give them clothes. To do the works of charity and mercy that we are called to do as His people. Not self flagellation and misery. Not heaping these carnal ordinances and requirements on to the people who are meant to be free to do His will. He promises if they do those things he actually asks of them, He will bless them and their light will shine, the glory of God our reward. The multitudes of blessings that would come upon them span the next several verses. But these false acts of piety aren't it, chief. God tells us, directly, in no uncertain terms, exactly what His stance on all these made up fasts and acts of communal suffering in His name is. It is inequity and sin. Doctrines of devils. And God promises us directly, the benefits of doing His will in this, and not our own: If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words: Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it. Take your foot off of God's rest. Delight in it, and in Him. Do things for others, with joy, not in the subjection of misery to yourself with rites of false piety, made up by men, not ordained by God, and He will bless you and your people. Amen. BTW, the term "penance" doesn't appear anywhere in scripture, even in the more corrupt modern versions, but Catholics draw their proof text from Isaiah 58:5, a chapter as we just saw that explicitly has God calling such practices sin. The New American Bible (NAB), a popular Catholic perversion of the word, twists the scripture and changes "afflict [your] soul" to "penance": “Is this the manner of fasting I wish, of keeping a day of penance: That a man bow his head like a reed, and lie in sackcloth and ashes? Do you call this a fast, a day acceptable to the LORD?” They don't even see the folly of using this, in its actual context, to justify the idea, or promote the yoke of abstinence and fasting, ashes and self- that God is literally telling Isaiah to preach against. They take from it only that they were being insincere, not that God calls us to delight in His day of rest, to celebrate the sabbath we have in Christ, and do for others that He be glorified. Only that the Hebrews just went about self flagellation wrong. 1 Samuel 15:22 And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.

Luke chapter 8 opens with a shout out to various women who ministered with Christ and the apostles, introducing us to Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, "and many others" who were an important part of Jesus mission. Fundamentalists often are accused (and by implication, the word of God) of not respecting women, or somehow being anti-Women. And while that may be true in some instances, a mature Christian who studies the word understands that men and women have unique roles, and a hierarchy in the home and during the assembly, but that in Christ all are equal, and the part women play in the ministry is often more important than what the average man in a church does. Most men may volunteer, soul win, maybe even lead studies and speak on men's nights, but they work and support their families. Their time isn't devoted to the ministry as their primary role. While women, ideally home, keeping the house and bringing up children, often are more involved in day to day labors in the Gospel. They can preach the Gospel soul winning. They are responsible for giving lessons in scripture to their children. They organize feasts of charity, visit one another in affliction and mourning, help each other with things that edify the congregation. Yes, Jesus is the head of the church, and a qualified pastor must be a male. Yes they must remain silent during services and submit to their husbands. It is the nature of our roles as children of God, and for the best interests of everyone, women included. But women are not subject to every man. They aren't there to be servants or slaves to every swinging Harry who walks through the door. They are subject to their father or their husband, in church, to the pastor (just as the men are), but not subservient to every male that comes along. This is a loving and healthy relationship between the male and female that God intends. Not "get me a sammich" despising of girls. Here we see that two well connected women provided wealth from their status and station to enable Christ His ministry. They traveled with the disciples. On Pentecost, they were among those preaching the Gospel to the crowd, getting people saved. Paul's epistles are filled with praise for women who labored with him in evangelism and in the churches he helped plant. Much is made of lamenting that women today are horrible. But the Bible teaches us they needn't be, and that it generally stems from men abandoning their roles, which in turn leads women to abandon theirs. (Looking at you Barack). Men are to lead, by being faithful to Christ, obedient to God, loving unto death for the women in their care. Men filling their biblical roles leads to women who do. And that in turn leads to a generation of godly children. And the glory of God increases. More souls are reached with the Gospel. Like Jesus earthly ministry and the early churches of the NT. We need to keep this in mind even more so today. Next, we are given the parable of the sower, a parable Christ gives to explain the different kinds of people who react to God's word. I have covered the parable extensively in our studies of Matthew and Mark. I would add to the points made about the parable of the sower in the other Gospels, that before explaining it to His disciples, as Jesus ended the preaching to the people who'd gathered to see Him, He cries out, "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." We have talked about how Jesus used parables that those seeking truth would hear, and understanding come to accept the Gospel, but those with hardened hearts were deaf to it. Unable to understand. They were like the well worn and compacted dirt of the pathway that the seed never takes to. But if we truly have ears to hear, it isn't enough to understand the meaning of the parable. It isn't simply "getting it" but understanding it and being pricked in the heart to be that fertile ground that produces abundantly, rather than the more worldly and unfruitful Christians. Hearing should compel us to be more than just saved. To whom much is given, much is expected. We are to prepare our hearts that we be fertile, to water the growing spirit inside us with the word. To grow deep roots in scripture and to branch out higher and higher as we seek the light. It is up to us whether we be the rock or the thorny ground, or if we are fertile soil. It's not just happenstance. It isn't just what it is. We have a choice. We can hide the light under a bushel or on the highest candlestick that others may see and be drawn in. We do that by obeying the word. Not being hearers only, but doers. Remember, to obey is better than sacrifice. Abstinence and fasting and not sinning in a manner we aren't prone to anyway is all well and good, but it is the keeping of the law, which Jesus boiled down to Love of God shown by keeping His commandments, and loving your neighbors which is the means by which we keep them. I keep coming back to Jesus' use of Isaiah 61 as a mission statement for Christian life, but it is key and given us for a reason: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. If we seek to be fertile ground, we need to make this our mantra. Our founding principle. We who are saved have been given the gift of having the Spirit of the Lord upon us. Are we frittering it away? Hiding it under a bushel? Do we allow the cares of the world to choke it out? Do we fall away having no roots? Do we live up to the ideal that to whom much is given, much is expected? Or, will we see it taken away, being only hearers of the word and never growing past that? It is impossible to spend time with Jesus and not have it change you. The more we diligently seek Him, the more we are given. And the more knowledge and understanding we are given, the harder and harder it becomes to live in sin. To not love others. To be lazy in our Christian life. To be afraid. To be blown away by the wind or choked out by the thorns, the cares of this world. Let him who has ears to hear, let him hear. Finishing out chapter 8 of Luke, we have in rapid succession Jesus healing the man containing a legion of spirits, sending them into a herd of swine that drove into the sea, the daughter of Jairus, who Jesus raises from the dead, and a woman with a blood disorder that, by faith only, touched the hem of Jesus' garment and was made whole as He made His way to see Jairus's daughter. Luke being a physician continuously shows us Jesus as healer. While on earth, Jesus takes compassion on those that suffer, and does what He can to ease it, in Jesus' case, the virtue of His holy being given to make the sick whole, the dead walk and the demons be cast out. But it was His mission to heal the sinners spiritually by the promise of faith. To make us whole, forgiven of sin and reconciled with God. But in everything, by grace and compassion, a charitable love, Jesus gave all. We aren't Jesus. We are weak vessels for the new man inside us. We can grow in faith and effectiveness for being used by God, as we are called to be, and amazing things will happen in our lives, but we can't literally raise the dead. We can't heal chronic illness. We can't cast out demons. The gifts of the Holy Ghost were for a sign until the completion of scripture, that a people unfamiliar with the Word could be drawn to the truth of Christ. But, do we do everything we can, giving all we have in our humble power to heal the sick, to set behind devils, to help the perishing escape death? There are weird sects calling themselves "apostles" and claiming the powers of the Holy Spirit, speaking "tongues," laying hands in dramatic fashion to "heal." Even using the sweat of their garments to act as "prayer cloth" guaranteed to cure what ails, "with just a small token of a love donation...." These vipers mimic the acts of the real Apostles, in a clown show grift, spouting gibberish and writhing on the ground as if it were them who were possessed by a demon. Claiming power that's not theirs. But that's not what I mean. Do we do everything we can, giving all we have in our humble power to heal the sick, to set behind devils, to help the perishing escape death? Do we live up to that saying of Christ that sets the tone for His mission in Luke 4? The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. The Spirit of the Lord is upon us. He has anointed us into His holy priesthood, the priesthood of believers given charge that we preach the Gospel to every creature. To the poor of spirit that they be made whole. To heal the brokenhearted by the hope we have in Christ. To preach deliverance to those captive by sin and the cares of this world, in chains to trying to work their own righteousness by the law, and coming short, perish in despair. Do we do all in our power to make the blind see? Spiritually, giving them the light that comes from the Lord, magnified in us, showing them the right and straight paths? Preaching the word that faith may come, and open their eyes to the truth? Do we set at liberty those bruised by their iniquities, freeing them from the yoke of sin? The liberty we share in Christ? Do we preach the acceptable year of the Lord, the Jubilee. The forgiveness of all debts as we are called home to be His people forever in a Kingdom not made of hands? Do we do everything in our meager power to show compassion on the spiritually sick that they may be healed? The best of us fall short. Most of us don't really even try. And we see how Jesus, who without sin despite being tempted in all ways like we are, studied the scriptures, committed them to heart as a boy, and in constant prayer, seeking to do God's will, loving others, doing whatever He could. And giving all, that those things be fulfilled in Him. Holding Himself up as an example, a light to the world calling all men, that we may be followers of Him, and thus be healed. Was Patrick a British Christian evangelist, with no ties to Rome? "The Patrick portrayed in public celebrations and by the Roman Catholic Church is mythical and useless. In Patrick’s Confession and Letter to Coroticus we meet a godly Christian missionary who both commands our admiration and deserves greater attention. Thus we shall consider his life, his message and his missionary labours, before concluding with an analysis of his significance." "There is no other God nor was there ever in the past nor will there be in the future except God the Father ingenerate, without beginning, from whom all beginning flows, who controls all things, as our formula runs: and his Son Jesus Christ whom we profess to have always existed with the Father, begotten spiritually before the origin of the world in an inexpressible way by the Father before all beginning, and through him were made things both visible and invisible; he was made man; when death had been overcome he was received into Heaven by the Father, and he gave to him all power above every name of things heavenly and earthly and subterranean and that every tongue should confess to him that Jesus Christ is Lord and God; and we believe in him and await his Advent which will happen soon, as judge of the living and the dead, and he will deal with everybody according to their deeds and he poured out upon us richly the Holy Spirit the gift and pledge of immortality, who makes those who believe and obey to be sons of God and coheirs with Christ and we confess and adore him, one God in the Trinity of sacred name." - Patrick of Britain, Confession 4 "That which I have set out in Latin is not my words but the words of God and of apostles and prophets, who of course have never lied. He who believes shall be saved, but he who does not believe shall be damned. God has spoken" (Letter 20).

Luke 9 sees the ministry of Christ grown to maturity, the Twelve acting as evangelists on their own, sent out to preach the coming Kingdom, bringing the Gospel, healing the sick, casting out devils all in Jesus' name. By sending them out without provision, He is trying to reinforce the idea that what they're doing is by faith. This is a subtle theme throughout the chapter, and something Jesus increasingly turns to as His time approaches. Knowing what He must do, the trials that afterwards the disciples will face, and the truth that by faith all things are possible, Jesus teaching on this both short term, practically, don't worry for food or shelter, just go, and preparing them spiritually, that they will be tested of His word, not to deny Him, not to be ashamed. To boldly command spirits. To shake the dust off those who won't receive them. He won't be around much longer to directly instruct them. The growth of the ministry and its success brings word of it to Herod, who in his guilt at having killed John the Baptist, wonders if it is him resurrected. The rulers of the time we're beginning to have an interest in what Jesus is doing, beyond the Pharisees and Sadducees He'd already contended with. All culminating as He goes to Jerusalem. But still, during this Jesus ministered to the people. And seeking to go off into the wilderness outside of Bethsaida without announcing it, still saw a crowd of multitudes follow them. 5,000 men. He taught on the coming Kingdom of God, and healed and as time went on, the Apostles bid that Jesus send them away so they could find lodging and eat. And so here Luke retells one of the accounts of Jesus feeding the multitudes with very little food; five loaves and two fishes. Dividing men into companies of 50, Jesus blessed the loaves and fishes and broke them up to be distributed by the 12. And all ate, and were filled, and there yet remained 12 baskets of leftovers. We have looked at these accounts in the other Gospels and I have pointed out the allegory of grace and faith being shown by Jesus; that God's grace is abundant. That by faith the apostles went out to share it, and each man was filled. So to is the Gospel. It is bread indeed, and all who eat of it are full. 5,000 or 5,000,000. Men of faith can share the grace of God through the word of God and feed multitudes. And come away themselves filled with more than they began with. Their own basket overflowing. Literally here and metaphorically, in the spirit. Jesus uses living parables to teach them on faith and grace that His disciples may face what's coming and do what they are called to, which is the will of God. Later on, Jesus brings up the rumors of Him going around to the Twelve, who had been journeying throughout the land, now returned. He asks who do the people say I am? They say, like Herod, people wonder if He is John, or a prophet returned. But when He asks them who they think He is, Peter answering said, The Christ of God. Here in Luke, the narrative moves to Jesus' admonishment to keep that quiet that His fate be allowed to play out. In John 16, in scripture that is taken out of context by Roman Catholics to justify their false church, Jesus replies to Peter's profession of faith that He is the Christ by saying that truth is the rock upon which His church is built. Catholic tradition twists this to make Peter that rock, and claim their earthly church was founded that day on a man, rather than Jesus and His Heavenly assembly of those who know He is Christ and believe. It is worth mentioning only in that if their version were true, it is odd that it's overlooked everywhere else in the Gospels, and in context, not even present in John. But affirming He is the Christ, as eleven of the Twelve believe, He again prepares them, that He must suffer and die, and rise again. Betrayed and rejected. And warns of any follow Him, to be prepared to take up their own cross daily, and follow Him unto death. That if they deny Him to save their own lives, they will lose it, but those willing to be faithful unto death will live. We draw a spiritual doctrine from this verse, inspiration to get up every day willing to sacrifice, follow His commandments, read the Bible, pray, etc. Taking up our cross. But here, Jesus means it literally, as well. They are going to face death for His sake. They will be tempted to deny Him. To be ashamed of the word. His Gospel. And Jesus wants them to understand if they don't truly have faith in Him they will falter, seek to save themselves and in doing so, lose out on the Kingdom, He will say He never knew them when He comes into His glory. "Lord, Lord..." and all. Again, we take from this spiritual application, and pastors will preach on how this is a lesson for us in improving our Christian walk, and it indubitably is. It is something that has comforted and edified me, and still does. It's something I try to remind myself of, especially those days you wake up not really feeling it. Cares of the world, infirmities of the flesh. Inspired by Jesus calling us to take up our cross and follow Him. But for us it's not sleeping in, or turning to the word instead of sin or remembering to pray. For His disciples, it was literal. Now, Jesus ends all this by saying: But I tell you of a truth, there be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the kingdom of God. And immediately, Luke brings us to the transfiguration of Jesus on the mountain: And it came to pass about an eight days after these sayings, he took Peter and John and James, and went up into a mountain to pray. So, follow that. He tells them that some of them shall see Him come into His glory, glimpsing the kingdom of Heaven before they taste death, and it came to pass eight days later that three of them do just that. This passage messes with people, where they come away with some kind of preterism or weird doctrines, because they don't rightly divide the word of God. They take a verse out of a larger narrative, stripped of context and then use their own foolish logic, try to make it make sense. Others who aren't familiar with the word pick up these errors and strange doctrines and repeat them. That's why we read all of it, in context, comparing scripture with scripture. And so, Peter, James and John, the three Apostles who are closest to Jesus, witness Jesus transfigured in His glory, with Moses and Elijah who appear in glory. They are a witness to the Kingdom, out of due time. It is often brushed over or minimized that Jesus was discussing His coming trials in Jerusalem with these great prophets of God, the culmination of God's will that these men preached in their day. What a conversation to be witness to, and add to that the understanding of the glory that awaits us in the Kingdom to come. Peter, who always says the wrong thing, suggests building tabernacles for Jesus and these saints, as he attempts to process what they'd witnessed. And a cloud overtakes them and envelopes them, and the voice of the Father says to them "This is my beloved Son: hear him." Peter and the brothers, James and John are witnesses to the presence of God, Christ in His glory, with the glorified Old Testament saints with everlasting life, not in a vision, but present with them on the mountain. They've seen the Kingdom of God. 2 Peter 1 16 For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty. 17 For he received from God the Father honour and glory, when there came such a voice to him from the excellent glory, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. 18 And this voice which came from heaven we heard, when we were with him in the holy mount. 19 We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts: In the second epistle of Peter, he recounts this episode, to lend credence to his testimony. He truly witnessed the promise of the Kingdom in all its glory, Christ in all His due honor, and heard God the Father Himself speak to them, praising Jesus as His Son. What a testimonial! Amen! But Peter reminds us that while he witnessed this all, that we have a more sure word, the scriptures. That he may have seen the faith in the Kingdom confirmed on the mount, it is by the word of God that we find the faith to reach it. And to that we should take heed. And so, we are told they come down from the mountain and find a company of men there, with the disciples and Apostles. And among them is a father whose son is possessed. He pleads with Jesus to help, as in His absence the other disciples tried to cast out this devil and failed. Jesus, again feeling the weight of what's to come and the short time with which He has to prepare the disciples, having just consulted with Moses and Elijah, in the presence of His Father, is again confronted with the limitations of man. His longsuffering patience tested, He cries out "O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you, and suffer you?" There are parallels here with Moses coming down from the mountain, having been in the presence of God, only to find the Israelites had gone after idols and engaged in wicked revelry while he was gone. In Moses case, he angrily smashed the stone tablets God had carved and written on, a sin of wrath he was made to correct, carving and chiseling the replacement stones himself. But frustrated Jesus, sinless Jesus, doesn't answer in wrath, but instead turns to the troubled and heartbroken dad, and says "Bring thy son hither," and heals him, casting out the demon that they could not, lacking the faith. And an exasperated Jesus says to His disciples; Let these sayings sink down into your ears: for the Son of man shall be delivered into the hands of men. But they understood not this saying, and it was hid from them, that they perceived it not: and they feared to ask him of that saying. In the retelling of this in Matthew 17, the Apostles later ask of Jesus why they failed to cast out that evil spirit. And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you. Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting. We have been talking about the role of fasting and prayer in finding the will of God, understanding it and accepting it. In the end, that's what faith is. Learning, believing and obeying the will of God. Jesus here is telling us that it was a lack of faith, and how to rectify that is by prayer and fasting. We may encounter things we struggle to overcome. If we had but a tiny bit of faith, this wouldn't be the case. If we seek to, then it is by prayer and fasting that we can grow in faith enough to overcome. Simple as. Just as Jesus fasted in the desert and prayed without ceasing throughout His ministry, especially when faced with a new undertaking or a difficult task, that's how we are to do it in similar situations. Christianity isn't a gnostic religion of secret revelation. God tells us everything we need to know in order to be successful in our Christian life. To better equip us to do His will. As frustrating as it may be for Him when we don't listen or understand or take it to heart. I thank God for His mercy and patience. If these men tried it, I can't imagine how much more frustrated He gets with me. Reading Luke 9:46-62, closing out the chapter, it seems like a litany of man trying Jesus patience, and His trying to impress certain lessons and understanding, His time growing short. Time is of the essence of what makes man, man. And Jesus, being fully God and fully man had to feel the weight of it more acutely than anyone who ever lived. As God, the Alpha and Omega, there from the beginning and through the end, the Godhead exists outside time, being trapped within it must have been trying, the infirmities of man constraining Him. Part of what Jesus suffered to be our savior. As much a part of His sacrifice as the cross. Time is a construct, a part of creation, the means by which life and death, creation and corruption are expressed. And Jesus being incorruptible, made a little lower than the angels, putting on corruptible flesh that we may be saved. And with full knowledge and understanding of the Father's will, and with time growing short, Jesus tried His best to give His followers and those who wished to be, the reality of what it would mean, who He was, what the Christ must suffer, and yet they understand not. O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you, and suffer you?

Beginning in chapter 10 of Luke we see what may be considered the highpoint of Jesus earthly ministry, in so far as success regarding the evangelism of the Gospel, reaching people throughout the region, the lost sheep of Israel, that they may come to repentance, turning towards God. (Jesus' work on the cross being the greatest single act in all human history, aside) Having successfully preached and reached multitudes, Jesus recruited the 12 from His disciples, and sent them out, two by two before Him. And now, adding an additional 70 to be sent out winning souls. Jesus says that while the harvest is great, there are too few laborers to bring it all in. This remains true, especially today. We note the pattern of evangelism given throughout the new testament, echoing what Jesus taught these envoys of the Gospel. Going forth in pairs (not unlike the animals saved from the flood, going forth from the ark of their salvation to multiply their kind), taking with them no provision other than what they carried on their backs, and the word of God. Preaching that the Kingdom of God is nigh. At each town on these mission trips, they are instructed to find a house to bless with peace and use as a base of operations, and accept what's given them to eat, the shelter offered, having faith that their needs be filled. That the wages of the laborer be paid by the Lord. He says, don't go begging door to door as they preach, just lodge in the first home that is provided them, taking what they are offered. But if the city reject them, if they find no habitations, to shake the dust and move on. Jesus openly curses the unreceptive cities, saying that with the acts of healing, the signs and wonders of these apostles shown to Capernaum and Bethsaida, even wicked places like Sodom and Tyre would have repented. Woe be unto those places that turned them away. And, we are told the 70 returned with great joy, carried away by the power they'd been granted to cast out devils in Jesus' name. And he said unto them, I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven. Jesus promises then that as they minister for Him they would be protected from the power of the enemy. That by no means would Satan be able to harm them in their work. But Jesus also cautions then to remember it is their salvation that they should rejoice in, their part in the Kingdom of Heaven. So, with a successful group of missionaries and Apostles, hundreds of disciples and multitudes of those saved by their work, Jesus rejoiced in prayer, thanking His Father for this great success, that what seemed good in God the Father's sight, His will be done. Similarly, we should be likewise thankful, counting the blessing of our part in the Kingdom above all other earthly blessings. Giving thanks to the Lord when we are given success in our labors for Him. Blessed by these things of God which we see. Lives changed. People healed. The spiritually blind made to see. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he that winneth souls is wise. Amen. If it isn't clear from scripture, the great commission, the call to be a laborer for Christ, a servant of the Gospel, bringing the good news of eternal life that we are blessed to have been made aware of, to believe on, to be healed by, to others. To love our neighbors enough to go out among the highways and hedges to call them to salvation. Jesus had followers. Disciples who not only were saved by their faith, calling upon His name, but also the few who left everything to do His work. Who, being called answered. Who took up their cross daily. Who were willing to go out and preach the salvation of the cross to all men. Apostles, messengers of Christ. Today we are called to do the same. Most of us don't. But the harvest is great and the laborers few. If we are serious in our walk with Christ, if we seek sanctification and separation as we grow in knowledge and faith, invariably we will come to the understanding of this great calling. To whom much is given, much is expected. The calling to share the Gospel becomes a driving force in our lives when we walk in His word, in prayer, in thanksgiving. As the Spirit works in us, helping to remove the thorns of sin from our hearts. As our faith grows. It's hard to resist that call. There are soul winning churches out there, seeking fellow laborers to minister the Gospel. If you want to really grow as a Christian, seek them out. Be wise. Win souls. The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few: pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest. Jesus tells us to pray that God provides laborers for the harvest. That He provide men and women willing to go forth, to the field as it were, to bring in the bounty that is ready to be picked. If you aren't in a position to go out yourself, pray that you can be. Work towards it. But pray without ceasing for those who are, and that more may come. Don't allow your own shortcomings, stumbling blocks and snares, perhaps embarrassment that you don't go soul winning for whatever reason (they aren't good reasons, but I am not judging. My excuses for when I don't do it are just as lame), but at least pray for those that do. Pray that God provides more who are willing to go door knocking and evangelizing. Pray you become one of them. If Jesus tells us to pray, then pray. Proverbs 11:30 The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise. And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles. The Bible says that when we are preaching the Gospel, we should preach to the receptive, rejecting the heretic after the second admonition, avoiding foolish questions, unprofitable arguing, not answering a fool in his folly, being gentle to all men. To understand that their acceptance or rejection of the truth that you're giving is reception or rejection of the Lord. It isn't personal. It isn't about you. Shake the dust. You are to come offering peace, and if it isn't reciprocated, to withdraw it. To move on to those with ears to hear. That the heretic is subverted and will be recompensed for his error by God, Whom it is he is that he actually is rejecting. Searching for and arguing with people who are wrong on doctrine, wrong about scripture, who have the wrong idea about salvation and who despise God, isn't how we are supposed to go about things. It takes away from the time we could spend on those who are willing to hear the truth. And it leads to our own sin, wrath and impatience, which clouds our testimony that otherwise may have convinced someone else. This is a snare I have fallen into plenty, and not a day goes by I don't witness it either in myself or by others. Luke 10 25 And, behold, a certain lawyer stood up, and tempted him, saying, Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? 26 He said unto him, What is written in the law? how readest thou? 27 And he answering said, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself. 28 And he said unto him, Thou hast answered right: this do, and thou shalt live. 29 But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour? 30 And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead. 31 And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. 32 And likewise a Levite, when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by on the other side. 33 But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him, 34 And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. 35 And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee. 36 Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? 37 And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise. Continuing in Luke 10, we see a lawyer, a religious position, one who examines the law of Moses, come to Jesus and this man seeks to tempt Him. He asks a typically bad faith question, as the Pharisees and Sadducees often do to Jesus, looking to trip Him up in matters of the law. The premise of the question he poses to Jesus is wrong from the start; that he as a man can justify himself. He asks what shall I do to inherit eternal life? And Jesus, as He is wont to do in these situations, answers in a question, asking this expert in the letter of the law, what it says in scripture. The lawyer answers Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself. Jesus replies Thou hast answered right: this do, and thou shalt live. The law certainly does say this, and as Jesus says elsewhere, the whole of it falls on these two commandments. And, if it were possible to keep the whole of the law, one would be righteous and obtain eternal life. But the Bible says this isn't possible, that all have fallen short. All have sinned. Sin is the transgression of the law, and so by the law comes knowledge of sin. The knowledge of sin brings understanding of our failings, and by this knowledge comes the need for salvation by faith, being unobtainable by man, driven by the needs and lusts of the flesh, and our own vain imaginings. This fallen state of man is there to remind us of our need for God to save us from our wicked hearts. For Christ to be the propitiation for our sin. To obtain eternal life not by our own doing, but by trusting in the promise of God, the blood of Christ, the baptism of the Holy Spirit, the circumcision of the heart. But the lawyer, we are told, seeking to justify himself asks, Who is my neighbor? The implication is that these holy men, claiming to be experts in righteousness, believe they are righteous by their own ability. Instead of showing them their own failings that they may be ripe for repentance, their pride sees them lie to themselves that they do not sin, and keep the law. And so the lawyer believes He is about to be shown justified by this Jesus. Confirming he is righteous by his works. And so Jesus tells him the parable of the Good Samaritan. We all know it. It may be one of if not the most famous of Jesus teachings. A man taken by robbers, left for dead on the side of the road. A priest of the temple crosses the street to avoid this poor soul needing help. A Levite, a servant of the temple, also a supposed man of God passes him by. But a man, not just any man, but a Samaritan, an enemy of the Jews, two people who despise each other as much for their shared lineage as their difference. No love lost between them. Enemies. And this Samaritan sees a man in need, and without thinking of self, without thinking of the enmity, he goes out of his way to help him. He takes time to care for someone near him, and in need. The moral of the story being that that's what defines a neighbor. Someone in your immediate sphere of influence who needs help, and to whom you can give help. The law says, in Exodus 23:4 If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again. How much more your enemy himself? And so, Jesus by His parable establishes just how high a bar the keeping of the law is. How much is expected of us who seek to justify ourselves, as this lawyer does. And with this, Jesus sends him on his way. What is lost on the lawyer is what's lost on mankind from the very beginning; That by our works we cannot be justified. This is the lesson of Cain. It's the lesson Jesus seeks to show this lawyer. And Paul, writing in the epistles hammers this need for salvation by self-righteous works that we innately cling to as often being a stumbling block to faith rather than a schoolmaster to lead us to faith. All who are saved by faith understand that by our nature, man sins and in sin, we die. That the wages of sin is death. That there are none righteous, no not one. It is a humbling experience. It drives us to our knees, often in tears, praising God for His undeserved mercy upon us. Thanking Him for His grace. That while we were yet sinners, He gave His only begotten Son that whosoever believes on Him shall not perish but have eternal life. And this knowledge of our salvation and the calling to share this good news, and hatred of every false way, leads us to standfast in the Gospel of grace and deny that there is any works-based way to Heaven. Proclaiming that it is by faith alone. That, contrary to the vain wisdom of man, that it is the "foolishness of the cross" that we hold our hope in. But that's not entirely true. Man may work his way to heaven. God gave us the means by which we are allowed to become self-righteous. If we only could. We see in Cain the desire of man's wicked heart to do it ourselves, to show God we are worthy. Despite His love, His encouragement, His grace. That we can by our own works, the sweat of our brow, bring forth a sacrifice that is so pleasing to the Lord that He must receive us and grant us what was lost in Adam's fall; eternal life in paradise in His presence. And we see in God's rejection of Cain's attempt that it falls short, and see the evil, the sin that knocks on the door, that follows such pride and arrogance. But more, it shows us that this inclination for self-righteousness is in man's heart. God, in His wisdom and awesome understanding of man, shows us this, first that by His wrath upon creation, and judgement of nations, flood and fire, but still mankind as a whole doesn't come to understand salvation by faith. God shows by promise and blessing His intention to offer salvation by faith to those who call upon His name, who diligently seek Him. And still man doesn't understand. Still they seek to justify themselves. They sought other gods and sacrificed to them that they may justify themselves and so God shows the Hebrews an acceptable works-based process of law and ordinances, that doesn't offend with idols, fornication, murder, sacrifice of children. If man was determined to have a system of works and ceremony, holy days and dietary requirements, sacrifice and ordinance, God decided to provide one through Moses. A clean and holy works-based salvation that they could strive to keep, while coming to the understanding that it is impossible and turn to Him in faith to redeem us from death and Hell. The glorious Old Testament. A Covenant. But God's glorious covenant, a law of works-based salvation, had a fault. Man. Hebrews 8:7-8 For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second. For finding fault with them, he saith, Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah And so it is incorrect to say that there is no such thing as a works-based plan of salvation. There is one, created by God that man cannot hope to rely on because of the fault of ourselves. What people call different dispensations, who try to divide the word of God by their own lack of understanding; the wisdom of men, is actually God's multiple attempts to teach us to rely on Him by faith alone. God speaks to us in all of creation, the natural order of things serving as a parable bringing us to the truth of the glory of God. In His wrath and in His blessing. And God, who is a reasonable God and just in all His ways, speaks to us throughout Scripture of what we should know just by observing his creation. He gave Adam and Eve one commandment and the advantage of eternal life and paradise to live in, and they failed and fell. He gave them instruction of the faith, and ordinances to follow to symbolize the blood of the lamb to come. And yet their son, not even a generation removed, rejected this simple faith to justify himself by his works. And man becomes exceedingly wicked, leaning into their own understanding and God destroys the world in a flood saving the only righteous man, saved by faith, and his family in an ark, representing salvation by faith in Christ. A generation later is Babel. Again man, seeking to make himself God by working their way to Heaven. Over and over again. God rewards the faithful with blessings and honor, as He did with Abraham. Isaac and his sons. And God showed His wrath from heaven against those who became consumed in their wickedness, Sodom and Gomorrah, for example. When the Hebrews fled their land in famine to egypt, the land He had given them in promise, He led them into slavery and then, through pestilence and plague, miracles and signs, He set them free and returned them once again to that promised land. He made covenants and vows that if the people followed the law and ordinances and maintained their status as a holy nation, separated unto Him that He would keep them in. In bless them that they may be a light to other nations. To bring them to faith. He gave to them a perfect law that they would understand that there is no way to justify themselves but to instead have faith on Him. They sought a king, rejecting God as the ruler of their land and wanting an earthly man to lead them, and He gave them their wish showing them the folly of their decision. God gave examples such as David, a man after His own heart, who had such perfect faith in the Lord and yet fell so many times backslidden to his own lusts. He gave us Solomon the wisest, gifted by the Holy spirit with wisdom and understanding that no man had ever seen, and he fell repeatedly into sin, lust, idolatry. He reproached the nation with invasion and captivity. He showed how a violation of His covenant would be met. He sent prophets, doing signs and wonders, brought droughts and famine, heroes and judges who brought about their salvation. He showed them redemption and a second chance out of Babylon. In all things, he taught the gospel to the people. He showed them the folly of depending on their works or the wisdom of man. Of thinking that sacrifice is and following commandments could ever bring them to be righteous enough to regain their place in paradise. In the presence of the Lord. He showed us that all his righteousness were as filthy rags. And in his mercy gave us hope in Jesus Christ, His Son. In every so-called dispensation, across generations, God gave man the truth of the Gospel, and a choice to accept it in faith. And in every time in diverse ways, He offered examples to serve as a way to understanding. Be it examples of righteous men of faith, symbols and sacrifices, revelation by nature or by prophet, scripture and promise. Even totems like the brazen serpent and the Ark of the Covenant, and every time the covetousness of man turned these things into idols, and worshiped the creation more than the creator. Romans 1 19 Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. 20 For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse: 21 Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. 22 Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, 23 And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things. Idolatry of ourselves, our works, our traditions, our adherence to the law, of political power, of being a chosen people by nature of our birth, of all these things, is shown fruitless and lacking in the law of God, and should lead us to faith, on our knees in tearful repentance when we hear the truth. The Bible says the sin of idolatry is covetousness. Seeking that which isn't ours. And justification isn't of self, but of God, and being God's, isn't ours to demand. If you're trusting in your works, like the lawyer from our reading in Luke 10, you are going after the error of Cain. Repent. Learn the lesson. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.
