I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O Lord my God. When my soul fainted within me I remembered the Lord: and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple. They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy. But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay that that I have vowed. Salvation is of the Lord. And the Lord spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land. Jesus says that the only sign they would be given is the sign of Jonah, the resurrection from death and Hell, the victory of the cross. To repent towards God or face His judgment. And unlike the wicked city of Nineveh, this wicked and perverse generation who refused to hear, would be destroyed.

Luke chapter 12 is almost entirely red-lettered preaching of Jesus Christ, both to the apostles and the people gathered in the assembly with them, and ultimately, a message to us, straight from the Word of God. Jesus is before a crowd, a multitude so great people are stepping over each other to move. But we see Jesus turning to His company of disciples to say, "Beware the leaven of the Pharisees," to beware being hypocrites. That the sin that consumes the Jewish religious leaders is their holier than thou act, while they themselves are in sin. Casting judgment down on others while they themselves are guilty of the same and worse. Many Christians today fall into this trap, and find themselves exposed and revealed. Nothing hidden remains hidden. Jesus says that what we whisper in secret will be proclaimed from the rooftops. Our sin is exposed when it is hidden, especially when we cover it by acting superior to others. We are all sinners and have fallen short. So fear God, not man. Be true. Not hypocrites. God chasteness every child, scourging every son. He tells them further, edifying them, not to fear men for the preaching of the word. Don't deny Christ because of threat and violence. God values His children. He knows us and loves us. Jesus is our advocate and brother. Here Jesus gives the teaching of the unpardonable sin; blasphemy of the Holy Ghost. Those that mock the power by which the Apostles act, the Holy Spirit which seals us as God's. The person of the Godhead which rebukes the world for its sin. Reprobates hate this pricking of their hearts, and the revealed judgment of God by the Holy Spirit, and it is that judgment that causes them to despise the truth that they may have their conscience seared, to do those things that are not convenient. To be given over and given up by God. To be rejected. Made reprobate. He gives advice to them that will be delivered up to the authorities by the Jews, that the Holy Ghost brings to them what to say. Don't plan arguments and speeches. God will bring to remembrance scripture, and give a measure of wisdom in peril through the Holy Ghost. Jesus is giving all this advice, straight doctrine, and is interrupted by a man with a petty dispute, seeking his brother to share an inheritance. Greedy and covetous, asking Christ Jesus, the son of God in the midst of preaching fire, to judge this trifling matter of earthly treasure. He gives the parable of the rich man who stored his excess wealth up on earth, while neglecting what matters, spiritual things, treasure for God. So that having stored this wealth and bounty in covetousness, God takes his life, leaving all of it to rust, rot and moth. Worthless to the man before the judgment of God. The life is more than meat, the body more than raiment. We should not care so much about these things, God will provide. Seek to store up treasure in Heaven and we will have what we need here on earth. He says, you can't think yourself taller, you can't change your height by worry, that's under God's control, so why worry about the rest? Trust Him. Have faith. Seek the kingdom of God. God wants to provide for us. Not wealth and riches and material things, these may come, we may have seasons of plenty, we might be poor, but learn to be content regardless as all comes from God, and we know this having the treasure of eternal life and a part in the Kingdom of God. Value that more than things or comfort. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. And by doing this, by waiting patiently doing the work of the Lord, diligently seeking His will and loving others, to do that which we who are anointed by the Spirit are called to do; preach the Gospel to the poor, heal the broken hearted, give comfort and liberty to those in bonds, when the Lord comes we will not be taken unawares. We will discern the times. We will be ready for the feast. Peter asks if Jesus just means the apostles or is this advice, touching on end times prophecy, for everyone that believes. Jesus says simply blessed is the servant who when the Lord comes He finds so doing. It's for all of us. And by doing His will, by being loyal and watchful servants, by storing up treasure in heaven, we will be rewarded as rulers with Him in the kingdom. Jesus then warns about becoming impatient and in doing so, slipping into the way of the Pharisees, the leaven of hypocrisy. Being slack. Worried about the things of this world. Feasting. Drunk. Mistreating others. He warns that such a person who in His name, who knows His will but does it not, they will be severely treated, beaten with many stripes. Even worse than the unbelieving, who act in ignorance. Jesus preaches the truth that to believe in Him brings division, that the faith will divide even families. It's how it is, be prepared and know the signs. Behave as if you're being taken to judgment by an adversary, being honest in your dealings that you're blameless before the magistrate and not cast into prison, for if you're not, you'll be given no mercy. You'll pay every cent you are found to owe. His warnings and edifying, to be good and faithful servants, to fear only God, to serve those we are called to, to act right, judge properly, placing your heart on the Kingdom not the cares of this world, given to inspire us in our walk with Him, are important to keep in mind, babe in Christ, or, and especially, as a more mature Christian. Not to lose sight of the prize. In patience and longsuffering we wait and do, that we may be blessed at the returning of the Lord. I feel weird about trying to give a study of what Jesus is saying here, when His words are so plain and easily understood, His parables in this passage aren't dark sayings, He is desperately trying to impart these things to His disciples before His eventual crucifixion. It's a ticking clock we see Jesus is all too aware of. But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished! Straitened, meaning constrained to a narrow path, Jesus laments showing frustration at this hypocritical generation. That they don't see it all clearly, and the press of time is all too real for Him that was before time, now made in corruptible flesh that He may deliver man. Some people say things like "we need to just focus on the red letters, and not worry so much about other doctrines and disputes over scripture!" But that's a natural man misunderstanding; the red letters ARE the scriptures, Jesus is the Word of God. His preaching and parables are the fulfilment of the law, the doctrines of God. They aren't isolated or contradictions. I mention this because, in my experience, people who say that don't actually read the red letters. It's a cope to not have to deal with the meaning and implications of the Bible. To really study the word and understand the fundamentalism Jesus is preaching. By the same token, we can be lost in the weeds of doctrine at times. It is a good thing to really consider the words of Jesus, and apply them to our lives. Praying on them that we can see the revealed will of God. Jesus lived in the flesh a short while, His earthly ministry only 3 and a half years, the Gospels our only record of His teachings, teachings He knew He had so little time to convey. Go back and really read and consider the chapter, in that light. Spend time with the words of Jesus, it will change you. Amen

Luke chapter 13 continues the general sermons covered in 11 and 12, where Jesus is preaching to both the disciples near Him, and to the multitudes gathered to see Him. A crowd of mostly unsaved, non-believers, Pharisees, scribes and others, some seeking healing, some caught up in the excitement, some searching for the Christ, ready for repentance. Chapter 12 ends with exhortation and warning to accept salvation or to receive their portion with the unbelievers. To be beaten with much stripes for their knowledge of the truth that they reject. That they have the Son of God among them, telling them the things of the kingdom of Heaven and yet are dull of hearing. Speaking to the unsaved He tells the parable of the man going before the magistrate, who should make peace rather than face the judgment and pay for all he owes. Continuing this, Jesus is told of news from Galilee, men killed by Herod and their own blood mixed with their sacrifices. He warns that whatever tragedy and tribulation they were struck by, they perish as any other sinner. That men killed in a building collapse in the city of Siloam weren't being punished for their sins any more than they who die unsaved. We are all appointed to die, and then the judgment. We are all dead in our sins without Christ. Jesus is calling them to repentance, warning of their destruction. Jesus gives a parable of a tree that has not given fruit in 3 years, a picture of His ministry among the Jews, and their refusal to accept salvation in Him. He is like the dresser, who when the Lord comes to cut the tree down, asks one last chance to manure the tree that it may yet fruit. But after that, it will be hewn down and cast into the fire that another tree may thrive. The tree is unbelieving Israel. His end being near, He tries to reach them. The scene shifts to Jesus teaching in a synagogue, a local assembly gathered on the sabbath, and seeing a woman with an infirmity in the congregation, He takes pity and tells her be healed. This triggers the rabbi of the place, who tells the Word of God that He ought not work on the sabbath, citing scripture, only to be reproached by Christ for his hypocrisy. They lose their livestock to drink on a sabbath, taking pity on their cattle, but not this woman in her affliction. And when he had said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed: and all the people rejoiced for all the glorious things that were done by him The crowd receptive, Jesus teaches on the Kingdom of Heaven, attempting to show how it grows and spreads, by faith to faith, each believer, as leaven spreads through the flour, as a tiny mustard seed grows to a giant tree. We who are saved, giving the Gospel to others who believe, and they in turn the same. Now Jesus has begun to make His way towards Jerusalem. His fate awaiting there, and He continues His mission, giving the Gospel to the poor that they may be redeemed. A person asks if few will be saved, Jesus replies that we must enter in the strait gate, the narrow path, through Him. That many seek the kingdom but by the way that seems easy. Similar passage to Matthew 7:13-14: Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it. Modern false translations change the narrowness of the gate, the one path to salvation, to "difficult," teaching that salvation is hard and of works. But in the abbreviated telling in Luke the meaning is reinforced. Jesus is desperately trying to reach people with the truth, that they may turn towards God and be saved. The kingdom is nigh. Repent. When once the master of the house is risen up, and hath shut to the door, and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are: Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity. Another parable warning then not to be shut out. Not to be like the virgins who didn't keep oil in their lamps, and when the bridegroom returned were shut out of the wedding feast. Like the wicked servant who abused his station while the master was away, only to be found out by the Lord's unexpected return. Not to be caught unawares like a thief coming in the night, but to be watchful and ready. Jesus preaches hellfire and brimstone. The destruction that awaits all men who do not come to believe. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out. The same day there came certain of the Pharisees, saying unto him, Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee. The spiteful Jews of Galilee threatening that Herod was looking to kill Jesus, that they would get Him to leave. He laughingly says tell that old fox that He still doing work and will abide a while. He's got devils to cast out and people to heal, that He'd be finished in three days. Showing no fear, because Jesus knows where and when His death should come. And, because Jerusalem is where the Jews always killed the prophets, He says to the Pharisees it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem. It is a slam against them, and must have pricked their hearts with shame and anger. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not! Behold, your house is left unto you desolate: and verily I say unto you, Ye shall not see me, until the time come when ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord. He is through with these reprobates. He is done, saying you won't see Me until the day of the Lord. The time of wrath. When every knee shall bow. He tried to get them to believe but they would not. And now, they are done. Twice-dead. Cut off. His destiny drawing near, but theirs is present before them. Weeping and gnashing of teeth, cast out into outer darkness in the lake of fire. I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. And if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down. Thou hypocrite, doth not each one of you on the sabbath loose his ox or his ass from the stall, and lead him away to watering? And when he had said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed... Then said he, Unto what is the kingdom of God like? and whereunto shall I resemble it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and cast into his garden; and it grew, and waxed a great tree; and the fowls of the air lodged in the branches of it. (Behold, a sower went forth to sow; And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up) And again he said, Whereunto shall I liken the kingdom of God? It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened. (Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth? This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you. A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.) Then said one unto him, Lord, are there few that be saved? And he said unto them, Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able. When once the master of the house is risen up, and hath shut to the door, and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are: Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity. (Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.) There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out. And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last. (So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests. And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless. Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel. And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.) The same day there came certain of the Pharisees, saying unto him, Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee. And he said unto them, Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow, and the third day I shall be perfected. Nevertheless I must walk to day, and to morrow, and the day following: for it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not! Behold, your house is left unto you desolate: and verily I say unto you, Ye shall not see me, until the time come when ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness. Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! because ye build the tombs of the prophets, and garnish the sepulchres of the righteous, And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets. Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets. Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers. Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of Hell? Wherefore, behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes: and some of them ye shall kill and crucify; and some of them shall ye scourge in your synagogues, and persecute them from city to city: That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar. Verily I say unto you, All these things shall come upon this generation. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not! Behold, your house is left unto you desolate. For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord. It is important to point out that in chapter 13 of Luke, which I covered somewhat this morning, much of the preaching done by Jesus, if not all of it, was not to disciples, to the saved, though many may have been present and there is application for us today as believers. It was to non-believers and, especially as His ministry wound down to His eventual crucifixion, He is preaching harder and harder against the reprobate Jews. The holy men, so called, hypocrites and vipers. And those they've made twice the child of Hell as themselves. They are the fowls of the air, perching on the mustard tree that is the Kingdom of Heaven. They are the leaven hidden in the meal that spreads throughout. They are those who seek to enter by the wide gate of their works and self-righteousness. They are those without the white raiment given the guests of the wedding who came when bidden, crashing the wedding. They are those saying "Lord, Lord, look upon my works." The virgins without oil in their lamps. The servant who didn't think the Lord would come, and instead ate, drank and was merry. They are the man counted among the share of the unbelieving. The man, given much who received the worse stripes. They, knowing the judgment of God reject it. They put off getting right with God, obeying the Gospel, thinking that when brought before the magistrate they will be able to plea their case. They are those who rather than striving towards the strait gate, contending for the faith, that they may be saved to do the work of the Lord, count on their genealogies and self-righteous works and adhering to the letter of the law, the ordinances and customs, but inside are whited sepulchers. Full of dead men's bones. Faithless and hopeless. Tares among the wheat, fit to be gathered and burned. The tree without fruit. Unable to come to repentance. Reprobate silver. It's important to understand that the Bible is deep, and it is complex, and when scripture is telling us God's word, when Jesus speaks it is to all men. Saved men. Unsaved men. Reprobates. There are lessons for us all, and deep with doctrine. But understand Jesus preaches hard against those too blind to see, dull of hearing, hearts hardened, as much as He speaks to His disciples, and for the same reason; to get those willing to listen to reconsider and obey the Gospel of reconciliation and grace. And of some have compassion, making a difference: And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh. Compare Jesus assessment of the hypocritical false teachers and the hypocrisy of their religion, vs the mission statement from Isaiah 61 that Jesus began His ministry with; The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Vs Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess. We aren't supposed to be working for Heaven, we are supposed to be workers of Heaven. That the Kingdom of Heaven draw nigh them, when we do the charity and humble service to others we are called to. When we give the Gospel to the poor, and heal the broken hearted. Clothe the naked and feed those in need. We didn't find Jesus, He found us, and set us to labor for Him, as we were bought with a price. This is the calling of discipleship that we all receive when we are saved. And yet few believers are able to commit to it. I being chief. Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. Young men need to join a Christian local church and help keep each other grounded and normal, that the glowy ops that rely on fear, on reaction coupled with loneliness and despair don't work. To fight the constant effort to bring our young men low, to corrupt the fatherless, a man needs unity in Christ and positive purpose, keeping each other accountable. Doing good for our people. Spreading the Gospel, judging the fatherless and caring for the widows indeed. Visiting our men in prison. Feeding our poor. Healing our brokenhearted.

Continuing a theme from Luke 12 that I touched on last night, where Jesus is preaching the Kingdom of Heaven, and specifically addressing those who would not believe, mostly among the Pharisees, as a way of contrast that the other people may see the chief among them's error, and come to repent towards God. Here, He has gone to supper bidden by a Pharisee, and sat among them on a sabbath, the Bible says, that they watched Him. Observing Jesus, looking to tempt Him as they've been. Looking to find fault. Some undoubtedly seeking status on f having supper with Him, as His ministry had grown. Looking for shared glory by proximity. It reminds us of Jesus having said in chapter 12: Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are: Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity. And here we see them eating with Christ, just as He said. The point is in the judgment, being in proximity to Christ isn't the same as believing on Christ. Doing works in His name, eating supper, His work done in your streets, in your church or even calling Him Lord, isn't sufficient to be saved. To receive the imputed righteousness of Jesus. To be washed clean in His blood. That comes by faith alone, coming to understand that you are a sinner deserving death and Hell, and accepting the free gift of grace, forgiveness and reconciliation. In the parable of the 10 virgins, waiting for the bridegroom that they may attend his wedding feast, Jesus says that some had oil prepared in their lamps, and when he arrived, went out and were taken into the feast. The rest, having no oil themselves asked for some of the other's, but they could not share. You can't be saved by being the son or daughter of a saved Christian. You cannot be made righteous by being the spouse of a believer. You can't be saved by going to a Christian church, partaking in the Lord's supper, or by trying to show up at the wedding feast in your own attire, clothes in the filthy rags of your own righteousness. That's what all these parables about weddings and being cast out into outer darkness, with wailing and gnashing of teeth, it's what all these are teaching. After healing a man with edema, there among the Pharisees on the sabbath, Jesus again puts the hypocritical men on the spot. They seek to hold the letter of the law against Him, while the spirit of it is revealed in the exceptions given to help a neighbor or even an enemy. Then He gives those bidden to the supper like He was some advice in humility and how the wisdom of men differs from that of God. Jesus says, if you're invited to a party, don't go in assuming you're asked to sit in the high places of status, instead be seated in the lowest room. Just happy to be there, and so when the lord of the supper bids you to sit in a more privileged seat, you are truly honored. If you presume, and you're asked to give up your spot to one greater than you, you will be humiliated. It's a basic teaching on how life works, and how it is in the Kingdom, that these social climbers and clout seeking Pharisees miss. Jesus goes on to say; when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just. If you have the means to call a feast, humbly seek to serve those who cannot do anything for you. Who are week. Honor them without thought for reward in this life and be rewarded for it at the judgment. It is the counterpoint advice for hosts, paired with how guests should behave. This pattern holds true in the Kingdom to come. He then gives the parable of the wedding feast, where the honored guests all refuse the invitation with their excuses, the cares of the world. Those bidden refuse to come. He is speaking to the Pharisees, saying they are like them. The feast will go on. The Lord will invite those poor and lame and of no status, that his house be filled. He will send his servants to the highways and hedges and compel the meek and lowly, bidding them to the feast. Those originally bidden, the Jews, the hypocritical religious leaders, they won't taste of this supper. Another message Jesus began mentioning increasingly as His time drew near, was that of discipleship. Of not just salvation by faith, and the fulfilment of the promise made of God for a Christ, but that of those who would pick up their cross and follow Him. Those who would, for love of Him, forsake everything to serve Him, and what that would mean. He called Peter, Andrew, James and John to be fishers of men, to forsake family and the family's business as fishermen, and they left all. Due to Jesus' intervention, they filled their nets so much so the boats began to capsize. They had the richest catch of their lives, and left it behind on the beaches of Galilee for others, in order to become disciples of Christ. This wasn't for everyone who believed. And it certainly divided off those who were there only for the spectacle; the signs and wonders, the miracles performed, the fiery sermons preached, the dead brought back to life and demons cast out. Jesus frequently warns there's a cost for following Him. His hard sayings brought division, and offended many that they no longer followed. His telling them that they'd be persecuted, brought before magistrates and beaten in synagogues for His name's sake, that they would see prison, and possible death for preaching the Gospel. Jesus told those who were faithful to follow Him and be His disciples that they should go out, among the highways and hedges, with nothing but the clothes on their back and the sandals on their feet, and want for nothing, to live on faith that God would provide. To leave their family, friends, the towns they knew, the sins they were comfortable in, the ways of their former life, that they may seek rewards in Heaven, afar off, ministering to the the poor in spirit, that they may come to know the truth of God. To do more than simply believe and be saved. To do more than be in the Kingdom of Heaven, but to help reign over it. To be willing to live for Christ and not themselves. This wasn't for everyone. Many in the crowds who believed fell away. Like the seed that falls on rocky soil that grows up with shallow roots and fades away in the heat of the sun. Some, in the joy of their salvation and the hope they were filled with tarried longer, seeking to do some service for Christ, only to fade by and by, consumed by the cares of this world. Many are called but few chosen. The harvest is ripe but the laborers few. The spirit willing, but the flesh weak. It is in this context that we see Jesus, on the road to Jerusalem and the looming weight of the cross already heavy on His shoulder, and He turns to the masses that are behind Him, some saved. Some already having given up much to follow Him. Some who believed unto salvation and others unsure. And gadflies and haters of God, seeking that He fall in some way that they could accuse Him. These same sort of mixed multitudes that had been with Him throughout His ministry. And it is in this context that He speaks to them, recorded here in Luke chapter 14. Jesus says essentially, if anyone comes to Him, to be His disciples, and hates not his family, not only his father and mother and wife, but his brothers and sisters and his own children, and more than that, his own life, he cannot be His disciple. Understanding that Jesus doesn't mean that we should hate them, or ourselves, but that we be willing to give them up and more, our very lives because we love Him all the more. That if the choice was given between them and Him, a disciple would choose Christ. He says of you're not earnestly expecting to bear your cross, the implement of death used by the Romans, the equivalent to this first century group of people, pre-crucifixion, pre-resurrection, to saying a firing squad, an electric chair, lethal injection. If you're not willing to be hung from a tree in public, a gazingstock in death for those passersby, a horrific sight they may have seen themselves as it was common, Jesus says, if they would follow Him they must be prepared to face. But even more common mistake, including among saved Christians, is that Jesus is describing the saved, just as they are. That by belief unto redemption that they have picked up that cross. Jesus wasn't trying to discourage us from being His disciples, but dividing the chaff from the wheat, being honest with those of us who remain. Every born again believer is called to be in service to Christ. It is time to consider the cost. Here in Luke chapter 15 we see that again, the Pharisees and scribes murmured amongst themselves, judging Jesus for the publicans and sinners that were drawn to hear His preaching. And again, Jesus shows them in parable that He is come to bring the lost sheep home. He has come to bring sinners to repentance towards God, not the righteous. A physician treats the sick. And Jesus tells how much joy there is in Heaven when one sinner turns towards God that they may be saved. He offered the example of the lost sheep, and another of a lost piece of silver, and the rejoicing of those who had found what was lost, comparing that to God the Father and His angels rejoicing over every saved believer, even the most wicked and wretched. To drive the point home, Jesus tells what has become one of the most iconic parables in scripture. The Prodigal Son. This story of falling and forgiveness, the love of a father for a son thought lost to the world, and the joy at his being restored home is well known even outside of Christian circles. It is an archetype used in secular stories, referred to throughout the culture, and the phrase "prodigal son" part of our lexicon. The tearful joy of the Father at having his son returned to him, all that he'd done forgiven in an instant, has been a moving inspiration to millions seeking redemption in Christ. The lesson that no matter how far we fall, we are still welcome home by God, Who celebrates our return with joy has helped heal so many similarly lost, and brought them home through Christ. It has moved me to tears to read it over the years. First as a sinner, come to God saying "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before you, And am not worthy." But especially as a father of grown children, being able to relate to that kind of heartache and love. The shift in my life's perspective, changing the meaning and adding depth to my appreciation of Jesus' words. But that's not who the parable is addressed to here. It's not addressed to the repentant sinner. It's not addressed to God the Father, for certain. It's addressed to those Pharisees and scribes, ostensibly righteous men, who are casting judgment on the sinners who're called by faith to Christ. They are the elder son. The son, who by nature didn't rebel and stayed, doing the work on the farm for the father, who was there while his brother went after whoredoms and drunkenness. Who stayed true. And who, feeling entitled by his works came to anger at his father, resenting his brother and refusing to celebrate his return. How many saved Christians today are like the elder son? Many who grew up in Christian homes, given the advantage of hearing the Gospel regularly, attending church where the Bible was preached, seeing the testimony of their own family, their parents, friends and congregants living out their Christian walk before them, and who, seeing new converts coming into the church, babes in Christ saved from a life of indulgence and sin, often scarred and broken, traumatized by the damage done in their lives and seeking to be healed, and came to resent them? To be holier than thou? Hypocrites? Fruit inspectors? It's happened. It was the case of the Pharisees, many of whom were not saved by faith but being so immersed in the culture of the religion believed they were righteous by their own works and in a place to judge others. The beam in their eye blinding them. Even those long-saved, but grown prideful, forgetting their previous state and losing sight of the mercy God showed them, the grace given to their undeserved salvation. Thinking they are better than. These are often those who seek to add works to the gospel of grace. Who push Lordship and outward signs of turning from sin before things like longsuffering, charity, instruction. Who have the leaven of the Pharisees in their hearts, which is hypocrisy. These types drive wedges between brothers, sow discord in the assembly, and have torn down entire church families, turning off an unknown multitude from receiving the Gospel by their bad report. Placing stumbling blocks before others, reminding them of their old man constantly. The Bible says As far as the east is from the west, So far hath he removed our transgressions from us. God says, their sins and iniquities will I remember no more. As Jesus puts it, Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth. This must be our attitude as Christians towards others. To love with the charitable love Jesus gave us. Longsuffering. Merciful. With grace. Forgetting about the past. Not holding grudges. Being understanding of the frailties of others, knowing with humility exactly how frail we are ourselves. This is not to say we ignore sin, or compromise what is right. There is church discipline for a reason, and it is outlined by Jesus and the epistles for our use. Right is right. If God says it's a sin, we ought have no other opinion on the matter. We teach and preach separation. Feeding the new man that the old man may fade away. Edifying one another. Steel sharpening steel. But we correct in love. We deal with the beam in our eye so that we may help others with the mote that is in theirs. We forgive when sincere apology is made. We forget, so that there is no resentment or grudge. We avoid the leaven of hypocrisy. We celebrate the return of the lost, rejoicing in their salvation. It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found. Amen

We are in Luke 16. The chapter opens with Jesus speaking to His disciples, again impressing upon them the lessons He must as He makes His way to Jerusalem. Here, Jesus tells them parable of the unfaithful steward. A dishonest steward is to be fired by his wealthy master for mismanagement of the lord's funds. Knowing he'd be out of a job, and not suited to labor or begging, decides to use his position to make deals with his master's debtors, forgiving their debts that they give him favor when he needs it. Buying their loyalty so when he's fired he can go to them for help. The master sees this scheme and, being corrupt himself can't help but be impressed by the servant's wisdom, his chutzpah and cunning. And the lesson here for His disciples isn't that these men are good, or saved, but that sometimes the unsaved, in serving Mammon, understand better how the world works. How to win friends and influence people. For the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light. And so, Jesus says make friends with your wealth. Spend it to others benefit. Forgive them debts. Gain favor the way the unscrupulous servant has, that those you've helped may hear the Gospel, having had the trust gained, and welcome them in the Kingdom one day. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. Your wealth does you no good here. Being stingy, miserly, storing up wealth in this world, is forsaking wealth in the next. In parallel passages the Bible says store up our wealth in heaven. If a worldly unsaved man understands that he can use his position and wealth, the forgiveness of debts to gain favor with men against his future calamity, how can a saved man not see it? There's more important things than money. Think of that future and how what you have can gain against our future in Heaven. So, if we are greedy and niggardly, unwilling to give all charitably that we may do the work of Christ, how can God trust us with actual treasure? Incorruptible crowns? Authority in the Kingdom. If we can't be just with unrighteous Mammon, how will we expect to be just with others souls? Ye cannot serve God and Mammon. This is a theme Jesus has been hammering home; the cost of discipleship. Jesus said we must be willing to hate our family for His sake, and willing to give up our lives. To love others more than ourselves. To not worry for earthly things like food, shelter, raiment. To be willing to forsake all in service to others, that the Gospel be shared. And, to use what wealth we have in that same service to Christ. Lay not up ye treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: for where your treasure is, there will your heart be. Of all the warnings of the costs of true discipleship, of truly following Christ, this one against Mammon, love of money, not only giving up trying to be rich and gaining stuff, but giving away the stuff you already have, is the hardest for most people to face. There is no "prosperity gospel." God provides what we need and knows our needs even when we don't. We may even be blessed with wealth but it's not our own. We are supposed to give all, and yet most of us don't even want to give a 10% tithe to our own church. This can be greed, and it often is. Jealously guarding our treasure here. That it's where our heart is, not Heaven. But for many, it's fear. Fear of doing without. Fear that God won't take care of us. That if we give away that which is extra in our lives that others benefit and by our works, God be glorified, we will suffer need. This fear grips especially tight in times like this where the debt economy, inflation and taxation and other worldly pressures weigh heavily upon us. We may not be called to forsake everything we own. But we are called to at least consider it and do it where appropriate, in the measure called for. To be hospitable. Charitable. To do unto others without thought of ourselves and our own comfort. In two more chapters we will see the rich young man sit down with Jesus and say in all things he is righteous before the law, and Jesus will say ok, sell everything you have and give it all away to follow Me. And the rich young man will walk away. He was being shown the error of his thinking that he was righteous by his works, and most of us won't be called to forsake all. God knows our limitations and infirmities. But we are called to give. To be as wise as this worldly unsaved steward. To not serve Mammon while claiming to serve God. The emphasis on discipleship that Jesus keeps preaching, the cost and expectations that he has for us to truly be called followers of Christ, not just saved from hell but laying up treasures in Heaven, should have us all feeling convicted. That we're not doing enough. Most saved Christians will tell you that they would gladly lay down their life for the cause of Christ. That rather than deny Him, we would suffer death in His name. Knowing we have eternal life and knowing that it was a gift, we would gladly lay it down. Out of love and gratitude for the grace that was shown us. And we may sincerely mean it, although it's easy to say, knowing that it's unlikely to ever come up. It's a cheap hyperbolic brag. Our lives are not our own and having the comfort of the blessed hope of eternal life means that threats of death are threats with Heaven. But even so we know it likely will never be asked of us and so it's easy to say. But how many saved Christians are willing to lay down 15-20 minutes of our morning to read the Bible? How many saved Christians are willing to go to church once a week, let alone three times a week? To go door knocking and soul winning? To give what extra they have in wealth and in time to the service of others that God may be glorified in us? How can we expect to seriously be willing to go to our death for professing the name of Christ if we won't be inconvenienced a little bit here and there? I speak this to my own shame. And understand there are unsaved people, people working their way to heaven with the false gospel of works, who do more to help those in need than actually saved Christians today. I'll tell you truthfully there are reprobates who for wicked reasons give of their time and their money, that benefit the poor and the needy, more than some saved Christians are willing to do. Count the cost of discipleship. Understand that Christianity isn't just an identity, a scene, a cheap ideological category to cosplay as, the way political and cultural identities are used today. It is not a set of arguments that we have prepackaged for us to spout off against others who have absorbed and regurgitated the ones they've consumed. Way too many of us who claim to be saved treat it that way. I say this out of love. I say this to chastise myself as much as to motivate you. When I count the cost, and reckoning my efforts, I find I do the bare minimum for Christ, and sometimes less than that. If you're honest with yourself, you'll find the same. There are people like this unfaithful servant who do favors for others that they may gain in this life, and in doing so bless other people more than saved Christians who profess the Gospel and have the spirit within them. Strive to do more. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches? This is a hard saying. This is difficult to hear. We are so caught up in touting our own righteousness that we missed the point of having it entirely. Jesus isn't Joel Osteen. He doesn't preach a gospel of comfort and wealth. If we seek to grow in our Christian life, we need to recognize the cost asked of us for following Him. And that starts with daily Bible reading and prayer. And the more we read the Bible, the more we understand what is expected of us. With more knowledge comes more expectation. To whom much is given much is required. The more you know, the more you realize you're half-assing it. Some will count the cost and fall away, castaway. Like the seed that falls on unfertile ground. Few will strive for the faith and contend for the crowns incorruptible. To produce fruit a hundredfold. We should consider this before feeling comfortable in our salvation. That we are prepared to do all for Christ. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. If you start with this basic premise and understanding, and apply it in your life, best you can, it provides you with the ability to call evil out when you see it, and have people respect and agree with you, and defend you because you you've been a blessing to them, which by your conversation, behavior, they see in you that light that shines. Taking the lesson of the parable of the unjust steward in Luke 16, as Jesus says And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations. And the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him. We see the transition here in chapter 16 of Luke, from Jesus addressing His disciples, to the Pharisees, who hearing His preaching, derided Him. They were covetous, the Bible says. Covering means to resent those with something we lack coupled with the desire to possess that which isn't ours to have. Covetousness, which is idolatry according to scripture, is a sin because by its very nature shows a lack of gratitude towards God, and makes us bring evil towards our neighbors. Here the Pharisees are hearing Jesus preach on serving God rather than Mammon, not taking care for the things of this world, but rather laying up treasures in Heaven, and Luke, writing in the Spirit points out their covetousness. This preaching offends them. He says they follow the Law, but since John the Baptist and his preaching of the Kingdom and Christ's coming, the Law is not profitable, salvation is here. They sought to be made justified by the works they did and the outward appearances they kept up, and by appealing to the justification before men, and when the Gospel of reconciliation is preached to them, where the praise of men matters not, but the humility and faith of a contrite heart towards God saves, they derided Him. They despised the gift. Like Jesus said to His disciples in the previous verses, the Pharisees couldn't be trusted with the things of this world, they certainly won't be trusted for the things of the world to come. Jesus says the Law and the prophets were to bring men to salvation when the kingdom of God is preached them. That they be fruit meet for repentance. They don't see the Christ before them, and missed the point that there are none righteous, no not one. All have come short of the Glory of God. And so, Jesus tells these covetous and hypocritical "holy men" a parable, the story of Lazarus and the rich man. We are introduced to a certain rich man. Often in Jesus preaching he uses "a certain man" to indicate someone who is a particular type of person, that we the audience would readily recognize and know. This certain man was rich, dressed in finery, and ate not just well, but sumptuously. We get the picture here, he is very rich. And by implication, someone when covetous Pharisees would see as one justified by the reckoning of man, the way they see themselves. An exaggerated version of their ideal, and in the context of their derision against His preaching on serving Mammon. And Jesus contrasts this certain rich man with Lazarus, a poor beggar which was laid at the gate of the rich man seeking the crumbs that fell from his plate. Moreover, Lazarus was full of sores, suffering physically, humiliated by the dogs licked his open wounds. Dogs being unclean to the eyes of the Jews. A more pathetic figure couldn't be painted. And it came to pass both died, and Lazarus went to Heaven, and the rich man to Hell. And we are told that the rich man lifted up his eyes to heaven while in torment, and across the great gulf fixed between hell and Heaven saw Lazarus being comforted by father Abraham, and cried out for mercy. To send Lazarus with just a little water, a finger dipped, that his tongue would feel relief from the burning hellfire. Where in life, Lazarus begged for his crumbs, the rich man is reduced to similar begging. But Abraham said, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented. And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence. Daunted, and seeking place for repentance where none can be found, the rich man begs that Lazarus return to the land of the living and preach the truth of salvation to the rich man's brothers that they may be spared this fate. Abraham saith unto him, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. And he said, Nay, father Abraham: but if one went unto them from the dead, they will repent. And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead. Jesus makes the point emphatically. They didn't come to salvation by faith, which comes by hearing the word of God. They served Mammon, like the rich man in Hell. And just as they didn't believe Moses and the prophets, they wouldn't be persuaded though a man rose from the dead. This has a double meaning, where there is the literal example of Lazarus, raised from the dead by Jesus in Bethany, whom the Jews saw come up from the grave after 4 days, made whole by the compassion of Jesus.
