I would be remiss if I didn't address some of the contentions that come from this parable. There are some who take this teaching of Jesus and draw conclusions from it for doctrine that amount to them attempting to fit their square pegs into round holes. Who are applying the logic of men to the things of God. There are some who deny Heaven and Hell entirely and to them they will say that this parable shouldn't be used to justify the doctrines of Heaven and Hell being real, fixed places in the cosmos. And the destination of the dead be they saved or unsaved. They take a general rule of thumb that is true and apply it here in a way that's foolish. We shouldn't draw doctrine from parables taken literally. We aren't literally having the faith of a mustard seed. We aren't literally sowing seeds upon the ground. We aren't literally sheep, the enemy's not literally wolves. We are supposed to see that creation serves as a way of understanding God's word, which is spirit and which is life. But what they fail to understand is that every parable that Jesus tells is of something we can understand. Of something real. Of lamps and oil and weddings and servants, of lords and stewards. Sowing seeds and harvesting the fruit. Jesus consistently uses creation as the backbone of his parables so that man can relate to what he's saying and take from it. The spiritual application that He's providing. That's no different here. God is not the author of confusion, and Jesus doesn't make things up. So even if this is simply a parable and not an actual retelling of events, it still uses as its basis, reality. Identifiable and understandable concepts. Death and the life thereafter, or condemnation to Hell which is burning and fire. Another mistaken doctrine that stems from this is the idea that Abraham's bosom is a place and not a body part. That prior to Jesus crucifixion there was no Heaven and Hell but waiting areas, that Lazarus went to a paradise that is part of Hell. That Jews who were saved in the Old Testament, All of the Israelite saints, that when they die they went to Abraham's bosom rather than to Heaven where Abraham awaited. This is often paired with dispensationalist heresies. It's foolishness and the other extreme of using parables for doctrine. We can't say for certain that the Lazarus of this story is Jesus' friend from Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha whom Jesus loved. But it's unusual for Jesus in a parable to use the specific name rather than a certain descriptor. It's not that important that we know this detail for sure. It's the spiritual application of the parable that matters. That there are some who see the richness of life as sumptuous living and worldly success. Who serve mammon rather than God. And their ability to believe, to come to saving faith is hampered by their pride and arrogance. Their hypocrisy and covetousness. They're placing the justification before men above being justified by God. There is a Heaven and there is a Hell and there is more to this life than the things that we store up here on earth. Don't allow your comfort or your wealth or your respect among your peers to confuse you regarding salvation. All have fallen short and failed to uphold God's law. And don't allow the low status of some to make you see them as less than. Don't be a respecter of persons.

Luke 17 continues the portion of the Gospel where Jesus preaches and teaches, making His way to Jerusalem. Here, again addressing His disciples Jesus says "It is impossible but that offenses will come." Understand that in the Bible, "offenses" refers to causing another to sin. To place a stumbling block in another's path, giving them occasion to sin. Jesus says it is impossible but that we be offended. That there will be stumbling blocks and snares and temptations brought before all men, including we who are saved. It is inevitable. "But woe unto him, through whom they come!" Jesus says woe unto the person offending, the person laying snares and stumbling blocks. The person tempting another to sin. Woe unto them, that it would be better that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the sea than that he should offend one of these little ones, speaking of the children brought before Him, as we see in the other Gospels. We tend to understand and focus on the direct application of this teaching, regarding sodomites who target and corrupt children, grooming them with abuse, guile, alcohol, corrupt speech, into becoming a reprobate like themselves. That they don't reproduce, they recruit and do so by offending little ones. It is a correct teaching to say that Jesus is telling these reprobate pedophiles that they should kill themselves to make it easier on them in Hell, for the added torment they will receive for offending against a child. It is true. The false idea that the Jesus of the NT is some hippy dippy "all is love" God, somehow different from the God of the Old Testament isn't supported by scripture. He comes in wrath on the day of the Lord, and all in Hell are tormented before His presence. I feel like the high incidents of suicide in the sodomite community comes from this basic understanding that they are escaping even worse punishment than the eternity in outer darkness, burning in a lake of fire, that they already face. Heeding Jesus' warning. But there is a broader application to this doctrine, one few of us are willing to apply to ourselves. How often have we in our lives brought offense to another? Even if it were intentionally making someone else angry and wrathful? It doesn't have to be tempting someone to share our sin. Getting them to drink booze, smoke cigarettes, fornication, to steal. It can be as basic as spinning up fear in their lives by promoting that which you know triggers their outrage, and pushes the buttons that lead them to spiral into fear, and wrath. We have a responsibility not to be a stumbling block for others. Jesus' warning is to us, too. In all matters, we are to seek the spiritual profit of others. It doesn't do that to aggressively red pill or black pill someone weaker in the faith than you. To "truth-rape" a normie. To put the cares of this world before that of the Kingdom to come. This isn't to say we don't speak the truth, stand for Biblical principles, provide guidance and knowledge that others may better navigate the world and grow in faith. But it does mean we don't try to offend, in the biblical sense of the word. Don't seek to trip someone up to an occasion to sin. And especially don't bring sin to a child, you should rather join the pedophiles at the bottom of the sea. Romans 14:13-23 Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way. I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean. But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died. Let not then your good be evil spoken of: For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. For he that in these things serveth Christ is acceptable to God, and approved of men. Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another. For meat destroy not the work of God. All things indeed are pure; but it is evil for that man who eateth with offence. It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak. Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth. And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin. In our Christian life we will be babes, and meet babes. Not everyone is at the same point as you are in your walk. Many you will meet have a head understanding of the word, and not the faith that comes from it, or they retain some of the ideas and doctrines of men that they still apply, convinced of their importance to the faith they've only just begun to have. They are like children. Babes in Christ. And if you're more solid in your faith, have a greater understanding of the liberty found in Christ, and yet seek to impose that understanding in a way that brings that child to be offended, you're doing them harm. Woe unto you. Honestly assess the times in your life where in judgment your rebuke and reproof was actually just pride and arrogance, and how in that sin you've brought others to sin. We can all recall times where we joined the evil of others, where we set wicked things before someone else's eyes. Where we encouraged another to join us in something we ought not do. Misery loving company. It is impossible but that offenses come, and so it is impossible but that we have been the means by which they do. But how many of us have done this subtly, and supposedly in Christ's name? Raise your hand. If we are honest with ourselves, we all have our hands up. Few Christians can say they haven't used poor judgment that could cause another to stumble. And it came to pass, as he went to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. And there Jesus saw ten lepers, calling out to be healed. And as was custom under the law as we saw earlier in Luke, Jesus says they are healed, go show the priests and do the sacrifices that they may be proved clean. And all but one go off. The remaining one, a Samaritan. By implication the others were Jews. (They might not be, but it seems the purpose of God to point this out.) The healed Samaritan stays, falling before Jesus in thanks, praising God. Jesus asks where the other 9 were, this stranger, a non-Jew, says they can't be found, that they were healed and took off. Jesus tells Him his faith has made him whole. Not only healed physically, but saved spiritually. Now to those of us saved spiritually, by faith, calling out "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us" that in His grace we be forgiven, there is a lesson here. Physical healing, a picture of our spiritual healing in salvation, we see Jesus tell them to go on their way. He doesn't ask they praise God or worship Him in thanksgiving. He heals them and says to go do what you're supposed to. In this case the ritual ordinances relating to the healing of a leper. In ours, the basics of the faith, showing we are clean as it were. Turn from sin, read your Bible, say your prayers, love God, love others. Bare minimum Christianity. Few, maybe one out of ten as is the example here, actually realize what a gift they've been given and rather than the bare minimum, seek to serve Him more, in praise and thanksgiving. All ten were healed. All who believe are given eternal life. But it is the rare few who follow it up with this level of devotion as pictured by the Samaritan. Luke's Gospel has been focused on the costs and consequence of discipleship. Of what following Christ actually means. That we are not only healed, justified by faith through the grace of God in Jesus name, but how we grow our faith that we may better serve Him in gratitude. The disciples here ask Jesus to show them how to grow their faith. He says if they had the smallest amount of faith they could uproot a sycamine tree, and plant it in the sea. A sycamine is known for its incredibly deep and strong roots. It is not just some shallow rooted pine. Jesus uses extremes in examples to give us a measure of what He means. But His answer as to how we grow our faith actually ties in and dovetails perfectly with the story of the 10 lepers. Jesus says that when a servant is finished with his chores in the day, the master doesn't treat him as if he's accomplished something extra. He doesn't have him come and sit and feast. What Jesus is saying is the servant did what he's supposed to do. And that the right attitude having done that bare minimum, should be We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do. This is how we grow our faith. This is Jesus answer to them to this specific pointed question. Just as the nine lepers went and did what they were told to do, what was expected of them, didn't make them remarkable. A leper healed from his incurable illness was meant to go to the priest and offer the sacrifices and perform the rituals of cleansing to prove they were healed. I have to note it again. The order of things here, where in the leper is healed already and then they do the things required of them. (Again, understanding that this Old Testament law was put into place as a foreshadowing of what Jesus would do specifically for the purpose of these instructions in doctrine. God is great. Amen?) Jesus says that we can grow our faith not by doing the bare minimum but realizing that doing bare minimum of what's expected of us makes us unprofitable servants. That in our realization we become as that Samaritan who, being healed, did more. Expressing his gratitude with humility. Again, Jesus doesn't demand this of the 10 lepers when they are healed. Only that they do what they're obliged to. Just as the servant who plows the fields and then comes in and makes the meal and serves the master is doing just the bare minimum. What he's expected to do. It is the humility and understanding the honor that we get to serve God, being unworthy and unprofitable, doing more than the bare minimum. Without expectation of praise for what is honestly the least we can do. The following of the law. Following the commandments of God. The least we can do. And if we seek to grow our faith, realize that that is the bare minimum and strive to do more. And so, we have to ask ourselves, are we like the one Samaritan? Followers of Christ, doing more, willing to forsake everything for the ministry of the Gospel? Growing in our faith the more we realize just how great a gift we've been given, and so loving Jesus that we devote ourselves to following Him. Picking up our cross. Or are we like the 9? Saved, for certain. Healed of our transgressions and doing the basics, following the commandments of the law, but little else. Doing what we ought to by obligation, and little else. Unprofitable servants. Bare minimum Christians. Or worse, are we not even holding up that weak standard? Is our faith so little that we don't even do that which is expected. Falling short of that bare minimum expectation? Caring so little about our healing that we don't stop to praise God and seek to do more for Him except the basics, and failing to do even that. This hits hard. I fall short. But it's the lesson that is being taught, and we cannot ignore it. If you fall short of that bare minimum, or if you do your best to do what you're obligated to, and little else, don't judge others and their Christian walk. Don't be a stumbling block or a cause of offense. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. Luke 17 20 And when he was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come, he answered them and said, The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: 21 Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you. 22 And he said unto the disciples, The days will come, when ye shall desire to see one of the days of the Son of man, and ye shall not see it. 23 And they shall say to you, See here; or, see there: go not after them, nor follow them. 24 For as the lightning, that lighteneth out of the one part under heaven, shineth unto the other part under heaven; so shall also the Son of man be in his day. 25 But first must he suffer many things, and be rejected of this generation. 26 And as it was in the days of Noe, so shall it be also in the days of the Son of man. 27 They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all. 28 Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot; they did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded; 29 But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all. 30 Even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed. 31 In that day, he which shall be upon the housetop, and his stuff in the house, let him not come down to take it away: and he that is in the field, let him likewise not return back. 32 Remember Lot's wife. 33 Whosoever shall seek to save his life shall lose it; and whosoever shall lose his life shall preserve it. 34 I tell you, in that night there shall be two men in one bed; the one shall be taken, and the other shall be left. 35 Two women shall be grinding together; the one shall be taken, and the other left. 36 Two men shall be in the field; the one shall be taken, and the other left. 37 And they answered and said unto him, Where, Lord? And he said unto them, Wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together.

When should the Kingdom of God come? Jesus, asked this question of the Pharisees, says that the kingdom isn't an earthly kingdom. It is within us to be part of it. It is spirit. It is in our hearts. We who are saved are of the Kingdom. Jesus taught His disciples that when we do good in the service of the Lord unto others, the Kingdom is nigh unto them. When a people reject the Gospel, Jesus said to shake off the dust, telling them that the Kingdom was nigh unto them. We carry the Kingdom of God in our hearts and the key to its entrance in the truth of the gospel. It sounds corny and sappy to modern ears, just as much as it did the scoffers and mockers of Christ's day. They expected an earthly kingdom led by an earthly king. They saw their religion as being about political power and breaking free of Roman oppression and the restoration of Judea. Their faith in wealth and man. But Jesus Christ came to offer something greater. But knowing the impatience of man, and the weight of the world on even the most devout, Jesus offers us the hope of His glorious return, the coming of His wrath, and the gathering of the elect in the resurrection and rapture. Jesus teaching on n end times prophecy is most extensively given in Matthew 24, but Luke's telling has the fundamentals and added insight. Jesus says as weary and impatient as we may be, don't be fooled. If someone comes claiming a secret return of Christ, not to believe them because Jesus will appear as the lightening that spans to all edges of the sky. Unmistakable. All will see His return. The dispensationalist heresy of a pre-trib rapture relies on a secret coming of Christ, which sets men up for being fooled by the antichrist. Let no man deceive you. Jesus return will be for the unbelieving like the days of Noah, where everyone went about their business, until Noah and his family were taken in to the ark as sudden destruction came up on the rest. The wrath of God poured out from Heaven. The same with Sodom, where the wicked vexed just Lot with their filthy behavior, and the people there did what people do, right up to the day Lot and his family were spirited away, gathered by angels, and fire rained down destroying the wicked cities. 2 Peter 3:3-6 Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation. For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water: Whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished Jesus says, in that day of the Lord at His return, which will be manifest to all, we who are saved will be gathered, like birds of carrion to a corpse. Where Christ is in the clouds we will go to Him, caught up together. And woe to those who turn back. Who doubt. Who like Lot's wife turn to their old life and things. Who believed in vain and put the things of this world before the kingdom. Those seeking to save their life lose it. Make sure you know where you stand. 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord. There are those who teach that there is no rapture, or that if there is, it is past. 2 Timothy 2:16-19 But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus; Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some. Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity. Jesus tells us, let no man deceive you. The signs of the times. To be watchful and sober. To be ready. Paul and Peter in their epistles emphasize the importance of patience in awaiting that day, that it will come and to ignore the scoffers and the heretics that seek to undermine the faith in regards to the rapture and the day of the Lord. These teachings on the end times, what to watch for and what to expect and what to do in the meantime are clear, consistent, and as we saw in our study on Revelation, necessary that the will of God be done, that His kingdom come. Revelation 6:10 And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth? Luke 18 opens continuing the teaching to Jesus' disciples on the coming of the day of the Lord, and He offers a parable that they understand to pray always for the kingdom to come, and not faint, not be worried or impatient. He gives an example of a man who is a judge, not God-fearing, not a respecter of persons, who when bothered repeatedly by a woman seeking him to avenge her against her adversary, decides to do it to avoid her constant bothering. Jesus says if this unjust judge will do the right thing to avoid the widow's incessant pleading, how much more will God the Father avenge His elect in answer to their prayers? When Jesus teaches us to pray, He says "Thy kingdom come" should be a part of it. We are told to pray for God's swift judgment, the day of the Lord, our salvation and redemption by the resurrection, and His glorious and righteous wrath being poured out on the earth and the wicked that remain. Jesus assured us, He will come speedily. God, to Whom a thousand years is like a day to man, will not tarry. He will repay. Vengeance is His. But, Jesus asks, Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? Luke 18 9 And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others: 10 Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. 11 The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. 12 I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. 13 And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. 14 I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted. 15 And they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them. 16 But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God. 17 Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child shall in no wise enter therein. And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others. The Pharisee who prayed thanksgiving that he wasn't a degenerate sinner like other men. Believing by his fasting and tithing he was made righteous. By his works. The publican aware he was most wretched among men, praying to God for mercy, calling upon the name of the Lord for forgiveness in faith. Jesus says in no uncertain terms that the publican went away justified rather than the Pharisee. That he who abased himself became exalted, and he who exalted himself in his self-righteous works, left humbled. Jesus then says to suffer the children, the innocent, to come to Him. That we must be as a child to enter into the kingdom of Heaven. Humbled and trusting. Not in our own mind worthy and prideful. Wise in our own conceits. Luke 18 18 And a certain ruler asked him, saying, Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? 19 And Jesus said unto him, Why callest thou me good? none is good, save one, that is, God. 20 Thou knowest the commandments, Do not commit adultery, Do not kill, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honour thy father and thy mother. 21 And he said, All these have I kept from my youth up. 22 Now when Jesus heard these things, he said unto him, Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me. 23 And when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich. 24 And when Jesus saw that he was very sorrowful, he said, How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God! 25 For it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God. 26 And they that heard it said, Who then can be saved? 27 And he said, The things which are impossible with men are possible with God. 28 Then Peter said, Lo, we have left all, and followed thee. 29 And he said unto them, Verily I say unto you, There is no man that hath left house, or parents, or brethren, or wife, or children, for the kingdom of God's sake, 30 Who shall not receive manifold more in this present time, and in the world to come life everlasting. 31 Then he took unto him the twelve, and said unto them, Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of man shall be accomplished. 32 For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on: 33 And they shall scourge him, and put him to death: and the third day he shall rise again. 34 And they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them, neither knew they the things which were spoken. 35 And it came to pass, that as he was come nigh unto Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the way side begging: 36 And hearing the multitude pass by, he asked what it meant. 37 And they told him, that Jesus of Nazareth passeth by. 38 And he cried, saying, Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me. 39 And they which went before rebuked him, that he should hold his peace: but he cried so much the more, Thou son of David, have mercy on me. 40 And Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought unto him: and when he was come near, he asked him, 41 Saying, What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee? And he said, Lord, that I may receive my sight. 42 And Jesus said unto him, Receive thy sight: thy faith hath saved thee. 43 And immediately he received his sight, and followed him, glorifying God: and all the people, when they saw it, gave praise unto God. Another telling of the rich young man, that we have covered in Matthew and Mark. The juxtaposition between the rich young man and the parable of the Pharisee and publican, and Jesus suffering the children, seems fitting, as the young man is justifying himself by his works, proud in his wealth and claims of righteousness. He asks Jesus what must he do to inherit eternal life. Calling Jesus "good master," Jesus tempts him asking why does he call Him good, for only God is good. Had the rich young man recognized that Jesus was the son of God, that He was God made flesh, he wouldn't have asked a self serving question seeking to be justified by his works. Lacking that faith, Jesus tells him the only other way; perfect obedience to the law, which in his pride the rich young man claims he has done since his youth. And so Jesus tells him if this is true he only lacks one thing, selling all to give to the poor, and he can follow Jesus, with the surety of treasure in Heaven. And hearing this, the rich young man becomes sorrowful, not wishing to give up those things he has. For it is harder for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God than a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. They who exalt themselves shall be made humble. This isn't an endorsement of works salvation, it is Jesus pointing out the folly of trusting in one's self to be righteous. To be justified before God. At this point, the Bible says Jesus taught all things that were to happen to Him in Jerusalem to His disciples. He told them all, the arrest, scourging, the shame of the cross and His death, and His resurrection after three days. And those closest to Jesus, who had forsaken all to follow Him, in faith, didn't understand. Finally, it wouldn't be a chapter in Luke without Jesus healing a physical infirmity. Here a blind beggar, who not being able to physically see recognizes Jesus for who He is. The blind man asks what the commotion was when Jesus passed by. He is told. His faith, which came by hearing, led him to call out to the Lord for mercy. And by his faith, he was healed. Jesus saying "Thy faith hath saved thee." And with the restoration of his sight, he praised God and followed Christ. Contrast the blind beggar with the rich young man. Faith vs works of self-righteousness. Who was healed and rejoiced and who was turned away sorrowful. Consider how it is you know you are going to Heaven (or why you aren't sure). The blind beggar had no doubt that Christ would heal him, taking mercy on him, a humble man of faith who called upon His name. The rich young man who didn't recognize Jesus for who He was while sitting right there next to Him, wanted reassurance that his works had saved him, and when told they weren't enough, that it would require him to humble himself and give up everything to be perfect, he walked away in tears. This is the contrast between salvation by faith and salvation by works. Humility and falling on the mercy of God, vs pride, boasting at your own righteous works. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. If you are counting on your ability to follow the commands of God, to perform ordinances and rites, sacraments and ceremony in order to enter into the kingdom of Heaven, you will be left sorrowful. If you are trusting in yourself to "be good," and "not like others who are wretched sinners," you will leave sorrowful as you're cast into outer darkness. With wailing and gnashing of teeth. If you believe on Jesus to do it all, you can rejoice, praising God, knowing His promises are true, and thus being healed, begin to follow Him. It's that simple, and yet so hard for so many to understand.

Once again, the timing of the Lord amazes me. I had some rough plan to go through the Gospel of Luke and to finish by Easter, God willing, and not only does that appear to be the case, we arrive on Jesus entering Jerusalem, upon the colt of an ass, the people praising Him, today, the Saturday morning entering into what is called Holy Week. His entrance to palms and praise was on a Saturday, not a Sunday, and so it is fitting. Jesus and a multitude of disciples make their way to Jerusalem by way of Jericho, through Bethany, where Lazarus, Mary and Margaret live, where He would stay and eat supper, and up the mountain road to Jerusalem. I have read it's a 8 hour walk from Jericho to Jerusalem, along Roman roads and we'll traveled pathways. In parts a steep climb, and a journey Jesus had made many times in His earthly life. But Jesus takes His time and the journey lasts several days. And as He drew closer to Jerusalem, His destiny must have been weighing heavily on His shoulders. But even in this, He sought the salvation of the lost and the glory of God. We learn of little Zacchaeus, the diminutive chief publican from Jericho, who seeking Jesus and unable to see by the press of the crowd, climbed a tree to witness Christ pass by. Seeing him there on the branch of a sycamore, Jesus calls to Zacchaeus, hailing him by name and says "make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Zacchaeus receives Jesus joyfully. And though the crowd gossiping about Jesus dining with a sinner, Zacchaeus seeks to assure that he has been just in his office, as a lover of the Lord. Jesus says that He has come to find the lost and save them. And tells the crowd a parable. A lord seeking his kingdom rides off to receive it, the people rejecting him and loathe to be ruled by him. Yet he leaves care of treasure, ten pounds with his servants while he is gone. The first who wisely and faithfully brings a gain of 10 pounds when the newly crowned king returns. To the servant, the king grants rule of 10 cities. The second increased by 5, he also receives command of 5 cities. Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority in his kingdom. We are similarly left with treasure of the Lord, His Gospel. And we are similarly expected to seek increase for God. But one servant agrees with the people who despise the king. He delivers back the original 10 pounds, having not used it to gain, but his it away judging the nobleman as the world judged him, cruel and unkind and undeserving of the increase he takes. And judging the wicked servant by his own words, takes away that which he'd been given, gives it to the profitable servant. He then orders those who spoke against him to be slain before him. Wew. What a powerful indictment of those Jews who had the truth, the wealth of His kingdom, and did nothing with it to bring the faith to others that He may have the increase. Zechariah 9:9 Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. Jesus nearing Jerusalem sends disciples to find a colt, the foal of an ass, which is awaiting them as He said, that the prophecy be fulfilled, and He rides triumphantly into Jerusalem, the crowds of disciples crying out Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest. Pharisees, offended by this call from along the route telling Jesus to silence them. Jesus says "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out." AMEN! And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it, Saying, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes. Jesus goes on to again prophesy the destruction that will come to Jerusalem. Not one stone left upon another, made desolate for their unbelief. Jesus again goes to the temple and casts out the money changers. My house is a house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves! And there He taught the people, and the priests and scribes sought how they could kill Him, wary of the people. Everything is in place. Jesus' final week as man has begun. I'm have posted on the timing of the Passion Week, that Jesus was the Passover lamb. Brought to Jerusalem on Saturday, killed on Passover, a Wednesday, the three Sabbaths in a row that bring us to Sunday, and His resurrection. It is a fascinating study, showing the continuity of scripture and the beauty of God's promises. I recommend anyone seeking a deeper understanding to go over it. It is beautiful .

And so, after Luke 19, where Jesus enters Jerusalem triumphantly, with the people worshiping Jesus as God and king, riding on the colt of an ass, in fulfilment of the prophecy, and ending with the chief priests and the scribes and the chief of the people seeking to destroy Jesus, we pick up immediately afterwards. Jesus is teaching in the Temple, giving the Gospel, and a delegation of the high priests, scribes and lawyers, the religious leadership of the Jews and elders of the community, their political leaders, comes to question Jesus, asking Him; by what authority does He do these things? Who does he think He is? They saw the spectacle, they, knowing scripture understanding the significance of what He has done, allowing Himself to be declared Lord, the promised Christ, chasing out again the money changers selling sacrifice in the Temple, and teaching the good news of the Kingdom of God and salvation, in their very seat of power. And, seeking to destroy Him, they ask Jesus; Tell us, by what authority doest thou these things? Or who is he that gave thee this authority? And Jesus, knowing their intentions and knowing that though this is His final few days before His trial and death, seeks to delay their murderous plot till the timing come, and He lay down His life on the Passover. But that time is not yet come, and so Jesus answers them with a question. Was the baptism of John from heaven or of men? Was this new thing John, whom the people considered a prophet, recently slain by Herod, was his baptism brought of God? Or did he come up with it on his own? The Jewish leaders were stumped. They reason with themselves that if they answer that it was of God's authority, then Jesus could ask why they didn't get baptized. Why didn't they follow him? And, if they acknowledged that John's authority came from heaven, it answers their question of where Jesus' authority comes from. And if they deny John, the people will turn on them. Unable to answer, Jesus says He won't answer them either. But then, in parable He gives them what they want, in a subtle way to deny them their opportunity to arrest and kill Jesus. Jesus tells the parable of the vineyard. A certain man, this is the LORD God, Jehovah. The Father. He plants a vineyard. As we see by scripture, this vineyard are the people of Israel, those He made covenant with, when taking them out of Egypt. And this certain man, who is God the Father, gave power to husbandmen to take care of his vineyard. These are the religious and political leaders, the same as who had come to Jesus to tempt Him. The leaders would know exactly what Jesus was saying. Jesus goes on and tells of how in the time to gather the harvest, the man, who is God, sent servants, who are His prophets, and those who were in charge of the vineyard, the leaders, abused them, beat them, treated these servants of the lord of the vineyard shamefully and sent them away with nothing. Then the lord of the vineyard sends his beloved son. That they may respect him. And seeing the heir they said, let us kill him and take the inheritance for themselves. And so they did. And Jesus, telling them their heart, that this was to be His fate as the beloved Son of God, He asks these husbandmen, left over Israel by the Lord, Jesus asks them; What therefore shall the lord of the vineyard do unto them? And Jesus, answering His own question for them says; He shall come and destroy these husbandmen, and shall give the vineyard to others. Shocked and angry, understanding exactly what Jesus is saying in parable, they said "God forbid." And citing scripture, again which these so-called men of God all know, Jesus asks; What is this then that is written, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner? John hits the ground running. No human genealogies. Not the human birth of Christ, but the divine godhead of Jesus. The Word is God's promise. The Word is the written testimony of God to man. The Word is who made all things and gave life, to creation and man. He was the light. He is God, and always was. John begins his testimonial of the good news letting the reader know beyond a shadow of a doubt that Jesus is God, and was with God in the beginning. Genesis 1 26 And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. John establishes first that Jesus always was. Always was God and always was with God, the Father. It's the first doctrine of the Gospel. You have to accept that there is a God, that His Word is true. That Jesus is fully of the godhead, and eternal, and God is the creator of all things and the spark of life for that creation. 5 verses that dispels modalism, oneness heresy. Dispels the "Jesus didn't exist until he was born" heresy. The "Jesus isn't God" heresy. 5 verses that lay a foundation for the faith. Next, the apostle John introduces us to John the Baptist, the voice crying out in the wilderness bearing witness to Christ. John the apostle again turns to explain Jesus is the true light which "lighteth every man." (RIP limited atonement). V10 states the matter plainly, the creator has come into the creation and the creation didn't even recognize Him, fallen as we are. Man doesn't recognize Christ (rip irresistible grace) V11 lays the groundwork for replacement theology. The "chosen people" the Jews don't recognize Christ V11 is the Gospel itself; the good news. "As many received him..." (that's an indeterminate number, meaning 'all who' (limited atonement BTFO, again), "...to them gave he power to become the sons of God" (the promise made by God), "even to them that believe on his name" (the means of obtaining the aforementioned power to be sons of God; BELIEVING, not works or any other means). V13 Sons born (you have to be born again to be a son or daughter of God). Not by blood (dispensationalism, ded), not by our fleshly desire (none righteous), not by our works (the will of man) but of God. V14 is the mystery of Christ made flesh revealed. V15-17 John the BAPTIST (hint) tells us his ministry has been preaching the coming Christ and salvation by grace, not the law. When JtB is questioned by the Pharisees he testifies that Jesus is the Christ come in answer to what was taught by all the prophets, the faith that saved OT saints was manifest. About halfway through one chapter and the doctrines are just boom, boom, boom... Next recounts Jesus baptism and JtB's testimony that Jesus was the Christ whose name he had been preaching and baptizing believers in. Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world. Again, Jesus is the sacrifice that takes away the sin of the whole world. Note in V30 JtB makes clear that not only is Jesus preferred before him, meaning to God, being above him. But that Jesus was before him. Again the eternal godhead. He describes the difference of being baptized with water as a declaration of faith and the baptism of the Holy Ghost which is the gift of that faith. That Jesus truly is the Son of God. Next we get into the recruiting of the apostles. It's important to recognize that as Andrew tells his brother Simon, this is the Christ they were waiting for, because all faithful Jews were aware that God promised a savior. There's a false doctrine that the OT doesn't talk about Jesus when the entire thing is about Him. The introduction of Peter contains the first reference of what Jesus meant when he renamed him; "when Jesus beheld him, he said, Thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone." Cephas/Peter means a stone, not 'rock.' (remember this when you're reading Matthew 16) The Bible defines itself and the translation is done in the text itself, so as to have no mistake about it. John gives us the word and translation (by interpretation) repeatedly throughout his Gospel, and it's for good reason. The remaining verses are wonderful and richly detailed account of Jesus gathering his fishers of men, that reads so true you can imagine it playing out exactly as written. Wonderfully authentic, as is all the dialogue in John. This was the challenge I saw in doing John chapter by chapter. It is so densely packed with doctrine there's so much to unpack. Oh, another thing that I love is the way John uses "come and see," here and in Revelation. It's an invitation of a witness to not just believe his testimony but to come and see for yourself. I hear it as a joyful call. "Hey check this out!" It moves me whenever I read it. We are called to "come and see." Not just to follow blindly, not just to take someone's word for it. Not to be led to gnostic revelation of esoterica, but to literally come and see the light. The truth. The Word. It's wonderful. Come on in, the waters fine!

In the Gospel of John, Jesus is quoted 7 times making affirmation of who He is, using the divine "I am," (as God the Father said to Moses from the burning bush). This formulation would be a sign to some, recognizing Jesus was Christ and a stumbling block to the hypocrites who challenged Jesus at every turn, leading eventually to His arrest and crucifixion. They are: 1) John 6:48 I am that bread of life. 2) John 8:12 Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life. 3) John 10:9 I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture. 4) John 10:11 I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. 5) John 11:25 Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: 6) John 14:6 Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. 7) John 15:1 I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. From these we see Jesus' nature as the source of eternal life and our salvation through Him. His sacrifice and His love. There is an 8th instance, in John 8:57 Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.” - which serves as an emphatic statement on the Son's divinity, and timeless origin. Jesus always has been. He is who am. And as always, the Jews reaction to the truth was anger and violence; "So they picked up stones to throw at him."

In John 4 we begin with something Jesus does frequently in His earthly ministry; he moves on when the heat begins to turn too hot too soon. He must be about His Father's business. Note the detail that Jesus baptized not. He was winning souls, baptism was left to the disciples for those who believed. Leaving Judea to travel to His home country in Galilee, passing through Samaria which had been the northern kingdom of Israel, the 10 tribes that split away after the death of Solomon, and then destroyed by God using the Assyrian empire, around 700BC. Rather than capture and exile, the Assyrians used immigration, interbreeding to dilute and overwhelm, much as we see happening to the West today. Great Replacement. This was a punishment by God for their falling away and worshipping strange gods in high places, and eschewing God's temple in Jerusalem. Following Jeroboam's setting up an alternative altar in Bethel which led Israel to sin, and their ethnic erasure, Jews looked down on Samaritans both spiritually and ethnically, despite shared origin of Jacob and quasi-shared faith of the prophets still being taught and known. It's in this context that Jesus meets the woman at the well. Asking her for a drink from Jacob's well, she questions him regarding the bias Jews have towards her people. The allegory that Jesus is spiritually Jacob's well. The Samaritans still drink of the physical waters of the well as their birthright, and He says if she knew, she would ask Him for salvation, ie the living water. She questions Jesus further to explain, and He gives her the Gospel in metaphor, much the same way we saw with Nicodemus. Similarly, she takes it literally but unlike the Pharisee, we see that she's an ear to hear. Testing her, Jesus asks about her husband, knowing already her sin, and revealing it to her when she answers guardedly but true. She says her people worship God in the mountain rather than the Temple in Jerusalem, "Ye" being plural and referring to the Jews. This is one of the dividing points, and still a sore subject centuries after the divide. He tells her that the time when both the temple and altars won't be needed is coming. The woman responds with understanding of the faith of her fathers, in a way Nicodemus wasn't able to. She knows a messiah was promised and coming. A Christ. Jesus affirms that He is the Christ. (BTFO those who falsely teach Jesus was just a teacher who never claimed to be a messiah) His disciples return at this moment and they are thinking to themselves what's up with Jesus speaking to a Samaritan woman, but keep it to themselves. And as they are, she leaves everything to go to her people and to tell them to "come and see." That she's met the Christ. Unlike the Jews like Nicodemus, who should know the promise preached by the prophets that salvation would come from the Jews, yet can't see it, this woman and her countrymen see and believe. Now His disciples who had returned with food try to get Jesus to eat, but he takes the opportunity to explain His meat is doing His Father's work; winning souls. As is often the case, Jesus explains by comparing their sharing the faith with harvesting. He points to the gathering Samaritans that they are ripe to be harvested. He tells the disciples that their labors in gathering will be rewarded, even as the sower will be. In our labors for Christ, some of us will sow seeds and never see if they germinate and grow to fruit ripe for harvesting. Some of us water the seeds sown by others. Some are blessed to reap. All will rejoice in Heaven when we meet those we've helped win to the Lord. Jesus preached for 2 days and they believed on Him, having seen for themselves that the report of the woman was true. The chapter ends with Jesus in Galilee, where he expects His own receive Him not. But it seems like having seen signs and wonders of Him, they are at least interested. It's in this atmosphere that the nobleman father from Capernaum comes to ask Jesus come and heal his son who is near death. Jesus tests the man, saying you're only here asking because you've seen signs and wonders, not faith. Just like the woman at the well, the father confesses his faith in Jesus to save his son, and with that Jesus heals the child. The father believes Jesus' word and his prayer is answered. That's all God asks of us. With Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman and the Capernaum father, we see Jesus test them. To see if they have faith. A Calvinist would say that God provides the faith, but imagine how cruel Jesus' testing would appear if this were the case. We have the power to believe Jesus' word, or not. The free choice to accept salvation.

John 5 opens with the miracle at Bethesda. A paralyzed man waits at a pool that the Bible tells us, is a healing pool where an angel will occasionally trouble the waters and the first to go in is made whole. (Verse 4 which describes this phenomenon is missing from the NIV, diminishing the greatness of God.) Jesus knowing how long the man had lingered there waiting asks him if he even wants to be healed. As we see so often in John, Jesus tests people, just as He does us. How many of us linger in vague belief and vain faith, waiting to be healed, trusting God that it's possible, and yet never get in the pool, so to speak. How many people are willing, but are spiritually crippled by weak flesh? The lame man believes God can heal him, but, in one of the most poignant lines of the NT, says "Sir, I have no man..." Imagine the faith to be there, day after day, and the desperation of knowing you could be made whole if you had but a man to do what your weak flesh cannot? We have such a man in Jesus. Seeing the lame man's faith and weakness of body, Jesus heals him, and makes him whole. Just as he is. Just as He will for us. And once healed we are called to take up the symbols of our infirmities, the earthly things we relied on, and carry them away. Now, it wouldn't be the Gospel of John without a lesson on the Jews resenting and hating Jesus for His doing His Father's work. It's a Sabbath, which in the Mosaic law is a picture of the rest we have in Jesus, and instead of seeing the miracle for what it is, the work of God, they use the letter of the law to condemn Christ. When Jesus answers their charge with "My Father worketh hither to, and I work" they cannot hear His meaning, only that Jesus called Himself the son of God. Their anger and fear, their status and beliefs threatened, the good news only further enrages them. The remaining verses of the chapter are all red letter preaching by Jesus. Jesus establishes His sonship with the Father. That He emulates and gets His authority from the Father. That His dominion as the Son is the authority of the Father, and to honor the Father you must honor Jesus. This is pure doctrine. Next Jesus again gives the good news of the Gospel; Saying He is telling us truthfully that any who hear God's word, His testimony of Christ, and believe, has everlasting life and shall not come I to condemnation. (Again showing that once we are saved it is forever. We HAVE everlasting life. We WON'T be condemned) Jesus preaches that the dead in spirit will hear His voice, His word, and live. Salvation quickens, or makes alive, our dead spirit inside and brings us into life. Jesus says not to marvel at the basic Gospel, just wait until the resurrection of the dead! Jesus again teaches He is not there for His own will, but that of the Father. Each member of the Godhead has His own will, are their own person, Father, the Son and the Spirit. But these three are one and obey the will of God the Father. Jesus accuses the Jews of not believing the witness of those testifying He is Christ and what He says is true. He points to John the Baptist as one, then the Holy Ghost, the works of God the Father Jesus does, and the very scriptures that the Pharisees claim their authority from, that testifies to who Jesus is. The Jews claim to believe in the resurrection of the dead and the salvation of the Christ, but they don't have the truth in them, and so they can't see it when He's literally in front of them. Jesus prophesies about the antichrist, who the Jews will believe on, even as they reject Jesus. He finishes reminding them that if they believe the scriptures, then they'd believe on Him, as Moses wrote of Him. Again this destroys the dispensationalist heresy, as well as the "oral tradition" of the Talmudic Jews. Scripture is written. God preserves it as His testimony. And the OT scripture is all about Jesus, and faith in His coming, and believing God's promise is how people were saved, in all times.

In the opening of John 6, we see one of the accounts of Jesus feeding the multitudes with the miracle of the loaves and fishes. 5,000 had followed Jesus seeking to see miracles of his healing of the sick. The disciples follow Christ's instructions and hand out what were 5 loaves of bread and some fish, and having fed the masses to the fill, had baskets left over. As we see, this is a picture of the salvation in Christ through God's grace, which abounds and is more than enough to fill all who come, and still there'd be more than man could fill himself with. The crowd, having earthly fill from this miracle sought to make Jesus an earthly king, not comprehending the spiritual nature of eternal life He was offering. Next is one of the accounts of Jesus walking on water. Note His miraculous coming and the fear of the apostles turns to their willingly accepting Him. Pictures of salvation. Now the crowd He'd fed and who wished to make Jesus king of their lives, followed across the sea to find Him, their bellies still satisfied by the bread He'd given them to eat, but Christ sees their hearts. "Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled." They are still seeking earthly things of the flesh. Jesus puts them in mind of the spiritual things of the Gospel. That He is offering far more than a meal for the belly, but eternal life for the spirit. The crowd asks what they have to do, what works they must undertake to receive the meat of everlasting life from God, Jesus replies "This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent." Again, works salvation takes the L. Now in testing the crowd, they respond seeking after a sign, and again look at their fleshly needs to be physically fed, asking Jesus to prove Himself like Moses "giving manna" to their fathers in the desert. Jesus corrects them that bread came down from Heaven from God, and having shown that they lacked understanding, Jesus begins to preach. Jesus tells us that He is the bread come down from Heaven, sent by God. He means this spiritually but the carnal crowd is still seeking things of the flesh and take it literally. Jesus says "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst." We believe on Him to receive this spiritual bread and drink, and once received we never hunger or thirst again, having been renewed unto everlasting life. Too many like Nicodemus or this crowd, trapped in their own carnal desires cannot see the spiritual, and begin to think Christ is speaking literally, physically. They have seen Him, His works and signs, and yet don't believe and so lack understanding. The preaching Jesus gives that follows is so important, let's look at it again: 37 All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. 38 For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me. 39 And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day. 40 And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day. These verses are often used by Calvinists to say the Father chooses who is saved, but as we see in v40 everyone could see Jesus and believe. Not everyone will. Those who say you can lose your salvation ignore that Jesus says those given Him by God's grace shall in no wise be cast out. That He shall not lose any who believe and are given Him. That they will have everlasting life and be raised up on the last day. Everlasting. You cannot lose your salvation. Finally we have those who say you have to do the will of the Father to be saved, which is true, but they take it to mean obeying the commandments, repenting of all sin. But that is not the "will of the Father" Jesus teaches. He says His Father's will is that all who believe have everlasting life. To obey the Gospel. To accept His word. Again, the Gospel of John is written to the unsaved so that they may know if they believe on Jesus they will have the gift of eternal life given by God. And just like we have seen in the previous chapters, this truth is given for those with eyes to see, who seek the truth. For others it is taken as literally as Nicodemus talking about being born again from his mother's womb, and they miss the message and thus, cannot believe and be saved. Now once again the Jews in the crowd hear Jesus preaching and take offense at the Gospel given. They REE at Christ. Jesus responds to this in much the same manner as His talk with Nicodemus, reiterating the message, but less simplified, further confounding the natural men among them. V44 is another taken out of context by Calvinists to justify their damnable heresy. As we see by reading the entire book, they are missing what He actually says. Jesus says man can't believe unless the Father draws them unto Christ. Sounds convincing for limited atonement and being chosen, but not so fast. John 12:31-32 31 Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out. 32 And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me. Christ being lifted up, crucified on a cross, will draw all men unto Him. All mankind in their hearts know the truth, and are drawn unto him. But drawn doesn't mean believe. That's up to each of us. So now, again, the Jews and especially the Pharisees among them, being natural men and not understanding the spiritual things of God, fail the test of understanding that Jesus held out to them, and so He moves further from the milk of the word to the meat. For if they cannot understand the simple things and the parables and analogies, then Jesus may as well preach harder things and more difficult, dark sayings. Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life. They don't get it. I am that bread of life. Nope. They can't understand. Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead. This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. Here Jesus gives the full Gospel, and compares it again to the manna from Heaven which fed the body, but not the soul. He explains his flesh, his actual physical body will be sacrificed on the cross, that He'll die physically to bring salvation to the world, that that is the way he is the bread of life. How spiritual bread can be His flesh. And again, like Nicodemus, the Jews do not understand the spiritual things of God, being natural men. And instead they take it literally to mean actually eating bread that is made of his flesh. They turn what is basic salvation into cannibalism in their lack of understanding. Many denominations today take that literal approach to what Jesus is saying, and make a sacrament of literally feeding their belly with literal bread that they claim is literally flesh. Some, like the catholics, invented a doctrine of Hocus pocus, that the priest blessing their wafers and alcohol miraculously turns it into literal flesh and literal blood that must be consumed by the body in order to be spiritually saved. That's wicked as hell. Other denominations try to split down the middle and claim that while yes, it is symbolic, it's still "the real presence of Jesus," and necessary for salvation to consume earthly bread and earthly alcohol or juice. They may as well be crawling up inside their mother's womb to be born again, these foolish Nicodemuses. By the way, the Bible says that wherever two or three are present in his name, the real presence of Jesus is there. Not inside a wafer or a cracker or a crouton. And although the analogy is clear to those who want to understand, and to those who believe, it confounds the unsaved and the natural man. We must eat the spiritual bread and the spiritual wine, the belief in Christ and God's promise to us to be saved. And he will live in us and we and Him if we do. Forever. Eternally. The Spirit inside us. We as the body of Christ. These dark sayings troubled even His disciples, and as often as the case, Jesus takes the time to explain what He's saying to them so that they have better understanding. Jesus says that it's the spirit that is quickened, and that the flash profits nothing, that this is spiritually meat and drink, not literal. That "the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life." He's literally telling them that it's an allegory for a spiritual salvation, and yet some couldn't believe despite being called His disciples. Despite having some semblance of faith, but not unto belief and thus missing the point and the mark, and not getting saved. But there are some of you that believe not. For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him There is a false doctrine out there that Judas proves you can lose your salvation, but of course that's untrue. Not only wasn't Judas saved, he was a reprobate and Jesus knew this. I've had people say to me "What? Did Jesus make a mistake choosing Judas? Clearly Judas believed and then rejected Christ and lost his salvation." But they speak in ignorance because they do not know the scriptures. Jesus answered them, Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil? He spake of Judas Iscariot the son of Simon: for he it was that should betray him, being one of the twelve. This literally couldn't be any clearer and is completely spelled out, And yet when showing this verse to people who deny once saved always saved, they cannot, and I mean this as a supernatural phenomenon of having their mind darkened in their eyes blinded, they cannot see this. Just to wrap up, it's important to see that when asked, Peter shows that he gets it and believes. As some of the larger group of the disciples leave, he asks the 12 apostles if they too will leave, offended. Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. This couldn't be further from the truth. God is not the author of confusion. God wants us to reason together with him. He wants us to understand and understanding, the Bible says, comes from God. John 7 opens with the common theme of John's Gospel account; the Jews hating Jesus and wanting to kill Him. It is in every chapter so far. Here Jesus is lingering in His home country of Galilee, with His family. His half-brothers who, at this point, do not believe that He is Christ, basically mock Him and tell him to go to Judaea and tell His story walking. They're all set. Two of Jesus' half-brothers we know for sure we're eventually believers, James and Jude, who write epistles later on after Christ's ascension. (BTW, the false doctrine of Mary remaining a perpetual virgin after Jesus' birth is unscriptural nonsense. We repeatedly hear about the half siblings and the Bible says Joseph didn't know Mary until after Jesus was born, indicating he eventually consummated their marriage) Jesus rebukes His brethren, but in His own time, does go down to the feast to teach. John gives us a good overview of the attitudes and opinions among the Jews regarding Jesus, including how many were afraid to openly follow Him or believe because of fear of the others, especially the Pharisees. Again, when confronted Jesus gives the good news; God has sent Him, that the Father's word is true. If any man do His Father's will (which we have seen already is to believe that Jesus is the Christ), he will know what doctrines are true or not. Jesus calls back to the healing of the lame man on the Sabbath, and preaches how the law allows circumcisions on the Sabbath, arguing how is what He did any different. Jesus tells them (and reminds us) to judge righteously, spiritually, not by appearance or superficial things. Note the confusion this bold preaching causes among the gathered Jews. V31 we see that some do get saved by this preaching, but that angers the Pharisees even more. Jesus tells them that they shall seek Him and not find Him, both literally at that moment, and spiritually, because thither ye cannot come. Again Jesus "dark sayings" confound them. V37 we see Jesus again preaching the Gospel. Again, the Bible shows us His clear meaning of the allegory He's used. That living water is a picture of the Holy Ghost, given to all who believe on Him, after His resurrection and ascension. The Gospels always show the reader the meaning, so we don't have to guess or take it literally like Nicodemus. Just have eyes to see and ears to hear. Never a man spake like this man. Now, we again encounter poor old Nicodemus, the Pharisee who came to Jesus by night. This description is unfavorable to say the least. Nicodemus, who doesn't believe but does seem to be worried about the crowds who do, offers a weak defense of Jesus under the process of the law the Pharisees put their faith in. Again, Nicodemus could have believed, boldly proclaimed Him, but yet again serves two masters. Every man went to his own house, the matter unresolved, reminds me of the verse in 1 Kings 12:16: So when all Israel saw that the king hearkened not unto them, the people answered the king, saying, What portion have we in David? neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David. So Israel departed unto their tents. In this account of the old kingdom being divided, between the northern tribes and Judah we see the people demanding that Solomon's son, Rehoboam who has just been anointed king, ease the enforcement of God's law, claiming it's too heavy a yoke to bear. They rebel, they kill the man sent by Rehoboam to collect tribute (picturing God the Father sending Jesus, and the Jews killing Him). They then name Jeroboam their king, (picturing men putting their faith in what they want, rather than what God tells us). So Israel rebelled against the house of David unto this day... This rejection led to God's wrath upon the northern kingdom, and their having renounced their inheritance, their portion of the promise in David, they were eradicated by the Assyrians. This is a picture of the Jews in Jesus' day, some choosing to follow God's anointed, most choosing their own way, and thus divided, each returns to their own house to do as they will. O Israel, return to thy tents, and every man went unto his own house, shows that this is a parallel passage.

John 9 is an interesting chapter, where almost all the action and dialogue happens away from Jesus and with the Pharisees in the synagogue. The opening exchange with the disciples asking Jesus who's sin caused the man's blindness and Jesus' reply that it was neither, but a chance to glorify God, His works made manifest in him is an awesome and often overlooked doctrine. While the wages of sin is death, and we see health issues and poor fortune may at times be the result of sin, infirmities from birth, or even hardship in life are not necessarily the fruit of sin, but to God's glory. Very similar to the lesson of Job. As fleshly humans, we sinfully become respecters of persons, and assume based on status, fortune and health that we are "better or worse than," and see God's hand in punishing and rewarding, relative to ourselves, when it's not how we should look at others. Sometimes covetous. Sometimes prideful. When we should look at every opportunity as to how we can glorify God, win souls and edify believers. It's hard. So, obvious "was blind but now I see" picture of salvation occurs in this miracle, and again the Jews seek to indict Jesus for, once again, healing on the sabbath. The Bible shows us the deliberations of the Pharisees. While the man blind from birth represents the sinner who has been born again, the Pharisees and even the man's parents, represent the unbelieving world, blind to the truth. We see them show pride, fall into the trap of assuming the man was born in sin to be cursed with blindness. They again show their faith is in following their carnal laws rather than the work of God. They claim Moses, and as we saw a few chapters ago, Jesus said if this were true they'd believe on Him, so this is a lying rationalization. The man's parents, witness to this miracle, show that fear of being out out of the synagogue keeps them from accepting the truth. Loss of status. Sort of the flip side of being a respecter of persons, and just as sinful. The blind man who now can see, who's eyes are open through the grace of God begins to reason with the Pharisees to lead them to the truth that by implication, Jesus must be at least a prophet and definitely sent of God. They won't see it and cast him out. Jesus finds the man and asks him if he believes, and, eyes open and trusting Jesus is from God, asks who it is that he may accept Him. Jesus tells him it is He. (again, the lie that Jesus never claims to be Christ is shown over and over to be false if we read the scriptures) The man believes and is saved. The Pharisees, meanwhile, who have claimed knowledge of God, who claim a faith in works, law and tradition, show that they are made blind to the truth. That Jesus exposes those who truly are blind just as much as He opens the eyes of those who can believe. We have to admit we are blind. We are halt and lame. That we need saving in order to be saved. In humbling ourselves we can truly see Jesus for who He is. Blinded by a false faith in ourselves, our position and status, our works, tradition or pride in our own weak understanding, we truly cannot see.
