Chapter 4 picks up immediately after 3, and the healing of the lame man at the Temple gate. The Jews are angry again, this time the Sadducees who were a sect that denied Heaven or the Resurrection. It's important to understand that they're denial of the literal body Resurrection of the righteous was their doctrine that predated Jesus Christ's coming. There are many who foolishly will say that the OT didn't teach on Jesus or a resurrection in the last day, that it was a concept invented later, yet there being a prominent sect opposed to the teaching established in the temple pretty much destroys that nonsense. The Sadducees are very much like today's reformed Jew, that carry the trappings as ceremony, but teach a vague, satanic deism absent the glory and power of God. Much of the conflict between factions of modern Jews reflects the split between the Sadducees and Pharisees, who claim a belief in God and the afterlife, but again deny His power, trusting their own. Think the Globohomo diaspora Jews vs the Orthodox, Chabad Lubavitch Zionist Jews. Both despise Christ and Christians. So the Jews, angry at how many believed the preaching at the temple by Peter and John and seeing the miracle of healing, got saved in their belief by turning to Christ, actually lock them up for the night. The following morning before council, Peter again preaches an indictment against the Jews for killing Christ, citing scripture (Psalm 118/Isaiah 28) that Jesus is that cornerstone of the foundation that we are to trust on and believe, an that the Jews had rejected. Quoting scripture is what Jesus had done to defend Himself to the Jews, and it's what Peter and the disciples do, filled with the Spirit. Jesus had told us to take no heed as to what to say, but that the Holy Ghost would bring all things to remembrance, that God's word would be in our heart and on our tongue if we lived in the word. Being released, blameless the Jews conspired again as to what to do with these troublesome Christ followers. Meanwhile, back at their gathering place, a commune by description, Peter recounts the story and they all of one mind, give glory to God. They ask God for boldness to preach His word and the Gospel of salvation, and the Holy Ghost comes upon them to facilitate this. This communal living, where the salvation of God is sufficient, and the excess of worldly possessions unnecessary, they gave to all so that none lacked. This is true Christian living. Not socialism. Not forced takings and redistribution, but hard working children of God providing for each other. The final verse leads to Acts 5. The narrative in this book flows in a fairly straight line as we will see tomorrow. It's also a fairly notable how the Acts and Epistles are very straightforward, of course that doesn't mean people don't cherry pick verses out of context to create hidden meanings that aren't there to support doctrines that don't exist in the Bible. But rather, the dark sayings and parables that Jesus used prior to his crucifixion and Resurrection are now no longer necessary, and while we still see through a glass darkly as it were, we can begin rightly dividing the word of God and having understanding of all things pertaining to salvation through Christ in Jesus name. I overlooked this this morning, but it's an important doctrine taken from Acts 4 verse 12, where Peter tells the accusers in the temple asking him by whose name and authority did Peter and John heal the lame man, and Peter says under the Spirit, Jesus Christ of Nazareth whom they had crucified. Then he says: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. This is very important. It is in Jesus Christ's name that we are saved, there is none who come to the Father except through the Son. There is no ecumenical path to heaven. There are none saved by other faiths, trusting in their works, praying in the name of another. Not the Hebrew roots nonsense about "Yeshua." If you are looking for righteousness and truth, you cannot find it in anyone else or belief in any other power but that of the Son. The matchless name of Jesus Christ. Also, to tie in to the theme of Jesus being the cornerstone, the stone not cut by hands which is a theme of the prophets preaching of Jesus in the OT, we can look at Daniel 2:34, where Daniel is interpreting the dream of the idol that is representing the various empires and ages to come. Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces. Jesus is that cornerstone. He is the rock upon which His church is built, the word made flesh. If you want to know if someone is a saved Christian, the evidence isn't their lifestyle or their adherence to the commandments. The only sure way to know is if they believe the word of God. When they hear preaching that is from the Bible and don't recoil from it, but accept it. That they hear Doctrine expounded upon from the word and, knowing that scripture is inspired by God indicate that they believe God. This is very difficult for people who were raised in false churches where they were trained to be hypocritical, Pharisees. Being fruit inspectors. You may need to see change in someone to have them justified before you, because you're a respecter of persons. But to be justified before God one needs only believe his testimony and accept it as truth. 1 John 4:6 “We are of God: he that knoweth God heareth us; he that is not of God heareth not us. Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error.” I despise holier than thou fake Christians, who have no Grace whatsoever within them, and rather than working out their own salvation with fear and trembling, they worry and fret about others who have at least believed the report.

Acts 5 picks up immediately following the last verses of 4, where the gathered believers of the assembly had just praised God in Jesus name, and been filled with the Holy Ghost to preach the scriptures boldly. They had all things in common, meaning they shared possessions as needed, forsaking materialism to edify the church and do great things for the Lord. One disciple, Barnabas had just sold property and donated the sum to the church at Jerusalem. Likely to praise and blessings. And so we meet a married couple, Ananias and Sapphira. Ananias and Sapphira, in the context of seeing Barnabas coveted his praise and honor in the church, and having land themselves to sell, sold it for a sum, but presented to the Apostles a lesser amount, keeping a portion of the proceeds for themselves while saying they gave all of it to the church. Peter, by the Holy Ghost calls out Ananias, who is present before them presenting the gift. Peter says he knows that it's not the full total, and asks why lie to the Holy Ghost about it considering they weren't required to sell the land at all, or to give any of the money to the church. They had every right to give a portion, as it was theirs to give. But the lying for praise and to be favored among the congregation is the problem, and confronted, Ananias collapses dead at Peter's feet. The brothers bury him, and a few hours later, as they are putting him in the ground along comes the wife, Sapphira. Peter gives her a chance to be truthful, and she sticks to the story her and her husband had concocted. Peter, again in the Spirit curses her to the same fate of her husband, striking her dead. The gathered now know Ananias' death wasn't just happenstance, but that the couple has been punished by God. Were Ananias and Sapphira saved? Didn't they just feel the presence of the Holy Ghost when the church prayed the chapter before? The Bible says in Acts 4 that the entire church was of one heart and one soul. They were of that church. I think the implication is clear they were. But their being in Heaven when they die, justified by faith and Jesus' imputed righteousness didn't keep them from sinning, nor did it stop God from punishing them with their lives. Many of the religion of works, who maintain that you must repent of sinning to be saved, and claim that the Gospel of Christ, salvation by faith in grace, is a "license to sin." And so, being fruit inspectors, take this story as evidence they were not believers. But what it shows is that God chastises His own for our iniquity. He takes the rod to His children when they sin. The Bible says He scourges His adopted sons and daughters. Even unto death. We saved are held to a higher standard than the unsaved, and we are punished here in this earth, sometimes more so than the unsaved, who are not God's children. This is why we should walk in the word, live for God, take up the cross and follow Jesus. Honoring our heavenly Father, which brings blessings upon blessings. It is an amazing gift to be given a chance by God to bless others, to help people. To give freely what we have to others in the church in need. But our own pride and greed can often stop us from receiving the blessings, and instead lead us to chastisement in our sin. Now we see that for the believers, this made them fearful but more determined to serve the Lord but others it a frightened to the point with a dare not join the church. These could be a mix of people saved and unsaved, who's seeing how tight a ship God is running through the apostles with the Holy Spirit, but still living a car in a life in their sin, we're afraid and In their fear were forsaking the assembly. But others unsaved in the general population, hearing this group of believers preaching the word boldly with one mind and soul, and seeing the power of their testimony, we're eager to believe and join them. And of course, this brings them into conflict with the Jews again. It wouldn't be a new testament scripture without mentioning the evil of the Jews. The Sadducees taking the place of the Pharisees as the big bad of Acts stems mainly from the disciples preaching in a resurrected Christ's name. And primarily from the true accusations that they killed Jesus. It's the same today, as we see groups like the ADL calling this biblical truth that they killed the Son of God "anti-semitism." This preaching, laying the blame squarely on the shoulders of the Jews of Jerusalem for killing Christ is what the early Acts of the Apostles references to repentance refers to. Peter and John and the others, tell The gather Jews listening to them at the temple that they may have acted out of ignorance but now is the time to repent and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ for the remission of their sin. And the high priests and officials, knowing their guilt, sought to imprison and threaten the disciples into silence. So we see when all of the disciples are imprisoned at the temple for preaching the truth of the Gospel and the healings being done by the Apostles (whom Jesus had anointed to have the power to lay hands when He had originally sent them out), and the multitudes being saved because of it all. An angel of the Lord comes and frees them. One of many jailbreaks in the book of Acts. They're told to redouble their efforts and continue preaching boldly, and they do. To the consternation of the Jews. So we see the problem as the Sadducees see it; ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man's blood upon us. And so Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. Peter again preaches the Gospel and indicts the Jews for Christ's death. Now we are introduced to a Pharisee on the council named Gamaliel. He is the same who Paul would later say taught him before his conversion. Gamaliel warns the council to just ignore the disciples, and names a couple of previous false messiahs they'd seen. That if they aren't of God it will come to naught. He warns the Sadducees, who are essentially religious atheists, that if they are of God then any effort to harm the disciples will not work. Still, they ordered them beaten and released, threatened not to speak in the name of Jesus. Often Christians will not boldly talk in Jesus name. They will talk about higher powers and a vague God, rather than proclaiming Jesus. It is from the same fear, I think, that the Jews sought to instill in the disciples. This persecution leads them to rejoice. And they take it as a sign they are doing Jesus' work, who had preached that they would be persecuted for His name's sake. We are similarly called. If you aren't facing personal persecution, it may well be because you aren't boldly proclaiming what you believe, or who your faith is placed in.

Now Act 6 opens with a problem for the early church at Jerusalem. The Apostles, disciples and converts, of one mind and soul, daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ. And to the congregation they added thousands, both Jew and Greek. Now we know the role of the church assembly is to teach and preach the Gospel of Jesus to the unsaved, the things of God and His doctrines from scripture to the edification of the saved, and to minister to the least among them, especially widows indeed. And even in this, the purest church with the purest doctrine, full of saved believers, full of the Holy Ghost, witness to signs and wonders by those whom had the power anointed unto them by Jesus through the Holy Ghost, people remained prone to sin, being of the flesh. They were respecters of persons. These saved Judeans favored their own in the ministering of the poor sisters of the faith, the Grecians. Faced with this issue, the 12 gathered the disciples, those dedicated daily to the word and the work, and had from among them 7 chosen to serve the needs of maintaining the larger church and its ministry to the poor members. This is the establishment of the biblical office of deacon. We see here in verse 3 some of the qualifications for deacon; men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom. This is expounded upon in 1 Timothy 3: 8 Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; 9 Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. 10 And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless. 11 Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. 12 Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well. 13 For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus. The Apostles and other disciples appointing them deacons, maintain their position as pastors and evangelists, to be continually in prayer and in the ministry of the word. It is important to understand that these are the only two offices given in the Bible, and that the deacons work for the church and answer to the pastor, not the other way around. We see also that this office is key in allowing the church to grow, that freed of the mundane daily tasks as the deacons serve full time to take care of matters, the numbers grew and multiplied. In this election of deacons, we meet several key members of the early ministry, chiefly Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost. We see that in addition to his duties, he maintained his soul winning, teaching and working signs among the Jews to bring them to Christ. Stephen being so effective that certain sects of the Jews in synagogue, Hellenistic freed slaves, returned to Jerusalem from where they'd been captive, disputing with Stephen and his doctrines of Jesus Christ. Unable to counter his preaching and pure doctrine, they instead get men to falsely accused him of blasphemy. By getting a mob worked up by these lies, they drag Stephen before the council. We see from their railing accusation that they are twisting Jesus prophecy of the temple destruction, and misleading about the law, which continues fulfilled in Christ, and the doing away of the carnal ordinances, sacrifices and diverse washings. We leave this short chapter in a cliff hanger, as they look upon innocent Stephen, with a face like an angel.... One reason I don't like Bible studies, including my own, is that they always are 5 times as long as the verses they cover. God's word is succinct and clear, and we can know all things from the Spirit inside us when we take the time to read it. I understand the need and am blessed to be apt to teach but I cannot stress enough, this is not of private interpretation but just knowledge that comes from studying to be approved by God, available to any saved Christians who read the Bible faithfully.

In the previous chapter, we meet Stephen, who had been elected a deacon by the disciples, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, who did great wonders and miracles among the people. Charged falsely by the Jews, saying "This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law: For we have heard him say, that this Jesus of Nazareth shall destroy this place, and shall change the customs which Moses delivered us." Stephen is brought before the council and as chapter 7 opens, is asked to defend himself. Stephen then gives a brief history of Israel, and of their stiff-necked rejection of the men of God. Their murder of prophets. Of their taking up idols and not obeying the law of Moses they claim Stephen and the early Christians threatened. Stephen calls out these Jews. Betrayers and murderers, whose fathers killed those who prophesied the coming of Jesus, and the very men who killed the Son of God. And thus, full of the Holy Ghost, convicted the Jews sitting in judgment of him, and in their anger, they took him and stoned him to death. Stephen then becoming the first martyr of the disciples. This is the escalation, from mocking derision to arrest, to beatings. And still the believers persisted and still they accused the Jews of the murder of prophets and Christ. This truth is enough to bring the enemies of God to murderous rage. We see a brief introduction to a young Saul, who witnessed the stoning and began his path to Christ. The history of the Israelites, given by Stephen, which had been preached about by prophets before, by John the Baptist and by Christ Jesus, and that would be repeated in the Epistles, is a searing indictment of them as a people, and of man in general. God pounds the message of their stiff-neckedness and disobedience, their rejection of His word, over and over again throughout the Bible. The idea of their being special or chosen as a race, outside of Christ, is unbiblical fiction. The idea of separate ethnic dispensations is a lie. "Replacement theology" itself is a misnomer, as the theology of God in scripture has remained consistent throughout, it is simply who has received the grace of God and His blessing that's changed.

So forgive me for almost skipping chapter 8, because it is a good one. We see Saul again, fresh from being the coat holder for the Jews who stoned Stephen to death, and are told he consented of that evil. The Bible says being a partaker in another man's sin is as bad as committing it ourselves. Saul, in his ignorance embraces the persecution of the believers in Jerusalem and in all of Judea, zealously thinking he is doing it for God, that the saints were blasphemous doing what they did in Jesus' name. We see once again that in persecution, all things work together for good to them that love God, and God in their affliction uses the scattering to bring the truth of the Gospel out of Jerusalem and into the whole world. Phillip, one of the deacons selected with Stephen and whom the Apostles laid hands on, filling him with the gifts of the Holy Ghost goes to Samaria, the capital of the province that was once the Northern Kingdom of Israel, before God used the Syrians to wipe them out. There, there are a mix of followers of the Hebrew religious practices, who followed scripture and knew of Christ to come, and unbelievers from every background. It was this mixed race mess that caused the Jews to look down on Samaritans, despite their cultural and racial similarities and origin. Phillip has tremendous success in getting Samaritans saved, through his preaching and the miracles of healing and casting out devils through the power of the Holy Ghost imparted to him by the Apostles and the laying on of hands. We meet Simon, AKA Simon the sorcerer, a charlatan who had great fame in the land, but who did trick people into believing he had some power from God. But his paltry parlor tricks were nothing compared to the truth of the word and the power of God moving through Philip, and as the masses believed on Christ, Simon too became saved, born again in faith and even joining Philip in his ministries. When the Apostles hear of the great things of God Philip was doing among the Samaritans, they went up to see and give the gift of the Holy Ghost upon the believers that they may continue to grow the church there and bring people to salvation. It is important to understand the difference between the quickening and indwelling of the Spirit upon belief and salvation, and the doctrine of laying on of hands. All believers were born again and had the Spirit inside them with the new man created at the time of their salvation, but the gifts of the Holy Ghost, in the Old Testament sense of having Him come over one and grant them power, was something that the Apostles were granted by Jesus, and given unto them to share as needed to the glory of God. Simon seeing their ability to imbue others with this great power, and perhaps missing the glory he had in the past, coveted it, and sought to pay Peter and John for the same gift earning a harsh rebuke from Peter, telling Simon to get his heart right with God. He tells Simon to repent of this wickedness and pray for forgiveness. Many grace-mixing works heretics point to this, one of the few times "repent" is followed by anything close to "of sins" as proof text for their false doctrine, but in doing so they omit that Simon was already saved. He believed on Jesus already. He did something wicked, but his repentance isn't for righteousness but as a believer who has sinned. And showing the conviction of his salvation, Simon accepts the rebuke and repents. Often you will see unbelievers, even those who claim Christ, bristle at correction. As the Bible says they despise it. But Simon, to his credit learns and grows from it. Now Philip is called by the Lord to go to the desert of Gaza, and being obedient, he goes. He is called to do a great thing because he had shown God his commitment. The more we do for God the more He gives us to do, and so Philip gets this opportunity to show us how soul winning is done. We meet the Ethiopian eunuch, who we are told was the queen of Ethiopia treasurer, and that she and he were followers of the Hebrew religion, or what the modern form of Pharisees it has taken. He's reading scripture when Philip comes upon him, and providence has it, verses of Elijah that prophesies Jesus. We see the elegance of God's word, that Jesus is Christ revealed throughout scripture. He asks the eunuch if he understands the scripture he's reading, and the reply is so true; unsaved people need saved people to explain scripture. "How can I unless a man guide me?" He is a receptive man, searching for truth. This is an excellent example of how God will move heaven and earth to get the gospel to someone earnestly contending for the truth that is written in every man's heart. It is an answer to the natural man scoffing question "What about the savage in the jungle, hmm? Are they damned for not being born where they can hear about Jesus?" Ask and ye shall receive. All men are called to Christ. Few who answer. Now, after Philip has given him the gospel and shown him, out of the Bible the truth of Jesus Christ, the eunuch asks what hinders him from being baptized in the water the caravan had come to, and Philip answers with pure doctrine; If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. This is the Gospel. This is how salvation works. This is the order of things, and baptism is but a public expression of the salvation that came from belief. And so Acts 8:37 is either removed or footnoted into doubt by all modern perversions of the Bible. The simplicity of the Gospel, that we are saved by our belief in this truth that Jesus is the Son of God, the Christ who saves us by His perfect work, as God promised from the foundation of the world. The removal or doubt-casting on this verse, the clearest and most explicit example of 1-on-1 soul winning thus far in the New Testament, can only be done for one reason, and to serve one agenda; Satan's. We see the eunuch saved, baptized and Philip carried away by the Holy Spirit, leaving one of the most powerful men in Ethiopia joyfully proclaiming Jesus Christ. Acts 8:37 is missing from most modern translations, the NIV, ESV and the CSB and is bracketed as not original in the NASB. The unsaved vipers who promote those versions will claim that "it's missing from the oldest and best manuscripts." They reject the received texts, thousands of copies of which agree, and instead cleave to texts found in garbage, that disagree with one another and contradict the preserved word. What a strange coincidence that all of the changes in the text that they prefer, diminishes the Divinity of Jesus and removes doctrine that shows their damnable heresies to be false. Then they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and ran upon him with one accord, And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul. And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep. And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles. And devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him. As for Saul, he made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison. The Bible says that even by his presence and holding the coats of those stoning Stephen to death that Saul/Paul was "consenting unto his death." 1 Timothy 5:22 Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins Giving even passive consent to sin is a sin. We are to loudly and boldly proclaim the word of God and stand against evil. Drinking is a sin. So is eating that extra cupcake. So are thoughts of foolishness. We all sin every day. The idea we can "Repent from sin" for righteousness is itself a foolish thought. We wrestle with the flesh daily, we are called to crucify ourselves daily. To mortify our members and being ourselves into subjection. To strive for that prize of rewards in Heaven by doing God's work which is honoring Him, spreading the good news of Jesus Christ and taking care of and being a good judge of the poor, lame, widows and fatherless. God knows we are in sinful flesh and He forgives us in Jesus name, and the Spirit and His word are there to help us overcome sin as Christ overcame the world, to our own edification and to be conformed to His use.

Acts 9 tells the story of Saul/Paul's 'seeing the light' on the road to Damascus. He had gone from a student of the Pharisees taught by the high priest Gamaliel, to a participant in the martyrdom of Stephen, to becoming a zealous persecutor of the church in Jerusalem, to the point where the disciples were scattered abroad. Now, seeking to further put down what he saw as a blasphemous uprising, he asked permission to go and arrest Jews in another nation, Syria. With that license, he set off on the journey only to be struck blind by the appearance unto him of Jesus Himself. Saul, astonished and fearful responds to Jesus' rebuke, asking "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" And, Saul blindly asks "Who art thou Lord?" Jesus identifies Himself, and repeats the charge against Saul of persecuting Him, through His church. Jesus tells him it is "hard for thee to kick against the pricks." A idiom of the time, referring to the pricked stick used to steer an ox in the field. It means that the more you fight it, the harder it's going to be, as an ox who kicked against the prick would only further imbed the sharp ends. (Modern versions omit this verse because they are written by reprobates who take away from the word of God). Blinded and desperate, Paul asks what he must do, and Jesus directs him to Damascus, where he will be told. In Damascus, a disciple Ananias is given a vision by the Lord to go to Saul, and give him the truth of the Gospel, laying hands on him that he might be gifted by the Holy Ghost to be a great man of God, preaching to kings and spreading the Gospel to the Gentiles. Naturally, Ananias protests. This is Saul who has been breathing threats and slaughter against believers. Who had a warrant to arrest them in the city. Now Jesus was asking him to go, in faith and visit him, that he might see. Three days without sight, fasting, without drink, Saul was praying to God for answers, visited with a vision of Ananias coming and healing him. Here we see that while Jesus appeared and struck Saul blind, He doesn't give Saul the answer to what he must do, but rather a man must go to him and bring him to Christ. We are called upon by God to bring people the truth. It is from faith to faith, by hearing the word of God from saved Christians, that brings them to salvation. Jesus could have told Paul in that vision, but that's not how it works. We are the laborers who sow, water and harvest. It is an awesome responsibility. One too many of us shirk, under far less threat and danger than Ananias here. He was called to go into the den of those who sought to arrest or kill him, on faith he obeys and brings perhaps the most influential Christian in history, to the Lord. If he can do that, we can give the Gospel to a coworker, friend or neighbor, with only the threat of being mocked or rejected standing in our way. So, it is with that understanding and faith that Ananias goes to his enemy, and heals him, and Saul, now Paul, able to see, believes and is baptized in Jesus' name. Paul himself tells the story again in Acts 22, with a bit more detail, which we will see. But his conversion, seeing the light, being once blind but now seeing, becomes the chief analogy for Christians being born again. Paul, being a brilliant student of the law and coming to understand all things in Christ, and filled with the boldness of the Holy Ghost, begins immediately preaching the truth of Jesus in every synagogues, and immediately we see the pattern repeat, that those who oppose Christ and hate the truth began plotting to kill him. And the multitudes grew, the various independent churches through the Levant were edified by his preaching, multiplying believers. God working through the man who had persecuted them the most, to win souls to Christ. 1 Samuel 8:5 And said unto him, Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations. This is the spirit far too many Americans find themselves in today, wanting to overthrow the current system entirely because it's leaders are corrupt and the people are wicked. Even the Israelites, with the perfect system of God being their King, the law literally set in stone, and Godly men given power by God to judge them, still went through cycles where they failed the system, and were captured or occupied. Where their own wicked deeds brought about decades of oppression, and it's only by turning to the Lord and repenting of that evil do we see them return to prosperity. It doesn't matter if we are a monarchy, democracy, fascist, socialist, a dictatorship... We are going to be judged by God if we turn away from Him. That's why all of this debate about political solutions to our spiritual problem is vain and foolish. Work on getting enough people right with God and the rest will sort itself. People don't want to hear this because they imagine vein things, and want easy answers that do not require them, themselves to change. They will seek out a thousand ways to ruin rather than the narrow and strait path of turning to God.

Now we find in Acts 10 the story of Cornelius, a Roman centurion stationed in Samaria, in the port city of Caesarea and someone who was devout to God, but not saved. Praying and giving alms, God-fearing and fasting, but in ignorance of the truth of the gospel. And God, seeing his searching for truth sends him a vision of an angel telling him to send men to bring Peter to him, that "he shall tell thee what thou oughtest do."Just as the Lord tells Saul in chapter 9 to wait on Ananias. And, similarly to Philip in chapter 8 with the Ethiopian eunuch and Ananias to Saul in 9, we see God telling Peter to go unto Cornelius. This is important. Things God repeats we should pay attention to. The angels and visions and even the glorified appearance of Jesus, none give the gospel but rather send saved men to preach the word and get other men saved. We are called to be ministers of reconciliation, that we may save some. Don't miss this point, for it applies as much today as it did here. It is by man acting as agents for God, a royal priesthood sharing the Gospel, that by hearing man may come to believe. Peter is in Joppa, and sees a vision from God showing every type of animal, clean and unclean according to Masoretic law, and God tells him to slay and eat. Peter, that stone, protests saying he has never eaten an unclean thing. God, using this illustration to show Peter he must preach to the Gentiles, says nothing is unclean if God has cleansed it. This is an allegory for preaching to the Gentiles, but it also serves as a reminder that the carnal ordinances and dietary laws that were a picture of the better Testament to come are done away with in Christ. That no meat is unlawful for a saved Christian to eat, that is blessed by God. It's interesting that the vision is repeated to Peter 3 times before he wakes from it. Just as Peter denied Christ 3 times and as he was instructed by the risen Jesus 3 times to feed His sheep. The translators calling this Passover mentioned in Acts 12 "Easter" in the KJV has caused confusion and consternation for many. This name is derived from the word “עשׁתּרה (‛ashterâh)” which means “increase” or “flock” (Brown-Driver-Briggs’ Hebrew Definitions). “עשׁתּרה (‛ashterâh)” is translated as “flocks” four times in the KJV. The etymology of “Easter” on the other hand has nothing to do with “flocks” or animal fertility. “Easter” (“Ostern” in German) is a Germanic word derived from the word “east” (“Ost” in German). Today, “east” refers to the direction from which the sun rises. The direction of east goes by that name because the Saxon word “east” meant “dawn”, “sunrise” or “morning.”' “Easter” means “dawn” The Old English word for the month of April was “Eosturmonað” coming from Old Germanic, Ōstar-mānod. So, mostly history of the early churches and Paul's second missionary journey, little doctrine but we continue the familiar themes of the book of Acts; Jews reacting badly to the Gospel, that Jesus was Christ. That many believed, and then were baptized (because baptism is for believers, not infants). That even as the churches sprang up and grew, persecution remained. Ten chapters remain in the Acts of the Apostles. If you're sticking with it, we will have read through 3 books of the Bible together! Amen. 63 to go!

As Acts 19 opens, we transition from Apollos, to Paul meeting others like him, those saved and baptized, that believed on the Christ to come by the preaching of John the Baptist, but hadn't been made perfect with complete knowledge of Jesus. Paul says that John "baptized with the baptism of repentance," not "...of sin" as some works-based false teachers present, but as Paul explains, towards believing on "him which should come after him, that is, on Christ Jesus." This is biblical repentance. To turn from whatever else you may be trusting on or believing in, to accepting the truth of the word, made flesh in Jesus Christ. After being baptized again in Jesus name, Paul through the laying of hands in the power given unto the apostles, fills the disciples there with the Holy Ghost, and the power thereof as we've seen since Pentecost. Paul again preaches at the local synagogue, and again runs against hardened hearts of the reprobates blind to the truth. We see the only mention of a school in the Bible, one of Tyrannus, which apparently teaches heresy and bad doctrine as the newly empowered disciples dispute scripture daily there. The preaching at Ephesus we are told, lasts 2 years and reaches all of Asia Minor, so that all who dwelt there heard of Lord Jesus, Jew and Greek. Next we see God working through Paul to heal people not only by his direct laying of hands but pieces of cloth Paul had touched, that both healed and drove out devils. There are sects of charismatics and pentecostals who today falsely claim they are Apostles, and that they have such power, but we see exactly who these charlatans are in verse 13. Some "vagabond Jews" (I love that), who play at being exorcists, seeing those like Paul, filled with the Holy Ghost, calling out devils in Jesus' name, give it a try to hysterical bad effect. They get dissed by the evil spirit, who knows Jesus and knows Paul but who are they? The possessed man beats them and sends them packing, naked. Word spreads of these fools and their failure, to the glory of God. And new believers came to Christ and, having been followers of this wicked spirituality new age nonsense, gathered the books of the "curious arts" they had purchased, 50,000 pieces of silver's worth, and burned them. Burning wicked books is biblical, amen. Paul begins his plans for moving on in his ministry, a controversy erupts among the cult of Diana in Ephesus, led by a maker of silver idols, and other craftsmen who see Paul's preaching and the attitude against graven images as a danger to their profession. And so they turn the crowds who worship the idols made of hands of the false goddess, Diana Queen of Heaven. I don't have to explain the modern parallel here. So there's great turmoil stirred up, we see the Jews, sensing blood, pushing one of Paul's companions, Alexander, to the front of the crowd. He signals to speak but we are told he is drowned out by the mob chanting praise to Diana for 2 hours. The town clerk calms things down after that, the crowd mostly appeased. He directs the idol makers to take it up with Roman law if they have just cause, and he dismissed the assembly. The more you turn to God when you're blessed, the easier it is to turn to Him when you have tribulation. Revelation 3 14 And unto the angel of the church of the Laodiceans write; These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of the creation of God; 15 I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. 16 So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth. 17 Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked: 18 I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see. 19 As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent. A carnal Christian, saved by faith but living mostly in the world, taking what are blessings given to His children for granted. Getting apathetic and weak in the faith. Jesus warns this church that He will correct and punish us for being lukewarm. Half in, half out. Not doing what they know they should. 1 Peter 3:15 “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:”

So we pick up after the events of Acts 19, where the idol-makers and the Jews stir up trouble, and Paul is continuing to travel back along his 2nd missionary journey, to Jerusalem, and in chapter 20, the feast he is aiming for is Pentecost. We see that the Jews are laying in wait to mess with him, as usual. Paul and his companions make their way to Troas, and on Sunday they come together with the disciples there to eat and listen to Paul's preaching. Paul, believing he won't be though this way again, goes to midnight. We are told about a young believer named Eutychus, who, like many of us, falls asleep during the sermon. However, unlike our snoring in the pews, this poor kid falls from the 3rd floor window to the ground below, dead. There is a lesson there for us all lol. (Also, some believe that this is where the doctrine of the young men carrying in enough chairs for everyone, in one trip, comes from!) Paul and his party continue their journey, and not passing through Ephesus, Paul sends for the elders of the church there to meet him so he can say his goodbyes. We see that this journey to Jerusalem by Paul has a sense of foreboding over it, a pall cast that he doesn't know what fate awaits him. As he wrote to the Philippians, "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." His to him, these goodbyes are final. His speech here is eloquent. He reminds them of his first interaction, that he maintained the same disposition and doctrines as long as he's known them. How he served the Lord despite the evils that befell him, mostly from the Jews. That he taught them all profitable doctrine from scripture, not only in public, but house to house. (As Jesus instructed us, out along the highways and hedges). That Paul preached the faith of repentance toward God and faith toward Jesus. Again showing that turning to God and to faith in Christ is biblical repentance. (The doctrine of adding "...of your sins" can't withstand scrutiny of the scriptures. We see it destroyed along with other false and damnable heresies, chapter after chapter, verse after verse.) He tells them regardless of what awaits him, as he is moved by the Holy Ghost to preach the truth, that he doesn't care if he dies, that he may finish his ministry that God appointed him to, with joy. Would that we all undertake our Christian lives with that same attitude, having joy despite tribulation, having no care for our lives or this world, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. Paul steadfastly acknowledges that in his course, of sharing the Gospel to the Gentiles and Jews throughout his ministry he has absolved himself. He did what he could to the utmost to save all who would hear him throughout Asia. We should be inspired to do the same, and chastened that there may be some we didn't try to reach. He then exhorts the pastors and deacons before him to be mindful of their charge, to feed the flock spiritually with the true doctrines of scripture, because as Paul warns, there will be reprobates, "grievous wolves," who come after the flock with heresy, and false teachers leading men away from the truth. He reminds them that he was diligent for years, seeking no reward or coveting anything of theirs, working to pay his way with his own hands. He reminds them of their obligation to do the same. And with prayer and tears they say their farewells, and accompany Paul to his ship.

Acts 21 sees the final leg of Paul's ill-fated journey to Jerusalem. For the past 3 chapters we have seen it written that it was Paul's will and desire to get to Jerusalem before Pentecost, and to celebrate in the Temple with the Jews, deliver alms to the saints at the church in Jerusalem and give the good news that the Gospel has spread out among the Gentiles, further and greater than the last Apostle could have imagined when he began. And in his journey we have seen strife, tumult in the cities of Asia as he went, and now we see multiple disciples in multiple cities prophesy in the Spirit that Paul should not go. But despite this, Paul remained determined. There are differing theories regarding this narrative. One is that Paul obstinacy in doing his own will was warned and opposed by God. This seems likely, as even the best of us get sidetracked into heeding out own desires and ignoring God, telling us not to as we think we should. Yet it remains our choice and all glory will come to God, even as we are chastised, and His will be done as all comes together for good. Another view is that Paul, heading to tribulation and suffering for Christ Jesus, was given warning by God so that Paul's decision was made with full awareness, in free will to better glorify God in his afflictions. We won't even get into the theological nonsense regarding the "permissive will of God" vs the "sovereign will of God." Theology is man trying to make God fit into their own notions of how things work, and theologians and their students are fools. Bible says it, believe it. Simple as. Anyway, we see Paul accepting the warnings, including of a man named Agabus, who we are told predicted the famine in the land back in Acts 11, so his gift of prophecy by the Holy Ghost is known. Either way, Paul is not dissuaded. And so, Paul and Luke and the rest of his company return to Jerusalem, and straight away Paul goes to the head of the church, James, and the elders, and personally tells them of his success in the Gospel. But there's a problem. Those believers among the Jews who had earlier stirred up trouble regarding the practice of circumcision are again unhappy with Paul. They may be saved by faith but they see perfection and separation through the keeping of the law. We know from Acts and Paul's epistles that while Paul (and James, Peter and the others) all are in agreement regarding not forcing the Gentiles to take up the Mosaic laws, that they all still, as Jews celebrate the holy days and go to temple and kept the traditions. That Paul even circumcised Timothy, not as part of salvation but to show the Jews he was born of their people having a Jewish mother. As Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 9:20-21: “And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law; To them that are without law, as without law, (being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,) that I might gain them that are without law." Elsewhere he instructs, under the Spirit that these things are nothing to him, but a means to get people saved. That the carnal ordinances, diverse washings and dietary laws of the Levitical priesthood are done away with. That the sacrifices do nothing to wash away sin, that only faith in Jesus saves. But while the temple remained and the believing Jews maintained the old ways during this transition between the resurrection and the destruction of the temple, there was great debate among them what Christianity would look like for the Jew. We see James reiterate their message to the Gentiles that they are not yoked to the law. But to satisfy the Jews in his church, James asks Paul to not only set their mind at ease, but to undertake a vow, shave his head and purify himself in the temple so that they are more receptive to his plea. (BTW verse 25 should be a nail in the coffin for the 'Hebrew Roots' nonsense) So Paul, who sees these things as nothing if they edify the church and give glory to the Gospel of Jesus, goes along with the plan, and it almost immediately blows up when unbelieving Jews from Asia, likely at the Temple for the holy days as Paul was, spot him there. The Jews stir up the crowd and accuse him falsely of teaching heresy and of bringing 'unclean' Greeks to the Temple. This gets the Jews of the city into a mob, and they were going to kill Paul, beating him to death, when he's rescued and arrested by the chief captain and his guard who have to carry Paul due to the extent of injury. The crowd, an unruly and angry mob shouts out all manner of accusations against Paul, and trying to ascertain who he is, the captain brings him into the castle there, and Paul corrects him, in Greek, as to who he is. Taking to the stairs, Paul is allowed to address the crowd, in Hebrew, and we leave off for the next chapter to see what he says.

Acts 23 opens immediately after the events of 22, where Paul has been captured by the guards, saving him from a mob of Jews in Jerusalem who had seen him in the temple and laid false accusations against him. Taking him up the stairs of the fortress, the captain of the guard allows Paul to address the crowd. Turning to them, Paul, in Hebrew, begins his defense. Paul gives a short biography by way of establishing his credentials as a Jew, and a zealot. He recounts the events that we read in earlier chapters of Acts, his complicity in the murder of Stephen and persecution of the saints. Paul tells them the story of his encounter with Christ on the road to Damascus, and his acceptance of the truth by Ananias. His baptism and given mission to the Gentiles. And despite all this, like all the prophets before him, even the Son of God, Christ Jesus, the Jews of Jerusalem seek his life for the truth offends them. The captain of the guard orders Paul scourged to find out what he must have done to anger the people like this, hoping to gain a confession by his stripes. But Paul cleverly asks the centurion if it is lawful for them to whip a Roman citizen without charge. This will begin a series of events that leads to the Gospel being spread to the seat of power in Rome, and great glory to God.

Again, this chapter picks up immediately on the last, and Paul is now before the chief priests and all their council, Sadducees and Pharisees alike. And Paul brilliantly plays the sects off one another by saying, truthfully, that he is being accused of nothing other than preaching if the resurrection of the dead, promised in Christ, that the Pharisees allege to believe. This sets them against the Sadducees who, being worldly and rejecting the things of God, take issue with the others of the council. This divide, between spiritual and worldly Jews remains today. The Orthodox, Chabad Lubavitch Jews, are the heirs to the Pharisee, and the atheist and reform Jews, the Sadducees. And they war with one another even as both seek to persecute Christians. Taking advantage of this divide, Paul lives another day. And he is visited by Jesus, who tells him he will preach to Rome as he did in Jerusalem. We see the spiteful and wicked Jews vowing to murder Paul, and a conspiracy set in place to do it, but his nephew hears of it and warns the guard captain, who ordered hundreds of men to protect Paul, sending the last Apostle to the Roman governor Felix in Caesarea. When God has a purpose for us, he will make ready the things of this world to protect us, even unbelieving agents of the state are His to use. "Be of good cheer."

Now in Acts 23 we find Paul already delivered to the Roman governor of the province, Felix in Caesarea, and his accusers called before Felix to hear charges against the Apostle. Having seen Paul's gift for rhetoric, Ananias the head Priest of the temple brings a ringer, the orator Tertullus. Tertullus flatters the Roman governor and government, praising their stewardship, and claims Paul and the "sect" of Nazarenes is sowing sedition against Rome. He throws the chief captain under the bus, and bemoaning the "great violence" of the centurions, the Jew cries out in pain as he strikes. The Governor then hears Paul's rebuttal, and Paul likewise appeals to Felix's honor as a judge, as he sets about the truth of the matter. He notes his business in Jerusalem was to bring alms, that he was found by certain Asian Jews while undergoing purifying in the Temple. That those same Jews aren't even present to accuse him. Paul testifies that it is his faith in the resurrection that's the real issue. He orders Paul held for the time being, and Paul is able to preach the Gospel to him and his wife, a Jewess named Drusilla, shaking Felix who allows Paul some liberty under guard, failing to entice a bribe from him. Two years pass in Paul's house arrest, and Porcius Festus takes Felix's place as governor under Nero, and to show the Jews a concession, continues to hold Paul. This all is taking place roughly 58-60AD. The political situation in Judea and among the Jews of Samaria is getting strained and rebellion is growing. This untoward generation of unbelieving Jews is rapidly approaching its judgement, the Jewish war of 66, followed by the desolation of Jerusalem scattering the remnant of Jews of the flesh and total destruction of the temple in 70AD. It's a fascinating dynamic, and Jesus' and His apostles and believers impact on the hastening of these events is obvious. We need not sow sedition or take up arms or anything else but have faith in God. Turning towards Him, trusting He will judge the nation using His means for His wrath in His time. Often Christians get impatient with God and His long-suffering, and eager for their perception of justice, try to take vengeance into their own hands. Their lack of faith and sin of fear grips them, and desperation fueled by provocation and deliberate humiliation is used by the enemy to tempt us. To have us turn away from God and towards an earthly solution. Reactionary spirals, further worsening the conditions we face. Dancing to the devil's tune. Slaves to Satan's plans. Tribulation and persecution is a part of the Christian life. The Bible promises us that as believers we will be hated of the world, because the world hates Him. That the greater things we do for God, the harsher the persecution. And, as we see through out the Bible, and in history, the more God's people are persecuted in His name, the more His people flourish. For we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. And knowing this, how can we be fearful? And being fearful, how can we be a light that shines? How can we be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you? Paul has been scourged repeatedly. Scared by stripes. Stoned to death and raised immediately. Chased out of countries, driven from cities. Plotted against and arrested multiple times. And like when he was held in a Philippian jail, singing songs and Psalms of praise to God for it. God has written to us to be not afraid 365 times in His word, once verse for every day of the year, and yet so many Christians live in misery and despair. They hide their light under a bushel, while the faithful shine it to beggars and princes alike. A common lament of the believer is that their friends and family are perishing, damned without faith. The worry and stress of having that knowledge and their inability to convince them of the truth leaves many feeling impotent and frustrated. But this is all the more reason to remain steadfast. To magnify God's love for us, reflecting it to those we care about. To be the rock that they can turn to when they are troubled, and maybe coming to see the truth of the word though our example. The reason for our hope. To be an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity. Why would someone believe someone telling them of the peace that passes all understanding found in Christ when we are as miserable and fearful as everyone else?

The plans of the Jews continue to be thwarted and the plans of God continue to unfold. Paul has made an appeal unto Caesar, and in doing so has ultimately drawn the attention of King Herod Agrippa II and his sister, Bernice, who ask a formal audience with the Apostle.... Not much in the way of doctrine, but we are told the primary offense of Paul to the Jews, according to Festus, was of "Jesus, which was dead and Paul affirmed to be alive." The truth of the Gospel is going to be preached before kings. Proverbs 22 29 Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men. Matthew 10 18 And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles.

Having been called before the king, Agrippa, Paul is given the opportunity to speak freely in his defense. Bound and chained before them, Paul explains himself. He again gives his testimonial, of how he came from the Pharisees with zeal against the believers of Christ, to his roadside visitation by Jesus, and his ministry to bring the truth, preached by all the prophets before then, that Christ must come and the resurrection that follows. Paul says he showed the truth of the Gospel first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judaea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance. For these causes the Jews caught me in the temple, and went about to kill me. We see Biblical repentance in regards to salvation is turning from what ever is being believed in regards to God's word, and turning towards God for salvation. That, as we have seen again and again, it's always used in this fashion. That the "...of sin," or whatever isn't mentioned. It is turning your trust from false beliefs, your own works, false gods and idols, and towards God. And once saved doing works suitable and proper for such a turning. This, Paul says is why the Jews want him dead, as the book of Acts has shown us again and again. This message of hope and good news of the resurrection, and their role in killing Christ, and their resentment at losing the inheritance to the Gentiles has always been why the Jew persecutest God's people. Even today, making Gentiles unworthy of God's inheritance is their goal, and the subversive nature of the Jew is dedicated to this cause, and preventing those of us who have obtained our portion of the kingdom of God from giving others the same adoption of faith. Festus yelling out, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" is a familiar tactic of those proud in their own conceits when confronted with the truth of the word. We see this mockery and derision often, when we speak out for the Lord. Especially when it's done confidently and with knowledge of the scriptures. Left with having to either acknowledge the truth or save face and defend the status they hold in pride, most choose to be scornful. And Agrippa, who history paints as a hedonist, possibly engaged in incest with his sister Bernice (who is present for this), laughingly says Paul has almost convinced him to be a Christian. I believe him to be reprobate, based on this mocking response. One quality of the reprobate mind according to Romans 1, is that knowing the truth, they reject it. I find this true in my own experience with them. Most reprobates when pushed understand the basics of salvation and Christ. Often better than some who call themselves Christian but who are caught up in damnable heresy. It's a head knowledge coupled with a hardness of heart and stiffness of neck, that brought them to be twice-dead, conscience seared. Paul expresses the fervent hope that all who hear him come to saving faith, that the hearers be as he is, absent his current bonds, and with that they dismiss him. Agrippa then says that while Paul hasn't done anything to be held, his appeal unto Caesar has sealed his fate. Paul is destined for Rome. It is in the hands of Christians, Bible believing, born again sons of God, to turn away from their wicked ways, their indulgence in the world, in sin, in the subversive and perverse things we are tempted with, and turn towards God the Father, in Jesus' name. All other methods of delaying the wrath that America deserves are vanity. We cannot vote our way out. We cannot shoot our way out. We cannot riot and murder and exact our own vengeance, and expect any relief. There is only one path. Turning to the right or left leads to destruction. Turning towards the Lord is all we have. #IndependenceDay #4thofJuly

I won't even try breaking down the narrative of this chapter, as Luke writing in the spirit paints a thrilling picture of the perilous voyage of the centurions taking Paul to Rome. Paul's visitation by a messenger of God, promise to save the crew and passengers. The fasting of the believers among them, the breaking of bread and the casting off of the wheat to the sea. The centurion saving the prisoners from death by his soldiers, for Paul's sake. Their eventual wreck, and being castaway on the shore. God has purpose for us, and in that use we see a hedge of protection that still allows for the free will of others to make bad decisions and ignore sound advice. Not a hair harmed as God carries us towards His purpose, in His time and manner. All of this journey serves as an allegory for the Christian life, in tumultuous times. That we should be as an anchor, steadfast in our faith. Trusting in God's promises. An example for others. Giving sound advice in a sea of storms to those seeking safety of the shore. Offering them salvation of the spirit, even as it was told unto you. So, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me. Amen

The final chapter of Acts. Thank God for His word. Luke writes of their being waylaid on the island they castaway on, Melita (Malta), and its barbarian population led by a man named Publius. The Maltese are hospitable to the crew, centurions and prisoners. We are told that after gathering a bundle of sticks (ahem), and burning them in the fire, a venomous snake bites Paul in the hand, causing the natives to assume he be a murderer that having escaped shipwreck was now being taken out by snake. However, as Jesus said if those apostles given the gifts of the Holy Ghost in Mark 16:18 “They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” And thus, Paul shakes the snake off into the fire and is fine. Further, he heals Publius' father of dysentery, and goes on to heal many of the Maltese people during their stay, lasting 3 months. They leave with a ship that had wintered in port, honored by the chief and his people, and so, as Paul writes in Romans 1:14, “I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians." There are snake handling sects claiming they are "apostles," and that venom cannot hurt them, who speak gibberish and call it 'speaking in tongues," and engage in other nonsense, LARPing at the things of God, more African voodoo than Christian. There is no record in the Bible of Publius' conversion or of any preaching of the word, or the Gospel having any effect on the people there. Generally there are mentions of 'some believed,' or a summation of Paul giving the good news of Christ and it is hard to imagine he didn't, given his zeal and the healings we are told he performed, but there's no indication either way. That hasn't stopped the RCC from declaring Publius a saint and naming him a bishop, posthumously. So, finally coming to Italy and heading to Rome, they meet brothers in Christ, and we are told this was an encouragement to Paul. And arriving in Rome, Paul is placed under house arrest. Tradition holds that Paul was chained to his guard, 24 hours a day, as was Roman custom in such cases. Roman guards typically restrained prisoners with chains. The prisoner’s right wrist was usually chained to the guard’s left wrist. This kept the guard’s right hand free. Paul referred to his chains, bonds, and imprisonment in most of the epistles he wrote during his house arrest in Rome..(Eph 3:1; 4:1; 6:20; Php 1:7, 13, 14, 17; Col 4:3, 18; Phm 1, 9, 10, 13) Paul calls on the Jews of Rome, and tells them of his plight and treatment by the Jews of Asia, in Jerusalem and leading to his being in Rome to appeal to Nero. He preaches to them from scripture, proving all things about Jesus being the Christ. And, as we have seen more than once, while many believed, most had stiff necks and hardened hearts. Here, quoting Isaiah 6:8-10 in the same way Jesus does in Matthew 13:15, we see them unable to understand the Gospel and believe, by their own choosing. But the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles, and they will hear it. Jews, so-called, to this day resent and hate the Gentile for this. We are told Paul remained in bonds in his own hired house for 2 full years, preaching of Jesus. We know of the epistles he wrote while under bonds. We know he must have reached some of Caesar's household as he says in his letter to the Philippians, 4:22, "All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household." We know Nero hadn't quite gone full Reprobate by this time, and we have no evidence Paul went before him or just simply was released. Tradition has it that he was freed after the two years, and that his mission then took him to Spain, preaching the word. Some later historians claim he was arrested again and martyred in Rome by beheading. Others have said the evidence is flimsy, and he likely died of old age while still evangelizing. We simply don't know. But the important thing to Paul was always Jesus, spreading the faith in Him, first to the Jew and then the Greek. Amen. Before beginning another book of the Bible, I just want to reflect back on what we have seen consistently: In John, the only book written explicitly to the unsaved that they may believe and receive eternal life, where in every chapter, Jesus teaches that it is by faith alone we are saved. In Acts, the Apostles from Pentecost, unto Paul, decades later in Rome, this message has been the same. We are all sinners, deserving death and Hell, but God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son that whosever believeth on Him shall not perish but have everlasting life. That Jesus was Christ, crucified and risen. That by calling upon His name, we are adopted as sons of God, heirs to the promise of the kingdom, and this free gift, given in God's grace can never be lost or taken away. It is this faith that saves us. Not our works. Not a denomination. Not anything other than believing in your heart this truth of the good news. That once we do, our spirit, dead in sin is quickened by the Holy Spirit, and we are sealed by Him unto the day of judgment, our sins washed clean in Jesus' blood, we are healed by his stripes. This is the good news. This is the Gospel. If you are not 100% sure today that if you were to die, you would go to heaven, please listen to this presentation of the Bible way to heaven. For faith comes by hearing and hearing by the word of God.

The epistle to the churches of Rome, written by the Apostle Paul prior to his arrest in Jerusalem and his being taken under house arrest to the seat of the empire, as described in the book of Acts. Paul describes himself in his greeting as first and foremost a servant of Jesus Christ. A minister doing the work of the Lord, which he specifies as being separated unto the Gospel of God. As we know, he was an evangelical Apostle to the Gentiles to give them the good news of God, the faith in His Son for eternal life. This good news. Paul tells us parenthetically that this is the same Gospel given by the prophets in the Old Testament, the holy scriptures. As evidenced by our readings, shown by the Spirit, and as taught by Jesus himself. The gospel of God is concerning His Son, our Lord, which was made of the seed of David concerning the flesh, meaning only the incarnate aspect of manhood, that it is of the lineage of David as promised. But more, Christ Jesus is declared to be the Son of God with power, meaning His godhood is shown by what? The spirit of holiness He possessed, and by His resurrection from the dead. These things testify that Jesus was God made flesh, again as promised by God through the prophets. Building on this; By whom we have received grace... Grace is God's mercy in giving salvation by the faith that acknowledges that all these facts are true. God promises a savior in the writings of the prophets, from the lineage of David after the flesh, but being the Son of God in the spirit by His holiness and resurrection. ...and apostleship; Paul transitions from establishing the faith common to himself and the intended audience of believers, giving the creed of what they all believe as Christians, to his specific calling as an Apostle. For obedience to the faith among all nations; For, meaning in the context for the purpose of, he is given to be an Apostle to bring the Gospel which is obedience to the faith he has just laid out, to all nations. To all Gentiles. For his name; whose? Christ Jesus. Among whom are ye also the called of Jesus Christ. The Romans are among the "all nations," and are also called to salvation the same way he was, in the same faith he enumerated, which is the same Gospel he preaches as Apostle, which is the same Gospel that God promises in the holy scriptures. To all that be in Rome; his greeting shifts from establishing baselines and his own credentials in the faith, to addressing the Roman believers, called to be saints, just as Paul was called to believe, so were they, saints just meaning those saved by faith. Grace and peace to them, well wishes, and again acknowledging that the grace and peace comes from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, His Son. Romans 2 17 Behold, thou art called a Jew, and restest in the law, and makest thy boast of God, 18 And knowest his will, and approvest the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law; 19 And art confident that thou thyself art a guide of the blind, a light of them which are in darkness, 20 An instructor of the foolish, a teacher of babes, which hast the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law. 21 Thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself? thou that preachest a man should not steal, dost thou steal? 22 Thou that sayest a man should not commit adultery, dost thou commit adultery? thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege? 23 Thou that makest thy boast of the law, through breaking the law dishonourest thou God? 24 For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you, as it is written. Jews, with the Law, commit the same sins and face the same condemnation. Boasting their own righteousness by being possessors of God's word, seeking to lecture the heathen in righteousness, and yet just as susceptible to sin, and so giving a bad report of the truth of God to all nations. And this leads to the crux of Paul's argument, a statement of logic using the key physical difference between the two peoples, circumcision. The outward sign of being of Israel, that is, the people of God: For circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law: but if thou be a breaker of the law, thy circumcision is made uncircumcision. Therefore if the uncircumcision keep the righteousness of the law, shall not his uncircumcision be counted for circumcision? And shall not uncircumcision which is by nature, if it fulfil the law, judge thee, who by the letter and circumcision dost transgress the law? If a Jew is circumcised it doesn't mean anything of they don't keep the whole of the law. If a Gentile being uncircumcised does the works of the law without the law, it counts to them for circumcision. If a non-Jew, uncircumcised, fulfils the law in Christ, and will judge over the circumcised, who with the law doesn't fulfill it, what then? Who is the real Jew in this scenario? Who is the actual child of God? Those circumcised of the flesh or those circumcised of the heart? And so Paul reaches this conclusion: For he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly; neither is that circumcision, which is outward in the flesh: But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God. This alone should be sufficient to kill the idea that Jews of the flesh have special favor with God over the Gentiles. Dispensationalism RIP in the mid-1st Century. And yet the idea persists because Jews, having the circumcision and the law, the oracles of God, demand they are special boys. Entitled to God's mercy without conforming to His law. Which is fulfilled in belief, the faith of Christ as laid out in the common gospel in chapter 1. The circumcision of the heart. To the Gentiles in the church of Rome, whose faith Paul said was known throughout the world, this is an encouragement, to not look at themselves as lesser-than the Jews, who in all cities throughout the empire, had taken to Judaizing and lording over converts in Christ. Remember the context of the epistles from the Apostles; To combat Judaizing, the demand of circumcision to be saved, and to establish the faith, edifying the church. Preaching salvation to every creature without deeds of the law. Paul spends the bulk of Romans doing this in the most concise rendition of the theology of Christianity ever written. Inspired by the Holy Spirit. And the lesson continues in chapter 3.

That the saved Gentile in uncircumcision is better off than the circumcised Jew that sins. The circumcision of the heart, the following the spirit of the law, makes the Gentile a Jew inwardly, and the Jews of the flesh who deny the judgment of God, their circumcision of the flesh profits them nothing. Again this argument Paul is making is to provoke the Jews to jealousy and into separation towards the Gospel, and to reject being holier than thou against the repentant pagans being converted in Rome. But this entire exchange is also important to understand when dealing with Zionism and the Dispensationalist error that Jews are favored by God. There is no respect of persons to God. The Jew and Gentile are judged the same. Given the same revelation of wrath. Have the law in their hearts, given a conscience, the Spirit working to convict them of sin. And our following the letter of the law doesn't make us better than those who aren't where we are spiritually. Only the grace of God is keeping us from the same fate. This doesn't mean we don't judge, it means we should try to judge righteously as God has with us. And never think you are a special boy, given favor by God for who you are, what tribe you're born to, how diligently you keep the letter of the law, but remaining humble in the grace of God. The things we should keep in mind reading Romans 1. Through 3, especially, Is that God is not a respecter of persons, that his nature is revealed to us in multiple ways so that we have no excuse, that the gentile is judged by the same law as the Jew and the Jew has no advantage having the law given them, for none keep the whole of the law. All have fallen short. He's building to a culmination in chapter 3. That there are none righteous. No not one. He's building the case for why we need salvation in Christ. And why it applies to both the Jews and the Gentiles. Answering a question with a brother about Romans 2 had me really rethink something that I missed, and it clarified a lot of the misunderstanding around the chapter, specifically who it is written to. Because of the language Paul uses, specifically at the end of the chapter, many assume he is directly addressing Jews there, despite the greetings in chapter 1 being to the church in Rome, which are Gentiles. In my study, I did what a lot of people do and just squared the circle by saying basically the church has both Jews and Greeks (which is likely true, but irrelevant to what Paul is doing). The entire epistle is a general one, and all believers are the audience. But there is a default understanding that some of it is actually targeted to Jews, in the church, based especially on the last half of chapter 2. But it's not. Paul's not writing to Jews. He's writing a rhetorical method of argument that addresses common points made about Gentiles, then Jews, in a methodical way. It's part of the larger argument that he's making in the epistle. It isn't literally him saying to the Jew the things he says, but addressing questions often raised by Jews against Christians who were preaching that Gentiles were now made accessible to the Gospel of Grace. When Paul says "O man..." is like when James says "a man may say..." It's a method of rhetoric common in the era. Anticipating and answering objections to stipulate certain points. And so after establishing that Gentiles, despite being pagans and many reprobate and given over, with no excuse, given up to all unrighteousness, have access salvation in Christ, Paul continues to hammer Jewish objections to this idea. Behold, thou art called a Jew, and restest in the law, and makest thy boast of God, And knowest his will, and approvest the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law...This is addressed to a rhetorical Jewish opponent who would make these claims, not specifically "to Jews." Chapter three changes to 3rd person, because it was always the arguments being made, not the audience being addressed. What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God. For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? Having chapters and verse helps to quickly reference scripture, but the breaks can cause confusion when a larger point is being made. Go back and read the entire epistle in one go, and consider it's Paul, in the Spirit, making several arguments, methodically. Not telling Jews one thing and Gentiles another.

Romans 3:21-31 But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference: For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law. But we know that no flesh was ever justified by the works of the law, but by the law was condemnation. Death.
