Continuing the look at dispensationalism in light of Romans. Chapter 2 saw Paul conclude that a Jew isn't one outwardly. It's not of the flesh. It is of the heart, and a Jew is one inwardly; meaning believers. Israel are the people of God who believe the covenant in Christ. Circumcision of the heart. And so, picking up from there in chapter 3, Paul begins to build on this idea. What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God. The prophets and the scriptures were given the nation that came from Jacob. The 12 tribes of Israel. And through Moses they received the law of the Old Testament, or rather the covenant. This advantage gave them the understanding and precepts to understand salvation by faith. The carnal ordinances, diverse washings, the dietary laws and sacrifices, holy days and sabbaths that were a picture of the Christ to come. But, anticipating arguments, Paul concedes that not all of Israel were saved. That the law wasn't perfect in converting all who said they were a Jew, just as not all Jews believed on Christ. For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? What then? are we better than they? No, in no wise: for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin; As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one... Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin. Paul is making the point that all are the same under sin and need of redemption to make it clear that the Judaizers are wrong to claim that believing Gentiles must adhere to the law to be saved. Even though it is by the schoolmaster of the law we can know we need salvation. The freedom we have in Christ was a threat to their power structure. And it still is to this day, to all who teach works-based salvation. Judaizing never stopped. And those of you who are saved by faith through grace witness this same pushback today as you give the gospel. To the people taken in by the false gospel, who are under the yoke of the law and subject to the authority of men, primarily in the Catholic Church and its daughters, and even in the evangelical movement, Lordshippers and the like, the appeal of works is they never have to confront the truth that they aren't good enough, that there are none righteous, that they are going to Hell. Talk with them, soul winning and even online, and they will say they know they are going to heaven because they are a "good person," or that they attend mass and take communion and go to confession. But in the back of their mind they know this isn't true, that they imperfectly follow the law of God, and even fall short of the traditions of man. And so they will hedge by saying it is presumption to claim to know if you're saved. That they "think so, but God decides at judgment." That unbiblical things like purgatory exist as a Plan B is a testament to the cope people will cling to to deny that they are sinners deserving death and Hell. And the Gospel reminds them of this, triggers them, and their anger has resulted in persecution and murder of martyrs, just as the prophets slain in the OT times. Just as it did Christ. Just as it did the apostles and the early church and through the dark ages. Man doesn't want to humble themselves to the truth of their nature and what they deserve. They seek reassurance that they are good. That they deserve salvation. But we know this isn't true. And so, Paul is writing to the churches in Rome, many of the congregation are saved Jews, surrounded by reprobate pagan excess and put upon by Pharisees among their own people. He established that the Gentiles were beholden to the same Creator. He established that the law wasn't sufficient to save the Jew. He established that all are under sin. And so we begin to get to the meat of things. There is none righteous, no, not one: There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one. This is quoting Psalm 14; The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good. The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, and seek God. They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one. Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people as they eat bread, and call not upon the Lord. There were they in great fear: for God is in the generation of the righteous. Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge. Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! when the Lord bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad. The workers of iniquity, those whose mouths are an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lip; those teaching men false doctrines, their words are like the stench of death, of an open grave, because that is what their false gospel brings. It is poison. They eat the people up as bread, that they don't call upon the name of the Lord and be saved. This should sound familiar. Matthew 23; 14 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation. 15 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves. 16 Woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor! 17 Ye fools and blind: for whether is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifieth the gold? 18 And, Whosoever shall swear by the altar, it is nothing; but whosoever sweareth by the gift that is upon it, he is guilty. 19 Ye fools and blind: for whether is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifieth the gift? 20 Whoso therefore shall swear by the altar, sweareth by it, and by all things thereon. 21 And whoso shall swear by the temple, sweareth by it, and by him that dwelleth therein. 22 And he that shall swear by heaven, sweareth by the throne of God, and by him that sitteth thereon. 23 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. 24 Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel. 25 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess. 26 Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also. 27 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness. 28 Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. 29 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! because ye build the tombs of the prophets, and garnish the sepulchres of the righteous, 30 And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets. 31 Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets. 32 Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers. 33 Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell? They devour widows houses. They make merchandise of the people. They make them twice the child of hell as themselves. They are as whited sepulchres, full of death. These are the workers of iniquity whom Jesus says on the day of judgement will call out "Lord, Lord, didn't we do many wonderful works?" and He will say to them "Depart from me, I never knew you." Jesus and Paul taught the same thing, because God's Gospel has always been the same, and opposed by the same forces. Chasing after the error of Cain. Trusting in their works. Hypocrites condemning others while excusing themselves. And so, going back to Romans 3, having the full context of things, and an understanding of the conflict between these two visions; God's revelation of His righteousness, and the filthy rags of man's, we proceed. Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin. Now we know. Everyone under the law should know that they all break the law. That all the world is guilty before God. That is the purpose of the law, to serve to humble us and reveal the holiness of God, that we may come to call upon His name to be saved. (If a man were perfect under the law, they would be saved, but the exceeding holiness that is God, only the Son could achieve this in the flesh) Therefore by the deeds, the doing, the works, none shall be saved. It is impossible for man to work their way to Heaven. We cannot attain the righteousness of God. And so what does this mean for us? Where is the good news? How can we attain righteousness if not by our works? But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference: For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. Read that again. And again. Jesus Christ is the propitiation, that is a sacrifice that is wholly pleasing to God, that is the blood of Christ serves to impart His righteousness to us, by faith, to show us the righteousness of God in our forgiveness. We are justified freely by His grace. Even the righteousness of God, that is by faith, upon all them that believe. That's the good news. This is the Gospel. This is the reason Romans is used to evangelize, because it is the clearest and most succinct summary of the Gospel. All have sinned. All deserve death. Jews under the law. Gentiles without the law. But God's grace is such that all who believe that His Son, Christ Jesus, the lamb without blemish, was given to be the propitiation for our sin, and that grace is given freely to all who believe. Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? of works? Nay: but by the law of faith. This is the end of the argument. There is no one who reads this and says "yeah, but you have to do works" who is seeking truth. They are blind in their own pride. Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. Read that again. Say it out loud. Three chapters of building argument against the judaizers, the works-based false gospel. The workers of iniquity. Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. Furthermore: Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also: Seeing it is one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith. Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law. By understanding that salvation comes only by faith, we actually establish the law. By believing God's word, by placing our trust in the sacrifice of Jesus, that in His blood we are washed clean, forgiven of sins, we then understand the nature and purpose of the law, and are free to become doers of the law. To seek to obtain the holiness of God out of love. To be holy because He is holy. To reveal His righteousness to the world by our forgiveness in His grace. I know that is a lot of Bible, and that these posts were long, but I implore those reading along to take the time and really understand what's being given to us to reveal God's will. If you've already called upon the name of the Lord, and are saved, I hope this helps make it easier for you to explain the Gospel to those who aren't. To separate yourselves to the Gospel of God. And to those of you who are still trusting in your works, who are still dependent on the works of the law to be justified. Who are under the yoke of the workers of iniquity, the blind guides who bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers, I hope this helped stir you to be convicted by the Spirit, to repentance from dead works and towards God. Amen

Unlearned and unstable people confuse the means by which God delivered us, Jesus' life, death, burial and resurrection, with the means of receiving the promise of God, belief. Abraham believed God's promise to him, by faith, without knowing the exact means by which He would make good on the promise, only that He would. And it was counted for righteousness. We have the mystery of the means revealed to us, by the post-resurrection teachings of Christ to the Apostles, and that faith handed down, believer to believer in an unbroken line by which we can say that Abraham and the OT saints are our brothers in Christ, through they did not fully understand the mystery that was Christ. This is what the Bible teaches. I am saved because I believe God, and it is counted for righteousness. If God told us we would be saved by any other means or manner, believing His word would still be why we have His imputed righteousness. We know as New Testament Christians that the only means and manner of salvation is by the blood of Christ.

Building upon the conclusions reached in Chapter 3, we see in Romans 4, Paul uses scripture to flesh out the ideas and demonstrate the truth of his argument. The veil lifted, so that by the reading of Moses a believer may understand God's word. He begins with the understanding that Abraham was not justified by his works or by circumcision, but by his faith. Abraham believed God and it was counted for righteousness. And when Abraham believed, it was decades before the institution of the carnal ordinance of circumcision. A practice giving an outward sign for the continuation of the people chosen to bear Abraham's seed, which is Christ. While Romans 4 is frequently cited to demolish the heretical argument that we are saved in any capacity by our own works, it is primarily an argument against the Judaizers who think to themselves to say they have Abraham as their father. But as John the Baptist says in Matthew 3:9; And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham. It wasn't circumcision that saved Abraham, but faith. It wasn't even his willingness to sacrifice Isaac. All the great works of faith by Abraham may be reason to glory among men, but not before God. They may be reckoned for reward out of debt, but not of grace which is freely given to those who believe, to the glory of God. As David wrote, Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Those who do no works, but have believed on Christ, that faith is counted for righteousness. It is an accounting. The only thing that is reckoned for forgiveness of sin and salvation from death, is faith. And so, if this blessing came by faith and not circumcision, there is no profit in circumcision. And if the righteousness of Abraham came by faith, there is no profit in being able to call Abraham your father after the flesh. The promise of God, that through his seed all nations shall be blessed, and that seed should be made heir to the whole world, was not made to Abraham, or to his seed through the law. Meaning his physical descendants, who under the law are inheritors. The promise to be made heir was through the righteousness of faith. This excludes unconditionally any claim Jews would have on the Abrahamic covenant, except by faith in Christ. For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect If dispensationalist Zionism were true, that by the law Jews are heirs to Abraham's promise, then faith is made void and the promises made of none effect. Saved Christians who believe that Jews are the inheritors by this promise, are like Esau, selling the promise for pottage. Despising their inheritance. Abraham believed. And in that faith, received the inheritance, which in Christ is given to all who believe. Whether they were circumcised or uncircumcised. And the righteousness and promises of faith given Abraham was not only to him, but to all who believe the Gospel of Grace, again recounted here by Paul; Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. This is the faith that imputed righteousness on Abraham and upon we who believe. Plus nothing and minus nothing. The same faith that saved Abraham saved us today, and will until the day of the Lord comes, and we are gathered unto Him. Jew or Gentile. At the great harvest of God. So, in 4 chapters we see that there is no difference between Jew and Gentile, all are under sin, all condemned, with the law or without. We see that all who are saved from that condemnation are saved by faith in the blood of Christ Jesus. By believing God's promise. By the imputed righteousness of Jesus, our own sins are not counted against us. Without works. Not by the law. Not by circumcision. Not by being physical heirs of Abraham, but spiritual heirs in faith. There is no replacement theology, only the continuation of the covenant made to Abraham, which is to all nations. There was no other dispensation given. There is no future dispensation to be had.

What shall we say then? Paul, having concluded that all are under sin, all being unrighteous, and the grace of God given to all who believe on the Son, and that no man may be justified by the works of the law but only faith, now begins the application of this knowledge. The implications of this law of faith, given us by God. And he uses scripture and the promises to Abraham to explain the Old Testament in light of the New. Abraham, the physical father of the Hebrews, including the remnant of Jews from the Children of Israel in Rome, what was Abraham's experience? A story every Jew would be familiar with. Paul starts by saying, if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory. Abraham could brag in his works, his decades of service to God that includes willingness to sacrifice his only begotten son, but we know that there are none righteous. That boasting is excluded when we are judged by grace, as all the glory belongs to God, and the righteousness of Christ. So Paul writes, if it were by works, Abraham could glory, boast, brag that it was due him being so righteous. But not before God, being in the flesh, a sinner. (Which we have already stipulated in chapter 3) What then? Well, scripture says in Genesis 15:6; And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness. Paul quotes this and argues that if it were of works, that means God would be indebted to us. To pay us for our works. That we were owed. And so the reward would be not reckoned, or accounted for, by grace. Because grace is an unmerited and unearned gift or favor. Debt is deserved. Grace is undeserved. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness. Abraham is the example Paul uses, given us in scripture as a lesson in justification by faith to God, by grace not of debt. That the glory in our salvation is God's alone. But what about before other men? A man may say that faith without works is dead, being alone. That, to men, justification isn't seen of faith but by a man's works. James 2:18-23 Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works. Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect? And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God. A man may say... The overlooked predicate for the argument James makes in his epistle, written to brethren, the saved, to encourage them to good works. A man may say that Abraham's faith was shown in his works and thus he was justified to others. But we know that scripture says it was faith that justified Abraham to God. For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God. For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. By comparing scripture with scripture we see that there is no contradiction, only context. That Paul is writing of justification before God in grace, while James is writing of justification before man, by doing good works in faith. The rhetorical question asked by a rhetorical man, "Was not Abraham justified by works?" is answered by the holy Spirit in Romans 4 and Genesis 15. Not before God, or he would have to glory. The boasting wouldn't be excluded. The law of grace would become one of debt. The misuse of James 2 to teach a false gospel of works is one of the great stumbling blocks to salvation and faith. But by comparison, context and understanding we see that there is no contradiction found, anywhere in the Bible. Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. But to him that worketh not, but believes, his faith is counted for righteousness just as Abraham's. Just as all who believe. Works has nothing to do with salvation. God doesn't owe us salvation. Our works, no matter how good we think they are, can never offset our sin, and the wages thereof. When someone says their salvation or their ability to stay saved is contingent on their works, they are saying they are good enough to please God. That they are owed salvation. That the glory is theirs. That their boastings before God are justified. That they don't need grace. Hebrews 11:6 But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. Their lack of faith in Christ to be the propitiation for our sin, the sole sacrifice pleasing and acceptable to God, means their works are dead. They have no grace and no works. They are incapable of pleasing God. Hebrews 6:1 Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God Repentance from dead works and to faith towards God. Turning from means turning towards. From trusting in our works of righteousness to faith in God. This is the foundation that is built on the rock that is Christ. And so, reckoned of faith, the man who does no works but believes, is saved by that faith alone. Paul quotes David from Psalm 32 Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, Whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, And in whose spirit there is no guile. The Lord will not impute sin, our ledger is clean, our transgressions forgiven. For what is sin? 1 John 3:4 Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law. But we who believe not only are forgiven of sins past, but God will not impute sin to us. Our transgression is forgiven. This is a promise of God. Hebrews 10:17 And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more. So this is the promise made by God that if we believe on the Son, we are saved by His grace. Our sins forgiven. No sin even being imputed upon us. Whether we work or not, because work is debt not grace. Paul continues using Abraham's example; Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? for we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness. How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. Abraham did not receive the ordinance of circumcision until decades after his believing God's promise, and being saved by that faith. He was blessed with the accounting of righteousness when he did not know circumcision. So this promise, predating this rite of the Jews, means it does not only apply to the circumcised, but also to the uncircumcised. And so the promise of grace doesn't require circumcision, but faith alone. This point is both specific to the issue of circumcision being introduced by the Judaizers in Paul's day, but also generally speaking, that there is no rite or ordinance that is required for salvation. Not baptism. Not any ritual or keeping of tradition. No works of the law. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteousness might be imputed unto them also. Abraham as the father of all who believe, the circumcision of the spirit, the generation of believers are partakers of the promise, that the righteousness of God is imputed upon us in faith. For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect: Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression. The promise of God that Abraham believed was that through his faith, he would be made father to many nations, and inherit the kingdom of God. This promise was made possible in Christ. Galatians 3:16 Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ. Unbelieving Jews felt they were owed the kingdom by God for being Abraham's seed under the law. That the inheritance was by blood, and the promise made to them after the flesh, and not in the spirit. This is the basis for Zionism and the false doctrine of dispensationalism. But the Bible teaches the exact opposite. There is no difference between Jew and Gentile. All are under sin. It is by faith only that we are made heirs. That the seed of the promise is Christ manifest in the flesh. Matthew 3:9 And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham. It is not an inheritance by the law but by faith. Like Esau and Jacob, the inheritance went to the younger. It was taken from the elder, who with tears sought repentance from God, but none was found. Luke 13:25-30 When once the master of the house is risen up, and hath shut to the door, and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are: Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out. And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last. The kingdom of God was taken from the Jew in their unbelief and given to the nations of people bringing forth the fruit thereof. Who had faith. There is no plan for the Jews after the flesh and those teaching dispensationalism to claim there is are teaching heresy. Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression. Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed; not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham; who is the father of us all, (As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were. Because the law brings wrath, because we are all under sin, it isn't by the law we are saved. It is impossible for all have sinned. As James writes in the parts of his epistles ignored-by-works salvationists; For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all. Remember, there are none righteous. Knowledge of the law brings wrath. But faith, the grace of God. We access His mercy and forgiveness through faith alone. Plus nothing, minus nothing. And in grace we receive the promise given Abraham, and count as his seed in the spirit. Adopted into the kingdom of God. Made sons of God. Abraham is the father of us all who believe. (As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were. God, who can see all things, the future which is not to us, and yet it appears as it were to God, who quickens the dead, who breathes life into our dead spirit, and who made this eternal promise to all who believe. The Jew has no claim to Abraham, outside of faith. None. And to none of the promises made, for they all are fulfilled in Christ. If it feels like I am beating a dead horse, understand that it is God's word that stresses this over and over again, because it is the Gospel, the good news, that is the entire point of scripture. To bring us into the promise through faith and the imputed righteousness of God. Paul continues to show that despite the unlikely nature of some of the specific promises to him made of God, the hope against hope that he father a child with Sarah in their old age, that they would through Isaac become many nations, to people more numerous than the sand of the shore, the stars of heaven. And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness. But was this for Abraham alone? No. This was written for our sake as well, that we may KNOW we have eternal life and the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ if we believe on the promise of God. Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. Amen, amen, amen! I pray to the Lord that this series continues to be a blessing to others and that my understanding grows from presenting it. That the undeniable meaning of the theology of God found in scripture changes hearts with the power of His word. Have a blessed Sunday, and remember to thank father Abraham on this father's day. For he is the father of all who believe. In Jesus name, amen

Abraham was justified by faith alone. We are as well. It's only the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ on those who believe on His salvation, and trust God's promises offered in grace "while we were yet sinners," that saves us from death and Hell. It is the Gospel, the good news. If we cannot advocate for our religious morals and convictions, lawfully and politically, then we are being persecuted. Make them say it. All believers will be persecuted. It's ok, God rewards us. Don't be afraid of the persecution, and kept in silence. Just speak out, in peace and love, and let them come.

Psalm 145:8-17 The LORD is gracious, and full of compassion; Slow to anger, and of great mercy. The LORD is good to all: And his tender mercies are over all his works. All thy works shall praise thee, O LORD; And thy saints shall bless thee. They shall speak of the glory of thy kingdom, And talk of thy power; To make known to the sons of men his mighty acts, And the glorious majesty of his kingdom. Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, And thy dominion endureth throughout all generations. The LORD upholdeth all that fall, And raiseth up all those that be bowed down. The eyes of all wait upon thee; And thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand, And satisfiest the desire of every living thing. The LORD is righteous in all his ways, And holy in all his works. The Lord tells us love our enemies. That we who are saved, that have received the atonement through Jesus Christ, Who died for us while we were yet sinners, who were His enemies now reconciled in the blood of the lamb, because God is kind to the unthankful and to the evil, should judge our enemies with the same spirit of grace, longsuffering and mercy that God has shown us. His mercy is such that we are promised by the Lord Jesus Christ that though we suffer loss, are despised for His name's sake, will be blessed. We are poor, and ours is the kingdom of God. We hunger, but we shall be filled. We weep, but we shall laugh. And when we are persecuted, we should leap for joy, because we are rewarded in Heaven. And here on earth, our generosity, our putting others needs before our own, even to the thankless and those that seek to do evil, we shall be rewarded greatly, here on earth as well as in Heaven. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again. It can be hard to not lose sight of the mercy of God that has been given to us. To take for granted so great a gift as Christ. To forget the pattern of prayer Jesus taught us, asking the Father to forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. Why? For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. I wasn't going to take detours in this exercise of Dispensationalism in light of the book of Romans, but I cannot overlook the beauty of chapter 5 and the understanding that everything is in Christ Jesus; By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Note this carefully. The Calvinist says the special boys chosen by God have access to faith by grace, but the Bible says the exact opposite. We access His grace, which abounds and is to all men, by faith. Just as Adam accessed death by the choice of sin, we access life in Jesus by the same free will choice. Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one, the free gift came upon all men unto the justification of life. Salvation is a free gift. Justification is of Christ. Offered to ALL MEN, by grace. Free. A gift, given without works, without being reckoned of debt. Without our having the glory. Without boasting, which is excluded. Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. This is the Gospel. And it is to all men. With the law or without. While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord. Again, it is impossible to read "Therefore being justified by faith..." and come away with "it's faith plus works." Just as it's impossible to read "to all men" and say it's only for special boys, chosen because of their unique wonderfulness, "Hey, don't question a sovereign God. He just thinks I am super special and awesome." God is not a respecter of persons. It is impossible to say the Mosaic law did anything other than show man our own sinful nature, just as Adam transgressed under one commandment, then so too man transgressed all the more abundantly under the 600 or so contained in the law. There is no fair reading of Romans that leads to these heresies. It is only by being a heretic first, and then searching for whatever scripture they can wrest with to torture into confirming their own vain imagination. There are some who say the complex sentences and thoughts can be difficult for some to understand, but luckily for us God is not the author of confusion, and has Paul in the Spirit provide clear and concise summaries of each point as he concludes each argument. "There is neither Jew nor Greek...." "Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight..." "To him that worketh not but believes..." "Therefore being justified by faith..." Isaiah 1:18 Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

It's not complicated. We make it complicated because we can't believe it's so easy. Because we feel like the prodigal son and say "And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants." Many want to do works because they don't feel worthy. This is a common problem with babes in Christ, saved but now feeling embarrassed at the generosity of the gift, and seeking to become slaves to a sovereign to earn it. It's sad and keeps you from knowing the freedom and liberty of Christ. Therefore. When we see this word we have to ask ourselves "what's it there for?" What does it refer back to? Well, 4 chapters of Paul logically and with irrefutable proof from scripture that all are under sin and need salvation, and that salvation is through faith in Jesus Christ, by the grace of God. Therefore. Therefore what? Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. As the heavenly hosts proclaimed in the hills of Bethlehem at the birth of the man Christ Jesus; Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men. The peace and goodwill on earth was come from God to man. Not the peace of men not warring. Not goodwill between tribes. But the enmity of wrath in the transgressions of man made justified by the peace offering of His only begotten Son. We are justified by faith alone. There is nothing more noted. We have already concluded that by the works of the law no man shall be justified. We already know that by faith, Abraham became father to all who believe. We already know that the judgment of God is upon Jew and Greek alike. And that Jesus as propitiation for our sin has given us salvation from the wrath we deserve. Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. What's more; By faith we have access into the grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Believing, we are given grace, and by grace, God is given the glory for our salvation. Note, "wherein we stand." This isn't the future, this isn't a process. This is now, at the time of our repentance towards belief in Christ as our redeemer we then, at that moment, stand in grace. And rejoice. And we not only rejoice in the glory of God's grace that provides us with salvation through faith, because it shows the mercy and judgment and righteousness of God (which remember is one way His glory is revealed to man from Heaven), we also glory in tribulations here on earth, knowing they are a refining fire; that worketh patience, which brings experience, and experience brings hope. Hope builds faith. Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. Hope is the sure knowledge that a thing will be that is not yet. The object of faith. Tribulation in our lives, not only persecution for our faith, but just general troubles like health, finance, whatever things common to all men, saved or unsaved, all of it gives opportunity to glorify the Lord, as it makes our faith sharper as we are brought out of it by His mercy and blessings, better for having experienced it. And our hope is fulfilled in the love of God, by the comforter, the Holy Ghost, which is given us, who indwells with us, quickening our spirit and leading us to that peace which passes all understanding, even in turmoil and crisis. Our faith in man, traditions, our own works, all will leave us ashamed at some point. But the hope we have in Christ Jesus will never bring us shame. God never lets us down. And how do we know that God's word is good, that our hope is true? Because But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. That when we were still enemies, working inequities, dead in sin, God reconciled us through the death of His Son. God loved His enemies, and offered the free gift of salvation by the shedding of blood of His only begotten Son. Think about this, for in it is the righteousness of God. And if He offered us such a gift, if a righteous man gave His life for us while we were enemies, dying for us while we were dead in sin, then how much more shall He do for us whom have been reconciled to Him in faith by the death of His Son? Who stand in His grace? We shall be saved by His life in the resurrection. And not only so, that we shall know we will be saved out of tribulation by His resurrection and the promise of God to us likewise for eternal life, but we also joy, rejoice, in God through our Lord Jesus Christ by whom we have now received the atonement. Our hope is that, today we who believe are spared wrath for our sins, adopted to the promise, and that in tribulation on this earth we will be saved by God's love for His sons, because of the atonement of Christ Jesus that we holdfast to in faith. Amen The first law was to Adam, and it was simple. Do not eat of the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden. For you will surely die. And Adam broke the single law in paradise. And by his sin, death came up on the world. Paradise was denied us, and the way of the world, short and brutish lives. And sin multiplied, and death. All through one man. This is not original sin, btw. There is no sin that follows man from birth, but only the understanding that it is in our nature, even under perfect conditions as Eden, that we still fall short. And so the law came, to Noah, to Abraham, to Moses, and by Sinai, so detailed and expanded, much more than the single commandment of the Garden, so that man had to know that the holiness of God was unattainable by their works, and that faith in His grace alone was our only hope. And with the law, sin abounded much the more, that God's grace may abound to His glory. So that by one man, the man Christ Jesus, and His righteousness and His willingness to die for us, and not only those who believe, but for every man and all sin, he gave His life that we may enter into peace with the Father by faith, in His grace. To His glory. That the righteousness of God be shown the world. It becomes impossible for those who maintain that "vicarious atonement isn't found in scripture," that Jesus wasn't the sacrifice for our sins, once we have reached Romans 5. The propitiation that is Christ is the atonement we have. The reconciliation is in His blood. Our hope is in His life from death. When we were righteous? No, as sinners. Did we earn it through works, the keeping of the law? No, that would be debt, it is the imputed righteousness from Christ that justifies us in faith. It is the law of grace. We don't deserve it. It is the free gift given by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ. The gift of His righteousness that we may be justified through Him to God. By His obedience to the end, and the death on the cross for all men, that in His resurrection we may enter into grace by faith. That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord. What shall we say then? Do you continue in the vain works of the law seeking to justify yourselves? To put God in debt to you for your own righteousness? Well, we have concluded by logical analysis that this is impossible. If you are counting on your works to justify you before God in any way, you do not have faith in Christ, you call God a liar, and you reject His free gift. If this is you, and you have been told all your life by men that you have to deserve grace to be saved or to keep your salvation, you cannot read the epistle to the Romans and not see the folly of that false gospel. Repent. Trust God, and enter into peace with Him through Christ. Have faith in the hope of the free gift of eternal life.

Romans 6 builds on the conclusion of the doctrine of the law of grace, and the implications for that liberty which we have in Christ. That we are no longer dead in sin with the judgment against us in unrighteousness, but born again a new man in the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ. Having proven this, that we are justified before God by faith, and standfast in His grace, what then? Shall we sin that grace may abound? If it glorified God to be forgiven our sin, would it be to His glory that we sin all the more? (Again, as some slanderously reported about the apostles, and those who continue this smear today, calling the glory of God "cheap grace" and "a license to sin") Again, God forbid. How should we, that are dead to sin, love any longer therein? We are free, in Christ, that when we are baptized as believers, it is into death with Christ, just as when we rise up from the water, it is a picture of our rising with Him into eternal life. Even so, we should walk in newness of life. If we are picturing the image of Christ in our baptism, death, burial and resurrection, then our old man, our sinful nature after the flesh should be considered nailed to the cross with Him. That the body of sin might be destroyed. Being dead in Christ we are risen with Him, and risen, death has no more dominion over Him, or us through Him. We are dead to sin but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Paul is really hammering this point home because it is not automatic that we who are saved turn from our sins. That the new man's presence doesn't preclude the old man's lusts of the flesh from warring in our members. Our eyes and tongue betray us. Our feet are swift to sin. If we automatically became holy by our salvation, this wouldn't have to be taught us, and it wouldn't be given us as a reminder in nearly every epistle. If we were given to "show fruit" to prove we are saved, as Lordshippers and other hypocrites suggest, it wouldn't be necessary to explain the old man vs the new. Being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness. We are free to serve God being pardoned by His grace. To work for righteousness, as its servant out of love for Him that justified the ungodly, while we were yet sinners. We who deserved death now are servants of life, unto God and should act like it. Note also in his appeal to walk in the new man, we are never told that we should lose the grace we standfast in. Rather, that we have our fruit unto holiness and the end everlasting life. We now earn rewards in the kingdom heaven, vs earning the wages of sin which is death. For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Gift vs wage. We do not earn gifts. A wage is debt owed. In sin, our debt is paid by death and hell, but in Christ we are given grace, a free gift, salvation and liberty that we may serve Him. And in that service we earn holiness, towards the righteousness of God, rewards. 1 Corinthians 3:9-15 For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building. According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble; Every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is. If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. We see here that as laborers for God, working as husbandmen in His vineyard, servants of His righteousness, that we will be judged as laborers, and earn rewards for our works. Each deed we do that is built up on the foundation of Christ will be judged by fire, and those of no spiritual importance will burn like wood, hay and stubble, but those of lasting impact, especially the salvation of souls, will be manifest as gold, silver and precious stones. And though some of our effort is burned by fire, as a loss, not being of real value, we ourselves are still saved, yet so as by fire. The same fire that reveals the fruit of our labors will be to us who believe a refining fire, but to them without hope, destruction in eternal torment. For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward. God repays. Be it the wages of sin with death or rewards in the kingdom to come.

Addressing the Jew, brethren after the flesh, those knowing the law, Paul continues his argument that the law is the ministry of death, while the gospel of grace is unto life. But to buttress the point, Paul uses the law to demonstrate how the law is made null by the death of Christ, just as a marriage is annulled by the death of the husband. The oldness of the letter is done away with for the newness of the Spirit. Paul is again dismantling the idea of salvation by the law. The same law that Judaizers sought to bring to the new believers of the Gentiles. The same law that dispensationalists claim was the means of salvation for the Jews, and that it will be implemented again. As if a widow should take her dead husband again as a spouse. Galatians 5 16 This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. 17 For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. 18 But if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law. 19 Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, 20 Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, 21 Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, 23 Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. 24 And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. 25 If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit. 26 Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another. 1 Corinthians 15 42 So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: 43 It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: 44 It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. 45 And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit. 46 Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual. 47 The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven. 48 As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. 49 And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly. 50 Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption. 51 Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, 52 In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. 53 For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. 54 So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. 55 O death, where is thy sting? And so, building on the implications of our faith, the law and grace, Paul comes to the matter of our flesh, in this world before the resurrection, but after our salvation and the quickening of our spirit in Christ. Christ, in whose death, we die also to the law, freed then to the Spirit, married to Him in grace. Just as the woman described by Paul is free from her marriage vows at the death of her husband, we are free from sin and death with Jesus. And baptism is a like figure representing this. We are born again, in the Spirit. But not in the flesh. That's the lively hope we have, Jesus being the first fruits of the resurrection with the same promise to us who believe. That we will shed this corruptible body for incorruptible. The dead in Christ and those that are alive and remain at His coming, all will receive glorified bodies that know not sin. Chapter 8 of Romans will delve a bit more into this, but then the question for Christians is; in the meantime, what? Our new man, inside, spirit quickened by the Holy Ghost, sealed unto the day of redemption, knows not sin. It can't, being dead to the law. For as Paul explains, with the commands of God to tell us what is righteous and holy, there is no sin. He says he was alive once without the law, we all have been. Innocent children who don't know there is a right from wrong, do no sin. But when the knowledge of the law comes, and they in the flesh choose sin, the spirit dies to the law. Had Adam and Eve not had the commandment in the garden, they wouldn't have sinned in eating the apple. Had the laws of God not come onto Noah and then Moses, showing us His light, we wouldn't know our flesh of the old man leads us to darkness. The law itself is holy and true. And being saved, our spirit is willing but our flesh is weak. The old man still reigns in our members. Our flesh. Sin takes advantage of the law to show we lust in the flesh. Not that the law is evil, but we are. And like Paul, we do what we would not. We don't do what we should, despite wanting to. Without the newness of spirit we can't. For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not. As Jesus admonished the Apostles who were to keep watch as He prayed at Gethsemane, who fell asleep multiple times; Matthew 26:41 Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. It is important to know as a Christian, we are not perfect and sinless perfection isn't possible in our flesh. We all are sinners. We all deserve death and Hell but in Christ we are given His righteousness that we may be given justification before God. We sin, every day. But unlike the unsaved (which we were and should never forget the mercy we were shown, that we not think too highly of ourselves before the unsaved), we have the Spirit within us, and our own spiritual new man cries out to do good. But to the flesh, we are called to sin. What do we do? The Bible says if we walk in the spirit, feeding that new man, praying, studying scripture, going to church to be edified with the congregation, practicing true religion which is care for the poor, widows, fatherless, and most importantly sharing the Gospel with others that they may be comforted as we are by the promise, that the flesh becomes easier to mortify. To subdue. And, if we walk in the spirit we will also learn more about the holiness of God and His law, and in that knowledge come to see more things that are sinful. It is impossible to feed the new man with the things of God and not come to be convicted by the Spirit that things we thought not sin, actually are. But the great mystery of that dichotomy is that, despite the knowledge increasing our occasion for the flesh, we have the grace and power to escape from it. 1 Corinthians 10:13 There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. It is a refining process. One that removes thorns in our flesh we didn't know we had. This process of sanctification makes us more valuable vessels for God's will. It makes us better able to serve His Gospel. To have real fruits of the spirit. To win others to Christ, and further, to instruct and guide babes in Christ to maturity that they may be able to better serve God as well. This is the point of our Christian walk. It's not about you. It's not about finding yourself, or happiness or whatever new age and pagan selfish nonsense our flesh comes up with to lead us away from the spirit. We are saved already, and justified by the perfect work of Christ Jesus that we believe on. Rejoice. In His blood we have overcome. Our sanctification isn't about salvation. It is about becoming acceptable tools in God's shed. To be workmen who aren't ashamed. Good and faithful servants. O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? But most aren't believers and just bring filthy rags before the judgment seat of Christ, saying Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? And He will say to them, depart from me I never knew you. And so we wait patiently for the reward of eternal life, and glorified bodies that know not sin. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Romans 7, like most of the chapters leads directly into the next, the theology building upon each argument. Chapter 7 sets up the arguments made in 8, just as it rests on the foundation of the previous chapters. We are blessed that we have the whole word of God. Preserved for all time. That we may study to be approved. Comparing scripture with scripture. Because, by doing so we are given power over our flesh that we may restrain the lusts of our members, and do what's right. That we may have access to the fruit of the Spirit; Galatians 5:22-23 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. Just because we are saved doesn't mean that we will do good. Just as it doesn't mean we will stop sinning. Paul, who many consider the greatest Christian of all time for his understanding of God's word, writes of himself here in Romans chapter 7; But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. Writing in 1 Timothy 1:15 This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. Paul has for the past 7 chapters laid out the factual, Biblical case for conditional election, that we must believe to be saved, starting with the testimonial of God in creation, the lack of excuse by the unbelieving, the refusal to accept the knowledge of God of the reprobate, and the surety of our salvation of placing our faith in God's promise. Here, tying together these themes, he speaks of the carnal mind that the saved still have, exhorting the saved by faith to live in the spirit, not the flesh, because in that righteousness given us is adoption into the promise; we become heirs of Christ, we call out to our Father. In verse 9, he makes it clear that this is a conditional state of being. You aren't adopted without first believing. Then, Paul begins building onto this foundational theme of being adopted as sons in the spirit by explaining how God's foreknowledge that we (the saved) then be used to His purpose. (Note the order of operations in verse 29, Calvinists reverse it, and thus get none of it). The glory of being joint heirs with Christ, in Christ. The hope, which is an earnest expectation for the thing we believe to come (not a long-shot wish as some use the term) being shared with all of creation, waiting for that kingdom to come. That we are blameless to charge by any because we are justified in our faith in Christ. That, in faith, none can stand before us as God gives us all things, according to His will. Having laid out the first faith and its terms and rewards, Paul is making the case to the saved to understand what their faith has opened them up to, what God's gifts mean to us if we now walk in the spirit, quickened by the Holy Ghost, that all things are for good to us for loving God, if we simply trust further in the word of God, building faith upon faith. By putting "predestinated" first, and to mentally add "to believing," and making the election unconditional of anything but God's whim, they deny the purpose of the Gospel, and make the arguments made by Paul to the saints in Rome who have already been saved, to now walk in the spirit, foolishness. Sanctification becomes a post hoc form of works salvation, wishing it be enough. Rather than giving hope, it cruelly removes it. Wicked "Ok, I think I understand the concepts. We are all totally depraved because God wants us to do all manner of evil, and he's gonna punish us for the sins he made us do, but some of us, if we try real hard to not sin might get his attention, and be given faith, so we have to try to make him our Lord in all things, and if we fail it just means we aren't elect and burn anyway? Yeah? And the works aren't giving good news of the free gift, but being fruit inspectors of others. Wow, this sounds... HORRIFYING" Also "you can lose your salvation" heresy is destroyed by this chapter and these verses (and by the rest of the Gospel and Epistles). THAT is the perseverance we have in Christ. Not hoping that we do the works well enough throughout our life, complete enough and to the satisfaction of the various "fruit inspectors" waiting to lay charge against us.

Quick exercise Romans 9 I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost, 2 That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart. 3 For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh: 4 Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; 5 Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen. 6 Not as though the word of God hath taken none effect. For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel: 7 Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children: but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called. 8 That is, They which are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God: but the children of the promise are counted for the seed. Paul is undeniably talking about the nation of Jews, his brethren after the flesh. According to a "reformed theologian" in my chat, Paul suddenly shifts gears to talk about individuals in the context of salvation, in the following verses. Let's look: 9 For this is the word of promise, At this time will I come, and Sarah shall have a son. 10 And not only this; but when Rebecca also had conceived by one, even by our father Isaac; Well, it seems Paul is continuing his thoughts about who the child of promise is. It's the same topic, Jews after the flesh vs adopted children of the promise. 11 (For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;) 12 It was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger. This is not a verse about a different doctrine. He's still talking about the physical nation of Jews compared to children of faith, and the promise. There's nothing to indicate a transition. There's nothing about salvation mentioned. It's for the purpose of showing that relationship reflected in the elder serving the younger. 13 As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. Again. Same topic. We know the context because it's quoting Malachi, which was about the nations of Israel and Edom. 14 What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid. So all that is about the physical nation. 15 For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. 16 So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. 17 For the scripture saith unto Pharaoh, Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth. 18 Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth. The question is "Is there unrighteousness with God?" Paul says no, God forbid. Why? Because as he told Moses He will have mercy on who he will. And harden some. The context isn't salvation, it's still the Jews. If God hardens them that refused Christ, it would be consistent with what He told Moses. 19 Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will? 20 Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? 21 Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour? 22 What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction: Israel of the flesh are who that's talking about. We know it is because in the next sentence; 23 And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory, 24 Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles? The Jews and also the Gentiles. As a group. 25 As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved. My people... 26 And it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people; there shall they be called the children of the living God. The children of the living God. Who are not my people... 27 Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved: 28 For he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth. 29 And as Esaias said before, Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha. 30 What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith. 31 But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness. It's entirely about Israel as a people. Not individuals. There is no transition. It doesn't go back and forth. The chapter isn't about salvation. It's about Paul's brothers after the flesh whom he wishes would believe and be saved. 32 Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone; 33 As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed. Whosoever... That's everyone, unlimited. Believeth on Him... That's the conditional clause for election Calvinism and "reformed theology" are foolish and unbiblical and rely on people knowing more about what the arguments of men are than the scriptures they torture to make them.

Romans 9:1-3 I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost, That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart. For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh... Paul, having just laid out the impossibility of losing one's salvation in chapter 8, immediately makes this appeal. That he would give up his own salvation if it meant his kinsmen after the flesh would be saved. Chapter 9 of Romans, like 11, is the most abused by dispensationalists (and greatly by Calvinists), to justify their doctrine. But it is important to look at them in the context of what's already been established. Paul has already made clear that there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles, all are under sin. All are judged. All need salvation. That salvation comes from faith alone without works of the law. That the same faith that justifies a Greek justifies a Jew. That Abraham received the promises by faith and they were to his seed, singular, the Lord Jesus Christ. That God predestinated that all who believe in Christ are to receive this promise. And it can never be lost or taken away by any means. The point being raised is to rebuke Judaizers, laying claim that new Christians had to adopt the law to be saved and that Jews, because of their having the law, were superior to the Gentiles. They had the advantage of the oracles of God, Paul concedes, but that was unto death, not the spirit of faith which is to life. But this saddens the "Apostle to the Gentiles." We know that in Acts, Paul makes multiple efforts to preach to the Jews. He gets run out of synagogues and towns in his early ministry for doing so. And he eventually shakes the dust. Acts 18:5-6 And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ. And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles. But in his epistles, Paul often tries to argue to the Jews the truth of Christ, from the very scripture they read in the temple and synagogues, showing how Jesus is the Christ promised. The Messiah. The fulfilment of those promises made to Abraham and David. How He was pictured in the Levitical laws and taught of all the prophets. Being a learned Jew, an Israelite of Benjamin, a Pharisee who studied under the chief Pharisees, Paul was frustrated that his countrymen couldn't see what was blinding obvious to him in the Spirit. And here, in the opening to chapter 9, he lays out his regret and frustrations. Paul writes of his kinsmen after the flesh; Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen. This is where the dispensationalist will stop reading. "See they were given the adoption and the glory and the covenants. Case closed!" But in truth this is just a restatement of the beginning of Romans 3; What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God. And, as there, we see that advantage was worthless if they did not believe; What then? are we better than they? No, in no wise: for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin...For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also: Seeing it is one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith. Therefore we already have seen this argument played out. We already know the actual disposition of the Jew relative to the Gentiles, and to God. So, we continue on and see Paul deal directly with this same conclusion; Not as though the word of God hath taken none effect. For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel: Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children: but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called. That is, They which are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God: but the children of the promise are counted for the seed. This could not be clearer. Paul states it 3 times in 3 different ways. The children of the flesh are not the children of God. They are not all Israel which are of Israel. There can be no confusion. It isn't open to private interpretation. Paul in the Spirit makes it crystal clear that, despite his own wishes that his brethren after the flesh would be his brethren after the Spirit, they aren't. They oppose themselves, and blaspheme. They are judged by the law of death. By the letter and not the spirit. Without faith they are condemned. For this is the word of promise, At this time will I come, and Sarah shall have a son. And not only this; but when Rebecca also had conceived by one, even by our father Isaac; (For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;) It was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger. As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. This is Paul using the scriptures again to back his point, that the promise is of one. Given to Abraham, passed to Isaac, and then given to Jacob over Esau, despite Esau being the heir according to the law, as the oldest. It was always to one, to the seed, and that seed is Jesus Christ, and the promises and blessings fall on Him. He is the inheritor of it, as Isaac was from Abraham. And we who believe are, as Jacob was over Esau, the younger over the elder. Just as the believing Gentiles have been made heirs to the promise over the unbelieving Jews. Esau, who is Edom, who sold his inheritance for a bowl of pottage, wasn't hated by God. He was blessed. But the people who are Edom, the nation he birthed were eventually destroyed. When Malachi wrote the scripture Paul is quoting, it wasn't the man it was the nation. The burden of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi. I have loved you, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us? Was not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob, And I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the dragons of the wilderness. As Obadiah prophesied; Obadiah 1:18 And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau for stubble, and they shall kindle in them, and devour them; and there shall not be any remaining of the house of Esau; for the LORD hath spoken it. Again, Paul is teaching this idea of what some people call replacement theology, by using the example of Jacob and Esau. He isn't bringing a new doctrine about predestination or being chosen in the womb. He isn't comparing unbelieving Israel to Jacob but to Esau. To Edom. Because it is a like figure to what is happening in his time with the election in Christ of Gentiles over the Jew.

Paul begins by expressing his sorrow that his kinsmen, the unbelieving children of Israel after the flesh are cut off. That they have had the Kingdom taken from them, as Jesus said. Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. This is pertaining to the seed, the promise of Christ, knowing Edom would be made desolate, the election is of Jacob/Israel, that Jesus would come from Judah, the root of Jesse, from the throne of David. That all are chosen in Christ, not unto belief. Not given faith by God, but predestined in Christ to be given the blessing, the promise and the inheritance, to all who believe. And so God, in His wisdom, shows mercy to who He will show mercy. And compassion on whom He will. And harden the hearts of those fitted for destruction. All to His glory. Because as we have established; the righteousness of God is revealed both in His mercy towards us, and the love that gave His only begotten Son for us, but in His wrath against those who hold the truth in unrighteousness. And so, as Paul in the Spirit testifies, he wishes that his brothers after the flesh would come to the faith. But they are cut off. Just as Esau become Edom, and they were made desolate, Jews were cut off and consumed. Is God's judgment unrighteous? No. Is His word unfaithful? Again no, for a remnant remains, those saved by faith as is Paul, and to believing Jews whom he writes to in Rome. But the unbelieving Jew, hearts hardened, had their chance, and their destruction served to show the glory of God. For the scripture saith unto Pharaoh, Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth. Just as Pharaoh was made reprobate, so too are the Jews after the flesh. God's promises were kept in Christ. The remnant is in Christ. All Israel was saved, in Christ. Both Calvinism and Zionism are about making the promises and the blessings, the election and our shaping to God's purpose, about man. They are special boys.
