They will be posting their PR's and sharing their routines for massive gainz, while using porn, having a profile on tinder, and laughing at skinny incels who are at least pure of this wickedness.

I owe you a 1 Corinthians 7, "Married couples and Incels stay winning" Bible study, but we have a few (very) minor crisis to deal with. (And yes, I believe Satan behind them but I have no fear and grand scheme, it's petty annoyances because it's all he could muster against us. Prayers appreciated but no concern needed. We are on the winning side, thanks to Jesus) Paul, having dispensed with the rebuke, moves on to answer questions asked pertaining to those who have taken a vow of virginity, and then marry, have they sinned? Paul gives a wide ranging answer, and speaks of his own situation as well as marriage in general. Much of this advice is given from Paul, not speaking in the Spirit and he says so repeatedly, yet its inclusion and his final judgment to say he believes he has the Spirit of God on this, tells us it's God's word. It would be good if Christian man stayed a virgin, volcel, if they have such a gift from the Holy Ghost. But as most don't, and fornication is wicked and self-destructive, God has given us marriage. Due benevolence in this verse is regarding marital relations in the bedroom. If we are married, we are not our own flesh, but our spouses. To withhold relations with our spouses for reason other than brief periods of fasting, is defrauding our spouse. If you are going without intimacy for a brief period, agreed upon, consummate at the end least your incontinence, that is your being hornt-up, leads you to sin. Paul's gives the same advice to widows and the unmarried. Regarding divorce, Paul echos the scriptures, that a wife out away shouldn't remarry. He says that being unequally yoked, married to a non-believer, isn't sufficient grounds for divorce, but that if they leave and break the marriage vows over your faith, it is no sin to the believing spouse to be divorced. Our behavior and expression of faith in how we carry ourselves in the marriage is the strongest testimony to our unsaved spouse, and to our children. Paul, as the Apostles agreed upon in Acts, then speaks again on the circumcision issue, that it's nothing. Paul continues this side note, away from matters of marriage and celibacy, explaining how we must remember that regardless of our station, servant or master, we are God's, bought with a price, in Christ's blood, and so to remember, as a slave we are free in Christ. As a master, we are bound to God in Christ. Where we are called and what state we are in, is immaterial, and this goes for marriage as well. Either way, we are to live for God, as His. As to the virgin by vow, if they can't keep it, but are in love and get married, that's ok. Better to do this, in Paul's opinion than break the vow, and lose your virginity in fornication. He briefly mentions that in taking the virgin as wife, she's gonna have a bit of discomfort, but I spare you. Paul points out that these worldly cares of marriage and sex are brief in the scale of things measured in eternity. So not to worry so much about it, but serving the Lord. Paul finishes this chapter giving his preference that the unmarried virgins stay this way, to better serve God and the church, as he has, but he understands that's not for everyone. Note this is not to justify celibate priests, as by Paul's own writing, they aren't qualified to be bishops or deacons. (Husband of one wife, father of children) "Muh nuns" perhaps. All the single ladies...

In chapter 8 of First Corinthians, Paul gets into an often misunderstood doctrine. It's regarding eating food sacrificed to idols in heathen temples and homes, but it can apply to many other things in our Christian life. Things that aren't explicitly sin, in our knowledge and understanding of both our salvation, and the liberty that's in Christ, and of God's law in our conscience, which is bulwarked by the Spirit. As Paul says, we who are saved should understand that there is only one living God, and that idols are dead, made by man and have no power, being graven images. But the unsaved man or a babe in Christ, still superstitious of the things of this world, may stumble or be snared by seeing our eating of the sacrifice. Knowing it's nothing but meat, and the pagan practice silly and stupid, we could, in good conscience eat the sacrifice and laugh at how silly the pagans are and give all blessing and honor to God. But if that thing done in our knowledge were to cause the weaker man to sin or not come to the faith of the one true God, we shouldn't do it. It is offensive. This can apply to the circumcision. Maybe to other practices not forbidden by the scriptures, or that is sinful only in intent of the heart, not in the doing for one at liberty. I would list a few things, but in doing so I risk offending a weaker conscience. Ultimately, we should be mindful of others and their infirmities, and seek to build up their faith, not please ourselves. Galatians 5 Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. 2 Behold, I Paul say unto you, that if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing. 3 For I testify again to every man that is circumcised, that he is a debtor to do the whole law. 4 Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace. 5 For we through the Spirit wait for the hope of righteousness by faith. 6 For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love. 7 Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth? 8 This persuasion cometh not of him that calleth you. 9 A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. 10 I have confidence in you through the Lord, that ye will be none otherwise minded: but he that troubleth you shall bear his judgment, whosoever he be. 11 And I, brethren, if I yet preach circumcision, why do I yet suffer persecution? then is the offence of the cross ceased. 12 I would they were even cut off which trouble you. 13 For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another. 14 For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. 15 But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another. 16 This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. 17 For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. 18 But if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law. Galatians 5 is a parallel passage of this idea. We are free of the bonds of sin and the law in Christ, yet though all things are lawful to me, not all things are convenient. Not all things edify. The liberty we have is freedom to serve others in Jesus name without fear of Hell, but fear of God. With trembling, knowing where we'd be without grace. Fear of the Lord here is understanding the nature of our salvation, and how by not offending others, hindering their belief or subverting their Christian walk, we honor Him for the gift we've received.

The sudden turn in chapter 9, to address another matter of contention among the church makes me believe we are seeing Paul's point by point replies without seeing the questions he's replying to. But we can discern the meaning as we go, based on his answers. Here, some had questioned his apostolic credentials. Paul makes the case that despite his not pressing the matter to not offend and to make the Gospel known, he was within rights to ask for a wage and support from the congregation. That other apostles, as is right, earn a wage for their service. A tithe of carnal things of meat and drink like the priests of the temple, in exchange for the spiritual things they bring to the believers. He notes that Peter and the others are paid enough to support a wife and yet he and Barnabas, being single, didn't ask for the same, even though they were within their rights to. Those whom the Lord has ordained as ministers of the word, evangelists and pastors, preach the Gospel and so should live of the Gospel. Paul says he'd rather die than any man could accuse him of doing it for his own glory. We know that Paul was a tentmaker by trade, and worked with Aquila and Priscilla in this during his ministry. Paul says he is compelled to preach the Gospel, a feeling many of us have the further we get into the word, building our faith. We will see later in this epistle that some are "addicted to the ministry of the saints." Working in the church, edifying the faithful, sharing the Gospel. Would that we all have this addiction. Paul makes the point that his sacrifice of doing without to service of the ministry is done willingly. That his reward from God would come only because he does it of his own free will and liberty. This is the same for all works we do. We are free in Christ from death and Hell. We are liberated from the law, being washed clean. Any work we do thereafter isn't by force or fear but love. It's a sacrifice to serve, and laborers are paid by the fruit of their labors, as God's law states. Even the oxen. Those working to gain or maintain salvation are working against their will, for a price, and so the reward they get is the bondage of having to be slaves to the whole of the law. It's not sacrifice, it's selfish, and they perish for it. Paul continues, explaining that in service to the Gospel he willingly suffers all things that it may spread, and that he may be a partaker of the glory of God. He compares this service to an athlete, temperate in all things, training his body for a prize, a corruptible crown of laurels, while we do it for the incorruptible crowns of life given to us as reward in Heaven. He tells us to run to win. To fight, not shadow boxing, but fully engaged. Keeping our bodies under subjection to be able to be blameless to others as we present ourselves as God's people, and spread His good news of grace. That we not be hypocritical and backslidden to those we seek to win to the Lord.

Skipping ahead, as I read through 1 Corinthians this morning, headed to chapter 12 and the meat of the word regarding spiritual gifts, which is the purpose of this study, I wanted to touch on chapter 3 and chapter 10, just to finish off the point about what we learned in Numbers, and how it is for our benefit. Paul in the Spirit gives us the rundown of events that should be familiar to us having just finished reading it, and how all those examples for our admonition. And understand that our sanctification is for other's sake. We are separated unto the Gospel, that to all men we can be fitted to win them to Christ. Not in compromise and enabling sin, but as an example. That even things we know aren't sinful for us in the Spirit, having a good conscience before God in Christ and not a heart of Idolatry, or covetousness or murmurings, we abstain from it if by any means it leads a weaker man to reject Christ, or brings a weaker brother to sin in his heart, and lead them astray. Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. God speaks to us through His word, not giving new revelations to men. From such turn away

Paul continues his teaching to the Church at Corinth, and reminds them all that their forefathers were baptized unto Moses by the passing through the sea, and by the cloud that followed them as they wandered, the Rock that provided water, a symbol of Christ. And despite this, those saved out of Egypt were backslidden and committed wickedness, as all sin common to man tempts us all. They committed idolatry and idleness, with the golden calf (Exodus 32). They were tempted by the daughters of Moab and led to slaughter by their fornication (Numbers 25). They complained of the Mana and were struck down by the fiery serpents (Numbers 21). They murmured and complained against Moses' leadership, and the gainsaying of Koreh was met with instant death (Numbers 16). These Israelites were faithful to leave captivity, made free by that faith, baptized of a sort, led to the promised land by a cloud and a pillar of fire, fed from the corn of Heaven, they did eat angel's food, and were given the water from the Rock, that was like the living waters of Christ. They ate of the communion the meat, and drank the common drink, and yet they fell to fornication and idolatry, and God did punish them for it, just as believers who are backslidden and castaway are punished by God. For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. (Hebrews 12). Paul says these examples are lessons given us by God to learn His ways. God will not allow us to be tempted beyond our ability to resist, but it is up to us to resist, by the path God provides us to escape each test and temptation. That way of escape is found in our knowledge of the word. By how much time we spend in it. It's why Paul uses examples of scripture to reason with the Corinthians, it's why he reminds us of the lessons from God's word. If you are facing sin, as thorns in your heart, and you want to be rid of it, or if you are engaging your lusts of the flesh or cares for the world, you will find relief and understanding from God, being in His word. It's the truth. The closer you get to Him the more clear your path becomes and the fewer snares and stumbling blocks there be. Now Paul having established this, gets to the heart of the matter; eating sacrifices. As he's already said it is nothing to a Christian, knowing that the gods they are sacrificed to are just dead stone and wood. And knowing that all things are fine for us to eat as blessings from God as long as we acknowledge that. Again all things are lawful to us, but not all things edify others. And just as we sit in common with our Brothers and sisters in Christ and are told, by Jesus, on those occasions that when we break the bread and drink the wine we are to remember him, Paul says that by being partakers in this, we shouldn't be partakers of the meat sacrificed unto idols. That although we could do it, there are reasons why we shouldn't. He draws the analogy between the communion of saints, the Lord's supper, symbolic act when we come together and bless the food we consume together in God's name, in remembrance of Jesus, we are like the levitical priests who partook in the sacrifice of the altars in the Old Testament. And where Christ died once for all men, the sole propitiation for our sin, we partake in the food and drink God has provided us in remembrance of him and that sacrifice. And if we so partake, how does it look to other people whether they not be saved yet, or maybe babes in Christ, and they see us sit down at the table of idolatry to partake in those sacrifices? And so we do not exercise our Liberty at the expense of others. We do not seek our own comfort and fortune, we should seek others. We should be pleasing to all men in service of the gospel. We should do without rather than offend. This aspect of Christianity, that we are both free from all sin in the blood of Christ, and the knowledge that most things people think of as sin is a sin of the heart, because what goes into the mouth doesn't defile us, but what comes out. And out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. It is our intent, it's the adultery we commit in our hearts. And the knowledge of that is the Liberty we have in Christ. But it is not a license to sin. Because if what we do in our Liberty hampers another person's ability to believe or come to faith, or makes them struggle with the loss of their own flesh which turn to sin when exercised by them, then we must do without. This is what Paul means by pleasing others. This is what loving your neighbor entails. We are to be weak to those who are weak that they might be strong. And unlike the Jew who is contrary to all men, we are to be agreeable with all men in God. That's not going along with earthly sins and lusts of the flesh, but it's being cognizant of how our actions on matters can be a snare or a stumbling block for others. There are many who criticize this as being a Christcuck. That it is this a good natured Christian impulse to not offend that has left us defenseless against those who would subvert and destroy us. That this is a slave mentality of sorts. But that's not what's being said here at all. When we act agreeable to others to win them to the gospel that is not the same as accepting wickedness in our presence or going along with these abominable people when they seek our destruction. Being mature enough in the word to understand the distinction is one of the goals of consuming the word daily. Rightly dividing the word of God. BTW if I wasn't clear, there is no sacramental aspect to this, no Lord's supper as it were, it's the meals we have together with other believers we're to remember Jesus, with the breaking of the bread and the drinking of the juice of the vine, or anything else that we eat together. The idea of a real presence, or the Hocus pocus of a transubstantiation, is neither implied nor even hinted at. When two or three are gathered together in his name Jesus is there. He's always present. Our taking the time to remember him and thank God for the food, and acknowledging Christ's sacrifice for us it's just something we should do when we gather together. People turning Christianity into a weird cannibal cult are the worst The physical things of the Old Testament, and honestly all of creation, are there to teach us the spiritual things of the New Testament. The better Testament. People who have not the spirit, cannot discern spiritual things and apply everything to the flesh. All their doctrines revolve around the worldly. They cannot rightly divide the word of God. 1 Corinthians 3:16-23 Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are. Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness. And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are your's; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are your's; And ye are Christ's; and Christ is God's. The gifts of the Spirit also come with responsibility, that we are the temple of God, and to defile it brings physical destruction. We see this clearly in the Book of Numbers, which we recently studied; how those that defiled the temple, or offered strange fire, were destroyed. That God admonished Moses to let the children of Israel know that they must cleanse themselves before coming before the Tabernacle. A picture of us now, in this present time a temple of the Spirit of God. How fornication, covetousness, sedition, whoredoms after strange Gods, complaint and sowing discord and fear among the brethren, the touching of disease and death, which is a like picture of sin...these things defile the temple, and him shall God destroy.

I've gone into detail about the first half of this chapter before and made my opinion about the second half known even yesterday, but chapter 11 is one of contention for a lot of people. The first half of the chapter, regarding "coverings" and shorn and shaven heads, is about hair and hair length. Women are to have long hair, not cropped short. Men are to have short hair. It is a shame for a man to have long hair just as it is an abomination for him to wear that which pertaineth to a woman. Some take this that women must wear a veil or head scarf in church. It's such a non-issue that the doctrine is again one where if a woman thinks she should, it's of not a big enough deal to argue with her. Just like the eating of meat vs herb, it's up to those of us in grace to not quibble about what in the end is nothing. The primary doctrine about men and women being made of God, and the order of who is put over whom, with God as the head, is what's important here. As for the second half, I point that "as often as ye eat and drink" give blessing and remembrance of Jesus. Simple as. The Corinthians appear to have some showing up when they gather who are in fornication and there for their gluttony, not in the spirit of the Lord. How various NT churches decide to engage in a Lord's supper together is really not important, so much the spirit by which it is done. Some do it in honor of the day leading to His death burial and resurrection. Some do it weekly. Some do it every meal they have at church or at home. I tend towards that, at least in the blessing and remembrance. What isn't good doctrine is placing more in the physical eating and drinking than the spiritual application. Or placing it as a source for grace and salvation. The Catholic version of this and the Protestant spin offs have at their heart the wrong motives spiritually, and so eat and drink damnation unto themselves. As Jesus says in John 6, It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life. Those that heard and didn't understand this were offended and many disciples left from following Christ, because they took spiritual things literally, just as the Jews condemned Him for these "dark sayings." One of the problems with replacing the spiritual application of biblical principles and examples with rites and ceremony, carnal ordinances and diverse washings, and dietary laws and restrictions, is that, as the Bible demonstrates, these sacramental ordinances become a religion unto themselves. Just as the Old Testament which was a symbol of the Christ to come, eventually devolved into the Pharisaical religion practiced in Jesus day, Christian churches who put all their emphasis in these vain traditions of men, the pomp and circumstance, lose the spiritual aspect of what it represents. And in doing so run the risk of running into a damnable heresy where their ability to perform a ritual or the frequency with which they do is tied directly into their salvation. The lesson of God's word should be for us to understand the spiritual nature of our eternal lives rather than the limited and short nature of our corruptible flesh. All things in creation point to the spiritual lessons and are there for our edification and learning. All ritual and levitical practices were there to point us to the spiritual meaning. Meats for the belly and belly's for the meats, but our spirit and what is in our hearts is what we take with us when our flesh dies. That's where our sin is. And that's where our salvation is in the quickening of our inner man. As Jesus said it's not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of it. A man who's committed adultery in his heart, feels hatred to another, has sinned just as much as those who commit the act. It's why Jesus spoke in parables because there are those among us who cannot live in the spirit, but only in the flesh and so they cannot receive the things of God.

Romans 12 I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. 2 And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God. 3 For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith. 4 For as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office: 5 So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another. 6 Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith; 7 Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering: or he that teacheth, on teaching; 8 Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness. 9 Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good. By the Spirit of God that has baptized us into the body of Christ, a spiritual baptism, pricked of the heart and sealed by the promise and made a child of God, we become partakers of the gifts given every man, according to the purpose of God. The selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as He will. Paul, comparing the assembly of saints to a body, Christ as the head (both literally, as ruler and figuratively in this anatomical allusion), gives examples of the talents expressed by believers towards the edification of that body. Building up the church of believers. The Corinthians, who we know were prideful, set at variance over who it was that led them to Christ, tolerating fornication among them, worse than the unsaved Gentiles, eating meats given to idols, profaning the ordinance of blessing the cup and breaking the bread when they gathered, believing heresies among them, and coveting, resenting and lording over each other when it came to spiritual gifts. Paul throughout the epistle models the meekness and humility which each Christian should have, understanding that it is God through His Spirit that has granted us knowledge, understanding, to each a minister of the faith that we came to believe, and to each talents in growing the faith, building His church. In Romans 12, the Apostle uses the same formulation; For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith. This humility and understanding that we stand by the grace of God, not of ourselves, as part of a single body, is an appeal to be of one mind, one towards another. None thinking they are more important than another. This is the context in both epistles. But, as we know, many have taken 1 Corinthians 12, and wrest from that scripture, a different doctrine than the understanding we are all joined as one under Christ, and make it about the gifts themselves, and applying them as evidence of salvation, resulting in entire denominations acting as the yet-unrepentant Corinthians. Pentecostal denominations, Charismatics and the like, take this rebuke against Corinth, reinforced in Romans and elsewhere, and forge a blueprint for doctrines that aren't being taught by scripture. But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. The things of the Spirit are for others' profit. But if they are used as a sign of salvation, or holiness, as an indicator of individual righteousness and worse, prominence in the assembly, they aren't of any benefit at all, except to those who seek to be seen as better-than. Holier than thou. Paul gives examples of the gifts of the Spirit. Note these may be supernatural but aren't superpowers. This isn't a comic book. While some may be miraculous, they are by God, to His purpose. But most are simply talents as are divided among men severally, or individually; each in turn. Wisdom and knowledge, which we know are from the Spirit for all men, that the knowledge of how the world is and the understanding of what that knowledge means is a revelation of God. Even among the unsaved and profane, and true wisdom of this world comes from God, and His word, inspired, taught and reproved by the Spirit, through the righteous in Christ. Even when a depraved and reprobate person like Jordan Peterson or Deepak Chopra expresses some kernel of truth within their nonsense philosophies of men, it is from God and His word and the recognition of that truth in men is by revelation of Him through the Spirit, reproving the world. That we who are of Christ and partakers of the gift of eternal life, are able to study the word of God, and to know His will through scripture, receiving the spiritual things of God, we are given knowledge and wisdom. Walking in the Spirit, we are given that gift, that the natural man receiveth not. That is why Peter and John, uneducated and common men, were able to speak with such excellency of knowledge and wisdom: Acts 4:13 Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus. As Christ promised, the Comforter brings to remembrance all that He spoke, and understanding of all that the prophets gave witness to. This is a gift that we can all enjoy, by walking in the Spirit. By studying to be approved. By humbling ourselves to know nothing but Christ, and Him crucified. Comparing spiritual things with spiritual. Scripture with scripture. Letting God tell us His will; Hebrews 4:12 For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. But that knowledge and wisdom is not to put ourselves above other brethren, but to humbly serve them that they may grow in the same. 2 Timothy 2:15; Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. Approved unto God. Not justified among men. Not to be pridefully arrogant in knowledge, (and showing a lack of wisdom) by applying the wisdom of men to the things of God, as so many do. Internet theologians, special boys well versed in the vain philosophy and traditions of men, who through much learning of those rudiments of "muh church fathers" and "the reformers," or worse, doctrines of devils drawn from their own invention, ever learning but never come to the actual knowledge of the Truth. Remembering that, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another. And remembering that our purpose is to profit others. Will continue with the other examples listed here, and elsewhere in scripture, tomorrow. But don't miss the context and point of what the Spirit is teaching us, that none who are of Christ are any better than another. Those weak in the faith we should receive for their edification, and that being a blessing to others by our talents, we are blessed of them, and all of God. Being servants to the whole body, just as the hand serves the heart, and the lungs serve the brain, and the eye serves the less comely parts...that by their profit, to God is the increase. Just as Romans 12 outlines some of the gifts of the Spirit given severally by God to every believer according to His purpose, as part of the body of Christ, 1 Corinthians 12 provides a similar list, and for the same purpose; to rebuke those in an assembly who are set at variance one another, that they be of one mind. Not coveting what talents others may have, and not lording over others for the gifts God has bestowed upon you. That we all work as one body, under the head that is Christ. As we will see, this is the more excellent way that Paul is referring to. These passages are not about the gifts, but about the hearts of Christians regarding them. Many cannot help themselves, and see the admonition against thinking too highly of themselves or desiring what others have to gain prominence for themselves, and take it as a challenge instead. The heart of man is desperately wicked, after all. We see something along these lines play out in Acts 8:9-25; But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one: To whom they all gave heed, from the least to the greatest, saying, This man is the great power of God. And to him they had regard, because that of long time he had bewitched them with sorceries. But when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip, and wondered, beholding the miracles and signs which were done. Now when the apostles which were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John: Who, when they were come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Ghost: (For as yet he was fallen upon none of them: only they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.) Then laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost. And when Simon saw that through laying on of the apostles' hands the Holy Ghost was given, he offered them money, Saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost. But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money. Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God. Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee. For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity. Then answered Simon, and said, Pray ye to the Lord for me, that none of these things which ye have spoken come upon me. And they, when they had testified and preached the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans. Simon coveted the gifts bestowed by Apostles upon his brethren, and having had great prominence among them by trickery in his life prior to repenting towards Christ, believing the gospel, the sight of those who received genuine power to perform miracles was a snare. He tries to buy it and is promptly rebuked by Peter, because Simon's heart isn't right with God. It is that heart that these things are written unto us, that we can know that envy, strife and pride are sins of the flesh but have no part in the talents and gifts given us by God by the Spirit. To avoid these stumbling blocks and better serve as ministers of the body of Christ. So. Knowing this, the list of examples given by Paul becomes incidental to the overall message. But in some false churches, the list became primary doctrine, and this heresy took hold precisely because of these sins in the hearts of men. Wanting to feel powerful, special, better than. Given over to jealousy and vainglory. Coveting the attention and respect of persons given to those who are talented in some of the more prominent and manifest ways. And so you have churches that place the expression of "spiritual gifts," as a witness to the "faith" of the person holding them. Of how special God must think they are, and wanting that for themselves. Now, knowledge and wisdom are given every man his measure, by walking in the Spirit and study of the word, and from that the skill of preaching and teaching. And some will be puffed up, taking the gift of intelligence and time, studying to be approved by men, rather than God. They use their knowledge to gain respect and power of others. And they guard dispensing it, rather than giving it freely as it was given them. They make themselves feel superior to others, and often seek to control those that they impress, rather than edifying others with humility and longsuffering. Their heart isn't right. And some take their gifts for governance; organizational talents and judgement, and in pride make it about themselves, and their own power and prominence, not in glory to God. And many take their ability to prophesy, preaching with great oration, and using that to gain a following and preeminence among the brethren. The more comely parts thinking themselves better than the less comely but equally important parts. And the less comely, envying and resenting the comely. If a man with wisdom and skill in leadership and teaching can be subverted by their own sin into taking advantage, imagine what deviltry the less skilled can of invent. Lacking knowledge or wisdom, not diligently seeking the things of God to improve it, because that requires humility and self-discipline, they may focus on obscure doctrines, picked up third hand, that fascinate others and allow them to be beguiled. They become like a gnostic "master," dispensing this wisdom of men and the doctrines of devils, to lead astray silly women (and silly men). They are like Simon, and want to be considered special, and that is their avenue to achieve it. These sometimes are the type that subvert whole houses. Unsaved vipers and apostates, who become false teachers. But they often are just pathetic saved people, who can't appreciate the gifts given them and the opportunity to serve others, because of their insecurities and own hangups. This same impulse directs others to take the gift of prophecy, and not being great orators or filled with real knowledge and wisdom, they instead lean on the more sensational aspect of being a prophet; "seeing the future." Having "visions and dreams of what is to come," or extrabiblical revelations, claiming "God told me..." It is attention seeking nonsense. But it is easy and many with itching ears want to believe. And the opportunity to manipulate others into validating your self-worth becomes more important truth, or serving God. Many may start as a lie, impulsively told, and then rationalized away as they experience the positive attention they coveted. Some are under delusion, given by God that they may be revealed a liar. The working of miracles, particularly healing, is another. God works through the fervent and effectual prayer of believers, often to heal the sick or bring about a miraculous outcome to a seemingly desperate situation. In the case of the Apostles, those who had seen Christ risen, and been gifted accordingly to perform signs and wonders, the laying on of hands and the responsibility of growing the early church, the gift of healing was more than the hope of faith, but the power itself. And to those that were given it, like those around Samaria that Simon witnessed, worked miracles that the power of the gospel be made manifest, before the sealing of scripture. And so, the evidence of miracles in our lives, or those that we are told about by others, is real. I have witnessed healing and recovery, miraculous events by my own reckoning, impossible becoming possible with the only explanation being the grace of God. Usually subtle. Sometimes not, but hardly ever "flashy." Rarely so definitive that the skeptic could be convinced, but to the believers, it adds to our faith. To some on the fence, it may help convict them in the Spirit. But for the unscrupulous, those wishing to gain that prominence by the "gifts of the Holy Ghost," healing becomes an opportunity. Taking advantage of the desperate and brokenhearted. Performing flashy "miracles" of "healing," for filthy lucre's sake. To gain power over others with false hope. I believe that these "faith healers" are all Reprobate. I believe they are blaspheming the holy Spirit when they claim they are performing miracles by His power. I think it is as wicked as those who claim to be mediums, talking to the dead to take advantage of mourning souls. And it is incredibly easy to fake. Whether by the placebo effect, plants in the audience, the gullibility of the crowd. Those wanting to be part of something miraculous. And sometimes, it might be through devils. And when the frauds are exposed, it brings a bad report of the genuine power of God among the heathen. It shakes the faith of some and becomes a stumbling block to others. Remember, that regardless of anything else if you are saved and you have been blessed by the indwelling of the holy Spirit, you have been gifted with talents by God for the purpose of ministering to others and edifying the brethren. Use them. Not for yourself, not selfishly, but with a heart right towards Christ and to serve the purpose God graciously gave them to you. Pray for opportunities to bless others with them, in your family, church and community. Diligently seek the spiritual things of God, that He can better use you for His purpose. Tomorrow, God willing, we will look at the most abused, misunderstood and easily faked of the spiritual gifts; Speaking in tongues.

At the time of this writing, there were many Apostles and disciples who had been granted gifts of the Holy Ghost, and others who were blessed with talents and aptitude, though not as supernatural, were just as much a gift and made each believer a valuable member of their congregation, and tools for to be used by God. But remember, the Corinthians have envy and divisions among them, and it is no different when it comes to these things. Paul lays out the gifts and builds the case that each member, like parts of the body, is as important to the whole and none should act better than or covet, because the glory of the whole is unto God, and in Christ. In Chapter 13, Paul has a more excellent way for them, to understand that regardless of gifts, charity is more important. (But we will talk about that tomorrow). One note I would have to this, regarding speaking in tongues and the understanding of tongues, regarding the Charismatics and Pentecostals; the gift of languages given by the Holy Ghost in those times was to the understanding by people of other languages. Not babbling and shouting nonsense that no one can understand. Partakers of the gift could be understood by those who didn't speak Greek or Hebrew or whatever the one blessed with the gift spoke, and interpreters could understand foreign tongues. And this gift was for the spreading of the Gospel to the ends of the earth in those days. Not to make a show of it in a church, flopping on the floor like a fish.

Paul's more excellent way, as promised in chapter 12; charity. That regardless of the spiritual gifts we all have, or the special gift of the Holy Ghost some in those days were blessed with, it is the unfeigned love, given for no personal gain, but genuine and selfless, that is above all else, and is a faint reflection of the love God showed us by giving His Son that we may be saved, and the love Jesus showed us while we were still sinners, to give His life for us, and taste death and Hell for our transgressions. We usually use the basic definition of charity to mean giving something away to help others, alms. And that certainly can be a form of expression for charity, but it is not itself charity as we see in verse 3. Paul defines it by what it's not or what qualities it has. And its qualities are those of the love, the charity of God shown towards us, that Jesus teaches us in His sermons. So many do so much as a form of "charity" but for selfish purpose, or taking pride or accolades for it. Storing up hay and stubble without ever gaining rewards for it, because they do it in the wrong Spirit. IMO, works done to "earn" or keep salvation being the most selfish of all, and the least charitable. This chapter also parallels with James 2, and the "faith without works is dead, being alone" lesson. It's the true meaning. We may have faith enough to move mountains, as Paul says here, but if we have not charity it profits no one. When the Kingdom is here and established in Christ's reign, and then when we know all things and are as an adult to a child, the mysteries all solved, charity will remain, even as all our other things we placed importance in fade. We need to read the Bible in full context. Chapters and verses are there to make navigation of the word easier, but these are not stand alone concepts, but entire thoughts that span entire books. If we look back at chapter 12, we see how Paul is leading to the lesson of charity: That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another. And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it. Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues. Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles? Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret? But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way You see the charity is caring for the others in the church, sorrow for each members' sorrow, and joy for their individual success. Not coveting the gifts each may have. Edifying one another. In Chapter 14 we will see that it is the gift of tongues driving much of the contention here, given its prominence in Paul's epistle. Thus if someone preaches in tongues, even with the language of angels, they become as sounding brass and tinkling cymbals, it's useless without charity. We can know all things in scripture, and all knowledge can be show us, and of we aren't edifying others and given to love people, it's for nothing. It's the motive not the gift. Matthew 6 Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven. 2 Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. 3 But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: 4 That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly. Now, as to what abides and what fadeth away, we see it is our faith, the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, our hope, a well founded expectation of good that comes from faith, the expression of that trust and belief, and charity, the unconditional love that is God's love, magnified through us, that cares for others and seeks to build them up, even at our own expense. These are what endure in the Kingdom of God. Not tongues, various languages or soaring rhetoric, not preaching and prophecy, that fails and fades. Not knowledge, that is imperfect at best in our current state, seeing through the glass darkly. In the end, these gifts may have been blessings for the holder, and may have fed others faith, given them hope and built them up in charity, but they aren't in themselves eternal the way faith, hope and charity are. One more example of the charity we should have, one to another: Romans 14 Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations. 2 For one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs. 3 Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him. 4 Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand. 5 One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. 6 He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord; and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it. He that eateth, eateth to the Lord, for he giveth God thanks; and he that eateth not, to the Lord he eateth not, and giveth God thanks. 7 For none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself. 8 For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's. 9 For to this end Christ both died, and rose, and revived, that he might be Lord both of the dead and living. 10 But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. 11 For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. 12 So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God. 13 Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way. 14 I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean. 15 But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died. 16 Let not then your good be evil spoken of: 17 For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. 18 For he that in these things serveth Christ is acceptable to God, and approved of men. 19 Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another. 20 For meat destroy not the work of God. All things indeed are pure; but it is evil for that man who eateth with offence. 21 It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak. 22 Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth. 23 And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin. Brothers in Christ can be wrong on doctrine but right in the heart. That is they, in the same faith of the same promise, and born again in Christ, might feel something or another is sin, despite your knowledge that it is not. Don't let your faith and knowledge be a stumbling block or a snare for a brother, weaker in his faith and knowledge. But be charitable, and not endlessly disputing. For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature: And likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly, and receiving in themselves that recompence of their error which was meet.

Speaking in tongues is described in Acts as the miracle of the disciples present on Pentecost, going out to the crowds of the feast in Jerusalem, and giving the gospel to those gathered from every nation in their own tongues. Their languages. Judeans and Samaritans, who knew Aramaic, Greek. Hebrew, suddenly were speaking Parthian, and Mede, and Elamite, and Mesopotamian, and Phrygian, and Pamphylian, Egyptian, and Libyan and Latin, and a host of other languages, of all the scattered Israelites and others, gathered there that day. Prophesying the word of God and preaching the risen Christ. This gift of the Holy Ghost continued in the early church, as it grew and served as a sign that brought the gospel to every nation, tongue and kindred. The God who had divided the nations and confused the languages in Babel, uniting them through the miraculous gifts of speaking in, and as we see in Corinthians, understanding or interpretation. Allowing them to be understood and to understand, that the gospel would be preached. Even today, absent miracles but by the same grace, the same gift is given many who are quick studies in understanding languages, and given to allow the furtherance of the Gospel, bringing many to Christ. The men in the church of Corinth, blessed with the more suspense gift, were puffed up, showing off, in the church. This was not only causing contention within the church, but as Paul says, gave a bad report to those without, that they were all babbling madmen. He admonishes them in Chapter 13 to seek rather Charity, the unfeigned and gracious love of others. Their profit and welfare. Their edification. Not our own. And in the case of being able to speak in a tongue foreign to others, it serves no one but the speaker. Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal...For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries. But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort. He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church. This is the sum of what Paul is teaching. He uses the idea that even if he were to speak in the language of angels, if no one understands it, it is useless, even to the speaker. Paul is not saying that they are speaking the language of angels. It is a hypothetical exaggeration given for instruction. That some make an entire doctrine from that goes to show that those who wrest with scripture do so to their own destruction, because in the same scripture lays the context and the truth. Pride and wanting to seem more spiritual, more holy, more blessed by God, in the eyes of others, feeds the Pentecostal movement and its foolish doctrines of speaking in tongues, the inane babblings of fools. Of all the spiritual gifts, it's the easiest to fake. And when everyone present is afraid to call it out, they not only enable and encourage it, they'll even have some "interpreters" sharing the delusion and claiming they can understand the other person. Since it is not any recognizable language, and because the noises being made have no bearing of prophecy, because they're not preaching the word of God but their own infantile speech, edifying no one, It is in direct conflict with what Paul is teaching here in 1st Corinthians. It's to no one's benefit but the speaker. There's no charity in it, only pride and dishonesty. It is always amazing to me that the strong delusion people are under when they twist a small portion of scripture to serve their heresies, manages to fool others and bring them into the same delusion. But the natural man receiveth, not the spiritual things of God for they are spiritually discerned. And because they seek after the error of Simon the sorcerer, they don't know the spiritual things of God. They're blinded to them. In chapter 3, Paul had already chastened the church for being carnal in regards to these gifts; For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal. That's the attitude they had was not spiritual, after the manner of God. He calls them children. And not in an endearing way. And understand he's speaking to people who actually possess these gifts. People who are actually saved by the Gospel through faith by grace. How much worse are these that fake it in order to seem spiritual? How much worse are they who, not being saved, not understanding the gospel, having faith in themselves instead of faith in Christ Jesus? Simon, the sorcerer was saved. He took rebuke when Peter gave it. We see in the second epistle to the Corinthians that they too were corrected by Paul's letter. One of the signs of a saved person is their ability to be corrected from scripture, by the word of God, because the Spirit that inspired it and the Spirit that indwells us are in harmony, being one. God is not the author of confusion. But you'll find that regardless of what you show them, Pentecostals and Charismatics will refuse to repent of their belief. They will double down. They will accuse you of not being faithful for trying to pop the bubble of their delusion. And ultimately if you scratch the surface with them at all on doctrine, They will usually admit to some forms of work salvation. Or some odd heresy like oneness/modalism. That baptism is necessary for salvation. And a host of other weird doctrines. Since these movements are led by wicked people who are often seen grifting the elderly and the desperate, begging for money for fake faith healing, prayer cloths, and assortment of other con jobs, but yet are not bringing anyone to Christ, You can see how Jesus warning that we shall know them by their fruits is so valuable. We can know they are false teachers because of the number of souls they've misled on the basic simple gospel of God. 1 Corinthians 14:18-22 I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all: Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue. Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men. In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord. Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophesying serveth not for them that believe not, but for them which believe Just to reinforce this point; that the purpose of the 1st century churches having members who could speak or understand foreign languages was to be as a sign for the unsaved, that they may hear the Gospel and believe, knowing the power of God. This means that God's word can be translated into all languages and remain powerful and give faith and keep the same meaning. Even if phrased in the manner and custom of the language itself. All languages are of God. From Babel to today. The gift of speaking to others that they may be saved hasn't gone away. It just requires some effort. But the same Spirit works in us, that if we begin a good thing for the work of Christ, He is faithful to help us achieve it. If any man think himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord. In other words, if some claim to be better than, more spiritual than others, more "gifted" then this epistle should set them right that they aren't. That these gifts and whatever talent we have been blessed with by God are to be used in an orderly and decent manner, with charity towards all. Galatians 5:16-26 This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. But if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law. Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit. Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another. The gifts of the holy Spirit are for the edification of others and to the glory of God. The fruit of the Spirit works to edify those who walk in the Spirit. Love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance are the result of the Spirit working in us, as we seek the spiritual things of God. If we stay in His word, remain in prayer. And deny the flesh. We are rewarded with this peace and love towards others, patient and humble, desiring the profit of others more than our own; a charitable heart. This promise of God isn't only to those who have more excellent gifts, flashy talents, the more comely parts of the body of Christ. It is to all believers, even to those whose talents are being helpers. Ministers to the little things. And maybe more especially to them. One of the most overlooked and least coveted gifts discussed by Paul, being a helper, is arguably the most needful in a congregation. This goes along with the gift of governance. Being an organizer, as well as being a ready and willing helper, that those with other talents can achieve even more for God. I would like to explore this aspect of Christian life more in the next few days.

Paul continues his teaching to the Corinthians on spiritual gifts, having put in place the doctrine that we shouldn't covet and envy those who have received talents to the edification of the church that differ from ours, that all in the body serve the same head, that head being Jesus and through Him, the Father. Then making the case that being charitable, the love for others that God expressed to us, and Christ demonstrated on the cross, then we've a better gift than even those the Holy Ghost bestowed on many in this time. Specifically the ability to speak and understand foreign tongues, or languages. The Bible is clear that this is the meaning. Not the nonsense gibberish of the pentecostal heathen. No where in the Bible does the term "speaking in tongues" exist (unless you read one of the perverted modern versions that sow false doctrine with confusion so often). This gift is rather the use of those who can interpret or prophesy scripture to those who speak another tongue. Like the Apostles and disciples on Pentecost, who spoke the Gospel to those pilgrims from all over the world, in Jerusalem for the feast. They spoke to understanding, and it amazed the crowd and acted as a sign, bringing thousands to belief as they heard the word of God in their native language. Prophecy in the Bible is the preaching of scripture, and bringing the relevance of the word of God to the people. It is giving the Gospel to the unbelieving. It is teaching the law. It is relevant preaching to the building up of the church. It is the advice of proverbs taught at a mother's knee. It is the exhorting of the pulpit to the flock. And if any of this be done in a language none of the hearers understand, as Paul says in chapter 13, it is of sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. This goes for false religion that gives entire services in a dead language. It is to no one's edification but the speaker. This goes for the "You must return to the Hebrew! You must return to the Greek! God's word is impossible to understand in English!" nonsense of puffed up "scholars" who take pride in their private interpretation and sowing confusion among the people to show how learned they are. This goes to the Ruckmanites who take the preservation of the Word in the KJV to be a further revelation that is more perfect than the Greek and Hebrew, which is nonsense. Paul says that if you have a gift of knowing a language that can be used for interpretation to the person being reached with the Gospel then use it, but not to show off to the believers who cannot understand it, which seems the case in Corinth. As Pentecost showed us, God's word is powerful in any language, and in every tongue God, who is not the author of confusion can make His word known. Verse 26 he wonders how it is so many in Corinth are puffed up by claims of their own doctrines and revelations and psalms, and strange tongues, etc. They apparently were many among them who, in covetousness and pride were deceitfully inventing whole doctrines and aping gifts they did not have, or bragging about gifts they were given and wasting them. As for tongues, today we have the inspired Word of God, preserved by the Spirit, in English in the KJV. And we should be grateful that we need no one to tell us it's lingual meaning, as every word and term is defined in itself. There is no need to appeal to a concordance or other work of an unsaved man to explain to us the plain meaning of His scripture. Paul notes, and it appears to be an issue in Corinth, that women in the church are to remain silent, so as to no usurp the authority of their husbands, and to protect the hierarchy God created, as enumerated in Chapter 11. This is not to say women cannot prophecy at all. They are called to teach scripture to their children, to convert their unbelieving husbands with their chaste conversation. We have multiple examples of women giving the Gospel and being active in spreading the word. But in church, under the leadership of a man of God, the pastor, who has very specific qualifications listed in the pastoral epistles, they are to learn in silence, and in their questions to turn to their authority, their husbands or fathers, first. As Paul had previously mentioned, each member of the body is important to the goal of the whole, and the "more important" parts shouldn't be puffed up, as they have reliance on the "uncomely" parts that serve the same head. It isn't the role but the goal. And we each have a responsibility to that larger goal, giving God the glory and increase of His harvest. And all who serve that goal shouldn't take pride in their role but humble themselves, which is the larger theme of this letter to Corinth.

Acts 17:26-31 And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent: Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead. Repent of the ignorance of men worshiping idols to believe in the living God. Acts 3:12-21 And when Peter saw it, he answered unto the people, Ye men of Israel, why marvel ye at this? or why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk? The God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob, the God of our fathers, hath glorified his Son Jesus; whom ye delivered up, and denied him in the presence of Pilate, when he was determined to let him go. But ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you; And killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead; whereof we are witnesses. And his name through faith in his name hath made this man strong, whom ye see and know: yea, the faith which is by him hath given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all. And now, brethren, I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers. But those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled. Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord. And he shall send Jesus Christ, which before was preached unto you: Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began. They denied the Holy One, Jesus Christ and they and their rulers had Barabbas freed and had killed Jesus. Peter tells them that was hopefully done in ignorance but now they know better, repent of denying Jesus is the Christ that their sins be blotted out. Acts 2:14- But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and said unto them, Ye men of Judaea, and all ye that dwell at Jerusalem, be this known unto you, and hearken to my words: For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day.But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams: And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy: And I will shew wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and notable day of the Lord come: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved. Paul moves on to his next point; some among the Corinthians who doubt the resurrection, and he spells out the Gospel of salvation that if we believe, saves us. But those who don't believe in the resurrection of the dead, and the promise of Christ risen, then their belief is in vain. It's for nothing. The apostles and disciples who preached to them did so in vain. Those dead in Christ and sleeping, never coming back. Our efforts at sanctification and spreading the word ,waster and so we should be most miserable. Without this truth, we remain in our sins. Paul reasons with them that, in Adam, man's earthly nature of sin promised death, but in Jesus, the last Adam, and heavenly in nature, the spirit is quickened and we are given eternal life. Paul brings this truth to the end times application, answering the mystery of those alive at the coming of the day of the Lord. He describes the rapture, resurrection of the dead and transformation of those living, in a twinkling of an eye, in to incorruptible bodies. He compares this to a seed, that's dead and dried and sown, that grows its own body and so likewise are we, in death sown to be raised in a new body. That in those times Jesus will reign until all enemies defeated, death being the last so that none will die again and the kingdom then handed to the Father for eternity, amen. Paul mentions "they who baptized for the dead." This is an other, not "us" or "we." But what does it mean? I believe it may just be a restatement of the main argument against supposed Christians who deny Jesus rose from the dead and that there is no resurrection. They are baptized in Jesus' name, but if He were dead still, then why bother? Essentially the crux of the chapter. Closing out his epistle, Paul takes care of some housekeeping. We see he is collecting for the church in Jerusalem during a famine in the land, that we read about in Acts. These alms are often cited by Jews and "Christcuck" mockers (BIRM) who say passages like this or in Romans, regarding it is a "command" to all Christians at all times to give Jews money. Never mind it's an example of believers helping on another. Never mind it's a special case. Never mind the church at Jerusalem had Jews, Greeks, Samaritans, etc. It's a foolish line of argument. The house of Stephanas who are addicted to the ministry, gets that special mention. What an honor. If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha. "What in the heck does maranatha mean?! See you need to know Greek!" But of course it's Aramaic... And it's untranslated from the original Aramaic because it had become a Latinized word with a known meaning in English simply from this one verse. That meaning being, "Our Lord comes," or "Come, O Lord." The poetic use with anathema, a clear meaning English word, and known use had the translators leave it in, as is.
