Paul writes his second epistle to the church at Corinth, approximately a year following the first. As we know from Acts, his plan to go to them was derailed, slightly and instead, elders of the church went to him as he traveled, and so he writes with some apology in his greeting. That the troubles he came to in his travels that prevented him from going to them, were actually blessings. He acknowledges the truth of the Gospel is in them, as it is in him, and that of the hope of eternal life we also receive the comfort of God in the Holy Spirit. The message, that in our tribulations and troubles, we have comfort, given by God's grace, and in that comfort, the ability to give the same comfort with grace an understanding to others in need. Thus, his tribulation and that which the churches experience are a gift, that gives us consolation and salvation from trouble, that we may provide the same to others. He reminds them that if our faith in God is to the hope of the resurrection and eternal life, then there's nothing we can't place on God to deliver for us. This is the goal of a Christian life, to see not only riches and good fortune as blessings, but troubles and tribulations even unto death, as giving glory to God. The gift of prayer for others is a gift that is repaid with thanks in prayer, towards God, "Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts." We are sealed unto the day of judgment, and the ernest, or the down payment on the promise of eternal life, is the Spirit living within our hearts. And so with this knowledge, the testimony of our faith living within us, we can trust in God. His promises are 'yea, yea.' It's a beautiful introduction and sober reminder that in God, all things are possible and we needn't be troubled by anything in this world, because in Christ we have already overcome it. The final line in chapter 1, regarding the apostle and the evangelists who have ministered to the churches throughout the region, and specifically to Corinth not being in dominion over the believers there, but helpers, because they are established and stand by their own faith as individuals. Their churches are independent as well. They may receive reproach or guiding, but it's not to dictate over them who are equal in the faith, members of the same body with Christ at its head. Quick sidenote to this and the series of readings and studies we are undertaking; I have all but stopped noting when the Gospel of faith alone and grace alone is mentioned, because it is nearly every chapter and it is inarguable at this point for those who come here daily. Paul doesn't write to them about being stablished in their works, or ceremonies, or how willing they are to turn from their sins, but by the faith they believed shared by those who ministered unto them.

Chapter 2 continues Paul's introduction, speaking now as to why he hadn't come to them, with a rod, as promised in his first epistle to them, saying he decided in part to not come to them "in heaviness" to grieve them. As we saw in 1 Corinthians, Paul had laid into them pretty hard, especially in chapter 5 regarding one member and his wicked fornication. Paul says to them that he considers them his sons in Christ, having asked them to follow him as a father who brought them to the gospel, and like a father, scourging those he loves, Paul says his chastisement was necessary but he doesn't want them to mistake it for anything other than his love of them. He says in verse 5 that it wasn't personal. He's not doing this out of hurt feelings. And likewise, as he's showing kindness to those he'd chastised, he says to them that they should be forgiving to those in the church that they punished as he'd called for, and they having repented, be welcomed back and comforted that they not fall back into sin. We are never to tolerate or enable other Christians sins, especially those that lead to church discipline, but when a Christian makes a sincere turn around, we are to be gracious like God is with us, daily. Forgiveness of trespasses. Paul says if they've forgiven some their sin and brought them back from being backslidden, it's good enough for him, because it is good enough for Christ. This may be specifically the man who was sleeping with his step-mother, but it reads as a more general item. We should be happy to forgive and forget, just as eagerly as we are to condemn and rebuke. As a parent treats their child, which is how Paul looks at those he's won to Christ, this is an incredibly important concept to master. How we love our children, including how we discipline and forgive, is an imprint in their minds of how God works, and by showing firm hand, but loving kindness and forgiveness, the same as He shows us, we are demonstrating to them His love and grace. When we are resentful, angry, taking it personally and overcharging them, failing to forgive and forget, they may be swallowed up with much sorrow. It is how Satan gains an advantage in their lives. Many parents create a barter system in place of love, where everything is transactional. They may forgive but not forget, throwing past behavior at their child, holding it against them. Many parents don't even realize they are doing it. This behavior builds within a child the seeds for a works-based relationship with God, and can cause all sorts of problems in their lives. Never being "good enough." Never having healthy relationships with others. Never really understanding the charitable love and grace we have in hope through Christ Jesus. Maybe even bringing them to reprobation in the end, bitter against you and so bitter against God. Paul shifts back to his delay of his promised visit, and talks of his going into Macedonia to give the Gospel. Verse 15 and 16 notes that to those who believe, the sincerely preached gospel by a saved Christian is a sweet smell, the savior of life, but to those perishing, they smell only the death that their sin is bringing them. This is the division Christ brings. This is the reason for their hating us in His name. One aspect of spreading the Gospel that most miss, and misunderstand, is that as many receive it, even more reject it, and in doing so, eventually run the risk of reprobation. Soul winning can and does create reprobates, and that is intended by God. Every hearing is a seed sown, or watered, and could be what leads to harvest. But the same message of truth is really required for the reprobate to know and reject to lead them to that state. Romans 1 21 Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. 22 Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, 23 And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things. 24 Wherefore God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts, to dishonour their own bodies between themselves: 25 Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

Paul has begun this letter to Corinth far less hostile than the last. His reproach cooler. His reframing of the question of letters of commendation to one of the Spirit and the heart of the persons saved by his or those he sent's ministry, that the believers' own salvation and behavior are the real epistles of the authority Paul and the others have is softer, and yet more biting. He spins from this to the idea of the letters of the law, of the old testament, being what condemned us, knowledge of the law bringing with it sin, which the Bible defines as transgression of the law (1 John 3:4), but in the Spirit is Liberty, the eternal life given in the new testament. This becomes a major theme for Paul in other epistles, the use of the law by God as a schoolmaster, bringing us to sure knowledge of our transgressions and death from sin, and the liberty found in Christ, which is more glorious than even the hand of God engraving stone and giving it to Moses. The veil Moses wore to protect the Hebrews in the wilderness from the lingering glory of God reflected in his face becomes a metaphor for the veil keeping the glory of God, through Christ, from the hearts of the Jew. But, with the veil taken away by belief on Christ, we see the glory manifest, and in that image, have it reflect in our own faces, the way it did to Moses, but unhidden and used to show others our faith that they might believe.

What a beautiful passage. "We faint not." And again, fitting with topics I've posted about in the past day, the reminder to look at the things unseen, not the seen, because they are temporal, and the unseen eternal. Paul writes that as we have obtained mercy in Christ, we have also received a ministry to share the light we've been given in that mercy. We are all ministers, servants to the glory of God. We don't hide the message, or teach it as "hidden things," gnosticism to be drawn out, but instead proclaimed in truth, in the light for all to see. Our making the truth known to be judged by others conscience in the sight of God. What we learn in the shadows shouted from the rooftops. Not hiding our light under a bushel. Amen. That, of the Gospel be hid, it isn't due to our lack of ministering, but because Satan, the "god of this world," who deceives the whole world, keeps it hid to those that are in unbelief. We are to be servants to others for Jesus sakes. Because we were changed and born again because His sacrifice for us, we serve others in sacrifice for His sake. Being a servant to the Gospel to administer it to the unsaved is our calling. Verse 6, tying the creation of Genesis and God summoning the light out of the void of darkness through Jesus, to the same light coming into our dark hearts, void and dead in sin. Paul reminds us that God is placing this treasure, the quickened spirit redeemed in Christ, in "earthen vessels," the flesh that perishes. Imperfect and plain, containing the riches of the spirit that God gets the glory, not us. We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed; That we aren't troubled because our corruptible body will see death but our spirit eternal life in the death and life of Jesus Christ. This is our faith, and having this faith, it is the good news we speak, and so on as it's spread. We will be together in God's glory, regardless of the trials of this world, and so we faint not. Amen This verse about earthen vessels with the light inside reminds me of the story of Gideon's 300, from Judges 7, where God tells Gideon to send home most of his troops before a battle, so that when the enemies were delivered unto them they couldn't take the glory for themselves, he tells the remainder to put a light, a lamp, in earthen pots. 15 And it was so, when Gideon heard the telling of the dream, and the interpretation thereof, that he worshipped, and returned into the host of Israel, and said, Arise; for the Lord hath delivered into your hand the host of Midian. 16 And he divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put a trumpet in every man's hand, with empty pitchers, and lamps within the pitchers. 17 And he said unto them, Look on me, and do likewise: and, behold, when I come to the outside of the camp, it shall be that, as I do, so shall ye do. 18 When I blow with a trumpet, I and all that are with me, then blow ye the trumpets also on every side of all the camp, and say, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon. 19 So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands. 20 And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands to blow withal: and they cried, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon. 21 And they stood every man in his place round about the camp; and all the host ran, and cried, and fled. The faint of heart and fearful are sent home, thousands are sent to their tents. Those 300 who remain placing lamps in earthen vessels, that are then broken to reveal the light and lead God to triumph over the enemy. This is such an amazing parallel to our lives, and an illustration of Paul's point.

Continuing the theme of the previous chapters, which of you recall, started regarding letters of commendation among men. Paul reminds that our letters of commendation are those who have believed because of our sharing the gospel. He says we are being judged by the conscience of the unbelieving, that our behavior should reflect the light that's within us, living as a light that guides them through the darkness put over them by the devil, winning them to Christ. That we are ministers of the same Gospel of mercy that changed our hearts and brought us to focus on the things unseen, our conscience clear in Jesus. Building on this, Paul writes about our physical bodies perishing, but our glorified body from Heaven assured. That the Holy Spirit within us is the earnest, the down payment from God on His promise. But our eternal body is naked, being new born. It is clothed and housed in raiment earned by our works here, judged by God, and so we should constantly strive in this body for that which we will receive in the next. Preferring being absent this body to be present with the Lord, we should live without fear. What are we threatened with? Heaven? As Jesus said "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you." We should live with the confidence that this is true and that we are furnishing the mansion He has provided us, winning souls to Christ. By focusing on the unseen, living the faith, we also give answer to those that judge by appearance rather than of the heart, as God judges. And in doing so, be able to pierce the veil of darkness and bring them to the light of God reflected in us. We are a new man, contained in the earthen vessels of the old, but reconciled with God in Jesus, and so, given the ministry, being a servant, to spreading that reconciliation to others. Ambassadors. Paul says it better than I can, go read the first 5 chapters again. And again, this is a much longer form of James 2's "faith without works is dead, being alone." Note that we have a tabernacle in Heaven for us by faith, but it is naked without works. To the unsaved who judge the world by appearances, respecters of persons, judging only the things they can see, being blind to the spiritual, are made to see by our works, which are reflection of the light, the mercy we've been shown. We are saved by faith alone. We share that faith by how we live. And by being mindful of that, we get others saved, and also brought into that ministry of reconciliation with us so that then others can be. Our letters of commendation. One of the hardest things to understand in faith is that the more we care about the things of God, despising even the flesh we have, our family, our comfort, and living for Jesus, the more we are blessed, the better things are in our lives and those we love. It's a paradox that many can't get around, but for those who do, you see how it works. When Jesus says "Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law," (Luke 12) he isn't saying you have to hate them, but rather be prepared to lose them. To be willing that you lose them all to gain Christ. To understand that many will reject Him and you, and die perishing. Many will hate you for it. But we aren't to be troubled. Because as Jesus also says, "And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.(Matthew 19)” Like Job, who having lost everything in this world but his life, yet he loved the Lord, and received it all back in abundance, so to if we are willing to lose everything, on faith, we will gain what we lost and more. If you have unbelieving children or parents you love, this can be difficult to get past. But if you're willing to let go and trust God, even if you may lose them, you will be surprised at how many come around. This goes for comfort, nation, work...all the cares of life. The more you are willing to suffer and yet trust Him, the more you will gain. If you're afraid of the future and desperate to see some kind of assurance, or place your faith in whatever reactions you think you should take, politics you get involved with, fed posting and red pilling, you will lose it all. But trust in Christ, despising those things for the Lord's sake, and you will gain so much more. I have seen it. I have been so blessed. Let go. Have faith.

Paul's establishing the understanding that we are servants in Christ, ministering the Gospel to the unbelieving, and living in a way that glorifies God, reflects His light within us, and piercing the darkness put on them by the devil, comes to a conclusion. We are workers with Jesus, having received the grace of God, we work so that our salvation is not in vain, but serves others to come to the same redemption. He quotes Isaiah 49:8, Thus saith the Lord, In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages. Now, having established no need for letters of commendation for Titus and the brethren that accompanied him, but the shared spirit and kinship in Christ, Paul actually gives his commendation, their bona fides. The purpose remains instruction, but specifically the gathering of the alms to bring to the church in Jerusalem, then stricken with a famine as described in Acts. There is doctrine here, that we who have are expected to share with brethren who lack, because worldly things being unimportant, and the blessings given by God to those that do without for others, our liberality, our generosity of materials leads to our receiving abundance of the spiritual. It's an even trade, not a burden. This is a reflection of the charity God shows us in His mercy and loving kindness. We lack, and He has abundance, and in His grace, sharing it with us, He loses nothing but gains. In the same manner, when we do the same among men we are rewarded. Psalm 40; "But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me." Psalm 41; "Blessed is he who considereth the poor: the Lord will deliver him in time of trouble." If you have troubles, people against you, peril and tribulation, seek first to put your fate in God's hands, asking for deliverance, and then having confidence through your faith in Him, seek those you can help towards delivering them from theirs. Pure religion, undefiled... This is the wisdom of man, not God. Idleness and being a sluggard have their own punishment, and our work has its wages. Each has its own reward. But "help" presumes already that there's effort or a will, but lacking the ability or strength to complete. To this cause, I support the locals, the NSCs and the other clubs of young men seeking discipline and honor, where it may have been lacking in their lives, or where they were raised with it and want to share with others. My only concern is they do it in Christ, and don't substitute it for a soul winning church. But it is something positive, and their food and supply drives to help White people in crisis are excellent examples of what needs to happen.

Continuing his encouraging of the church in Corinth in their collection of alms to be sent to the church in Jerusalem, Paul speaks that he had boasted of their generosity and charity throughout Asia Minor, and that as he sends Titus and others to gather their offering together, they be not ashamed. That the boasting is true. He gives more instruction on the idea that God blesses those who give in the right spirit. That God's given us the greatest gift in salvation by His Son's sacrifice, and fulfilled His promise in Jesus resurrection, and with the earnest of the Spirit within them. Knowing we are recipients of such charity, the greatest love man can know, as Jesus preached, Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends, how can we be any less generous in our gifts of charity, especially the giving of worldly things. That the rewards of spiritual things in return are another promise of the same God we have faith in. The issue of raising money for the saved Christians in Jerusalem is often used by the perishing on the Right, as well as the Zionist dispensationalists, to say Christians are required to give money to Jews. This is a lie, promoted by Jews, and echoed by their minions of whatever stripe. A lesson in charity is not the doctrine of Gentiles having to support godless Jews.

Up until this point, Paul has made a conscious effort to be kinder and gentler in this second epistle to Corinth. Writing in response to a request of some sort of letters of commendation for the workers in Christ coming to collect alms from them, and set the church there right, especially after the problems they had with fornication and other sin in the assembly the year before. First Corinthians being harsh, 2nd is far more friendly, as Paul has laid out the reasons why the very idea of letters of approval from men towards others, giving bona fides, is foolish given they are all servants of Christ in the same faith and to the same ends of edifying the believers and spreading the gospel. But now, here in chapter 10, Paul turns harshly towards those who may, at this point of reading his epistle, still have doubts of him, his authority, the authority of those sent, and of the shared understanding of salvation in Christ. Rhetorically, he destroys them. He says that he's come to them in meekness, like Christ, and that some may judge him as unimposing physically, compared to the boldness he showed in his first epistle. That they are judging him as if he were just some unsaved person, and not by the authority of the gifts he has received or as the father of their salvation that he was, bringing them the Gospel. That he could boast more of this, and not be ashamed in the boasting. He could come with a rod, and in spiritual gifts, destroy the nay sayers, despite being weak in the body and his manner of speech. He's telling them they are lucky he isn't coming there to crack heads, because whatever they think, he has the power to. He adds some cutting lines about those who measure themselves with themselves, to commend themselves being "not wise." Then in a stinging rebuke, cleverly worded to shoot down those unwise, reminds them again of his position in bringing them the Gospel while insinuating that the boastful seeking the letters of commendation from Paul are puffed up over what was his work. Labors of another. He ends reminding again it is being approved by God that matters, not of other men and certainly not of ourselves. It is worth reading through a couple times, out loud if you can, because the grammar is dense in places and can be confusing in print. There is no doubt the power of the Spirit is in these writings. Imagine talking smack about Paul behind his back and asking him to provide references

If you recall yesterday's reading of chapter 10, Paul had begun his reproach of those in Corinth who had sought letters of commendation from Paul and of his fellow evangelists, which, given the nature Christianity, and Paul's having begat many in the faith there, was insulting. They said he was bold in his first epistle reproaching them, but if he'd come to them personally he wouldn't be so tough. That physically he was weak, and just "talked tough." He corrected them saying essentially they should be thankful he didn't come to them with the rod. That they're estimating the flesh rather than the Spirit of God and the power of Paul's faith and gifts. And now, he continues. He says bear with him a little folly, because he is going to speak as a fool (subtly calling those challenging him fools), as he gives their arguments a rhetorical beating. He first tells them that he's doing this out of love. That he begat them in Christ, and is jealous over them as God is of us who believe. Jealousy in the Bible is a virtue. The righteous desire to keep and protect that which is rightfully yours. Modern use links it to covetousness and envy, but God is a jealous God, and in Him is no such sin. He says he hopes to present them in the day of Christ as virgins to a groom, but that if the men he sends are bringing a false gospel, a false Jesus, corrupting the simplicity of salvation that is in Christ, they could have complaint. But he is an Apostle, humbly saying he's a hair less than the others. And as such, he may have offended them in his previous letter, with rude speech, and yet didn't he give them knowledge of Christ and wasn't all things made manifest to them through him? Stinging rebuke incoming. He asks, rhetorically, didn't he abase himself to bring them the word? That he didn't ask them for money or support while he preached to them, other churches funded his mission where he was lacking. (We know Paul, a tentmaker by trade, would support himself with that as much as possible, so as to not offend or give the impression of grifting). He says he would have preached the Gospel there in Acacia regardless of his material comfort, because the truth of Christ is within him. It is in all of us that have believed. It compels us to give the gospel of reconciliation to all, even if we don't heed it. Paul says he was powerless against it, having to preach it. He compares himself to the false apostles and the vipers who even then were creeping into the early churches, and what they do. He again asks them to think him not a fool, but allow him to act as a fool for this argument. Clarifying that these things he's saying here aren't doctrine of God but his rhetorical device showing how foolish this line of demanding bona fides of him is given his history and zeal. That even if they are Hebrews, seed of Abraham, well so is he. And if they claim to be ministers of Christ, well ok, but so is Paul, and even more so by any reckoning, especially in his tribulation for preaching the word. He's not conceding that these false teachers are ministers of Christ, but if they are leading them astray into questioning Paul's authority in God, then consider these things. That Paul was repeatedly scourged, beaten, stoned, imprisoned, shipwrecked and more, all for the Gospel's sake. With all responsibilities that he has taken on, and in all the peril and tribulation, yet they called him weak. Bold in letter but afraid to come to them with that boldness. That he was meek, and physically unimposing. He says, sure I am weak. Let me boast of my infirmities, let's glorify those because look at what I have gone through for the Lord and still he is here to reprimand them. He's like, "I had to escape a city in a basket for crying out loud." And still these people knowing his history dared to question him, his motives and his emissaries. To mock him as weak. Paul's ability with words to cut to the heart of fools is amazing. Inspired by the Spirit.

Continuing the building rebuke to the Corinthians who had doubted Paul, were offended at his previous epistle that pointed out the sins of some in their church, and who had insulted him and essentially cast doubts on his apostleship by demanding letters of commendation and we're suggesting his collection for the church in Jerusalem was a grift. They had insinuated that, since he is weak and unimposing and meek in their presence before, and bold in his first epistle, that he was a paper tiger. That he wouldn't say it to their face. For the purpose of the ministry and to set things right for those in the church who hadn't been involved in this disputation, Paul wrote with love and patience through the first few chapters, but in 10, he began his rebuke and it is building to a crescendo. He says in the previous chapter that glorying of himself he could do, after all the things that have happened to him for the cause of Christ. After all he did, the punishments he received, the stripes on his back. That he could glory for all the souls he'd won, including some there at Corinth. But that he would not glory in those things, but where he was lacking. That if he wasn't physically imposing as they said, then all the more glory to God that Paul's mission had been so full of tribulation and persecution. Now, he says that if he were to glory in the gift of revelation, it would be in things like a man he knows, who had a revelation from Heaven (be it physically taken there or in the Spirit, Paul doesn't know), and seen things that were yet unlawful to speak of. It's just an example of how Paul would glorify a gift given another, greater than his. That he'd rather, for himself, glorify God for using such a weak and infirm vessel as himself. I have heard it preached that the man taken up to the 3rd heaven is Paul himself, and he's being a little sardonic and coy. I don't believe so. I take it plainly. That it sounds like the experience of John from Revelation seems coincidental given the time frame of Corinthians being in the 50s AD, and fourteen years prior to that is well before the assumed date of John's exile (either mid-60s AD, or in mid 90s, depending). But regardless of who it was, Paul's point is made. Paul goes on to say that he is blessed by his infirmities, that he'd prayed for a particular 'thorn in the flesh' to be healed, and God told him no, that Paul's accomplishments would be God's to take credit for and that thorn keeping Paul weak, so that God can be seen as strong. Amen. We all have such thorns. Some of the flesh, some of the heart in the sin we struggle with. We should pray to God for relief, and accept that if we have weaknesses, it is God who is strong and overcomes. We are to just do His will. Paul continues his rebuke. He says he performed the gifts and signs of an apostle among them, and yet they doubted. He lived among them preaching, without taking a dime from them. And now, they are asking him for letters from others to give him and those he sent to them credentials. Wew. The audacity. He says as a parent should bestow an inheritance on the children they love, not being a burden, he has and will of he came again give to them again, without being a burden, out of love, even as his loving chastisement makes them not love him. He's calling them spoiled brats in other words. And it's understandable. And, building upon this case he is making, he begins to suggest that maybe the reason they are doubting and backbiting and making subtle accusations of being a grifter, and a fake apostle, is that if he were to come to them that they are still mired in sin and resent him telling them so. This is about to get turned up a notch in chapter 13... Another aside, Boomers take note: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children. The spending of the children's inheritance, be it personal, buying toys and taking trips, or through use of government for debt, ponzi schemes and wealth transfers, is wicked as Hell. One more thing, given the amount of content Paul contributes to the New Testament, and the amount of Doctrine he explains in that content, the Epistles to the Corinthians, especially this last half of the second, is written to address all the naysayers and scoffers that were sure to come against Paul. God included this as much to future readers as to the actual church there. If you've spent any time online in Christian circles, or in theological social media debates in general, you have seen Paul be accused of multiple things, including not being a real apostle, not having actual gifts of the Holy Ghost to prophesy, his writing as not being inspired, that he has presented a different gospel than that which Jesus taught...all manner of accusations by unsaved and lazy believers, buying in to every thing they read on Reddit without ever reading the Bible themselves in the Spirit. And much like the scoffers at Corinth, the people who hold those views are generally either offended at the gospel, offended by the preaching of doctrine they don't like, condemnation and rebuke of sin they enjoy or believing in vain false doctrines given by vipers. As for Paul, there are Corinthians justifying grave sin by saying the Apostle isn't qualified to rebuke them. He levels exactly his credentials; Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you. For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God... Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates? He cities the work of salvation in them by his own testimony of the gospel towards them. If he isn't qualified to rebuke them, then how were they begotten of Christ through him? Are they reprobates? And if they have Christ in them due to Paul's preaching, could he be a reprobate? Here is wisdom; that we can establish who is of God and who isn't by the works done. False teachers are judged by their fruit. They don't produce thousands of salvations, ordained pastors, multiple churches planted, if they are not of God. Paul certainly shut up those protesting his qualifications by reminding them of this simple fact.

Final chapter, Paul finishes his rebuke of the Corinthian church in stinging fashion. He says he's coming back, and in the manner established in God's law and Christ's teaching on church discipline, before 2 or 3 witnesses Paul will establish who is telling the truth, and who exactly it is that needs credentials to be established. That if he has to come there again it will not be to spare those who seek proof of his having Christ in him. He says examine your own selves, if they have Christ within them. If they think Paul doesn't, and that Christ is within them so mightily, sarcastically accusing them of not being saved. Of perhaps being reprobate. This seems harsh. We hear all the time that we shouldn't "reprobate someone." Even when the person is exhibiting the signs of reprobation, sodomy, being a false prophet with a damnable false gospel, many Christians today will say we cannot judge what is in another's heart. But we can judge what they say and do, if not the reason. The Corinthians who disputed Paul's salvation were passively accusing him of being a reprobate. Of preaching a false gospel. Of being a grifter. And so Paul opens both barrels and questions if they are still in the sins he'd written to them about before, if perhaps they themselves are reprobate. Paul does take pains to make room for the sincere believers within that church. And he says, he'd hope that even if he and his associates were reprobate, they'd still comport themselves without sin, doing evil. It's hard preaching, because it puts those balking at giving alms and using the railing accusations against the Apostle to do it, on the hook that regardless of others, they should live as befits saints, (knowing they do not). He concludes the rebuke with a threat of coming with the sharpness of the gifts he has through the Holy Ghost, but assuring it would be to their edification, not destruction. Again it's a sarcastic dig at the problems in the church while assuring the brethren. He finishes with a flourish of kindness and grace, and salutations in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Amen. I feel remiss that I haven't done this before, but if any book needs it, it's this. Go listen to the audio version of 2 Corinthians. It is so powerful

Everyone should really read this introduction to the Epistle to the various churches throughout Galatia. Paul is writing to churches he founded on the gospel, the only good news that we are forgiven all sin and given eternal life through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. He is writing them because Jews have come behind him, telling the Gentile believers they must follow the law and be circumcised to be saved. Trying to drag who they can back to bondage. To judaize the churches, and to damn the people who had believed in vain, never really trusting in Christ alone. And these judaizers had badmouthed Paul, claiming he wasn't a real Apostle, that he preached a different Gospel than Peter and even than Jesus Christ. Sound familiar? (It's a trend in our circles and on pol, for example, that comes around like clockwork every few months. There are patterns to heresy. They come in waves.) Discrediting Paul, who God chose to give the authoritative theology for people saved by faith, Jew or Greek, to write the afterwards and lay out everything that came before it and the implications for a Christian life, just as James, Jude, Peter and John. For there is one gospel and anyone bringing another is accursed. And the Apostles agreed with Paul when he went to them in Acts about this very thing, which prompted those other epistles and more like them not in scripture. But the first thing they do is change the Gospel to works. To the bondage of the law. They bring another gospel that isn't a gospel. If people don't bite, they discredit Paul. "White knuckle sobriety" describes one who gives up alcohol or other addiction, but doesn't seek support, preferring to go it alone, on their own plan. Lacking guidelines, guidance and accountability it generally is a recipe for relapse. The individual is just using pure willpower to stay sober. It is like they are just hanging on, waiting for the ride to end, hence "white knuckles." As I understand it, the difference between "white knuckle" sobriety and a "dry drunk" is subtle; both are relying on themselves to maintain sobriety, but the "dry drunk" does nothing else to change the underlying behavior or causes that feed their addiction, while the white-knuckler may take steps, as near as his own understanding allows, to make some changes in their life. Some of which may be good ideas if part of a well-supported recovery, some old wives tales or misled by bad advice found online, from friends, media, self-help books, etc..., some just plain rationalizing. The point is that outside of proper support and absent real accountability, they are usually going to fail, often harder than they were before the futile effort. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement. Amen

We who believe are freeborn sons of God, heirs to His Kingdom. Paul exhorts to standfast in that liberty, and not to be drawn back to self-righteousness of sacraments and observances, works and deeds, which is bondage. If they trust in their circumcision to justify them, even partially, then Christ will profit them nothing. This could be any other work of the flesh you're trusting to save you, even if it is added to faith. Even if it is done in zeal. It makes null the promise. Be it adding baptism, turning from sin, church membership and attendance, rites of man, communion...all things done by those calling themselves Christian by yoking themselves to the bondage of the unregenerate Jew. Christ profits them nothing. They become debtors to the whole of the law, and there are none righteous, no not one. None who can do the whole of the law. And so they perish. If this is you, you're perishing. Repent. And what is the whole of the law? Paul again, echoing Christ who quoted Leviticus; Loving our neighbors as ourselves. In all things. And as Jesus taught in the parable of the Good Samaritan, your neighbors are those you meet along the way, even your enemies. And what does loving them look like? Sacrifice of time, material wealth, comfort, status, gain, health, even life to aid them in their need. Can any of us love this much? Jesus Christ, sinless and blameless sacrificed Himself, yet while we were sinners so that we may be forgiven. No greater love than this. A standard we strive for, to which we crucify ourselves daily to achieve. Our spirit willing, but the flesh is weak. So how do we shore up the spirit to bring us closer to following Christ? By being in the word. In prayer. In thanksgiving to God for the gift of salvation. And it is reflected and made manifest in our walk, through love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance. As to the flesh, Paul lists the sins, common to man, that violate the law the Galatians seem eager to put themselves under. Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. They are counting on their cutting off of foreskin to save them, to adhere to the law to please the Judaizers among them, making them debtors to the whole of the law; meanwhile the lusts of the flesh, made manifest, indict them. We all have committed adultery, in our hearts if not physically. We envy and covet and engage in emulations, the comparison of ourselves to others in a competitive way. We feel wrath, murder in our hearts, with hatred for others. Plot sedition. Spread heresy. None of that can be forgiven and erased by keeping a ceremonial part of the law. Carnal ordinances can't get you the inheritance. Only faith can. And those in faith have crucified our sins so that our flesh may be dead in Christ, but our spirit alive with the risen Jesus. And not to damn the Galatians with faint praise, but at least they were being beguiled into obeying something that actually was ordained by God in the Old Testament, if done away with in Christ. How many people calling themselves Christian are putting their faith in something that isn't even in the Bible? That has no actual examples in scripture? That are twisted from incoherent cherry picking? You can almost see the errors of those trusting baptism to save them, a natural man reading of scripture could lead them to that I suppose. Unsaved people might be persuaded to think that the Lord's supper is some kind of magic ritual bringing them an installment of grace. (I'm speaking kindly of those holding on to damnable heresy, that it might jostle some in to repentance. But that benefit of the doubt doesn't mean they aren't damned). But the entirety of the Mystery Religion of Babylon, practiced by the whore and her harlot daughters, is extra-biblical, vain traditions of men. Repent and trust in Christ alone. Believe God's word alone.

1 Corinthians 7 18 Is any man called being circumcised? let him not become uncircumcised. Is any called in uncircumcision? let him not be circumcised. 19 Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God. 20 Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called. ... We see Paul's view that it's not the act of circumcision but the heart of those seeking justification with God through the act, and being placed in bondage under the yoke of the law. That false prophets crept in to mislead the early churches and by doing so make the Gospel to none effect of those who took heed of them. And so the demand of Titus to be circumcised prompted the council in Jerusalem, and the decision of James the half-brother of Jesus and the rest to make certain this heresy was warned against. The last chapter of the epistle to the Galatians. Paul seeks to edify those remaining hearing his words who are saved (after accusing some who'd gone along after the Judaizers of not being saved at all). Great doctrine in a few passages, of our call to bear each other's burdens, and to love one another. That we reap what we sow, so sow that which is spiritual. Paul indicates that the Jews pushing circumcision on the Gentiles as a way for them to glory among the Jews in leading them astray, to avoid persecution by those that tempt them. But Paul reminds us he bears the stripes and scars of being beaten by these Jews for preaching the Gospel. And still, having this physical sign of his glory, for not buckling to the Judaizers, Paul still gives all glory to Christ and seeks the spiritual new man. Not the weak flesh. It's a beautiful sentiment. His physical scars, far greater than a snip of skin, bear record of his faith, and yet he doesn't count on that for his own righteousness, but the faith Paul preached and shared among them. Our reading of the NT so far, from the Gospel of John to Galatians, has touched mostly on the milk of the word, the basic doctrines of God, Christ Jesus, reprobation, salvation and liberty from works of the law. Judaizers and false gospels. Church discipline and sin. Tomorrow begins the epistle to the Ephesians, a culmination of this teaching, tying it all together, as it is a thorough instruction for all saved Christians.

What an introduction. Paul lays so much doctrine in what is only the greeting of his letter to believers at Ephesus. It's fantastic, and dense and due to the extensive use of prepositional clauses, causes many believers and all natural men to struggle in understanding. One aspect of understanding the Word is understanding God's use of conditional logic, if-then statements, often complex with multiple factors. This method of reasoning together with God is evident in this epistle. Paul is an Apostle, by the will of God. He's writing to the saints, the faithful in Jesus Christ. He wishes grace and peace to the reader from God and Jesus. God has blessed us with all spiritual blessings. Keeping this in mind, consider verse 4-6: According as he hath chosen us in him (Jesus) before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he (God) hath made us accepted in the beloved (Jesus). The error of Calvinism is to misapply the focus of predestination to those benefiting from it, rather than by whom, Jesus Christ. God has chosen us in Jesus. Predestinated by Christ. Accepted in the beloved, His Son. Jesus is the Son of God, beloved of the Father, the lamb slain before the foundation of the world. Jesus was predestinated to be the means by which we received grace. We weren't chosen. He was. We are only adopted sons, because of Jesus In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace. Paul is lauding God the Father and the Son, Christ Jesus, he is not indicating that the believers are special boys, predestined, but that in Christ through God's grace, we are. In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will. We obtain the inheritance in Jesus who was predestinated according to the will of God. And this isn't a question of perspective and interpretation, because Paul then makes our role in this process abundantly clear: That we should be to the praise of his glory, who first trusted in Christ. In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory. Follow that? We gain this inheritance IN Christ who we trusted when we heard the Gospel, and after hearing and believing, being sealed by the Holy Spirit. These are the conditional terms of our obtaining the inheritance, our salvation. Not God picking and choosing us, but God having predestinated Christ, that those who first trusted in Him are included in the inheritance. It's an order of operations that is focused on God and His Son. Our part is in believing it to be true. Further, once we believe we are sealed by the Holy Spirit as the earnest, the down payment as it were, until redemption, where God makes good on His promise, on the day of the Lord. Once you are saved you are purchased by the blood. To let you know God's promise is good, He sets the Holy Spirit to seal you, to quicken your spirit, to awake the new man inside, and that seal is until the day He redeems you. He makes good on the promise. He raises you from the dead in glorified bodies to inherit His Kingdom. It is a contract entered in to by faith with God by believing His testimony. Taking Him at His word. And what is that promise? Paul writes that we should be in prayer and thanksgiving for this salvation, that we may have the spirit of wisdom and eyes to see, having been enlightened by the Spirit, that we may know what is the hope of this calling, His offer that we've answered in faith. We can know we are saved, confident we are given eternal life, partakers of the glory of Jesus to whom all things are given to rule, as He is the head to which we become the body. In 23 short verses, God packs in the entire foundation of the Gospel and its purpose and affect on those who trust in Him. An amazing and breathtaking bit of writing that, once looked at in its entirety, rather than cherry picked without context, shows how the inspired Word of God has power. Another point to make regarding the introduction, that Paul addresses to the saints and believers, terms which are interchangeable in the New Testament. All believers are saints. It's a title bestowed throughout to all who believe. It is not a select few whose Works were so good that they are honored here on Earth with the title. By making a church of man the arbiter, and basing it on works, the Catholic church has cheapened the term. I am a saint. If you believe you are a saint as well. Even if your backslidden, even if you need to turn from sins that are consuming your life. And as saints we should turn from sin, we should live a righteous life as possible. Live up to it. Secondly Paul frequently writes that he prays for Grace from God to us the reader, and with that grace, peace. The only piece we have with God is through his grace, and Christ Jesus. At the nativity the Angels announced peace on Earth. Goodwill towards men. This is a message from God to man, that he is granting them peace with Him, and goodwill through the birth of Jesus. The angel isn't saying that they'll be peace upon the Earth between men, but rather peace between God and men.

One thing that greatly confuses many searching for truth, and leads them into the damnable heresy of Lordship salvation and reformed Calvinism is they use modern perverted bibles, that insert words and concepts that aren't in the text, and that are then manipulated to deceive the ignorant. I would that any deceived by this doctrine to repent and believe the testimony of God, that the only way to salvation is to trust His word, that He so loved the world He gave His only begotten son that WHOSOEVER believe shall not perish but have everlasting life "Oh yeah? What about Pharaoh? God hardened his heart! See he had no free will!" This is a common argument made by people who lack even basic understanding, have their own ideas and just don't read the Bible and let God teach them doctrine. In Exodus, we see God through Moses, give Pharaoh multiple chances to acknowledge God and repent, freeing the Hebrews. God sends 10 plagues, and at each we see the pattern: Blood: Pharaoh’s heart “became hard” (7:22) Frogs: Pharaoh “hardened his own heart” (8:15) Gnats: Pharaoh’s heart “was hard” (8:19) Flies: “Pharaoh hardened his own heart” (8:32) Livestock die: Pharaoh’s heart “was hard” (9:7) Boils: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (9:12) Hail: Pharaoh “hardened his own heart” (9:34) Locusts: God announces that he has “hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (10:1,10:20) Darkness: God “hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (10:27) Death of the firstborn: God “hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (11:10) It isn't until the 6th opportunity that God gives Pharaoh what he has chosen repeatedly, to not acknowledge God when called to. As Romans 1 shows: Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. That "for this cause God gave them up," And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient. Reprobate simply means rejected. Unable to come to saving faith having already rejected God, utterly and finally being given up on by God. Pharaoh is an example of how reprobation works. The Bible says they are conscience seared, twice-dead, dogs, sons of the devil, sons of Belial. Reprobation in the Bible is shown to be as much of a choice as salvation. A Spiritual condition. And it is entirely by free will. I think the pattern shows that once God sets out to reject someone, they are given one last chance, seeing what reprobation becomes like. As with Cain's works-sacrifice, God wants them to simply correct their behavior and have them get right with Him. From that time on, his spiritual fate is sealed. Keeping with the week's theme, Reprobate Doctrine: Jude 1 Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called: 2 Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied. 3 Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. 4 For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ. 5 I will therefore put you in remembrance, though ye once knew this, how that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not. 6 And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day. 7 Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire. 8 Likewise also these filthy dreamers defile the flesh, despise dominion, and speak evil of dignities. 9 Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee. 10 But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves. 11 Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core. 12 These are spots in your feasts of charity, when they feast with you, feeding themselves without fear: clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots; 13 Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever. 14 And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, 15 To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him. 16 These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words, having men's persons in admiration because of advantage. 17 But, beloved, remember ye the words which were spoken before of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ; 18 How that they told you there should be mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts. 19 These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit. 20 But ye, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost, 21 Keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. 22 And of some have compassion, making a difference: 23 And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh. 24 Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, 25 To the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen. We see in Jude an epistle to saved Christians, to whom the Gospel had already been delivered, warning them of those others who are reprobate in the faith, trees without fruit, twice-dead, plucked up... Titus 1:16 They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate. Reprobates are the children of the devil, who work all unrighteousness. Acts 13:10 And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? It's important to recognize that normal unsaved sinners are not reprobates. They haven't been turned over by God. Sons of perdition, sons of Baal, of their father the devil, are spiritually twice-dead as the saved are born again. The normal unsaved person are spiritually Ishmael. First born of the flesh, born of water They aren't heirs of the kingdom, aren't sons of God, aren't receiving the blessing, etc, where as the second born (or born again by the Spirit) are Isaac, and so heirs to the promise. Ephesians chapter 1 built the theme of the first 3 chapters; the promise of God, predestinated in Christ and redeemed in us through faith, to be heirs to His Kingdom, and being bestowed with spiritual blessings as His sons. The immediate application of this for the Galatians and other Gentiles to whom it is written was the Jews attitude towards them, even in the early church. That they were not joint heirs. That they were somehow less than believing Jews in the Kingdom of Heaven, not having been of the "chosen people." It's one of the reasons for Paul's emphasis on being elect in Christ. Being all chosen to members of the body of which Jesus is the head. Here in chapter 2, Paul builds on the idea of adoption of grace, to being sons of God, and compares the sonship of believers to the 'children of disobedience,' or the 'children of wrath.' which we all were, Jew or Gentile, without grace from God, His mercy and the blood of Christ, that we who believe are quickened, our spirit born again as His sons. Even when we were dead in sins, Christ died for us all. That we may sit together, raised up together, by the grace and mercy of God. Something we all needed to be there, Jew or Gentile. Together in Christ. And all bestowed with blessings of the exceeding richness of our Father, given by God's grace. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. Grace is unmerited, unearned and unconditional love. Things given in grace are given not because of anything we have done or who we are, by by faith in Christ, God's gift is made accessible to us all. Not of circumcision of the flesh, or the law of commandments contained in ordinances. But by grace through faith in God's mercy and Jesus' blood shed for the word. Paul acknowledges that at times, before Christ, that the Gentiles were "afar off," kept in twain, ignorant of the law and of the promise. But now, made nigh by the blood of Christ. The partition between peoples and who were elect by grace through faith, removed after the coming of Jesus. All saved become a new man. For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father. No more strangers or foreigners, we are all made part of the temple of God, with Jesus as the cornerstone, the foundation laid by the prophets and apostles. Each believer, a pillar.

For the cause of the good news, that all who believe are joint heirs, in Christ, Paul is writing as a prisoner. In chains, under tribulation, but free in Christ, he wants the Gentiles reading this epistle to understand the depths of his devotion towards the ministry unto them that he has received from God. A dispensation of grace given unto the Gentiles as it already had been to the Jews, in faith through Christ. What had in times past been a mystery. How God would achieve the promise of all nations being blessed in Abraham's seed, Jesus. Now Paul understands the mystery and is explaining it to them. That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body and partakers of His promise, in Christ by the Gospel. Paul's mission is to reveal the answer to this mystery, to proclaim the good news. To make all men see. This dispensation of grace is being extended to all, is not a different dispensation as some would claim, but the same as given the Israelites, and all men, from Adam. Since Seth and his sons called upon the name of the Lord. All who bow their knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named. And as such, with Christ dwelling in our hearts by faith, we are able to know the breadth, length, depth, and height of all the bounty of blessings made available to God's children. Amen. Again the focus of these first 3 chapters is attacking the idea that Jews are God's "chosen people," and that Gentile believers are somehow less-than in their inheritance. The Jews having sold it in their fornication for the pottage of earthly things. The change is to extend it to all men, through Jesus Christ regardless of lineage. There is no limit to the atonement, but the free will to believe the Gospel by those that receive it, and In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him. This destroys the damnable "mortal sin of presumption" made by the Catholic Church to snare the unsuspecting into never coming to salvation, and never having that confidence, put in bondage to dead works of the law, and reliant on the RCC to save them in the end. Sending millions to Hell.

Psalm 68 18 Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts for men; yea, for the rebellious also, that the Lord God might dwell among them. 19 Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah. Leading captivity captive. Freeing those in bonds only to bind that which had captured them. Jesus Christ, fulfilling the promise of God. Paul draws the parallel with Psalm 68, David prophesying the Christ to come and our salvation. Ephesians 4 is a beautiful devotional of the love we have received and should magnify with one another. That as Jesus both descended into Hell for 3 days and nights, to leave captivity captive, ascending to Heaven with our liberty from death, the keys of Hell, to rule all things. Adopted by the Father, forever, amen. Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. Note the doctrines here, that unity of faith into the body, where Christ is the head. That we are sealed by the Spirit, given eternal life, testified by the new man within us, that we may know and have confidence in our trust in God. This is the promise of salvation. Denominations that teach you can lose your salvation, that you must earn it, that only they can give it, that they are the head and the body, teaching the vanity of the mind and tossing their members to and fro with every changing wind of doctrine, rather than standing fast upon the unmoving rock of the Word...these false churches cannot save. They are the bondsmen, keeping people in chains. Some take the admonition against corrupt communication to be simply not to use vulgarity, lewdness or potty talk, but while all those things can be the type of corrupt communication Paul's writing about, it isn't what he means. In this context, he's regarding the things we say in wrath and anger, envy, strife, backbiting, tale bearing, railing, false accusations, etc. Not the words used, as if a naughty word has power to corrupt, but the means and meaning of what's being said. Is it edifying? Does it leave you blameless to share the good news without embarrassment or hypocrisy? That's the meaning, and while a cuss word can be something that can be corrupting in this context, it isn't always and discernment should be given. Jesus wasn't using corrupt communication when he said "Raca." When scripture says "ass," or "pisseth." When Song of Solomon gets a little spicy. Overly legalistic types lose their mind at a stray vulgarity while accepting hypocrisy, backbiting and railing, being holier than thou. Finally, consider that we are to edify, building up the body that is Christ's, speaking the truth in love, that they may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ. Fellow believers are in various stages of this work, babes in Christ to those more sanctified by time and experience. The backslidden and the just. Those of incredible faith, born out of tribulations we can't imagine, others struggling in tribulation right now. And our own place in that journey, in our Christian walk. We should be cognizant of this, with the same mercy and grace and love that we have received (unmerited as we are sinners), and show the same to others where we can. Being understanding. Charitable. The true kindness, not as the world measures kindness, with wickedness, enabling and justifying evil as good, but speaking the truth of God in love. 1 Peter 2 Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings, 2 As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: 3 If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious. 4 To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious, 5 Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ. 6 Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. 7 Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, 8 And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed. 9 But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light; 10 Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy. 11 Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul; 12 Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation. 13 Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme; 14 Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well. 15 For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men: 16 As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God. 17 Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king. 18 Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward. 19 For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully. 20 For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God. 21 For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps: 22 Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth: 23 Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously: 24 Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed. 25 For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.

People often say they are waiting on the revelation of the "will of God" to make decisions or a sign to show them the way. They don't know if they have the faith to make a change in their lives or the understanding to do what God wants in a given situation. They express fear at circumstances or tribulation that befalls them. They may pray for guidance and strength, but struggle to find what God wants for their life. The Bible tells us where faith comes from. It tells us God's will for us as His children. It gives instruction for how to gain knowledge, insight, understanding and peace. How to live, what our roles are. To obey those in charge of us, to love those under us. In all things, doing it for God, for that is His will. To abstain from fornication. To flee Idolatry. To trust in Him to guide us. To live by faith and to gain faith by His word. (The just shall live by faith) If you are feeling rudderless. If you are searching for more faith. If you don't know what you should do. Start with the word. Make sure you are doing the things God has told us are His will (obviously starting with obeying the Gospel, and believing on the Lord Jesus Christ). Tomorrow's study on Hebrews 11, the Hall of Faith heroes of the OT, will demonstrate how faith led them to serve the will of God.

Are you a child of God or a child of disobedience? As heirs, by Christ, we are of God the Father. And so we should walk as such. Carrying ourselves as befitting our station, in meekness because only grace has brought us in, and blameless in mercy and righteousness, a light that shines so that others may become fellow brothers, who are as what we were. The children of disobedience are fornicators, unclean, covetous, filthy and foolish talkers, jesters joking rather than giving thanks, whoremongers, idolaters. They have no share of the inheritance and God's wrath is upon them, so why walk with them? Why act as they act? Why sin as they sin? Why partake in the things unbefitting heirs? So we should walk in the light, where the sins of the dark are made manifest. Christ is that light. Making the most of our short time here, in these evil days. Not being as fools, but wise with the wisdom God has given us in his mercy. Not drunk, but in the Spirit. Paul in a few short paragraphs gives God's will for us that He's adopted. It isn't asking much, considering the gift we've been given. But the flesh is weak and wars against our spirit. Still we should strive for this bare minimum. And how are we filled with the Spirit? It's not gnosticism. It's not a secret. The Bible gives us answers. Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God. Not drowning out your thoughts with music that dishonors God. Listening to others talk, often blasphemy, all day as you work, pushing out the spiritual and filling your head with foolishness and earthly cares. Consuming the latest Jewish fables to talk about with coworkers. Sporting contests brought to you by drunkenness, gambling and vice. We all waste time, not redeeming the day, rather than being in prayer, song and praise. But the more we walk as we should, the more we are in the Spirit and absent distractions of this world, the easier it is to be in the light, and the more useful we are to God. And the more useful we are to God, the more he blesses us with the Spirit That's really what it's all about. Another way we can be drawn to the spirit over the flesh is submission to fellow believers, and obedience to the hierarchy of God. This becomes controversial, as Paul begins with wives submitting to their husbands. That as Jesus is the head of the body, the members, so to the husband is head of the wife. Far too many, male and female alike, stop reading there and take up the "war of the sexes" stances, trad v feminist, digging in heels and bringing wrath, covetousness, envy and strife to what is a unifying principle of God. Women are shown "submit" and taught to resent it. Men are shown it, and taught entitlement, and none look at how the roles are described and the responsibility being the head entails, or consider why a wife should submit to a husband who has abandoned their God-given roles. Men are called to love their wife as their own flesh. Protecting and providing for them as Jesus has for us. When men shirk this responsibility, women see no profit in submission. And the entire thing breaks down. And the two who become one flesh, under God, tear themselves asunder. Men complaining about women being loose women are part of a culture that has abdicated our duty, not loving the wives as ourselves. (Let alone neighbors to whom we have no physical attachment) MGTOW/PUA/BAP and the other gay ops designed to stoke resentments and give men the rationalizations needed to place all the blame on women, is just the boy version of the feminist that makes women feed on the fear and insecurities that male dereliction has created, to make them rebel. It's a self-perpetuating subversion. It leads inevitably to the kind of Sodom we see today. Where children are left vulnerable to predators, and trauma-induced reprobation runs rampant. So, again, the question of why we as a nation (because God judges nations here on earth), ...why as a nation are we failing, slouching to Gomorrah? Is it the children of darkness, of wrath? Doing the unseemly things they do, not having the light within? As they flail around in the darkness? Or is it the people who call themselves by His name, going along with it? The children of the light? Not shining the light but walking after the ways of the unsaved and unbelieving? Compromising, and so being compromised... It starts with us. We lead revival. Not with flowery words and enabling our own sin. Not with judgment designed to puff us up, and rationalize our faults as, "at least, not as bad as those sinners over there." We do it by walking in the Spirit. We do that by staying in the word, in prayer, in praise and thanksgiving. By being honest in our dealings. In meekly having a ready answer to our hope, which isn't in our works and good deeds, such as they are, but in Christ. By submitting to God, and His will for us. To honor our roles. This is what brings blessings to a nation, when the people who call themselves Christian act like it, and in doing so bring others into the same light.
