Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women... For the non-English speaker, understanding basic grammar can be a stumbling block for understanding God's word. "Neither... nor" is a negative correlative conjunction that connects two or more parts of a sentence to indicate that both options are not true. "Neither... nor" must be used in parallel structures, meaning both sides must be balanced. For example, if "neither" is followed by a verb, "nor" must also be followed by a verb, or call back to the original verb, and apply it equally to the object of the sentence. For example; "Neither shall he regard": "Shall" is the main verb, with "he" as the subject. "Neither" is a coordinating conjunction modifying the verb "shall regard." "The God of his fathers" is the direct object of "regard." ("The" modifies "God." "Of his fathers" is a prepositional phrase modifying "God.") "Nor" introduces the second object, "desire" which parallels "God." ("The" modifies "desire." "Of women" is a prepositional phrase modifying "desire.") So in the verse about the antichrist, taken from Daniel 11:37 Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god: for he shall magnify himself above all. ...the Bible says that the antichrist shall not regard the God of his fathers, shall not regard the desire of women, nor shall he regard any god, (small L lords.) Why? For (because, for this reason) he shall magnify himself above all. It's easy to get caught in strange doctrine and weird beliefs when you don't understand how our language works. Especially when you refuse to attend church and despise correction.

There are others, many well meaning believers, who have been raised with false Bible versions, or taught by honest pastors misled by Bible college or extrabiblical reading, into appending "...of your sins" to the word repent. Why Doctrine Matters For Baptists, doctrine is the bedrock of faith, derived only from the KJV Bible (in English) as God’s preserved and inerrant Word. It distinguishes truth from error, throughly equips believers for godly living, and protects against heresy, ensuring the church remains faithful to Christ, giving unity to believers and fellowship between independent churches (1 Timothy 4:16; 2 Timothy 4:3) Jesus’ Doctrine from the Father and the Religious Leaders’ Hatred Jesus Stressed the Doctrine Given by the Father Jesus emphasized that His doctrine was not His own but came directly from God the Father, teaching with divine authority. John 7:16 : “Jesus answered them, and said, My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.” The people and the Religious Leaders Heard and Were Astonished by His Doctrine The Jewish religious leaders, including Pharisees and scribes, heard Jesus’ doctrine and were amazed, yet questioned His authority, revealing their growing opposition. Matthew 22:33 : “And when the multitude heard this, and the Pharisees also, they were astonished at his doctrine.” (Context: Pharisees present, reacting to Jesus’ teachings on the resurrection and commandments, Matthew 22:23-34.) The Religious Leaders Sought to Kill Jesus Because of His Doctrine The religious leaders’ astonishment turned to hatred, as Jesus’ doctrine exposed their hypocrisy, leading them to plot His death. John 7:19 : “Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keepeth the law? Why go ye about to kill me?” (Context: After Jesus taught His doctrine in John 7:16-18, the Jews, including religious leaders, sought to kill Him for His teachings, as seen in their reaction in John 7:1, 25.) Doctrines are authoritative and essential for salvation, matters of faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16). Example: Salvation by faith alone (Ephesians 2:8-9). Theology: The study and systematic organization of biblical truths, often involving human interpretation. While useful, it is secondary to doctrine and not authoritative in KJVO IFB churches, which rely solely on Scripture (2 Timothy 2:15). Example: The Trinity (1 John 5:7) Opinion: Personal beliefs not explicitly taught in Scripture, often non-essential (e.g., timing of ordinances). Opinions should not divide believers (Romans 14:1). Tradition: To do things a certain way that may or may not be explicitly taught, but which have been done by our forefathers in the faith. Example: Standing for the reading of the word. Heresy: False teaching contradicting core KJV doctrines, such as denying Christ’s deity or salvation by works. Heresy is condemned and leads to spiritual destruction (2 Peter 2:1; Galatians 1:8). Shadows and Substance: Why the Old Testament Practices

Shadows and Substance: Why the Old Testament Practices Shows that the Tabernacle, sacrifices, and washings were shadows that sanctified the flesh and pointed to Christ, while righteousness has always come by faith. One deck covers the subject, ending with the new heaven where God and the Lamb are the temple. Shadows & Substance – Old Testament Practices and Salvation by Faith Adult Sunday School Shadows & Substance Old Testament Practices and Salvation by Faith ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move through the study. Tap any gold reference to read the verse. The question There is a misunderstanding among many about the Old Testament’s commands for building a temple to offer blood sacrifice to God. People ask, how does this line up with the understanding that we are saved by faith in the sacrifice of Jesus alone in the New Testament? Does this mean works were needed to be saved in the Old Testament? God commanded Moses to build the Tabernacle. And let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them. Exodus 25:8 God also commanded Moses that the people would bring sacrifices and offerings, culminating each year in the Day of Atonement, a statute for Israel to keep continually. And this shall be an everlasting statute unto you, to make an atonement for the children of Israel for all their sins once a year. And he did as the Lord commanded Moses. Leviticus 16:34 A shadow on the ground Imagine a shadow on the ground. It shows the shape of a person but is not the person. The Tabernacle and its sacrifices were shadows cast by Jesus, the real thing standing just out of sight. Hebrews 8:1-5 Hebrews 10:1 Key Point: The Tabernacle, Temple, sacrifices, washings, and dietary laws were God’s instructions to Israel, but they never saved a single soul. Salvation has always been by faith, exactly as it is for us today in Christ. The Tabernacle & Temple A dwelling place, first mobile, then permanent, where God’s presence would meet with His people. The Tabernacle “Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them.” Exodus 25:8 The Temple Later made permanent: the Ark, the mercy seat, the glory-cloud filling the house of the Lord . 1 Kings 8:8-10 1 Kings 8:10-11 These were special places marking Israel as God’s own nation, but they did not save souls. The ritual restored ceremonial cleanliness , allowing a person to approach God’s presence without defiling the sanctuary. It was never about justifying the soul, which required faith. Hebrews 9:1-10 Sacrifices, washings & dietary laws Sacrifices Animal offerings, like on the Day of Atonement, covered sin temporarily. Blood cleaned the outside; it could not fix the heart forever. Their yearly repetition underscores a temporary, external effect. Ritual purity to maintain access to the tabernacle, not a transformation of the heart. Leviticus 16:15-19 Washings & dietary laws Ceremonial cleansings and food rules kept Israel distinct and addressed ritual uncleanness. These were about physical purity and obedience, not eternal salvation. Leviticus 15:13-15 Numbers 19:1-2 Numbers 19:17-19 Carnal ordinances “Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.” These were “carnal” (fleshly) rules, temporary until Christ came. Hebrews 9:10 Purifying the flesh, not the soul For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh: Hebrews 9:13 These rituals purified the body, not the soul. Why God required them To make Israel holy, set apart among pagan nations, and to point ahead to a greater sacrifice: Jesus, who would truly save. These rituals were a “picture” of the spiritual cleansing and atonement Christ would accomplish. Hebrews 9:11-15 These rituals were like a picture book pointing to Jesus, the real Savior. Where they fell short Limitation: They could never permanently remove sin. Sacrifices offered “year by year continually” could never make the worshipper perfect. For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect. For then would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins. But in those sacrifices there is a remembrance again made of sins every year. For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. Hebrews 10:1-4 Animal sacrifices were a temporary fix, like a bandage, not a cure. The Day of Atonement The slain goat A sin offering whose blood was shed for the sins of the nation, a picture of Christ’s atoning blood. Leviticus 16:15-19 The High Priest Carried the blood of the slain goat into the Holy of Holies within the Tabernacle, sprinkling it upon the Mercy Seat, foreshadowing Christ our great High Priest. Hebrews 9:1-10 The scapegoat Bore Israel’s sins into the wilderness, symbolizing guilt removed. Leviticus 16:20-22 Jesus is the scapegoat, the Lamb slain, and the High Priest. More shadows of Christ The Passover lamb And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt. Exodus 12:13 The temporary, external protection of the Passover lamb prefigures Christ’s blood, which provides eternal spiritual redemption. The scapegoat And when he hath made an end of reconciling the holy place, and the tabernacle of the congregation, and the altar, he shall bring the live goat: And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins, putting them upon the head of the goat, and shall send him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness: And the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited: and he shall let go the goat in the wilderness. Leviticus 16:20-22 A ritual act pointing to Christ, who “bare our sins in his own body” 1 Peter 2:24 , but symbolic and external, requiring annual repetition, unlike Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice. Abraham believed God Before any Tabernacle or Law existed, Abraham was already saved by faith. Before the Law, salvation was by faith. The sacrificial system dealt with ceremonial cleanliness, but righteousness before God was always tied to faith, not ritual. And he believed in the Lord ; and he counted it to him for righteousness. Genesis 15:6 Abraham was saved by believing God’s promise, not by sacrifices or rules, and long before circumcision was given at 99. Romans 4:1-5 Romans 4:9-13 Faith in the Old Testament The Old Testament itself critiques leaning on sacrifice for spiritual standing. God sought faith and obedience over the blood of bulls and goats. Counted for righteousness And he believed in the Lord ; and he counted it to him for righteousness. Genesis 15:6 The just shall live by faith Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith. Habakkuk 2:4 A broken and contrite heart For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise. Psalm 51:16-17 Cease to do evil To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the Lord : I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats. Isaiah 1:11 Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. Isaiah 1:16-17 Hebrews 10:4-6 Hosea 6:6 Christ fulfills the law Jesus’ death was the one-time, perfect sacrifice that saves the soul forever, accomplishing both sanctification and forgiveness, resolving what the Old Testament system never could. Hebrews 10:5-14 Wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, redemption Jesus doesn’t just cover sin. He makes us holy in God’s eyes. 1 Corinthians 1:30 I will remember their sins no more The covenant that makes it so. Hebrews 10:15-17 Saved by faith today Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: Romans 5:1 We are saved by trusting Christ, not by rituals or works. Faith gives peace with God that no sacrifice could fully give. Old Testament rituals were like a map leading to Jesus, the destination. No temple needed In the New Jerusalem, no physical Temple is needed. God and the Lamb are the temple. We do not need rituals or buildings, because Jesus’ sacrifice makes us holy forever. And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it. Revelation 21:22 Revelation 21:21-24 Christ’s work means we are fully sanctified by faith, not by repeated washings or sacrifices. The Old Testament pointed to this future, where God’s presence is enough. We are His temple 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 2 Corinthians 6:16 1 Peter 2:5 The Tabernacle was like a tent for God’s presence; now, Jesus Himself is our home. Key takeaways Fleshly sanctification Sacrifices and washings restored ritual purity to allow access to the tabernacle. They addressed external states but could not cleanse the conscience or remove sin’s guilt. Spiritual sanctification Righteousness before God came through faith. Sacrifices were never a substitute for faith, but a means to maintain covenantal relationship in the physical sphere. Christ as fulfillment Christ’s sacrifice transcends the Old Testament system, purifying both flesh and spirit. His blood cleanses the conscience and grants eternal redemption, what the rituals could only symbolize. Practical application: Encourage trust in Christ’s finished work, not in personal efforts to earn salvation. Read Hebrews 9 and Hebrews 10 at home to see how Jesus fulfills the Law. Conclusion The Tabernacle, Temple, sacrifices, washings, and dietary laws were God’s way to teach Israel about holiness and point to Jesus. Salvation has always been by faith, and Christ’s sacrifice makes us holy forever, as we will see in Heaven, with no need for a Temple. Old Testament practices addressed outward holiness, not the saving of the soul. Salvation is by faith alone, as it was for Abraham, and is for us in Christ. Jesus’ sacrifice makes us holy forever, replacing every ritual. 2 Corinthians 5:21 But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: 1 Corinthians 1:30 No sacrifice but Jesus. You are saved by faith, and Jesus has already made you holy in God’s eyes. Rest in that! ‹ Prev Contents Next › Scripture Close Contents Close

"Are Saved" or "Being Saved"? 1 Corinthians 1:18 and 15:2 Looks at the Greek participle in 1 Corinthians 1:18 and why the KJV's "are saved" fits the settled work of God, compared with the modern "being saved." Connects the wording to eternal security. The Greek term σῳζομένοις is a present passive participle (dative masculine plural) from the verb σῴζω (“to save”). It literally means “to those saved.” The present tense in Greek participles can indicate either an ongoing action or a state resulting from a completed action, and the passive voice emphasizes that the action is performed by an external agent—God—rather than by the subjects themselves. The King James Bible renders σῳζομένοις as “are saved,” using the simple present tense to emphasize a completed action with an assured future state. This translation aligns with the doctrine of eternal security: salvation is a definitive, irreversible act accomplished by God, and “are saved” presents it as a settled, present reality for the believer. Modern versions (NASB, ESV, NIV, etc.) typically translate it as “are being saved,” using the English present progressive. While this reflects one possible aspect of the Greek present tense and highlights ongoing effects, the progressive form can introduce ambiguity, suggesting a process that is incomplete or could potentially be lost. In 1 Corinthians 1:18 the word of the cross is the power of God precisely to those who stand in the state of having been saved—God’s effective, completed work secures the believer. In 1 Corinthians 15:2 Paul writes, “by which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you.” The “if” clause is not a condition for retaining salvation but the evidence of genuine faith; true believers will hold fast because they are already saved (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29). The present passive participle here carries its common New Testament sense of a current state resulting from a past, completed action. Scripture repeatedly presents salvation as a finished act (Romans 8:30; Ephesians 2:8–9) that guarantees eternal security for everyone truly in Christ. Therefore, in both 1 Corinthians 1:18 and 15:2 the rendering “are saved” more accurately conveys the assured, completed, and eternally secure state of the believer, while “are being saved,” though grammatically possible, risks undermining that certainty by implying an unfinished or losable process. The word σῳζομένοις is best understood as describing a permanent present condition of salvation fully accomplished and eternally kept by God.

Six Predecessors Paved the Way Earlier English Bibles. William Tyndale Why Was Translating the Bible Considered “Heretical”? Challenging Church Authority: The Catholic Church held absolute authority on religious issues and guarded its power. Translations of the Bible into vernacular languages like English threatened that authority. Providing the Bible in English allowed literate individuals to read and interpret Scripture for themselves, often arriving at conclusions that differed from unbiblical Catholic doctrine. “Lord, open the King of England’s eyes.” William Tyndale, before his execution This prayer was partially answered when King Henry VIII later allowed the English Bible to be available in every parish church. Translation, Text & Impact The King James Version was created by a team of 47 scholars (54 were originally appointed), including the greatest linguists of the time, from various backgrounds, ensuring a more comprehensive and accurate translation. Collaboration Textual Sources. Translators of the KJV utilized earlier translations and the original preserved manuscripts: the Masoretic Text for the Old Testament, and the Antioch manuscripts, called “The Received Text,” or Textus Receptus, for the New Testament, striving for accuracy while adapting the language to be accessible and beautiful to the English-speaking public. Literary Style A Literary Masterpiece. The KJV is renowned for its poetic and rhythmic style, making it not only a religious text but also a literary masterpiece that has influenced English literature significantly. The King James Version has left an indelible mark on Christianity, used for 400 years to win souls on every continent and country, shaping the culture, language, and literature of the world, and the expressions and idioms that remain in common use even today. Its Powerful, Preserved Nature The King James Version has profoundly influenced literature, language, and art, but its powerful, divinely inspired and preserved nature, as the complete Word of God without error in English, the “lingua franca” of this age, has shaped nations, influenced kings and presidents, converted millions, fed the spirit of believers, and served as the rock of Christianity since 1611. But the truth of the matter is (not to detract from the labours of those men in any way) it should be noted, definitely more often than it is, that there was a great company of men who laboured much harder and sacrificed much more than they did to give us the word of God. William Tyndale, a courageous reformer, devoted his life to translating the Holy Scriptures into English, ensuring the common man could access God’s pure Word. His work laid the foundation for the Authorized Version, preserving biblical truth against Roman Catholic corruption. Betrayed and condemned, Tyndale was martyred in 1536, strangled and burned at the stake by Rome’s authorities for his unwavering commitment. As he faced death, he boldly declared, “Lord, open the King of England’s eyes,” a final plea for the spread of God’s truth, cementing his legacy as a faithful hero. It is estimated that the KJB contains well over 80% of William Tyndale's work. Taking into consideration the purification that took place between Tyndale's work and the KJB, the KJB Translators actually made relatively few changes to the text. Much of the work was done by men who risked... and lost... their lives to give us the Book. The KJV committees had rules established by King James for how they would translate, and what they could use of previous translations: Translation Rule #14 - "These translations to be used, when they agree better with the text than the Bishops' Bible: Tyndale's, Coverdale's, Matthew's, Whitchurch's [Great], Geneva." Not martyred, died peacefully. John Rogers (c. 1500–1555): Edited Matthew Bible (1537) under pseudonym “Thomas Matthew.” Martyred, burned at the stake by Roman Catholic authorities under Queen Mary. William Whittingham (c. 1524–1579): Led Geneva Bible (1560) translation. Not martyred, died peacefully. Matthew Parker (1504–1575): Led Bishops’ Bible (1568). Not martyred, died peacefully. Prophecy Power : Over 1,800 prophecies, with 300+ about Jesus fulfilled perfectly, like His Bethlehem birth ( Micah 5:2 ). Self-Referencing Scripture : The Bible cites itself over 1,000 times, with phrases like “It is written” affirming its authority. The KJV is its own Dictionary !: You can generally find the meaning of a word by looking for its first appearance and seeing the context. Year-Long Read : 1,189 chapters—read 3.3 chapters daily to finish in a year , or read 30 min. daily and finish in under 5 months! 66 Books, One Story : 39 Old Testament + 27 New Testament books weave God’s redemptive plan from Genesis to Revelation . Verses Galore : 31,102 verses in the KJV, packed with wisdom, history, and God’s Word for all. No Contradictions : Despite centuries and authors, the Bible’s message stays unified, a testament to divine inspiration. Three Tongues : Written in Hebrew (Old Testament), Aramaic (parts of Daniel, Ezra), and Greek (New Testament). Shortest & Longest Chapters : Psalm 117 (2 verses) is the shortest; Psalm 119 (176 verses) is the longest, a meditation on God’s Word. Shortest Verse : John 11:35—“Jesus wept”—shows Christ’s humanity and mercy in just two words. How the KJV Bible Is Broken Down The KJV’s 66 books are grouped by purpose and style, telling God’s story from creation to eternity. Here’s the breakdown: Pentateuch (5 Books) : God’s creation, salvation from Egypt, giving of the law and Israel’s origins. Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy. Historical Books (12 Books) : Israel’s journey from conquest to exile, and return from captivity. Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 & 2 Samuel, 1 & 2 Kings, 1 & 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther. Poetic/Wisdom Books (5 Books) : Songs, prayers,wisdom. Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon. Major Prophets (5 Books) : God’s word through bold prophets (longer books). Isaiah, Jeremiah/Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel. Minor Prophets (12 Books) : Short, powerful prophetic books. Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Gospels (4 Books) : Jesus’s life, death, and resurrection. Matthew, Mark, Luke, John. History (1 Book) : The early church’s growth. Acts. Pauline Epistles (13 Books) : Paul’s letters to churches and leaders. Romans, 1 & 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 & 2 Thessalonians, 1 & 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, and Hebrews. General Epistles (8 Books) : Letters by other Apostles and saints, written for all believers. James, 1 & 2 Peter, 1, 2 & 3 John, Jude. Prophecy (1 Book) : Christ’s return and final victory. A line of believers, not a chain of churches The Trail of Blood follows a simple, observable truth: in every age since Christ there have been believers living faith to faith, holding the same gospel and the same Bible distinctives, and paying for it in blood. What history shows An unbroken line of believers, saved by grace through faith, who held believer’s baptism, the authority of scripture and the independence of the local church, under different names in every century. Romans 1:17 What it does not prove An unbroken chain of one church, of pastors laying hands on pastors back to the apostles. That claim (Landmarkism, the “bride” doctrine) builds a rigid system on more than history or scripture can show. We learn from this history; we are not married to a system. The line that matters is faith, and the Bible decides what a church is, not a chain of ordinations. The gates of hell shall not prevail And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it . Matthew 16:18 Christ promised His church would endure. He also promised it would suffer. The world has always hated those who hold His word without compromise. John 15:20 2 Timothy 3:12 And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints , and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration. Revelation 17:6 The early church 33–100 Apostolic Era. The church founded by Jesus Christ spreads by apostolic preaching. Believers, first called Christians at Antioch, practice believer’s baptism and local church autonomy, persecuted by Jewish and Roman authorities for holding to scripture. Acts 11:26 100–313 Post-apostolic persecutions. Groups like the Montanists (c. 150) hold to biblical purity against an emerging hierarchy, under Roman persecution, and work to put Scripture in the common tongue. The rise of the imperial church 313 The Edict of Milan. Constantine legalizes Christianity, and the state church that follows persecutes the churches that will not submit to it, like the Donatists (300s), who reject infant baptism and the hierarchy. 313–600 Rome comes to restrict Scripture to the Latin Vulgate and suppress the common tongue. Dissenters face death, exile, and the burning of their writings. The same pattern repeats for a thousand years: the Bible in the people’s own language, believer’s baptism, and no master but Christ, answered with the sword. Acts 5:29 Medieval dissenters 600–1200 Paulicians and Bogomils. They keep believer’s baptism and Scripture-based worship, through Catholic crusades and executions. Councils condemn Scripture in any tongue but Latin, and the translations are burned. 1200–1500 Waldensians and Albigenses. Peter Waldo’s followers (c. 1173) and the Cathars preach biblical simplicity and put the Bible into the common tongue. The papal bull Ad Abolendam (1184) orders them put down. 1209 Béziers: up to 20,000 killed in one day 1209–29 the Albigensian Crusade: hundreds of thousands killed 1545 Mérindol: Waldensian villages massacred Anabaptists and the Reformation Anabaptists (c. 1525) revive believer’s baptism and separation from the state church, and are persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. 1527 Felix Manz drowned in Zürich 1529 George Blaurock burned 1536 William Tyndale strangled and burned Tyndale gave England the Bible in English, and his books were burned under Rome’s decrees. Under Queen Mary (1553–1558) more than 280 were burned at the stake, John Rogers, Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley among them. The French Wars of Religion (1562–1598), with the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre (1572), took up to three million lives. Baptists by name 1609 John Smyth forms a Baptist congregation of exiles in Amsterdam; English Baptists follow, under Anglican persecution, their preachers jailed and their Bibles burned. 1651 John Clarke and Obadiah Holmes are fined, and Holmes is whipped in Boston, for preaching Baptist principles in Puritan Massachusetts. 1655 The Piedmont Easter massacre of the Waldensians, in the Savoyard wars (1655–1690). 1660s–80s Virginia’s Anglican laws fine and jail Baptists for preaching without a license. Liberty Persecution drove believers to the American colonies, where the Pilgrims landed in 1620. In time, the Baptist conviction of soul liberty became the nation’s. The Great Awakening (1730s–1740s) spread the gospel, and unlicensed preachers were arrested for it. The new states, many settled by those fleeing state churches, adopted the Baptist principle of religious liberty: the First Amendment forbids a state church. With that freedom, the gospel spread and Baptist churches formed throughout the nation. Terms & Conditions – The Vocabulary of the Faith Adult Sunday School · Week 6 Terms & Conditions The vocabulary of the faith: plain definitions for the words we build our doctrine on ✦ ✦ ✦ Every field of study has its own language, and theology is no exception. Before we can rightly divide the Word, we need to agree on what its key terms actually mean. Tap any gold reference for its supporting Scripture. A Working Glossary How We Are Saved: Grace, Faith, Repentance Soteriology : the doctrines and teachings of salvation. Six terms that describe how a sinner comes to stand right before a holy God. Grace The unmerited, unearned, undeserved favor of God. Mercy extended to someone by the unconditional love of another. The favorable influence of God on persons and situations. Romans 11:6 Faith The persuasion of mind that something is true, trustworthy, and able to be counted on, without having seen direct evidence. Belief and trust in someone’s word are the characteristics of faith. Every man is given a measure of faith by God ( Romans 12:3 ). Hebrews 11:1 Ephesians 1:12-14 Repentance A change of mind or heart when presented with new information. The Greek metanoeo means “to change one’s mind.” The emphasis is on a shift in thinking and perspective, not on feeling remorse or regret. Sorrow at wrongdoing being pointed out can lead to repentance, but is not repentance itself. Jonah 3:10 Acts 19:5 2 Corinthians 7:10 How We Are Saved: Salvation, Justification, Propitiation Salvation The deliverance from sin and its consequences, by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. It is a gift of God, not something earned by works, a one-time event that, once secured, cannot be lost. “Save,” “saved,” and “salvation” are also used in Scripture for physical rescue, depending on context. Ephesians 2:8-9 John 10:28-29 Jude 5 Justification The act of God by which He declares a sinner to be righteous and free from the guilt of sin. This is a legal declaration based on the righteousness of Christ imputed to the believer through faith: “just as I’ve never sinned.” Romans 5:1 Romans 4:5 Propitiation The act of appeasing or satisfying God’s holy wrath against sin. Jesus Christ, through His death on the cross, is the propitiation for our sins. 1 John 2:2 Hebrews 11:1 Hebrews 11:1 Grace: God’s Riches At Christ’s Expense Grace: God’s Riches At Christ’s Expense Ephesians 2:8-9 Biblical Repentance Biblical Repentance Past, Present & Future Justification, sanctification, and glorification are three tenses of the same salvation: a past event, a present process, and a future certainty. Past, Present & Future: Justification, Sanctification, Glorification Every Belief System Reduces to One of Two Doors Every Belief System Reduces to One of Two Doors The Godhead: Trinity, Godhead, Holy Who God is: His triune nature, and the attributes that belong to Him alone. Trinity The theological name for the concept of the Godhead: the three persons of God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 1 John 5:7 Godhead The essential being, or nature, of God. All persons of the Trinity are of the Godhead. Colossians 2:9 Holy Hallowed; consecrated or set apart to a sacred use, or to the service or worship of God, as with the holy sabbath, holy oil, holy vessels, a holy nation, the holy temple, a holy priesthood. God Himself is holy, being perfect and separated from all things that aren’t holy. The Godhead: Omnipotent, Omniscient Omnipotent All-powerful. A trait found only in the Godhead. Revelation 19:6 Omniscient All-knowing. A trait found only in the Godhead. 1 John 3:20 The Shield of the Trinity The Shield of the Trinity God’s Sovereign Plan How God’s choosing and man’s believing work together in salvation. Elect Chosen. The saved: the sons and daughters of God. God determined that all who believe on Christ Jesus would be the elect. Predestination The act of God determining something to be so before it occurs. Jesus was predestined to be the Lamb slain to take away the sins of the world. In terms of salvation, God predestined the means and results of salvation, not who specifically would be saved. Revelation 13:8 Romans 8:29-31 Ephesians 1:4-11 Reprobate Rejected. In the context of salvation, it refers to those given over to a reprobate mind because they rejected the truth of God and held it in unrighteousness: conscience seared as with a hot iron, filled with all unrighteousness, unable to come to the knowledge of the truth. Romans 1:28 The Christian Life: Sanctification and Separation Salvation is a gift, received once. What follows, a lifetime of being set apart and following Christ, is a different matter altogether. Sanctification The process by which a believer is set apart from sin and made holy: both a lifelong process that begins at salvation and continues until the Rapture, AND the finished work of the Spirit on our spirit, made clean by the blood of Christ. Our sanctification will never be perfect; the sanctification of the Spirit is perfect. 1 Thessalonians 4:3 1 Thessalonians 5:23 Separation A biblical doctrine commanding believers to be separate from sin, the world, and false doctrine: personal separation in conduct and character, as well as separation from churches and organizations that do not hold to sound doctrine, and from people who compel us toward sin. We are separated not only from the world, but toward the doctrines of God. 2 Corinthians 6:17 1 Peter 2:11-12 The Christian Life: Disciple and Apostle Disciple A follower of someone or something. In Christianity, it is following Christ not just as a saved believer, but walking in Him, in the Spirit, and denying yourself to serve others. It is not a requirement for salvation, but a calling we all have. Not all believers are disciples. We must choose to pick up our cross and follow Him, and being a disciple has a cost. Matthew 16:24 Luke 14:28-30 Apostle Literally, a person sent by another; a messenger, an envoy. A special follower of Christ, used as a witness to His life and to spread the Gospel, generally applied to the twelve chosen for this purpose. Rapture Latin for “caught up,” a theological term for the resurrection of believers on the day of redemption, the gathering of the elect. The exact timing of this event is disputed by differing interpretations of Scripture surrounding it, but the reality of it is indisputable. Matthew 24:31 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 Millennium The period of time between the end of the wrath, where Satan is bound for 1,000 years in Hell, and his release to deceive the nations for “a little season.” This view is called Premillennialism by those holding a “postmillennial” or “amillennial” position. Rightly Dividing the Word Two opposite approaches to Scripture: one starts with the text, the other starts with a conclusion already in hand. Exegesis Receiving doctrine from the interpretation or understanding of Scripture. “The Bible says it, I believe it.” You start with the text and let it speak. Eisegesis Using the text to justify existing traditions or opinions, and to confirm biases. You start with a conclusion and go looking for a verse to support it. Watch for it: “Faith without works is dead” ( James 2:20 ); “Baptism doth now save us” ( 1 Peter 3:21 ); “Make Jesus Lord of your life”; “Repent of your sin to be saved.” Context matters: God is not the author of confusion ( 1 Corinthians 14:33 ), and it is not up to you to square a contradiction for the person who introduced it. Every man is given a measure of faith by God.( Romans 12:3 ) Repentance: A change of mind/heart when presented with new information. In the New Testament, the Greek word most commonly translated as "repent" is " metanoeo " (μετανοέω), which means "to change one's mind". The related noun, metanoia (μετάνοια), means "change of mind" or "repentance". The meaning emphasizes a shift in thinking and perspective, rather than feeling remorse or regret. God repents 14 times in the Bible. ( Jonah 3:10 And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not. Acts19:5 T hen said Paul, John verily baptized with the baptism of repentance , saying unto the people, that they should believe on him which should come after him, that is, on Christ Jesus. ) Sorrow at wrongdoing being pointed out can lead to repentance, but is not repentance. ( 2 Corinthians 7:10 For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.) Trinity : Theological name for the concept of the Godhead, the three persons of God; The Father, Son and holy Spirit. (1 John 5:7 For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one .) Godhead: the essential being or the nature of God. All persons of the Trinity are of the Godhead. ( Colossians 2:9 - For in [Jesus] dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily .) Salvation: The deliverance from sin and its consequences, by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. It is a gift of God, not something earned by works. ( Ephesians 2:8-9 For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. ) It is a one-time event that, once secured, cannot be lost. ( John 10:28-29 And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand. ) Save, saved and salvation are used for physical rescue as well, depending on the context.( Jude 1:5 I will therefore put you in remembrance, though ye once knew this, how that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not .) Elect: Chosen. The saved. The sons and daughters of God. God determined that all who believe on Christ Jesus would be the elect. Predestination: The act of God determining something to be so before it occurs. Jesus was predestined to be the lamb slain to take away the sins of the world. ( Revelation 13:9 And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. ) In terms of salvation, God predestined the means and results of salvation, not who would be saved ( Romans 8:29-31 For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?, Ephesians 1:4-11 According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace; Wherein he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence; Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself: That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him: In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will. ) Reprobate: Rejected. In the context of salvation, it refers to those who have been given over to a reprobate mind because they rejected the truth of God, and held it in unrighteousness. Conscience seared as with a hot iron, psychopaths. Filled with all unrighteousness. Sons of Belial. Twice-dead. Unable to come to the knowledge of the truth. ( Romans 1:28 And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient. ) Justification: The act of God by which He declares a sinner to be righteous and free from the guilt of sin. This is a legal declaration based on the righteousness of Christ imputed to the believer through faith. “ Just as I’ve never sinned” ( Romans 5:1 Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: Romans 4:5 But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness ) Propitiation: The act of appeasing or satisfying God's holy wrath against sin. Jesus Christ, through His death on the cross, is the propitiation for our sins. ( 1 John 2:2 And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world .) Sanctification: The process by which a believer is set apart from sin and made holy. This is both a lifelong process that begins at salvation and continues until the believer is redeemed at the Rapture, AND the work of the Spirit on our spirit, made clean by the blood of Christ. Our sanctification will never be perfect. The sanctification of the Spirit is perfect. ( 1 Thessalonians 4:3 For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: 1 Thessalonians 5:23 And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ .) Separation: A biblical doctrine that commands believers to be separate from sin, the world, and false doctrine. This includes personal separation in conduct and character, as well as separation from churches and organizations that do not hold to sound doctrine, and people who compel us towards sin. ( 2 Corinthians 6:17 Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you. ) Holding biblical standards in behavior, dress and attitudes. We are separated not only from the world, but seprated towards the doctrines of God. ( 1 Peter 2:11-12 Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul; Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation .) Holy: Hallowed; consecrated or set apart to a sacred use, or to the service or worship of God; frequently in Scripture; such as the holy sabbath; holy oil; holy vessels; a holy nation; the holy temple; a holy priesthood. God is Himself is holy, being perfect and separated from all things that aren’t holy. Omnipotent: All powerful. A trait only found in the Godhead. ( Revelation 19:4 And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. ) Omniscient: All knowing. A trait only found in the Godhead. ( 1 John 3:20 For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. ) Disciple: A follower of someone or something. In Christianity, it is following Christ not just as a saved believer, but walking in Him, in the Spirit, and denying yourself to serve others. It is not a requirement for salvation, but a calling we all have. Not all believers are disciples. We must choose to pick up our cross and follow Him ( Matthew 16:24 Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. ) Being a disciple has a cost associated with it ( Luke 14:28-30 For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish. ) Apostle: Literally, a person sent by another; a messenger; envoy. A special follower of Christ, used as witnesses to His life and to spread the Gospel; generally applied to the 12 chosen for this purpose. ( Mark 3:14 And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach. ) Rapture: Latin for “caught up,” a theological term for the resurrection of believers on the day of redemption, gathering of the elect. The exact timing of this event is disputed by differing interpretations of scripture surrounding the event, but the reality of it is indisputable. ( Matt 24:31 And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. , 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him. For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep. For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words. ) Eschatology : The doctrines and teachings of the End Times Millenium : The period of time between the end of the wrath, where Satan is bound for 1,000 years in Hell, and his release to deceive the nations for a “little season.” ( Revelation 20:1-3 And I saw an angel come down from heaven, having the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain in his hand. And he laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years. And cast him into the bottomless pit, and shut him up, and set a seal upon him, that he should deceive the nations no more, till the thousand years should be fulfilled: and after that he must be loosed a little season .) Called Premillennialism by those holding a “ postmillennialism ,” or “ amillennialism ” position. Soteriology : The doctrines and teachings of Salvation Exegesis : Receiving doctrine from interpretation or understanding of scripture, “Bible says it, I believe it.” Eisegesis: Using the text to justify existing traditions or opinions, confirm biases.

Week 8: The Doctrine of Christ Presents Jesus as promised, pre-incarnate, Creator, eternal Son, fully God and fully man, and the only way of salvation. Includes the Old Testament theophanies, the seven I Am statements, and a match-the-verse worksheet. Opening Scripture And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory. 1 Timothy 3:16 The Promise of Christ From the Garden onward, Scripture points forward to one coming Deliverer. Genesis 3:15 The first prophecy of Christ, as a coming deliverer. The promise to Abraham Now the Lord had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing: And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. Theophanies / Christophanies Old Testament appearances of Jesus — the “Angel of the Lord ” and other pre-incarnate visitations widely understood as the Son of God, seen before Bethlehem. The Angel of the Lord and Hagar And the angel of the Lord found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur. And he said, Hagar, Sarai’s maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? And she said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai. And the angel of the Lord said unto her, Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands. And the angel of the Lord said unto her, I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude. And the angel of the Lord said unto her, Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the Lord hath heard thy affliction. And he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren. And she called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me? Week 9: The Doctrine of the Holy Spirit

Week 9: The Doctrine of the Holy Spirit Studies the Comforter, His deity, His work in convicting the world, and His role in salvation and sanctification. Also covers gifts, fruit, and blasphemy against the Holy Ghost. The Doctrine of the Holy Spirit – The Comforter Adult Sunday School · Week 9 The Doctrine of the Holy Spirit The Comforter: His nature, His promise, and His work in the life of every believer ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move through the study. The Comforter Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you. And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment: Of sin, because they believe not on me; Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more; Of judgment, because the prince of this world is judged. I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now. John 16:7-12 He reproves the world The Spirit of God, who was in the beginning, who inspired the prophets, who fell upon the men of God throughout the Old Testament, has other roles and responsibilities in the New Testament we are under. He reproves , convicting the world of sin. That is, saved or unsaved people; that little voice is our conscience. He reproves the world of righteousness, silently pointing the lost toward faith in Christ. And of judgment, showing us that the prince of this world, that is, Satan, is wrong and will be destroyed. The Spirit of truth He is the Spirit of truth. When we hear the truth, especially from the Word of God, the thing that catches our attention and makes us listen is the Spirit. He moves saved believers into the path of the unsaved that they may hear the gospel: divine appointments. He softens hearts and opens ears. He helps lead people to salvation, if they respond. Once we believe Once we believe, He indwells us. He quickens our spirit so that we can know Him; this is regeneration. He sanctifies that new man inside us, sealing us unto redemption. The Bible says He is the earnest of our inheritance, the down payment of God upon us, His purchased possession. He is the Spirit of adoption that lets us know we are the children of God, crying “Abba!” or “Father.” The Spirit testifies within us that we have eternal life. He guides, remembers and intercedes He guides us to all truth and lets us know truth from error. He brings to memory the word of God when we need it. He intercedes in our prayers, even when we don’t know what to pray for. He opens up knowledge to us and understanding when we read the Bible. When we walk in the Spirit, the Bible says, we don’t fulfill the lusts of the flesh. He keeps us honest. We are His temple. The Bible uses “Spirit” and “Ghost” interchangeably. The Holy Spirit and the Holy Ghost are one and the same. The nature and attributes of the Spirit The Holy Spirit is a distinct person of the Godhead, possessing all the attributes of God. Eternal Omnipotent Omniscient Omnipresent The promise of the Spirit Poured out upon all flesh And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions: Joel 2:28 A prophecy fulfilled in Acts 2. Gifts of the Spirit Diversities of gifts, the same Spirit The Spirit gives a variety of gifts for the edification of the body. 1 Corinthians 12:4-11 Gifts differing according to grace A list of gifts including prophecy, ministry, teaching, exhortation, giving, ruling, and mercy. Romans 12:6-8 Gifted men to the church Christ gives gifted men to the church. Ephesians 4:11 Gifts and fruit The gifts and the fruit of the Spirit are often discussed together, but they are different in purpose. Gifts are supernatural abilities given by God to a believer for the benefit of others and the church (teaching, helps, prophecy), given as the Spirit wills; not every believer has the same gifts. Fruit , on the other hand, is the character produced by the Spirit living in a believer’s life. It is not an ability but a reflection of the Spirit’s work, and all believers are commanded to cultivate it. A person may have a powerful gift, but the true mark of spiritual maturity is the presence of the fruit. The fruit of the Spirit Galatians 5:22-23: nine qualities, one fruit, produced in every believer who walks in the Spirit. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. Outline of the Covenants: Rightly Dividing

Outline of the Covenants: Rightly Dividing Sets out a framework in which many Old Testament promises were conditional on Israel's obedience, traced through a timeline from Genesis to the prophets. Explains how the New Testament presents the fulfillment under the new covenant. The "Rightly Dividing" Framework: From Conditional Promises to New Covenant Reality This document presents a framework for reconciling apparent contradictions between Old Testament prophecies and their New Testament fulfillments. The core principle is that many Old Testament prophecies were conditional , dependent on Israel's obedience and repentance. When these conditions were unmet, God's plan shifted, and the New Testament presents a reconfigured, often spiritual, fulfillment of those promises. This framework views the Old Testament prophecies as "what could have been" and the New Testament narratives as "what will be" under the new covenant, explaining the differences in timing, scope, and detail between the two testaments. The shift from Old Testament's conditional, national promises to the New Testament's unconditional, spiritual realities is best understood through a historical timeline of Israel's progressive rejection of the "kingdom offer". The framework also distinguishes between individual judgment by faith and national judgment by works, emphasizing God’s longsuffering and the free will he offers between life and death. God's foreknowledge allows him to offer conditional promises while respecting human choices, adapting his plan and redirecting blessings to a "new nation" of believers when conditions are not met. A Biblical Timeline of Conditional Promises, Choices, and Changed Outcomes This section traces a biblically consecutive timeline of conditional promises and their outcomes, from Genesis through Revelation. Genesis: The Foundation of Winnowing Promise: God promises a great nation and land to Abraham. God also promised that Abraham’s seed, singular, which is Christ Jesus, would be the light of nations. The promise of spiritual salvation is unconditional, only faith is required. But the physical promise and the land's immediate possession requires obedience. Choice: Cain chooses disobedience by offering an improper sacrifice and murdering Abel, leading to his exile and a shift of the godly line to Seth. Abraham's lack of faith also delays the fulfillment of God's promise. Outcome: God’s plan adapts, winnowing the unfaithful while preserving the promised line. Exodus and Leviticus: National Promises and Priesthood Promise: God promises to deliver Israel from Egypt and give them Canaan, on the condition of covenantal obedience. The priesthood is also conditionally offered based on faithfulness. Choice: Pharaoh’s defiance leads to judgment on Egypt. Israel’s murmuring and Moses’ disobedience in striking the rock forfeit his entry into Canaan. Israel’s idolatry with the golden calf leads to the Levites being chosen for the priesthood due to their loyalty. Outcome: The land promise is delayed. The priesthood shifts from the firstborn to the Levites. Numbers and Deuteronomy: Forfeiture of the Promised Land Promise: God reaffirms the land promise, contingent on Israel’s trust and obedience. God outlines blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. Choice: The Kadeshbarnea rebellion, spurred by the spies' unbelief, causes God to declare that the rebellious generation will not see the promised land. Korah’s rebellion also leads to his destruction. Outcome: The land promise is delayed for forty years, and that generation dies in the wilderness. The promise persists for future generations, but national disobedience ultimately leads to exile. Joshua to 1 Kings: Fulfillment, Disobedience, and Forfeited Dynasties Promise: The land promise is fulfilled under Joshua, but continued possession requires obedience. God promises Saul a lasting dynasty, contingent on his obedience. God also promises Jeroboam a sure dynasty like David’s, on the condition of obedience. Choice: Achan’s sin brings defeat at Ai, and Israel’s failure to fully expel the Canaanites leads to future idolatry. Saul disobeys God's commands, leading to his rejection as king and the forfeiture of his lineage in the Messiah’s line. Jeroboam’s idolatry leads to the destruction of his house. Outcome: The fulfilled land promise under Joshua is annulled by the curses God laid out for their disobedience. The Messianic lineage shifts to David from Saul. The promise to Jeroboam’s line is gone, because he rejected the faith of his fathers for a religion of idols that he invented, leading to the destruction of the 10 northern tribes. The Prophets: Reprobate Silver and Conditional Eschatology Promise: God promises judgment on nations and conditional restoration for Israel. He promises restoration if Judah repents. Ezekiel 40–48 promises a restored temple and land, contingent on Israel’s repentance and shame for their iniquities. Zechariah promises a kingdom "if ye will diligently obey". Choice: Babylon's pride leads to its destruction. Judah’s persistent idolatry renders them "reprobate silver," and they are rejected. Israel's failure to repent forfeits Ezekiel's vision, rendering it "what could have been". Their failure to obey Zechariah's commands forfeits the promises. Outcome: God’s mercy offers a remnant a return from exile. The promise of a restored kingdom and temple is forfeited, and the blessings redirect to the "new nation" of believers. Hope: There is always an offer to repentance. The natural branches can be graft back in. Old Testament believers are joint-heirs with Christ and will see their Kingdom in the Millenial, ruling and reigning from Jerusalem with Jesus, just as the believing Gentiles, the wild branches grafted into the Vine will rule with Him throughout the nations of men. The promise to Abraham and to David will be fulfilled. The Kingdom Offer Timeline: The Road to Final Rejection The Opening of the Kingdom Offer : John the Baptist and Jesus both preached, "Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand". This was a literal offer to Israel, confirmed by Jesus' miracles and a message exclusively to "the lost sheep of the house of Israel". The Rise of National Rejection : The Pharisees committed the "blasphemy against the Holy Ghost" by attributing Jesus’ power to Satan. Jesus’ subsequent teaching in parables symbolized the concealment of truth from those with hardened hearts. The Official Rejection : The ultimate rejection occurred at the Cross, where the nation's leaders and people rejected Jesus as their King and chose a murderer instead. The Final Offer and "The Last Straw" : After the cross, God extended one final chance, with Peter promising that Jesus would return if the nation repented. The definitive "last straw" was the martyrdom of Stephen in Acts 7. His sermon exposed their complete rejection, and their act of stoning him confirmed their "no". New Testament Fulfillment and Resolution (The "What Will Be") After Israel's final rejection, the kingdom offer to the nation was withdrawn, and the establishment of the earthly kingdom was delayed until Christ's Second Coming. God's plan shifted, and the prophecies were fulfilled in a reconfigured, spiritual way under the new covenant. The focus shifted to a universal, spiritual kingdom for all believers. New Testament Narratives and Reconfigured Fulfillment Ezekiel’s Gog and Magog vs. Revelation’s Gog and Magog : Ezekiel's conditional prophecy, tied to a national victory for Israel, is reconfigured in Revelation 20:7–10 as a global, spiritual conflict for the "camp of the saints" that occurs after the millennial reign of Christ. Ezekiel’s Temple vs. The Spiritual Temple : The conditional promise of Ezekiel’s physical temple is reconfigured in the New Testament. The church is now the temple of the Holy Spirit, and Christ is the cornerstone. The New Jerusalem, which descends from heaven, has no temple, for "the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it". This spiritual reality reflects the shift from a conditional promise to a universal, spiritual kingdom. Zechariah’s Messianic Kingdom vs. Revelation’s Millennial Kingdom : Zechariah's physical, earthly kingdom is fulfilled as a spiritual reign with Christ and the saints. Revelation's New Jerusalem descends from heaven with no physical temple, fulfilling Zechariah's conditional prophecy in a spiritual manner necessitated by Israel's rejection. Isaiah’s Peace vs. Revelation’s Tribulation : Isaiah's vision of immediate peace is fulfilled in Revelation 6–19 as an intense period of suffering before final peace is established. This shows the suffering that must precede Christ's spiritual kingdom due to Israel's failure to bring about immediate peace. Joel's Day of the Lord vs. Acts & Revelation : The initial part of Joel's prophecy—the outpouring of the Spirit on "all flesh"—was fulfilled in Acts 2 , marking the beginning of the new covenant. The latter part of the prophecy, the "Day of the Lord," is reinterpreted in Revelation as a global judgment on the unrepentant world. Conclusion The prophecies are not contradictions but different pictures reflecting a conditional covenant. Israel's failure to meet the conditions of the Old Testament covenant, the death, burial and resurrection of Jesus Christ was the blood of a new covenant, the death of the Testator ushering in the New Testament, all culminating in the definitive rejection of the Messiah by the Jews at Stephen's martyrdom. This new covenant shifts the focus from a conditional, national, and physical fulfillment to an unconditional, universal, and spiritual one. The New Testament, therefore, presents the ultimate reality of God's plan, while the Old Testament prophecies reveal the path that could have been. The fulfilled land promise and redirected blessings to the "new nation" of believers affirm God’s sovereignty and His desire for all to choose life, by believing on Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, promised by the Father from the foundation of the world.

And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day. And the evening and the morning were the second day. And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also. And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth, And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good. Genesis 1:24-25 Day 6 · vv. 26–28 Living Creatures & Man — The Plural God Speaks And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness : and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it : and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth. Genesis 1:26-28 Day 6 · vv. 29–31 Very Good And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat. And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so. Genesis 1:29-30 And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day. Genesis 1:31 Cross references · Genesis 1:26 Jesus in Genesis 1 — “Let Us Make Man in Our Image” Genesis 1:26 The Plural. “Us / Our”: God speaks in the plural within Himself. Man is made in God’s image, not angels’. This cannot be God addressing angels. This is the Triune God deliberating within Himself. John 1:1 John 1:1, 14. The One who said “Let us make man in our image” later became the Man, taking on the very nature He designed. John 1:14 Colossians 1:15-16 Man was created by Christ and for Christ. The Creator later became the Redeemer of what He made. Cross references · Genesis 1:26 Jesus in Genesis 1 — “Let Us Make Man in Our Image” Proverbs 8:22-30 Wisdom personified, present with God at creation, rejoicing. The Father calls Christ the Creator of heaven and earth. 1 Corinthians 8:6 “By whom are all things, and we by him.” Paul includes our very existence as coming through Christ the Creator. Cross references · Genesis 1:26 Creation and Redemption “Let us make man” is not a detail to pass over. The Son who spoke those words in eternity past is the same Son who took on that image in Bethlehem ( Phil. 2:7 ), died for those who bore it, and will one day present a redeemed humanity perfectly conformed to His own glorious image ( Rom. 8:29 ). Creation and redemption are one unbroken story. Day 7 · Genesis 2:1–3 · The Sabbath God Rested, Sanctified the Seventh Day Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. Genesis 2 – Marriage Young Adult Sunday School · Genesis Series Genesis Chapter 2 Marriage · God’s Design from the Beginning Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh. Genesis 2:24 ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move. Tap any reference to read the verse. Gen 2:1–3 · The Sabbath, Creation Complete God Rested & Sanctified the Seventh Day Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made ; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made. Genesis 2:1-3 Gen 2:7–8 · The Formation of Man Man Formed from the Dust And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life ; and man became a living soul. And the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed. Genesis 2:7-8 Cross references · Genesis 2:7 Man Formed by God, Made in His Image Genesis 1:26-27 The Image of God. Man is unique among all creation, made in God’s own image. The distinction between male and female is built into that image from the very beginning. 1 Corinthians 11:7-9 Man the Image, Woman the Glory. Paul grounds male/female roles directly in the Genesis 2 creation order, not culture, but design. Psalm 139:14 Fearfully and Wonderfully Made. Every person is the direct handiwork of God, personally formed, not accidentally produced. Job 33:4 The Breath of the Almighty. The breath of God in Genesis 2:7 is not merely biological, it is spiritual. Man alone among creation received this direct animating breath. Man is not the product of time and chance. He was personally formed and animated by the living God. This dignified origin is the very reason marriage, between two image-bearers, carries such weight. Gen 2:15–17 · Man’s Purpose & Command Dress It and Keep It And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it. And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die. Genesis 2:15-17 Gen 2:18 · The First “Not Good” · Foundation of Marriage It Is Not Good That the Man Should Be Alone And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone ; I will make him an help meet for him. Genesis 2:18 Cross references · Genesis 2:18 “Not Good to Be Alone”: Marriage Throughout Scripture Proverbs 18:22 Finding a Wife. Marriage is not merely permitted, it is a gift and a sign of God’s favour. Proverbs 31:10 A Virtuous Woman. The “help meet” God promised is portrayed in Proverbs 31 as a woman of remarkable character and godliness. Ecclesiastes 4:9-12 Two Are Better Than One. Solomon’s wisdom reflects Genesis 2:18. The aloneness God called “not good” is answered by the companionship God designed in marriage. 1 Corinthians 7:2 Marriage as God’s Provision. Paul acknowledges both the gift of singleness and that marriage is God’s ordained provision for companionship and purity. God Himself declared aloneness “not good,” the only time before sin that God pronounced something in creation as lacking. The help meet He provided was His answer: not a servant, but a complement perfectly fitted for the man He had made. Gen 2:19–20 · Adam’s Authority Adam Names the Animals And out of the ground the Lord God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof. And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him. Genesis 2:19-20 Gen 2:21–22 · Creation of Woman God Made He a Woman And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof ; And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man. Genesis 2:21-22 Cross references · Genesis 2:21–22 Woman Created, the Help Meet 1 Corinthians 11:8-9 Woman from Man, for Man. Paul does not invent a gender hierarchy. He traces it directly to Genesis 2’s creation order. 1 Timothy 2:13 Order of Creation Matters. The order of creation is cited by Paul as the basis for roles within the covenant community. Ephesians 5:25-27 Husbands Love as Christ Loves. The husband’s calling is not dominance but sacrificial love, just as Christ gave Himself for the Church. Proverbs 31:11-12 The Help Meet Fulfilled. The “help meet” of Genesis 2 is portrayed throughout Scripture not as lesser, but as indispensable. Woman was not an afterthought. She was the crown of a creation that God Himself declared incomplete without her. Taken from man’s side, not his feet nor his head, she stands beside him as companion, counterpart, and co-bearer of the image of God. Gen 2:23 · Adam’s Proclamation, First Words About Marriage Bone of My Bones, Flesh of My Flesh And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. Genesis 2:23 Cross references · Genesis 2:23 “Bone of My Bones”: Union & Recognition Ephesians 5:28-30 Husbands & Their Own Bodies. Paul directly echoes Adam’s words and applies the same intimacy to Christ’s relationship with the Church. Marriage is a living picture of the gospel. Song of Solomon 2:16 Mutual Belonging. The Song of Solomon celebrates the joyful recognition of belonging that Adam first expressed. Genesis 29:14 “My Bone and My Flesh.” The phrase “bone and flesh” becomes a covenant expression of belonging throughout the Old Testament. Adam’s first words were poetry, a joyful cry of recognition. This was no cold arrangement but a moment of wonder. The first human speech recorded in Scripture is a husband celebrating his wife. Gen 2:24–25 · The Institution of Marriage Leave · Cleave · One Flesh — God’s Design Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh. And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed. Genesis 2:24-25 Cross references · Genesis 2:24 Leave · Cleave · One Flesh Matthew 19:4-6 Jesus Quotes Genesis 2. Jesus settles the marriage question by going back to creation: permanent, exclusive, one man and one woman. Mark 10:6-9 From the Beginning of Creation. Marriage predates the Fall, the Law, and every culture. It is anchored in creation order itself. Ephesians 5:31-32 The Great Mystery. Paul reveals the ultimate meaning: marriage has always been a picture of Christ’s union with the Church. Cross references · Genesis 2:24 Leave · Cleave · One Flesh 1 Corinthians 6:16 One Flesh Is Not Casual. “One flesh” is a real and binding union. Sexual union always creates a covenant bond. Malachi 2:14-15 The Lord Witness Between Thee and the Wife. God Himself is witness to the marriage covenant. Hebrews 13:4 Marriage Honourable. The New Testament upholds the honor of marriage as God designed it: pure, exclusive, and guarded by God’s own judgment. Genesis 2:24 is the most-quoted verse in the New Testament on marriage, cited by Moses, Jesus, Paul, and the writer of Hebrews. One man leaves his family of origin, cleaves exclusively to one wife, and the two become one new covenant unit. This is what God joined. This is what man must not divide. Gen 3 · The Fall, Marriage Under Curse But It Wasn’t to Last… God had called it very good. Man had a purpose, a garden, a companion, and communion with God. Then came the serpent. Genesis 3 will show what sin does to the marriage God designed, and why redemption must restore what the Fall corrupted. The story of marriage is not finished at Genesis 2. It runs through every page of Scripture, climaxing in Christ and the Church. ‹ Prev Contents Next › Scripture Close Contents Close
