Psalm 22: A Cry from the Cross

Psalm 22: A Cry from the Cross Reads Psalm 22 as David's prophetic song that Christ prayed from the cross, with tap-to-see notes on how verses point to Calvary. The Cry From the Cross: Psalm 22 Sunday School The Cry From the Cross A study of Psalm 22, the prophetic song of David that Christ Himself prayed from the tree ✦ ✦ ✦ “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” Matthew 27:46 Mark 15:34 Psalm 22:1 Scripture Reading Psalm 22 (KJV) Read together as a class. The words in gold are the verses that point to Calvary. Tap any of them below to read the verse. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me ? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent. But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel. Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them. They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded. But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. All they that see me laugh me to scorn : they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, He trusted on the Lord that he would deliver him : let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him. But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother’s breasts. I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou art my God from my mother’s belly. Be not far from me; for trouble is near; for there is none to help. Many bulls have compassed me: strong bulls of Bashan have beset me round. They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion. I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels. My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death. For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet . I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me. They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture . But be not thou far from me, O Lord : O my strength, haste thee to help me. Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns. Psalm 22:1-21 I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee. Ye that fear the Lord , praise him; all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him; and fear him, all ye the seed of Israel. For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard. My praise shall be of thee in the great congregation: I will pay my vows before them that fear him. The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the Lord that seek him: your heart shall live for ever. All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the Lord : and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. For the kingdom is the Lord ’s: and he is the governor among the nations. All they that be fat upon earth shall eat and worship: all they that go down to the dust shall bow before him: and none can keep alive his own soul. A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this. Psalm 22:22-31 Psalm 22:1 Psalm 22:7 Psalm 22:8 Psalm 22:16 Psalm 22:18 I. The Cry Itself A Prophecy Fulfilled in the Ninth Hour In the ninth hour, Jesus cried out from the cross the opening words of Psalm 22, a song of desperation penned by David centuries earlier. It is recorded twice in the Gospels. Matthew 27:46 Jesus cries with a loud voice, quoting the opening line of the Psalm. Mark 15:34 The same cry, in the Aramaic Jesus spoke daily: “Eloi, Eloi.” The man Christ Jesus, after a day of betrayal, abuse, beaten beyond human recognition, scourged, shamed and mocked, cursed, hung on the tree, and made sin for all mankind, acknowledges in that moment that, having taken on all the sin of all creation, He is no longer looked upon by the Father with Whom He has been since everlasting. Jesus cried out in Aramaic, the daily language of the people, the language He grew up speaking, conveying His humanity in that moment. The Hebrew words, long sung by Israel in the congregation, translated into Greek and given to us in English, never lose a scintilla of power. Hebrews 12:2-3 Looking unto Jesus, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross. II. Our High Priest The Scapegoat, Once for All Jesus, our scapegoat, received our sin in atonement, without the camp, taking it utterly away. Not as the blood of bulls and goats offered yearly for sanctification by the High Priest of the Tabernacle, but once and for all, shed for man. And He, as the true High Priest, entered into the Heavenly Tabernacle and applied His own precious blood upon the mercy seat in Heaven. Consider. No greater love has ever been shown than this: that God became flesh and lived among us, sinless and perfect, that He might drink of this cup. Going to the cross that we might live. While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. III. The Ground of Hope He Has Never Failed to Keep His Word The Psalm turns from desperation to the certain hope of a holy, promise-keeping God. We cry out and feel He is far from us, that He doesn’t hear, that He may have abandoned us to our plight. But there is always the hope of faith and trust, because those who trusted Him were never confounded. He heard the cries in Egypt and brought them out of the land. He heard their cries in the wilderness. He delivered their children to the promised land. He heard them in the days of the judges, sending deliverers to raise them up out of the evil their own sin had brought upon them. Hebrews 12:1 Compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses. We know God is good and cannot lie. Our deliverance is assured, even when the flesh is weak and we feel abandoned. His consistent faithfulness to those He foreknew gives us confidence and strength. These things were written for our admonition, that we may know Him as a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him. Romans 15:4 Written aforetime for our learning, that we might have hope. IV. A Shadow of Calvary Through a Glass Darkly In David’s personal pain, we see a shadow of the suffering of Jesus: a reproach of men, despised of the people, laughed to scorn. Matthew 27:39-43 They that passed by reviled Him, wagging their heads. Compassed about by bulls, by dogs, men like lions, surrounded by Roman soldiers doing the work of the Jews, piercing His hands and feet with nails. Splayed out upon the cross, His joints distended and twisted to bear the weight of His own body. Death settling in His guts as He struggled to breathe. His bones in sharp relief against His stretched-out skin. At the cross He was given vinegar mingled with gall, a bitter drink, and when He had tasted it He would not drink. The soldiers then parted His garments by lot. Matthew 27:34-35 They crucified Him, and parted His garments, casting lots. The desperation and loneliness Jesus suffered on the cross He had also carried with Him for thirty-three years, understanding, all along, the anguish that awaited Him at Calvary, while at all points touched by the infirmity of the flesh and tempted as we are. His prayer at Gethsemane, Son to Father, asked that the cup might pass, yet He remained steadfast to the Father’s will, knowing full well the physical and emotional cost. Romans 8:28 All things work together for good to them that love God. V. From Desperation to Praise The Condemned Man’s Prayer of Certain Hope Compassed by dogs, scorned, ridiculed, pierced and heartbroken, feeling abandoned by God, the Psalm turns to a prayer of certain hope. We know God has delivered every promise He has made. He has heard the cries of His people and, in due season, saved them. We may persist in prayer, reminding God, and ourselves, of His faithfulness, even as we ask for more immediate relief. His timing may not be ours, but at our weakest He shows His strength. From the Text (vv. 20–21) Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns. Psalm 22:20-21 From the proverbial horns of a dilemma, from the immediate threat, we call upon the name of the Lord. Not only the saved, His darling, but the lost often find His strength in their time of trial. Foxhole converts. The Potter often moves the clay in such a way that we finally see our own shortcomings and impotency, and our need for His hand to lift us up, that we may become what He has planned for us to be. If even Jesus Christ was made a reproach and murdered by wicked men, that we might know eternal life as the risen and triumphant Son of God, then our trials are an opportunity to overcome by His power and give the Lord the glory. VI. Declared in the Congregation Go to Church I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee. Psalm 22:22 In the midst of tribulation, we shall praise Him. That is the mind of a mature Christian. It is difficult to see sometimes, and we may feel isolated, alone, but in our most desperate hour, we praise Him. We declare His holy name to our brethren; in the congregation we hold up His excellence. A Plain Application. It may not be a primary, or even secondary, application of this Psalm, but consider: we cannot lift our voice in praise to the congregation, or declare His name unto the brethren, if we avoid church. If we forsake the assembly. Go to church! The praise, glory, and fear of the Lord come from the knowledge of the doctrines of God: the understanding of His ways, the past performance of His promises, the teaching of the fathers through the inspired and preserved word of God. Faith cometh by hearing. Romans 11:3-4 I have reserved to myself seven thousand men. Hebrews 10:23-25 Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together. That communal exhortation is invaluable to a believer in tribulation. Hearing the victory Jesus has given others provides the strength to go on, to know the meek shall eat and be satisfied, seeking the Lord and finding Him, unto eternal life. John 6:35-37 I am the bread of life; him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. VII. To Every Generation A People Not Yet Born The truth of this gospel goes to the ends of the world, and every knee shall bow, for the kingdom is the Lord ’s, and He is governor among the nations. Our hope rests on the truth that what God has promised to deliver, He will. The present suffering pales in comparison to what is to come. Romans 8:18 Not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this. Psalm 22:30-31 Our suffering becomes cause to praise the Lord before the brethren, to bring others to the knowledge of Christ, to proclaim His power and promise, and to partake in the spreading of His gospel to all people, that every tongue shall confess that He hath done this. Discussion For Class Discussion Why is it significant that Jesus quoted this Psalm in Aramaic, the language of His everyday life, rather than in formal Hebrew? Verses 16 and 18 describe pierced hands and feet and garments divided by lot, written roughly a thousand years before Jesus was crucified, and centuries before Rome practiced crucifixion. What does this tell us about the nature of prophecy and the authorship of Scripture? The Psalm moves from “why hast thou forsaken me” to “I will declare thy name unto my brethren.” What causes that turn, and where do we see the same pattern in our own trials? How does Hebrews 10:23-25 connect the Psalm’s call to praise “in the midst of the congregation” to our own responsibility to gather with the local church? In what sense was Jesus a “foxhole convert’s” answer and also the Savior of “His darling,” both the lost and the saved, in verse 20? ‹ Prev Contents Next › Scripture Close Contents Close

Psalm 50: God Is Judge Reads Psalm 50 as a courtroom in four movements: the summons, the sacrifice God seeks, the indictment and the verdict. Applies the case against His people to us. Psalm 50: God Is Judge A Psalm of Asaph God Is Judge Himself Psalm 50 and the case the mighty God brings against His own people The mighty God, even the Lord , hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof. Psalm 50:1 ✦ ✦ ✦ Tap any gold reference to read the verse. The Text Psalm 50 in four movements The whole psalm is a courtroom. God summons the court, sets aside what He is not charging, brings the indictment, and then gives the verdict and the promise. Psalm 50:1-6 The Summons (vv. 1–6). The Judge comes out of Zion and gathers His saints Psalm 50:7-15 The Sacrifice God Seeks (vv. 7–15). Not bulls and goats, but thanksgiving and calling on Him Psalm 50:16-21 The Indictment (vv. 16–21). The charges against those who take His covenant in their mouth Psalm 50:22-23 Verdict and Promise (vv. 22–23). A warning to those that forget God, and salvation shewn to the faithful Read the whole psalm Contents The lesson I The Author and His Seer II Our God Shall Come III Not Thy Sacrifices IV The Offering God Seeks V The Indictment VI The Case Against Us VII Consider This I · The Author and His Seer God speaks in the first person The mighty God, even the Lord , hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof. Psalm 50:1 Psalm 50 is a song written in the voice of God Himself, His own perspective spoken directly to man. It is instruction in doctrine and in prophecy, given by His word, in the first person. The psalm opens by introducing its Author: the mighty God . All scripture is given by inspiration of God ( 2 Timothy 3:16 ). It is God-breathed and God-spoken. But this psalm is set apart as the word of God delivered as a message of judgment for His people. I · The Author and His Seer Asaph, the seer God spoke these words through a psalmist other than David. The superscription titles it “A Psalm of Asaph,” the first of the twelve Asaphite psalms in the Bible. Asaph was a prominent Levite, appointed by King David as the chief musician and worship leader before the Ark of the Covenant when it was brought to Jerusalem ( 1 Chronicles 16:4-5 ). He was more than a song director. Scripture credits him as a prophet, and calls him a seer . 2 Chronicles 29:30 “…sing praise unto the Lord with the words of David, and of Asaph the seer.” Prophesying May refer to preaching and declaring the word of God. Seeing The specific term for a visionary given glimpses of the future by God: prophetic understanding of things that are not, but will be. I · The Author and His Seer The Word who called the earth The psalm first establishes the primacy of God the Creator. By His Word the earth and the heavens were made. John 1:1-4 “All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” 1 Corinthians 8:6 “…and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.” When the Bible credits creation to God, remember that this includes Jesus. We read the Old Testament revelation with a New Testament understanding. The nature of the Godhead is revealed in the creation, and it matters for this psalm: the God who called the earth is the God who will come to judge it. II · Our God Shall Come Out of Zion God hath shined Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined. Psalm 50:2 Zion is the place God chose to put His name. His presence in the Tabernacle and later the Temple, God dwelling with His people through their worship, is an echo of the true coming of the Lord in the flesh, and of His return on His day to judge the nations upon that holy mountain. Tabernacle God among His people in worship Incarnation God come in the flesh Return God come to judge on His holy mountain II · Our God Shall Come A fire shall devour before Him Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him. Psalm 50:3 The Second Coming, the return of Christ, is the day we look forward to with gladness. He will come with power, a consuming fire proceeding from Him, and the sword of His word from His mouth shall slay the wicked. 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9 “…in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God…” Revelation 19:15 “And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword…” The future judgment of the world was a key part of Israel’s understanding, though they saw it through a glass, darkly ( 1 Corinthians 13:12 ). With the full revelation of the completed Bible, we see clearly what they only glimpsed in faith. II · Our God Shall Come Gather my saints together He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people. Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice. Psalm 50:4-5 He comes as Judge, the Son calling up to heaven and down to earth, with a shout, with the trump: the call to judgment of His people, before His wrath is poured out on the world. 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 “…caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air…” The gathering of the elect, those sanctified by the Spirit in Christ, is not a “new doctrine,” as some would claim. The Rapture was a key part of prophecy for the Lord’s people, sung by Asaph the seer. II · Our God Shall Come A covenant made by sacrifice And the heavens shall declare his righteousness: for God is judge himself. Selah. Psalm 50:6 The covenant Moses made between the people and God was sealed with blood that represented the blood of Christ, and with it the promise of a better covenant made by a better sacrifice: the sacrifice of the Son. Hebrews 9:19-23 “…without shedding of blood is no remission.” The heavens declare the righteousness of Christ Jesus, and His righteousness is upon all His people. The Judge Himself The Atonement Himself The Mediator Himself The saints are secure in His righteousness. But now God speaks to Israel in judgment, beginning with His own people. III · Not Thy Sacrifices Hear, O my people Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I am God, even thy God. I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices or thy burnt offerings, to have been continually before me. Psalm 50:7-8 The psalm turns from the future prophecy to the present call. The sacrifices had been kept. Israel maintained the Levitical ordinances on which God had based His promises, the constant offerings that preserved ritual cleanliness and kept His presence among them. Those offerings stayed His hand from reproving them harshly. He is not asking for more sacrifice. No additional bulls or goats need shed their blood. III · Not Thy Sacrifices The better sacrifice Under the old covenant the blood of bulls and goats was offered continually by the Levites, each one signifying the Sacrifice to come. We have that better sacrifice, once and for all: a covenant made by the blood of Jesus, the burnt offering for our sin. Hebrews 9:11-14 “How much more shall the blood of Christ… purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” III · Not Thy Sacrifices The cattle upon a thousand hills I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he goats out of thy folds. For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills. I know all the fowls of the mountains: and the wild beasts of the field are mine. If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof. Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Psalm 50:9-13 Every beast is His. If He were hungry, wanting the savour of the fat and the sustenance of meat, He would have His pick and His fill. He does not need them. Israel’s sacrifices were a picture, and a necessity of the covenant, but they did not please Him in and of themselves. III · Not Thy Sacrifices Mercy, and not sacrifice The prophet For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. Hosea 6:6 The Lord Jesus But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless. Matthew 12:7 The same sentiment, spoken by Hosea and repeated by Christ. What God was after in Psalm 50 is what He is still after. IV · The Offering God Seeks Offer unto God thanksgiving Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High: Psalm 50:14 God makes it plain that the offering is thanksgiving. Their vows were to be paid to keep their part in the covenant as His nation: tithes and firstfruits as acts of faith. Unlike the offerings to other gods, it was not a meal for Him to consume. It was thanksgiving, offered in gratitude for all He had supplied, and to keep themselves unspotted as His people. God desires mercy toward others: right judgment, defending the weak, and hating the workers of iniquity. Matthew 23:23 “…and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith…” These are not the repeated acts of priests, but matters of the heart, which God judges and which He seeks from us. IV · The Offering God Seeks Call upon me in the day of trouble And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me. Psalm 50:15 Having established His ways, God gives the gospel: good news to all men in all ages, the dispensation of grace. Calling upon the name of the Lord for salvation, that we may glorify Him before all men. It is the promise of salvation and the heart of the Great Commission, joined to the truth that when we are in Him we magnify His light, so that men see our works of righteousness, mercy and thanksgiving, and glorify God. Matthew 5:16 “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.” This is our purpose as believers: to make known the judgment of God and to be an example of His mercy, praising His name in thanksgiving, all openly before men, that He may be glorified. V · The Indictment The charge of formalism But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? Seeing thou hatest instruction, and casteth my words behind thee. Psalm 50:16-17 Having summoned the court and stated His position, God begins the indictment. Having shown that He has no need of bulls, goats or fowls, He lays the charge of formalism against His covenant people. The religious practices are being kept, the bare minimum of service to maintain the covenant. The Lord is not accusing them of failing there, but in the weightier matters, just as Jesus accused the Pharisees. V · The Indictment A light to all nations God gave Israel promises and practices to keep them as His people, but they were failing to declare His statutes and proclaim His law. The whole point of Israel was to be a light to all men, not to selfishly reap the benefits while doing nothing to teach the nations by example. They squandered their blessings by not fulfilling that role. Deuteronomy 4:5-6 “…Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” V · The Indictment Near with their lips, far in their heart God accuses the wicked among His people of missing the entire point, the same charge Jesus would bring against the religious leaders of the Jews. Matthew 15:8 “This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth… but their heart is far from me.” Matthew 23:27-28 “…ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward…” V · The Indictment The counts against them God’s accusations are sharp. ( vv. 18–20 ) Consent “When thou sawest a thief, then thou consentedst with him.” They went along with the thief. Partaking “…and hast been partaker with adulterers.” Both the literal engagement with the world, and the spiritual adultery of general ecumenicalism. Deceit “Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit.” They speak evil things, and lie. Slander “Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother.” They not only fail to love their neighbour, they lie against their own brother. V · The Indictment “And I kept silence” These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself: but I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes. Psalm 50:21 God is longsuffering and merciful, not willing that any should perish ( 2 Peter 3:9 ). He gave them space and time to reconsider their ways. Instead they considered themselves holy as God is holy. They thought that by their religious practice, keeping the letter of the law, they could ignore the purpose and spirit of the law. It is the same indictment as Matthew 23, and it could be said of so many supposed Christians today. VI · The Case Against Us The leaven of the Pharisees For Christians today, the indictment is the same leaven of the Pharisees: hypocrisy. ( Luke 12:1 ) Just as the Pharisees had the Old Testament sacrifices, we have the once-and-for-all sacrifice of Christ and the total remission of sins. Hebrews 10:8 “Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and offering for sin thou wouldest not, neither hadst pleasure therein…” VI · The Case Against Us No more sacrifice As God told Israel He was not seeking to add sacrifices to those they already offered, He is not asking us for additional acts of atonement. He remembers our sins no more. For those in Christ And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more. Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin. Hebrews 10:17-18 For wilful sin For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins, But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries. Hebrews 10:26-27 Like Israel in Psalm 50, we are covered by the blood. We are His people. But are we bound by formalism and the outward appearance of being clean, while failing at the good work He saved us for, the work that gives Him glory? VI · The Case Against Us Taking His covenant in our mouth If we are not declaring His righteousness and glory in thanksgiving, and showing mercy and judgment to others, loving our neighbour, how are we taking His covenant in our mouths? How are we telling the world we are Christians when we are not acting like it? Who does it benefit? James 2:14-17 “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” VI · The Case Against Us This is not legalism God is not saying that we must do works to be saved, or to be His. We are not justified before God by our works, but before men. Yet God does have works for us to do. Before God Justified by faith, through the blood of Christ alone. Before men Shown to be His by the good works He ordained for us. Ephesians 2:10 “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…” VI · The Case Against Us The buried talent The indictment against His people is that while we have availed ourselves of His covenant and promises, we have squandered the talents of silver He has given us. ( Matthew 25:14-30 ) Five talents Traded, and gained five more. “Well done, thou good and faithful servant.” Two talents Gained two more. “Well done, good and faithful servant.” One talent Afraid, went and digged in the earth, and hid it. “Thou wicked and slothful servant.” To whom much is given, much is required ( Luke 12:48 ). There are professing Christians who have taken the offer and buried it. They never took it in as their own, nurtured it, or used it to increase God’s kingdom. Again, this is not works-based salvation. Had the servant kept his one talent in his own care, he would not have been cast out. Instead he buried it and went through the motions. VI · The Case Against Us Not forsaking the assembling Hebrews 10 sets the command to gather between its two statements on sacrifice: no more need of sacrifice for those in Christ, and no more sacrifice for wilful sin. Hebrews 10:23-25 “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together… but exhorting one another…” We are commanded not to forsake the assembly, and its purpose is to love one another: edifying, building each other up, so much the more as the day approaches. Yet some treat church as a checkbox for their righteousness, proving themselves holy by attendance alone. They wash the outside of the cup ( Matthew 23:25-27 ) while within they are whited tombs full of dead men’s bones. To them religion is rituals and obligations that benefit only themselves, sacraments as their sacrifice rather than the blood of Christ. VII · Consider This Ye that forget God Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces, and there be none to deliver. Psalm 50:22 Christians in name only go through the motions and never once consider God. God goes out of His way in this psalm to stipulate that His righteous people are protected under His care. His case is with the false professors of His name, who think the formalism of their worship is enough to spare them from His wrath. They forget God, and He will tear them in pieces. They bury their talent out of fear, while never truly fearing God. VII · Consider This Whoso offereth praise Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God. Psalm 50:23 But God, ever gracious, ends on a note of promise. Our purpose as His people is to praise His name, that He be glorified among men. We are the salt of the earth, preserving the world against judgment, and He encourages us to continue in praise and thanksgiving. Matthew 5:13 “…but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?” Revelation 3:16 “So then because thou art lukewarm… I will spue thee out of my mouth.” Revelation 2:5 “…or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick…” Salt can lose its savour. A lukewarm church can have its candlestick removed, and be of no further use to God. VII · Consider This Stay salty God’s case against Israel is God’s case against all who call themselves by His name and fail to live to proclaim His glory. Let us then keep our savour: Do all things with mercy and judgment Forgive those who trespass against us Consider the poor, the widow and the fatherless Exhort one another, so much the more as the day approaches Offer praise and thanksgiving, that God be glorified among men So that at the coming of Christ, when He brings fiery judgment upon the world, we will be found acceptable: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant.” ( Matthew 25:21 ) Amen ‹ Prev Contents Next › Scripture Close Contents Close
So You're a Saved Christian, Now What?

So You're a Saved Christian, Now What? A seven-session study for new believers on the gospel, baptism, witnessing, prayer, Bible study, a life that pleases God and the hope of glory. Begins by rooting assurance in Christ's finished work. So You're a Saved Christian, Now What? New Believer’s Foundations · A Beginner’s Guide to Christian Living So You’re Saved… Now What? Seven sessions for the new believer: the gospel, baptism, witnessing, prayer, Bible study, a life that pleases God, and the hope of glory. As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: 1 Peter 2:2 KJVO Sunday School Resources · Fundamental Foundations Training ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move. Tap any reference to read the verse. The Contents button lists every session. KJVO Sunday School Resources · Fundamental Foundations Training Session one Session One: the gospel confirmed Before we talk about growing, let’s make sure the ground is solid. You have already believed the gospel and been saved. This session is not to make you doubt that, but to root it so deep that no one, including the devil himself, can shake it loose. We begin where the Bible begins the good news: God’s love, man’s need, and Christ’s finished work. The Gospel in a verse For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved. He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. John 3:16-18 Notice the shape of it: God’s love is the source, Christ’s gift is the means, and belief, simple trust in Him, is the only response required. Not belief plus baptism, not belief plus church membership, not belief plus a certain feeling. Belief alone, in Him alone. The Romans Road Paul’s letter to the Romans lays the same truth out step by step. Walk it slowly. This is the road you walked to get saved, and it is the road you will walk with others. All have sinned For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Romans 3:23 The wages of sin For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Romans 6:23 Christ died for us But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Romans 5:8 Confess and believe That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Romans 10:9-10 For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Romans 10:13 You can know you have eternal life He that believeth on the Son of God hath the witness in himself: he that believeth not God hath made him a liar; because he believeth not the record that God gave of his Son. And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life. These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God. 1 John 5:10-13 Teaching point. John didn’t write “that ye may hope” or “that ye may wish”; he wrote that ye may know . Assurance isn’t pride; it’s simply taking God at His word. If He said it, and you believed it, it’s settled. Eternal security: once saved, kept If salvation depended on you keeping yourself saved, none of us would make it. But salvation was never a transaction you maintain; it’s a gift God keeps. Nothing in all creation is strong enough to undo what Christ has done. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Romans 8:35-39 Everything that follows in this course (baptism, prayer, Bible study, godly living) is not how you stay saved. It’s how a saved person grows in faith and grace. Session two Baptism: an outward sign Baptism saves no one. You were already saved the moment you believed. But the very first thing the early church did with a new believer was baptize him. It’s not a suggestion for the “serious” Christian later on; it’s the normal, immediate next step for every believer. Think of it as a public wedding after a private engagement: the commitment was already real, but now everyone gets to see it. Or think of a wedding ring: that ring is the outward sign, but without it you are still married. Baptism works the same way: it doesn’t create the marriage between you and Christ, it displays one that already exists. Two reasons to be baptized An outward sign to others It tells the world, without a word, that you have died to your old life and been raised to a new one (buried under the water, raised up out of it). An act of obedience to God Christ commanded it, and a saved heart wants to obey, not to earn anything, but because it loves the One who saved it. What the picture means Why go under the water at all? Because baptism isn’t just a ritual. It’s a picture Paul explains in plain terms: going down into the water pictures Christ’s death and burial, and coming back up pictures His resurrection. You are acting out the gospel with your own body. Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection: Romans 6:3-5 A new believer gets baptized: the Ethiopian Acts 8 gives us the clearest picture in Scripture of what happens the moment a new convert understands the gospel. Read it as one flowing account. And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert. And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship, Was returning, and sitting in his chariot read Esaias the prophet. Then the Spirit said unto Philip, Go near, and join thyself to this chariot. And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him. The place of the scripture which he read was this, He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth: In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth. And the eunuch answered Philip, and said, I pray thee, of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man? Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus. Acts 8:26-35 What doth hinder me to be baptized? And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized? And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him. And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way rejoicing. Acts 8:36-39 Notice what the eunuch did the moment he understood: he didn’t wait for a “right time,” a special service, or years of preparation. There was water. He believed. He was baptized. He went on his way rejoicing. That’s the pattern for you too. Going on toward maturity Baptism is a foundation stone, not the finish line. The writer of Hebrews names it as one of several “first principles” a believer lays down once, and then builds on for the rest of life. The next five sessions of this course are that building. Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this will we do, if God permit. Hebrews 6:1-3 Session three Every believer a witness The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise. Proverbs 11:30 Here’s good news you may not have heard yet: you don’t need years of Bible school to point someone to Christ. You just need to have met Him. Scripture’s clearest illustration of this is a woman who had known Jesus for less than an hour before she was leading her whole town to Him. The woman at the well John 4:4-42, in brief: Jesus, tired from His journey, stops at a well in Samaria at noon and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, a request that broke two social barriers at once, since Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and a rabbi did not speak to a woman alone in public. He offers her “living water,” and when she asks for it, He gently exposes the real thirst in her life: five failed marriages and a man she isn’t married to now. Rather than running from that, she runs toward Him, perceiving Him as a prophet, then questioning Him about worship, and finally hearing Him say plainly, “I that speak unto thee am he,” the Messiah Himself. John 4:4-42 She does not wait She does not go get trained. She does not wait until she has her own life sorted out. She leaves her water pot standing right there and goes straight into the city, telling everyone, “Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?” And John tells us many of the Samaritans believed on Him because of the woman’s testimony , before they ever met Jesus themselves. A woman with a broken past and no theological training became the first missionary to Samaria, simply by telling what she knew. Teaching point. You already know enough to win someone to Christ. You know that you were lost, that Jesus saved you, and how. That is a testimony no one can argue with, and it’s exactly what the woman at the well had. The Great Commission And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen. Matthew 28:18-20 Witnesses unto the uttermost part But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. Acts 1:8 This wasn’t given only to preachers. It was given to every believer in the room (fishermen, tax collectors, ordinary people) and it still stands today. Soul-winning is not a specialty; it’s the normal Christian life. Living so your witness isn’t undone What you say about Christ matters. So does how you live in front of the people watching you say it. Chaste conversation Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives; While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear. 1 Peter 3:1-2 Let your light so shine Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. Matthew 5:14-16 Abstain from all appearance of evil Abstain from all appearance of evil. 1 Thessalonians 5:22 Conversation means conduct “Chaste conversation” here doesn’t just mean clean speech. Conversation in the King James English means your whole conduct, your manner of life. A watching world reads that conduct like a letter, long before it ever reads a Bible verse. Guard it carefully; a single careless season can silence years of testimony. Session four Prayer: talking with the Father Prayer is simply talking to God as your Father, because that’s exactly what He’s become to you. Not a formula to unlock blessings, not a performance for others to hear, but a relationship. Paul tells believers plainly to pray without ceasing ( 1 Thessalonians 5:17 ): not one long unbroken prayer all day, but a heart that stays in conversation with God through everything the day brings. The model prayer When His disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, He didn’t hand them a theory. He gave them a pattern. After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen. Matthew 6:9-13 The ACTS pattern Bible teachers have long noticed that the Lord’s Prayer naturally breaks into four movements, an easy pattern to carry into your own prayer time, remembered by the word ACTS. ADORATION · CONFESSION · THANKSGIVING · SUPPLICATION Psalms for the pattern: A and C The Psalms give us some of the best examples in Scripture of each part of that pattern. Read each one slowly. Better yet, pray it back to God in your own words. A, Adoration (praising God for who He is) O Lord , our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth! who hast set thy glory above the heavens. Psalm 8:1 Great is the Lord , and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable. Psalm 145:3 C, Confession (agreeing with God about sin) Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions. Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me. Psalm 51:1-3 I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord ; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah. Psalm 32:5 Psalms for the pattern: T and S T, Thanksgiving (gratitude for what He has done) Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name. Psalm 100:4 Bless the Lord , O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord , O my soul, and forget not all his benefits: Psalm 103:1-2 S, Supplication (asking for what we need) Bow down thine ear, O Lord , hear me: for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee. Psalm 86:1-2 Teach me to do thy will; for thou art my God: thy spirit is good; lead me into the land of uprightness. Psalm 143:10 When you don’t know how to pray Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God. Romans 8:26-27 Teaching point. Yes, you can pray amiss. James 4:3 warns that asking with wrong motives, purely to spend it on yourself, gets you nowhere. But don’t let that make you afraid to pray. The Spirit corrects and carries your prayer even when your words fall short, and God answers prayer with what you actually need , not always what you asked for. Asking amiss, and a Father who gives Asking amiss Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts. James 4:3 God shall supply all your need But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus. Philippians 4:19 A Father who gives good gifts Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone? Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent? If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him? Matthew 7:9-11 The confidence we have in prayer And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him. 1 John 5:14-15 Session five Bible study: feeding on the word Prayer is you talking to God. Bible study is God talking to you. A believer who prays but never opens the Word ends up with a lot of opinions and very little truth to test them against. You need both. Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth . But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. 2 Timothy 2:15-16 “Study” here isn’t a suggestion to skim. It means to work at it, the way a tradesman works at his craft until he no longer has to guess. You are not expected to master the whole Bible this week. You are expected to start, and to keep going. Desire, meditate, walk by the light Desire the sincere milk of the word As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: 1 Peter 2:2 Meditate therein day and night This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success. Joshua 1:8 A lamp unto my feet Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. Psalm 119:105 A simple start A simple start. Read a little every day rather than a lot once a week. The Gospel of John is a good place to begin. It was written, in John’s own words, “that ye might believe” and, having believed, keep believing more deeply. And a caution: reading a devotional, a random verse of the day, or a one-line calendar entry is not a substitute for reading the Bible itself with a plan and a purpose, taking each passage in its context. Those tools are fine as seasoning; they were never meant to be the meal. John 20:31 Session six A life that pleases God God’s commandments were never meant to cage you. They were meant to protect you and, quite literally, to lengthen your days. The very first commandment with a promise attached tells us so directly. Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right. Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise; That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth. Ephesians 6:1-3 The commandment restated Honour thy father and thy mother, as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee; that thy days may be prolonged, and that it may go well with thee, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee. Deuteronomy 5:16 The benefit is the point Every command God gives is aimed at your good, not just your obedience. He isn’t fencing you in. He’s fencing out the things that would wreck your life. A few examples: Ephesians 4:25 Don’t lie , because trust, once broken, is slow to rebuild; guard it instead. Ephesians 4:28 Don’t steal , because a life built on taking never has anything left to give. Exodus 20:17 Don’t covet , because a heart fixed on what it doesn’t have can never enjoy what it does. Titus 2:12 Be sober , because a clear head is what lets you make good decisions in the moment they actually matter. 1 Corinthians 6:18 Don’t commit adultery or fornication. It is a sin against your own body; it doesn’t just wound others, it wounds you. God is not trying to make your life smaller. He’s showing you the path that actually works. Your life is an open book test People may never read the Bible you carry, but they are always reading you. That’s not a burden; it’s the privilege of being useful to God. You might be the only Bible they see. Known and read of all men Ye are our epistle, known and read of all men Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men: Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart. 2 Corinthians 3:2-3 All scripture is given by inspiration of God All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 Quick, powerful, and sharper than a sword For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. Hebrews 4:12 The Book is open to you But there’s a second sense in which your life is an open book: the Book itself is open to you. God didn’t leave you guessing about how to live. He wrote down the answer to nearly every question you’ll face: money, marriage, work, suffering, the future. Scripture isn’t a restriction on a good life; it’s the blueprint for one. The point of reading it isn’t to collect information. It’s to find out what God thinks, so you can walk the path that actually leads somewhere good. Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. Proverbs 3:5-6 Psalm 119:105 Psalm 119:130 Expect trouble, and a way through it Godly living was never promised to be easy. Christ said it plainly, and Paul confirmed it: living for Him will bring resistance, sometimes from the last people you’d expect. All that will live godly shall suffer persecution Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. 2 Timothy 3:12 A way to escape temptation There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. 1 Corinthians 10:13 A sword, not always peace Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword. For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law. And a man’s foes shall be they of his own household. Matthew 10:34-36 Division, even in a household Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law. Luke 12:51-53 When family pushes back Teaching point. If a family member pushes back on your new faith, you are not failing. You are exactly where Jesus said some believers would be. Stay loving. Stay patient. Don’t force the issue, but don’t hide the change God has made in you either. Love, in every direction The proof that we belong to Christ is not how well we argue doctrine. It’s how we love the people around us. The brethren 1 John 3:14 John 13:34-35 Your spouse Ephesians 5:25 Ephesians 5:33 Your parents, if you’re a child under their roof Ephesians 6:1 Those in authority over you Romans 13:1-7 Titus 3:1 1 Peter 2:13-17 Your boss 1 Peter 2:18 Colossians 3:23-24 Your enemies yes, even them Matthew 5:44 When you sin (because you will) Nobody in this course, including the one teaching it, has stopped sinning. Even Paul, decades into his walk with Christ, wrote honestly about losing the fight against his own flesh. O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? Romans 7:24 He doesn’t leave himself there. The very next breath answers the question, and the chapter that follows is the answer in full. No condemnation There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death. For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh: That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. Romans 8:1-4 Teaching point. Your flesh will keep sinning until the day you’re glorified. That’s not news, and it isn’t cause for despair. No temptation that comes at you is anything new; it’s common to everyone. But your standing before God isn’t decided by your flesh anymore. In Christ, you’ve been given a new man that isn’t a slave to sin, even while the old nature keeps fighting for control. New every morning No temptation but such as is common to man There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it. 1 Corinthians 10:13 His mercies are new every morning It is of the Lord ’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. Lamentations 3:22-23 Take up his cross daily And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. Luke 9:23 Falls seven times, rises again For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief. Proverbs 24:16 As far as the east is from the west As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us. Psalm 103:12 Following Christ was never a one-time decision that runs on autopilot. It’s a daily choice to lay the old self down again. Some days that means starting over more than once. That’s not failure; that’s the Christian life. Mercy meets you fresh every morning, and a fall doesn’t define you. Getting back up does. Every sin, past, present and future, already covered Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Romans 4:6-8 That’s not imputation one sin at a time. It’s a settled account. Every sin you had committed, are committing, and will ever commit was already covered when God declared you righteous in Christ. That truth isn’t a license to sin freely; it’s the very thing that makes honest confession possible instead of terrifying. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. 1 John 1:9 Confession isn’t groveling to earn back what you never lost. It’s agreeing with God about what happened, so fellowship stays open and clean. Walking in the Spirit The real answer to sin was never willpower. It’s who you’re walking with. Walk in the Spirit This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. Galatians 5:16 The fruit of the Spirit But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. Galatians 5:22-23 That fruit isn’t something you manufacture by trying harder. It grows out of walking close to Him. The more you do, the less the flesh has room to win. Don’t do this alone Not forsaking the assembling of yourselves And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching. Hebrews 10:24-25 Charity unfeigned Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently: 1 Peter 1:22 Charity suffereth long Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth; Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things. 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 Church is not an optional accessory to the Christian life. It’s where you’re loved, checked, fed, and kept from drifting. No believer in the New Testament grows alone. Sober and vigilant Your adversary the devil Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: 1 Peter 5:8 Let us watch and be sober Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober. 1 Thessalonians 5:6 As the day of Christ’s return draws nearer, Scripture doesn’t tell us to relax. The Epistles Placed in the Book of Acts

The Epistles Placed in the Book of Acts Lists the epistles in the order they were most likely written, set against the chapters of Acts, followed by the post-Acts epistles and Revelation. Serves as a reading guide for placing each letter in its setting. List of the Epistles placed in the context of Acts chapters where they were most likely written (based on a conservative, fundamentalist timeline aligning with Acts events). - Acts 1–12 → Read James (written ~AD 44–49 from Jerusalem, addressing early persecution and trials among dispersed Jewish believers) - Acts 13–14 → Read Galatians (written ~AD 48–49 from Antioch, shortly after the first missionary journey to the Galatian churches) - Acts 15–18 → Read 1 Thessalonians and 2 Thessalonians (written ~AD 50–51 from Corinth, to encourage the new church planted in Thessalonica during the second journey) - Acts 19 → Read 1 Corinthians (written ~AD 55 from Ephesus, addressing issues in the Corinthian church) - Acts 20:1–2 → Read 2 Corinthians (written ~AD 56 from Macedonia, as a follow-up to 1 Corinthians) - Acts 20:3–38 → Read Romans (written ~AD 57 from Corinth, as Paul planned his trip to Rome) - Acts 21–28 (Paul's arrest, trials, and journey to Rome) → After Acts 28, read the Prison Epistles: Ephesians, Colossians, Philemon, and Philippians (written ~AD 60–62 from house arrest in Rome) Post-Acts Epistles (after Acts ends ~AD 62): - 1 Timothy and Titus (~AD 63–65) - 2 Timothy (~AD 66–67) - Hebrews (~AD 60–68, possibly from Italy) - 1 Peter (~AD 62–63, from Rome/"Babylon") - 2 Peter (~AD 65–68) - Jude (~AD 65–80) - 1 John, 2 John, 3 John Revelation (~AD 85–95)
The Old Testament in Light of the New: Stephen

The Old Testament in Light of the New: Stephen Retells Old Testament history as one story with many witnesses, following Stephen's account and similar surveys such as Nehemiah 9. Reads it with the New Testament's own explanation. One History, Many Witnesses – The Old Testament Retold Throughout Scripture The Old Testament Retold Throughout Scripture One History, Many Witnesses The Old Testament’s narrative, God’s covenant with Abraham, the Exodus, the wilderness, the kings and the prophets, is not told once and set aside. It is retold again and again across Scripture, always to teach the grace and mercy of God, His longsuffering towards His people, and the tendency of those people to be prone to wander, to become puffed up, to harden their hearts and stiffen their necks, and to disobey God and provoke Him. Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition , upon whom the ends of the world are come. 1 Corinthians 10:11 This lesson follows four of those retellings, chosen because, read in order, they trace a single arc: confession, accusation, repetition, and redemption. I. Confession Nehemiah 9 II. Accusation Acts 7, Stephen III. Repetition Acts 13, Paul IV. Redemption Hebrews 11 ✦ ✦ ✦ The Pattern in Scripture This is not unique to these four. Retelling Israel’s history is one of Scripture’s standard tools, used by psalmists, prophets, and apostles alike to call God’s people back to Him. Corporate Confession Psalm 78; Psalm 105 and 106; Psalm 135 and 136: the history sung and confessed in worship. Prophetic Confrontation Ezekiel 20; Joshua 24; 1 Samuel 12: the history used as an indictment, or a charge to choose. New Testament Theology Galatians 3–4; Romans 9–11: the history used by Paul to explain the Law, faith, and the difference between unbelieving Israel and the believing. We will look closely at just four, chosen because they trace one arc from confession to redemption. I. Confession Nehemiah’s Confession Generations before Stephen ever stood trial, the returned remnant stands in Jerusalem, reads the Law aloud, and confesses this same history as their own failure, verse for verse. The Exodus and the Wilderness God chose Abraham, delivered Israel from Egypt with signs and wonders, and led them by cloud and fire to Sinai, giving them the Law, manna, and water. Nehemiah 9:6-15 The Golden Calf and God’s Mercy They hardened their necks and made a molten calf, yet God’s mercy did not depart from them, and He brought them in to possess the land. Nehemiah 9:16-25 The Cycle of Rebellion In the land, the pattern repeats for generations: they rebel, God delivers them to their enemies, they cry out, and He hears and saves them again. Nehemiah 9:26-31 The Confession The prayer ends by justifying God and condemning themselves. Nehemiah 9:32-37 Howbeit thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly : Nehemiah 9:33 II. Accusation Stephen’s Accusation: Abraham to Moses Brought before the council of Jews in Jerusalem, Stephen uses the very history Nehemiah’s generation confessed as an accusation against his accusers. Indicting them for their rejection of God’s Messiah, Christ Jesus. Abraham Called out of his own country to a land and an inheritance he never lived to receive. Acts 7:2-8 Joseph Sold by his own brothers in envy, yet God was with him, and made him ruler over Egypt. Acts 7:9-16 Moses Rejected the first time he tried to deliver his people on his own, but forty years later, was chosen by God to lead them from captivity. Acts 7:17-34 Genesis 12:1–3 Now the Lord had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing: And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. Genesis 12:1-3 mark: Get thee out of thy country Exodus 3:5, 7, 10 And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground. Exodus 3:5 And the Lord said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows; Exodus 3:7 Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt. Exodus 3:10 II. Accusation Stephen’s Accusation: Idols, the Temple, and the Indictment Idols The same Moses who delivered them was refused again. While he was on the mountain, Israel turned back to Egypt’s idols and built a golden calf. Acts 7:35-43 The Temple David wanted to build God a house but was denied because he was a man of war and had shed blood ( 1 Chronicles 28:3 ); his son Solomon was given the role instead. “The most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands”: the building was never the point, but a shadow of good things to come. Acts 7:44-50 Stephen quotes Amos 5:25–27 Have ye offered unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, O house of Israel? But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves. Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus, saith the Lord , whose name is The God of hosts. Amos 5:25-27 mark: beyond Damascus Stephen quotes Isaiah 66:1–2 Thus saith the Lord , The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest? For all those things hath mine hand made, and all those things have been, saith the Lord : but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word. Isaiah 66:1-2 mark: where is the house that ye build unto me The Indictment “Ye stiffnecked... which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?” The same history Nehemiah confessed, Stephen turns into a charge. Acts 7:51-53 II. Accusation Saul, Consenting The council is cut to the heart, not persuaded, but enraged. Stephen is dragged out of the city and stoned, praying for his killers as he dies. And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man’s feet, whose name was Saul . And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge . And when he had said this, he fell asleep. Acts 7:58-60 Standing in the crowd, at whose feet the witnesses laid down their clothes, is a young Pharisee named Saul, consenting to Stephen’s death. Acts 7:54–60 Acts 8:1 Stephen is the first martyr, a powerful witness against unbelieving Israel. Saul will hear this testimony, and soon be the one giving it. III. Repetition Paul’s Repetition: The Second Witness This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established . 2 Corinthians 13:1 Stephen is not the first to preach this against unbelieving Israel. Peter does, and Jesus certainly did in His own ministry. But Stephen’s witness, and his consenting unto death for the cause of Christ, was a powerful testimony to the truth, a truth Saul, now called Paul, would echo. Years later, in a synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, the very man who watched him die for it becomes the second, independently preaching the same history, to the same end: that it all points to Jesus. The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt, and with an high arm brought he them out of it. Acts 13:17 And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will. Of this man’s seed hath God according to his promise raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus : Acts 13:22-23 Paul walks the synagogue through Egypt, the wilderness, the judges, and the kings, the very shape of the history Stephen preached, and lands it on the same name: Jesus. Acts 13:16-25 Interlude A Rejection as Old as the Prophets Before Stephen ever stood trial, Jesus leveled the same charge against the very city that would kill him, and named the pattern going all the way back to the beginning. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! because ye build the tombs of the prophets, and garnish the sepulchres of the righteous, And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets. Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets. Matthew 23:29-31 That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar. Verily I say unto you, All these things shall come upon this generation. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not! Behold, your house is left unto you desolate. Matthew 23:35-38 Jesus names Abel first, the very same Abel that Hebrews 11 is about to commend by faith. The line runs from the first martyr, to the prophets, to Jesus Himself. Matthew 23:29–39 IV. Redemption Hebrews’ Redemption: By Faith The same names are recited a fourth time, not as accusation, not as confession, but as a roll call of faith. Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. For by it the elders obtained a good report. Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear. By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain , by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh. Hebrews 11:1-4 Abel, Enoch, and Noah obeyed God by faith before the Law ever existed, proof that faith, not ritual, has always been the standard. Hebrews 11:1–22 Abraham and Sarah believed a promise neither of them lived to see fully kept, and died still looking for “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.” Hebrews 11:10 IV. Redemption Hebrews’ Redemption: “Time Would Fail Me” Moses refused the treasures of Egypt, choosing to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. Hebrews 11:23–40 And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets: Hebrews 11:32 (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth. And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us , that they without us should not be made perfect. Hebrews 11:38-40 Of whom the world was not worthy. Hebrews 11:38, the same men Stephen’s accusers claimed to honor. V The Lesson Four settings, one history. What changes is not the facts, but the posture toward them. Nehemiah Confession Stephen Accusation Paul Repetition Hebrews Redemption Saul stood by consenting when this history was preached as judgment against a stiffnecked people. Years later he stood up and preached it himself, and in his own epistles, came to hold up the very same men and women as redeemed by faith, a great cloud of witnesses. The Old Testament story is both an indictment of men, who with the advantage of God’s grace and protection, the oracles of God, still fell short in their sin, but also a powerful example of His redemptive plan for man, through faith in His Word, calling upon the name of Jesus. ‹ Prev Contents Next › Scripture Close Contents Close

Brother Mark and His Lies Judge righteous judgment, not by appearance: Job's friends, respect of persons, and suffering that is chastening, for God's glory, or just time and chance. Then, in fun, a defense of Lazarus the beggar against a brother's sermon, closing on Romans 14 and loving brethren who differ on secondary things. John 7:24 Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. We as believers are called to judge (judge angels) Not hypocritical judgement, but righteous according to God’s word Luke 13:1-5 ; There were present at that season some that told him of the Galilaeans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And Jesus answering said unto them, Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay : but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay : but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Our nature to see all hardship of others as “karma” - Deserved Sometimes we may even comfort ourselves, rationalizing our own sin because we aren’t as bad off as others are This is the leaven of the Pharisees; Hypocricy Don’t have to turn there but the story of Job (breifly summarized; Job, a righteous man, suffers immense loss—his wealth, death of his children, and his health, Job was afflicted with painful pusey sores, boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head— All due to Satan’s challenge to God that Job’s faith would falter under affliction. That it’s easy to be a believer when things are good, but what about in tribulation?) Job's three friends; Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite visit Job to comfort him They sit mourning with Job for 7 days, but then one by one, end up critiquing him, asserting that his suffering must be due to grave sin; that he is experiencing divine retribution. Eliphaz " Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite? " (Job 22:5) Bildad " If thou wert pure and upright; surely now He would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous. " (Job 8:6) Zophar doubles down - "Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth." (Job 11:6) With friends like these… Finally God appears to correct the record, and God rebukes Job’s “friends”, declaring they judged wrongly, by appearances: " My wrath is kindled against thee” God says, and He instructs them to make a burnt offering and seek Job’s intercession to avoid punishment for their faulty judgment. So we should be careful to assume anything by appearances Don’t be a respecter of persons: James 2:1 ; My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. In other words, don’t judge people differently based on appearances.Just because someone looks rich and well off, don’t give them more respect than the poor in vile raiment. … Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him? …if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin - Acts 10:34 Peter says God is not a respecter of persons God commands us to be like Him, to uphold justice and compassion for the vulnerable—specifically the fatherless, widows, brokenhearted, and poor…Those who would appear the least among us. Psalm 82:3-4 , " Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked, " James 1:27 ; “ Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world .” It is true that God chasten backslidden believers, He scourges every son he receives, the Bible says. Sometimes a believer in terrible straits is being punished. But there but for the grace of God go I. How merciful is the Lord when considering our own sin, that we be merciful to others when we judge their situation. God’s grace is sufficient. When Paul says in 2 Corinthians 12:7-10 that he was plagued by a thorn in his flesh, pleading with God three times to take it from him, to heal him, God says “My grace is sufficient for thee.” The apostle finally recognized that humbling truth.
