Simeon was there when Mary and Joseph brought in the baby Jesus, and he took the child up in his arms, embracing Him , and blessed God, and said, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation, Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people ; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel. The title of my sermon tonight is Watch . Simeon is an example of an OT saint, faithful and waiting patiently for the coming of Christ and was rewarded to see his faith fulfilled. Embracing the hope he had watched for. A light to lighten the Gentiles , quoting Isaiah 49 , the prophets all gave witness Looking down to verse 36; we meet Anna, of the tribe of Asher, a prophetess of great age, who departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day. And there, seeing the Christ child, she gave thanks to the Lord, and spake of Him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem. The OT is full of examples of those who watched and waited for that redemption, in Christ. We should look at our forerunners in faith, and to be like them: To show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end: That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises . Those who watched and waited: Hebrews 11 - The Hall of Faith, tells us of OT saints who watched, waiting for the promises of the Lord: By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain (blood of the lamb vs works) Noah by faith found grace in the eyes of God, being warned of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark , watching for the promised rain Abraham believed God and it was counted for righteousness. God made a promise to Abraham… Saying, Surely blessing I will bless thee, and multiplying I will multiply thee. And so, after he had patiently endured , he obtained the promise. (Heb 6) For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God. Knowing It is impossible for God to lie, We like Abraham can have a strong consolation , to lay hold upon the hope set before us , Like Simeon, who embraced his hope, Jesus Christ. Looking forward to the cross. Hebrews 11:1 Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. For by it the elders obtained a good report. Hope is a tangible thing, though we have not seen it or touched it, we know that it IS. By faith the elders Watched patiently: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Issac, Jacob, Moses, Rahab, the judges, the prophets and kings… Hebrew 11:13 These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them , and embraced them…. 16 But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city. A Fundamentalist View on Atonement, Salvation and Election

A Fundamentalist View on Atonement, Salvation and Election Sets out a plain-reading view of the atonement as Christ's propitiatory death, cosmic in scope and offered to all, with salvation received by faith. Keeps God's sovereignty and human responsibility together without leaning on Calvinism or Arminianism. Fundamentalist View on Atonement, Salvation, and Election Dealing with the doctrines of atonement, salvation, and election are approached with a strong emphasis on the plain, literal reading of Scripture, prioritizing biblical balance over systematic frameworks like Calvinism or Arminianism. This view seeks to uphold God's sovereignty in providing redemption while affirming human responsibility in responding to it, without over-philosophizing the interplay. The atonement as described in the Bible as Christ's propitiatory death on the cross—His shed blood serving as the ultimate fulfillment of the Old Testament mercy seat (hilastērion)—which objectively reconciles the world and all creation to God. This work satisfies divine justice and pays the cost for redemption, a propitiation for not our sins only, but the sins of the whole world, removing the things that prevented God's grace from being extended to humanity. Key aspects include: Objective and cosmic scope: The atonement accomplishes a real, foundational, cosmic in scope, total reconciliation (e.g., 2 Corinthians 5:19; Colossians 1:20), making peace possible between God and creation regardless of individual response. It is effective in this sense "even if no one ever believed," as it deals with sin's imputed guilt, the fallen world, the tally of the wages of sin - universally and individually - by providing the necessary condition for salvation's offer to all (e.g., 1 Timothy 2:6; 1 John 2:2). Universal provision: Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for the sins of the whole world, enabling a genuine gospel invitation to every person, without limitation in extent or intent. Substitutionary and propitiatory nature: While sharing elements with Penal Substitutionary Atonement (PSA), fundamentalism avoids strict Reformed theology formulations because the Bible emphasizes broad reconciliation over effectual application limited to a predestined group. The cross is not merely potential but achieves an actual change in God's relational stance toward sinners. This perspective integrates substitution (Christ dying in place of sinners) with broader biblical themes like victory over death, but centers on the blood's role in propitiation as the grounds for mercy. Salvation: Salvation is understood as deliverance from sin's penalty, power, and presence, received by grace through faith alone in Christ's finished work. It builds directly on the atonement's objective foundation: Personal application: While the death provides reconciliation objectively (Romans 5:10—"reconciled... through the death of His Son"), full experiential salvation—eternal life, justification, and regeneration—comes through belief in Christ's resurrection and risen life ("saved by His life"). Faith is a free, personal response to the gospel, not irresistibly imposed or conditionally foreseen. Necessity of faith: The atonement makes salvation available to "whosoever will," but it is not automatic or universal; individuals must trust in the crucified and risen Savior (e.g., Romans 10:9; John 3:16). We reject universalism while maintaining the gospel's general accessibility. Holistic process: Salvation encompasses initial justification (forgiveness through the cross) and ongoing sanctification (transformation by His life, walking in the Spirit), leading to the ultimate glorification, which all believers are elect to at the resurrection. The Bible stresses the simplicity of the gospel: Christ died for sins, rose again, and offers eternal life to all who believe, without requiring works or predestined selection. Election is never presented as an individual, personal selection by God for salvation, we reject both Calvinist (unconditional predestination to eternal life) and Arminian (conditional election based on foreseen faith) models as two sides of the same deterministic coin. Purpose-oriented: Election refers to God's sovereign choosing or ordaining for a specific role, service, benefit, calling, or future result (e.g., holiness, ministry, or conformity to Christ's image). It is not synonymous with being saved in scripture; Saved believers are elect unto certain things, but election itself pertains to vocation or purpose within God's plan (e.g., Romans 8:29–30; Ephesians 1:4). You have to be saved to be elect. Not elect to be saved. It is conditional, by faith. Unconditional election is a lie. Election is corporate or categorical - emphasis: Often applied to groups (e.g., Israel as a chosen nation, the church as a royal priesthood) or to believers as a class set apart for holy living and witness (1 Peter 2:9; 2 Timothy 1:9). Foreknowledge: In passages like Romans 8:29 ("whom He foreknew"), this is not God previewing who would believe (Arminian) or decreeing based on sovereign will alone (Calvinist). It may mean a broader determination that those fitting the category of believers will receive blessings (e.g., glorification), or specifically in Romans 8, a prophetic past tense assuring NT believers of the same outcomes believed by OT saints, the promise of what will happen to believers (to be justified and then glorified). "Foreknow" carries relational intimacy with God, especially the Old Testament saints had trusted, rather than false idea of election by the foresight of “God knows who will believe!” determinism. Arminianism and Calvinism both start from a false premise of what these terms mean, and all their theology falls apart when compared with scripture. Overall, this Fundamentalist framework promotes assurance for believers through God's faithful purposes, while preserving the mystery of divine sovereignty and human free will. It critiques overly rigid systems for potentially undermining the Bible's universal language (e.g., "world," "all") or the call to personal faith, aiming instead for a practical, evangelistic theology that encourages proclaiming the gospel to everyone. This summary reflects a commitment to Scripture's plain sense, as discussed, without endorsing or critiquing external traditions like Eastern Orthodoxy or Reformed views.

Augustine and Pelagius Looks at the early fifth-century clash between Augustine and Pelagius as a turning point in how grace and the human will came to be taught. Argues that Augustine's views, carried into the Roman church, are the root of later Calvinist and Arminian systems. Augustine and Pelagius God's gospel is simple: grace through faith in Christ's finished work, which not only saves us from Hell and gives us eternal life in Jesus, the Spirit indwelling us, quickening our spirit, sealing us unto redemption, but God also graciously empowers us to choose obedience, His paths, His commandments, allowing us to strive for maturity in Him, and live separated lives as the New Testament demands. But over the centuries, and even today, that simplicity has been complicated, twisted, and poisoned by human systems that shift blame from personal choice to inherited inability or divine decree, and make grace no more grace. Leading men to destruction, and to pridefully destroy those that remind them of their error. A major turning point came in the early 5th century with the clash between Augustine of Hippo and Pelagius, the ascetic monk from Britain. Augustine's doctrines of Manichaean gnostic determinism, which he championed (including his novel theory of "original sin" as inherited corruption, "prevenient/irresistible grace" as the sole cause of good, and redefining predestination as preordainment) were advanced by redefining orthodoxy against a constructed "Pelagian" strawman opposite, and attributing to Pelagius heresies which were not held by the ascetic monk in Britain. This approach functioned as a Hegelian dialectic: Augustine pitted his views against an exaggerated opposite to legitimize them as the necessary middle ground. By securing Pelagius's condemnation through imperial and ecclesiastical pressure, Augustine's theology gained dominance in the emerging Roman Catholic Church, influenced by political patrons in the late Empire. This pressure of being made anathema and labeled a heretic served to make others who held the Eastern, Greek traditions of New Testament Christianity and understanding fearful of being similarly labeled. The writings of Pelagius and others who held his actual beliefs were either destroyed or allowed to fall into obscurity due to this fear, and so the lack of an extensive record lends even more credibility to Augustine's false doctrines. Regarding original sin, Augustine's formulation—where Adam's sin transmits inherited guilt and an inevitable inclination to evil from birth—was not a settled orthodox doctrine in the earlier churches. Pre-Augustinian Christian asceticism generally viewed human nature as inclined toward goodness, if incapable of being good outside of grace entered into by faith. That man is capable of moral progress in Christ, with sin arising from personal choices, habits, or imitation of bad examples rather than a deterministic corruption inherited biologically or legally. Despite the smears, Pelagius explicitly affirmed God's grace and the Spirit's work as essential: grace opens the heart, reveals truth, exposes snares, enlightens with heavenly gifts, and forgives sins gratuitously. In his Letter to Demetrias and other texts, he described virtue as resulting from cooperation—human consent and effort partnering with divine aid to battle sin and imitate Christ's example of holy living. This was not sinless perfection by fleshly will alone (he acknowledged ongoing weakness and the need for maturity, or perfection in Christ), nor salvation by Old Testament law-keeping (which he recognized all fall short of), but pursuit of Christ's new commandment: loving God fully, with all your heart and loving your neighbor as yourself, all enabled by grace in the regenerated life of the believer. Rather than portray Pelagius as claiming flawless, sinless perfection or denying God's grace and human weakness/sin, we see a view of grace-enabled free agency and moral responsibility that was orthodox into the late 4th/early 5th-century Christian theology, particularly in the ascetic context—before Augustine's influence shifted the boundaries, and changed the conversation to say men are beyond responsibility, and can only be as "good" as God predetermined they be. In the Eastern church, again predominantly Greek, Antioch tradition, they had grown to see the natural end result of following the New Testament was living simply, loving others, being charitable, not given to drink, gluttony, fornication, adultery, coveting, etc. To put others' profit above your own. This contrasted with late empire libertine culture in Rome, and the gnostic influence from Alexandria, which saw excess, and to the ascetic mind, sinful living being supported by the religious leaders there. Augustine, from North Africa with roots in Alexandrian thought, a deep Manichaean past, and limited Greek proficiency, which introduced interpretive errors and conclusions, because he lacked the ability to understand the Greek texts. So Augustine diverged from earlier traditions, and his heresies have over time become foundational for many supposed Christians. Pelagius's outspoken criticism of Roman hedonism and clerical hypocrisy made him unpopular among those Augustine later influenced to support his theology and anathematize his critic. This reevaluation of the false charges of "Pelagianism," isn't meant to idealize Pelagius but recognize that the traditional "heretic" label stems more from polemical and political wrangling by Augustine and others, than from his actual teachings. In that context, we should reconsider how Augustine's legacy shaped Western Christianity—often at the expense of biblical exegesis and understanding of choice, responsibility, and grace-empowered obedience. That the simplicity of the Gospel and simplicity of life we should strive for, has been complicated by systematics of men. That the separated life and sanctification believers should strive for has been abandoned by many professing Christians. And that the teachings on lack of responsibility, or "inability to respond," has allowed those influenced by Augustine to fall well short of the potential given us by grace through faith, and the example of Christ we should actually be striving for. The pattern is clear once you see it. Groups that actually try to live the separated, simple, holy life the New Testament calls for—loving God with all the heart, loving neighbor as self, putting others first, avoiding the flesh’s excesses—have always drawn persecution from the powers that be. Look at the Cathars (the "pure ones"): extreme ascetics who rejected Roman wealth, hierarchy, sacraments, and papal authority in favor of purity and spiritual living. Rome branded them dualist heretics with false charges and launched a full crusade to wipe them out, massacring thousands in genocidal campaigns like the siege of Béziers in 1209, where "Kill them all, God will know His own" became the motto. Their crime? Living too separated from the corruption they saw in the Church, exposing the hypocrisy just like Pelagius did. The Waldensians ("poor men of Lyon") did the same in a more biblical way: lay preaching, poverty, charity, vernacular Scripture (KJV-like emphasis on the Word for all), no oaths or excess, and rejection of papal authority and indulgences. They wanted apostolic simplicity. Rome excommunicated them, hunted them with crusades and Inquisition, burning them at stakes, drowning families, and slaughtering villages in the Alps—murderous false witness calling them heretics for rejecting infant baptism, purgatory, and clerical pomp. Why? Because their separated life exposed clerical hypocrisy, echoing the smears Augustine used on Pelagius. This false witness—strawmanning true believers as heretics to justify murder—didn't stop with Augustine and Rome. It continued through the Reformers: Luther labeled Anabaptists "fanatics" and supported their execution; Calvin had Servetus burned and drowned Anabaptists in Geneva for rebaptism; Zwingli oversaw the drowning of believers in Zurich rivers; Anglicans imprisoned and executed Puritans and early Baptists for nonconformity. Even "Bloody Mary" (Queen Mary I of England) burned hundreds of Protestants at the stake during her reign (1553–1558), including men, women, and children who rejected papal authority and held to Scripture alone—false witness and torture to enforce high-church conformity. Add in the Paulicians: 7th-century ascetics rejecting icons, hierarchy, sacraments, and papal-like authority, emphasizing Scripture and simple faith—they were massacred by Byzantine emperors and labeled Manichaean heretics (ironic, given Augustine's past). The Bogomils followed, dualistic but ascetic, persecuted by Orthodox and Catholic alike with burnings and exiles. Petrobrusians and Henricians (12th century) preached against infant baptism and corruption, only to be burned alive. Arnoldists rejected clerical wealth—hunted down. And the Lollards, followers of Wycliffe, pushed Bible in English, poverty, holy living, and rejection of papal authority—branded heretics, burned at stakes under English law, their bones dug up and scattered. Even quasi-Augustinian sects like the Puritans and Plymouth Brethren, who pursued disciplined, world-denying holiness—plain living, strict Sabbath, moral rigor—faced hostility. Puritans fled England under Anglican pressure, facing starvation and native attacks; Brethren separated from established bodies and were often mocked or marginalized, even as they carried some Calvinist errors. Rome and high-church Protestant systems alike use political power to silence those who live too close to Christ’s example. The simple gospel—grace through faith enabling obedience, choice, and separated living—threatens any institution that has grown fat on compromise. When believers start striving for the real thing, the powers that profit from laxity always push back with false witness and murder. History proves it: purity draws fire, leaving a trail of blood from NT martyrs through these groups to the burnings under Bloody Mary and beyond. Augustine’s legacy perverted the gospel and weakened responsibility which excused the excess and rationalized the evil done to separated Christians with standards; the faithful who keep trying to live Biblical lives and are persecuted for it. The pattern hasn’t changed. The Bible says, Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. Jesus warns again and again that Christians will be hated for His name. That we will suffer persecution. Paul, Peter, John and Jude all write about scoffers, mockers, persecution for the faith, and the patience of the saints who endure it. We count ourselves blessed that in America, today, we aren't facing any real persecution. That we are free to worship, pray, read and own the Bible, go soul-winning...all without facing the same challenges our spiritual forefathers faced. Partly because our system of government was influenced by those fleeing persecution and sectarian violence. This gave us some protection against politically connected apostates coming against us for Godly living. But, another reason why Bible believing Christians today, including you and I, aren't facing the same level of persecution those 1st century NT Churches faced, or the various Christians throughout the last 2,000 years have faced, is because of our own lack of separation. Hebrews 6:9 But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation, though we thus speak. … Others use 2 Timothy 2 to say that a believer can fall away from the faith. 2 Timothy 2:13 (KJV) “If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.” The surrounding context of this verse is found in 2 Timothy 2:8–14: “Remember that Jesus Christ of the seed of David was raised from the dead according to my gospel: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound. Therefore I endure all things for the elect’s sakes, that they may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory. It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him: If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us: If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself. Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.” The passage is not primarily about individual apostasy of previously saved believers. It forms part of Paul’s larger instruction to men of God regarding sound doctrine, endurance, and the unchanging nature of the gospel. The statement that God remains faithful even if “we believe not” underscores the immutability of God’s character, His word, and His decrees. The truth of the gospel does not depend on human belief; it stands regardless of whether people accept it. Immediately preceding verse 13 is the conditional warning of verse 12: “if we deny him, he also will deny us.” Isolating verse 13 while setting aside this earlier clause produces an incomplete reading. Verse 13 does not teach that a person who once believed and later ceases to believe is nevertheless guaranteed heaven by God’s faithfulness. Rather, it affirms that God cannot deny Himself—His own character, gospel, and justice. If God has decreed judgment upon those who deny Him and remain in unbelief, He remains faithful to that decree. The claim that the Greek term apostasia (“a falling away” or “departure”) can apply only to those who were genuinely saved represents a significant logical leap. Departure can occur from a visible community, a theological position, or a religious system without the individual ever having possessed the corresponding spiritual reality. Judas Iscariot provides a clear illustration: those who “went out from us” demonstrated by their departure that “they were not of us.” Visual or institutional departure does not prove prior genuine possession of saving faith. An interpretation that treats verse 13 as a permanent safety net for later unbelief or apostasy produces a distorted picture of God—one who would compel a hostile, self-professed atheist into heaven solely on the basis of a past intellectual assent. Such a view reduces the blood of Christ to something closer to a mechanical formula than a transformative covenant, resembling the very “sinner’s prayer” approach that is often criticized for treating salvation as a mere verbal transaction rather than a genuine work of grace.

Creation Ex Nihilo Defends creation out of nothing and answers the Divine Council theory of Michael Heiser from John 1, Colossians 1, Hebrews 11, and Genesis. Holds that God made all things alone by His Word. Creation Out of Nothing – Defending the Biblical Doctrine IFB · KJVO · Sunday Morning Class Creation Out of Nothing Defending the Biblical Doctrine of Ex Nihilo and Answering the Divine Council Theory of Michael Heiser Scripture Alone Settles the Question ✦ ✦ ✦ Why This Matters The Question Before Us Historic Christian doctrine holds that God created all things out of nothing ( ex nihilo ), by His word alone. A popular academic theory, associated with the late Michael Heiser and the “Divine Council Worldview”, claims the Old Testament originally taught a council of spirit-beings, a “pantheon,” ruling alongside God, and reads a watery chaos as pre-existing His act of creating. This is not a harmless footnote. It quietly relocates God’s unique, incommunicable glory as Creator onto other beings. We will test the theory against its own proof texts, then set the whole matter under the plain testimony of the New Testament and the grammar of Genesis. Text One John 1:1–3 The Pre-Existence of the Word In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made . John 1:1-3 The Defense “Not any thing” made without Him leaves no crack for pre-existing matter, chaos, or a council of co-workers. Every category of created thing, spirit or matter, passes through the Word, and the Word passes through no one. Text Two Colossians 1:16–17 The Scope of Christ’s Creation For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers : all things were created by him, and for him: And he is before all things , and by him all things consist. Colossians 1:16-17 The Defense Paul names the very categories a divine-council reading depends on, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, and puts every one of them on the created side of the ledger. If the “council” is made by Christ, it cannot have stood alongside Him at creation. He alone is “before all things.” Text Three Hebrews 11:3 The Origin of Visible Matter Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God , so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear. Hebrews 11:3 The Defense This is the New Testament’s own definition of ex nihilo . The visible universe was not organized out of some pre-existing, visible material, a chaotic deep sitting there before God got to work. It came strictly from His spoken word. Text Four Romans 4:17 The Sovereign Power of God (As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were . Romans 4:17 The Defense God’s creative power is described as calling what does not exist into existence, not reshaping, not organizing, not commissioning help from beings already on hand. “Things which be not” is as plain a denial of pre-existing raw material as Scripture offers. Text Five Revelation 4:11 The Ultimate Purpose Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things , and for thy pleasure they are and were created. Revelation 4:11 The Defense The heavenly host itself, the very beings a council theory would promote to co-creators, falls down to say the glory belongs to God alone. If they knew of colleagues in creation, this would be the moment to name them. They don’t. Text Six Isaiah 44:24 “By Myself”: God’s Own Claim Thus saith the Lord , thy redeemer, and he that formed thee from the womb, I am the Lord that maketh all things; that stretcheth forth the heavens alone ; that spreadeth abroad the earth by myself ; Isaiah 44:24 The Defense God does not merely say He made all things. He specifies the manner: “alone,” “by myself.” This is not a passage that leaves room for silent partners. Any theory that populates creation week with a working council must first explain past this verse, not around it. Answering a Proof Text Job 38:4–7 The Foundation Is Christ Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding. Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line upon it? Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof; When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy ? Job 38:4-7 The Defense Bible-believers hold more than one view of who the “sons of God” are here, some angels, others the redeemed line from Seth onward, and that is a secondary question, not the point at issue tonight. What matters for our purpose is the foundation itself. Scripture names a foundation deeper than day one’s dirt: Christ Himself, the cornerstone laid before the world began ( 1 Corinthians 3:11 ; 1 Peter 1:20 ), the very foundation Abraham himself saw by faith and rejoiced in ( John 8:56 ). On either view of the “sons,” this text gives no committee of co-creators. It gives worshippers glad for a foundation God alone laid in Christ. Answering a Proof Text Psalm 82:1, 6–7 The “Gods” Who Die Like Men God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods. Psalm 82:1 I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High. But ye shall die like men , and fall like one of the princes. Psalm 82:6-7 The Defense This is the Divine Council Worldview’s cornerstone text, and it refutes itself. Whatever these “gods” are, the Psalm’s own verdict is that they will die like men . An eternal pantheon does not die. Christ Himself applies this psalm to those “unto whom the word of God came” ( John 10:34-36 ), corrupt human judges under divine indictment, not a co-eternal spirit council. Answering a Proof Text Deuteronomy 32:8–9 A Textual Argument, Not a Scriptural One When the Most High divided to the nations their inheritance , when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. For the Lord ’s portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance. Deuteronomy 32:8-9 The Defense The Divine Council argument here rests on preferring a variant reading, “sons of God,” found in some Dead Sea fragments and the Greek Septuagint, over the Hebrew Masoretic Text the King James translators followed under God’s providential preservation. We do not rebuild doctrine on disputed fragments against the received, settled text. And even granting that angelic princes are set over nations elsewhere in Scripture ( Daniel 10:13 ; Daniel 10:20-21 ), that describes derived, creaturely authority under God’s appointment, never a council sharing in His work of creation. A Question of Method Reading Scripture Through Canaanite Eyes The Claim Much of the Divine Council Worldview is built by importing Ugaritic and Canaanite mythology, the Baal Cycle, the god El and his council, as the lens for reading Hebrew words like “council,” “sons of God,” and “Most High,” on the assumption that Israel’s writers shared their pagan neighbors’ cosmology. The Support Scripture is its own interpreter and needs no pagan mythology to explain what it means ( 2 Peter 1:20-21 ; 2 Timothy 3:16-17 ). And where the Bible does speak of the “gods” of the nations, it does not describe them as junior members of a real heavenly bureaucracy. It calls them nothing: “all the gods of the nations are idols” ( Psalm 96:5 ); Israel’s sacrifices to them were sacrifices “unto devils, and not to God” ( Deuteronomy 32:17 ; 1 Corinthians 10:20 ). Building doctrine by reading Canaan’s myths into Moses gets the authority backwards. Foundations in Genesis The Grammar Itself Answers Three grammatical and structural facts that rule out a plural “council” of creators at the very source text. The Grammatical Rule of Elohim The Structure of Genesis 1:1 as an Absolute Beginning The Singular Execution in Genesis 1:26–27 Genesis, Point One The Grammatical Rule of Elohim The Hebrew word Elohim (אֱלֹהִים) carries a plural ending (-im). Yet in Genesis 1:1 , its verb is bara (בָּרָא), strictly singular: “He created.” The Support A plural noun paired with a singular verb, in Hebrew, signals majesty or a single entity acting as one, never a voting committee. The King James translators rendered it correctly as the singular “God.” It points to the unified Godhead, Father, Son, and Spirit, acting in absolute unison, and rules out a plural council of separate gods watching or helping Him work. Genesis, Point Two The Structure of Genesis 1:1 An Absolute Beginning The Claim Heiser and other academics argue Genesis 1:1 is a dependent clause, “When God began to create... the earth was a watery chaos,” which requires reading the first word, Bereshit (בְּרֵאשִׁית), as “in the beginning of.” The Support The traditional, received reading is the independent, absolute form: “In the beginning...” a foundational announcement of an absolute start. Verse 1 is the completed creation of everything from nothing; verse 2 simply zooms in to describe the earth’s initial unformed state before the six days of forming and filling begin. No pre-existing chaos is required, only a text willing to stand as it was handed down. Genesis, Point Three Genesis 1:26–27 The Singular Execution And God said, Let us make man in our image , after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. So God created man in his own image , in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. Genesis 1:26-27 The Support The consultation of verse 26 uses the plural “Us,” the fellowship within the Trinity itself. But the execution in verse 27 drops to strictly singular pronouns: his, he, he . A council did not create mankind; the singular Godhead did. Angels never share the image or the creative power of God. Sorting the Claims What the Theory Gets Wrong The Overreach The Actual Testimony That a heavenly host implies co-creators. Angels are creatures who worship, not architects who build ( Job 38:4-7 ; Revelation 4:11 ). That “gods” in Psalm 82 means an eternal pantheon. Scripture’s own “gods” die like men ( Psalm 82:7 ), no eternal rivals to the Most High. That a disputed textual variant should override the received Hebrew text. God made all things “alone” and “by myself” ( Isaiah 44:24 ), a claim no council can share. Summary Scripture Speaks Clearly John 1:1-3 Nothing was made without the Word. Colossians 1:16-17 Christ is before all things, visible and invisible. Hebrews 11:3 The seen was not made of things which appear. Romans 4:17 God calls things which be not as though they were. Revelation 4:11 All things were created for His pleasure. Isaiah 44:24 God stretched forth the heavens alone, by Himself. Job 38:4-7 Whoever the “sons” are, the foundation is Christ, not a council’s handiwork. Psalm 82:6-7 Scripture’s own “gods” die like men; Christ applies it to earthly leaders. 2 Peter 1:20-21 Method: Canaanite mythology is not the lens Scripture hands us to read itself. Genesis 1:1 Singular verbs, an absolute beginning, and singular execution. Conclusion One God, One Word, One Work The Bible consistently presents one sovereign God who created all things out of nothing by the power of His word. There is no eternal matter, no pre-existing chaos that limited Him, and no council of lesser gods that shares His creative work, however loudly modern scholarship dresses the claim in Hebrew grammar and ancient Near Eastern parallels. Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things , and for thy pleasure they are and were created. Expository: James 2:14-17 A short draft exposition reading James 2 as written to saved Christians, urging faith to be shown in serving others. Notes that works justify a man before men, not before God. Expository: James 2:14-17 What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him? If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit? Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. James 2 misunderstood writing to saved Christians, to encourage those of us justified by the law of liberty ( James 2:12 ), to exercise our faith in the service of others What good is our faith if we don’t also do for others? Justified before men “Yea, a man may say Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works” Knowing this, that God so loved the world He gave His only begotten Son, that Jesus so loved the brethren that He gave His life for us that we may by faith receive the gift of eternal life, to be made sons of God and heirs to the Kingdom and the promises and blessings we have in this life and the next, sealed by the Spirit unto redemption…The least we can do in return is be a blessing to others. To show them the same love as Jesus showed us.

Fundamentalism vs. Vain Philosophy Shows that where Scripture presents mystery, the fundamentalist stops, while the philosopher and theologian press on and answer heresy with counter-heresy. Traces the back-and-forth of early church controversy and rests on the witness of God in 1 John 5 and the warning of Colossians 2. Fundamentalism versus Vain Philosophy A lesson on the Bible alone Fundamen­talism versus Vain Philosophy Where the Scripture presents mystery, the fundamentalist stops. ✦ ✦ ✦ I The Mystery of Godliness And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness : God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory. 1 Timothy 3:16 Where the text of scripture presents mystery, “great is the mystery of godliness,” the fundamentalist stops, where the philosopher and the theologian continue, pressing on in their vain imagination. Revelation and Faith The truth is not found by the reasoning of men. It is by the revelation of scripture, and by understanding that some things our finite brain cannot comprehend. And accepting those things by faith. God revealed it. God did not explain it. We believe it. Compare scripture with scripture Deuteronomy 29:29 1 Corinthians 13:12 II Heresy Answered with Heresy We see people debate the various vain philosophies of men used to explain the position of the Father, the godhood of the incarnate Jesus, the Trinity, the person of the Spirit, and the unity of it all, in the fallible and weak terms of men. Biblical fundamentalism is superior to theology. Heresy answered with heresy is not how we find the truth. Compare scripture with scripture 1 Corinthians 1:20 2 Timothy 2:23 The Trap of the “Closer” Answer Way too many Christians, saved, Bible-believing Christians at that, see an answer to a clear heresy that is closer to the truth, and accept that doctrine as solid. They lean on the understanding of traditions. The consensus of the crowd. Closer to the truth is not the truth. An error that corrects another error is still an error, and the man who adopts it has only traded one tradition of men for another. Compare scripture with scripture Proverbs 3:5-6 III The Back-and-Forth Away from the Bible The pure light of preserved Scripture, untouched by either side. Each error provoked a reaction. Each reaction became its own error. Thesis produced antithesis, and both sides pulled on the same chains: the categories of Greek and Latin philosophy. Neither one stood in the light of the plain text. The Hegelian Cycle, c. 90–381 AD Thesis (action) · Antithesis (reaction) · Synthesis c. 90–150 AD 1. The Gnostic Spark (underlying thesis). Valentinus, Marcion, and the Gnostics. Introduced Greek dualism: matter is evil, spirit is good. Denied the real physical body of Jesus (Docetism), or claimed the divine Christ-spirit only temporarily inhabited the man Jesus. Abandoned: “the Word was made flesh” John 1:14 and the reality of Christ’s true humanity 1 John 4:2-3 . c. 150–165 AD 2. The Apologists’ Logos Theory (first antithesis). Justin Martyr and the early Greek Apologists. Answered the objections of pagans and Jews with Greek Logos philosophy instead of the plain text. Presented the Father as the supreme, hidden God and the Son as a secondary, generated instrument, “another God” made reasonable to the Greek mind. The Gnostics had already brought Greek dualism into the church through the back door. Now the defenders of the faith brought Greek philosophy in through the front door. Heretic and apologist were working in the same categories. Result: Birthed subordinationism, the Son inherently lesser than the Father, and set the terms for the back-and-forth that followed. c. 190–268 AD 3. Dynamic Monarchianism / Adoptionism (reactionary thesis). Theodotus of Byzantium, Paul of Samosata. Reacted against the “two-God” trajectory of the Apologists. Sought to protect strict monotheism by human logic. Result: Taught that Jesus was a mere man adopted by God at His baptism, denying His eternal deity. c. 200–250 AD 4. Modalistic Monarchianism / Sabellianism (counter-antithesis). Noetus, Praxeas, Sabellius. Over-corrected against Adoptionism to defend Christ’s absolute deity. Result: Taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are only temporary modes or masks of one divine person (Modalism, Patripassianism). c. 210 AD 5. Tertullian’s Materialistic Legalism (philosophical synthesis). Tertullian of Carthage. Sought to defeat Modalism without returning to Adoptionism. Imported Latin legal and physical terminology: una substantia, tres personae , “one substance, three persons.” Result: Defined the Father as the whole substance and the Son as a portion derived from it. c. 230–250 AD 6. Origen’s Platonic Invention (Alexandrian thesis). Origen of Alexandria. Blended earlier ideas with Neo-Platonic philosophy. Invented “Eternal Generation”: the Son is timelessly and continuously begotten from the Father’s substance. Result: Forced the Bible word “begotten” out of its scriptural context. c. 318–325 AD 7. The Arian Outbreak (logical conclusion, ultimate thesis). Arius of Alexandria. Took subordinationism and eternal generation to their logical extreme. Declared “there was a time when the Son was not.” Abandoned: The eternal deity of the Word, reducing Christ to a created, exalted being John 1:1-3 . 325 AD 8. The Nicene Creed and the State Synthesis (imperial antithesis). Athanasius, Constantine, the Council of Nicaea. Answered Arianism with more philosophy rather than pure Scripture. Canonized the extra-biblical term homoousios , “of the same substance.” Result: Locked Origen’s “eternally begotten” language into a state-enforced creed. 325–381 AD 9. Post-Nicene Fragmentation (the cycle continues). The new philosophical vocabulary produced further warring camps: Semi-Arians, Homoiousians, Anomoeans, and more. Result: Human creeds generated more human error instead of biblical unity. The Core Pattern Each step refused to stop where Scripture stops. Thesis produced antithesis. Both remained inside Greek or Latin philosophical categories. The result was progressive distance from the plain statements of the preserved text, and from the humble acceptance of mystery. The philosopher’s way The fundamentalist’s way Answer error with a counter-theory. Answer error with the text. Borrow the world’s vocabulary to close the gap. Speak in the words the Holy Ghost teacheth. 1 Corinthians 2:13 Enforce the result by creed and council. Stop where Scripture stops, and believe. IV Where Scripture Stops, We Stop The fundamentalist does not feel obligated to supply the missing metaphysical machinery that finite minds invent to close the gap. And we don’t need to take sides in the back-and-forth debates of differing heretical schools of thought. We are not on the stone side or the gold side. We are not obligated to pick the lesser error. We stand where the light falls: on what God said. No Prepackaged Beliefs Fundamentalists should never accept presuppositions and systematics that require us to adopt a set of beliefs that come prepackaged, regurgitating apologetics because others before us accepted them whole cloth. Always search the scripture to see if it is so. And if you cannot draw a clear, direct understanding of a doctrine or view from plain language and context, then it is okay, and in fact wise, to leave it to faith and admit your ignorance as fallible, finite man. Compare scripture with scripture Acts 17:11 Deuteronomy 29:29 V Pure Bible, Not “Sola Scriptura” The fundamentalist rejects the theologian’s “Sola Scriptura” for pure Bible. The theologians use the logic of men, the writings of church fathers and reformers and past generations of men, to claim the Bible should be the final arbiter of doctrine. That sliver of daylight given to the authority of tradition and man’s philosophy invites error just as much as the other attempts to answer bad doctrine. “Final arbiter” The Bible judges, but tradition, the fathers, and the reformers sit at the table. Only authority The Bible alone speaks for matters of faith and practice. Nothing else sits at the table. Scripture Compared with Scripture Taking scripture compared to scripture as the only means of finding truth, and allowing the Bible to be the only authority for matters of faith and practice, avoids these traps. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works . 2 Timothy 3:16-17 Throughly furnished. The man of God does not need a supplement. Liberty on Secondary Matters The general understanding of Romans 14, that on secondary matters men may disagree and be fully persuaded in their own minds, without judging another man’s servant, makes fundamentalism the way. Primary doctrine is clear. God is not the author of confusion. But where we see through a glass darkly, there is room for brotherly disagreement. Compare scripture with scripture Romans 14:4-5 1 Corinthians 14:33 1 Corinthians 13:12 VI Three That Bear Record For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one . 1 John 5:7 The Bible does not demand that we figure out the metaphysical mechanics of how three can be one. It simply states the fact of their heavenly record and their absolute unity, leaving no room for human rationalization. What Scripture Does Not Say Scripture doesn’t get into the mode, the essence, the hypostatic union, the filioque, or any other nonsense used to debate endlessly the vain wisdom of man. The words of man’s wisdom Mode. Essence. Substance. Hypostatic union. Filioque. Eternal generation. The words the Holy Ghost teacheth The revealed names, Father, Word, and Holy Ghost, and the fact that these three are one. 1 John 5:7 It identifies them by their revealed biblical names, Father, Word, and Holy Ghost, and states the undeniable fact that these three are one. By Water and Blood This is he that came by water and blood , even Jesus Christ; not by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit that beareth witness, because the Spirit is truth. 1 John 5:6 God anchors the reality of Jesus Christ to historical facts. He was born of water, the incarnation, and He came by blood, the death and resurrection. And the person of the Spirit bears witness to Christ’s factual existence and the truth of the gospel. There is no need to explain what we know is true. It is just true. The Witness of God Is Greater If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater : for this is the witness of God which he hath testified of his Son. 1 John 5:9 The theologian and the seminarian and the other “experts” seek to gain our confidence in them. In their arguments and their theories and their jargon. But the witness of God is greater. The Witness in Himself He that believeth on the Son of God hath the witness in himself : he that believeth not God hath made him a liar; because he believeth not the record that God gave of his Son. 1 John 5:10 We have the Spirit of truth, who teaches us all things. Who does not speak of Himself, but the good things of God. Compare scripture with scripture John 14:26 John 16:13 Comparing Spiritual Things with Spiritual Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. Which things also we speak, not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual . 1 Corinthians 2:12-13 What more do we need? This Is the True God And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life . 1 John 5:20 This speaks expressly of the truth we have known, and the gift of eternal life, that we may know Him. The truth that is the true God. So don’t let theologians and men wise in their own conceits tell you that you need to be “educated” as they are to know the truth. Compare scripture with scripture Romans 12:16 VII Lest Any Man Beguile You For I would that ye knew what great conflict I have for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh; That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ; In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. And this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words . Colossians 2:1-4 The beguiling men with enticing words seek to lead us from the truth. Paul in the Spirit is giving prophecy that applies to Christians today as much as it did the Colossians and the Laodiceans. Our hearts may be comforted with the full assurance of understanding, even as we acknowledge the mystery of God. Of the Father, and of Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Rooted and Built Up in Him As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him: Rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith, as ye have been taught, abounding therein with thanksgiving. Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit , after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Colossians 2:6-9 We have received Christ, sealed by the Spirit; we are rooted in Him. We are called to walk in Him. And because we are established in the faith, secure in our knowledge of the truth, we can never deny Him. But we can be spoiled by deceivers. Led away by vain traditions of men, following the ways of the world, the logic of men. Following the theology and theory and disputations of denominations and schools of thought, instead of Christ. All the Fulness of the Godhead Bodily The fulness of the Godhead is stated as a fact, in Christ. The scripture does not seek to define His “essence,” substance, or the mechanics of that fulness. God’s word simply declares it as truth, and then warns against the very methods that later generations of men would use to elaborate it. What Paul warned against Philosophy. Vain deceit. The tradition of men. The rudiments, the elementary principles, of the world: the natural man’s view. What came after Vain and puffed-up philosophy. Groups of men with creeds and confessions that add to and take away from the things of Christ. Teaching for doctrines the commandments of men Matthew 15:9 Intruding into Things Not Seen Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen , vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, Colossians 2:16-18 These are the tip of the iceberg: the various ways false teachers use their own imagination to invent how we should live and what we should do, condemning those of us who place our trust entirely in Christ and His word. The Witness Is God’s You do not need the seminary’s vocabulary, the council’s creed, or the philosopher’s system to know the Son of God. The Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost bear record, and these three are one. Christ came by water and blood. In Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Where God has spoken, we believe. Where God has drawn the curtain of mystery, we stop, and we worship. God Himself testifies with us the truth of His Son. Amen. For Discussion Memory Verse Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit , after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. At what point should each side have simply stopped and said, “Thus saith the Lord, and no further”? What is the difference between the Bible as the “final arbiter” and the Bible as the only authority? Why does the sliver of daylight matter? Name a doctrine you were taught that you have never checked against the plain text. How would you search the scripture “whether those things were so”? Where is the line between primary doctrine, which is clear, and the secondary matters of Romans 14? Text 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 John 5:6–10, 20; 1 Corinthians 2:12–13; Colossians 2:1–18 Memory verse Colossians 2:8 Length About 55 minutes, 26 slides in seven sections Materials The interactive deck, KJV Bibles for each student, a printed copy of the timeline for anyone who wants to take it home Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. Transition “Let’s see how this actually played out in history, because it did not happen once. It happened over and over.” III. The Back-and-Forth Away from the Bible Slides 6–8 · 10 min Show the image. The cracked stone statue is the thesis, the action. The gold statue is the antithesis, the reaction. Both are pulling on the same chains. The light of Scripture falls between them and neither one is standing in it. Open the nine steps of the timeline one at a time. For each, ask the same question: where should they have stopped? Gnostic Spark (c. 90–150): Greek dualism; Docetism. Abandoned John 1:14. Note 1 John 4:2–3: John was already fighting this in his own epistle. Apologists’ Logos Theory (c. 150–165): answering pagans and Jews with Greek Logos philosophy instead of the plain text; the Son a secondary, generated instrument. The Gnostics brought Greek philosophy in the back door; the apologists brought it in the front door. Birthed subordinationism and set the terms for everything that followed. Adoptionism (c. 190–260): protecting monotheism by human logic; Jesus a mere man adopted at baptism. Modalism / Sabellianism (c. 200–250): over-correcting the other way; Father, Son, and Holy Ghost as masks of one person. Tertullian (c. 210): Latin legal and physical terms, “one substance, three persons”; the Son a portion derived from the whole. Origen (c. 230–250): Neo-Platonic “Eternal Generation”; “begotten” forced out of its scriptural context. Arius (c. 318–325): the logical conclusion of subordinationism; “there was a time when the Son was not.” Nicaea (325): Arianism answered with more philosophy; homoousios and “eternally begotten” locked into a state-enforced creed. Post-Nicene Fragmentation (325–381): new vocabulary, new warring camps; human creeds generating more human error. Key statement Each step refused to stop where Scripture stops. Thesis produced antithesis; both remained inside Greek or Latin philosophical categories. Teacher’s caution Keep this section moving. The point is the pattern, not the personalities. Do not let it become a church-history lecture. We are showing the error of those who cite these men, not building on them. IV. Where Scripture Stops, We Stop Slides 9–10 · 5 min Key statement The fundamentalist does not feel obligated to supply the missing metaphysical machinery that finite minds invent to close the gap. Teaching points We don’t need to take sides in the back-and-forth debates of differing heretical schools of thought. We are not on the stone side or the gold side. Never accept presuppositions and systematics that come prepackaged, regurgitating apologetics because others before us accepted them whole cloth. Always search the scripture to see if it is so (Acts 17:11). If you cannot draw a clear, direct understanding from plain language and context, it is ok, and in fact wise, to leave it to faith and admit your ignorance as fallible, finite man. V. Pure Bible, Not “Sola Scriptura” Slides 11–13 · 7 min This is the section most likely to surprise students, because “Sola Scriptura” sounds like our position. Slow down here. Key statement That sliver of daylight given to the authority of tradition and man’s philosophy invites error just as much as the other attempts to answer bad doctrine. Teaching points The theologian uses the logic of men, the writings of church fathers and reformers and past generations, to argue the Bible should be the final arbiter . Tradition still sits at the table. The fundamentalist takes scripture compared with scripture as the only means of finding truth, and the Bible as the only authority for faith and practice. 2 Timothy 3:16–17: the man of God is throughly furnished by scripture. Romans 14: on secondary matters men may disagree and be fully persuaded in their own minds, without judging another man’s servant. Primary doctrine is clear; God is not the author of confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33). Where we see through a glass darkly (1 Corinthians 13:12), there is room for brotherly disagreement. Ask the class “What’s the difference between a judge who has the last word and a judge who is the only one allowed to speak?” VI. The Witness of God Is Greater Slides 14–20 · 9 min Now show what Scripture actually says. Have students read each verse from their own Bibles before you comment. 1 John 5:7. The Bible does not demand that we figure out the metaphysical mechanics of how three can be one. It states the fact of their heavenly record and their absolute unity. No mode, essence, hypostatic union, or filioque. Just Father, Word, and Holy Ghost, and these three are one. 1 John 5:6. God anchors the reality of Christ to historical facts: born of water, the incarnation; came by blood, the death and resurrection. The Spirit bears witness. There is no need to explain what we know is true. It is just true. 1 John 5:9. The theologian, the seminarian, and the other “experts” seek our confidence in their arguments, theories, and jargon. But the witness of God is greater. 1 John 5:10. The believer has the witness in himself. We have the Spirit of truth, who teaches us all things (John 14:26) and does not speak of Himself (John 16:13). 1 Corinthians 2:12–13. Not the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. What more do we need? 1 John 5:20. The Son of God has given us an understanding, that we may know Him that is true. Don’t let men wise in their own conceits (Romans 12:16) tell you that you need to be “educated” as they are to know the truth. VII. Beware Lest Any Man Spoil You Slides 21–24 · 6 min Colossians 2:1–4. Beguiling men with enticing words seek to lead us from the truth. Paul’s warning applies to us as much as to Colosse and Laodicea. Our hearts are comforted with full assurance of understanding, even as we acknowledge the mystery of God, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Colossians 2:6–9. We have received Christ and are rooted in Him. We can never deny Him, but we can be spoiled by deceivers: the tradition of men, the rudiments of the world, the theology and disputations of denominations and schools of thought. The fulness of the Godhead is stated as a fact, in Christ. God declares it, then warns against the very methods later generations would use to elaborate it. Matthew 15:9. Creeds and confessions that add to and take away from the things of Christ, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men. Colossians 2:16–18. The tip of the iceberg: false teachers using their own imagination to invent how we should live, intruding into things they have not seen, condemning those who trust entirely in Christ and His word. Closing Slides 25–26 · 7 min Read the closing slide, then say the memory verse together twice. End on the line: God Himself testifies with us the truth of His Son. Amen. Discussion questions 1 Timothy 3:16 calls the mystery of godliness “without controversy.” Why did men turn it into centuries of controversy? Look at the cycle. At what point should each side have simply stopped and said, “Thus saith the Lord, and no further”? What is the difference between the Bible as the “final arbiter” and the Bible as the only authority? Why does the sliver of daylight matter? Name a doctrine you were taught that you have never checked against the plain text. How would you search the scripture “whether those things were so”? Where is the line between primary doctrine and the secondary matters of Romans 14? How do we keep brotherly love on the second without compromising the first? Questions You May Be Asked “Isn’t ‘Trinity’ an extra-biblical word too?” Whatever word a man uses as shorthand, the content has to be exactly what 1 John 5:7 says and nothing more: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one. The problem is not shorthand. The problem is the machinery men attach to it and then require others to confess. “So was Nicaea wrong to say Jesus is God?” Jesus is God because the Bible says so: “the Word was God” (John 1:1), “this is the true God” (1 John 5:20), “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Colossians 2:9). We don’t need a council to tell us. The error was answering Arius with philosophical vocabulary and an imperial creed instead of with the text, which put the authority in the council and the vocabulary rather than in the word of God. “If everyone just reads the Bible for himself, won’t everyone believe something different?” God is not the author of confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33). Primary doctrine is clear. The believer has the witness in himself (1 John 5:10) and the Spirit of truth to guide him (John 16:13). On secondary matters, Romans 14 already tells us what to do: be fully persuaded in your own mind and don’t judge another man’s servant. The creeds did not produce unity either. They produced Semi-Arians, Homoiousians, and Anomoeans. “What does ‘begotten’ mean, then?” Let scripture interpret scripture. Psalm 2:7 says, “Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee,” and Acts 13:33 tells us how God fulfilled it: “in that he hath raised up Jesus again.” Read the word in its own context before reaching for a philosopher’s definition. “Aren’t you just rejecting education?” No. We are rejecting the claim that a man needs the theologian’s education to know the truth. The Bereans were commended for searching the scriptures daily (Acts 17:11), not for consulting the scholars. Study hard. Just study the Book.

Romans 9 Reads Romans 9 in the context of Israel, showing God's mercy to the nations through the gospel and the hardening of unbelieving Israel, rather than individuals chosen for heaven or hell. Paul has been talking about Israel. He has just said God has the right to show mercy to whom He wills and to harden whom He wills. In context that is not “some random humans elected to heaven, some elected to hell.” It is God showing mercy to the nations through the gospel and hardening unbelieving Israel—the same Israel that had the covenants, the law, the promises, and still stumbled over the Messiah: Romans 9:30–33 (KJV) «“What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith. But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness. Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone; As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.”» That is why the question in 9:14 is “Is there injustice with God?” It is the covenant people asking why God would treat them the way He treated Pharaoh: raise them up, harden them in their rebellion, and use that hardening to make His name known among the Gentiles. Romans 9:14–18 (KJV) «“What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid. For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. For the scripture saith unto Pharaoh, Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth. Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.”» So the objector in 9:19 is not a reprobate crying, “I never had a chance.” It is a self-righteous Jew crying, “How can God find fault with us? We are the chosen nation. Who resists His will?” Romans 9:19–21 (KJV) «“Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will? Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?”» In other words: “God promised us. He cannot set us aside and graft in those dirty Gentiles. That is not how the story is supposed to go.” That is why Paul answers with the potter. He is not quoting a philosophy textbook on compatibilism. He is echoing Jeremiah 18. In Jeremiah the clay is a nation, and the potter remolds it in response to whether that nation turns. The point is not “the pot has no say.” The point is “the Potter has the right to do something you did not expect with a vessel that refused to repent.” Jeremiah 18:6–10 (KJV) «“O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel. At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it; If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them. And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them.”» Keep reading and the Calvinist objector disappears. • 9:30–32: Gentiles obtained righteousness by faith; Israel did not because they pursued it by works. Romans 9:30–32 (KJV) «“What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith. But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness. Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law.”» • 10:21: “All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.” That is not a people God never wanted. Romans 10:21 (KJV) «“But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.”» • 11:11: They stumbled so that salvation would come to the Gentiles—to make Israel jealous. Romans 11:11 (KJV) «“I say then, Have they stumbled that they should fall? God forbid: but rather through their fall salvation is come unto the Gentiles, for to provoke them to jealousy.”» • 11:20–23: They were broken off because of unbelief. If they do not continue in unbelief, they can be grafted in again. Romans 11:20–23 (KJV) «“Well; because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear: For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee. Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity; but toward thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off. And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again.”» The same “hardened” people are not stuck in a decree of reprobation. Their condition is contingent on faith. If the objector were a man damned by an eternal decree he could never resist, Paul’s answer in chapter 11 would be cruel nonsense. You do not tell a vessel prepared for destruction, “Stop persisting in unbelief and you will be grafted back in.” So the Calvinist has to treat 9:19–23 as a self-contained philosophy of individual election and then quietly change the subject when Paul keeps talking about Israel, unbelief, jealousy, and restoration. The objector Paul actually answers is the one standing in the story: the covenant member who thinks God’s mercy to the nations and His judicial hardening of unbelieving Israel is unfair. That objection makes sense in the argument of Romans 9–11. The “why did God create me to be damned” objection does not. Paul is not defending God against the charge of authoring unbelief. He is defending God’s right to use a rebellious nation’s unbelief to save the world—and then invite that same nation back if they will believe.
