The Biblical Doctrine of Reconciliation and Atonement

The Biblical Doctrine of Reconciliation and Atonement An outline beginning at Luke 2 on reconciliation through Christ's blood, distinguishing atonement as the means from reconciliation as the result. Presents the reconciliation as objective and wide in scope, with personal salvation received by faith and kept secure. Outline: The Biblical Doctrine of Reconciliation and Atonement Luke 2:9-14 And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid. And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord. And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men . I. Introduction: The Heart of the Gospel - Reconciliation Through Christ's Blood The Bible presents the cross as God's great plan to make peace and restore what sin broke. Atonement (covering, satisfaction for sin) is the means God uses to accomplish reconciliation (restoring harmony, ending enmity). Jesus’ death and blood is the propitiation (the price needed to satisfy God) 1 John 2:2 And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. Christ's death on the cross is sufficient and powerful enough to address the entire curse of sin on all creation Yet personal salvation comes by faith in His resurrection, with eternal security for the believer. 1 Timothy 2:5-6 For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time. Key principle: Reconciliation is objective and cosmic in its scope and accomplishment (through His death); personal salvation/justification is applied and secured through baptism into Christ, by faith in His risen life. These are two separate concepts. Without the atonement, justification would not be possible. But without justification of sinners, the atonement still has been paid. Romans 5:10 For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. II. The Scope of Reconciliation: All Things Reconciled to God Christ's blood makes peace for the whole creation disrupted by sin (the Fall affected everything mankind, nature, heavenly powers). Romans 5:12 Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned Romans 8:22-23 For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now. And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body. This is not a Universalist idea (the false doctrine that everyone is saved, with or without faith) Atonement/Reconciliation is not synonymous with personal salvation Despite reconciliation hell remains for the unsaved; and is reserved for the fallen angels. It is the triumphant, objective victory where all things are brought under Christ's lordship, where He has overcome the world. The cross subdues enmity, defeats powers, and prepares for the new heavens and new earth. Colossians 1:20 And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven. Ephesians 1:10 That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him. Supporting cosmic impact: Creation groans under the curse but awaits deliverance ( Romans 8:19-23 ); Christ triumphs over principalities and powers ( Colossians 2:15 ). All things are not yet subjected under Christ Hebrews 2:8 Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him. The total subjection purchased with the atonement, takes place in the End Times, after the resurrection, and His millennial reign. And once Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, the LORD of Lords and King of kings has subjected all under Him, Jesus gives it to the Father: 1 Corinthians 15:28 And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all. III. The Means of Reconciliation: By the Death of God's Son God Himself initiates and accomplishes reconciliation while we were still sinners and enemies no human merit involved. The atonement is substitutionary: Christ died for sins, bearing the penalty, making peace through His shed blood. This objective work is finished It is finished ( John 19:30 ) sufficient to reconcile the world with God from its fallen state. Romans 5:8-10 But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son... 2 Corinthians 5:21 For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. IV. The Application to Believers: Personal Salvation by His Life While reconciliation is accomplished by His death (objective, for enemies), believers receive personal justification, peace with God, and eternal life through union with the risen Christ. 1 Timothy 4:10 For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe. Salvation is by grace through faith alone once received, it is secure forever (OSAS), because Christ ever lives to make intercession , so believers are assured final salvation for those reconciled by faith. Romans 5:1, 9-11 Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ... Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him... And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement [reconciliation]. Romans 5:10 ...much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. Hebrews 7:25 Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. V. The Ministry We Have Today: Proclaim the Reconciliation Believers are ambassadors with the message: Be ye reconciled to God! The gospel invites sinners to receive by faith what Christ has already accomplished. 2 Corinthians 5:17-20 Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation. Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God. VI. Conclusion: The Biblical Doctrine of Atonement Destroys The False Dichotomy of Limited/Unlimited Atonement Christ's atonement is mighty: sufficient to reconcile all things through His blood (all creation’s victory over sin's curse), yet personally applied to save believers eternally by faith in His risen life. Calvinism (Particular Redemption/Limited Atonement): Christ died efficiently and intentionally only for the elect (those unconditionally chosen by God before creation), securing salvation infallibly for them alone; His atonement is limited in scope and design, though sufficient in power for more if God had so decreed. Arminianism (Unlimited Atonement with Conditional Application): Christ died provisionally for all mankind without exception, making salvation genuinely available to every person; the atonement is unlimited in scope but limited in efficacy—applied only to those whom God foreknew would believe—thus election is conditional upon foreseen faith rather than sovereign decree alone. Both Calvinism and Arminianism misunderstand the atonement by confining it primarily to the question of individual salvation ("for whom did Christ die?"). – Calvinism limits its scope and power to the arbitrarily elect. – Arminianism , while claiming unlimited provision of the atonement, still ties its efficacy to foreseen individual faith, making election conditional rather than sovereign decree. Both systems reduce the cross to an individualistic framework and miss its grand biblical purpose: the cosmic, triumphant reconciliation of all things—ending enmity, defeating powers, and restoring creation through the blood of the cross Two sides of a heretical coin - Arminianism essentially keeps the same Calvinistic framework (unconditional election based on God's decree) but swaps "arbitrary decree" for "foreseen faith"—so the atonement still ends up functionally limited in scope to the foreseen elect, just determined differently. Scripture presents a finished, objective victory already accomplished, rendering the debate moot. 2 Peter 3:9 The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. Hebrews 2:9 But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man. Scripture shows a finished, powerful work that glorifies God and is the power to secure the saved. Christ died for all sinners, rose for our justification, and keeps us forever by the power of God. John 3:16 For God so loved the world , that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
The Biblical Truth About Perseverance of the Saints

The Biblical Truth About Perseverance of the Saints Starts with the question of how a person knows he is saved and compares Calvinist and Arminian teaching on perseverance. Contrasts both with the Bible's eternal life promised by a God who cannot lie, so that believers may know they have it. The Biblical Truth About Perseverance of the Saints vs Eternal Security 1 John 5:13 — These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God. Introduction: How Do You Know You're Saved? When asked "How do you know you're saved?", many religious systems answer with uncertainty: "If I persevere to the end..." "If I continue in faith and good works..." "If I keep the sacraments and don't fall away..." Their assurance rests on what they have done or will do—always looking inward at performance. But the Bible-believing Christian answers differently: "Because Jesus died for my sins and rose again—He did it all!" "Because God, who cannot lie, promised everlasting life the moment I believed." Titus 1:2 — In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began; John 5:24 — Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life. Today we'll expose the false doctrine of "perseverance" taught in many theologies, contrast it with biblical Once Saved, Always Saved in context, and rejoice in the objective, finished work of Christ that ye MAY KNOW we have eternal life by faith alone. I. What Other Theologies Teach About "Perseverance of the Saints" Calvinism/Reformed Theology: True saints will persevere in holiness and good works as inevitable evidence of election. If you don't endure in faithfulness, you were never truly saved. (Tied to their "P" in TULIP) Arminianism/Wesleyan Theology: Believers can lose salvation if they don't persevere in faith and obedience; "enduring to the end" is required to be finally saved. Roman Catholicism: Salvation is maintained through sacraments, cooperation with grace, and avoiding mortal sin—no full assurance until death. In fact, Catholicism officially teaches that claiming to know with 100% certainty that you are in a state of grace (and will persevere to the end) is the sin of presumption against the Holy Spirit. Lutheranism (varying views): Some emphasize perseverance through Word and Sacrament; assurance is hoped for but often tied to ongoing faith/repentance. Common thread: Assurance is subjective—based on personal endurance, fruit, or continued performance. No one can fully know until the end. II. What Biblical "Perseverance" and "Enduring to the End" Actually Mean in Context These phrases are not about eternal salvation but physical deliverance/safety through tribulation and persecution for kingdom inheritance and rewards. Matthew 24:13 — But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. Context: Olivet Discourse about the Great Tribulation (v. 21—" For then shall be great tribulation "). "Saved" here means delivered physically/safely from tribulation, the persecution of believers in this world (as in v. 22—" And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened "). Revelation 2–3 (letters to churches, not individual people!): "Overcometh" and hold fast for rewards, crowns, and ruling with Christ—not gaining or losing salvation. Biblical perseverance for believers today: Standing firm in faith amid trials, but eternal security is guaranteed by God's power, not ours. James 1:12 — Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him. 1 Peter 5:9 — Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world. John 10:28-29 — And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand. Philippians 1:6 — Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. III. "Repent of Your Sins" and Back-Door Works Salvation: Teaching Probation, Not Justification The modern demand to "repent of your sins" (turn from all sin to be saved or stay saved) confuses biblical repentance (a change of mind) with works—it turns the gospel into probation (ongoing performance required) instead of instant justification by faith alone. Romans 4:5 — But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. Ephesians 2:8-9 — For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. God Himself "repents" multiple times in Scripture (over a dozen), yet He cannot sin—proving repentance means a change of mind or course, not turning from sin. Jonah 3:9-10 — Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not? And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not. Genesis 6:6 — And it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart. Exodus 32:14 — And the LORD repented of the evil which he thought to do unto his people. Sinners repent (change mind) about Christ—believing the gospel—not promising to clean up their life first or maintain it afterward. IV. Why This False Teaching Leads to Hypocrisy and Spiritual Pride It breeds fruit inspectors and holier-than-thou attitudes—the leaven of the Pharisees, which Jesus directly calls hypocrisy. Matthew 16:6 — Then Jesus said unto them, Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees. Matthew 16:12 — Then understood they how that he bade them not beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees. (The leaven is hypocrisy and false doctrine— Luke 12:1 ) Luke 18:11-12 — The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. It's hypocritical back-door works salvation: Claims "grace alone" but ties assurance to ongoing effort. Makes perseverance the root instead of the fruit—turning the gospel upside down. Good works aren't automatic—if you don't walk in the Spirit, don't expect to do the works God has appointed for you ( Eph. 2:10 ). True fruit is primarily the others we bring to Christ with the gospel ( Rom. 1:13 ; John 4:36 ). Works will be rewarded at the Judgment Seat, but even if they are wood, hay, stubble—you yourself are still saved. 1 Corinthians 3:15 — If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. Men may justify us by outward works, but not before God. James 2:24 — Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only. (Context: justified before men, v. 18—"shew me thy faith") Romans 4:1-2 What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found? For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God. V. How It Creates Doubt, Hinders Salvation, and Robs Believers of Joy For the seeking sinner: "I must turn from sins, make Jesus Lord, and persevere" becomes vague, hopeless, and impossible—leading to trust in self instead of Christ. Lordship Salvation / "repent of your sins" / "make Jesus Lord of your life" is subjective and undefined—what sin level disqualifies? How much commitment is enough? Keeps people from simple trust: They never rest because they're always inspecting fruit or fearing failure. For the believer: Constant doubt—"Have I endured enough? Is my faith real?"—steals peace and assurance God intended. Romans 5:1 — Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Colossians 2:2 — That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ. VI. The Biblical Alternative: Objective Assurance in Christ's Finished Work Salvation is received the moment you believe—eternal life is a present possession. John 5:24 — Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life. John 6:47 — Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life. Assurance is objective: Anchored in God's unbreakable promises and Christ's resurrection, not our performance. Ephesians 1:13-14 — In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory. Ephesians 4:30 — And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. Hebrews 7:25 — Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. 1 Peter 1:5 — Who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. Jude 24 — Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy. We are commanded to know we have eternal life—not hope or examine fruit. 1 John 5:13 — These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God. Fruit follows naturally from abiding in Christ ( John 15 ), but it's never the basis of assurance. VII. Conclusion: Rest in the Sure Promises of God Reject vague, hopeless demands ("make Jesus Lord," "repent of sins," "persevere in works"). Trust the simple, objective gospel: Christ died for your sins, rose again, and gives eternal life freely to whosoever believeth. 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 — For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures. Acts 16:31 — And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. Romans 8:38-39 — For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. How do you know you're saved? Because God said it, and He cannot lie. Jesus' Unbreakable Promise of Eternal Security John 6:37-40,44,47 — All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me. And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day. And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day…No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day…..Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life. Jesus promises four times in this chapter that He will raise up every believer at the last day—it's the Father's will, and Christ guarantees He will lose nothing. "In no wise cast out" means once you come to Him by faith, you're never rejected or lost—eternal security from the Lord's own mouth. If you've never trusted Christ alone—do it today. Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved. Believer—stop doubting. Don’t let the hypocrites and the holier-than-thous make you doubt your salvation. Rejoice in your eternal security and live for the One who saved you completely!
The TULIP Trap: Rejecting Calvinist and Arminian Premises

The TULIP Trap: Rejecting Calvinist and Arminian Premises A planned four-to-six lesson series outline arguing that the TULIP debate rests on faulty premises. Goes through the points one at a time, affirming what Scripture says while rejecting the Calvinist and Arminian framework. Beyond TULIP: A Biblical Rejection of Calvinist/Arminian Premises ### Series Overview (4–6 lessons) Goal: Show that the entire TULIP debate rests on faulty premises that Scripture does not require us to accept. The Bible presents a straightforward gospel of grace through faith alone, with a finished atonement sufficient for all, applied to whosoever believes, and eternally secured by the power of God. 1. Lesson 1: The Wrong Question – Why the Limited vs. Unlimited Debate Misses the Point - Use your atonement/reconciliation outline as the foundation. - Both Calvinism and Arminianism confine the atonement to the question of individual election/salvation. - Scripture presents a cosmic, triumphant reconciliation already accomplished (Col. 1:20; 2 Cor. 5:19), rendering the debate moot. - Key: Christ’s work is bigger than either system allows. 2. Lesson 2: Total Depravity – Biblical Truth Without Calvinistic Inability - Affirm: Man is dead in sins, none seek God, totally affected by sin (Rom. 3:10-23; Eph. 2:1). - Reject the premise: This does not mean moral inability to believe the gospel when convicted by the Spirit through the Word (John 16:8; Rom. 10:17; Heb. 4:12; John 1:9; Rom. 1:16). - The gospel is the power of God unto salvation—the Word quickens, the Spirit convicts all who hear, and whosoever will may come. 3. Lesson 3: Unconditional Election – The Biblical Doctrine of Election is Not About Individual Salvation - Election in Scripture is primarily corporate (in Christ), to service, holiness, and inheritance (Eph. 1:4-5; Rom. 8:29-30 understood as conformity to Christ). - Reject the premise that God arbitrarily chooses some for salvation and passes over others before creation. - God desires all to be saved (1 Tim. 2:4; 2 Pet. 3:9); the gospel is a genuine offer to all. 4. Lesson 4: Irresistible Grace vs. the Resistible Drawing of the Spirit Through the Word - The Spirit convicts the world (John 16:8), but men can resist (Acts 7:51; Rom. 1:18-28). - Grace is not an internal overpowering but the external provision of Christ and the gospel call—effective when believed, resisted when rejected. - Faith comes by hearing; the power is in the message, not a secret inward work only on the elect. 5. Lesson 5: Perseverance of the Saints – The Biblical Truth vs. the Calvinist/Arminian Counterfeit - This is where your insight shines. - Calvinist "P" teaches that true believers will persevere in holiness/works as evidence of election—often leading to doubt and introspection. - Arminians accept the same premise (real saints must endure in faith/works) but conclude salvation can be lost—also breeding fear. - Biblical truth: Once a person believes, God keeps them eternally secure by His power (John 10:28-29; Heb. 7:25; Rom. 8:38-39; Eph. 1:13-14). - Passages about "enduring to the end" (Matt. 24:13; Rev. 2–3) refer to physical deliverance through tribulation/persecution for kingdom inheritance, not eternal salvation. - True believers are sealed and kept forever; fruit follows naturally but is not the root of assurance. No back-door works salvation. 6. Conclusion Lesson: Once Saved, Always Saved – The Simple Biblical Gospel - Salvation is by grace through faith alone, not of works (Eph. 2:8-9). - Eternal life is a present possession the moment one believes (John 5:24; 6:47). - God finishes what He starts (Phil. 1:6); Christ ever lives to intercede. - Call to rest in the finished work, rejoice in assurance, and proclaim the gospel freely to all.

Wise as Serpents A Sunday School lesson on Matthew 10:16 and the two charges Jesus gives, to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. Warns against the dove-only trap and looks at handling doubtful disputations and sowers of division. Wise as Serpents A Sunday School Lesson Wise as Serpents Handling doubtful disputations and sowers of division Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves. Matthew 10:16 ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move. Tap any gold reference to read the verse. Two commands, not one Jesus sends His disciples out as sheep among wolves, and in the same breath He gives them two charges: be wise as serpents, and be harmless as doves. Many Christians keep the second and quietly drop the first. We are good at being doves. We are not nearly as good at being serpents — at understanding the context and nature of those who come into our lives and exert a negative influence. Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves . Matthew 10:16 Matthew 7:15 sheep’s clothing Acts 20:29-30 grievous wolves Discuss. Why would Jesus pair these two qualities? What does a Christian look like who has only one of them? The dove-only trap We feel the need to show grace, to bridge peace, and to avoid conflict in every situation — to be sheep in both mind and spirit. The wolves take advantage of this. Part of the problem is that we can’t imagine how evil people might behave. We cut them slack. We extend grace on our own conscience’s terms, and show a kindness and mercy that only encourages and emboldens them. The wolf rarely comes with an obvious lie. He comes with a grain of truth. In the interest of fairness, and to seem reasonable, we validate his premise — but the premise was offered in bad faith. He was never seeking dialogue or understanding. His intent is to throw bombs, sow discord, and validate slander to promote his own agenda. Grace without discernment is not biblical peace; it is an open door. Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them. For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple . Romans 16:17-18 2 Corinthians 11:13-14 an angel of light Hebrews 5:14 senses exercised Discuss. Think of a time a “reasonable” point turned out to be a wedge. What was the grain of truth, and what was the real aim? Weak brother or wolf? Not everyone who comes in wrong is a wolf. Some are weak in the faith — confused on a doctrinal point, turned around by something they heard, or convicted about something the Bible doesn’t explicitly teach. Those we receive. We bear with the ignorant, and we correct them in love. But Paul attaches a limit to the receiving: not to doubtful disputations. When a man comes in to argue, to stir turmoil, and to break the unity of the brethren, he is not to be received on those terms. The difference is the intent of the heart. That is what the serpent’s wisdom is for. Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations . Romans 14:1 Galatians 6:1 restore in meekness 2 Timothy 2:24-25 patient instruction Discuss. What signs tell you someone is asking to learn, and what signs tell you they are looking for a fight? First and second admonition Even the one who is simply in error gets a limit. Admonish him kindly. Admonish him again. If he is too proud to accept rebuke, the Bible does not tell you to keep the conversation going forever. It tells you to reject him. Notice what Paul puts right before that command: foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and strivings — unprofitable and vain. The church has no obligation to keep hosting them. Matthew 18 gives the order: go to him alone, then with witnesses, then before the church. If he will not hear the church, he is to be treated as a heathen man and a publican. But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject ; Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself. Titus 3:9-11 Matthew 18:15-17 the order of church discipline Discuss. Why does God give a limit to admonition instead of telling us to keep reasoning indefinitely? Answering the slanderer Defending yourself against a false accusation built on a bad-faith premise does nothing but legitimize the other person’s point. If someone accused you of something vile and absurd about your own mother, your answer should not be “I am not!” It should be “You’re wicked!” You don’t defend yourself from slander by reasoning with the slanderer. You identify what he is doing, and you rebuke it. This is especially true at the door when soul winning. It does no one any good to get bogged down in a doubtful disputation. When the hearer is plainly after contention and not the truth, shake off the dust and go to the next door. Answer not a fool according to his folly , lest thou also be like unto him. Answer a fool according to his folly , lest he be wise in his own conceit. Proverbs 26:4-5 Nehemiah 6:3 a great work Matthew 10:14 shake off the dust Matthew 7:6 pearls before swine Discuss. Proverbs 26 gives both answers back to back. When do we refuse to engage the folly, and when do we expose it? It will eat as doth a canker The real damage comes when sowers of division are entertained in the house of God or in a place of fellowship, and not put out at the first sign of their behavior. Their contention grows and draws others in. Sheep who aren’t yet wise as serpents are pressured to compromise the truth to bring peace — to smooth things over, to debate slander as if it had merit. That only encourages the wolves, and keeps the confused, weak brother in his error. It doesn’t matter what form the vain babbling takes: denying the resurrection to come, slandering men of God and their works, discouraging first love and soul winning, or teaching a false gospel that says men are made elect by their genealogy. It increases ungodliness and overthrows the faith of some. Frowardness is in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually; he soweth discord. Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy. These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him: A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief, A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren . Proverbs 6:14-19 2 Timothy 2:16-18 Hymenaeus and Philetus 1 Timothy 1:20 delivered unto Satan 1 Corinthians 5:6 a little leaven Discuss. God names the sower of discord alongside a lying tongue and hands that shed innocent blood. Why do you think it ranks so seriously with Him? Where the line is drawn Serpent and dove are not opposites to balance. They work together: see clearly, act rightly, and keep your own heart clean while you do it. Situation Response Passages Error, with humility and teachability Patient instruction Romans 14:1 Galatians 6:1 Error, with pride and refusal after admonition Reject Titus 3:10 Discord sown by design Identify, remove the influence, and treat as an outsider once the process is complete [[Proverbs 6:14-19 Proverbs 6]] [[Matthew 18:15-17 Matthew 18]] At the door, soul winning Don’t be drawn into disputations — shake the dust when they want contention, not truth Matthew 10:14 Nehemiah 6:3 Many Christians default to dove-only behavior because they cannot imagine the calculated malice, or the strategic use of partial truth, that wolves employ. Biblical wisdom requires us to see it when it appears and to act accordingly — without losing the innocence of the dove. For your obedience is come abroad unto all men. I am glad therefore on your behalf: but yet I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil . Romans 16:19 Grace without discernment is not biblical peace; it is an open door. Take it home. Which comes more naturally to you, the serpent or the dove? What is one way you’ll practice the one that doesn’t? ‹ Prev Contents Next › Scripture Close Contents Close

Amazing Grace A short devotional on the hymn written by John Newton in 1772 and what it says of God's grace to a wretch. Reflects on grace shown even now. Amazing grace! How sweet the sound, That saved a wretch like me! I once was lost, but now am found, Was blind, but now I see That hymn, “Amazing Grace” (which is one of my favorites), was written by John Newton in 1772, just before 1776 and American Independence. And as Pastor Tefft has often pointed out, Newton was a truly a “wretch.” Before his conversion to Christianity, John Newton was a wayward sailor, living a reckless and morally depraved life marked by profanity, drunkenness, debauchery, and involvement in the brutal Atlantic slave trade. And the song is about how amazing God's grace is, “To save a wretch like me.” And that is true for all of us. What an amazing, glorious and wonderful grace, that God abundantly gives, even when we were wretches. Even as sinners, Christ died for us. But when I sing Brother Newton's inspired hymn, I often think about the grace God shows me even now. What a wretch I continue to be, and yet God's love is constantly shown to me. The Lord is still with me, and shall not forsake me. His grace for me is not only sufficient, but an amazement. That He loves wretch like me, even me. How amazing is His grace.

Baptist Groups Compared Compares Independent Fundamental, Particular (Calvinist) and Arminian-leaning Baptists on grace through faith, eternal security, free response and the Baptist distinctives. Uses the IFB position as the baseline. Baptist Groups Compared Adult Sunday School Baptist Groups Compared An IFB / KJVO baseline ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move. Tap any reference to read the verse. The five groups Prepared for IFB / KJVO adult Sunday school use. The Independent Fundamental Baptist position is presented as the baseline; other groups are evaluated by that standard. IFB baseline Southern Baptist Reformed / Particular Landmark Free Will / Arminian All Scripture quotations, Authorized (King James) Version. Foundation Core gospel foundation This chart treats classic Independent Fundamental Baptist doctrine as the closest practical match to New Testament church order and gospel preaching. These four points are non-negotiable. Variations that subtract from or add conditions to them are treated as serious error. Grace through faith alone No front-loaded or back-loaded works. Faith is the empty hand that receives Christ. Ephesians 2:8-9 Provisional / general atonement Christ died for the whole world. The invitation is genuinely “whosoever will.” John 3:16 Once Saved Always Saved The believer is sealed and kept by God. Apostasy proves a person was never saved. John 10:28-29 Human responsibility Man is genuinely responsible and able to respond in free response to the gospel call. Romans 10:13 Reformed Calvinism and Free-Will Arminianism are viewed as two sides of the same coin. Both move away from this simple, provisional gospel center. Baptist distinctives The BAPTISTS acrostic Most historic Baptists formally affirm the BAPTISTS acrostic. Differences appear in application and in the doctrines underneath. B · Biblical Authority Scripture alone is final authority. No creed or confession may bind the conscience above the text. Preservation implies a pure English text (KJV). Common drift Confessionalism elevates 1689/Westminster language above plain reading. Multiple versions undermine preservation. A · Autonomy of the Local Church Each local assembly is independent under Christ. No hierarchy, convention, or association has authority over the church. Common drift SBC Cooperative Program and association pressures. Some Reformed networks function semi-presbyterially. Baptist distinctives Priesthood, ordinances and soul liberty P · Priesthood of the Believer Every believer has direct access to God and the right/responsibility to interpret Scripture under the Spirit. Common drift Heavy confessional gate-keeping or elder-rule systems can functionally limit this. T · Two Ordinances Baptism (immersion of believers) and the Lord’s Supper only. Neither is salvific. Common drift Some Free Will / Separate groups add foot-washing as a third ordinance. I · Individual Soul Liberty No civil or ecclesiastical power may coerce conscience in matters of faith. Common drift Generally retained, though some Landmark or confessional circles tighten practical application. Baptist distinctives Membership, offices and security S · Saved Church Membership Only those who give credible evidence of regeneration and believer’s baptism are received. Common drift Practically weakened where open membership or weak discipline exists. T · Two Church Offices Pastor (bishop/elder) and deacons. The pastor is under-shepherd; plurality of equal elders is not required by the text. Common drift Reformed Baptists often insist on plurality of elders as normative. S · Security of the Believer Eternal security / OSAS. The truly saved are kept by the power of God. Apostasy proves the person was never saved. Common drift Arminian groups teach conditional security. Some Calvinists reframe it as perseverance that can look like works. Baptist distinctives Confession or Scripture Holding a detailed confession (e.g., the 1689 London Baptist Confession) as binding tends to drift from pure biblical authority. The confession becomes a lens that can override the plain reading of individual texts. Soteriology Soteriology: the gospel core Grace through faith plus OSAS is the foundation. Systems that condition salvation on human performance (Arminian) or restrict the gospel offer and redefine security in terms of perseverance works (Calvinist) both miss the mark. The next six slides compare the five groups, one question at a time. Soteriology Salvation by faith alone Group Position IFB baseline By grace through faith, not of works ( Ephesians 2:8-9 ). No Lordship front-loading. Southern Baptist Generally affirms sola fide. Growing Calvinist minority introduces nuances. Reformed / Particular Affirms justification by faith alone, yet ties true faith so tightly to perseverance that assurance is disturbed. Landmark Generally holds faith alone; some circles emphasize local-church baptism heavily. Free Will / Arminian Often mixes faith with ongoing obedience or the possibility of falling away, effectively adding works. Soteriology Atonement scope Group Position IFB baseline General / provisional. Christ died for the world ( John 3:16 ; 1 John 2:2 ; 1 Timothy 2:4-6 ). Southern Baptist Majority Traditionalist/Provisionist view is general atonement. Calvinist minority holds limited atonement. Reformed / Particular Limited / particular atonement. Christ died only for the elect. This restricts the free offer of the gospel. Landmark Usually general atonement, consistent with IFB on this point. Free Will / Arminian General atonement, but paired with conditional security. Soteriology Election and free will Group Position IFB baseline God elects according to His foreknowledge; man is genuinely responsible and able to respond ( Romans 10:13 ). Southern Baptist Mixed. Many hold a soft view of election; growing 5-point minority. Most still preach “whosoever will.” Reformed / Particular Unconditional election and irresistible grace. The free offer is effectively only for the elect. Landmark Usually closer to IFB: responsibility and free response emphasized. Free Will / Arminian Strong free-will emphasis, often at the expense of God’s sovereignty. Salvation becomes man-centered. Soteriology Eternal security (OSAS) Group Position IFB baseline Once saved, always saved. Sealed by the Spirit ( Ephesians 1:13-14 ; John 10:28-29 ). Southern Baptist Officially affirms eternal security. Vast majority of churches teach OSAS. Reformed / Particular Perseverance of the saints. The elect will persevere; those who fall away were never elect. Can functionally resemble works-based assurance. Landmark Generally holds eternal security / OSAS, consistent with IFB. Free Will / Arminian Conditional security. A believer can lose salvation through willful sin or apostasy. Treated here as a grave error. Soteriology Apostasy passages Group Position IFB baseline Hebrews 6, 10, etc. describe those who tasted but were never regenerated. “They went out because they were not of us” ( 1 John 2:19 ). Southern Baptist Most interpret consistently with eternal security. Some softer voices exist. Reformed / Particular Usually interpreted as evidence of non-election. The warning passages function as means God uses to keep the elect. Landmark Generally the same as IFB. Free Will / Arminian Taken as proof that true believers can fall from grace and be lost. Misreads the texts. Soteriology Works and assurance Group Position IFB baseline Good works follow salvation but never secure or prove it. Assurance rests on Christ’s finished work and the Spirit’s witness. Southern Baptist Generally similar. Some Calvinist circles push Lordship or fruit-inspection that unsettles weak believers. Reformed / Particular Strong emphasis on fruit and perseverance as evidence. Can produce a practical works-righteousness of introspection. Landmark Usually closer to IFB simplicity. Free Will / Arminian Ongoing obedience is often treated as a condition of remaining saved. Ecclesiology Ecclesiology, Scripture and separation A New Testament church is local, autonomous, evangelistic, and under the pure preserved Word. The next eight slides compare the five groups, one question at a time. Ecclesiology Local church autonomy Group Position IFB baseline Absolute under Christ. No convention, board, or association has authority over the local assembly. Fellowship is voluntary. Southern Baptist Officially autonomous, yet the Cooperative Program and convention structures create practical interdependence and pressure. Reformed / Particular Autonomous in theory. Many practice elder-rule and association accountability that can limit congregational freedom. Landmark Very strong emphasis on local-church authority, often the strongest among Baptist groups. Free Will / Arminian Generally autonomous; associations exist but the local church remains primary. Ecclesiology Succession and Landmarkism Group Position IFB baseline Many IFB hold a practical Baptist succession or “trail of blood” view, emphasizing continuity of New Testament order rather than an unbroken institutional chain. Southern Baptist Generally rejects strict Landmark successionism. Accepts broader evangelical baptism in many cases. Reformed / Particular Rejects Landmark succession. Sees continuity through doctrine and the true church. Landmark Core distinctive: only Baptist churches (in succession) are true churches. Closed communion; rejects “alien immersion.” Free Will / Arminian Usually does not hold Landmark succession. Ecclesiology Communion Group Position IFB baseline Typically close or closed: local-church members or those of like faith and order. Not open to the unbaptized or those in known error. Southern Baptist Varies widely. Open, close, and closed all exist. Trend toward more open practice. Reformed / Particular Often close (baptized believers of like faith). Some stricter. Landmark Closed communion, restricted to members of the local church (or churches of like faith and order). Free Will / Arminian Varies; many practice open or close communion. Ecclesiology Offices Group Position IFB baseline Pastor (bishop/elder) and deacons. One primary teaching pastor is the New Testament pattern; plurality is permitted but not required. Southern Baptist Pastor and deacons standard. Some churches move toward elder plurality. Reformed / Particular Strong preference for plurality of elders as the normative model. Landmark Usually pastor and deacons, consistent with historic Baptist practice. Free Will / Arminian Pastor and deacons; some groups have additional practices. Ecclesiology Scripture and preservation Group Position IFB baseline Verbal plenary inspiration + providential preservation. In English this leads to the King James Version. Modern critical-text versions are rejected. Southern Baptist Inerrancy officially affirmed. Majority use modern versions (ESV, NIV, CSB); KJV preference exists but is minority. Reformed / Particular Inerrancy held. Almost universally use modern translations based on the critical text. Confessions treated as highly authoritative summaries. Landmark Many Landmark churches are KJV-preferred or KJVO, similar to IFB. Free Will / Arminian Generally accept modern versions; some older groups retain KJV. Ecclesiology Evangelism and missions Group Position IFB baseline Essential mark of a NT church. Aggressive soul-winning, local evangelism, and faith-mission support of church planting ( Acts 1:8 ; Matthew 28:18-20 ). Southern Baptist Strong missions emphasis through the Cooperative Program and IMB. Methods and theological breadth vary. Reformed / Particular Missions affirmed, but limited atonement and emphasis on the elect can dampen aggressive “whosoever” evangelism in practice. Landmark Strong missions emphasis in many Landmark/Missionary Baptist groups, often through their own associations. Free Will / Arminian Evangelism affirmed; conditional security can affect how the gospel is presented and followed up. Ecclesiology Ecclesiastical separation Group Position IFB baseline Clear separation from apostasy, liberalism, and neo-evangelical compromise ( 2 Corinthians 6:14-18 ; 2 Thessalonians 3:6 ; 2 Thessalonians 3:14 ). First- and second-degree separation practiced. Southern Baptist Officially conservative since the Conservative Resurgence, yet remains in cooperative structures including broader evangelicalism. Separation generally weaker. Reformed / Particular Doctrinal separation on Calvinistic distinctives is often strong; fundamentalist-style separation from neo-evangelicalism is less consistent. Landmark Often strong separation, especially regarding baptism and church order. Free Will / Arminian Varies widely; many are less separatist. Ecclesiology Confessionalism Group Position IFB baseline No binding creed beyond Scripture. Statements of faith are descriptive, not magisterial. Elevating a confession drifts from sola Scriptura. Southern Baptist Baptist Faith & Message is a consensus document, not a rigid confession. Churches may differ within limits. Reformed / Particular Highly confessional (1689 London Confession or similar). The confession functions as a secondary authority and interpretive grid. Landmark Often use historic Baptist confessions or abstracts, but emphasis remains on local church and Scripture. Free Will / Arminian Some have treatises or confessions; less rigid than Reformed Baptists. Summary Where others miss the mark The gospel center must not be moved Reformed Calvinism (by limiting the atonement and reframing security around inevitable perseverance) and Arminian Free-Will systems (by making security conditional) both move the gospel off center. This affects how the gospel is preached, how assurance is given, and how the church understands its mission. Biblical authority vs. confessional drift When a detailed confession becomes the functional authority or required interpretive grid, the church has begun to drift from sola Scriptura. Historic Baptist practice treated confessions as useful summaries, not binding secondary standards. Preservation and the English Bible If God inspired His Word and promised to preserve it, then in the English-speaking world that preserved Word is found in the King James Version. Churches that treat modern critical-text versions as equal or superior have accepted a different doctrine of preservation. Evangelism and missions are not optional A New Testament church is a soul-winning, missionary-sending body. Any system that dampens the free offer of the gospel or shifts energy away from aggressive evangelism has missed a central mark of the early church. Separation protects the testimony Ecclesiastical and personal separation are obedience to clear commands, not mean-spiritedness. Cooperation with unbelief or persistent doctrinal error eventually erodes the gospel and the purity of the church. Prepared for IFB / KJVO adult Sunday school use. Baptist Names in History Traces the many names worn by the people of God from Antioch onward, such as Novatianists and Cathari. Shows the same conviction beneath each, that a church is a company of the saved baptized upon profession of faith. Baptist Names in History Adult Sunday School · The Baptist Succession Baptist Names in History A study of the many names worn by the people of God through the long centuries between the apostles and today, and the one truth that held beneath every name. ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move. Tap any reference to read the verse. A name is usually given Religious bodies rarely choose their own names. A name is usually given by a leader, a town, a doctrine, or an enemy’s sneer. Yet trace the names back far enough, and the same conviction keeps appearing: a church is a company of the saved, baptized upon a profession of faith. And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch . Acts 11:26 Part One · First to Third Century From Antioch to the Novatianists For nearly three hundred years, one name sufficed. Then the church’s purity began to be tested from within. Christians The earliest and simplest name, given at Antioch to the followers of Christ. Acts 11:26 Novatianists Followers of Novatian, who withdrew from a church he judged too lax toward those who had denied Christ under persecution, contending for a pure, regenerate membership. 1 John 2:19 Puritans A name applied to the same separatist conviction, a church cleansed of unconverted membership, not merely reformed in ritual. 2 Corinthians 6:17 Cathari, “The Pure Ones” Greek for “the pure,” this name traveled alongside Novatianists and Puritans in the third century and would resurface centuries later among the Albigenses, always marking the same insistence on an unmixed, holy church. Ephesians 5:26-27 Part Two · The Schism Within Traditores, Infant Baptism, and a State Church The deepest wound to the early church did not come from Rome’s sword alone. It came from compromise inside the church, and was then sealed into law by an emperor’s embrace. The Traditores During the Diocletian persecution, some clergy surrendered copies of Scripture to be burned rather than suffer, earning the name “traditores,” those who handed the Word over. When restored to office afterward without repentance, faithful believers separated from them. 1 John 2:19 Apostates Others recanted the faith outright under threat of death, then sought readmission to church leadership without discipline, the very compromise that Novatian and his followers refused to accept, at the cost of being cast out themselves. 2 Thessalonians 2:3 Part Two · The Schism Within Infant Baptism and the State Church Infant Baptism Takes Root Alongside this compromise, the doctrine of baptismal regeneration spread, and with it the practice of baptizing infants, formalized as unofficial custom in the third century and later established by imperial law in 416 A.D. Mark 16:16 Constantine and the State Church In 313 A.D. the pagan emperor Constantine ended the persecution, but what followed was no less costly. Church and state were fused into one institution, membership by citizenship replaced membership by new birth, and a hierarchy grew up to govern it. John 18:36 Part Two · The Schism Within Persecution Redirected Persecution Redirected Persecution did not end with Constantine, it changed direction. The sword that had once fallen on all Christians now fell on those who refused the new state church and its infant baptism: Novatianists, Donatists, and every group after them that kept to New Testament faith and practice. Acts 5:29 Revelation 17:1-2 A church joined to civil power, pictured in judgment Galatians 1:6-7 A warning against a gospel reshaped by compromise Part Three · Third to Seventh Century Donatists and Anabaptists Arise Out of the traditores controversy and the new state church, dissenting bodies multiplied, each still contending for a regenerate church and believer’s baptism, and each paying for it in blood. Donatists North African believers who refused fellowship with a state-favored church they considered compromised, insisting the church must remain pure. Romans 16:17 Anabaptists Literally “re-baptizers,” a name of derision given because they baptized believers who had only received infant baptism, insisting baptism must follow a profession of faith. Acts 8:36-38 Matthew 3:8 Baptism follows repentance, never precedes it Colossians 2:12 Baptism as burial, requiring prior faith Part Four · Seventh to Eleventh Century The Paulicians and Their Heirs Through the Dark Ages, dissenting churches persisted in Armenia, Bulgaria, and Italy, hunted, scattered, and renamed with every migration. Paulicians A dissenting movement across Armenia and Asia Minor, later driven into the Balkans and Italy, planting seed that would surface again as new names in new lands. Hebrews 11:37-38 Petrobrusians Followers of Peter of Bruys in southern France, who rejected infant baptism and the veneration of the cross. 1 Peter 4:14 Henricians & Arnoldists Named for Henry of Lausanne and Arnold of Brescia, both of whom preached against clerical corruption and for a church gathered by conversion. Galatians 1:8 Part Five · Eleventh to Sixteenth Century Albigenses, Waldenses, and Lollards By the eleventh century the names multiply again, a sign not of confusion, but of a movement too widespread to be governed by any single hierarchy. Albigenses Named for the town of Albi in southern France, the target of a papal crusade in the thirteenth century for their rejection of Rome’s authority. Revelation 2:9-10 Vaudois & Waldenses “People of the valley,” followers of Peter Waldo who preserved vernacular Scripture and sent missionary preachers across Europe from their Alpine strongholds. Matthew 5:10-12 Lollards Followers of Wycliffe’s teaching in England, translating and spreading Scripture in the common tongue at great personal cost. John 8:31-32 Part Six · The Unbroken Thread One Way, Many Names Lay the centuries side by side, and a single line runs beneath every name: churches gathered by conversion and baptism, never by birth or decree. 100–300 Christians · Asia Minor, Italy, England, Africa 300–600 Traditores fall away · Constantine’s state church, 313 · Novatianists · Donatists · Ana-Baptists · Spain, France, Wales, Armenia 600–900 Paulicians · Ana-Baptists · Armenia, Italy, Bulgaria 900–1300 Petrobrusians · Henricians · Arnoldists · Albigenses · Ana-Baptists · France, Wales, Germany 1300–1600 Waldenses · Lollards · Baptists · Holland, France, England 1600–present John Clarke · Roger Williams · Sandy Creek · Baptists · England, Russia, America Matthew 16:18 Christ’s promise that His church would never be extinguished Matthew 28:20 A promise of perpetuity to the local church Part Seven · The Mark That Never Changed The Nature of the Church Every name in this study points back to one contention, argued in every century against every pressure to abandon it. The nature of the church has been the most distinguished mark of difference between all of our ancestors and the Roman Catholic Church. The Montanists, Novatianists, Donatists, Paulicians, Petrobrusians, Henricians, Arnoldists, Albigenses, Waldenses and all of our Baptist ancestors have contended for the purity of the church. To them, a church was a group of saved people, baptized upon a profession of faith. Since infants can make no profession of faith, infant baptism was rejected. True Baptists today believe the same thing. The truth of the Lord’s church is a great truth with far reaching effects. Hisel Part Seven · The Mark That Never Changed Three Marks Mark One · A Regenerate Membership A church is composed of saved people only, never a mixed body of the converted and unconverted gathered by birth or geography. Mark Two · Believer’s Baptism Baptism follows a profession of faith; since an infant can profess nothing, infant baptism was rejected in every century by every name. Mark Three · Separation from the State Church From Donatist to Waldensian to Baptist, this conviction repeatedly meant standing apart from, and often suffering under, a church allied with civil power. 1 Timothy 3:15 The church as the pillar and ground of the truth Acts 2:41 The apostolic pattern, receiving the word, then baptism Closing Thought One Church, Called Out Ekklesia , a called-out assembly. Whatever the century called them, and whatever the world called them in scorn, they held the same truth we hold: a visible, local, regenerate, baptized church, standing on the sole authority of Scripture. Pedobaptist and Campbellite Immersions. Southwestern Publishing House, 1858, p. 150. (By the “church” Zwingli means the Roman Catholic church.) Daniel Merrill, A Forgotten Baptist Tells how Daniel Merrill, a Congregational pastor in Sedgwick, Maine, studied baptism and became a Baptist in 1805. Notes his firm later writings on baptized church membership. Daniel Merrill, A Forgotten Baptist Daniel Merrill (1765-1833) pastored the Sedgwick Congregational Church, the largest church in Maine. He came from a family of minsters and was a convinced pedobaptist. However in 1802 some Baptists came to his town. Merrill began to earnestly study the doctrine of baptism. Soon he was convinced the Bible only taught believer's immersion. He shared the results of his study with his congregation in several sermons. On February 28, 1805, the church voted unanimously to become a Baptist church. They sent for help from the Baptists of New England. On May 13, 1805, in the waters of the Benjamin River, Merrill, his wife and sixty- four of their number were baptized by Thomas Baldwin of Boston and Elisha Williams of Beverly, Massachusetts. The next day, nineteen more were baptized and the First Baptist Church of Sedgwick was officially constituted. While some students of Baptist history know this part, very few know the rest of the story. Merrill's studies of the Scriptures led him to become a staunch Baptist. So strong that he wrote: "We purposely exclude from our communion all Churches, which admit to their community any of the unbaptized: for all such pollute, if not destroy, the Church of God, and are not baptized Churches; but are Churches, or Societies, of spurious origin; or Churches bewitched... the Paedobaptist Churches are NOT of the visible Church of Christ." (The Kingdom of Heaven Distinguished from Babylon, 1808) Not only that, but in his 1812 Miniature History of the Baptists, Merrill wrote, "The origin of the Baptists can be found no where unless it be conceded that it was at Jordan or Enon." He goes on to write of the Anabaptists, the Waldenses, and the Petrobrusians. Those who ignorantly claim such Baptist views originated with J.R. Graves or G.H. Orchard would do well to study the life and writings of Daniel Merrill. See the slides: Early American Baptists, Disestablishmentarianism
