Early American Baptists: Establishment, Disestablishment and Soul Liberty New England and Southern Baptists such as Roger Williams, John Clarke, Obadiah Holmes, Isaac Backus and John Leland. Covers what they fought, including tax-funded churches and licensing laws, and what they argued for, soul liberty and believer's baptism, with the middle way between them, through to the First Amendment. Early American Baptists – Establishment, Disestablishment and Soul Liberty Baptist history Early American Baptists Establishment, disestablishment and soul liberty: three answers to the question of who rules the church. Acts 5:29 Galatians 5:1 ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move. Tap any reference to read the verse. Three answers Early America asked one question: what should the state do about religion? There were three answers. 1. Establishment The state backs the church with taxes and laws. One church (Cotton, the Mathers, the Anglican South), or all the Christian churches alike (Patrick Henry’s 1784 bill, Massachusetts after 1780). 2. Disestablishment, the middle way No tax-funded church, but the laws, oaths and proclamations keep the state friendly to Protestant Christianity. John Jay. 3. Soul liberty No state support and no state control at all. A church lives on the gifts of its members, and a man’s conscience is his own. The Baptists. The Baptists fought the first answer and then pressed against the second. A friendly state, they said, is still the state in the church. The long word “Antidisestablishmentarianism” comes from the nineteenth-century British fight over whether to disestablish the Church of England, and it means holding that the state church should stay. In early America the word fits the first camp. The second camp wanted disestablishment, but not the Baptists’ kind. What they were fighting Tax-funded churches Everyone paid for the Congregational church in New England and the Anglican church in the South, whatever he believed. Licenses to preach A man could not preach without the state church’s permission, and unlicensed preaching was a crime. Infant baptism as a civil duty Babies were baptized into the church and the commonwealth together, and refusing it marked a man as a troublemaker. Enforced conformity Fines, whippings, jail and banishment for those who would not conform. What they argued for 1 Soul liberty. Every man answers to God for himself. Romans 14:12 2 Voluntary membership. A church is the saved, baptized upon their own profession of faith. Acts 8:36-37 3 No coercion in religion. Faith cannot be forced, and the sword is not the church’s weapon. 2 Corinthians 10:4 4 Liberty for all. Not only for Baptists, but for every conscience, even those they disagreed with. Render unto Caesar They say unto him, Caesar’s. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s ; and unto God the things that are God’s . Matthew 22:21 Two realms, and two kinds of authority. The magistrate keeps the peace. He does not keep the soul. John 18:36 Romans 13:1-4 Let both grow together Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field: But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way. But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also. So the servants of the householder came and said unto him, Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares? He said unto them, An enemy hath done this. The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up? But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest : and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn. Matthew 13:24-30 Roger Williams leaned on this parable. If the tares are among the wheat until the harvest, then the sword has no business sorting them now. Luke 9:54-56 We ought to obey God Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men . Acts 5:29 The answer every one of these men gave when the court told them to stop preaching, stop baptizing, or stop meeting. Acts 4:19-20 Thomas Helwys The Baptist argument for soul liberty began in England, before any Baptist reached America. 1609 John Smyth forms a Baptist congregation of English exiles in Amsterdam, and Thomas Helwys is among them. Acts 8:36-37 c. 1612 Helwys leads part of the congregation home to England, and publishes A Short Declaration of the Mystery of Iniquity , a plea for liberty of conscience that may be the first in the English language. 1612 → He sends a copy to King James I. Helwys and others are thrown into Newgate prison, and he probably died there about 1616. Let them be heretics, Turks, Jews, or whatsoever, it appertains not to the earthly power to punish them in the least measure. Thomas Helwys, 1612 The same conviction, a century and a half earlier, that Holmes, Backus and Leland would suffer for. The New England core 1636 Roger Williams banished from Massachusetts Bay; founds Providence. 1639–40s Providence and Newport. The first Baptist churches in America take form. 1651 Obadiah Holmes whipped on Boston Common. 1663 Rhode Island’s charter guarantees religious freedom. 1770s Isaac Backus carries the fight against the tax-supported church. Roger Williams 1635 The Massachusetts Bay court banishes him for “newe and dangerous opinions”, chiefly that the magistrate has no authority over the soul. He flees into the winter wilderness in January 1636. 1636 He founds Providence , a colony where no man would be compelled to worship. 1639 Baptized, he helps form the Providence church, often counted the first Baptist church in America. He left it within months and ended as a “Seeker”, so we claim his argument and not his later path. 1644 The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution argues that forcing conscience is itself the sin. John Cotton of Boston answers him, and the debate runs for years. John Clarke 1640s A physician, he helps found Newport and gathers its Baptist church. Sources date it anywhere from 1638 to 1648; it is among the first two Baptist churches in America and still stands. 1651 Arrested at Lynn with Obadiah Holmes and John Crandall for holding a private worship service, and imprisoned in Boston. Clarke is fined £20, Crandall £5 and Holmes £30. 1652 Publishes Ill Newes from New England in London, exposing Massachusetts to the English public. 1663 After years in England as agent, he secures Rhode Island’s royal charter from Charles II: “a lively experiment” in full liberty in religious concernments. Obadiah Holmes Born in Lancashire about 1610, a weaver and glassmaker, Holmes left Salem and then Rehoboth for his Baptist convictions, was excommunicated, and fled to Newport in 1650. July 1651 Arrested at the home of blind William Witter in Lynn for preaching, baptizing and the Lord’s Supper. Sept. 5, 1651 Thirty lashes with a three-corded whip on Boston Common. He declined wine beforehand and preached through the whipping. 1652 → Succeeds Clarke as pastor of the Newport church, and serves it for some thirty years until his death in 1682. You have struck me as with roses. Obadiah Holmes, to the magistrates, after the whipping Read the full study: Obadiah Holmes ↗ Holmes and the apostles And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name . Acts 5:41 Holmes read his stripes in the light of Peter and John. He prayed that the sin not be laid to the charge of his persecutors, as Stephen did. Acts 7:60 Galatians 6:17 Isaac Backus 1724–1806 Converted in the Great Awakening, he left the established church, became a Baptist in 1751, and pastored at Middleborough, Massachusetts, for fifty years. 1768–71 Baptists at Ashfield have their property seized to pay the Congregational minister’s tax. They petition the General Court and carry the case to the King in Council, which disallows the law. Backus takes up their cause. 1773 An Appeal to the Public for Religious Liberty , the plainest Baptist argument against a state-taxed church. 1774 Goes to Philadelphia with James Manning, president of the Baptists’ Rhode Island College, and meets the Massachusetts delegates to the First Continental Congress, to ask relief for Baptists taxed for ministers they did not choose. Backus refused to take out the “certificates” that excused Baptists from the tax, because to ask the state’s permission was to grant its authority. He also wrote the history of New England Baptists. Colleges, associations and Hezekiah Smith Baptists in New England built the institutions to carry their case: a college, an association, and pastors who would travel for both. 1764 Baptists found Rhode Island College, later Brown University, under its first president, James Manning. Hezekiah Smith helps raise its support, spending eight months in 1769–70 in the South. 1765–1805 Smith pastors the First Baptist Church of Haverhill, Massachusetts. 1767 The Warren Association unites the New England Baptist churches and, in time, carries their grievances to the courts and Congress. 1775–80 Smith serves as a chaplain in the Revolution. Daniel Merrill A Congregational pastor in Sedgwick, Maine, and a convinced pedobaptist, who studied the Bible on baptism when Baptists came to town in 1802. 1805 His church votes unanimously to become Baptist, and Merrill, his wife and sixty-four others are baptized in the Benjamin River. 1808 Writes The Kingdom of Heaven Distinguished from Babylon , holding that churches that admit the unbaptized are not baptized churches. 1812 Miniature History of the Baptists : their origin can be found “no where unless it be conceded that it was at Jordan or Enon.” Read the full study: Daniel Merrill ↗ Pennsylvania and the associations Not every colony fought. Rhode Island and Pennsylvania offered liberty of conscience from the start, and Baptists there built the first networks. 1682 William Penn’s Pennsylvania grants liberty of conscience, and Baptists gather in and around Philadelphia. 1707 The Philadelphia Baptist Association forms, the first in America, and for generations helps the scattered churches stay together. 1758 The Sandy Creek Association forms in North Carolina, and Separate Baptists across the South join it. 1767 The Warren Association unites the New England churches, and by the 1770s it keeps a grievance committee to carry their cases. The associations are why the Baptists could speak with one voice, and why their agents went to the legislatures on behalf of many churches, not as lone men. Separate Baptists The Great Awakening reached the South through the Separate Baptists, preachers who came out of the revivals and preached whether the Anglican parish permitted it or not. The older Regular Baptists were more formal and kept ties with the Philadelphia Association. The two groups united in Virginia in 1787. 1755 Shubal Stearns , a Baptist since 1751, leaves Connecticut and plants the Sandy Creek church in North Carolina on November 22, with sixteen members. From it the Separate Baptists spread into Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. c. 1770 Daniel Marshall , Stearns’s brother-in-law, carries the work to Georgia, where he is arrested in St. Paul’s Parish and ordered to stop preaching. He preaches on, and settles at Kiokee in January 1771, where the church is constituted in 1772. Acts 4:19 Their preaching was warm, their meetings were long, and the parish clergy did not like it. They preached under open sky and in houses because no one would give them a pulpit. Jailed for preaching June 1768 Spotsylvania County. John Waller, Lewis Craig, James Childs and others are seized and arraigned as “disturbers of the peace”. A lawyer complained they could not meet a man on the road without ramming a text of Scripture down his throat. They refused to promise to stop preaching, and lay forty-three days in jail, preaching through the grates. 1768–70s Baptist preachers are jailed in Spotsylvania, Caroline, Chesterfield, Culpeper and Orange counties. Again and again they preach through the jail grates to crowds outside. 1770s Lewis Craig and Elijah Craig , both jailed (Elijah in Culpeper and Orange counties), later carry their congregations to Kentucky. Patrick Henry and the Baptists Patrick Henry (1736–1799), the Virginia lawyer who cried “Give me liberty or give me death” in 1775 and later served as governor, stands on both sides of this story. The friend Legend has him pleading for these jailed preachers in a famous speech. That speech is apocryphal, written later by a minister, according to Semple’s editor. But Henry did act as counsel for some imprisoned Baptist preachers in Caroline County, and Semple calls him a friend in the fight to license their meeting places. The opponent In 1784 he backed a general tax to support teachers of the Christian religion, and the Baptists opposed it. See “Multiple establishment.” He was a champion of liberty against Britain, yet he held that a republic needs the state’s support of religion. The Baptists thanked him for the first and opposed him on the second. Reuben Ford Born about 1742, Ford was awakened under George Whitefield at about twenty, and baptized some seven years later after hearing the Baptist preachers Read and Harriss. 1771 He gathers the Goochland church, with about seventy-five members, among the earliest Baptist churches in Virginia, and pastors it for the rest of his ministry. Dover follows in 1773. 30+ years Clerk of the Dover Association. Aug. 1785 Clerk of the General Committee at Du Puy’s meetinghouse, Powhatan County, which resolved against the assessment bill. The committee appointed him to carry its remonstrance and petition to the General Assembly. 1786–87 Reports that the assessment did not pass, and that Jefferson’s act on religious liberty passed instead. He and John Leland then served as the committee’s agents against the Episcopal incorporation act. Not a brilliant preacher, wrote his biographer, but his simplicity, affection and a blameless life won the confidence of everyone who knew him. Sources: James B. Taylor, Virginia Baptist Ministers (1859); Robert B. Semple, A History of the Rise and Progress of the Baptists in Virginia (1810). Ford was the clerk and messenger of the General Committee, not the author of its resolution. The Anglican establishment In Virginia and much of the South the Church of England was the law. Its parish and county officers did not merely favor it. They enforced it. Preaching licenses Granted by the parish and the county court, and withheld from dissenters. Parish taxes Everyone paid the Church of England’s tithe, Baptists included. Legal penalties for dissenters County courts, parish vestries and crown-appointed governors enforced it all. Not always one famous name, but a whole system. The English Toleration Act let dissenters license a few meeting places, but Semple notes a few licensed places in each county was a small gain to people who wanted to preach to every creature. The establishment side They were not always villains. Many believed society could not hold together without the state’s support of religion. John Cotton (1585–1652) The leading minister of Boston. Defended a close church-state relationship in early Massachusetts, and answered Roger Williams. Increase (1639–1723) and Cotton Mather (1663–1728) Boston ministers, father and son. Upheld established church structures and the ideal of a godly commonwealth. The Anglican system Parish vestries, county courts and crown-appointed governors enforced the Church of England in the South. Their motives were order and morality. The Baptists’ answer was that Christ is the only head of the church, and conscience cannot be commanded. Colossians 1:18 Multiple establishment Patrick Henry wanted no single favored church, but he held that a moral republic could not stand without the state’s support of religion. 1784 The Bill Establishing a Provision for Teachers of the Christian Religion would tax every Virginian, and each taxpayer would name the Christian church that received his money. If he named none, it went to schools. 1780 Massachusetts’ constitution had already done the same, letting towns tax for “public Protestant teachers”, each taxpayer’s money going to his own denomination. Isaac Backus and the Baptists contested it. Whereas the general diffusion of Christian knowledge hath a natural tendency to correct the morals of men, restrain their vices, and preserve the peace of society… Preamble to Henry’s 1784 bill Henry’s case is civic, not gospel: Christian teaching is valued for good order. Scholars compare it to a public good that taxes should fund, like roads. That comparison is theirs, not Henry’s words. This was the harder argument for the Baptists, because it sounded fair. Their answer: a tax for religion, even an even-handed one, makes the state the judge of what is a church. Romans 14:4 The middle way: John Jay The middle way sits left of Henry. Jay rejected a national church and a single state denomination, yet he believed civil order and liberty were tied to Christian morality, and that the states could shape their laws to keep that heritage. 1777 At New York’s constitutional convention he moved to bar Roman Catholics from land and civil rights unless they renounced the Pope. That failed, but his naturalization oath, renouncing foreign ecclesiastical as well as civil authority, was adopted and stood until 1806. 1795–1801 As governor he followed New England precedent in proclaiming days of Thanksgiving, and pressed for laws requiring observance of the Sabbath, the “blue laws” that closed work, trade and amusement on Sunday. 1816 Writes to Jedidiah Morse that “it is the duty as well as the privilege and interest of our Christian nation to select and prefer Christians for their rulers.” Sources: John R. Vile, “John Jay,” First Amendment Encyclopedia (Middle Tennessee State University); on blue laws, The New York Times, Oct. 7, 1963, “The Archaic Blue Laws.” This is the middle way in a single man. No state church, but a state that leans on Christianity and limits the civil standing of those outside it. The Baptists’ soul liberty asked more: equal liberty for every conscience. Galatians 5:1 Baptists and the Revolution Virginia’s Baptists had been ground under the established church, and Semple writes that they were “to a man” favorable to any revolution that would give them freedom of religion. Aug. 1775 At Du Puy’s meetinghouse in Powhatan County, the united Baptist body resolves to petition the Virginia Convention to abolish the church establishment and to leave religion to stand on its own merits. Aug. 1775 It also asks leave to preach to the army, which is granted. Jeremiah Walker and John Williams preach to the soldiers, but find little encouragement and drop it. 1775–80 In New England, Hezekiah Smith serves as an army chaplain. Mere toleration was not enough, Semple notes, since they had been jailed even where the toleration law was thought to be in force. Virginia, 1776–1786 1776 Virginia’s Declaration of Rights, drafted by George Mason, guarantees religion in Article 16. Madison, then a young delegate, amends Mason’s “toleration” to “free exercise”. 1784 Patrick Henry’s general assessment bill (an assessment is a tax) would have taxed every Virginian for the church of his choice. Baptists petition against it through their General Committee. 1785 James Madison’s Memorial and Remonstrance helps defeat it. Jan. 1786 The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Jefferson, passes. Madison answers Henry James Madison, then a young Virginia legislator and later the fourth President, answered Henry’s civic argument head on in his Memorial and Remonstrance (1785). The Bill implies either that the Civil Magistrate is a competent Judge of Religious Truth; or that he may employ Religion as an engine of Civil policy. The first is an arrogant pretension falsified by the contradictory opinions of Rulers in all ages, and throughout the world: the second an unhallowed perversion of the means of salvation. James Madison, Memorial and Remonstrance , section 5 During almost fifteen centuries has the legal establishment of Christianity been on trial. What have been its fruits? More or less in all places, pride and indolence in the Clergy, ignorance and servility in the laity, in both, superstition, bigotry and persecution. James Madison, Memorial and Remonstrance , section 7 Madison argued from the good of the state. The Baptists argued from the gospel, as the slide “Different roots, same conclusion” shows. The General Committee resolves On August 18, 1785, the Baptist General Committee met at Du Puy’s meetinghouse in Powhatan County, with William Webber moderator and Reuben Ford clerk. Semple records its resolution. …it is believed to be repugnant to the spirit of the Gospel for the Legislature thus to proceed in matters of religion; that no human laws ought to be established for this purpose; but that every person ought to be left entirely free in respect to matters of religion; that the holy Author of our religion needs no such compulsive measures for the promotion of His cause; that the Gospel wants not the feeble arm of man for its support; that it has made, and will again through divine power, make its way against all opposition; and that should the Legislature assume the right of taxing the people for the support of the Gospel, it will be destructive to religious liberty. Baptist General Committee, August 1785, in Semple’s History of the Baptists in Virginia It urged every county that had not yet petitioned to do so against the engrossed bill, and appointed Reuben Ford to carry its remonstrance to the General Assembly. Matthew 16:18 Zechariah 4:6 Semple’s own judgment: the Baptists, he believed, were the only sect who plainly remonstrated, and the bill’s defeat owed much to them. Not all histories would put it that strongly. The petitions Madison’s essay was not the only answer. In the fall of 1785 a printed petition went through central and southern Virginia, and far more people signed it than signed the Remonstrance . …that they are inwardly moved by the Holy Ghost to take upon them that Office, that they seek the good of Mankind and not worldly Interest. Let their doctrines be scriptural and their Lives upright. Then shall Religion (if departed) speedily return, and Deism be put to open shame… Virginia petition against the general assessment, 1785 Its answer to Henry was the gospel’s own: ministers are called by God, and the church needs no tax collector to keep it. Copies went to the General Assembly from many counties. Acts 20:28 1 Peter 5:2 Source: quoted in The Heritage Foundation, “Did America Have a Christian Founding?”. The original forms are in the Legislative Petitions collection at the Library of Virginia. Whether Baptists wrote this one is not yet confirmed. John Leland Born in Massachusetts in 1754, Leland spent about fifteen years as a Baptist preacher in Virginia, and became the Baptists’ best-known voice for liberty of conscience. 1775 Ordained in Virginia, he pastors there until he goes home to Massachusetts in 1791. 1788 Tradition holds that Leland, who opposed the Constitution for lacking a bill of rights, met Madison in Orange County in March and stood aside for his election to the Virginia ratifying convention, on an understanding that Madison would seek one. The details vary by source, and Madison’s own public stance was more guarded. 1791 The Rights of Conscience Inalienable : liberty for all men, “Pagan, Turk, Jew or Christian”, not for Baptists alone. Leland’s conviction was the Baptist one: the same freedom he asked for himself, he asked for those he disagreed with. Matthew 7:12 Different roots, same conclusion In Virginia the Baptists found allies in Jefferson and Madison, who wanted the state out of religion for other reasons. The Enlightenment wing Jefferson and Madison reasoned from natural rights: religion is a private matter, and government has no jurisdiction over it. The Baptists They reasoned from the gospel: faith must be free, because a faith that cannot be refused means nothing. John 6:44 Acts 8:36-37 Both pressed past the middle way, where the state still leans on Christianity through taxes, oaths and laws. The Baptists did not become secular for it. They asked the state to leave the church alone, so that the church would be free to be the church. John 18:36 The First Amendment Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free , and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. Galatians 5:1 Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof… First Amendment, ratified December 15, 1791 The Baptist voices of Backus, Leland and the Virginia committee were among those that carried the argument. In 1801 the Danbury Baptists of Connecticut, where the state church still stood, wrote to President Jefferson that religious liberty there was held as a favor from the state and not as a right. His 1802 reply spoke of a “wall of separation.” In their case it is a wall to keep the state out of the church, not the church out of society. Disestablishment, state by state 1786 Virginia ends its establishment. 1818 Connecticut ends tax support for its Congregational church. 1819 New Hampshire ends its religious tax (some sources give 1817 or 1818). 1833 Massachusetts is the last state to disestablish, almost two centuries after Holmes was whipped. The First Amendment bound only the national government at first. The states had to follow one at a time. The thread Holmes, Merrill, Backus, Leland and the rest are one thread. Willing to suffer for believer’s baptism. Unwilling to submit to state church authority. Strong for religious liberty for everyone, even those they disagreed with. Faith was a matter between a man and God, not a matter of law. 1 Timothy 2:5 Hebrews 11:36-38 2 Timothy 3:12 A line of believers The Trail of Blood These men stand in the line of believers who held the same distinctives and paid for them in every age. Hebrews 12:1 Our inheritance Soul liberty, the local church and believer’s baptism are not American inventions, but Bible convictions people bled to keep. I Reject the Nicene Creed Explains why the author rejects the Nicene Creed, holding that its Greek terms such as begotten and homoousios brought new errors in answering Arianism. Stands on the Godhead as stated in Scripture alone. Critique of the Nicene Creed Summary of My Rejection of the Nicene Creed As an independent fundamental Baptist standing on the word of God alone—no church fathers, no reformers, no councils, no vain philosophy (Colossians 2:8), I reject the Nicene Creed outright. In trying to fight Arian heresy (the idea that the Son was created and not eternal God), the council of men in 325/381 imported Greek terms and logic that actually birthed new errors. The Conflict: By calling the Father the "unbegotten" source and the Son "begotten" of Him, the Creed establishes a hierarchy of origin rather than of role. Even if they call the Sonship "eternal," the language implies the Son is derivative. If the Father is the "One God" (the Monarchia), and the Son is "from" Him, the Creed essentially describes a "process," which by definition,becomes a characteristic of the Son’s creation, not a description of a static, eternal Godhead. The Creed uses Homoousios (of the same substance) to try to fix the "creational flow" problem this language introduces. But this brings another problem; the Bible doesn't say they are of the same substance, but fully and eternally the Godhead, one God Who is three persons. Not one God the Father and a Son made , or begotten, of the same substance by the Father. Use of the word "begotten" (implying origin and derivation) denies the eternal nature of Jesus, while the use of "through him" for the Creation (making the Son sound like a secondary tool used by the Father), creates confusion. Add to this the Creed’s assertion that the Spirit is issued from the Father and Son, rather than the Spirit being coeternally God as well, further complicates what the Bible describes. The introduction of this “Filioque” false dichotomy (Orthodox; Spirit issued only by the Father, vs Rome; issued by both) gives the unbiblical understanding that the Spirit, rather than being God, co-equal in the Godhead as God, is a created being. All of this rationalizing use of “begotten,” "consubstantial" and "proceeds" becomes non-biblical philosophy of men, turning the Godhead into a chain of ontological origin rather than the biblical triune God. If the Creed says the Son is “from the Father’s substance” (the very wording behind “begotten… consubstantial”), then by the plain meaning of language He is derived. There is no honest way around it. “From” denotes source. “Substance” denotes something He is taken out of or issued from. That is the definition of “made,” no matter how many qualifiers like “eternally,” “not made,” or “before all ages” you stack on top. You cannot escape the logic: something taken from another thing is secondary to it. The men at Nicene also chose to elevate faith in a visible "holy catholic and apostolic Church" and in their “sacrament” of water baptism "for the forgiveness of sins," to salvific essentials that must be professed, alongside their re-definition of Who and What God is . The result? A creed that claims to defend biblical truth but subtly subordinates the Son and Spirit through implied creational hierarchy, rather than a hierarchy of roles, contradicts its own "not made" claim with creational-flow language, and adds extra-biblical requirements that damn by vain tradition. Creeds aren’t necessary. Scripture alone is sufficient: the eternal, co-equal, co-eternal triune Godhead (Father, Word, Holy Ghost, these three are one) needs no conciliar patch. The Creed didn't refute heresy, it dressed up a different version of the same root error, and passed it off as truth. 1. The Creed's Use of "Begotten" Implies Origin, Creating a Contradiction Creed Language : "the Only Begotten Son of God, born of the Father before all ages... begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father" The Argument : "Begotten" is a term of origin or source, implying a "before" and "after." This introduces a creational hierarchy that contradicts the denial of creation ("not made") and suggests the Son is derivative rather than fully co-eternal God. Biblical Support : Scripture ties "begotten" to time-bound events, such as the resurrection, rather than an eternal pre-temporal state: Acts 13:33 — "God hath fulfilled the same unto us their children, in that he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee." Hebrews 1:5 — "For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee?" Revelation 1:5 — "...Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead..." Verses asserting the eternal deity of Christ without "begotten" origin language: John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." John 8:58 — "Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am." Micah 5:2 — "...whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting." 2. Framing Creation "Through Him" Subordinates the Son Creed Language : "through him all things were made." The Argument : While creation by Christ is biblical, the Creed’s wording makes the Son sound like a secondary agent or instrument of the Father. Scripture presents all three Persons as directly and equally involved ("by him"). Biblical Support : John 1:3 — "All things were made by him ; and without him was not any thing made that was made." Colossians 1:16 — "For by him were all things created... all things were created by him, and for him. " Hebrews 1:2 — "...his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds ." 3. "Homoousios" and Procession Language Introduce Non-Biblical Philosophy Creed Language : "consubstantial with the Father"; "who proceeds from the Father and the Son" The Argument : The Bible does not use terms like "same substance" or describe ontological "processions." These terms turn the Godhead into a chain of origin. Scripture teaches three co-equal Persons in one Godhead with functional roles but no ontological derivation. KJV Support : Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily." 1 John 5:7 — "For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one." Note: John 15:26 refers to a "sending" role, not an eternal ontological origin. 4. Elevation of the Visible Church and Baptism to Salvific Essentials Creed Language : "I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church"; "I confess one Baptism for the forgiveness of sins" The Argument : This equates institutional membership and water baptism with core doctrines of the Godhead, suggesting they are essential for salvation. Scripture teaches that the church is a spiritual body and baptism is a symbolic ordinance following faith. Biblical Support : Church as a spiritual body : Ephesians 1:22-23 — "...the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all." Baptism as symbolic : Romans 6:3-4 — "Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death..." Baptism of the Spirit : Ephesians 1:13 — "...ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise" ; Titus 3:5 — "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost." Final Summary: Why This Matters In the end, the Nicene Creed's attempt to combat Arianism with human wisdom and philosophy (instead of pure Scripture) backfired. By forcing "begotten" onto eternity, it creates a logical contradiction: a term of origin ("source" and "result") while denying any creation happened. Framing creation as "through" the Son after calling the Father the primary "maker" subtly demotes Him to an instrument. Terms like "consubstantial" and "proceeds from the Father and the Son" (Filioque) introduce non-biblical chains of derivation, turning co-equal Persons into a hierarchy. Then it compounds the error by confessing "one holy catholic and apostolic Church" and "one Baptism for the forgiveness of sins" as if these are on par with the doctrine of God—elevating institution and ritual over the blood of Christ and Spirit regeneration. Once you bind people to the Creed as a test of orthodoxy (as the council and every creed-affirming denomination does), you force them to swallow the whole package: The Son becomes a kind of eternal demiurge—continually “begotten” out of the Father’s substance, never created yet never fully self-existent in the same way the Father is. The Spirit is reduced to something “proceeding from” or “issued by” the Father and the Son (Filioque) or just the Father (Eastern version)—either way, not the co-equal, co-eternal, complete Person the Bible presents, but a derived breath or influence. You must confess the visible “one holy catholic and apostolic Church” (their denomination or communion) as an article of saving faith. You must confess “one baptism for the forgiveness of sins” as the act that actually remits sin, not the symbolic testimony that follows the remission already granted by faith and the baptism of the Holy Ghost. None of that is in the Bible. Not one word. This is the danger of creedalism: good intentions against one heresy open the door to others. Protestants who wave "Sola Scriptura" as a fig leaf while leaning on councils and fathers miss the point. I stand on the Book alone—the living God doesn't need men's improvements. The Bible reveals the simple, eternal Jehovah: three co-equal Persons, one God, no origins, no processions, no add-ons required for salvation. The Nicene Creed codifies error under the guise of orthodoxy. I'll take the KJV over Nicaea every time. Amen.

Ignatius and the Lord's Table Answers the Catholic transubstantiation proof text in Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 7:1, in its own context. Shows that Ignatius was fighting the Docetists, who denied Christ came in the flesh, and measures him by the KJV. Ignatius and the Lord’s Table Answering the transubstantiation proof text Ignatius and the Lord’s Table Smyrnaeans 7:1 in its own context, measured by the King James Bible ✦ ✦ ✦ Use the arrow keys or swipe to move. Tap any gold reference to read the verse. Section One Who Was Ignatius? A pastor in Antioch, writing on his way to die. ✦ ✦ ✦ A Prisoner’s Letters Ignatius led the church at Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians. Around 107 to 110 AD he was arrested and taken under guard to Rome to be thrown to the beasts. On the road he wrote seven short letters: six to churches, and one to Polycarp. Same rule as the Didache. Ignatius is a valuable early witness. He is not Scripture. Where he agrees with the Bible, he confirms it. Where he goes beyond it, the Bible corrects him. Acts 11:26 Isaiah 8:20 Section Two The Real Enemy Ignatius was not fighting about bread. He was fighting about the body of Jesus. ✦ ✦ ✦ The Docetists From the Greek dokeō , “to seem.” They taught that Jesus was pure spirit who only seemed to have a human body. So He only seemed to suffer, only seemed to die, and only seemed to rise. John had already called this the spirit of antichrist. The real question in Smyrna. Did Jesus Christ come in the flesh? Everything Ignatius says about the Lord’s Table answers that question. 1 John 4:2-3 2 John 7 John 1:14 Luke 24:39 Section Three · Smyrnaeans 7:1 The Proof Text The verse most often quoted to prove transubstantiation. ✦ ✦ ✦ What Ignatius Wrote “They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again.” Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 7:1 Who abstained? The Docetists. Why? Because the meal remembered a body they said never existed. Ignatius is exposing their denial of the Incarnation, not defining the bread. A Figure of Speech Ignatius calls the meal by the name of what it represents. Grammarians call this metonymy : naming the sign for the thing signified. The flag. If a man refuses to salute a nation’s flag because he denies that nation has a right to exist, his protest is against the nation, not the cloth. The Docetists refused the meal because they denied the body it remembered. Jesus spoke the same way. No one thinks He is made of wood or grows on a trellis. John 10:9 John 15:1 A Memorial of Thanksgiving And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me . Luke 22:19 The Greek word is anamnēsis : a memorial, a calling to mind. The elements point back to a finished act on Calvary, not to something happening in the eating. And they point forward. For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come . 1 Corinthians 11:26 Luke 22:19 1 Corinthians 11:24-26 Section Four Jesus at the Table What the first Supper shows about every Supper since. ✦ ✦ ✦ His Body Was Holding the Bread When Jesus said “This is my body,” His own body was whole and sitting at the table, holding the bread in His hands. After the blessing, He still called the cup “this fruit of the vine.” After the blessing, Paul still calls it “this bread.” Stated in Scripture The Lord Himself and the apostle Paul both named the elements as bread and fruit of the vine after they were blessed. Matthew 26:29 1 Corinthians 11:26 Expect This Answer Ignatius calls it the flesh “which suffered for our sins, and which the Father raised up again.” It is tempting to say, “So the bread was crucified?” Don’t lean on that A Roman Catholic will simply agree that the body present is the same one that suffered and rose. That argument answers a view they don’t hold. Stand here instead His sacrifice was offered once for all, and is finished. He sat down at the right hand of God. His body is in heaven until He returns. Hebrews 10:10 Hebrews 10:12 Acts 3:21 Section Five In His Own Words Let Ignatius define “flesh” and “blood” for himself. ✦ ✦ ✦ Faith Is the Flesh, Love Is the Blood “Be renewed in faith, that is the flesh of the Lord, and in love, that is the blood of Jesus Christ.” Ignatius, Trallians 8:1 “I desire the bread of God, the heavenly bread, the bread of life, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ… and I desire the drink of God, namely His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.” Ignatius, Romans 7:3 In Ignatius’s own vocabulary, eating the flesh and drinking the blood describe living by faith and abiding in love. Eating Is Believing Ignatius is echoing John 6. Jesus Himself explains what coming and eating mean. And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger ; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst . John 6:35 Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life . I am that bread of life . John 6:47-48 It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life . John 6:63 Section Six The Altar Is the Assembly Where the “altar” really is in Ignatius’s letters. ✦ ✦ ✦ Christ Is Our Altar Some use Ignatius’s word “altar” to turn the thanksgiving meal into a new and continual sacrifice. Scripture says we already have an altar, and it is Christ, who suffered without the gate. Hebrews 13:9-12 “Let no man deceive himself: if any one be not within the altar, he is deprived of the bread of God.” Ignatius, Ephesians 5:2 “Within the altar” means within the gathered church. To be outside it is to separate yourself from the local congregation, and so lose your place at the memorial. One Eucharist, One Altar “Take ye heed, then, to have but one Eucharist. For there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup to show forth the unity of His blood; one altar; as there is one bishop, along with the presbytery and deacons, my fellow-servants.” Ignatius, Philadelphians 4:1 The point is unity: one meal, one cup, one gathered body. “Eucharist” means the whole thanksgiving gathering, which the Docetists were boycotting. The “one altar” is the one local assembly. 1 Corinthians 10:17 What “Catholic” Meant “Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude of the people also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.” Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 8:2 This is the first known use of the phrase. Katholikos means “whole” or “universal.” It is defined by where Christ is, not by Rome. In his letter to the church at Rome, Ignatius never mentions a bishop there at all. Measured by Scripture Ignatius sets one bishop above the elders (presbyters). That is already a step beyond the New Testament. Stated in Scripture Paul calls the same men “elders” and “bishops” (overseers). In the Bible these are one office, not two. Even so, Ignatius’s bishop was the pastor of one church in one city, not a ruler over many churches. Titus 1:5 Titus 1:7 Acts 20:17 Acts 20:28 Section Seven The Answer Putting it together when Smyrnaeans 7:1 comes up. ✦ ✦ ✦ In One Breath “Ignatius is not defining the substance of the bread. He is exposing the hypocrisy of the Docetists. They cannot join a thanksgiving meal meant to memorialize a physically broken body when they deny Jesus ever had a physical body to break. You are reading a 13th-century Roman Catholic definition of transubstantiation back into a 2nd-century defense of the literal, physical Incarnation.” The enemy was Docetism, not a low view of the bread. Ignatius defines flesh and blood as faith and love. Jesus and Paul still called it bread and fruit of the vine. Christ’s sacrifice is finished, once for all. Obadiah Holmes: A Testimony of Perseverance in Christ

Obadiah Holmes: A Testimony of Perseverance in Christ Tells the life of Obadiah Holmes, from his youth in Lancashire to his conversion and Baptist convictions. Recounts the steadfast faith he showed under persecution in New England. The Steadfast Faith of Obadiah Holmes: A Testimony of Perseverance in Christ Let us consider the life of Obadiah Holmes, a man whose unyielding commitment to the Gospel of Jesus Christ serves as a beacon for all Baptists. Born around 1610 in Reddish, Lancashire, England, near Manchester, Holmes grew up in a humble farming family. Baptized on March 18, 1609/10 at Didsbury Chapel, he was the son of Robert Hulme, a husbandman, and Katherine Johnson. As a youth, Holmes described himself as rebellious and wayward, immersed in "folly and vanity," admitting in his later testimony that he "minded nothing but folly and vanity... I was not only rebellious against my parents but against the Lord... continuing in such a course for four or five years." He blamed his disobedient acts for hastening his mother's death around 1630, an event that sparked a profound spiritual awakening. Reflecting on this, he wrote, "It struck me that my disobedient acts caused her death, which forced me to confess the same to her—my evil ways." This turning point led him to embrace repentance and faith in Christ, transforming his life from rebellion to devotion. At age 20, on November 20, 1630, Holmes married Katherine Hyde at the Collegiate Church in Manchester. They had nine children, though their infant son John died in England in 1633. Holmes worked as a weaver and glassmaker, skills that would later sustain his family in the New World. Seeking religious freedom amid England's turbulent spiritual climate, the couple emigrated during the Great Puritan Migration, enduring a stormy six-week voyage to arrive in Boston around 1638. Tradition holds they brought the first tall-case grandfather clock to America. Settling first in Salem, Massachusetts Bay Colony, Holmes joined two others—Ananias Concklin and Lawrence Southwick—in establishing what may have been America's first glass-making operation, producing window glass. He received land grants, served on juries, and became a freeman in 1640, joining the First Church of Salem. Yet, even here, his growing convictions began to stir unrest. By 1645, religious tensions mounted as Holmes increasingly opposed the Puritan practice of infant baptism, embracing instead "believer's baptism" by immersion—a hallmark of Baptist faith. In his testimony, he reflected on this shift: "After many years in death and darkness, this good news of salvation brought light in my soul." The Puritans viewed Baptists with deep suspicion, labeling them as "loathsome" heretics and "incendiaries of commonwealths, and the infectors of persons in main matters of religion, and the troublers of churches in all places where they have been." They accused Baptists of holding "other errors or heresies" alongside rejecting infant baptism, often concealing these until an opportunity to "vent them, by way of question or scruple." Seeking a more tolerant environment, he relocated his family to Rehoboth in Plymouth Colony (now Seekonk, Massachusetts), where he became a freeman in 1648 and soon became involved in the local church under pastor Samuel Newman. However, doctrinal differences quickly emerged, dividing the congregation over issues like infant baptism and church authority, with Holmes growing dissatisfied with the rigidity of the established Puritan practices. Influenced by Baptist ideas from nearby Rhode Island, Holmes and eight others underwent "new baptism" by immersion, marking their formal separation from the official church. This led to a prolonged schism that took about three years to fully manifest, splitting the church on doctrinal and legal lines. Holmes emerged as the leader of this dissenting faction, known as the "Schismists" or "Schismatists," a group of about 14 individuals including John Hazell, Edward Smith and his wife, Joseph Tory and his wife, the wife of James Mann, William Devell and his wife, and others. Clashes arose with the established church's pastor, Samuel Newman, escalating personal and religious tensions. The Schismists were accused of setting up an unauthorized, irregular church meeting in opposition to Newman's orderly, approved congregation, holding separate gatherings on the Lord's Day from house to house, baptizing adults, ordaining officers, and breaking bread together—actions seen as direct challenges to Puritan orthodoxy and social order. In October 1649, Holmes sued Newman for slander, seeking £100 in damages after Newman publicly accused him of taking a false oath in court—essentially perjury—though Newman later confessed in court that his accusation was based solely on hearsay from others, not personal knowledge, leading to Holmes winning the case. The conflict intensified in June 1650 when a multi-part petition was brought against Holmes and the Schismists before Plymouth's General Court, urging that all such "schismatical activity" cease. On October 2, 1650, a grand jury—including Plymouth leaders like William Bradford, John Alden, and Miles Standish—indicted Holmes and his followers for holding unauthorized Sunday meetings from house to house "contrary to the order of the court" and promoting Baptist views. The court ordered them "to desist, and neither to ordain officers, nor to baptize, nor to break bread together, nor yet to meet upon the first day of the week." Newman excommunicated Holmes, a severe ecclesiastical penalty that, in the theocratic context of colonial New England, carried profound civil and social implications. In Plymouth Colony, freeman status signified full citizenship, granting adult males the right to vote in colonial elections, hold public office, own and transfer land without restriction, participate in town meetings to shape laws, and serve on juries—privileges essential for influencing governance and community affairs. Unlike the stricter Massachusetts Bay Colony, where church membership was mandatory for freemanship, Plymouth did not explicitly require it; instead, candidates were elected by the General Court after demonstrating moral character, economic stability, and loyalty to the colony's Puritan-influenced laws. However, excommunication for religious dissent like Holmes's often blurred the lines between church and state, leading to significant repercussions. It branded the individual as a moral and spiritual outcast, eroding social standing through community ostracism, loss of business opportunities, and familial strains. Politically, while not automatically revoking freemanship in Plymouth, it could prompt civil authorities to view the excommunicated as "opposers of the good and wholesome laws of the Colony" or threats to social order, potentially resulting in the denial of voting rights, disqualification from office, confiscation of property, or even banishment. For Holmes, this excommunication amplified the court's indictment, diminishing his ability to engage fully in colonial politics, defend his interests in legal matters, or maintain economic security, as dissenters risked being sidelined from land grants and civic roles. Amid the ongoing persecution, Holmes refused to comply, declaring his obedience to Christ above man-made laws. In 1650, Holmes and his family fled to Newport, Rhode Island, a refuge for dissenters founded on tolerance by Roger Williams. Here, his Baptist convictions deepened, leading to one of early America's most infamous acts of religious persecution. On July 16, 1651, Holmes joined Baptist leaders Rev. John Clarke (physician and founder of Newport's church) and John Crandall on a pastoral visit to elderly, blind Baptist William Witter in Lynn, Massachusetts. The next day, during a private worship service at Witter's home—where "the word was proclaimed, converts were baptized, and the elements of the Lord’s Supper were served"—constables burst in, arresting the men as "erroneous persons" and "strangers" promoting heresy. The Puritan authorities condemned Holmes specifically for meeting at Witter's house to preach and baptize privately, for keeping his hat on during prayer in "disrespect to the ordinance of God and his worship," for receiving the sacrament while excommunicated, for rebaptizing those previously baptized (thereby denying prior baptisms as invalid and churches as nullities), and for denying the lawfulness of infant baptism. They charged that all this "tends to the dishonor of God, the despising the ordinances of God among us, the peace of the churches, and seducing the subjects of this commonwealth from the truth of the gospel of Jesus Christ, and perverting the straight ways of the Lord." A court found them guilty of "a half-dozen crimes of heresy," with Magistrate Encrease Nowell retorting to Holmes's claim of suffering for his faith, "No, it is for your error and going about to seduce the people." Imprisoned in Boston for nearly a month, they were tried before the Court of Assistants. The court fined Clarke £20, Crandall £5, and Holmes £30—a sum equivalent to much of his estate—with non-payment yielding whipping. Friends paid for Clarke and Crandall, but Holmes refused, proclaiming, "I bless God, that I am worthy to suffer for the name of Jesus." He declined wine or comforts before punishment, resolving "not to drink wine nor strong drink that day, until his punishment was over," lest others claim the "strength and comfort of the creature" sustained him, instead showing reliance on God alone. On September 5, 1651, stripped to the waist on Boston Common, he endured 30 lashes from a three-corded whip wielded by executioner James Smith with full force. Witnesses noted Smith spitting on his hands for grip. Holmes neither cried out nor showed pain but preached to the crowd, declaring, "The Lord, having manifested his love towards me, in giving me repentance towards God and faith in Christ, and so to be baptized in water by a messenger of Jesus, into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, wherein I have fellowship with him in his death, burial, and resurrection, I am now come to be baptized in afflictions by your hands, that so I may have further fellowship with my Lord, and am not ashamed of his sufferings, for by His stripes am I healed." As the flogging began, he affirmed, "Though my flesh should fail, and my spirit should fail, yet my God would not fail," and broke forth praying "unto the Lord not to lay this sin to their charge," feeling such a "spiritual manifestation of God's presence" that the pain was "removed" and "easy to me." As the scourging ended, a bleeding Holmes turned and said, "You have struck me as with roses," adding to the magistrates, "Although the Lord hath made it easy to me, yet I pray God it may not be laid to your charge." Holmes’s suffering echoes the trials of the early apostles in Acts 5:26-42, where Peter and others faced persecution for preaching Christ. The captain and officers, fearing the people, brought them "without violence" before the council, who were enraged that the apostles defied their orders to stop teaching in Jesus’s name, saying, "Ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man’s blood upon us" (Acts 5:26, 28). Peter boldly replied, "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), proclaiming Christ’s resurrection and exaltation. The council, cut to the heart, sought to slay them, but Gamaliel’s counsel prevailed, urging restraint lest they "be found even to fight against God" (Acts 5:39). Still, they beat the apostles, commanding them not to speak in Jesus’s name. Yet, the apostles "departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name" (Acts 5:41), and "ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ" (Acts 5:42). Like Holmes, they faced imprisonment and scourging for their faith, yet rejoiced, seeing it as fellowship with Christ’s sufferings. Holmes’s cry, "You have struck me as with roses," mirrors their joy in persecution, his resolve to obey God over man reflecting Peter’s stand. So too, the Apostle Paul bore "in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus" (Galatians 6:17), enduring stripes for the Gospel, as he wrote, "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned" (2 Corinthians 11:25), counting it all joy to suffer for Christ. Stephen, the first martyr, faced death for his bold testimony, praying as stones fell, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge" (Acts 7:60), a plea Holmes echoed in his own affliction, beseeching God to forgive his persecutors. These saints, like Holmes, stood firm, their trials proving that "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2 Timothy 2:3). Governor John Endecott reportedly declared Clarke "deserved death and was worthy to be hanged," underscoring Puritan intolerance for Baptists, viewed as threats to social order. Roger Williams protested in a letter to Endecott, decrying the "tyranny and persecutions." The event drew international scrutiny when Clarke published Ill Newes from New England (1652) in London, including Holmes's account. English Puritan Richard Saltonstall criticized the colony's "tyranny and persecutions in New England," and it influenced Harvard's first president, Henry Dunster, to adopt Baptist views, refusing infant baptism for his son in 1653 and leading to his dismissal. Returning to Newport in 1652, Holmes was ordained and succeeded Clarke as pastor of America's second Baptist church (now First Baptist Church in Newport), serving faithfully for 30 years. A respected civic leader, he acquired extensive waterfront land in Middletown along the Sakonnet River, shaping the area's development. In 1665, he subscribed to the Monmouth Patent for lands in New Jersey, assigning a house lot in Middletown (lot #20); sons Jonathan and Obadiah Jr. settled there, the latter becoming a judge and sheriff. During King Philip's War (1675–1676), Rhode Island's General Court sought his "advice and concurrence" as one of 16 "most judicious inhabitants." In 1675, at age 69, Holmes penned a heartfelt letter to his children and 42 grandchildren, exhorting biblical living tied to their names—e.g., urging son Joseph to emulate the "bold" Joseph of Arimathea who claimed Christ's body. He reflected on faith's trials: "God in His own time chose a people to Himself and gave them His laws and statutes in a special manner, though He had always His chosen ones in every generation." Holmes died October 15, 1682, in Newport, buried on his Middletown farm in the Holmes Burial Ground, his gravestone reading: "In Memory of the Rev. Obadiah Holmes Baptist Minister from Great Britain who died October 15th 1682 in the 76th year of his age." Katherine died shortly after. His will, dated April 9, 1682, and witnessed by prominent Rhode Islanders, provided for his family while affirming his legacy. Holmes's endurance advanced the cause of individual soul liberty, securing Rhode Island's 1663 royal charter under Charles II, granting tolerance that influenced America's First Amendment. Remembered as an "eminent citizen—a champion of soul liberty," he is a direct ancestor of Abraham Lincoln through daughter Lydia. His Last Will and Testimony, a cherished Baptist exhortation, reminds us: Persecution refines faith, for "by his stripes am I healed." May we, like Holmes, count suffering for Christ as joy, holding fast to the promise that faithfulness endures eternal reward. See the slides: Early American Baptists, Disestablishmentarianism

Relics Heresy: Vigilantius vs. Jerome Looks at the debate around 406 AD between Vigilantius and Jerome over relic veneration, night vigils and praying to saints. Presents Vigilantius as holding to Scripture against creeping pagan customs. The abomination of corpse worship is a pagan, eastern practice that has no support in scripture. It is a heretical tradition originating with vipers.The debate between Vigilantius (c. 370–after 406 AD) and Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) is one of the clearest early flashpoints over creeping paganism and carnal traditions like relic veneration, ascetic practices, and other emerging customs in the church...Jerome’s Against Vigilantius was a defense of the practices (written in 406 AD in a single night) is the main surviving source of this debate. Vigilantius’s own writings are lost (likely destroyed by the Roman Church).Jerome, who had hosted Vigilantius in Bethlehem, wrote in reaction to an epistle by the presbyter from Gaul, which criticized the growing trends of veneration of relics, the bones and ashes of martyrs, night vigils at gravesites that had pagan cultish overtones, as well as the growing gnostic aestheticism, doctrines of devils, demanding celibacy, dietary prohibition, praying to and invoking the saints intercession, and the collection of alms by churches to send to the church at Jerusalem, which was growing in wealth while local poor were neglected.Similar to modern debates defending these then-new practices as "traditions," it came down to biblical fundamentalism being opposed by people with a financial stake in making merchandise of gullible people.Vigilantius called relic-venerators “ashmongers” (cinerarii) and idolaters for worshiping “a bit of powder wrapped up in a costly cloth,” seeing it as pagan-like under a Christian cloak. Saints’ souls are with God in heaven and have no special ongoing link to their earthly remains.Jerome's response is exactly the sort of rationalizing cope we are used to today. He said it was "honoring, not worship," similar to the "veneration!" semantics. He claimed supernatural occurrences were reported at the death vigils. That V was promoting sexual immorality.This event shows that the tradition that the Catholic Church and Orthodox claim is from the Apostles was a later development, and the labeling of Vigilantius as a heretic for opposing these new customs, destroying his writing was how the emerging political entity dealt with critics.

Saint Patrick Was a Baptist A ministry essay presenting Patrick as a missionary sent from an independent church in Britain. Quotes his Confessio on salvation by grace through faith. A Ministry Essay · Jag’s House of Wews The Missionary Behind the Legend Patrick was a Baptist missionary sent to Ireland by the independent church in Britain to preach the gospel. In his own surviving words, the Confessio, Patrick describes salvation by grace through faith with a clarity that would be at home in any evangelical pulpit today: Confessio 4 “…He poured out his Holy Spirit on us in abundance, the gift and pledge of immortality, which makes the believers and the obedient into sons of God and co-heirs of Christ who is revealed… Let every tongue confess that Jesus Christ, in whom we believe and whom we await to come back to us… is Lord and God. He is judge of the living and of the dead; he rewards every person according to their deeds.” Confessio 14–15 “In the knowledge of this faith in the Trinity… it is right to make known the gift of God and his eternal consolation… I didn’t deserve at all that the Lord would grant such great grace, after hardships and troubles, after captivity, and after so many years among that people.” Patrick affirms that obedience to the gospel, and receiving the gift of eternal life and sonship as co-heirs with Christ, is by the grace of God and received by faith. Confessio 3 “Hence I cannot be silent… about the great benefits and the great grace which the Lord has deigned to bestow upon me in the land of my captivity… for this we can give to God in return after having been chastened by Him, to exalt and praise His wonders.” The New Birth: Coming to Faith Confessio 38 “I am very much God’s debtor, who gave me such grace that many people were reborn in God through me and afterwards confirmed… for a people just coming to the faith, whom the Lord took from the utmost parts of the earth.” Patrick saw the new birth—eternal life, regeneration—as coming by grace to those “coming to the faith.” Faith is the response to the gospel call. His isolation from the Augustine–Pelagius controversy meant he was notably silent on determinism, preaching instead a pure gospel of grace received by faith. Confessio 12 “Before I was brought low, I was like a stone lying deep in the mud. Then he who is powerful came and in his mercy pulled me out, and lifted me up… That is why I must shout aloud in return to the Lord for such great good deeds of his… which the human mind cannot measure.” In Confessio 12, Patrick echoes the same amazement at the grace of God that saves a wretch—the same sovereign grace that reaches every sinner who believes. A Great Soul Winner Confessio 33 “The Spirit was fervent within me… I pray to God to give me perseverance and to deign that I be a faithful witness to Him to the end of my life for my God.” That same drive is what we should strive for today. Patrick was a great soul winner. We should emulate him and his passion for the gospel—not the drunken revelry and excess that Catholics have attached to his legacy. Green beer and bawdy behavior are more fitting with the pagans he preached to than with those professing Christ. Confessio 41 “How has it lately come about in Ireland that those who never had any knowledge of God… have now been made a people of the Lord, and are called sons of God… How many have been reborn there so as to be of our kind, I do not know…” It was this love of God and the people of Ireland that gave him innumerable souls won to the Lord. Reclaiming his legacy from Catholic hagiography reveals what he truly was: an inspiration to not faint in adversity or fall into the snares of the world. Confessio 16 “The love of God and His fear came to me more and more, and my faith was strengthened. Faith grew, and my spirit was moved…” Patrick’s doctrine shines clearly through his writings: eternal life is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. An Independent Church, Free from Rome Stripping away the invented Catholic hagiography reveals that independent churches existed in the 4th and 5th centuries with tenuous or no ties to Rome or papal authority—and that their understanding of the gospel was the same biblical understanding held by Baptists today. Patrick, as an evangelical figure from a non-Roman British church tradition independent of papal authority, does away with the common tropes Catholics claim always existed in the church. He relies on Scripture alone, emphasizes a believer’s response to the gospel, and avoids entirely Catholic elements such as intercession of saints, Mary, purgatory, falling from grace, priestly confession, and veneration of images—all completely absent from his writings, which are entirely gospel-focused. His Confessio shows no appeal to Rome for legitimacy, but a strong focus on personal faith and grace. His mission stands as the first documented major independent missionary enterprise in the post-apostolic era. The most reputable biographies confirm that Patrick was British (born approximately late 4th–early 5th century), enslaved in Ireland as a youth, escaped, then trained and ordained in Britain—likely in the church his father and grandfather served as elders—and returned as a missionary around 432 AD. A third-generation Christian, his patriarchal lineage carried a near-direct line to first-century Christianity. He describes his authority as divinely called; he appeals to no pope or hierarchy for validation. His Confessio defends his mission against British critics who questioned his calling to the very people who had enslaved him. Believer’s Baptism: No Infants in His Writings Patrick does not describe or mention infant baptism (paedobaptism) at any point in his writings. The two surviving documents universally accepted as genuinely from Patrick himself—the Confessio and the Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus (Epistola)—contain several references to baptism, but every one of them describes the baptism of converted believers: adults or those who had come to faith through hearing the gospel and confessing their faith. Patrick emphasizes baptism in the context of missionary preaching: teaching first, then baptizing those who believe—aligning precisely with the Great Commission, which he quotes repeatedly. All water baptisms Patrick mentions are of converted believers who have responded to the gospel. No babies or infants are referenced anywhere. The true gospel of eternal life and believer’s baptism were all he knew, and all he related to others. “Patrick’s doctrine shines through his writings: eternal life is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.”

The Apocrypha Shows from Christ's own words about the Old Testament canon why the Apocrypha is not Scripture. Treats the law, prophets and psalms as the whole canon Jesus taught. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect , thoroughly furnished unto all good works . … Jesus taught the OT scripture canon: Luke 24:44 And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me. The law is the first 5 books. Prophets are the words of the prophets in the historical books and major and minor prophets. Psalms includes all poetic writing and proverbs. Jesus says in Matthew 5:18: For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled... Jots and tittles are explicitly terms from the Hebrew alphabet and written Hebrew. A jot refers to yod, the smallest letter in their alphabet, and tittles a pen stroke or accent mark that differentiates one Hebrew letter from another. Section One Before We Begin What the Didache is, and where it stands next to the Word of God. ✦ ✦ ✦ A Witness, Not Scripture Didache (DID-ah-kay) simply means “Teaching.” What it is One of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament. A window into what early assemblies believed and practiced. Where it agrees with the Bible, it shows the doctrine was held from the beginning. What it is not It is not inspired. It does not add to the canon. Where it goes beyond the Bible, the Bible remains the final authority. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 Isaiah 8:20 Didache quotations appear in quote blocks. Scripture appears in gold. Quotations are from the public-domain Roberts-Donaldson and Lightfoot translations. Section Two Origins When it was written, where, and how a lost book was found again. ✦ ✦ ✦ When and Where Written about 70 to 110 AD No popes, no regional hierarchy, no priesthood over the people. Just local assemblies, each led by its own bishops and deacons. That simplicity is itself a mark of an early date. Compiled in Syria or Palestine The bread prayer speaks of grain scattered “over the hills.” That describes hillside wheat farming, common in Syria and Palestine. Lost and Found For centuries the West knew the Didache only by name. c. 70–110 The Didache is written. 4th century A papyrus copy is made in Egypt. Fragments of it are later dug up at Oxyrhynchus. 1056 “Leon the Notary” copies it into a manuscript now called the Codex Hierosolymitanus. 1873 Philotheos Bryennios discovers that manuscript in a library in Constantinople. 1883 Bryennios publishes the text, and it spreads around the world. The ancient papyrus fragments agree with the medieval copy where they overlap, showing the text was handed down faithfully.
